paragraphs.text: Commentary on the Prophet Hosea by our Father among the Saints, Cyril, Archbishop of Alexandria. Preface.

Someone might perhaps think it superfluous and ill-judged, and not at all necessary for anyone's benefit, to try to rake over again what many have already said, and to add fresh labours to the labours of those who came before. After all, their work is quite enough to make the writings of the holy prophets thoroughly clear. I, however, would say that the matter is not so; far from it. For I shall remember Paul calling out to those he had initiated into the mysteries: "To write the same things to you is no trouble to me, and for you it is a safeguard."

See how true this saying is. If some matter that we need to understand is set before us, and then many people say many things about it, no harm at all will come of it; on the contrary, it will greatly benefit those who listen. If those who usually do the interpreting give accounts that agree with one another, the knowledge planted in eager listeners will surely be all the more secure. And if something new should appear in what each of them says, so that a point another writer perhaps did not quite grasp rightly and beyond reproach occurs to the mind of someone else, what is the harm? Indeed, is it not better that the ideas should be set out more fully and more distinctly? So even though many before us have written to interpret what is in the holy prophets, we will not keep silent for that reason. Instead we will thrust aside hesitation as a sign of weakness, and whatever grace he who reveals deep and hidden things may give to us, we will make that plain to others too, remembering that Christ said, "Freely you have received, freely give."

As I begin a clear interpretation of the blessed prophet Hosea, then, I will first set out some points that also concern the writings of the other prophets. It is the custom of them all to shape whatever they say readily to what seems good to the Holy Spirit. So at one moment they rise easily from the history, that is, from things perceived by the senses, events that have happened and lie before our eyes, so to speak, to what is innermost and spiritual. At another moment they come down again, and often quite without warning, to things perceived by the senses. They very often bring in different speakers, together with laments and outcries, the remembrance of things already past, and the foretelling of things to come. So we must carefully distinguish each point as far as we can, and keep close watch on the order of the thoughts and on the change of speakers. In this way our account will surely be clear, free from confusion, and rid of every difficulty. I also think it necessary first to recount some of what happened to those of Israel's blood, so that the minds of readers will not be confused when they hear at one time of Ephraim and Israel, and of Samaria too, and at another of Judah and Benjamin. For such names are mentioned again and again in the holy prophets.

So that they may know each point clearly, let them hear this. In his time Solomon, who held his father's kingdom in Jerusalem, built for God that famous and admirable temple. Yet although he became exceedingly distinguished for his splendid wealth and abundant riches, when he reached old age he offended God through his weakness for women. Holy Scripture will tell us what form his offence took, for it reads as follows: "And King Solomon took foreign wives, including the daughter of Pharaoh: Moabite, Ammonite, Syrian and Edomite women, Hittite and Amorite women, from the nations of which the Lord had said to the children of Israel, 'You shall not go in to them, and they shall not come in to you, lest they turn your hearts away after their idols.' To these Solomon clung in love. He had seven hundred wives who were princesses and three hundred concubines. And when Solomon was old, his foreign wives turned his heart away after other gods, and his heart was not perfect with the Lord his God, as the heart of David his father had been. Solomon went after Astarte, the abomination of the Sidonians, and after Baal of the children of Ammon. Solomon did what was evil in the sight of the Lord, and did not follow the Lord as David his father had done. Then Solomon built a high place for Chemosh, the idol of Moab, and for Baal, the idol of the children of Ammon, and for Astarte, the abomination of the Sidonians. And so he did for all his foreign wives, who burned incense and sacrificed to their idols. And the Lord was angry with Solomon, because he had turned his heart away from the Lord God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice and had commanded him concerning this very thing, that he should not go after other gods, but keep and do what the Lord God had commanded him."

Solomon's outrages in his old age went beyond all ungodliness. For what could be more grievous than such monstrous sins? Or how is it not beyond all words to disregard the honour and love due to the one God, who alone is God by nature and in truth, and to assign the dignity that belongs to him alone to herds of demons, or rather to attach it to stones and pieces of wood? Since he was caught thinking and doing things it is not even lawful to speak of, and was found guilty of such shameful sins, the God of all then said to him: "Because this has been done by you, and you have not kept my commandments and my ordinances which I commanded you, I will surely tear the kingdom out of your hand and give it to your servant. Yet in your days I will not [do] these things, for the sake of David your father; I will take it out of the hand of your son. Yet I will not take the whole kingdom; I will give one sceptre to your son, for the sake of David my servant and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city that I have chosen." For as I said, Solomon, though very wise, was overcome by desire for women, and so, as far as his actions could do it, he all but tore apart the kingdom of God by attaching to idols the honour and glory that befit God alone. For this reason, and quite rightly, God threatened to tear apart his kingdom, paying him back grief for grief in equal measure, as it is written in the prophet Ezekiel: "As you have done, so it shall be done to you; your recompense shall be returned upon your own head."

When Solomon died, his son Rehoboam was called to the throne. It was then that Israel was finally split, and the ten tribes, together with the half-tribe of Ephraim, broke away from Jerusalem. For Ephraim and Manasseh, the sons born to Joseph, were reckoned as one tribe, since their forefather Jacob wished it so. He had said to Joseph, "Now then, your two sons, who were born to you in Egypt before I came to you in Egypt, are mine: Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, as Reuben and Simeon are." So the ten tribes, and half of the one tribe, that is, Ephraim, went off to Samaria and left Rehoboam's kingdom, while those of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin remained in Jerusalem. Now those in Samaria, being without a king or a general, feared attacks from Rehoboam and expected that they would perish along with their dearest ones, so they sent for Jeroboam. He was a servant of Solomon who had fled to Egypt, to King Shishak. When he came, they at once appointed him their leader and honoured the wretch with the sceptre of the kingdom. Jeroboam was from the hill country and tribe of Ephraim. Once he had been made king, he set about contriving how his kingdom might be established and remain secure, so that those who had appointed him would not change their minds and turn to some other plan and purpose. Then, afraid that Israel might be reminded of the worship prescribed in the law and of the feasts celebrated in Jerusalem, and choose to go back to how things had been at the start, and so fall under Rehoboam's yoke, he made two golden heifers. Leading Israel back to the worship they had known in Egypt, he commanded them to bow down to these and offer burnt offerings to them. "And he set up one," Scripture says, "in Gilgal, and the other in Dan." These were the most renowned cities in the land of the Samaritans.

So the apostasy of the ten tribes and the half-tribe of Ephraim was twofold. They departed not only from Jerusalem but from godliness itself, bowing down to golden heifers, sacrificing to them and worshipping "the works of their own hands," as it is written. Those who stayed in Jerusalem, I mean Judah and Benjamin, did show some respect and regard for the decrees given through Moses, since they sacrificed in the temple. Yet they did not hold wholly to the love of God, but they too were divided and drawn into apostasy. For they sacrificed to idols "on every high hill and under every leafy tree," in the words of the prophet. So when you hear the holy prophets name Israel, or Ephraim, take them to mean those in Samaria; and when they name Judah and Benjamin, those who remained in Jerusalem. There were also prophets among them, who prophesied without distinction about those in Samaria and those in Jerusalem. Some lived in Jerusalem and others in the land of the Samaritans, and they carried God's words to those who heard them.

It should be understood that after the ten tribes and the half-tribe of Ephraim broke away from Jerusalem, both those in Samaria and those in Jerusalem had their own kings. This lasted until the time of the last captivity, when they returned to Jerusalem after Cyrus had come to power and allowed them to go back, with Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, of the tribe of Judah, as their leader, and Joshua son of Jozadak as priest. Then they rebuilt the temple, came under a single rule, and lived in Jerusalem, with all division removed. The various captivities that befell, at different times, the ten tribes and the half-tribe of Ephraim, and also those in Jerusalem, I mean Judah and Benjamin, the course of this work will show clearly. The times in which each of the holy prophets spoke have necessarily been recorded as well, so that we may know exactly what the state of affairs was, and how things stood, when God's words came to them.
BOOK ONE

The word of the Lord that came to Hosea son of Beeri in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel. So the blessed Hosea prophesies in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel, and the time of his prophecy is understood to have extended over this whole span. I think we must now give a clear account of what concerns each of them, so that, as I said before, we may understand what sort of men they were: whether they were good and well disposed toward God, or had turned aside to the opposite; and what befell each of them, both those in Samaria and those in Jerusalem. In this way we will see quite easily what the aim of the prophecy is. Now the last named is Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel. He lived before Azariah, who is also [?]. It should be noted that this is a different Jeroboam from the first, who lived in the time of the reign of Rehoboam son of Solomon; yet he was of the same character and like him in impiety. For this is written about him: "In the fifteenth year of Amaziah son of Joash king of Judah, Jeroboam son of Joash became king over Israel in Samaria, and reigned forty-one years. And he did what was evil in the sight of the Lord; he did not turn away from all the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who made Israel sin." Do you see how he became an imitator of that man's ways, travelling the same road, as it were, and following right in the footsteps of his ungodliness? Then what does the sacred text say? "In the twenty-seventh year of Jeroboam king of Israel, Azariah son of Amaziah king of Judah became king. He was sixteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem, and his mother's name was Jecoliah of Jerusalem. And he did what was right in the eyes of the Lord, in everything that Amaziah his father had done; only he did not remove the high places; the people still sacrificed and burned incense on the high places. And the Lord struck the king, and he was a leper until the day of his death." Uzziah, then, was devout and loved God, but not entirely. For he did not take away the high places, it says, but those who had gone astray burned incense on them and brought sacrifices to demons. Then Azariah, that is, Uzziah, was carried away into outrageous notions and thought it befitted the glory of kingship that he should also perform the rites prescribed to God and take up the sacred ministry; and so he actually offered sacrifice himself, disregarding the laws given through Moses. And because he had stepped up into a ministry that in no way belonged to him, I mean the priestly one, "the Lord struck him," it says, "and he was a leper until the day of his death." Now under the law a leper is unclean, and those seized by such an affliction were sent out of the camp. For God once said to Moses, the revealer of sacred things: "Speak to the children of Israel, and let them send out of the camp every leper and everyone with a discharge, and everyone unclean through contact with a corpse." So he was punished with the disease for daring what was not lawful, and God sentenced the king to dishonour for having seized the glory of the priesthood.

But since the force of the prophecy looks not to Judah alone, that is, to those in Jerusalem, but extends also to Israel, that is, to the ten tribes in Samaria, we must necessarily speak of those who reigned over Israel in the days of Azariah, also called Uzziah, and of the calamities that overtook them as they sickened so outrageously with profane idolatry. When Uzziah, also called Azariah, was already in the twenty-eighth year of his reign, another Azariah, [son] of Jeroboam, reigned over Israel for six months. And since he too walked in the way of his father and did what was evil in the eyes of the Lord, he was given over to slaughter by some of his own people, and so he perished. As time went on, in the thirty-eighth year of Uzziah's reign, Shallum was in turn anointed over Israel and reigned for a month; for he was immediately killed by Menahem son of Gadi from Tirzah. The sacred text noted that they had become sons [?], and that both were of the blood of Jehu, who killed Ahab and his sons and Jezebel, and to whom God had promised, saying: "Your sons to the fourth generation shall sit on your throne." So Menahem reigned over Israel after killing Shallum. "And he did," it says, "what was evil in the eyes of the Lord; he did not turn away from all the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who made Israel sin." While he, Menahem I mean, was reigning and offending God through his great devotion to the [?] of idols, Pul king of Assyria marched against Samaria. Since Menahem could not fend him off by arms, he persuaded him with a great deal of money to leave the land and end the war. When Menahem had died, then in the fifty-second year of Uzziah's reign, Jotham in his turn was anointed over Judah in Jerusalem after his father's death; of him it is written that "he did what was right in the eyes of the Lord, in everything that Uzziah his father had done; only he did not remove the high places; the people still sacrificed and burned incense on the high places." Over Israel reigned Pekahiah son of Menahem. "He reigned," it says, "two years, and did what was evil in the eyes of the Lord. Then Pekah son of Remaliah, his captain, conspired against him," it says, "and struck him down in Samaria, and reigned over Israel in his place; and he did what was evil in the eyes of the Lord; he did not turn away from all the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who made Israel sin." During his reign Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria came up, took all Samaria by force, and deported Israel to Assyria. Pekah too died when Hoshea son of Elah conspired against him; Hoshea then reigned in his place, in the twentieth year of Jotham son of Azariah. But "in those days," it says, "the Lord began to send Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah against Judah." Here the narrative goes backwards for us: we said that Pekah died when Hoshea son of Elah formed a conspiracy and plot against him; yet the text brings forward an event that happened in his time. "For in those days," it says, "the Lord began to send Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah against Judah."

For Pekah son of Remaliah made war on the people of Jerusalem, since they were his neighbours. But when he saw that their resistance was fierce and unbreakable, he persuaded Rezin, king of the Syrians, to become his ally and helper and to join him in besieging Jerusalem. While the war was under way, Jotham son of Azariah died, and his son Ahaz succeeded to the kingdom. He was exceedingly wicked and an idolater, and was so drunk with the delusion of idol-madness that he even made his own son pass through the fire, turned aside to every kind of outrage, and burned incense "on the high places and under every leafy tree," as it is written. So Ahaz, thrown into panic, gathered all the wealth found in the house of the Lord and sent it by messengers to Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, begging to be saved by him. The Assyrian therefore took up arms against Rezin's kingdom; he captured Damascus, the chief city of Syria, and killed Rezin. Then Ahaz went down from Jerusalem to Damascus to see the Assyrian. There in the precincts of the idols he saw an altar of novel and unfamiliar design, and being greatly pleased with it, he took a pattern of it and sent it to Uriah the priest in Jerusalem, ordering that one be made after it. He brought it into the house of the Lord and, all but dishonouring the altar that had been made through Moses according to God's will, ordered the prescribed rites to be performed on the new one. Besides this he introduced other innovations in the temple as he saw fit, thoughtlessly and in a way displeasing to God. In his time too, while Hoshea son of Elah king of Israel was still alive, Shalmaneser king of Assyria came up against Israel; he laid Samaria waste and deported Israel to the mountains and rivers of the Medes. He also killed Hoshea himself. And for what reason? Because, it says, he had not brought him the manaa, which was a token of submission, but instead called on the tyrant of the Egyptians for help.

After this, when Ahaz had died, his son Hezekiah reigned over Judah in Jerusalem. He was a devout man, and one of those who cared most for righteousness, so that in this respect he stood beyond comparison with the others. "He tore down the high places," it says, "and cut down the sacred groves; and the Lord was with him." During his reign Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against the fortified cities of Judah, besieged them and took them without effort. It was then that the Rabshakeh assailed Jerusalem itself and, opening his unguarded mouth against God, let loose those utterly blasphemous words; and it was then too that one hundred and eighty-five thousand fell from the camp of the Assyrians in a single night, consumed by the hand of an angel. All this has been usefully said for the present purpose, for the words of the prophecy will be skilfully fitted to each of these events. At one time it rebukes those in Samaria; at another it threatens those in Jerusalem with invasions; it foretells captivities; it announces terror in advance; it promises help; it calls to repentance. No word or method necessary for the benefit of those who had then gone astray has been left out of the prophecy. So it says:
The beginning of the word of the Lord in Hosea. And the Lord said to Hosea:

God begins to reveal mysteries in the prophet, very much in line with what was clearly said through another prophet: "I will stand at my watch and mount upon a rock, and I will keep watch to see what the Lord God will speak in me." For the God of all reveals things to the saints by putting the knowledge of what is to come into their minds. So the blessed David says: "I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me, for he will speak peace to his people." And the blessed prophet Zechariah speaks to us in just the same terms, for he said: "And the angel who spoke in me answered." For it was customary among the holy prophets to call the Word of God an angel, that is, a messenger, since he announced to them and made plain the will of God the Father. The prophet Isaiah will bear witness to this, saying of him: "For they will repay every garment gathered by deceit, with compensation, and they will wish they had been burned with fire; for a child has been born to us, and his name is called Angel of Great Counsel." And that the revelation in the saints was subtle and not outwardly visible, and was not carried out by tongue and words as with us, Paul will assure us when he writes: "Or do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?" So the statement that the word of God came in Hosea would, as far as I can understand, indicate nothing else to the hearers than that a revelation took place in Hosea, and the knowledge of what was to come flashed like a light that illuminates not the eyes of the body but the mind and heart. Again, the words "And the Lord said to Hosea" lead us to thoughts like these. The command given was not common to all who would read it, nor was it set out for anyone who wished to carry it out from time to time; it was spoken specifically and to Hosea alone. For taking a wife of harlotry and children of harlotry could not be understood as good and beneficial in the way that a general and useful precept is, such as: "Thus says the Lord: Do not learn the ways of the nations, and do not be afraid of the signs of heaven." That precept would usefully apply to everyone, but this one would fittingly be spoken by God specifically to the prophet alone. This, I think, is the meaning of "and he said to Hosea"; it is as if it were saying: such a word is not addressed to everyone without distinction, but to Hosea alone. For what was said by divine dispensation to one man on a particular occasion must not become a pretext for many to live a shameful and pleasure-loving life. What, then, did God say to the blessed Hosea?

Go, take for yourself a wife of harlotry and children of harlotry, for the land will surely go whoring away from following the Lord. And he went and took Gomer daughter of Diblaim, and she conceived and bore him a son.

No argument will persuade us to reject the letter, to condemn the narrative as pointless, to declare the deed itself unseemly, or to suppose, as some do, that it did not happen this way and that Gomer was not taken in marriage or in marital union. For the sacred text says that conception took place and indeed childbirth; it records the name of the child, names the woman's father, and gives the woman's own name as well. Since those who choose to side with the truth of what took place must acknowledge that these things really did happen this way, let us first set out the arguments of those who are in the habit of mocking, and only then go on in due course to the account of the divine dispensation.

I came across a short treatise by a man of some note who wished to explain this passage. He spoke disparagingly, and not moderately, of the literal narrative and of those who say that these things happened in this way. He said that lovers of continence ought, on this very point above all, to cry out plainly and without any fear: "The letter kills." Attacking the letter as though it had no defender, and rushing headlong as it were, he put together arguments like these: "Moses," he said, "the inspired man, was once commanded to lead Israel, redeemed from slavery in Egypt, into the holy land promised long ago to the fathers, I mean the land of promise. The prophet Jeremiah, too, heard God say plainly: 'Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you came out of the womb I sanctified you; I have appointed you a prophet to the nations.' How then," he says, "are they not to be admired, who declined even so venerable and noble a ministry and did not refuse to hesitate? For the one said: 'I beg you, Lord, appoint someone else who is able, whom you will send'; while the other, pleading his youth, tried to dissuade God. The prophet Ezekiel too," he says, "when he was commanded to make bread for himself over cakes of human dung, was greatly distressed, and so he heard: 'See, I have given you cow dung instead of human dung, and you shall bake your bread on it.' And indeed the inspired Peter himself, when the sheet was let down from heaven with all the four-footed animals and beasts depicted on it, and he heard God say, 'Rise, Peter, kill and eat,' refused," he says, "saying: 'By no means, Lord, for I have never eaten anything common or unclean, nor has any profane meat entered my mouth.' But Hosea, on hearing that he must unite himself with a shameful, harlotrous woman living an accursed life, does not refuse the thing, admits no hesitation, offers no plea begging to be let off; instead, like one of the most licentious men, he all but snatches at the thing at once and without delay, perhaps because he was overcome by desire for the woman." Then, closing his argument in absurdity, he added a few feeble remarks. For he makes a show of defending the prophet and says in turn: "He would have made the strongest possible refusal had he known that God was commanding a bodily union; but since what was being done was something spiritual, out of his great love for God he comes forward almost of his own accord to do what was commanded. Besides," he says, "the God of continence would not have wished such a thing to happen, that so great a man should be defiled by such shameful and abominable embraces, I mean with a woman, and a lewd and harlotrous one at that." Then, as it were, reshaping the force of the narrative into spiritual meanings, he said that Gomer stands as a type of the soul that has chosen to live shamefully and indecently, while the prophet fills the role of an image of the one from above and from heaven, that is, of God the Word from the Father, who, uniting himself spiritually with our souls, implants in them the seeds of a life that loves virtue.

These, then, are the inventions of his plausible reasoning, and I was greatly astonished. First, because, sparing no thought for the truth, he dared to say that the letter kills. Then, besides this, because he cited Moses and the others we have just mentioned as having objected to the oracles from above, but wrongly kept silent about the fact that those who dared to oppose the divine decrees were not free from blame. For when Moses, the revealer of sacred things, refused and shrank from his mission, pleading slowness of speech, God rebuked him as weak in faith, saying: "Who gave man a mouth? And who made the deaf and the mute, the seeing and the blind? Is it not I, the Lord God? Now go, and I will open your mouth." And when after this he still shrank back and hesitated, "the Lord was angry with Moses," it says, "and said: Is not Aaron your brother here? I know that he will speak for you." Again, when Jeremiah said rather rashly, "I am too young, and I do not know how to speak," God answered him no less, saying: "Do not say, 'I am too young,' for you shall go to all to whom I send you, and you shall speak whatever I command you." For it was by no means without danger to say, or even merely to think, that the supreme will had missed the proper reckoning in calling a young man to prophecy. Likewise the inspired Peter, when the sheet was let down from heaven, heard: "Rise, Peter, kill and eat." But since he cried out in Jewish fashion, "By no means, Lord, for I have never eaten anything common or unclean," he was rebuked at once, and as one who dared to set himself against the divine purposes, he heard plainly: "What God has cleansed, you must not call common." For even if the God of all chose to rebuke them gently, and was not immediately and immoderately angered at them for objecting, their refusal was still not free from blame. I say that we must at once grant that the decrees from above are right and beyond reproach, and hasten to carry out what has been commanded, even if the matter is not altogether pleasing to our souls. For example, the God of all commanded Saul to slay Agag for the unholy things he had done against the Israelites. But Saul thought it a kindness to deliberate about him, and judged that the man condemned by the decree deserved to be spared. So in this way he gave great offence to God. He took care of the one commanded to die, all but crying aloud and saying by his very action that God had not passed a just sentence on him. For this reason the blessed Samuel was deeply grieved and shared God's indignation; he slew Agag himself, declaring the reasons: "As your sword has made women childless, so shall your mother be childless among women." And he foretold to Saul that he would be thrust out of the kingdom and pay a bitter penalty for his disobedience.

If we should also bring in the account of another story beside this one, it is written in the Third Book of Kingdoms that Hadad, the leader or king of the Syrians, once made war on Israel. Ahab, the king of Israel, was in great distress. He feared the attack and expected that before long his whole army would be captured. Then God promised through a prophet to hand the enemy over to him. But once he had him in his power, Ahab chose to spare him, against what God had decided. And what does the sacred text say after this? "And a certain man of the sons of the prophets said to his neighbor, by the word of the Lord, 'Strike me.' And the man refused to strike him. And he said to him, 'Because you have not obeyed the voice of the Lord, see, as soon as you go away from me a lion will strike you.' And he went away from him, and a lion found him and struck him. And he found another man and said, 'Strike me.' And the man struck him, striking and wounding him. And the prophet went and stood before the king of Israel by the road, and bound his eyes with a bandage." After saying a few things in between to Ahab as he returned, he went on: "Thus says the Lord: Because you let a man doomed to destruction go out of your hand, your life shall be for his life, and your people for his people." Do you hear how the man who refused to strike the prophet was pitiably killed, falling prey to a fierce beast? And yet surely one could truly say that it was the fruit of reverence not to dare to strike a holy man and a prophet. But the order was given by the word of the Lord, and the disobedience became a charge hard to escape. Ahab too unreasonably spared Hadad, although God had commanded him to destroy him, and he himself was given up in exchange for that man's life. It is therefore necessary for us to carry out whatever pleases God without hesitation or delay. To do anything other than this, or even to choose to think otherwise, brings the charge of arrogance. For such people have all but resolved to rebuke God himself, as though he sometimes deliberated wrongly.

We say, then, to those who do not hold the story beyond reproach, but find fault with it ill-advisedly: Does it seem unseemly to you, sirs, that a prophet should share a home with a lewd woman? Well, is it not far more unseemly that people should be slaughtered by holy prophets? How, then, did Samuel kill Agag, and Elijah the prophets of Baal, many as they were? And tell me, what about the prophet Isaiah, who took the sackcloth from his loins and went about Jerusalem naked and barefoot? Would not anyone at once condemn a man in such a state as indecent, out of his mind, and deranged? And how can this be doubted, if it is entirely praiseworthy for us to do everything with fitting decorum? But you will say that in doing such things on those occasions they were yielding to the divine will. Then tell me, what ought we to think about the blessed Hosea? Did he go to a harlot of his own accord and make so shameful a woman his wife, or was he commanded to do so by God? I am no less amazed at the man who wanted to mock what is written about him and dared to disparage the unpleasantness of the story. He does away with the event because of its absurdity, and insists very plainly that the prophet did not have union with a harlot, but that the divine Word sometimes joins himself to souls that have gone whoring. He has evidently not noticed what nonsense he has fallen into. For it seems he would have the prophet be more dignified than the all-holy God! Tell me, would not anyone say that it amounts to the same thing for the prophet to be joined to a wicked woman and for the Word of God to choose fellowship with an unclean soul? I think there is no difference at all between them. So let them either reject this along with that because of its absurdity, or else allow human considerations to come second to the divine will. I think it right also to cite something from the Gospels. Our Lord Jesus Christ reclined at table with tax collectors and sinners. But once again the fault-finding Pharisees accused him, and openly approached the holy disciples, saying, "Why does your teacher eat and drink with sinners?" What, then, did Christ say to this? "Those who are well," he says, "have no need of physicians, but those who are sick." No one would doubt in the least that God, out of his boundless love for humankind, receives even those who are defiled and not yet washed clean of sin. Above all, then, we must not fix our attention on the unseemliness of the story about the blessed Hosea, since in itself it depicts for us most beautifully that while we are still loathsome and unclean the divine Word graciously grants us spiritual fellowship with himself.

So the God of all said to the blessed Hosea, "Go, take for yourself a wife of harlotry and children of harlotry." He takes Gomer, not making the matter an occasion for pleasure, but fulfilling a work of obedience and service and becoming the minister of a type, which we shall shortly describe, in which spiritual things are given shape, as far as possible, in fleshly and more earthly ones. Still, someone might, I suppose, fault the prophet's purpose as improper. But the word of divinely inspired Scripture does not forbid choosing to marry, being joined to a wife, and desiring children. Rather, it everywhere frees these things from blame and reproach: "For marriage is honorable, and the marriage bed undefiled," in the words of the blessed Paul. Those who wished to live rightly and to achieve a virtuous and godly life were permitted to do so even if they longed for offspring. That is how the blessed Abraham lived, and those after him were also approved by God. Tell me, then, what is absurd about it, or how could it be faulted at all not to refuse marriage, when God commands that something spiritual, needful for the benefit of readers, should be depicted in bodily and perceptible things? For my part I would say without any fear that the prophet actually saved Gomer. She was a woman so shameful and common to many, and he persuaded her to attach herself to one man alone. She who had once offended nature itself, because she did not give herself to bearing children but sold her youthful bloom for the pleasures of whoever came along, was a snare of death, a door and a road leading down into the deep and utmost darkness. He persuaded her to abstain from such detestable songs and practices, and made her a respectable mother of children. Not to care greatly for one's own concerns, but to choose rather to accomplish what is useful to another and needful for salvation, would seem a pursuit worthy of the saints and deserving of admiration. Shall we not likewise count the blessed prophet Isaiah worthy of all praise, if he took off his tunic, removed his sandals as well, and, setting very little store by decorum, walked about naked, so that by showing the Israelites the appearance of the captivity to come he might make them attach themselves to God and persuade them from then on to love the ending of their sins? And tell me, did not our wise Paul plainly say, "For I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh"? Does he not also say that he became all things to all people, so that by all means he might save some, and that he became to the Jews as a Jew, to those without the law as one without the law, not being without law toward God but under the law of Christ, so that he might save those without the law? But why do I go on saying these things and leave aside what is greater still? The only-begotten Word of God himself, in order to save the human race, "did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men; and being found in fashion as a man," he endured the cross, despising the shame.

It is no wonder, then, if the prophet departed a little from what is fitting and saved Gomer, and brought the lost woman back to decency. That God commanded him to be joined to the woman for a useful and necessary purpose, he made fully clear at once, affirming that he had given that command for this reason: "Because," he says, "the land will go whoring, whoring away from following the Lord." And he speaks to the prophet not of a future harlotry of the land, but of one that had already happened. For there were the heifers at Dan and Bethel, the precincts of Baal had been set up, and the rites of Israel were being performed throughout the whole country of the Samaritans. So divinely inspired Scripture is indifferent as to tenses, or rather, to put it more truly, those who translated it for us are. In the same way, indeed, the person of Christ himself is introduced through the voice of Isaiah, saying, "I gave my back to the whips and my cheeks to blows." And the prophet himself says of him, "Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb silent before its shearer, so he does not open his mouth. In his humiliation his judgment was taken away." Do you see how the word of prophecy has presented to us what was to happen in due time as though it had already happened? So "the land will go whoring, whoring" must be understood in place of "the land has gone whoring." And in what way has it gone whoring? "Away from following the Lord," that is, by abandoning the following that one should practice toward God. For it is written, "You shall walk after the Lord," that is, you shall follow without turning back the laws given from above by God. So it has gone whoring away from following the Lord, refusing to follow after him. It became an apostate and profane, and by giving itself to the worship of idols it offended the Master. For this reason, then, the prophet Hosea is joined to Gomer: because the land had gone whoring away from following the Lord. For, as I said, what was done may be understood as a type of a mystical reality. Then Gomer gave birth.

And the Lord said to him, "Call his name Jezreel, for in a little while I will avenge the blood of Jezreel on the house of Judah, and I will put an end to the kingdom of the house of Israel. And on that day I will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel."

In these words the passage gives birth for us to a twofold interpretation. Another reading is also current among some, which must now be mentioned for the sake of accuracy, for it is of no small benefit for us to take account of both texts. Our own edition, that is, the Septuagint, says, "And I will avenge the blood of Jezreel on the house of Judah." The other says, "And I will avenge the blood of Jezreel on the house of Jehu." If some choose to understand it in this way, the explanation must be given in a more historical manner. It runs as follows.

Ahab became king in Israel, and he had Jezebel as his wife. He sought Naboth's vineyard, but Naboth answered, "Far be it from me to give you the vineyard of my father." So he was murdered, falling victim to Jezebel's wicked schemes. After he had been murdered, Ahab took possession of Naboth's vineyard. He was also given over in other ways to the worship of demons, and that to an extraordinary degree, so the God of all was angered. He then commanded the prophet Elisha to anoint Jehu as king over Israel. The prophet sent his servant and fulfilled the divine command. Once anointed, Jehu went down to Samaria and carried out the divine wrath on those who had given offense. He killed Ahab and threw him into Naboth's vineyard. After that he killed Jezebel, and he also put to death seventy sons of Ahab who lived throughout Samaria. To these he added Baal as well: he burned his pillars, demolished his precincts, and slaughtered the priests themselves. For these deeds God approved of him, and indeed promised him, saying, "Your sons to the fourth generation shall sit on your throne." But Jehu, who had won such approval, offended God no less. For he did not remove the heifers, and he too was found to have walked impiously in the sins of Jeroboam. Then from Jehu came first Jehoahaz, himself also an idolater who worshiped the heifers. In his time, it says, "the Lord was angry with Israel in his wrath, and gave them into the hand of Hazael king of Syria and into the hand of the son of Hadad." Second, Joash reigned after Jehoahaz, and he too was a wicked man. Third came Jeroboam, in whose reign Hosea began to prophesy. Fourth was Azariah, son of Jeroboam, himself also an idolater; Shallum killed him. So then, Jehu had been anointed to avenge the blood of Naboth, who was from Jezreel (this is a city of Samaria), and to do away with Israel's idolatry and so persuade them from then on to devote themselves to God. But he himself became a worshiper of the heifers, and his descendants were no less impious. Therefore God says, "I will avenge the blood of Jezreel on the house of Jehu." For just as he exacted vengeance on the house of Ahab through Jehu's reign, so he will exact vengeance on the house of Jehu as well. For in the days of his sons Hazael king of Syria made war, and Hadad too, and they defeated Israel and sacked a great many of the cities of Samaria. So a child is born to the prophet whose name is Jezreel, as though God were in some way recalling the sin committed against Naboth. For when a just and devout man had been unjustly put to death, how could the protector of the just keep still? He therefore promises to break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel. For, as I said, the tribes of Israel were defeated by Hazael and by Hadad.

So much for the account of what took place historically. Now let us say what is fitting about the other reading, carrying the words spoken by God up to a spiritual interpretation. The synagogue of the Jews is of noble descent because of the fathers. Those around the divinely inspired Abraham worshiped the living and true God. They also took care to practice righteousness, were richly crowned with every kind of good work, were outstanding in sincerity, unshaken in faith, and had cultivated every form of goodness. But when famine drove them down and they mingled with the Egyptians, and then spent a long time there, their descendants took on other ways and other ideas, choosing from then on to follow the customs of the inhabitants, and caring very little for the piety that had been familiar to the fathers and that they had practiced so outstandingly. For they worshiped the creature rather than the Creator, and the works of their own hands, as it is written. They sank so far into abomination and a profane life that there was perhaps no form of wickedness they had not practiced. They seem to me to have suffered something like what would happen to a wise and well-born woman who abandoned her own character and all but bade farewell to the practices of decency, taking pride instead in being seen in the look and dress of harlots. For just as such a woman satisfies everyone's pleasures with herself, every scruple having been removed, so too a human soul that has turned away from the pursuits of piety, disregarded love for God, and inclined toward Satan, fulfills the desires of the evil spirits. So the synagogue of the Jews went whoring in Egypt in a spiritual sense. For, as I said, it lay open to the desires of the demons, easily carried away to anything at all that pleased them. But God visited and had mercy on her who had been so cast off, and wished to make her chaste again. The all-pure and holy one all but made the profane woman his wife, made her a mother of children, and counted her worthy of love because of the firstborn who came from her, that is, Jezreel, which is interpreted "seed of God."

See, then, how Hosea was set as an image and type of what God arranged with such perfect wisdom. A holy prophet is joined to Gomer, a harlot, and she bore him Jezreel. So too God, through the all-wise Moses, called the synagogue of the Jews to intimacy with himself and into spiritual fellowship, because of the firstborn who was to come from her, that is, Christ, who is in truth the seed of God. For the Son was begotten of the Father, even though he became flesh.

But since the spiritual interpretation cannot be set out clearly and distinctly in any other way unless the historical events are brought forward, let me recall them once more. The passage has already told us plainly that Jezreel is a city, but as a man from the city of Jezreel it signifies Naboth. He too would be a type of the dispensation understood to be in Christ, for his name is interpreted "the one who comes." The sacred text very often signifies Emmanuel by this name. It was said to the blessed prophet Habakkuk, "Yet a little while, and the one who comes will come and will not delay." David too sings somewhere, "Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord." And indeed the divinely inspired Baptist himself sent some of his disciples to our Lord Jesus Christ and asked him, saying, "Are you the one who comes, or should we look for another?" That Naboth was an image of Christ we shall also learn clearly from what is written about him. Ahab desired to acquire his vineyard and turn so choice a plot into a vegetable garden. But Naboth was indignant at this and declared plainly that he would never give up his father's vineyard. "Far be it from me," he says, "to give up the vineyard of my father to you." When the God-hated and profane Jezebel, who persecuted the prophets and plotted against the righteous, learned of this, she contrived the murder of the just man with wicked schemes. And having arranged for him to be put to death, she told her husband, Ahab I mean, to take possession. At this God was rightly angered, and he promised to avenge the blood of Jezreel. So Ahab was killed by Jehu, as we have already said, and the utterly wicked Jezebel was added to him.

Come, then, let us apply to Christ what happened to the people of old as a type. The prophet Isaiah says, "The beloved had a vineyard on a hill, in a fertile place," and "the vineyard was the man of Judah, a new planting, beloved." But the leaders of Israel, of whom Ahab in his kingship may be taken as a type, wanted to possess his vineyard. They did not want it to be a choice inheritance, that is, a vineyard, but to be turned into a barren vegetable garden; in other words, they wanted it brought down to something incomparably lower, for there is the greatest possible difference between a vegetable garden and a vineyard. What is more, the deeper meaning here is not obscure. If the Jewish people had come under Christ, how could they not have been, and been seen to be, like vines rich in branches and most fruitful? But living by the customs and ways of the Pharisees, and learning as doctrines the commandments of men, they were in no way different from the lowliest vegetables, which very easily fall and wither. So the teachers of the Jews longed to have Christ's vineyard as their own inheritance and to make it a vegetable garden, but they could not persuade him to betray the vineyard of the Father to them. Then what did the God-hated Jezebel do? Jezebel stands for the common crowd under the leaders' hand, that is, the Synagogue, which joined in the leaders' resentment. She went after the righteous man, the holy Naboth, that is, "the one who comes," with deceit, and indeed she arranged for him to be killed. For Emmanuel was put to death on false charges. But that the thing was intolerable to God becomes clear from what is said to the prophet Hosea: For in a little while I will avenge the blood of Jezreel on the house of Judah, and I will put an end to the kingdom of the house of Israel. For, as I said, the blood of Christ has been avenged on all Israel. At the time when the prophecy was given, the people were called by separate names: those who remained in Jerusalem were called Judah, and those in Samaria were called Israel. So, in order to be seen to mean all Israel, he necessarily says that he will avenge the blood of Jezreel on the house of Judah and also put an end to the kingdom of the house of Israel. The blessed Jacob foretold this too when he said, "A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until he comes for whom it is reserved, and he is the expectation of the nations." When Emmanuel, the expectation of the nations, shone upon us, then indeed the kingdom of Israel was taken away. And so Herod, son of Antipater, an Ascalonite, was ruling the land of the Jews when Christ was born. He will also break the very bow of Israel on that day, that is, at that time. For "the bow of the mighty has grown weak," as it is written, even though they supposed they would overpower Emmanuel. And "the swords of the enemy have failed utterly," and "the sinews of their arms were loosened," for they did not conquer the unconquerable. Then, as if to lay a foundation for the depth of the spiritual interpretation, he immediately comes down to the historical events, saying, I will break the bow of Israel in the valley of Jezreel. For it was there that Hazael king of Syria defeated Israel when it marched out against him. But since I think it right not to withdraw the discussion from the necessary spiritual interpretation, I say this: nothing prevents us, in my view, from understanding the valley of Jezreel, that is, of the seed of God, namely Christ, to be the tomb in the garden. There the resurrection that followed the Passion overcame every kind of Jewish audacity. For through the resurrection their perverse, God-hated and murderous audacities were undone. They thought they could get rid of the Son, so as to have his vineyard as their own inheritance. But after he was laid in a tomb he came to life again, showing that the schemes of their plot had achieved nothing, and all but breaking their bows, since he could no longer suffer anything. And he casts them out of the vineyard as God-hated, wicked and murderers of the Lord, and he lets it out to other tenants, good, grateful and most diligent, according to the parable in the Gospel.

And she conceived again and bore a daughter, and he said to him, "Call her name Not-Pitied, for I will no longer have mercy on the house of Israel, but I will surely set myself in battle against them. But I will have mercy on the sons of Judah, and I will save them by the Lord their God; and I will not save them by bow, nor by sword, nor by war, nor by chariots, nor by horses, nor by horsemen."

After Jezreel was born, a girl was born to the prophet from Gomer, and he commanded that she be given the name Not-Pitied. Immediately he adds the reason for this and at once makes the cause plain, saying that Israel would no longer be thought worthy of any mercy. He would rise up against them, as it were, and take his place among their bitterest enemies, and would vigorously oppose their prosperity, so that they would slide into the utmost misery and endure a truly unbearable calamity. For when God stands against them, those who suffer can find help from nowhere. "If he shuts a man in, who will open?" it says; and as the prophet says, "His hand, who will turn it back?" Or who will have mercy on one condemned by the sentence from above? For all things follow the divine will. Whatever the Master chooses to accomplish is carried through without delay, in every way and without fail, since creation works together with him and follows the decrees of the Ruler. So it was that he punished the Egyptians: the waters were changed into blood and the soot into gnats, unbearable hail was sent down, a three-day darkness was poured over them, and all the other plagues were brought upon them. So the name Not-Pitied was given to the girl usefully and necessarily. The point was that those who at that time had offended God through the error of many gods would always be eager to learn the cause of the matter, and by learning it would be persuaded to think and do what was better and more fitting. Then they might turn to make a sensible choice and at least, on second thoughts, shake off the wrath, rendering the God of all, whom they had grieved, kind and gentle toward them. Here again the prophetic word seems to point to the captivities that befell Israel under Tiglath-pileser and also Shalmaneser, kings of Assyria. They deported Israel from Samaria to the territories of the Persians and Medes, after laying waste the cities in Samaria. But they would not have fallen into such terrible calamities if God had been willing to help them, or rather, if he had not in some way marched out against them and taken his stand against them in the ranks of their enemies. For he said plainly, I will surely set myself in battle against them. But he promises to have mercy on the sons of Judah and to save them, not by the law of war, for that is the meaning of not by chariots, nor by horses. This was in fact fulfilled when Sennacherib had Jerusalem surrounded. At that time Rabshakeh babbled against the divine glory, saying that God would not be able to rescue Jerusalem and those in it. As proof that they too would be captured in every way and without fail, he put forward the fact that the gods in Samaria had not been able to deliver their own people. But Judah, that is, the two tribes living in Jerusalem, was saved beyond all expectation. "For an angel of the Lord went out," it says, "and killed in one night a hundred and eighty-five thousand from the camp of the Assyrians." And those who had been saved sang like this, recounting the ways of the mighty work done on their behalf: "Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will be made great in the name of the Lord our God. They were tripped up and fell, but we have risen and been set upright."

But let this much be said by us on the historical level. Let us go on in turn to other meanings, I mean again those that concern Christ himself. For after the birth of Jezreel, that is, the seed of God, by which you should understand Emmanuel, whose blood he promised to avenge, a daughter, that is, a multitude, is born to Gomer, that is, to the Synagogue of the Jews which had committed fornication. It would be fitting for her to be called Not-Pitied, for she killed Jezreel, that is, Christ. For this reason she justly finds God an enemy and a most bitter foe. And she immediately suffered incurable calamities when she was sacked by the Roman forces and underwent that notorious war, when women even boiled their own children. As the prophet Jeremiah says, "The hands of compassionate women boiled their own children": they disregarded the laws of human nature, as famine forced them to neglect an invincible natural love. All these things befell the ungodly. But he promises to have mercy on the sons of Judah, that is, on those who through instruction and the rebirth that comes through the Spirit have become sons of Christ, who is of the tribe of Judah. For if some are begotten in Christ through the Gospel by the holy apostles, how much more by Christ himself? Concerning them he also says through Isaiah, "Behold, I and the children whom God has given me." So they are saved in Christ, the Lord and God of all, not by wielding earthly and fleshly weapons, but by the power of the one who saves. He shakes principalities and thrones, triumphs over the hosts of the adversaries by his own cross, overthrows the evil powers, and grants to those who love him "to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy." He does very well to compare the disobedient, unruly, Lord-murdering multitude of the Jews to a woman, I mean to Not-Pitied. For a woman is a sign of weakness, and may very clearly be understood as a type of an unmanly and broken spirit. Such are all who did not accept the instruction given through Christ and would not consent to follow his divine and holy decrees. So the prophet Hosea says, "Return, Israel, to the Lord your God, for you have grown weak in your iniquities." And again the same prophet says about the Savior's commandments, "For the ways of the Lord are straight, and the righteous will walk in them, but the ungodly will grow weak in them." And the same Hosea says somewhere about those who killed Jezreel, that is, Christ, "And the insolence of Israel will be humbled before his face, and Israel and Ephraim will grow weak in their iniquities."
And she weaned Not-Pitied, and she conceived again and bore a son. And he said, "Call his name Not-My-People, for you are not my people, and I am not yours."

Close on the heels of the first, not long after, another child is born to Gomer, which God said must be called Not-My-People. And again the reason is placed right next to the name: For you, he says, are not my people, and I am not yours. From this too it is now clear that these things were done historically to convict those who had sinned and to bring sure correction to those who had chosen to despise God and had turned aside into error. But they were also types of what would happen in due time to those of Israel, once the Only-Begotten had become man and had endured the precious cross for us. But if we must recount the historical meaning before the spiritual, we say this: after Israel had been deported from Samaria to the territories of the Persians and Medes by Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria and also by Shalmaneser, those who were still left, the remnant of those who had been in danger, fell away completely from being called the people of God, because they clung to the same pursuits that led to apostasy from God. For they never stopped devoting themselves to the most abominable worship of demons.

But you will understand the meaning, the true sense concerning Christ, in another way. After that unholy multitude, which was justly not pitied, for it had murdered the Lord, those who were born immediately after them as sons of the Synagogue that had committed fornication, or who already existed, clearly fell away from being, and being called, the people of God. For the Roman war did not consume the whole multitude of the Jews. A vast multitude, beyond counting, did perish, but those of them who were saved and escaped the net of death were scattered to every wind, as it is written, and dispersed through the lands of the nations, no longer, as I said, bearing the name of God's people. For grace passed over to those from the nations, and with them was mingled the remnant of Israel, that is, those who were saved through faith in Christ, for not a few of Israel also believed. And that, when Israel kicked against him, the God of all himself also withdrew from his close relationship with them, he indicated by saying not only, You are not my people, but by necessarily adding, And I am not yours. But concerning us, who have been justified in Christ and sanctified in the Spirit and have been enriched with closeness to him, he says through the voice of a prophet, "And I will be their God, and they will be my sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty." And to the Jews Christ said at one time, "I am with you a little while longer," and at another, "Behold, your house is left to you"; but about those from the nations, "My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life."
And the number of the sons of Israel was like the sand of the sea, which will not be measured or counted.

The blessed Isaiah explains this to us in another way: "And if the people of Israel become like the sand of the sea," he says, "the remnant will be saved. For he is completing and cutting short a word in righteousness, because God will make a shortened word in the whole world." But whether it is understood this way or some other way, though Israel is great and countless, equal in measure to the sands of the seashore, God takes little account of them when they have chosen ungodliness; whereas even one person who is righteous and devout is singled out as worthy of his love and mercy. Indeed, he looks even upon one who is humble and quiet and trembles at his words. And this is not all for the good and gentle, who fear him and serve him sincerely; they are also able to help others and sometimes to rescue those who have offended him from the punishment hanging over them. As proof of this you may take what was said about the Sodomites, when God, who is all-powerful, promised to spare them the judgment by fire if only five righteous people were found among them. And so Lot was saved together with his wife and children. And why do I speak of five righteous and good people? When he held his wrath over Jerusalem, he says, "Run through the streets of Jerusalem, and see and know, and search in her squares, if you can find a man, [?] to them, says the Lord." So you see how he holds on to even one righteous person and does not disregard him when he prays for a whole city. But, as I said, he takes no account even of a countless multitude if it is seen to be profane, turned aside to what is evil, and savagely caught up in the deceits of demons.
And in the place where it was said to them, "You are not my people," they too will be called sons of the living God.

Very close to the harshest wrath comes the release from sorrows, and the end of gloomy things is not far off, as far as the words go. That Israel would in due time be cast off, he clearly foretold in what we have just discussed. But that they will not go away forever and perish utterly, but that there will be a time for them to return to their former state and to regain love for God, namely through faith in Christ, he has again fully assured us. For those who were to hear the prophetic words had to know the whole mystery clearly and not be ignorant of the ways of the divine plan. So, he says, in the place where it was said to them, "You are not my people," they too will be called sons of the living God. Let us say precisely what in the place is meant to show. Those of Israel were taken captive at certain times and, as I said, were carried off to the land of the Assyrians. But there they wept and lamented and could do nothing about the Law. The blessed David made this plain to us when he said, "By the river of Babylon, there we sat down and wept when we remembered Zion"; and again he said, "How shall we sing the Lord's song in a foreign land?" But when they returned to Jerusalem through God's compassion, they were, and were called, the people of God no less than before. They continued in prosperity, worshiping freely and offering the sacrifices according to the Law. For it was not permitted at all to carry out what was prescribed anywhere else, but only in Jerusalem and in the temple, since the Law given through Moses clearly commanded, "Take heed to yourself that you do not offer your burnt offerings in every place, but in the place which the Lord your God chooses for his name to be called upon there; there you shall bring your burnt offerings." So when they returned to Jerusalem at various times and left the land of foreigners, they again fulfilled what had been ordained through Moses and bore the name of God's people. But after the Savior's cross and the siege and sack that befell them, they were scattered with all their households through the cities and lands of the nations. How, then, will they in due time become the people of God? Will they return again to Jerusalem and gather in the temple? Or will they do so while remaining in the places where each of them has been scattered? What does the prophet say? In the place where it was said to them, "You are not my people," they too will be called sons of the living God. For they fell away from being the people of God and were scattered through the lands of the nations, as one can see still holds true to this day. But in the last times of the age, "when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in," then indeed even Israel, which was cast off, will be received as sons of God, even while living in whatever places they may happen to be found. For nothing will compel them to go up to Jerusalem and still seek the temple built of stones, since they will no longer honor God with the ancient customs, I mean the sacrifice of oxen and the slaughter of sheep. Rather, their manner of worship will be faith in Christ and his decrees, sanctification in the Spirit, and the rebirth through holy baptism, which secures the glory of adoption for those who are worthy of it and have been called to it by the Lord.

And the sons of Judah and the sons of Israel will be gathered together, and they will appoint for themselves one head, and they will go up from the land, for great is the day of Jezreel. We will find that this too came to pass, both historically and spiritually. Both those who had been taken captive from Samaria, that is, Israel, and also those from Jerusalem, that is, Judah and Benjamin, were in the territories of the Persians and Medes. When Cyrus son of Cambyses captured Babylon and transferred the power of the Persians to himself, he released both Israel and Judah from captivity and ordered them to go home together with the sacred vessels. They came to Jerusalem, and from then on they no longer lived divided as before the captivity, nor did each have its own kings. They all lived in unity of mind in Jerusalem alone, with Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, who was of the tribe of Judah, as leader at that time, and Joshua son of Jozadak, the high priest, serving as priest. It was then that they built the divine temple and devoted themselves to the work on the house. So, he says, the sons of Judah and the sons of Israel will be gathered together, and they will appoint for themselves one head, and they will go up from the land, by which you should understand the land of the foreigners to which they had been carried off as captives. But for great is the day of Jezreel will not fit the historical account. So we say this: when Israel is called the people of God, though because of its great ungodliness it had been named Not-My-People, as we said before, then they and the sons of Judah will be gathered together, that is, the whole multitude of the Jews found in the last times, and they will all be under one head, that is, Christ. The God of all proclaimed something like this in advance through the voice of Ezekiel, saying about Christ, "And I will raise up over them one shepherd, and he will shepherd them, my servant David, and he will be their shepherd." He calls Christ, who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh, David. So when the flock of the nations has already been called, Israel will be brought in last, and they will all be under one head; and they will go up, he says, from the land. To those who understand rightly, I think this shows either that those who have accepted the Savior's yoke will by all means turn away from setting their minds on earthly things and rise above a fleshly mind (for such are all who have come under Christ, and the blessed David will confirm this when he says, "For the mighty ones of the earth belong to God"; [?] "those who are of Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires"), or else that they too will attain the resurrection of the dead.

For Christ said somewhere, "Truly I tell you, everyone who believes in me, even if he dies, will live." And yet, how can we avoid asking: will those who do not believe, tell me, remain dead and not come back to life along with the others? What, then, is the surplus that belongs to those who have believed? The Saviour himself showed us, saying, "The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy; I have come that they may have life, and have it in abundance." So all will rise, the wicked and the good alike; but not all will have the abundance. Those who do not belong to Christ, because they are seen to be caught in the charges of disobedience, will have a life at the end that is harder than death, for they will give account both for their sins and for their disobedience. But those who belong to him, who through the Spirit have been enriched with kinship with God and are good in their ways of life, will without fail have, besides the common resurrection and the return to life, what follows upon it: the gifts, the honours, the crowns, the rewards, the splendour. Paul will bear witness to this when he says, "Behold, I tell you a mystery: we shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at [?] … will be imperishable, and we shall be changed." "They will go up, then," he says, "from the land"; that is, they too will live the life of the saints. "For great is the day of Jezreel." For truly great is the day of Christ, on which he will raise all the dead, and will come down from heaven, and will sit, as it is written, on the throne of his glory, and will repay each according to his works. And if anyone should wish to understand the "day" as the time of his sojourn among us, in which forgiveness of sins was given by Christ to Greeks and barbarians, and to the Jews who had sinned against him, he too will walk straight along the path of the truth. So David also points to the time of our Saviour's sojourn among us when he says, "This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it."
Say to your brother, "My people," and to your sister, "Shown mercy."

He very fittingly adds this to what has already been said. For since he has said that all will be under one head, with nothing any longer walling them off or cutting them apart into discord, but with concord prevailing instead, and with faith in Christ gathering everyone into unity in the Spirit, the Spirit then fittingly commanded those already enriched with faith and brought under Christ no longer to be inclined to shake off peace with those who had justly been called "Not my people" and "Not shown mercy." For once Israel has been received, has obtained forgiveness, and has come under Christ, how would it be consistent for those called into brotherhood by the one Spirit of adoption still to be at odds, and not rather to continue in harmony? "You, then," he says, "who have been made radiant by faith in Christ and have received the glories of true sonship: to your brother, who was once justly called 'Not my people,' now say 'My people'; and to your sister, 'Not shown mercy,' say 'Shown mercy.'" For it is necessary that the peoples under his hand should be seen to share their Master's mind, and that those called by grace into sonship should will the same things as the Father, and rather rejoice that the remnant of Israel has been saved, and that those who were once cast off for their great disobedience have now become accepted and sanctified in Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.
By the Same Author: On the Prophet Hosea, Second Volume.
Plead with your mother, plead, for she is not my wife, and I am not her husband.

He had said beforehand that Israel would justly be cast off and would, besides this, be called "Not my people"; and indeed that she too [?], and very fittingly. Then, not long after, he added to these words the return through faith in Christ that will take place in the last times of the age, by saying, "And the sons of Judah and the sons of Israel shall be gathered together, and they shall appoint for themselves one head." Having narrated the whole dispensation from beginning to end, he now goes on in these words to lay bare the charges against those who were rightly cast off, and to bring clearly into the open the reasons it befell them to suffer those things. Accordingly he says to those who have been shown mercy, received, and made into God's people, yet were born, as it were, of a harlot, the Synagogue: Plead with your mother, plead. "For if you wish," he says, "to learn the reasons why, in the times before the return, you became and were called 'Not my people' and 'Not pitied,' you will not find that I was harsh toward you or careless in my affection. Rather, plead with your own mother, because she did not keep her love for me genuine but denied our bond. She thought very little of the purity of spiritual communion with me, and she would not bring to birth the fruits of my will. She has become not my wife, and for this reason I am no longer her husband. She bore you not to me but to others; for surely I would have recognized my own. One who is a father by nature is not slow to show mercy, but he hesitates to be kind to illegitimate offspring." Someone might perhaps say these things as though in the person of God. But he will also reason, and rightly consider, that when the Synagogue had turned to apostasy from God and chosen the worship of demons, and was all but a harlot, her children were neither purely and steadfastly God-loving nor gentle in their ways. Rather, brought up in the habits of those who begot them, they went heedlessly after what grieves God: on the one hand sacrificing to Baal and to the golden heifers, on the other rushing thoughtlessly into every kind of uncleanness. They will therefore blame, and very fittingly, their own mother, and not rather the truly virtue-loving and all-pure Master, who does not consent to have as his consort one who has played the harlot. The kind of harlotry meant is of course spiritual, even if it is spoken of in bodily terms.
And I will remove her harlotry, so that I may strip her naked and restore her as in the days of her birth.

For those who do not turn to God of their own will, and will not bear to do what pleases him, but cling tenaciously to the wickedness they somehow hold in honor, some penalty and punishment is devised, which in the end moves them, as if by necessity and fear, to the very thing toward which it would have been better for them to go by their own choice. Among bodily wounds, those that are troublesome and hard to treat, if they do not yield to the power of medicines and take some turn for the better, are either cut with iron, since the physicians' skill calls for help of this kind, or else are overcome by fire. In just the same way, a human soul that has strayed far into apostasy from what is good, if it will not yield to the voices of those who admonish it nor choose to pass over from what is more shameful to what is better, is overcome by penalties, and, caught in the snares of punishment, makes its return under compulsion. Such is the word spoken through Jeremiah: "With pain and the whip you will be disciplined, Jerusalem." And the divine David sings something similar about those who have loved being drawn on and on into sin: "With bit and bridle you will bind tight the jaws of those who do not draw near to you." For those who are used to breaking colts turn the hard and untrained among brute animals with bridles toward what seems right; and so too God deals with those who are very fond of sin, for their benefit. So the prophets and righteous men advised the Synagogue to abandon the worship of idols and to keep away from an error invented who knows where. And not only that: God himself threatened to bring upon them the most shameful of all evils if they did not choose to run back to thinking and doing what seemed good and pleasing to him. But they remained harsh and unyielding, inflexible in mind. For this reason they were taken captive by the spear to the Assyrians and the Medes, and spent long years there. Once they were there, weighed down by the yoke of slavery, they no longer sacrificed to the heifers (for how could they, or with what?), since they were already in evils from which there was no escape. Nor did they call on Baal himself; rather, they spent their time lamenting their own misfortunes. This, then, is what the Master of all says: And I will remove her harlotry from my presence, and her adultery from between her breasts. "For she will go away captive," he says, "and I shall no longer see her sacrificing to Baal or offering burnt offerings to the golden heifers, all but baring her breasts to her lovers in her great insolence. Instead I shall gloat over her as she is distraught and wretched, suffering an incurable misfortune in a land not her own, under harsh and bitter masters. I shall bring these things about by stripping her of my help and leaving her unsightly, so that she is seen to be as she was at the beginning, when, bearing the yoke of the Egyptians' greed, she remained naked of my grace and love and of the wisdom of the Law." So the Synagogue went into reverse and, as it were, back again to where she had been, forfeiting through her ignorance the honor and glory she had had in the meantime.

The Savior himself also taught us this when he said, "When the unclean spirit goes out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, and does not find it. Then it says, 'I will return to my house from which I came out.' And when it comes, it finds it unoccupied, swept, and put in order. Then it goes and takes along seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and they enter and dwell there; and the last state of that person becomes worse than the first. So it will be with this evil generation." For while the Israelites were still living in Egypt, the evil spirit dwelt in them, since they were idolaters; but in the meantime it was cast out, for they were called to the knowledge of God through Moses. But since they became killers of the Lord and liable to countless charges, their last state has become worse than the first, with a herd of demons, and no longer just one, dwelling in them. For a soul that has cast off the covering of heavenly grace will be easy prey for Satan in every way and altogether.

And I will make her like a wilderness, and set her like a waterless land, and kill her with thirst. And I will not have mercy on her children, because they are children of harlotry. For their mother played the harlot; she who bore them brought shame on them.

He says that she who has played the harlot will be barren, dry, and thorn-bearing, parched and waterless; deprived, perhaps, not of earthly waters but of the richness that comes from above and from heaven, that is, of the gifts supplied through the Spirit, which he distributes to every wise and good soul. For the blessed David sings somewhere to God and says, "But the sons of men will shelter under the shadow of your wings, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight; for with you is the fountain of life." Those worthy of so venerable and abundant a supply would be the genuine, who have lived rightly and put nothing before love for God. But she who has played the harlot, he says, will become [?], and indeed will die of thirst. And this, I think, is what was said about her through the voice of other prophets.
