For one said, "Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, when I will send out a famine on the land: not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord. And they will run about from east to west seeking the word of the Lord, and shall not find it." And Jeremiah, again speaking as in the person of God: "With pain and the whip you will be disciplined, Jerusalem, lest my soul depart from you, lest I make you an untrodden land that will not be inhabited." For, as I said, God sends into the mind of each of us, through the Spirit, words able to turn us toward eternal life, and often he also enriches us through the voice of the saints. He said, then, that the children must perish together with their harlot mother, and without pity. For what reason? Because they are children of harlotry. And we certainly do not say that a child is answerable for its mother's offenses; otherwise what would become of the saying spoken through Ezekiel: "They shall not die [?] ... he shall die in his own sin"? Rather it should be understood that, even if the figure of a harlot mother is conceived as a type of the Synagogue, those born of her would nonetheless be the same people. And by saying that they are children of harlotry, he showed clearly that they stand liable to the charges of spiritual harlotry, having been impious, so to speak, from their very swaddling clothes and from the womb, never having laid hold of the works of piety, but having been wholly unpractised in virtue and having paid no honor to the path pleasing to God. So also the Psalmist says (Ps. 57:4): "Sinners were estranged from the womb; they went astray from the belly; they spoke lies." Yet every pious person, nurtured in the works of righteousness, can cry aloud to God, "Upon you I was cast from the womb; from my mother's belly you are my God." And just as those who live splendidly and decently, as in light and in day, may fittingly be understood as sons of light and sons of the day, so too, if some are called children of harlotry, you will again understand them as those who live as in harlotry and in an utterly perverse life. These he does not consent to pity, Because their mother has played the harlot; she who bore them has brought shame on them. Clearly she brought shame both on herself and on the children who sprang from her. For just as the righteous man glories in virtue, so every impious man lives in shame and disgrace.
For she said, "I will follow my lovers, who give me my bread and my water, my garments and my linen and my oil, and all that is fitting for me."

He says that her lovers are the unclean demons, with whom, one might say, the harlotry was committed. For to follow their wishes and do what seems good to them is, I think, to be wanton in sins, to live shamefully, and to be filled with the utmost wickedness; indeed, all but to be in labor with every kind of uncleanness. For just as those who are in labor with the fear of God have cried out to God, "Because of your fear, Lord, we conceived and were in labor and gave birth; we brought forth the spirit of your salvation upon the earth," so too those who abandon the divine laws and practise every wickedness, giving up their minds to the desires of demons, at once have them full of every impiety. The apostate demons, then, are the wicked and accursed lovers of those who have turned aside to impiety; and if anyone chooses to attend to them as gods, he will be terribly impious. For he credits them with whatever blessing he may have, and often honors them with praises and offers them thank-offerings, having abandoned the one God, who alone is God by nature: the God who supplies what sustains life, who clothes us with grace as with garments and overshadows mind and heart with help from above, who enriches us as with oil and feeds us with spiritual bread for a glorious and unfading life, who nourishes us with life-giving water for spiritual well-being. But whoever has turned aside to impiety, just as the Synagogue that played the harlot did, said that she must follow her own lovers and render her thanks to them, and believed that it was from them she received what she had for food and clothing. For this, I think, is the meaning of For she said, "I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my water and my garments and my linen and my oil, and all that is fitting for me." But the wise and good, who are known to God and are his closest friends, would surely credit him with the gift of heavenly blessings and the supply of earthly ones. For they will say, and very wisely, "Is there among the idols of the nations one who sends rain? And if the heaven gives its abundance, is it not you? And we will wait for you, for you have made all these things." And they will cry out together with the divine David himself, "You visited the earth and drenched it; you greatly enriched it."

Therefore, behold, I am hedging her way with thorns, and I will wall up her ways, and she shall not find her path. And she will pursue her lovers and not overtake them; and she will seek them and not find them.

"For since she has plotted evil against herself," he says, "and has left out nothing of what is by nature wrong (for she said she must choose to follow her own lovers, that is, to give the bent of her mind to the unholy wishes of those who have led her astray, so as to do their will alone); and since, besides this, she renders thanks for what I have given her to the demons, who have done her no good at all, for this reason I will show her designs to be vain and will oppose her altogether. For I will hedge her way with thorns and wall up her path, so that she may neither follow her own lovers nor find those who led her astray of any use, even if she should choose to pursue them, that is, to devote herself zealously to honoring and worshipping them." By thorns he means the hardships that befell Israel: I mean the wars, the captivities, the famine, the dangers, the grinding life of slavery. For once they had come under the Medes and Persians, they had no leisure to approach Baal or the golden heifers. Rather, it was in a way inevitable that, deprived even of the freedom they had long had and held most dear, longing for home, living in poverty and pressed by the greed of their rulers, they could no longer carry out their customary rites, but instead lamented and were drunk with incurable calamities, already condemning those who had led them astray, since nothing of what they had placed their empty hopes in was theirs to enjoy. For they were helped in nothing, neither by Baal defending them (for what could voiceless wood have done?) nor by the heifers devising some way to help them, for they were of gold, "works of human hands," as it is written. So the ways are blocked: God does not smooth the path to wickedness for those who love sin, but roughens it for their benefit, and does not let them rush easily toward what their foolishness approves, so that, even against their will, they may be checked and move over to what is better, having learned through experience itself that sin brings loss to everyone.
And she will say, "I will go and return to my former husband, for it was better for me then than now."

The discourse still keeps its fitting manner, for it has been composed from beginning to end as if about a harlot. Therefore, he says, she will change her mind and say, I will go to my former husband, for it was better for me then than now. But observe here too the God of all, who disciplines even in his wrath, helps in many ways, reins in those who have gone astray by bringing terrors upon them, and remakes them for their good. "For when she sees her ways blocked with thorns," he says, "then, then indeed she will change her counsel; and what it would have been better for her to choose to do before the distresses came upon her, she will seize at least late, and after experience. For then she will love the things of God and, as if from sober reflection, disregard the offenses of the time between, and will at last turn to wanting what she wanted at the beginning; she will marvel at the things of God and, as one who has come to her senses after drunkenness, she will at last perceive how incomparably they excel." Being disciplined, then, is not without profit, even if it perhaps brings pain for the present. Knowing this, the prophets say (Jer. 10:24), "Discipline us, Lord." And the divine Paul writes (Heb. 12:7), "If you endure discipline, God is treating you as sons; for what son is there whom a father does not discipline?" And he shows how sweet and beneficial it is to be disciplined when he says (Heb. 12:11), "All discipline seems for the present to bring not joy but grief; but afterwards it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it."
And she did not know that it was I who gave her the grain and the wine and the oil, and I multiplied silver for her; but she made things of silver and gold for Baal.

"No one would doubt," he says, "that she will no longer choose to follow her own lovers. For he will accomplish this, and very easily, by blocking her way, walling up her paths, and letting her prosper in no way at all. But since, besides thinking that Baal is a god, she has also offered him thanks for what I supplied to her, I will plan what is fitting for this too, so that she may learn who it is who gives and holds authority over all things. For I gave her what sustains life: I multiplied grain and wine and oil and silver for her. But when she ought to have given thanks for my generosity, she made them into things for the glory of Baal." This is clear proof of utter insensibility and ingratitude together; and the matter is quite enough, and very justly, to provoke God, even though he is understood to be the source and origin of all gentleness.

It is therefore utterly dreadful, and not without penalty, to seek to credit the generosity of God's gifts to those who undermine his glory, that is, to the unclean demons. Some in the world do just this: the pagan Greeks and the heretics. For the former, when God gives a man wisdom, bestow it on their own opinions; while the God-hated and unholy gangs of heretics ruin some with their inventions of convoluted notions and overturn the minds of the simpler, "and they set snares to destroy men," as it is written. So both have honored Baal, all but bringing to him, as if from spiritual wealth, the things concerning God as a splendid offering for his glory. And this, I think, is the very fitting spiritual sense of I gave the grain and the wine and the oil, and I multiplied silver for her; but she made things of silver and gold for Baal. We must therefore render to God what is his. For it is fitting that he who is the giver and supplier of every good thing to us should be adorned with gold from what we have received from him, whether that is splendid eloquence or a mind well fitted to grasp true mysteries.

Therefore I will turn back and take away my grain in its season and my wine in its time, and I will take away my garments and my linen, so that they no longer cover her shame. And now I will uncover her uncleanness before her lovers, and no one shall deliver her out of my hand.

You see how he threatened to take away what brings gladness, and this for her benefit. For just as roughening her way with thorns led her to choose to think better things, and brought her, even as it were against her will, to say, "I will return to my former husband, for it was better for me then than now" (for she learned through experience what leads to benefit, and where it was better to stay), so too, he says, "if I take back what is mine, then surely she will seek the one who supplies it, and will stop rendering thanks to the demons and thinking that they are truly gods, able to save those under their power." He says that he will take back the grain and the wine and the linen in their season, perhaps because the crops fail at times and the harvest comes late for them, so that even their labors at farming are endured in vain.

If someone should choose to understand that the Jews will in due season be deprived of grain and wine, having fallen away from the mystical blessing, he will understand rightly. By "linen" he means the covering, as it were, and the help from above, under which a person becomes seemly. But if he is carried outside it, he is no longer beautiful; he becomes very unseemly indeed, and will go on as though naked in the world. This, then, is how you will understand the removal of the linen, "so that her shame is not covered." He promises to uncover her uncleanness even before her lovers. In what way? We said just now that, having fallen among the thorns, that is, the evils of war and the calamities most able to strike terror, she will neglect even those whom she reputed to be gods. She will have no leisure to offer them sacrifices, nor be able to perform the customary rites for their glory. Rather, she will mock them, since she has gained no profit from them at all, and, reproaching as it were their utter feebleness, she says: "I will return to my former husband, for it was better with me then than now." "When, therefore," he says, "I strip her of my help, and she falls into terrible things and disregards the honor and love she owed them, then she will appear shameful to them as well, having spat on them too with an unsound and faltering mind." For as far as their pleasure and liking went, she ought rather to have been seen enduring hardship, and not forgetting what pleased them even in the very worst calamities. So, as far as their wishes are concerned, Israel is shameful in the eyes of those it had considered gods, since it did not choose to love them to the end. The blessed Elijah seems to me to say something of this kind: "How long will you limp on both your legs? If the Lord is God, go after him; but if Baal is he, go after him"; which elsewhere he puts this way: "Either Baal, Baal; or God, God." And that no one could rescue those who have once come under divine wrath, nor could anyone raise up one whom God has cast down, he has shown by saying, "and no one shall rescue her out of my hand."
And I will put an end to all her mirth, her feasts, her new moons, her sabbaths, and all her festal assemblies.

For how could people keep festival who are caught in evils so harsh and inescapable that they have fallen under a barbarian hand and serve their enemies as captives of the spear? Or what occasion for gladness could they have, weighed down by such bitter cares and wasted away by unbearable griefs? And indeed, is it not better to understand it this way: that it would rather befit those brought to such wretchedness to cry out what is sung so beautifully on the psalmist's lyre: "By the river of Babylon, there we sat down and wept when we remembered Zion"? And since keeping festival was altogether impossible for them, they likewise say, "How shall we sing the Lord's song in a foreign land?" For the Babylonians, I suppose, did not allow them to perform their customary worship and the rites that were dear to them at home and familiar by custom.

But perhaps someone will say: If Israel had turned aside to worship idols, how would it not also have fallen away from the feasts prescribed by the law, the sabbaths and the new moons? To this we say that they slipped from their love of God and worshiped Baal and the golden heifers, yet they did not entirely reject what had been given through Moses. Rather, they went on walking on both sides and limping, as the prophet put it, choosing neither to worship Baal wholeheartedly nor to worship the God of all with a pure heart. Therefore Israel has lost its feasts, festivals, mirth and sabbaths, being neither permitted to fulfill for God what is in the law nor able to celebrate the customary festivals for Baal.

It would also be true in another sense, and quite reasonably, that those who depart from God and have made light of their love for him must necessarily be downcast and remain outside everything that is able to gladden. "For there is no rejoicing for the ungodly, says the Lord"; for them the worm has been reserved forever. But for the gentle, who have a pious and God-loving aim, it would rightly be fitting to rejoice in all good things. "For everlasting joy is upon their heads," as it is written, "and pain and sorrow and sighing have fled away." To them also the divine Paul writes, saying: "Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, rejoice. Let your gentleness be known to all people." For just as punishment must follow the wicked, so too an abundance of good things from above must follow those whose aim is to live a splendid life.

And I will destroy her vine and her fig trees, of which she said, "These are my wages, which my lovers gave me"; and I will make them a testimony, and the wild beasts of the field and the birds of the sky and the creeping things of the earth shall devour them.

This, again, is another way of saying, "I will take away my grain in its season and my wine in its time." For Israel attributed the fruitfulness of the seasons to the powers and generosity of the demons, and, acting most foolishly, offered its thank-offerings to them and not rather to God. Therefore he says that he will destroy and ruin the things by which she had been led astray for the worse, when she said she had received them as hire from her own lovers. The passage is cleverly framed as though about a lewd woman, but in truth it refers to Israel, which [supposed?] that the abundance of ripe produce and the possession of a fruitful land were their wage and recompense for the honor and worship they gave the idols. And that they thought this was the sole reason why they enjoyed every other kind of well-being, anyone could easily learn by reading the words of Jeremiah. Jerusalem had been captured, and some who had escaped the height of the war went down into the land of the Egyptians, and the prophet went with them at the divine command. There he counseled them to cease from the defilements of idolatry and to choose to run back to God. Then a wretched and utterly foolish crowd of women opposed the prophet's words, and shamelessly said: "As for the word that you have spoken to us in the name of the Lord, we will not listen to you. We will certainly do every word that goes out of our mouth: we will burn incense to the queen of heaven and pour out libations to her, as we and our fathers and our kings and our rulers did in the cities of Judah and outside Jerusalem. Then we had our fill of bread and were well off, and we saw no evil. But since we stopped burning incense to the queen of heaven, we have all been brought low, and we have perished by the sword and by wrath." Do you see how she all but says that she had received the necessities of life, and prosperity besides, as a reward for going astray? "Therefore," he says, "I will destroy the things of which she said, 'These are my wages, which my lovers gave me,' and I will make them a testimony." For once these things are taken away they will bear witness, as it were, against Israel's wickedness; they will make their punishment more conspicuous and make the wrath plain to see. And the wild beasts of the field and the birds of the sky and the creeping things of the earth will eat them. This may be understood not in one way only; rather, its meaning can be taken in three ways. Either he means that the produce of the fields will be food for wild beasts, since there will no longer be anyone living in the land. For very many, driven from their homes and cities, went away against their will to Babylon and the Medes, and many others were consumed by the war, so that the country of the Samaritans was now inhabited by wild beasts and reptiles alone. Or again he means that the Babylonians, like wild beasts, will feast on the fruitfulness of the land, while its inhabitants are shut up in the walled cities and dare not go even a step beyond the gates, although famine was destroying them. But if anyone wishes to understand it spiritually, he can take another path. For the vineyard and the fig tree may very well be compared to the instruction through the law that leads us to Christ, since the law acts as our tutor to bring us to him, as the blessed Paul says. The vine may be understood as a symbol of gladness, and the fig tree of sweetness. And who could doubt that the law of God is truly sweet to a God-loving soul and able to gladden it? Israel, then, has necessarily been left without a share in the spiritual goods from above. These have been given for others to share: to the wild beasts and reptiles, as it were, by which I mean those from the Gentiles. Before the Savior's coming they might have been thought to differ little from wild beasts and venomous reptiles, because of the perversity of their ways. Yet they did not remain in that state, for they chose to follow Christ, who says: "Learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls." To what has been said I would add this as well: those who lead an accursed and God-hated life must necessarily slip away from every good and fall into the worst miseries of all.
And I will punish her for the days of the Baals, in which she sacrificed to them and put on her earrings and her necklaces and went after her lovers, but she forgot me, says the Lord.

He at once adds the reason for such terrible, or rather most fitting, indignation against them. Since they persisted in their error for a long time, he says that they will suffer the wrath for an equal length of time. This, I think, is the meaning of "I will punish her for the days of the Baals," that is, of the idols. For the penalty and punishment, he says, will exactly match the days of error in which she burned incense to Baal. She never ceased to adorn herself and to please her lovers in many ways. And for souls that have chosen idolatry, adornment consists in doing what the unclean demons approve. For just as we say that a human soul is admirable when it is seen to excel in virtues, so too we must suppose that the sin-loving soul appears very beautiful to the herds of demons when it chooses to think and do everything that is sweet and dear to them. Such a soul may be compared to a woman of bad character who decks herself in gold that soon fades and all but bewitches the hearts of her lovers with the ornaments on her ears and neck. So every kind of uncleanness is a source of pride to the wicked. And that those whose aim is to look toward such things will habitually and inevitably slip from the very remembrance of God, he has shown by saying, "but she forgot me, says the Lord." For since she was sick, he says, with leaning toward the demons, or rather with abandoning entirely all desire and zeal for the good, she slipped even from the remembrance of God. And this is clear proof of complete impiety.
Therefore, behold, I will lead her astray and make her a desert.

"Since she has run aground in many ways," he says, "and I have quite rightly exacted the penalty for her apostasy ('for I have punished her for the days of the Baals,' and brought on her a wrath equal to her offenses), therefore I will now turn to mercy and bring her over to what is better, so that she can do the things by which she may become dear to God." What, then, he asks, will be the manner of her cure? "Behold, I lead her astray." This does not mean leading her away from what is necessary and useful for life to what is not, but from what is more shameful and by nature harmful to what brings benefit. For just as a soul strays from virtue into wickedness, so in the same way, I think, when it turns back, as it were, from the ways of wickedness, it would seem all but to have strayed, since it has been carried away from its own aim and no longer travels the path it had set before itself. And just as her ways were usefully fenced in with thorns so that she might not catch up with her lovers, so now, as she runs headlong, as it were, to ruin and destruction, she seems to be led astray by God's mercy. She is moved to desire virtue and receives into her mind and heart the light of the true knowledge of God, and, as I said, she no longer finds the old path. It should be noted that the other translators have rendered "I lead her astray" differently, but it comes to one and the same sense. Some have rendered it, "For behold, I will carry her away"; others, "For I entice her." They express in a different way, as I said, this very same thing: the "I lead astray" understood in a beneficial sense. And although she was easy to walk through and like a well-watered land for the herds of demons, he promises to make her a desert. He teaches that he will make her hard, trackless and waterless to their designs, so that, finding no place of rest any longer, they will give up and depart.

So also our Lord Jesus Christ says that the unclean spirit, when it has gone out of a man, passes through waterless places seeking rest and does not find it. For just as a waterless region is not habitable for people, so the God-loving and holy soul, which will not consent to think or do what pleases unclean spirits, may reasonably be understood as a bad and hateful land for them, as it were trackless and waterless. So the "leading astray" spoken of here is a form of help, and so too is being made into a desert land, as we have just explained.
And I will speak to her heart, and I will give her her possessions from there.

In these words the passage splendidly promises us the salvation that comes through Christ, and recalls the times of his coming, in which we say this was fulfilled: "In those days and at that time I will put my laws into their minds, and I will write them on their hearts." For so also the most wise Paul writes to those who have been enriched with such splendid and truly precious grace, saying: "You are our letter, written on our hearts, known and read by all people; and you show that you are a letter of Christ, delivered by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God." For we who have believed have been taught by God; and indeed the divine John declared, saying: "And you have an anointing from the Holy One, and you have no need for anyone to teach you; but as his Spirit teaches you about all things." Having received the Spirit, then, and having Christ himself dwelling within our hearts from then on as our instructor in what is needful, we have at once been enriched with the form of every virtue and with the abundant and inalienable possession of spiritual gifts. And Paul confirms us in this when he writes: "What eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and has not entered the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him." He promises, then, to speak to her heart. For the synagogue of the Jews will be called to knowledge, taking into its mind the divine laws engraved by the Spirit, just as the church from the Gentiles has done. And her possessions will come "from there," which stands for "from here," that is, from this very thing. For God speaks within us and makes us hear, through the Spirit, all that is necessary for life and for the knowledge of God that is understood in Christ, through whom and in whom we have beheld the Father. From this, as I said, we have been enriched with the unfading hope, the glory, the boast of adoption, grace, and reigning together with Christ himself. These are the possessions of the saints; this is the heavenly wealth. For they will not consent to set their minds on anything earthly; they have hated the world and the things in it.
And the valley of Achor, to open her understanding.

The words "I will give" must again be understood here. "For I will give," he says, "her possessions from there; and likewise I will give the valley of Achor to open her understanding." What he wishes to convey is this. We who have believed are eager to take what happened to the ancients as a kind of pattern for what we ought to do. So we avoid offending God, since that leads to ruin, and instead we seek and take care to accomplish what pleases him. For the most wise Paul urges us to this, saying: "Now these things happened to them as examples, and they were written down for our instruction, on whom the ends of the ages have come." So it is a way of training in virtue to think it necessary to look closely at what happened to those of older times.

That the disobedient and unruly, who despise the divine commandments, will fall into a terrible and inescapable penalty when Christ judges could be shown very easily, as in a type, by what was done long ago in the case of Achar. Achar disregarded the divine command and stole from the things devoted to God, and he was punished together with his whole household, when Joshua the son of Nun inflicted the ultimate penalty on him. Joshua fulfilled the image of Christ: he led the army after Moses, he brought the sons of Israel across the Jordan, and he allotted them the land of promise as their inheritance. What is written about Achar runs as follows. When he had been caught in the theft and had confessed his sin, "Joshua," it says, "took Achar the son of Zara and led him to the ravine of Achor, with his sons and his daughters and his calves and his beasts of burden and his sheep and his tent and all his belongings, and all the people were with him; and he brought them up to Emekachor. And Joshua said to Achar, 'Why have you destroyed us? May the Lord destroy you, as he does this day.' And all Israel stoned him with stones, and they raised over him a great heap of stones." Now Achor is interpreted as "turmoil," and when Emek is added, it is understood as "valley of turmoil." There the sons of Israel killed Achar as one hated by God and a lover of wealth, and destroyed all that was his along with him; for it is written, "The ungodly shall perish root and all from the earth." So it will be in the last times of the age, when Christ comes down to us from above, from heaven, to repay each according to his works. For he will bring down into Hades, as into a deep ravine, those who chose to disobey the divine commands and preferred to love the things of the world, and he will destroy those wicked men wretchedly. "I will give," then, he says, "the valley of Achor," that is, Emekachor, "to open her understanding." For the things done long ago in the valley of Emekachor, he says, will be very useful to her for coming to her senses and from then on opening wide the eye of her mind after its old hardening. He called the place the valley of turmoil because not a few of the Israelites fell there when the men of Gai pursued them, and great turmoil arose, since Joshua thought that Israel had lost God's mercy and help. "The things done in the ravine of turmoil," he says, "to the one who dared to break the divine command will open her understanding, so that she knows clearly what end awaits those who choose to show contempt." Observe how the valley of Achor is not given to open her understanding until he has spoken to her heart. For the Jewish people would not understand the divine commandments, nor would they perceive the mystery of Christ in the types, unless, like us who have already believed, they were enriched with a share in the Holy Spirit and were shown to have received illumination from above. The blessed Paul will assure us of this when he writes about those who are of Israel by blood: "For to this very day the same veil remains at the reading of the old covenant, not lifted, because only in Christ is it taken away. Indeed, to this day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart. But whenever one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed. Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom." He promises, therefore, first to speak to her heart, as the Holy Spirit engraves the divine laws and the instruction from above upon them; and only then will she understand what was done in the valley of Emekachor, both as type and as history. These things are well able to open her understanding and free her at last from her old hardening. "For a partial hardening has come upon Israel," as the wise Paul also writes.
And she shall be humbled there as in the days of her infancy, and as in the days when she came up out of the land of Egypt.

When I speak to her mind and heart, he says, and give her the valley of Achor to open her understanding, there — that is, at that time — she will be humbled. This does not mean that she will be brought low and sink under the things that usually cause grief. It means that she will at last have abandoned her disobedient and intractable ways, which were guilty of the charge of arrogance. For the disobedient person is boastful, steep and unbridled, as it were, and has made a practice of counting as nothing the reverence owed to fulfilling the law. But the one who is quick to obey is truly humble, approachable as it were, and greatly loved by God. Indeed, he said somewhere through one of the holy prophets, "And upon whom shall I look, but upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?" So when I speak to her heart, he says, then indeed she too will be humbled, just as in the beginning. Then, when Moses called them and the compassionate God had commanded them to depart from the land of the Egyptians, they were most eager to do it and ran away from the land of their oppressors. And when he laid down the laws at Horeb, they gathered with Moses at Mount Sinai and made a solemn promise, saying, "All that the Lord God has said to us we will do and obey." So she will be humble and docile, just as in the beginning, when she received through the law her birth into the knowledge of God and gladly accepted what pleased God. By the "days of her infancy," then, he means the rebirth into the knowledge of God through the law. That is why he said, "Israel is my firstborn son."

"And it shall be in that day, says the Lord, that she will call me 'My husband,' and she will no longer call me Baalim. And I will remove the names of the Baalim from her mouth, and their names shall no longer be remembered."

In these words he calls the time of our Saviour's sojourn "day." The time of the incarnation of the Only-begotten will properly and truly be called day, for in it the mist in the world was dispelled and the darkness vanished. Bright rays dawned, as it were, in the minds of those who believed, and the sun of righteousness shone forth, sending the light of the true knowledge of God into those who know how to open wide the eye of the mind. At that time, then, he says, she will be called to the knowledge of the one who is truly God, and she will cease from that ancient and hateful idolatry. She will no longer be easily led astray into apostasy. How so? Rather, standing firmly and soundly, she will keep her mind unshaken in piety, so that the names of the idols will not come into her speech even so much as to be uttered. For she will call me, he says, "My husband," and will no longer call me Baalim. That is, she will stop being a harlot and refuse to prostitute herself any longer. She will set great store by being a lawful wife and will acknowledge the relationship, clearly the spiritual one. She will in no way call upon the Baalim, thinking that things made of stone are gods, and by the [?] of certain [?]. So she will call me, he says, "My husband." Like a chaste and most modest wife she will turn to me, will love none of the others from now on, and will no longer call upon the Baalim. But if anyone wishes, he may take the saying in another way as well.

Everyone agrees that the Baalim signify the idols. Now it was a custom among Hebrew women to call their own husbands by the names of the falsely named gods. They say that [the originator?] of this practice was Ninus the Babylonian, who renamed his own father Belus after the idol they worshipped, I mean Bel. That she will also cease from so shameful a custom he has indicated by saying, "She will call me 'My husband,' and will no longer call me Baalim." For if she should choose, he says, to call me husband, she will certainly address me as "My husband." She will no longer call me by the names of the idols, as though she were honouring me with them. That is why he says, "And I will remove the names of the Baalim from her mouth, and their names shall no longer be remembered."

"And in that day I will make a covenant for them with the beasts of the field and with the birds of the sky and with the creeping things of the earth, and I will break bow and sword and war from the land."

In the passages read earlier he said, "And I will destroy her vine and her fig trees, of which she said, 'These are my wages, which my lovers gave me.'" And he added to this, "The beasts of the field and the birds of the sky and the creeping things of the earth shall devour them." In interpreting that text we said that the beasts, birds and creeping things obliquely indicate the enemies who plundered the land of the Jews: the Persians, Medes and Babylonians, and the whole abominable crowd of other foes. They might reasonably be thought to differ little from wild beasts because of their bloodthirsty ways. They are birds because of the swiftness of their attack, and creeping things because they are dreadful, utterly wicked and keen in malice. While Israel was shut up in the cities of Samaria, these enemies devoured everything in the fields, leaving no outrage untried. But when I remove the names of their idols from the land, he says, then I will also make a covenant of peace for them with every savage and barbarian race. The attacks of their enemies will now cease, and they will remain untouched by war and terrors. For I will break bow and sword. And we shall find that this was indeed brought to fulfilment in history. For when the most illustrious generals of the Romans won dominion over all and brought the whole world under heaven into their hands, with God in his providence granting them the glory, the Persians concerned themselves only with their own realm, and the raids of the other barbarians against lands and cities also came to an end. The blessed Isaiah clearly recalls this event when he says, "And they shall beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into sickles, and nation shall not lift up sword against nation, and they shall no longer learn war." For once they had come under one yoke, they turned instead to useful labour and reshaped the implements of war into tools for farming. There will be peace, then, he says, and the terrors of old will cease, for God lulls them to rest and gladdens those who love him with the blessings of peace.

I think we shall also need to add this. Formerly, while we lived on in error and were called children of wrath, the wicked and hostile powers were destroying us, like evil beasts, birds that feed on flesh, and the most dangerous serpents. But when we came to know in Christ the one who is God by nature, and through faith washed away the charges of the ancient deceit, then we were saved. We received authority "to tread upon serpents"; we trod upon asp and basilisk, and trampled lion and dragon. For Christ shielded us, walled his own about with invincible power, and put his own peace into our minds. For he says, "My peace I give to you; my peace I leave with you." And Paul too writes, "And the peace of Christ, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts."
"And I will settle you in hope, and I will betroth you to myself forever."

Not only will I free you from the terrors of the enemy, he says, but I will add to this that from now on you will be well off in the hope of good things, so that your good cheer will be secure, firmly grounded and unshakable. For I will betroth you to myself, and that forever. And what does this mean? In a way he had betrothed ancient Israel, that is, the synagogue of the Jews, and called it into a close relationship, I mean the one through the law, with Moses ministering and angels mediating. But that kind of betrothal was not perpetual, nor was it forever, far from it. The types were not going to hold sway for all time, since they were things "imposed until the time of reformation." At the time of reformation, however, that is, the time of our Saviour's sojourn, another kind of betrothal has been revealed. It is perpetual and unshaken, far more splendid than the first, and better than the shadow. The God of all granted the bride, as a kind of bridal gift, release from bodily slavery, and through shadow and types he called her to spiritual purification. But he set a limit of time on that betrothal. For the first was not faultless, as Paul says, nor was it ageless and far from vanishing away. For this reason a place was sought for the second, that is, the new one, I mean the gift and grace given through Christ, which brings us a freedom that is neither temporary nor carnal. For it enrols us among the children of God, lavishes on us "the pledge of the Spirit," and lays down perpetual laws. Indeed, the divine David said to him somewhere, "Your righteousness is righteousness forever, and your word is truth." I think he is clearly showing that the things in the law do not remain forever, since the shadow is to be transformed into truth, and that no one could behold the beauty of the truth in the writings of the law. For the law, as I said, was shadow and type. So he betroths her, having set aside the original, first marriage. The law is not able to unite us to God perfectly and purely. We approach him through the Son and through the decrees he gave, that is, those of the gospel, which bring a spiritual union or intimacy. For we are united to God in the Spirit and are enriched with a share in his divine nature. It is likely that "I will betroth you to myself" also hints elegantly at something else, for here again you will understand it in another way. He says "to myself" in place of "through myself": not as formerly, with angels mediating, nor with some minister taken on for this purpose, as Moses was. For, as it is written, "it was not an envoy, not an angel, but the Lord himself." The Word from God the Father, who became man like us, presented the church to himself and "created the two peoples into one new man, making peace, and reconciling both in one Spirit to the Father," as the blessed Paul says.

Or, if you like, you may take the saying in another way. As I said, he once betrothed the synagogue of the Jews in Egypt, but in a way he betrothed her to another rather than to himself, I mean to the divine Moses. To him he said somewhere, "Go, get down from here quickly, for your people, whom you brought out of the land of Egypt, have acted lawlessly." Do you hear how he assigned the betrothed, that is, the people, to Moses, not yet considering her worthy of a close relationship with himself? For, as I said, the law, or Moses, was not able to unite us to God purely and completely. That was reserved, as the best of all achievements and one truly befitting God, for the mediator between God and men, that is, Christ, through whom and in whom we are united to God. For he is "our peace," according to the Scriptures. He removed the sin that stood in between, and he joined us to himself, cleansed, washed and sanctified in the Spirit, and through himself to God the Father.
"And I will betroth you to myself in righteousness and in judgment and in mercy and in compassion, and I will betroth you to myself in faith, and you shall know the Lord."

He explains clearly what kind of intimacy this would be and through what acts the mystery of the dispensation would unfold. It will be, he says, in righteousness and in judgment, and also in mercy and in compassion. It seems necessary, then, to say what this righteousness is, what the judgment is, and also what the mercy is. We wretches were being oppressed. Satan was tearing us apart like a wild beast, leading us off into error and casting us at his pleasure into the pits of sin, and we had no strength at all to help ourselves. For that beast is truly most dangerous, most violent, and a killer of men. When human affairs had been brought to this depth of misery, the blessed prophets made frequent supplications to the one who was able to help. Wearing, as it were, the mask of our common humanity, they begged the Son to come from heaven as our helper and aid. Thus the divine David said, "Arise, O God, judge the earth"; and again, "O God, save me by your name, and by your power you will judge me." So God judged in righteousness. He saved those who had been wronged, drove off the bloodthirsty and accursed Satan, thrust him away from his oppression of us, and pulled down the arrogant and fearsome dominion of the demons. He himself explained this mystery to us in his own words when he was about to endure the cross for the life of all: "Now is the judgment of this world; now the ruler of this world will be cast out. And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all to myself." Surely we do not say that he meant he would pass judgment on this world at the time of his sojourn. For, as he himself said again, "God did not send the Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him." Rather, by judgment he means a right and blameless verdict, as it were, between two parties. For, as I said, he judged between us and that enemy rightly and in a manner befitting God. He saved us by drawing us to himself, and he cast out of his tyranny over us the one who oppressed us and destroyed us in many ways. So we were saved because God had mercy and compassion on us. For we were justified "not by works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his great mercy," as it is written. We were called through faith into a spiritual intimacy, and having been called in this way, we have come to know the one who is God by nature. That is why he says, "I will also betroth you to myself in faith, and you shall know the Lord." So faith came first, and in this way we were also enriched with the knowledge of Christ. I think this is what was said to some: "For if you do not believe, neither will you understand." That a clear understanding of the mystery of Christ wins a share in eternal life for those worthy to receive it, the Son himself will assure us, when he says to his Father and God in heaven, "And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God,

and Jesus Christ, whom you have sent." "And it shall be in that day, says the Lord, that I will hear the heaven, and the heaven will hear the earth, and the earth will hear the grain and the wine and the oil, and they will hear Jezreel."

Here again he gives the name "day" to the time suited to the calling, for this is the custom of the divinely inspired Scripture. He hints in a riddling way that Israel too, made radiant by faith in Christ, will in due time share in an abundance of every good and of the gifts that come from above and from God. He says that there will be an abundance of rain, since he will consent to it; I think that is what "I will hear the heaven" means. He also says that on the earth below the fruits most useful and necessary to us will be produced. For without God and the will from above, heaven would never rain on those on earth, nor would the earth bring forth its own fruit in season. Knowing this, the prophet Jeremiah pleaded, saying, "Is there among the idols of the nations one that sends rain? And if the heaven gives its fullness, are you not God? And we will wait for you, for you have made all these things." For when the Creator consents, as I said, and opens his hand to those on earth, heaven will be the giver of rain, and the earth will be at once mother and nurse of the fruits we need. "I will hear the heaven," then, he says, meaning, "I will consent to send down rains on those on the earth." When this has happened, the earth too will hear the grain, the wine and the oil. That is, it will yield abundant fruit to those who live on it, and nothing necessary for sustaining life will be lacking.

That is the historical meaning. But from bodily things, as from a most vivid image, we must ascend to spiritual ones. As long as Israel was still unbridled, disobedient and fighting against God — Israel, the vineyard of the Lord of hosts, "the beloved new planting" — God commanded the clouds not to rain upon it. By the clouds we must understand the holy rational powers above and in heaven, through whom the word of consolation comes to us, clearly from God. For they are ministering spirits, as the blessed Paul says, running to and fro between heaven and earth and "sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation." But the time of punishment has passed. The one who once killed the Lord has been saved through faith and at last received in righteousness and in judgment and in mercy and compassion, and so God, who richly distributes all things to all, has sent down on him the blessings from above. For he commanded the clouds to send down the rain, I mean consolation for the mind and heart. But he also taught that even the nature of the angels has nothing of its own and receives all its riches from God, when he said, "I will hear the heaven." That is, I will fill heaven with what comes from me — that is, those who are in heaven, the rational and holy powers — so that they too are able to console those who have received mercy. And then the earth will surely hear the grain and the wine and the oil, meaning that those on earth will bear the fruit of hope in life, gladness and cheerfulness. Grain is a type of life, wine of gladness, and oil of cheerfulness and well-being. For in those who have believed there is a good hope, firm and well grounded. A person turns away from wickedness, longs for every good, and bows his neck under the Saviour's yoke. He is nourished by a good, unambiguous and wholly true hope of the life to come, so that he may rejoice together with the other saints and have a most cheerful heart. For the prophet Isaiah said somewhere about the saints, "And everlasting gladness shall be upon their head; for upon their head shall be praise and exultation, and gladness shall overtake them; pain and grief and groaning have fled away." So in the hope of life, cheerfulness and gladness, the earth — that is, the people who live on the earth — will surely obey the consolations from above, that is, the spiritual rains. And the fruit of the saints' life will be for the glory of Christ: "For one died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and was raised for them." This he has shown by saying, "and they will hear Jezreel." For it is to him, as I said, that we shall bear fruit, since we owe him our very life. It has been said many times that Jezreel is interpreted "seed of God," and this is the Son, since he was begotten from God the Father by nature and in a way beyond words, even if the matter is expressed in bodily terms.
"And I will sow her for myself in the land, and I will have mercy on Not-Pitied, and I will say to Not-My-People, 'You are my people,' and he will say, 'You are the Lord my God.'"

Here again you will understand "for myself" in two ways. I will make her, he says, flourishing and fruitful, as it were. He clearly means the synagogue of the Jews, which will no longer carry out the law that I do not want, nor choose to cling tenaciously to the types, but will choose to do what is most dear and pleasing to God and is held to be good. So I will sow her for myself, for she will receive my seed. By this we are to understand the decrees of the gospel, and no longer the seed sown through Moses, as in the beginning, for in former times she was cultivated by means of types. Or you may take "for myself" in another way. I myself will do the work of caring for her, he says, and I will sow her like rich, well-ploughed land, not through anyone else but by myself. For God the Father has spoken to us in the Son, though to those of old he had spoken through holy prophets "in many parts and in many ways." The Saviour himself also likens the countless multitude of believers to crops in a field. Indeed, he said to the holy apostles, "Do you not say, 'There are still four months, and then the harvest comes'? Look, I tell you, lift up your eyes and see the fields, for they are already white for harvest. The reaper receives wages and gathers fruit for eternal life." And again elsewhere: "The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. Therefore pray the Lord of the harvest to send out workers into his harvest." So when our Saviour Jesus Christ sent down on us the spiritual rain, we became "a desirable land," as the prophet says. For he sowed us for himself, and Israel came to be called "God's field." He will have mercy on Not-Pitied, and the one once called Not-My-People he will call "people." And Israel too, leaving behind the ancient error, will come to know the true God and will say, "You are my God," though in former times, out of boundless madness, they cried out, "We know that God has spoken to Moses; but as for this man, we do not know where he comes from." So because they did not know the Son, they did not know the Father either. The Saviour himself will testify to this when he says, "If you knew me, you would know my Father also." But when they were called to knowledge and confessed the Son, they then beheld the Father through him and in him. For it is true, as the wise John says, that "whoever denies the Son does not have the Father either; but whoever confesses the Son confesses the Father also."
And the Lord said to me, “Go again, and love a woman who loves evil and is an adulteress, just as God loves the children of Israel, while they look to other gods and love cakes with raisins.”

What the matter is this time, or what the mystery, we must learn. I think we ought to investigate such things carefully and examine them in fine detail. After the first woman, the lewd and wanton one, another woman is assigned to the prophet, one guilty of adultery. And what is the reason? Before our Saviour came, the multitude of the Jews went rather carelessly and very readily into error. They worshipped the golden heifers, and bowed down and sacrificed to Baal, that is, Baal of Peor. So they might be likened to a harlot, and very fittingly, since they lay open, as it were, to every evil and unclean spirit that wished to satisfy its own pleasures. For they took up the objects of worship of the neighbouring nations that shared their land, each as he fancied, impiously and without examination. But since she went so readily into apostasy, she was justly punished: she was sent into captivity and fell beneath the feet of her enemies. Yet God made it plain to the prophet that at the time of the day of Jezreel, the truly great day, they would go up out of the land, that is, they would run away from the country of the foreigners. Once more this was a riddling way of showing that they would cease to be strangers and sojourners, or rather captives of war, living in a foreign land without freedom. For the Saviour proclaimed “release to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind,” in the words of the prophet. He also clearly made known that they would be received through faith in mercy and compassion, and would be called the people of God, and indeed “those who have received mercy.” For after the Saviour came, suffered on the cross and returned to life from the dead, the remnant was saved, since no small number of the [?] believed. “…already white for harvest; and the reaper receives wages and gathers fruit for eternal life.” And again elsewhere: “The harvest is plentiful, but the labourers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers into his harvest.” So when our Saviour Jesus Christ sent down the spiritual rain upon us, we became “a desirable land,” in the words of the prophet. For he sowed us for himself, and Israel has been called “God’s field.” He will have mercy on Not-Pitied, and will call the one that was once Not-My-People his people. And Israel too will give up its ancient error and acknowledge the true God, and say, “You are my God,” though once, in its boundless madness, it cried out, “We know that God has spoken to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he comes from.” So, not knowing the Son, they did not know the Father himself either. The Saviour himself bears witness to this when he says, “If you knew me, you would know my Father also.” But since they have been called to knowledge and have confessed the Son, from now on they have beheld the Father through him and in him. For it is true, as the wise John says: “Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father either; whoever confesses the Son confesses the Father also.”
And the Lord said to me, “Go again, and love a woman who loves evil and is an adulteress, just as God loves the children of Israel, while they look to other gods and love cakes with raisins.”

What the matter is this time, or what the mystery, we must learn. I think we ought to investigate such things carefully and [?] from Israel too. But the disobedient multitude again stayed behind, and it should be likened to an adulteress. It did not choose the Bridegroom from heaven, and it rejected the one who wooed it in faith. Instead it gave its mind over, as it were, to adulterers, the scribes and Pharisees: “For they taught as teachings the commandments of men.” The prophet lived with the harlot as a type of God, who bore with Israel’s fornication, punishing it in due measure so that it might turn back, and bringing it back to knowledge. In the same way, I think, the mystery is again elegantly given shape for us in the present passage. As a type of God, the prophet takes in the adulteress who loves evil things. He cherishes her, as it were, nourishing her richly with promises and good hopes, and he does not let her fall into despair. That the whole mystery lies in these things God showed when he said to the prophet: “Love the adulteress who loves evil things, just as God loves the children of Israel; and they look to other gods and love cakes with raisins.” For although, he says, they chose to disobey, gave their love to falsely named gods and wished to do what pleased those gods, God loves them out of his innate goodness, he “who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.” The Word of God also gives us in some way to understand that even at the time of his coming there were perhaps still many among the Jews who wavered between the two. They were neither purely devoted to the commandments given through Moses nor wholly freed from the filth of error, but rather looked to other gods as well. To these gods they also offered cakes with raisins, perhaps sacrificial cakes and honey-cakes. For they brought such cakes to the demons as sacrifices, as experience bears witness.

So I hired her for myself for fifteen pieces of silver, a homer of barley and a nebel of wine. And I said to her, “You shall wait for me many days; you shall not play the harlot or belong to another man, and I too will be yours.”

So the prophet hires the woman and settles her at home. He orders her to refrain from her habitual wickedness and to cease from the defilements of adultery. And he promises that if she chooses to be chaste and resolves to look to him alone, he too will be hers, that is, he will take her to himself in marriage and become one with her: “For the two,” it says, “shall become one flesh.” And what is the riddle? After Christ returned to heaven, God settles the multitude of the Jews, disobedient and Lord-slaying, adulterous and profane, without a husband. But he promises to join it to himself in due time, provided it no longer plays the harlot, that is, does not go back to choosing to honour other gods. Evidently the multitude of the Gentiles has been brought in first, for those from Israel have been placed at the back, that is, as an afterthought, behind and in the last times. Notice that no marital union at all took place between the prophet and the wicked adulteress. There was only a promise of it after many days, if she did not again belong to another man, that is, if she abstained from the charges and defilements of spiritual fornication. For, as I said, in due time the Bridegroom from heaven will receive the adulterous multitude, provided it has not served idols. After the Saviour’s cross, Israel has been devoted only to the laws given through Moses. It has kept them very feebly indeed and carelessly, but it has not turned aside to honour the false worship of demons. But what is the manner of life of the adulteress who waits for union with the prophet in due time? And what were her wages? “Fifteen pieces of silver,” it says, “a homer of barley and a nebel of wine.” For Israel has spent the time until its final calling feeding on a counterfeit word and heeding the mythical, truly old-wives’ teachings of its own leaders. Its life has become fit for beasts, and its mind is sunk in drunkenness and darkness. The silver would be a very clear type of the teaching word. So it is said, “Your silver is counterfeit,” and in the Saviour’s words he justly rebukes the wicked and lazy servant, saying, “You ought to have put my silver with the bankers.” So you will take the silver to mean the word of the teachers.

But if someone chooses to apply it to the law of Moses itself, he will say that the number is fifteen because the law is at once perfect and imperfect. It is perfect if understood spiritually, for it tells us the mystery of Christ. It is imperfect, on the other hand, if the mind of those under instruction goes no further than the letter. For the coarseness of the historical sense stands, as it were, at half of knowledge. The number ten is a symbol of perfection, being perfect in every way, as in “Be over ten cities” and “To one he gave ten talents.” What is not perfect would be meant by five, for, as I said, it is half of ten. Or you may approach what has been said in another way. The number fifteen contains seven and also eight. In the divinely inspired Scripture, seven always signifies in some way the whole period of the law up to the holy prophets, because of the sabbath rest on the seventh day. Eight, in turn, signifies the period of the new covenant, in which the resurrection of our Saviour Jesus Christ took place, on the eighth day. And this, I think, is what the riddling saying means: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight.” That is, let the law and the prophets after it, who honour the sabbath rest on the seventh day, have a place with you. And let the eight have one too, that is, the apostles and evangelists who came after the Saviour’s day of resurrection. This also agrees with what is indicated indirectly by the voice of the prophet: “And seven shepherds shall be raised against him, and eight bites of men.” For when our Saviour Christ shone upon us, the proclamations of the law and the prophets, together with the apostolic teaching, rose up, in a sense, against Satan, who had crippled us. Through these he was in a sense bitten and despoiled. And, in the Saviour’s words, his goods were plundered, since those who had once gone astray left their slavery under him and came to know the one who is by nature and truly God and Lord of all. So “shepherds” rose up against him [?] of the coming, together with those after the eighth day, calling those who had gone astray to salvation through the writings of the law and the new writings. So, as I said, Israel has gone on feeding on the counterfeit words of its own teachers, or on the bare letter of the law, though the law also contains the things of the eighth, that is, the mysteries of Christ. That its life is fit for beasts and has turned to fleshly things alone would be very well indicated by the barley given to the adulteress as food. That food is fit for beasts, and the wine would be a sign of drunkenness. It was said to them, “You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed look but never see.” These are the afflictions of the drunk and the failings of those sick from drinking: to look without seeing, and to hear without being able to understand anything, and to have a mind thickened, as it were, and filled with hardness.

For the children of Israel shall wait many days without king or ruler, without sacrifice or altar, without priesthood or manifestations. And afterward the children of Israel shall return and seek the Lord their God and David their king, and they shall be amazed at the Lord and at his good things in the last days.

From here on the meaning is clear and beyond dispute, at least in these words: the adulteress was taken in and was to stay at home many days until the prophet should be hers. That is how it is written. What was done foreshadowed what was to befall the adulterous synagogue of the Jews in due time. For our Lord Jesus Christ willingly endured the cross for the salvation of all, after those of Israel had behaved outrageously toward him. Then indeed their land was laid waste, and they were scattered as it were to every wind. To this day they are unable to practise the law, since the temple in Jerusalem has been burned, the altar removed, sacrifice abolished, the priesthood left idle, and the manifestations are no longer seen. For when there is no high priest robed in priestly fashion according to the law, how could the manifestations still be seen? The lover of learning perhaps knows what the manifestations are thought to be, but it is not unprofitable to recall it briefly.

When the God of all commanded the adornments of the high priest to be made, he said to holy Moses, “And you shall make an oracle of judgment, woven work, a span long and a span wide; it shall be square.” Then he commanded that twelve stones be skilfully and artfully woven into the work, in the name of the tribes, and two others between the rest, named Manifestation and Truth. This oracle of judgment then hung from the ephod by golden chains and lay upon the high priest’s breast, and the Manifestation and the Truth were a type of Emmanuel. For he has proclaimed to us everything he heard from the Father. He has made manifest the will of the one who begot him and has shown plainly the way of salvation. And how could anyone doubt that he is also the Truth, when he himself clearly says, “I am the truth”? This is also why it hung upon the very heart of the high priest. The type all but shouted, crying out openly that the priestly race will keep in mind and heart the Saviour and Redeemer of all, the Truth and the Manifestation. Or else it cried out that those who perform the sacred rites must by every necessity always remember Christ and carry him dwelling within them through the Spirit. And his house is a pure mind and a cleansed heart. “So the children of Israel shall wait many days,” it says, “without king or ruler,” that is, without a king and without anyone set over them. For those of the tribe of Judah will not reign, nor will the rulers according to the law, that is, the priests, preside. Nor, it says, will there be altar or sacrifice, priesthood or manifestations. Yet Israel will not remain in this state forever, nor will it be utterly cast off. For in due time it will be called and will return through faith. It will acknowledge the God of all, and with him David, that is, Christ, who is of the seed of David according to the flesh, the King and Lord of all. Then indeed they will be astonished at the greatness of his generosity and the boundless grace of his gentleness. For they will share in the hope prepared for the saints, and, mingled with the flocks of believers, they will graze “in good pasture and in a rich place.” The time for such splendid and admirable grace for them is the last, in the final times, and in Christ. Through him and with him be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.
BY THE SAME AUTHOR, ON THE SAME PROPHET HOSEA: VOLUME THREE.

Hear the word of the Lord, you children of Israel, for the Lord has a case against those who dwell in the land, because there is no truth, no mercy, no knowledge of God in the land. Cursing and lying and murder and theft and adultery have spread over the land, and they mingle blood with blood.

If we want to make the meaning of this passage clear, we have to go back, as it were, to what came at the beginning and chew over again the whole purpose of the prophecy. So, gathering it up as briefly as I can, I say this. "The beginning of the word of the Lord came through Hosea." When we explained those words, we rightly said that the words from God came to the blessed prophet Hosea while God was, so to speak, initiating him into the mysteries and foretelling what was to come through both types and words. So Gomer was taken at the beginning, and she bore Not-My-People and Not-Pitied. Then after her a second woman was taken, an adulteress and a wicked one, and the prophet, as I said, was instructed carefully and precisely about the meaning of each of these. Having thus gathered within himself a sufficient grasp of the force of the mystery, he now begins to foretell the future to those of Israel's blood. He makes plain the cause of the disaster that was all but upon them, and he shows very clearly the things over which God had been grieved, so that those being punished might know that they suffered justly whatever it might befall them to suffer. They were about to be captured by enemies and then be exposed to the mockery of those who had held the highest opinion of them and had thought Israel the hardest of all nations to conquer. He did not want them to think that the hand that defended and saved them had grown weak. He wanted them rather to repent and choose to turn back to better ways, realizing that in their ignorance they had offended the One who knows how to save, and that this was why they had fallen under divine wrath. So he had to announce the charges to them even before the things they were to expect, and he says: Hear the word of the Lord, you children of Israel, for the Lord has a case against those who dwell in the land. God enters into judgment with human beings by convicting them, not by being judged, and by setting before those who have acted impiously toward him the charges laid bare. This is perhaps in line with what is sung in the Psalms: "I will rebuke you and set your lawless deeds before your face." He does this so that they may not claim that wrath has been brought on them for nothing, but may see it as coming like a debt [?] that falls due, befalling of necessity those who make a habit of the gravest offenses. And what does the one who enters into judgment, that is, the one who convicts, say? There is no truth, no mercy, no knowledge of God in the land. To say that there is no truth would quite reasonably suggest that at that time slander, perjury, deceit and guile, the most shameful of all evils, were widespread among everyone. To say that there is no mercy would indicate that they had no love for one another and no compassion, that they were unbending and hard, and that their minds had grown callous. And he will make clear that they were lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, wholly devoted to the falsely named gods, by saying further that there is no knowledge of God in the land. Besides, it may fittingly be said of people caught up in such dreadful outrages that in a sense they seem not even to know God, if indeed, thinking rightly, we say that it is those who follow his divine will who know him. To these he adds that cursing and lying and murder and theft and adultery have spread over the land, and they mingle blood with blood. Do you hear how the people in question have reached the limit of every evil and gone beyond even unholy deeds, leaving none of the most outrageous things untried? And what is even more astonishing, he says, they mingle blood with blood. This too would be a clear sign that the wicked allowed themselves no respite, and that those who did these things never came to repent of what they had dared. Their sin stretched on, as it were, continuously and without a break.

So much for the more obvious explanation. But the blessed prophet seems again to give us a more mystical account, accusing Israel of its drunken outrages against Christ and its murders of him and of the saints. For the Lord has a case against those who dwell in the land. Why, and on what grounds? Our Lord Jesus Christ appeared to us and was sent, as he himself says, "to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." He came to enlighten those in darkness with the torch of the Spirit, to free them from the shadow of the law and lead them into the ways of true worship, and to justify by faith those caught in sins and join them through himself to God the Father. But the people of Israel did not see fit to think rightly. They cast out the one who had come from heaven for these purposes. They rejected him. They would not keep among them the truth, the mercy, the knowledge of God the Father. That Christ is truth and mercy needs, I think, no long proof, since the divinely inspired Scripture is enough for this, calling Christ mercy and truth again and again. That he is also the knowledge of God can be learned with no effort at all, since he cried out most clearly and plainly, "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father." So the Lord, he says, has a case against those who dwell in the land, clearly the land of the Jews, because truth and mercy and the knowledge of the Father are not among them. He enters into judgment, then, with those who do not have these things. But those who have embraced the faith have escaped being judged with him, or rather by him. This becomes clear when Christ says again, "Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes in me has eternal life and does not come into judgment."

What, then, has spread over the land? Cursing and lying and murder and theft and adultery; and they mingle blood with blood. And what is the cursing? Slander and insult. The crowds of the Hebrews never stopped insulting Jesus and assailing him with an unguarded, unbridled tongue, calling him now a Samaritan, now a drunkard, and saying he was born of fornication, since they had decided among themselves that the holy Virgin had committed adultery. That, then, is the cursing. They also lied against his glory, saying that he had a demon and ascribing his divine signs to the powers of Beelzebul. That they would be convicted of harboring murderous intent against him can be seen from the fact that they even led him to the very brow of the hill to throw him down headlong. Nor do the charges stop there. They also set a high value on theft, for they hired the traitor Judas against him, a man greedy for gain and a thief through and through. And the Pharisees became like wicked adulterers of the synagogue of the Jews. They drove away from her the Bridegroom from heaven, that is, Christ, and they committed fornication with her, persuading her to serve their own pleasures. They also mingled blood upon blood. How, or in what way? Having killed the holy prophets, they added to them the very Master of the prophets. So the blessed Stephen in the Acts of the Apostles justly reproaches them, saying, "Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? They killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, whose betrayers and murderers you have now become." And the Savior too said to the Pharisees, "Fill up, then, the measure of your fathers."

Therefore the land shall mourn and be diminished, with all who dwell in it, with the wild beasts of the field and the creeping things of the earth and the birds of the sky, and the fish of the sea shall fail, so that no one may go to law and no one may reprove.

He means that they have lived a life so hateful to God and so grievous, impious and unbridled, and have thought and done what is unlawful, behaving outrageously toward God. For this reason, as it were, [?] of the land. For the land will be turned wild. It will change its form and wear a joyless face, with its cities burned, its houses shaken down and its fields cut down. Its inhabitants will share the land's condition, lamenting and wailing with it. For they too will mourn, that is, they will be very far from all cheerfulness and prosperity. And who are the inhabitants? Beasts and creeping things, and flying creatures as well. If we understand rightly, we will surely not suppose that the prophetic word has cried out to us about wild beasts, or creeping things, or birds. To take it that way is utterly simple-minded and full of folly. Rather, since we have learned to think rightly, we hold that the ways of the Jews are being likened to the creatures just mentioned. By the beasts the word would suggest the most powerful, those well able to terrify others: the savage and aggressive, who are used to committing murder and are extremely fierce. By the creeping things it suggests those thoroughly practiced in bitterness of character, who have already reached the limit of all wickedness. So the wise John too rebuked the most depraved crowd of Pharisees and scribes, crying out, "Serpents, brood of vipers!" By the birds you will rightly understand those who are readily stirred to fly off into apostasy from God, or those sick with accursed arrogance, who are used to being borne aloft and thinking high thoughts. And he seems to call fish those who are rabble and herd-like, drowned in the cares of life and with minds, as it were, under water: the voiceless and utterly irrational, for the fish is the most voiceless of creatures. In another way the fish are also those who, as it were, swallow up the weaker, for among fish devouring one another is held in the highest honor. So the land, he says, will mourn together with its inhabitants. And what is the reason for this? So that no one may go to law and no one may reprove. Since cursing, lying, theft and murder and adultery have spread over the land, and they mingle blood with blood, the land will mourn, and from then on lying, deceit and slander will cease. Lamenting over what has befallen them beyond all expectation and weeping over the disaster at hand, they will refrain from such offenses, even against their will. For going to law and reproving would be nothing else, I think, than accusing and condemning people, that is, bearing false witness. Another of the holy prophets of Israel's blood also cried out to us about this, saying, "Woe is me, my soul, for the godly man has perished from the earth, and there is none among men who does right. All go to law for blood; each afflicts his neighbor with affliction."

That, then, is the historical sense. Now, directing the word of the prophecy toward its innermost meaning, we say this. In the land of the Jews, that is, among the Jews themselves, there is "no truth, no mercy, no knowledge of God," and we have said that these are what Emmanuel is and is called. Instead, cursing and lying have prevailed, theft has been prized, and they mingle blood with blood, for having killed the prophets, as I said, they also killed Jesus himself. So from now on the land will mourn together with its inhabitants, set on fire by the hands of the Romans. And these things will happen, he says, so that no one may go to law or reprove. This plainly accuses the Jews of having impiously brought Christ to trial and convicted him, that is, of having borne false witness against him. For the leaders brought him to Pilate, pressing their case and accusing him.
