Some came forward and testified against him, and all but dared to convict him, the wretches telling lies: at one point that he was perverting the people, at another, "We heard him say that in three days he would destroy the temple of God and raise it again." So, he says, lawsuit will be done away with, and reproof, that is, false testimony, and untrue verdict, since there will be no king or ruler accustomed to judge. For this reason, I think, the prophetic word likens the peoples of the Jews to the animals that have no king: beasts, I mean, and creeping things and birds and fish. So too the blessed prophet Habakkuk said somewhere to the God of all, "Why do you look upon the scornful? Will you keep silent while the ungodly swallows up the righteous? Will you make men like the fish of the sea, and like creeping things that have no leader?"
But my people are like a priest who is spoken against, and he shall grow weak for days, and the prophet too shall grow weak with you.

Notice, please, how the blessed prophet presents in a different way what was said to him by God. He had plainly heard, "The children of Israel shall remain many days without king or ruler, without sacrifice or altar, without priesthood or manifestations." But as if he himself foresaw that his hearers were quick to give unbridled rein to their anger, he reproves them with restraint and veils his words in a measured obscurity. He subtly hints that they will spend long times without leaders or anyone to reign over them and will remain without instruction, by likening them to the animals that have no king. And he indicates that they will also be thrust out from sacrifices and from the ministry of holy things by saying that they have become equal to those priests who are spoken against. And who might these be? That is, who is the priest who is spoken against? The one who has a blemish and a bodily infirmity, and for this reason is barred from ministry. Some were sent away from the priesthood because of a leg, or an affliction of the eyes, or a broken foot, or for some other cause, even though they were born of the tribe and blood of Levi, for so the law given through Moses ordained. So, he says, will my people be. Although it is holy because of the fathers and has been deemed worthy to offer sacrifice, it will sit outside the holy tabernacle, outside the ministry and the holy things. It will not offer sacrifices, nor send up a fragrant aroma to God, for it has fallen gravely sick with an affliction of the mind. Its heart is maimed, and it has justly been sent away and become hateful. And he has made known that it will also befall Israel that its prophets fall silent, by saying And the prophet too shall grow weak with you. This is fully in line with what God said to the blessed Ezekiel: "I will bind your tongue and you shall be mute, and you shall not be to them a man who corrects them," that is, who reproves them, "for it is a rebellious house." All this will happen because of their impiety toward Christ and their crimes against the prophets. Yet he says that Israel will not grow weak forever, but for days, for a time of salvation and of return through faith has been kept in store for it.

I have likened your mother to night; my people have become like one who has no knowledge. Because you have rejected knowledge, I too will reject you from serving me as priest; and since you have forgotten the law of your God, I too will forget your children.

These words, then, are addressed to the unrestrained and unholy multitude of the Jews. He calls the Synagogue its mother, just as the Church is the mother of those justified in Christ. He rightly likens the Synagogue of the Jews to lightlessness and darkness. That is why the most wise Paul says so well about himself and those made radiant by faith, "We are not of night or of darkness, but sons of light and of day." And my people, he says, are like those who have no knowledge, although they had been enriched with the guidance of the law. They were called to the knowledge of the One who is truly God, they were given full assurance through miracles, and nothing at all was lacking of the things that can enlighten those in darkness and are fully able to implant admirable knowledge in the more teachable. But since, he says, you have rejected knowledge, that is, Christ, through whom and in whom the Father is both approachable and known, you will from now on be thrust out from being holy and from offering sacrifices, as one profane. And since you have slipped into forgetting the divine laws, neither understanding the writings of Moses spiritually nor applying a keen and receptive mind to the teachings given through Christ, I too will, as it were, fall into forgetfulness of your children. That is, I will no longer remember them so as to count them worthy of mercy and care, for those whom God sees fit to remember are the ones to whom he grants his own loving-kindness. Israel also forgot the divine law and rejected knowledge in another way, by worshiping idols. In proportion to their multitude, so they sinned against me; I will turn their glory into dishonor.

The divine and ineffable nature is the source and origin of all gentleness, and is goodness itself. Yet it does not put up with offenders forever, but inflicts fitting penalties on those who rush into sin without restraint. He insists, then, that Israel has sunk to such depravity that its madness is no longer bearable, and its sins appear, as it were, equal in number to the people themselves. For they were "as the stars of heaven in multitude and as the sand by the shore of the sea," as it is written, and he said that their offenses fell nothing short of their numbers. This, I think, is the meaning of In proportion to their multitude, so they sinned against me. And since they slid into such wretchedness and folly and did not stop offending God, I will turn their glory into dishonor. That is, they will be put to shame over the very thing on which they had resolved to pride themselves. How, or in what way? They will lose their boast in their great numbers, as war consumes not only the fighting men but every other age as well, for houses and cities will be left empty of men. Over this very thing the prophet Jeremiah lamented Judea, saying, "How the city once full of people sits alone! She who ruled among the provinces has become subject to tribute."

It can be taken in another sense as well. When we offend God by doing what is unlawful, we will lie very far from all good repute. Sometimes we even boast and raise our brows high over the very things we ought to be ashamed of, so that it may justly be said of us too, "whose glory is in their shame." So you may take the saying I will turn their glory into dishonor in this sense as well. For how can anyone doubt that some are given up "to a debased mind, to do what is not fitting," when the blessed Paul has said so plainly?
They will eat the sins of my people, and in their iniquities they will take up their souls. And it shall be: as the people, so the priest.

Having set out the causes of the wrath against the multitude, he turns his discourse to the priestly order. And I think the words just quoted, "I will turn their glory into dishonor," would fit this too. The glory of the Synagogue of the Jews was its renowned priesthood and the preeminent and holy race within it, that is, the Levitical race. Some from the tribe of Judah were kings, but human affairs ranked second to the priesthood and far below it. The glory of the Synagogue of the Jews, then, is the holy and chosen race. So it will be clothed in dishonor, he says, and will pass into unsightliness. And for what reason? Because they neglected what most befitted them and were carried off into apostasy. They did not keep their own office. They did not know the proper conduct of the priesthood. They did not understand that they will eat the sins of my people, and in their iniquities they will take up their souls.

But since the saying is very obscure, come, let us once again explain as best we can how it ought to be understood. A male goat was slaughtered for sin, and for this reason the victim was also called "sin." The priests serving at the time brought the goat to the altar and offered up the entrails and the fat, but ate the rest themselves, as the divine law prescribed. The priest is thus taken to be a kind of mediator between God and human beings. He receives the people's offerings and shares them with the altar, as it is written, and he, as it were, offers himself in sacrifice for the people's offenses, just as our Lord Jesus Christ did. To show that what I say is true, I will quote the actual law concerning the goat. It runs thus: "And Moses searched carefully for the goat of the sin offering, and behold, it had been burned up. And Moses was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar, the sons of Aaron who were left, saying, 'Why did you not eat the sin offering in a holy place? Since it is most holy, he has given it to you to eat, so that you may take away the sin of the congregation and make atonement for them before the Lord.'" Do you see how those who stand at the divine altar act as mediators by eating what is offered for sins? With the purest prayers they lull to rest the wrath against sinners, and all but consecrate their own souls to God as a fragrant aroma on behalf of the people's offenses. This is just what the godly Aaron did when the people were beginning to be struck down. For it is written: having seized the censer and put incense on it, "he stood," it says, "between the dead and the living, and the plague ceased." In the same way the blessed Moses acted as mediator and entreated God when the Israelites had made the calf in the wilderness. He, as it were, put himself under the penalty, pleading and saying, "If you will forgive them their sin, forgive it; but if not, blot me also out of this book that you have written."

They shall eat, then, the sins of my people, that is, the sacrifices brought for sins. And "in their iniquities," that is, at the time of their iniquity (clearly the iniquity of those of Israel, that is, of the people), they themselves "will take their own souls," meaning, they will bring them to God. For the divinely inspired Scripture uses the word in this sense: whatever was brought to God and made ready for sacrifice was said to be "taken." And the word is used above all in this sense, as I said just now. Thus in Numbers, when he was laying down the laws concerning the red heifer, God said to Moses, the revealer of sacred things: "This is the ordinance of the law which the Lord commanded, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel, and let them take to you a red heifer without blemish." Do you hear "let them take"? That is, let them bring, or let them offer. And again, concerning the leper who is about to be cleansed, he says this: "And the priest shall go out of the camp, and the priest shall look, and behold, the plague of leprosy is healed in the leper. And the priest shall give orders, and they shall take for the one who has been cleansed two live clean birds." So when it says "they shall take" with reference to the priests as well, the word may reasonably be understood as meaning "they shall offer." At the time of the iniquities, then (the people's, obviously), they themselves will take, that is, they will offer their own souls to God as a sacrifice and a spiritual fragrance, by living rightly, of course, leading a life fully in keeping with the law, and striving as hard as they can to think and do what befits priests. For such a person is able to save peoples even when they have offended God and broken the law. But those who were appointed for this, he says, slid down along with the rest. For this reason the sacred rites will justly cease, the chosen and honored race will come to an end, and it will be "as the people, so the priest." For there will no longer be any difference between people and priest. And this, then, was the meaning of "I will turn their glory into dishonor."
And I will punish him for his ways, and I will repay him for his schemes.

By "ways" he seems to mean conduct in deeds, and by "schemes" the failings that spring from wicked thoughts. Since, then, he says, he has not walked rightly but has turned aside from the straight road and chosen, as it were, the path of every impiety, and has planned the most shameful and outrageous things of all, dishonoring the God of the universe and himself turning aside to the worship of idols, "I will punish him," that is, I will bring on him a penalty that matches his offenses. That those who desert the love of God will, in every way and without fail, fall into every evil, how can anyone doubt? For such a person will neither travel a straight and blameless path nor ever take wise counsel, since he does not have the divine wisdom and power to help him.
And they shall eat, and shall not be satisfied; they have committed fornication, and shall not be set right.

Again he has kept a remnant for those of Israel's blood. For he makes it plain that the priests' portion will not vanish altogether, when he says that they will eat but will not be satisfied. Whether one thinks of those ancient deportations and captivities of Israel, or of the devastation of Judea by the hand of the Romans after Christ, one will find both Israel itself and the worship according to the law preserved in remnants. For when they were carried off at that time by Shalmaneser and Tiglath-pileser to the Assyrians and Medes, the few, the scanty survivors of Israel nonetheless brought the customary offerings to the priests, honoring them with whatever they had at hand, and did not abandon their customs entirely. In the same way, in the last war too (I mean the one under Caesar Augustus), when their land was laid waste, they were scattered to every wind and into every country and city; yet, still honoring the sacred and chosen race in some measure, they brought what they could. And they still do so, although the ancient sacrifices have been abolished, for now that they are outside Jerusalem it is unlawful for them to sacrifice any longer. "They will eat," then, he says, "and will not be satisfied," that is, they will receive little, and that with difficulty, and not enough to fill them. And this shows no less the overthrow of their ancient honor and the loss of their former good cheer. And since they have committed fornication, he says, "they will not be set right." For it is impossible, as I said, for those who desert God (and this, I think, is both the name and the reality of spiritual fornication) either to have the supply of divine goods to the full, that is, to be able to gather the food that comes from heaven and from above, or to be set right in their counsels or in their deeds. For God is the giver of every good to us, and the helm of the mind that is in us.
Because they have forsaken the Lord to keep fornication; and the heart of my people has received wine and strong drink.

Here he states the reasons why the sacred ministers will neither be filled with food nor be set right any longer. For since they too, he says, went away from the Lord, and the teachers slid down together with those they taught, those whose lot was to lead together with those under their hand and authority, for this reason they will justly fall under divine wrath and pay the penalty for their unceasing failings. For they have kept fornication, that is, they saw to it that error was preserved among those under their hand, when they ought rather to have cast it out from among them and wiped it out. For the vigilance of teachers consists in zealously removing from among the people whatever harms them, and in overthrowing without delay whatever is hateful to God. But if, not bearing to do this, they themselves allow the works of error to remain and, as it were, be preserved, or rather even promote them, contrary to their duty, then surely the mind of those under instruction will also take in something like wine and drunkenness. For from where, or how, could the disciples be sober and able to open the eye of the mind to the one who is truly and by nature God, if their instructors, the very people who should guide them toward what is profitable, further confirm them in the belief that they ought to go astray? And this, I think, is what was clearly said through another prophet: "The priests did not say, Where is the Lord? And those who handle my law did not know me, and the shepherds acted impiously against me, and the prophets prophesied by Baal." And again: "My sons and my sheep are no more; there is no longer a place for my tent, a place for my curtains. For the shepherds have acted foolishly and have not sought the Lord; therefore the whole flock did not understand, and they were scattered."
They inquired by signs, and by their rods they gave him answers.

He makes it plain in what way they have forsaken the Lord but kept fornication. For he shows the teacher to be a willing accomplice of those who go astray. Those who might be expected, or rather who were bound, to follow the divine laws and to bring those under their yoke to do the same, these, as I said, he clearly shows to be committing the offenses of error. For some people went to them, he says, wishing to learn perhaps what was to come, or about their own affairs, and in what times or circumstances they would find themselves. But they impiously persuaded those who came to them no longer to seek such things from God; instead "they inquired by signs," that is, they sought to learn from unclean spirits through certain signs and observations, just as Balaam once attempted to divine against those of Israel. For Balak son of Beor ordered him to do this. And he said, "Build me seven altars here, and slaughter for me seven calves and seven rams," and I will go to meet the omens. For either they watch the smoke rising from the sacrifices, to see where and how it shoots up on high, or the wretches examine the quiverings of the liver, or they busy themselves with the flights of birds. Augury, divination and such evils are the charges of an impiety that has reached its limit, and they belong in the lowest recesses of idolatry. "And by their rods they gave him answers." When those of Israel came to them, he says, eager to find out something about their own affairs, they answered them not only by signs but also by their rods. This is another kind of deception. The thing is rhabdomancy, perhaps an invention of Chaldean curiosity. For Nebuchadnezzar divined in this way concerning Jerusalem, as the inspired [?]. Chanting some secret spells over the rods, they made them fall under the workings of demons, and as they fell they watched which way they went, whether forward or backward, to the right or to the left; and so they gave those who came to them whatever answer seemed right. This is "by rods they gave answers." It is truly dreadful, then, when the instructors of others, who were able to bring them to what is pleasing to God, led them astray instead and, as the prophet says, "fixed madness in the house of the Lord." For by "madness" he means false divination. Those who are accustomed to doing this pretend not even to know any longer where they are. And some said that they were in a frenzy and possessed, as though filled with the divine. For they did not know that the heart of those who go astray is, as it were, a house and a cave of unclean spirits.

They have gone astray by a spirit of fornication, and have gone whoring away from their God. On the tops of the mountains they sacrificed, and on the hills they made offerings, under oak and poplar and shady tree, because the shelter is pleasant.

He teaches clearly that such things are not done without unclean and evil spirits. For every kind of wickedness comes from them, and there is nothing shameful that those who have chosen to do their will leave undone. "They have gone astray," then, he says, "by a spirit of fornication," and have gone as far as possible from God, being lovers of pleasure and making the works of idolatry an occasion for indulging the flesh. For they sacrificed on the hills and mountains they occupied, honoring the groveling nature of demons with earthly heights. Then, raising altars under oak and poplar, they brought libations to nymphs, perhaps paying honors to the hamadryads, as in the myths of the Greeks. For the Greek poets and men of learning say that the unclean demons, whom they named nymphs, love plants and trees, according to some notion of theirs, I do not know how. They liked, then, he says, to enjoy the shade and to luxuriate under the most flowery groves, and to praise this and say, "because the shelter is pleasant." So the lover of pleasure could not also be a lover of God. And Paul will bear witness, saying of some that they are "lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God." "Blessed, then, are those who mourn now," as the Savior says, and who strive as hard as they can to honor and love the endurance of hardship in profitable labors.

Therefore your daughters will play the harlot, and your brides will commit adultery. And I will not visit your daughters when they play the harlot, nor your brides when they commit adultery; for they themselves mingled with harlots and sacrificed with the initiated.

For since you think it admirable, he says, to luxuriate under a tree and in the shade, and you have made a pleasure of what grieves me, that is, accursed error and impurity, for this reason your daughters will play the harlot, and your brides, that is, your sons' wives, will be defiled in adultery. And even if these things happen, he says, I too will keep still and will not visit. By this he seems to foretell the harms that war will bring upon those who have sinned, and the things that follow upon captivity. For those who have once captured and conquered do whatever they please to their captives. They wield unbridled power and rush with unchecked impulses after anything at all that pleases them, neither taking any account of law nor bearing to consider what is reasonable or fitting. With minds hardened, as it were, and inclined strongly toward savagery, they think those who have fared so miserably deserve no mercy. So he has clearly foretold that the children of those who committed fornication will lie exposed to their enemies for outrage and shameful acts.

But if anyone prefers, he may also understand it in another way. For the God of the universe visits those whom he wishes to honor and love; and if he sees them drifting into carelessness and wanting to do what is not lawful, he rebukes them in due measure, persuading them to run back to what is better and needful for their good. Therefore the inspired Paul also says to those called to a commendable life: "If you endure discipline, God is dealing with you as with sons. For what son is there whom a father does not discipline?" And the most wise author of Proverbs testifies and says, "For whom the Lord loves he disciplines, and he scourges every son whom he receives." So those whom he disciplines he also counts worthy of his oversight, as being in every way good and beloved; but he does not look upon those who have gravely offended him at all, all but saying, "I do not know you." "For the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous," as it is written. So even if they sin, he says, "I will not visit," that is, I will take no thought for them at all, I will not turn them back to myself, I will count them worthy of nothing. For what reason? Because you yourselves, he says, who stand in the place of fathers, are so far from being willing to rebuke yourselves and your offspring, even if they take up the worst wickedness, that you mingle with harlots. For you have sacrificed together with the initiated.

By "harlots" he means specifically the priestesses of Baal-peor. Baal-peor is the one called Priapus. And women who honor so shameful an abomination are, by common consent, harlots. Again, by "the initiated" he means the initiates in the mysteries of Baal-peor. They were men who could not bear to be what they are, but went over instead to a womanish frame of mind, impiously effeminate in speech and manner. Some call such people womanish men and softlings. With women's shrieks and cymbals, and running about together with torches, they made a show of performing initiation rites, acting out the games of Baal-peor's shame. "They sacrificed," then, he says, "with the initiated," that is, they had been initiated into their rites, and together with men so utterly corrupted they brought sacrifices to Baal-peor.
And the people that understood became entangled with a harlot.

He turns the discourse to Judah, that is, to those of the tribe of Judah and Benjamin, who [?] and had the divine altar, for the temple was still standing. They claimed to keep the commandments of Moses and to have the understanding that comes through the law. But they too served "Astarte, the abomination of the Sidonians." They say that Astarte is the one whom the Greeks, I do not know why, call Aphrodite. Her statue stands naked, in the guise of a harlot, shamelessly baring to the eyes of all even the parts of the body that ought not to be seen. So, he says, it was not only Israel, sick as it was with the greatest folly, that "mingled with harlots and sacrificed with the initiated"; even "the people that understood," that is, the people that still pretended to preserve the understanding that comes from the law, became entangled with a harlot. For they worshiped Astarte, as I said. Solomon built her a sanctuary, granting the wishes of a lustful foreign woman.
But you, Israel, do not be ignorant; and Judah, do not go into Gilgal, and do not go up to the house of iniquity, and do not swear by the living Lord.

I have already said many times that the words of the prophets call the ten tribes in Samaria "Israel," while by "Judah and Benjamin" they sometimes mean the two tribes in Jerusalem, that is, the tribe of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin. The present passage, then, concerns both, and exposes the sickness of each multitude. See how he reproaches Israel as utterly without understanding and senseless, and for this reason an apostate as well, if indeed devotion to the worship of idols and estrangement from the love of God may reasonably be regarded as a charge of the utmost lack of understanding. Here, then, "do not be ignorant" means "do not be foolish, nor full of a lack of understanding that has reached its limit." Again, he shames those in Jerusalem too, that is, Judah, as a hypocrite and an impious offender, for walking on both sides, or rather for limping on both legs, as the prophet puts it. For Judah pretended to practice and love piety toward God, and it performed the sacrifices according to the law; but it was by no means free of a zeal to worship the demons themselves as well, if not very openly, then at least in a hidden and secret way. Thus the blessed prophet Ezekiel was commanded to dig through the wall, and then he saw all the idols of the house of Israel portrayed on the walls. And what does the God of the universe say to him? "Have you seen, son of man, what the elders of the house of Israel are doing here, each of them in his secret chamber? For they have said, The Lord has forsaken us; the Lord does not look upon the earth." The prophet says he also saw women sitting and weeping for Tammuz, who is Adonis in the Greek tongue. See, then, how even though they attended the divine temple and pretended to lay claim to the worship according to the law, they were secretly defiled, being divided between it and forms of worship that were strange, demonic and hateful to God. So you, Israel, who have turned aside completely, "do not be ignorant," he says, that is, abstain from ignorance, cease from so rash and profane a way of thinking, and receive the understanding that comes through the law and the prophets, that is, the understanding that comes through Christ and the gospel. "And Judah, do not go into Gilgal" (it is a city much given to idolatry), "and do not go up to the house of iniquity, and do not swear by the living Lord." For it is absurd to call God to witness in one's oaths and to have the living Lord on one's tongue, [?] worship. For Jeroboam set up the one heifer in Bethel and the other in Dan. He does not allow them, therefore, to make a show of piety toward God by naming the Lord while being carried off to outlandish false worship, going up to Gilgal and to the house of iniquity. He calls Bethel the house of iniquity. For what reason? Bethel means "house of God." But it became the house of an idol, so that in a way both the thing itself and its very name were wronged; for, as I said, the house of God became the house of an idol. And so he said somewhere through the voice of Jeremiah concerning the multitude of Israel: "Why has the beloved committed abomination in my house?" And the God of the universe might reasonably say of those of Judah and Benjamin: "This people draws near to me; with their lips they honor me, but their heart is far from me."
For as a heifer stung to frenzy, so Israel has run wild; now the Lord will pasture them like a lamb in a broad place.

One of the saints wisely leads us to the pursuit of what is profitable, saying: "Son, let not your heart envy sinners, but be in the fear of the Lord all day long." For how would anyone choose to emulate those whom he would condemn? The God of the universe says something of this kind to Judah: Do not let Israel's frenzy become an excuse for your own apostasy, nor its bolting from the herd, so to speak, like heifers. When a gadfly, or "ox-striker," settles on a heifer (this is a kind of gnat with an unbearable bite), it drives her away from the herd and sends her racing off wherever she happens to go. Or shall we not find that this is what happened to Israel? For she went away from Jerusalem and, leaving her own herdsman, that is, God, committed a terrible and accursed apostasy.

So do not emulate her, O Judah, he says. For even if Israel, in a frenzy like a heifer, went off into apostasy, the venture will not go unpunished. She will go away a captive and, leaving the land that bore her, will be pastured in the land of the Persians and Medes, no longer bold, unbridled, as it were, and straying from the herd (for such is always the way of a heifer stung to frenzy), but become like the gentlest of lambs. For the lot of captives is always lowly and fearful, never far from the expectation of ill-treatment, and weighed down by the greed of their masters. He calls the land of the Persians and Medes a "broad place," as if to say something like this: she will be pastured in a wide and boundless land and will pass through many countries, not always having the same master, but being moved on to the land of whoever takes her in. A human soul too might suffer this very thing when it neglects love for God. For it will be carried about toward anything at all that the demons love, captive, cowardly and feeble, and it will justly hear God saying, "Your apostasy will discipline you, and your wickedness will reprove you."

Ephraim, a partner of idols, has set stumbling blocks for himself; he has chosen the Canaanites. They have gone whoring wantonly; they have loved dishonor because of their insolence. You are a whirlwind in her wings, and they will be put to shame because of their altars.

The prophet is still speaking to Judah. As I said, Judah pretended to lay claim to the law and to hold piety toward God in no small esteem, but had secretly come round to thinking that the images of demons ought to be honored. So then, he says, Ephraim, that is, Israel, has admittedly become a partaker of idols. Israel is given this name from the tribe that held power among them, namely the tribe of Jeroboam, for he was from the hill country and tribe of Ephraim. Just as he calls the people in Jerusalem "Judah," keeping the name of the royal tribe, so too with Israel: when he names Ephraim, he takes the name from the ruling tribe. Ephraim, then, has partaken of idols, he says. For he worshiped the object of Egyptian reverence. That object was Apis, that is, a heifer. And he shared no less in the impiety and boundless madness of the Canaanites, who chose to cherish and worship that most shameful idol, Baal-Peor. But by doing this Ephraim set stumbling blocks for himself, for he offended the God who both defends and knows how to save. "He chose the Canaanites" means that he made the customs of the Canaanites desirable and worth adopting. These were neighbors of the land of the Jews, ungodly and idolaters. Besides all this, those of Israel, "committing fornication, committed fornication utterly." Clearly this means that because they pursued spiritual fornication beyond all measure and reason, the charges of their apostasy reached the very limit of shamefulness. They also "loved dishonor from their arrogance," that is, from the lofty boasts they once had in God and in the glory that came from him. So they truly became dishonored and cast down, pitiable and trampled underfoot, once they had slipped from their former pride. For they will no longer be called free. Instead they will go into insult and dishonor, and will be under harsh masters. "But even if," he says, "the most foolish multitude of Ephraim was carried away by all these things, you, Judah, became for it like a gust of wind in the wings of a bird." It is plain to everyone that flying creatures always fly faster when a violent wind pushes them and all but forces them along. So Israel ran aground when it turned to apostasy, but you became a gust of wind in its wings. How, or in what way? Israel saw you, who were still being schooled by the law, who sat beside the divine temple and offered the sacrifices the law prescribed, growing careless and falling away, and caught in the same offenses. So it made its flight from God all the swifter. But they will find that their altars bring them shame and become the cause of disgrace and dishonor.

The same holds for us. We seem to stand, and we ought to live well and blamelessly. When we are found sluggish and careless about this, or worse, when we choose like the others to set aside what pleases God, we wrong not only ourselves. We destroy others besides, and so we shall suffer a double punishment. We ought to be set before those who have gone astray, or who do not wish to live rightly, as an image and pattern of virtue, but instead we have become an occasion of stumbling. What then does Christ say? "Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him to have a great millstone hung around his neck and to be drowned in the depths of the sea."

Hear these things, you priests, and pay attention, house of Israel, and give ear, house of the king, for the judgment is against you. For you have become a snare to the watchtower, and like a net spread over Tabor, which those who hunt game have fixed in place.

He first accused Judah of having become a gust of wind to Israel, in the way we have just described. Now he turns his rebuke to the inventors of the deceit and error, who brought on the people the disease of senselessness. These were the falsely named priests, who were not of the blood of Levi but had purchased their priesthood and bought with money the right to serve idols. For it is written of Jeroboam that "whoever wished, he filled his hand, and he became a priest of the high places." So the word fittingly extends both to these officiants and to the house of the king, and Israel itself is included in the charges. The priests said and did whatever served to establish idolatry: they set up altars, offered libations and sacrifices, and widened the road of destruction for those they deceived. But the kings were the inventors of the error. Therefore he says to them: "You have become a snare to the watchtower." By "watchtower" he means the multitude that was watched over both by the priests, if indeed they really were priests, and by the rulers themselves. For these oversee their subjects. Or else the rulers are the ones their subjects look to, and they turn their subjects toward whatever seems good to those in power, since those under the yoke follow the wishes of their leaders. "You have become, then," he says, "like a snare to the multitude you oversee," or perhaps, "to the multitude that looks to you." "And you have become like a net spread over Tabor." This is a most conspicuous mountain in Galilee, which offers abundant and plentiful hunting of beasts and birds, because it rises high and is thickly covered with woods and thickets.
But I am your chastiser. I know Ephraim, and Israel is not far from me.

The priests, then, and indeed those of royal blood, became a net, a snare and a hunt for the peoples. They commanded them to burn incense to demons and did so themselves ahead of the others. They persuaded them to think what is unlawful, and to their impious inventions they added further kinds of error: I mean the high places, Baal-Peor, the abomination of the Sidonians, Baal, and Chemosh. But God promises that he himself will be their chastiser, and before long, since he is about to bring upon them the evils of his wrath and anger. And the word is exactly true. Some of the royal house were caught in terrible and inescapable calamities and perished, as the holy scriptures attest; others were carried off to be subjected to the greed of the Babylonians and Medes. And the falsely named priests, priests for money, died miserably, or rather deservedly, some at the hands of Jehu and others at the hands of Josiah, who came from the tribe of Judah, that is, of David. For the man of God prophesied this too, once when Jeroboam was sacrificing and standing at the altar. He said: "Altar, altar, thus says the Lord: Behold, a son is born to the house of David, Josiah by name, and he will sacrifice upon you the priests of the high places who offer sacrifices upon you, and he will burn human bones upon you." So he threatened to chastise in wrath and anger those who had become a snare to the watchtower, I mean the priests and those of royal blood. But he by no means left the one they deceived, that is, Israel, free of blame. That is why he says: "I know Ephraim, and Israel is not far from me." This is equivalent to that other saying: "Who is this who hides counsel from me, who keeps words shut up in his heart and thinks he is hiding them from me?" "For I know Ephraim," he says, "and I have not stood far off from Israel." "For I am a God who is near, says the Lord, and not a God far off. If a man hides in secret places, shall I not see him?" And again: "Shall anything be hidden from me?" "For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart. And no creature is hidden before him, but all things are naked and laid bare to the eyes of him with whom we have to do."
For now Ephraim has committed fornication; Israel is defiled. Their schemes did not allow them to return to their God, for a spirit of fornication is in them, and they have not known the Lord.

The God of all sees into hearts and minds, and nothing at all is hidden from his sight. So he knows that Israel, or Ephraim, has committed fornication and reached the height of wickedness. Yet Israel did not let into mind or heart even the slightest thought that he ought to repent, because he was mastered by the spirit that urged him to fornication and had no wish to seek the true Master. It is true, then, as the Savior says: "No one can serve two masters. For either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other."
And the arrogance of Israel will be humbled to his face. Israel and Ephraim will grow weak in their iniquities, and Judah too will grow weak with them.

Here he calls that accursed haughtiness "arrogance," for the boaster is insolent. He says, then, that Israel's haughtiness will be humbled when Israel suffers, and very justly, things that would show him to be humbled, pitiable and cast down. He would be stripped of the boasts he had in God, and deprived even of the freedom that had been theirs from of old, from their fathers. The arrogance is said to be turned back on his face because every kind of dishonor is somehow like a blow to the face. He says that those of Israel will grow weak together with Judah. For when the kings of Syria and of Persia ravaged Samaria, they did not let Judah remain unscathed, but added to the cities of Israel some of the cities that belonged to Judah and Benjamin. Impiety and arrogance toward God admittedly brought every calamity upon them, as a matchmaker brings about a match. He taught this by saying that the affliction of weakness would come upon them for no other reason than "in their iniquities." Piety toward God, then, is useful and truly most precious. Through it one becomes able to rule over nations and to accomplish all things with ease. The Savior spoke truly when he said, "Apart from me you can do nothing." And David, who chose to think rightly, sings somewhere: "The Lord is my strength and my song."

With sheep and calves they will go to seek the Lord, but they will not find him, for he has turned away from them. For they have forsaken the Lord, because they have begotten alien children. Now the blight will devour them and their portions.

The facts show it to be true that, as the divine Paul says, "it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins," and that God cannot be approached through the law. By "law" I mean the worship the law prescribes, with its blood and sacrifices. So even if those of Israel offered the prescribed victims, asking forgiveness for the impious wrongs they had committed, or seeking to be brought near to God, they would not reach him, he says. They would not manage to find God, nor would he become approachable to those who repent in this way. For he is found only through the life in Christ. The entry into this life is understood to be the word of faith, and beyond this the saving baptism, which brings about closeness to God in the Spirit. So Israel would not find the Lord through the worship of the law. For he has turned away from them, because they too have forsaken him, and have leapt so far away as to become fathers of alien children. By "alien children" he means those who, as it were, from the womb and from their very swaddling clothes were dedicated to the worship of idols, perhaps because their parents offered thank-offerings to the demons and sacrifices for the pangs of birth. Alien children, then, are those who are not in God. Or, in another sense, they are children born of foreign women. For those of Israel heedlessly mingled with the daughters of the nations, who were still idolaters, even though the law plainly says that one must not be joined in marriage with foreigners. "You shall not give your daughter to his son," it says, "and you shall not take his daughter for your son. For she will turn your son away from me, and he will go and serve other gods."

Because they have done these things, "the blight will devour them." Here again he speaks figuratively, signifying the harm and damage that would come upon them from the onslaught of war. War is quite able, like a blight, to destroy them terribly along with all they have, for that is what "portions" means. That the war would not be put off or delayed but would come at once, close on their heels, he made certain by saying, "Now the blight will devour them." It is as if he said: "The experience will follow hard on these painful words; the calamity is already near, at the very doors." So this will be the lot of those who grieve God: they will be unable to find him even if they choose to seek him. They will become fathers of alien children, that is, they will bear no noble and genuine fruit, the fruit that comes from virtue and a holy life. Rather, they will perish, ravaged as if by a blight by their own wickedness and wretchedness. And besides all this, they will lose the very portions that come from God. Of these the divine David sings to God, the Savior of all: "My portions are in your hands." For every lot of ours and every share is in God's power, and he is the one who hands out the crowns.

Blow the trumpet on the hills, sound it on the heights, proclaim in the house of On. Benjamin is beside himself; Ephraim has become a desolation in the days of reproof. Among the tribes of Israel I have shown what is sure.

It has already been said clearly that the accursed Jeroboam introduced to those of Israel, besides the golden heifers, other kinds of idolatry, ruin and error. They worshiped Chemosh and Baal-Peor on mountains and hills, "under oak and poplar and every shady tree." And, as I said, the golden heifers stood in Bethel and in Dan. Such was Israel's error. But Judah, or Benjamin, that is, those of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, went astray no less. They served "Astarte, the abomination of the Sidonians," and they also worshiped the sun. This too will become clear to us through the words of Ezekiel. He was brought, as he says himself, to Jerusalem "in a vision of God," and there he saw the error of its inhabitants. "For I saw," he says, "about twenty-five men with their backs to the temple of the Lord and their faces turned the other way, and they were worshiping the sun toward the east." See, then, how they divided their ruin between them, offending and grieving God in many ways. There were those who wished to ravage Samaria and were expected at any moment, and who were about to throw Jerusalem into no small turmoil: I mean the Assyrians and Persians, and those from Damascus, that is, the Syrians. Both attacked at various times, spurred on to it now in one way and now in another. To these he all but complains that they are slow to attack, and he has commanded them to begin the war at once, making the trumpets resound and striking the first terrors into the souls of those who had gone astray.

He had said, "Now the blight will devour them and their portions," and we explained that the harm and destruction brought by war is called a blight. Now he teaches that it has come to the doors and will happen before long, and so, as I said, he has commanded that the trumpet be sounded loudly, and above all over the places of the idols. These places were about to be burned and shaken at any moment, or else they themselves had become the cause of the war and of the incurable calamity for those who had gone astray. So when he says that the trumpet must be blown on the hills and on the heights and in the house of On, you will understand him to mean the places of the idols. But it should be noted that the Seventy did not agree with the other translators about "in the house of On." Some of them said "into the house of the useless one," that is, of every idol; others, "in the house of On." We shall take it, then, that the prophetic word here means to indicate to us that they must sound the trumpet not only over the hills and the heights, that is, not only against the idolatry of Israel, the ten tribes in Samaria, but also against the idolatry in Jerusalem among Judah and Benjamin. For, as I said, they worshiped the sun, and On is the sun. They thrust God behind them and turned away from what is his. This, I think, is what is meant by their having their backs to the temple of the Lord and their faces turned the other way, toward the sun, clearly. So when you hear "in the house of On," you will understand a house or sacred precinct of some falsely named and man-made god, namely the sun. Nor should anyone think it absurd or implausible that those who worship the sun should be understood and named a house of the sun, just as those who think and do the things of God and offer him their reverence would be understood as a house of God. And if someone wishes the golden heifer to be called On, the interpretation will hold up this way too. For Jeroboam, hated by God, made the heifers after the Egyptians' object of worship, I mean Apis. The Egyptians honored Apis, saying that he was the child of the moon, which is why he had a crescent-shaped mark on his forehead. They also believed him to be, as it were, the offspring of the sun, because in their view the moon is lit by the sun. So they honored Apis as child of the moon and offspring of the sun. It was the crafty dragon, that is, Satan, who led them to this pitch of error and wretched reasoning. So he commanded that the trumpet be sounded on the hills and the heights and in the house of On, that is, of the golden heifer. What the charges against both were, and why they had to be punished, he makes plain by adding at once: "Benjamin is beside himself." That is, Benjamin has wandered away from his own customs, or slipped from the best frame of mind; for this is truly how being "beside oneself" should be understood when said of the wicked. And Ephraim too has been utterly destroyed. Yet he does not say these things idly. "For in the days when the offense of both was exposed, I showed what is sure," he says, "proving my words firm and true. For what I foretold has happened to them, and none of my words has proved false." Because they departed from their ancient customs and went out of their right minds, they were also driven out of their own land, and they fell away together from love toward God and from all prosperity.

In another sense, too, it will follow that those who forsake God must depart from every good thought, and indeed from every work directed toward virtue. They will go to destruction, as God reproves and rebukes them and exacts the penalty for their carelessness. Being with God, then, is useful and necessary for life, as is all but crying out those words in the Psalms: "My soul has clung close behind you." For then the right hand of the Almighty will take hold of us and readily help us, and from it no one will snatch us away, as the Savior says.
The rulers of Judah have become like those who move boundaries. Upon them I will pour out my onrush like water.

This is the figurative meaning of "Benjamin is beside himself." For they have become, he says, like those who move boundaries and want to overstep what was fixed long ago. Some transfer to others what befits God alone and was rightly dedicated to him, I mean love, honor and worship, by worshiping perhaps the sun, or the moon and the stars. Such people, in all likelihood, are doing nothing other than moving boundaries. That Judah, or Benjamin, gave to the sun and moon and stars the glory that befits God can be clearly seen from what God said to the prophet Jeremiah: "Or do you not see what these people are doing in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem? Their sons gather wood, their fathers kindle the fire, and their women knead dough to make cakes for the host of heaven. And they have poured out libations to foreign gods to provoke me to anger." So the rulers of the tribe of Judah moved boundaries. These were the people invested with the highest and royal glory, and the common multitude was likely to choose to follow them in their error. "But like a most violent torrent," he says, "I will pour out my onrush upon them." For what comes from divine wrath is hard to bear, insufferable and altogether irresistible, just as a great and abundant flood of water is hard to withstand.
Ephraim oppressed his adversary and trampled on judgment, for he began to go after vain things. And I will be like a disturbance to Ephraim and like a goad to the house of Judah.

How Benjamin was beside himself has been clearly shown, for he said that "the rulers of Judah have become like those who move boundaries." And now he explains again how "Ephraim became a desolation," adding: "Ephraim oppressed his adversary." Here the word seems to have been framed for us in a moral sense. So what is the charge against those of the tribe of Ephraim? And who is the adversary that, according to the divine oracle, Ephraim oppressed? I shall try to explain this as well as I can.

The people of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin still showed some respect and regard for the laws given through Moses, and they practised righteousness. Not all of them had turned aside. There were a good many who wept and lamented over the apostasy of those who had gone astray, and who were deeply distressed that some, dishonouring the God of all, were following the ways of idolatry. Indeed, as the blessed prophet Ezekiel says, certain ones were sent against Jerusalem carrying axes, and they clearly heard God say that they must follow the one girded with the long robe and spare no one. He says: “And I saw, and behold, six men came through the gate that faces north, and each had an axe in his hand. And he said to the man girded with the long robe, ‘Go through the middle of Jerusalem, and put the mark on the foreheads of the men who groan and grieve over all the iniquities committed in her midst.’ And to the others he said, in my hearing, ‘Go into the city after him and strike. Do not spare, and have no pity. Kill old man and young man, infants and women, until they are wiped out; but do not come near anyone who bears the mark.’” Do you hear that some were marked out as exempt from punishment, wrath and all blame? This was because they chose to think rightly, and indeed to live according to the law, to hold fast to righteousness, and to love God with a love beyond reproach. In Samaria, however, Israel had run completely aground. It did not think the things of Moses worthy of even a passing memory. Instead it lived a life that was at war with them, so to speak, and wholly opposed to them. So it regarded the law of God as an enemy, as far as one could tell, not even wishing to know it, and it dishonoured its tutor, though the law knew how to save and was well able to lead them to an upright and blameless life.

This, then, it seems, is what the prophetic word is hinting at, and as I said, it is spoken with a certain irony. It says that Ephraim overpowered his adversary. That is, Ephraim won a most outlandish victory, one that brought about his own destruction. He overpowered it as his personal enemy; in other words, he utterly fought down the law that he hated. But since the saying is obscure, the prophet makes it clearer in another way when he says, he trampled down judgment. That is, he paid no attention at all to the righteousness contained in the law. For whatever is trampled underfoot is always understood to be held in dishonour, and is shown to be worth nothing. So our Lord Jesus Christ says, “Salt is good; but if the salt loses its savour, with what will it be salted? It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled underfoot by people.” So when he says “judgment”, you are to understand the law. The divine David uses the same name for it when he cries out to God, “You have executed judgment and righteousness in Jacob.” For the law belongs to God, even though it was spoken through angels. But why did Ephraim regard the law as an enemy and trample down judgment? The prophet showed this as well, adding at once that he began to walk after vanities. The disease of this kind begins, he says, with choosing to honour vain things and to follow idols. For it is impossible to follow God and the wicked and unclean spirits at the same time. That is why the divine Paul writes, “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons; you cannot share in the table of the Lord and the table of demons.” For the one who loves God is single-minded. The unsteady person, by contrast, is fickle and wavering, knows how to walk on both sides, and easily goes off wherever chance takes him.

So then, it says, the rulers of Judah became like people who move boundaries, and Ephraim overpowered his adversary and trampled down judgment. From now on, therefore, I will be as a disturbance to Ephraim and as a goad to Judah. We must look carefully into what this means. The other translators said “moth” in place of “disturbance”, and “rot” in place of “goad”, but the Seventy used the words “disturbance” and “goad”. Ephraim, that is, the ten tribes, was thrown into great turmoil by the war that broke upon them. Part of it came from their neighbour, I mean the Syrian, and part from the Persian, who came from the land of the Assyrians. Meanwhile Judah was in pain and in no small fear, or rather in great anguish. For Judah expected, and soon, to be caught in the same evils, or perhaps in far worse ones. As the war pressed hard and fell upon the cities of Samaria, it was almost inevitable that the neighbouring cities, I mean those of Judah and Benjamin, would be destroyed along with them. So in this passage the disturbance signifies the onset of war, and the goad signifies the pain that comes from grief and despondency. Those who choose to set their minds on the things of Christ would surely be entirely free of these. Through him and with him be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.
BY THE SAME AUTHOR, ON THE PROPHET HOSEA: FOURTH VOLUME.
And Ephraim saw his sickness, and Judah his pain; and Ephraim went to the Assyrians and sent envoys to King Jareb; but he was not able to heal you, and the pain will by no means cease from you.

When God had become like a disturbance to Ephraim, and indeed like a goad to the house of Judah, Ephraim saw his own sickness, that is, his feebleness and weakness, and Judah too saw his pain; for, as I said, the territory of Benjamin was being ravaged together with those in Samaria. Then Ephraim, worn out by this, unable to withstand what had happened with his own forces or to shake off the damage of the war, offended once again against God, who is almighty. Not even under the very lashes, so to speak, did he perceive what was for his good. When the time had come at which he ought rather to have turned back to God, that was precisely when he chose to grieve him and to depart from him more savagely. He was not ignorant that God was the provider and governor of all their glory, the one who always gave them the power to overcome those who opposed them; yet he thought the matter of no account, even though the all-wise Moses had cried out, "The Lord who crushes wars, the Lord is his name," and had taught plainly that through him and in him "one will pursue a thousand, and two will rout ten thousands." Then, when he ought to have asked him, and him alone, for his customary help once more, and to have persuaded the Saviour with prayers to come to his aid, he devised bitter things against his own head. For he sent embassies to foreigners and called for alliances with enemies; that is, by persuading the advancing Assyrian with money, they thought they would be rid of the evils hanging over them. And indeed, when Menahem was reigning in Samaria, Pul king of the Assyrians came up against Israel; then they persuaded him with money and embassies to keep away from the land. This is the meaning of "Ephraim went to the Assyrians." Again, Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, once hired Rezin king of the Syrians and made war on Judah and on those of the tribe of Benjamin, while Ahaz son of Jotham was reigning. Ahaz, fearing the attack, persuaded the Assyrian Tiglath-pileser with embassies and money to come to the aid of Jerusalem; and he took Damascus by storm and did away with Rezin himself. But even if, he says, Ephraim went to the Assyrians and bought a postponement of the attack with money and entreaties, and even if Judah sent envoys to King Jareb, that is, to an avenger or defender (for that is what "Jareb" means), still they have not overcome the divine wrath, nor will they prevail when God exacts punishment for so dreadful an apostasy. For, he says, the one persuaded by money to keep quiet for a little while was not able, nor was any other of those who served for hire, to heal you; and the goad of the pain will by no means cease.

It is a terrible thing, then, not to desire rather to be saved by the gentleness from above, but to put one's confidence in help from human beings. And yet the Spirit cries out through the voice of the blessed David, "It is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man; it is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in rulers," and again through the prophet Jeremiah: "Cursed is the man who has his hope in man, and will lean on the flesh of his arm, and whose heart turns away from the Lord. He will be like the wild tamarisk in the desert, which will not see when good things come. And blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord will be his hope. He will be like a tree flourishing by the water, and it will send out its roots toward the moisture; it will not fear when the heat comes, and there will be leafy branches on it; in a year of drought it will not fear, and it will not cease to bear fruit." It is better, then, to attach ourselves to God and, from a good mind, to say that wise word: "I am yours; save me, for I have sought out your ordinances."

For I am like a panther to Ephraim and like a lion to the house of Judah; and I will seize and go and take, and there will be no one to rescue. I will go and return to my place until they are made to vanish.

He makes plain the reason why those who came to Ephraim's aid did him no good, and why their pain will not cease. For I am, he says, like a panther to Ephraim and like a lion to the house of Judah. It is evident, then, that when God withdraws there is no one who will save. "For who will turn back the uplifted hand?" as it is written. And that what befell them happened with all gentleness taken away, he has hinted in a riddle, comparing his own onslaught to the most fearsome and powerful of beasts. For the panther rushes with exceedingly swift speed upon whatever it chooses, and darts on such light feet that perhaps not even a track can be seen, nor any mark left on the ground. The lion roars in the mountains, terribly, heavily, like thunder, and can strike terror into those who hear it. "For a lion will roar," it says, "and who will not fear?" Its attack is irresistible and its onset very hard to withstand; and if it seizes anything, that thing is destroyed at once, and no one could rescue what it has caught. That the panther is a swift beast, and flies off, as it were, once it has snatched whatever it comes upon, while the lion, as I said, is unbreakable, fearless and hard to withstand, he himself has shown by adding, And I will seize and go and take, and there will be no one to rescue. The last of these suits the might of lions; but "I will seize and go," as I said, is what a panther would do. And that the Lord will depart from those who have grieved him, and will all but withdraw his help [?] and take away his favour, he has made known by saying, I will go and return to my place until they are made to vanish. For the divine is entirely unbounded by place; but it is said to be present with some when it grants them its favour, and again to be absent from those who have sinned when it turns away from them and cuts off its gentleness. Things about God are spoken in human fashion, but they are understood as befits him.
And they will seek my face when they are afflicted.

He teaches again that it is not for nothing that God often brings terrible things on those who have an unbridled inclination toward what is shameful, or on those who are accustomed to sin without ceasing, but rather for their benefit and as a kind of cure. For those who despise the divine gentleness, not knowing that the greatness of his forbearance calls them to repentance, will not escape the movements of his wrath. How could they? Rather, being broken by the harshness of misfortune, they come to recognize what is for their good; and those whom kindness did not help at all are brought to a knowledge of what is profitable by being afflicted with hardships. For just as the savage diseases of the body, those that do not yield to gentle remedies, are often overcome by fire and the knife, so in the same way and on the same principle, I think, the passions that arise in human souls, if they are not driven out by kind words or overcome by sober reasoning, give way to hardship and the lash and to grievous misfortunes. So, he says, when they have been sorely afflicted, then at last they will seek my face. For when good things lie within their reach, the foolish have little sense of what gives them joy; but if it happens that they are deprived of things so greatly to be desired, then above all we go after them with keener longing, and we take in a strong and overwhelming sense of what pains us. So when they are afflicted, then they will seek my face.

The passage seems to rise fittingly to the mystery of Christ, and to point very clearly to the redemption through him and the return to God. For the face of God that is sought may be understood, and quite rightly, to be the Son himself, "who is the image and radiance and imprint of the substance" of the Father. The Son, then, is the true face of God the Father, since he is known in him, and "whoever has seen him has seen the Father." So too the divine psalmist names him when he cries out to the God of all and says, "Make your face shine on your servant"; and again, as though speaking for those who have believed and have already been conformed to the Son through the Spirit, "The light of your face has been stamped upon us, O Lord." For, as the prophet says, "The light of our face is Christ the Lord."

They will rise early to come to me, saying, Come, and let us return to the Lord our God, for he has seized, and he will heal us; he will strike, and he will bind up our wounds. He will make us whole after two days; on the third day we will rise up and live before him, and we will know. We will press on to know the Lord; we will find him ready as the dawn, and he will come to us like the early and the late rain upon the earth.

"They will rise early" seems here to suggest that, roused as from sleep from the folly that was in them, and brought, as it were, out of night and darkness into light and day at last, they will call out eagerly to one another that it is now fitting to return to the Lord. This is the coming to their senses of those who had slipped into deception and been caught up in the worship of idols. For it is already the fruit of sobriety to seek to escape the mist, the demonic mist, that is, and, being now filled as it were with the divine light, to press on with a straight aim toward the knowledge of the one who is by nature and in truth God and Master, even though long ago they were of the opinion that there are "many gods and many lords" in the world, and had sunk to such folly as "to say to a piece of wood, You are my father, and to a stone, You gave birth to me."

The passage keeps to its figure. See how they say, He has seized, and he will heal us, as though of a lion or some other beast. Since he had said, "And I will be like a panther to Ephraim and like a lion to the house of Judah; and I will seize and go and take, and there will be no one to rescue," they have kept the form of the metaphor and say that the one who seized will surely heal. For just as the wrath grieved them, so the good things that come from his gentleness will surely gladden those who have suffered. At the same time we shall also understand this: when God afflicts people, no one could help them; the condition of those who have suffered needs him, and him alone, for its restoration.

But if we should also extend the force of the prophecy to all who are on the earth, we shall understand it this way. In the beginning Adam seized human nature; for he made it accursed at once, subjecting it to death and corruption. So wrath struck, but grace bound up the wound. For it healed us in Christ; it called us to the knowledge of the true vision of God; it made us steadfast through the Spirit in keeping the commandments; it made us enviable once more, placing us beyond corruption and freeing us from our ancient diseases, I mean sin and the passions. These things have happened to those on the earth not in the first time, as it were, nor in the second, but in the third, that is, the final and last. For all the ages are counted as three, the first, the middle and the last, in which Christ appeared to us. This is why they say that our binding up will take place, as by medical skill, after two days, the prophetic word measuring a day for us as a period of time. Then, he says, we will press on to know the Lord ("we will press on" they take to mean "we will hasten"); then we will also rise up and live before him. For we have been raised together with Christ; and since "one died for all," we live his life, no longer lying out of God's sight because of the transgression, nor cast behind him because of sin, but now brought into his presence and having boldness before him because of the righteousness that is in Christ. And that through him we have come to know the Father himself, and that the Son, having become like us, is for us the fullness of every good thing, they confess when they say, We will find him ready as the dawn, that is, as a rising light, as the sun, as the brightness of day when the darkness has passed. And he will be to us like the early and the late rain. For he waters us who have received the faith and have rightly recognized his appearing, in a twofold way, I think. He reveals in the Spirit the knowledge of the ancient teachings of the law, and of the prophetic teachings besides; and this, I think, is the early rain. As a late rain he gives, in addition to that, the understanding of the teachings of the Gospel and the much-longed-for grace of the apostolic preaching. And we have become, as the prophet says, "a land of delight." And perhaps it is about us that the blessed David sings, saying, "You visited the earth and drenched it; you enriched it abundantly." And indeed it has yielded its fruit, a hundredfold, sixtyfold and thirtyfold, according to the Saviour's word.
What shall I do with you, Ephraim? What shall I do with you, Judah? Your mercy is like a morning cloud, and like the early dew that goes on its way.

These are not the words of someone at a loss; for God could not fail to know what is useful for those who have gone astray, nor could he be too weak to accomplish what naturally benefits those caught in the devil's snares. Rather, he is accusing them, since nothing needed for their healing was lacking to them, but they had of their own free will turned aside to do what is unlawful. It is as if he were saying, perhaps: What way of sparing and helping you have I not devised? What shall I do after all that? How will you throw off your sickness? Or with what remedies will you now be made well? For you could have shared, and that abundantly, in my gentleness and incomparable love for humankind, as from a cloud that enriches very generously and as from the morning dew that waters the ground. But you thought the matter, he says, of no account; you treated so holy and so longed-for a grace as nothing.

The force of the prophecy would fit best of all with the gift given through Christ. For he is the watering cloud, the enriching dew. It is morning dew because it came down from heaven after a kind of night, understood as the mist and darkness of the devil; for the Word came to us from above and from the Father. It goes on its way because it goes over the whole earth under heaven. For the saving proclamation is very broad and all but extends across the whole earth under heaven, whereas the law was in a way confined and went about only in the land of the Jews. For "God was known in Judea," in the words of the psalmist; but the whole world has come to know the Saviour and Redeemer of all, that is, Christ.
Therefore I mowed down your prophets; I killed them by the word of my mouth.

The destruction of those who led them astray was a proof of his care and love for them. For from time to time false prophets arose against Israel, serving at the shrines of Baal, deceiving and being deceived, as it is written. But from time to time they were destroyed, God having foretold this too and pronounced a just sentence on them. Some Elijah killed beside the altar of Baal as they babbled in vain, saying, "Hear us, O Baal, hear us." Others Jehu killed, whom the blessed prophet Elisha anointed king over Israel through one of his young servants, God having commanded that this be done. When he had been anointed, since God was angry with those who led the people astray, he first killed Ahab, and after him Jezebel, and then his sons throughout all Samaria. Then, pretending that he wished to hold a festival for Baal, he gathered all the false prophets together, and, making a show of sacrificing, he slaughtered them when they had been assembled in one house; he also pulled down Baal himself and burned his pillars. For so it is written. So he has taught that the destruction of the false prophets was, as I said, a proof of his care and love for Israel by saying, Therefore I mowed down your prophets. And the phrase "I mowed down" is very apt; for they fell in great numbers, reaped like ears of grain.
And my judgment will go forth like light. For I desire mercy and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than whole burnt offerings.

He sets out for us another way in which he showed his care and love for them, one which, had it been fulfilled as he intended, all Israel and Judah [?]. For not only did he cut down the multitude of the unholy false prophets, appointing for them the death they deserved, but God the Father also sent his own Son in due time to make known, and to those of the blood of Israel before all others, his good will, and to make his judgment plain. So he said, through the voice of David, "But I have been set as king by him on Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming the decree of the Lord"; and he himself, when he had become like us, that is, a man, said in his own person, "I do not speak on my own; but the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment, what I should say and what I should speak." So my judgment, he says, will go forth like light; that is, my will shall not be shadowed in riddles, but will be set openly and unconcealed in the minds of all. And that Emmanuel, having come in due time, will not bring those who had gone astray over to the worship of the law, nor persuade them still to honour things in types and shadows, but will rather lead them on to gentleness and kindness and compassion, to love for one another, and to a true and undeceived knowledge of God, he makes the aim of his judgment clear, and says, I desire mercy and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than whole burnt offerings. For what did the Saviour say? "So whatever you wish that people would do to you, do the same to them." And showing that love is something especially precious to God, he says, "By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another." And who could doubt that he led the minds of those who came to him up to the knowledge of the God who truly is? For he presented himself to us as the image of the one who begot him, saying to his true disciple (this was Philip), "Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. I and the Father are one." And if anyone should choose to say that the Son himself is the Father's mercy, which surpasses sacrifice and whole burnt offerings, he will understand rightly. For he is called so in the divinely inspired Scripture. God the Father himself said to us somewhere concerning him, "My righteousness is quickly drawing near, and my mercy to be revealed"; and the prophets say to him, "Show us your mercy, O Lord, and grant us your salvation, O Lord." For Christ is truly the mercy that comes from the Father, since he takes away sins, releases from charges, justifies by faith, saves the lost and makes them stronger than death; and what of all that is excellent does he not bestow? So the knowledge of God, as brought to fulfilment in Christ, is better than sacrifice and whole burnt offerings; for through him and in him we have come to know the Father, and we have been enriched with justification by faith.
But they are like a man who transgresses a covenant.

Since we are eager to search out the truth carefully from every side, it is necessary to say now as well that the Hebrew version, instead of "like a man," reads "like Adam transgressing a covenant," so that the transgression of the Israelites may be understood to be of the same kind as that which took place in Adam. For although it was open to him to enjoy intimacy with God, to remain in incorruption and to delight in the pleasures of paradise, he neglected the divine commandment; then he slipped into what was worse and was unexpectedly deprived of his former blessings. So too, I say again, were the Israelites. Though they had the God of all gracious and friendly toward them, saving and protecting them, setting his mercy before them like a morning cloud and like the early dew that goes on its way, bringing forth his judgment like light and crowning them with a worship beyond the law, they grew careless about what was necessary and useful for their own prosperity and glory, and they too despised God who rules over all, even though he had said plainly through the all-wise Moses, "You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor a likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or on the earth beneath, or in the waters under the earth," and again, "You shall have no other gods besides me." And since they slipped into apostasy just as the first man, that is, Adam, did, they too are surely cast out, away from the one who knows how to give joy; for they have transgressed the covenant.

If the oracle is understood in a more mystical sense, as referring to Christ, we will again say the following, making plain the meaning of the words. God the Father sent the Son from heaven to enlighten the people of Israel and to make his judgment plain. He sent him to persuade them to give up the ancient sacrifices and the burnt offerings of the law, and instead to show them mercy, justifying them by faith, and to call them to the knowledge of the One who is truly God. Through him and in him we have seen the Father and have gained access, as holy Scripture says somewhere. But the people of Israel became like a man breaking a covenant. What this means I will again explain as well as I can. A man who breaks a covenant, or will, drawn up by someone else either does not himself come into the portion assigned to him by its author, or deprives others named in it of what is owed to them. The Jews did something of this kind, and did it in the case of Christ. How, and in what way? God the Father was granting the Son rule over the nation as a splendid and choice inheritance. As I said, the Son has cried out: "But I have been established by him as king on Zion, his holy mountain." The Father also gave the Son the spiritual vineyard, that is, Israel. As it is written: "For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the man of Judah, a beloved new planting." But, as the blessed evangelist John says, "He came to his own, and his own did not receive him." They threw him out of the gate and handed him over to death, saying, "This is the heir; come, let us kill him and take the inheritance."

See, then, how they became like a man breaking a covenant. You recognized the heir, so give him the portion assigned to him!
