So they broke the Father's covenant, as far as it lay in their power, by depriving the heir. Nor did they themselves come to grace; they did not accept the portion given to them by God. For God said through the prophet: "Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not like the covenant I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt." If the new covenant is weighed against the first, the difference between what each promises will be seen to be very great. In the first he had promised them the land of the Amorites, the Girgashites and the Hivites, and indeed of the Jebusites. But the new covenant, that is, the decrees given through Christ, called them through faith to adoption as sons of God, to glory, to incorruption, to endless life, to a share in God through the Spirit, and to the kingdom of heaven. Yet they did not want to have the portion assigned to them by God the Father through the Son. So they gave offense in two ways by breaking the covenant. As I said, they thrust the heir out of the portion the Father had given him, as far as it lay in their power. And they themselves fell away from the gifts God had given them in Christ.
There Gilead despised me, a city working vain things, stirring up water; and your strength is like that of a pirate.

The discourse returns again to listing the charges for which the unholy crowd of false prophets among them was justly destroyed. "There," he says. This means at the time when Israel turned aside and came into such a state that it even chose to worship demons. "There" here refers to circumstances rather than to a place. At that time, he says, Gilead utterly despised me. Gilead is a city beyond the streams of the Jordan, which was also allotted to the Levites under the law of Moses; so it was a city of priests and Levites. These men ought to have led others away from error and guided them to the truth and to the knowledge of what is good for them. As Scripture says, "The lips of a priest shall guard judgment, and they shall seek the law from his mouth." Yet they themselves became inventors of idols and craftsmen of vain things. For they worked vain things, that is, idols. They also stirred up water, which again means that they became a cause of confusion for the common herd. Holy Scripture is accustomed to compare the countless multitude of people to water. So, when the city of the Babylonians, and Nineveh, were very populous, it says, "Her waters are like a pool of water." This means that her multitude was like a pool full of water.

Or they stirred up water in another way. They set a muddied and, as it were, slimy teaching before those who came to them, and dulled the minds of the simpler people, for they taught them to worship idols. Indeed, the God of all accused them again through the voice of Ezekiel, addressing them as rams and leaders of the flock: "And you, my sheep, thus says the Lord: Behold, I will judge between sheep and sheep, and between rams and goats. Is it not enough for you that you fed on the good pasture, that you must trample the rest of the pasture with your feet? Is it not enough that you drank still water, that you must muddy the rest with your feet? And my sheep grazed on what your feet had trampled and drank the water your feet had muddied." Those of the blood of Levi were learned in the law. They had, as it were, a most excellent pasture and fine, clear water: the instruction given through Moses, which was quite able to lead people to the truth. Yet in a sense they trampled the pasture. They also muddied the water, setting a thick, slimy teaching full of earthy filth before those who followed them like sheep following rams. So the citizens and inhabitants of Gilead are charged with stirring up water. They are also convicted of having the strength of a pirate. We will make clear how this too should be understood as we interpret what follows.

The priests hid the way of the Lord; they murdered Shechem, because they had committed lawlessness in the house of Israel. I have seen horrible things there, the fornication of Ephraim; Israel and Judah are defiled.

The words of the holy prophets sometimes recall certain past events. If someone chose to pass over these in silence, he could not make clear the meaning of what is said. So those who wish to interpret such passages clearly must overcome any reluctance and be eager in every way to work out what will benefit their hearers.

So now we come to something of this kind. Shechem is a small town beyond the streams of the Jordan, neighboring and bordering on Gilead. As we said earlier, Gilead was given to those of the blood of Levi when Joshua son of Nun was distributing the promised land. A holy feast came round, that is, the Feast of Tabernacles prescribed by the law. At that feast it was the custom for everyone from everywhere to go up to Jerusalem, since the law commanded this to be observed. At that time some of the people of Shechem were pricked in conscience and repented of their error, or were called by God to sober up. They wished from then on to submit to the divine laws. So they sought to go up to Jerusalem, intending to offer sacrifices and to keep the feast there according to the law. This was, as it were, a beginning of conversion and of giving up their attachment to the worship of idols. For Jeroboam had devised the heifers at the outset precisely to stop some of Israel, that is, of the ten tribes, from going up from Samaria to Jerusalem for the sacrifices and feasts of the law. He feared they might then gradually return to their original state and come under the kingdom of Judah. So he ordered the customary rites to be performed before the heifers, and the wretch attached to his own inventions the glory that befits God. In this way he himself could reign securely, while God was, so to speak, deprived of what was his. So some of the people of Shechem were trying to go up to Jerusalem. But the people of neighboring Gilead prevented them, even though, as I said, they were of Levitical blood and appointed by the law to sacred service. They worked vain things, for they were craftsmen of idols. So they became bitter and angry, as if their craft were about to come to nothing if Israel should refuse from then on to serve idols. When they could not persuade the Shechemites with words, they turned to unholy plans and deeds. They got certain men ready to ambush them like robbers halfway along the road and savagely murder any Shechemites who chose to go up to Jerusalem against their wishes. A great many perished. Those who escaped altogether and managed to get out of their hands were stripped of what they were bringing for sacrifice, and barely made their way back to their own land. So the Lord of all accuses the people of Gilead. As Levites and priests who had been given the leadership of others, they ought rather to have shown plainly, according to the law, the way of godliness to those who had gone astray. On the contrary, they actually hide it. Some people, whether of their own will or through favor from above, had been pricked in conscience and chosen at last to throw off the burden of the demons' error. Yet the Levites do not allow these people to think rightly.

"The priests hid the way of the Lord," he says. This again says in other words what was said clearly through another prophet: "The priests did not say, 'Where is the Lord?' Those who handle my law did not know me, and the shepherds acted impiously against me." But the charges against the Gileadites do not stop there. Besides hiding the way of the Lord, they also killed Shechem, delivering it into the hands of robbers. That is why he also said to Gilead, "And your strength is like that of a pirate." See how God brings us to recall ancient history and remembers the old charges against Levi. What I mean is something like this.

Dinah was the daughter of Jacob, or Israel, for Jacob's name was changed to Israel. She once went out of her father's tent because she wanted to see the daughters of the local people; she was then in Shechem. Shechem, the son of Hamor, found the girl and unexpectedly forced her; he violated her virginity. Her brothers Levi and Simeon were deeply aggrieved at this and contrived a trick: they persuaded the men of Shechem to be circumcised. When this had been done, and the men were still in pain and overcome by their suffering, the brothers killed them all. Their father rebuked their unbridled anger, but they answered him, "Should they treat our sister like a harlot?" Now he brings us to recall this story, saying with a certain irony, "They murdered Shechem, because they had committed lawlessness in the house of Israel." He means that this was their charge at the time: the Shechemites had wronged the house of Jacob, or Israel, by violating the girl. "That is why we killed Shechem."

"But now," he says, "they resolved to return to God, to love what is in the law, to offer sacrifices, to keep the feasts, and to leave behind at last the defilements of idolatry. What, then, did the Levites do? They hid the way of the Lord and murdered Shechem. Or can they perhaps make the charge now too that the Shechemites committed lawlessness in the house of Israel? What girl was outraged now? Against what Dinah did they sin? What charges can be brought against the Shechemites? They had honored God, they had chosen at last to think rightly, and they were eager to carry out what is in the law." "So I have seen," he says, "the most horrible fornication of Ephraim there." One might well be astonished, and with good reason, to see the holy and chosen race turned so far away from love for God. Not only did they become inventors of idols for others; they even hindered people who chose to love the things of God. "So Israel and Judah are defiled," he says. Therefore, even if they suffer any of the things that are expected, let no one blame God for being angry. "Begin to gather the vintage for yourself, when I turn back the captivity of my people, when I heal Israel." Chapter 7. Again the word is addressed to the inhabitant of Gilead. It teaches this: "As God, I began to heal Israel and turn it back. Indeed, the Shechemites wished at last to bow their necks to God and to keep feasts, no longer those of Jeroboam but rather those of the law, and to escape from the deception devised who knows how. But you, Gileadite, all but sheared them, or rather stripped them like a vine, and made unjust wealth for yourself out of what you took by robbery." Again he adds with irony, "Begin to gather the vintage for yourself." He is all but saying something like this, or rather, though he does not say it, he subtly hints: "I too will make you the first of those to be punished. When I begin to shear Israel and to strip like a vine those who practice such terrible impiety, I will make you the first spoils of my wrath." It is necessary to know that Pul, king of the Assyrians, was the first to come against Samaria and Israel, and that he first carried off into captivity the tribes beyond the Jordan. Gilead was one of the cities there. "So, just as you, Gileadite, harvested for yourself the proceeds of robbery when I was turning Israel back and had begun to heal it, so I too, when I hand Israel over to the Assyrians, will make you the first of those to be carried away."

The ancient charges are akin to those brought against the Jews in the case of Christ. God the Father was calling all Israel to choose at last to think better things. He called them to give up the worship of the law and choose instead the new worship of the gospel. But they strongly opposed those who were turning back and being called to healing. For it is written: "The Jews had already agreed that if anyone confessed him to be the Christ, he should be put out of the synagogue." And their leaders heard: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you have taken away the key of knowledge! You do not go in yourselves, and you do not let those who are going in enter." So they have been handed over to their enemies and have paid bitter penalties for their outrage against Christ. "And the wickedness of Ephraim will be revealed, and the evil of Samaria, for they have worked falsehood. And a thief will come in to him, a robber stripping people on his road, so that they may sing in harmony, as those who sing in harmony in their heart."

The Lord of all is truly good by nature and forbearing, "long-suffering and abounding in mercy." As long as he still bears with those who stumble, their charges somehow remain hidden. But once he proceeds against them, brings penalties, and no longer endures to stay quiet, then the charges become plain. They seem, as it were, to be revealed already, and are all but brought into the open for everyone to see. This, he says, will now happen to Ephraim and Samaria. Here you should understand Ephraim as the royal tribe in Samaria, from which came Jeroboam and his successors. Samaria means those in Samaria, that is, the ten tribes. He says their sins will be revealed for reasons such as these. First, because they worked falsehood, practicing a cold and stale worship and becoming, as I said, craftsmen of idols. Second, because a thief, that is, a robber, "will come in to him," which means that a thief came in and rested and lodged with him, a thief who strips people on the road. From this, he says, it will appear that their hearts sing in harmony, that is, are in agreement and of one mind. For some were robbing those who wished to go up to Jerusalem, while others shared the guilt with them by taking a share in the plunder in an unholy way.

The leaders of the Jews too rejoiced when war was waged beyond all measure against those who believed in Christ. They became partners in the assaults and robbery committed by others and delighted in the persecution of the faithful. They received Satan into their minds and hearts like a robber, who strips their minds of all godliness, so that their hearts might be in harmony with him. For just as "he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit with him," in the same way, I think, he who is joined to Satan will have one heart with him.
I remembered all their wickedness. Now their schemes have surrounded them; they have come before my face.

As human beings, we have a nature that easily slips into sin. As long as our offenses are tolerable and moderate, God lets them pass out of his innate love for humanity. For he knows, he knows "our frame; he remembers that we are dust," as the Psalmist says. But sometimes we do something great, monstrous and truly intolerable. Such a deed can provoke even the gentleness of the judge and all but force it into anger against its will. Then he hastens to recall, so to speak, every offense people have committed. That is why he says of Ephraim and Samaria, "I remembered all their wickedness." It is also likely that the prophetic oracle means to hint at the following here. "In my goodness," he says, "I passed over the slaughter of the people of Shechem who died at Levi's hands because of the outrage done to Dinah, Jacob's daughter. But since they have killed again now, I will also remember their ancient injustice. I will treat Levi as a murderer and a cruel one, and I will exact penalties for the old offenses too." "For their schemes have surrounded them," he says. It is as if he were saying, "They are now besieged by their own designs and unholy plans." Once they killed the Shechemites by trickery and deceit, and now they kill them by robbery, even though they were turning to God. Since their offenses are now beyond all reason, "they have come before my face." "For I will not overlook such evils," he says, "nor will I put them out of my sight any longer and be slow to punish."

Their schemes surrounded the Jews too, especially in what they did against Christ. They killed the prophets while God was still forbearing. But since they also became murderers of the Lord, their schemes surrounded them, and the God of all remembered all their wickedness. "In their wickedness they gladdened kings, and rulers with their lies."

"They ought rather," he says, "to have done good and chosen to live according to the law. In that way they would have made the Redeemer gentle toward them and gladdened the Savior, who has irresistible power to save them." But they did not do this. They became very careless about what was necessary for their life and useful for their prosperity, and they thought nothing of offending God. Instead they played along with their kings and leaders, gladdening them by going along with whatever these decided. They offered what grieves God as a pleasure and delight to those who were leading them astray. Again he accuses them of siding with Jeroboam and the rulers under him. When Jeroboam devised the profanation of the golden heifers and wanted to carry them off in an unholy way to another worship, they consented at once. They should, they really should have opposed their rulers' schemes and utterly outrageous undertakings with genuine love for God, all of them together. They should have tried to restrain them in their folly, rather than readily agreeing with them and so gladdening them.

The saying is also true if it is understood of those who crucified Emmanuel. By lying about him and slandering him, they made Herod and Pontius Pilate glad, and the leaders of the synagogue as well. For the inspired Peter too said somewhere to the Father and God of all: "For truly in this city there gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel."
All of them are adulterers, like an oven heated for baking, burning hot from the flame, from the kneading of the dough until it is leavened. The day of your kings.

In these words he explains clearly to us how they gladdened kings in their wickedness and rulers with their lies. The history runs as follows, and anyone who happens to know it will surely understand the meaning of the prophecy. When the ten tribes broke away, the accursed Jeroboam became king over them. He was very much afraid that if they went up to Jerusalem for the feasts of the law, they might gradually be persuaded to choose the scepter of Judah again. Reminded of their ancient customs, they might either kill him or drive him from his rule over them against his will. For this reason the God-hated wretch planned to set up the golden heifers for them. He devised the form of this unholy false worship and set about introducing new feasts in honor of the heifers, as the Hebrew tradition relates. At first he was extremely fearful. If they spoke up for the worship that had come down to them from of old and from their fathers, they might drive him from the throne or even kill him, as I said. They might reject his scheme and choose to go back to their original practice, grieved and naturally indignant that Moses had been insulted and the divine commandment trampled underfoot. So, being bitterly cunning, he sent many people out among Israel to spread the word that they ought to make calves, to devise feasts of their own, and to ask the king for this very thing. When he learned that the crowds were very ready for this and agreed with and welcomed those who had given such advice, he gathered them all together. He declared openly that it was right to worship the golden heifers and announced the day of the feast, the fifteenth of the eighth month, as it is written.

When Jeroboam said these things at that time, the people applauded and cried out, “This is the king’s day; we too will follow this aim,” and they wanted to gladden him with other praises of the same kind. Those whose lot it was to lead were carried along with the crowds too, echoing them and agreeing with them. This is what the prophet’s word has now made known to us. For he says, “All are committing adultery, like an oven burning for baking, with a scorching from the flame.” They had turned aside to spiritual fornication, that is, to apostasy from God, for that is what fornication means. So they were like ovens already fired and ready to bake whatever might be put into them, because they were filled with flame, that is, with hot and, as it were, burning desire. They were also like a kneading of dough that already had the leaven in it but became fully leavened on the day of their king. As I said just now, when Jeroboam openly declared that they must sacrifice to the heifers and celebrate the feasts in their honour, they shouted, “This is the king’s day,” as the account of the tradition has it. Then the dough was fully leavened, that is, it became wholly and entirely possessed by impiety. So their minds were already set ablaze with hot, unrestrained desires for transgression, and they had already been leavened in just this way on the king’s day. In this state they slid down to the very limit of wickedness.

The Jews did something similar once again in the case of Christ. The scribes and Pharisees told lies about his glory and little by little drew the crowds away from their love for him. In this way they committed spiritual fornication, turning the common multitude away from him.
“The rulers began to rage from wine; he stretched out his hand with the pestilent, because their hearts were set ablaze like an oven.”

By “wine” here he seems to mean the wine from the vine of Sodom, which makes hearts drunk, clouds the mind and fills it with a deadly and loathsome fog. Some people were vexed at the innovation of the heifers and of the feasts too, and this provoked certain of the rulers to anger. They did not want the more sensible part of the multitude to be noticed, those who kept silent and could not bring themselves to applaud. So the rulers themselves stretched out their hands together with the crowds, shouted all the louder, “This is the king’s day,” and welcomed these unholy ways. So they raged, he says, drunk with an unholy drunkenness, and gnashed their teeth at those who did not run along with such shameful things, stretching out their own hands together with the pestilent. By “the pestilent” he means the crowds. For, as I said, the rulers applauded, though they ought to have guided the people toward piety and shown them the path of what is beneficial. But they too, he says, were hot in heart, having taken into their minds the deadly flame of desire for transgression.
“While they were dashing down, Ephraim was filled with sleep the whole night; morning came, and he was set ablaze as with fire.”

I said that Jeroboam, hated by God, was extremely fearful while he was still only planning his unholy undertakings. He thought, quite reasonably, that Israel would be indignant if it learned of any such thing, and would not take the transgression of ancestral customs lightly. But he himself announced to the crowds that they must worship the heifers, and they gladly accepted the plan and applauded together with the rulers, as though they had chosen to think and do what was right and beneficial. Then he let go of his fears and set aside his suspicion; from then on he remained cheerful and was full of luxury. So “while they were dashing down,” that is, at the time when they were falling into ruin and destruction, nodding assent and agreeing with him and preferring transgression to love for God, then, he says, Ephraim slept the whole night. Ephraim means Jeroboam, who came from the tribe of Ephraim. It is as if he said: though he had long been kept awake by fears and suspicion, he was now free of care, lived in luxury and slept the whole night on soft beds. And when morning came, he was hotter than the others. For he was set ablaze like the light of fire and grew hot along with the crowds. He did not think the matter deserved even the slightest delay, but very eagerly carried through to the end the display of his unholy undertakings. “All were heated, their hearts like an oven, and it devoured their judges; all their kings fell; there was no one among them who called on me.”

What I said, then, is true: those around the accursed Jeroboam were heated, and “they were set ablaze like the light of fire.” Did impiety, then, go no further than what he had dared? Not at all, he says. For all were heated, including those who came after him, and the deadly fire of this heat consumed all their judges and destroyed all who reigned after him in succession. For there was no one among them who was willing to worship me, who thought it right to entreat the God of all, or who could boast of the true knowledge of God.
“Ephraim mixed himself among his peoples; Ephraim became a cake baked in the ashes, not turned over.”

He sharply censures those of the tribe of Ephraim who took up the royal dignity over Israel in Samaria. They were in the habit of thinking no better than their subjects and the common herd, running along with them in everything and easily carried away with them. Yet as leaders they ought to have guided them toward the good, and by loftier reflection to have seen what leads to their salvation. But this they did not do. Instead they mingled with the crowds, all of them sick with one and the same thoughtlessness. Besides this they were persistent in wickedness, with an unchangeable mind that would by no means give up whatever it chose to do, even if these things should bring them ruin and destruction. So he says that Ephraim became a cake baked in the ashes, not turned over. He is using the image or example of loaves baked on stones: if no one turns them over, they inevitably get scorched and are then seen to be useless, and the abundance of flame ruins them as food.
“Strangers devoured his strength, and he did not know it; and gray hairs blossomed on him, and he did not know it.”

He calls “strangers” those of a foreign race and stock: I mean the Persians and their neighbours who border on them, the Moabites and Idumeans, and the nations of the Syrians. They all but devoured Ephraim; for since he had called him a loaf baked in the ashes, he keeps to the same figure of speech. By “his strength” he means a multitude beyond number. The tribe of Ephraim in particular was very populous, and on that account it raised its brow high and thought it would be formidable and invincible even to the commanders or generals of the Assyrians. But when these arrived, having undertaken war against them, they were consumed without a struggle and led into captivity. “But he did not know it,” he says, that is, he did not perceive the cause of the calamity, though he ought at least to have come to awareness through what had happened. For what is not seen by foresight, experience often sets before our eyes. It is better to look out for what is beneficial without waiting for experience. But if we should fail in this, those who have suffered will still be able at least to grasp from the experience itself what is necessary and profitable. Ephraim, then, he says, did not know, though he had grown gray, that is, though a long time had passed. That time was quite capable of instructing him and persuading him to learn how these things had come upon them: that because they had offended the One who is able to save, they slid into terrible and unexpected evils.
“And the insolence of Israel will be humbled to his face, and they did not turn back to the Lord their God, nor did they seek him in all these things.”

He clearly explains what he has said, for he again makes plain what it was that Ephraim did not know, though grown gray. The insolence of Israel, he says, that is, the apostasy he fell sick with out of arrogance, through which he also turned aside to foreign gods and dishonoured the One who is God by nature and in truth, will be turned back upon his face. It is as if he said that it will prove to be the cause of insult and dishonour to him, for that is what it means for something to be turned back upon someone’s face. But although he suffered such things, again he did not know God. Nor did they take any thought of turning back to him, hard and unyielding as they were and very sick with godlessness, even when they found themselves in the midst of terrible things. This is a charge of the utmost insensibility and a clear proof of a folly that has reached its limit.

“And Ephraim was like a senseless dove, having no heart; he called on Egypt, and they went to the Assyrians. As they go, I will cast my net over them; I will bring them down like the birds of the sky; I will chastise them by the report of their affliction.”

We must again recall what is written in the fourth book of Kingdoms, for in this way we will easily understand the sense of the passage before us. Hoshea son of Elah reigned in Samaria over Israel. Shalmaneser the Assyrian sent messengers to him, demanding the customary gifts in a rather tyrannical way and all but wanting to levy tribute on Israel. But Hoshea refused servitude and planned instead to resist, even if the Assyrian should perhaps choose to impose the law of war on Israel. Then he sent envoys to So, the tyrant of Egypt, asking for help, for he thought that with So he would prevail over the hand of the Assyrians. The Assyrian, greatly vexed at this, made war on Israel. Then Hoshea became his slave, and Israel too was taken captive along with him and deported from Samaria. So Ephraim became like a most guileless [?] dove, but his guilelessness was not to good purpose. That is why Christ too says, “Be wise as serpents and innocent as doves.” Simplicity of character and a free disposition may rightly be thought worthy of all esteem; but when understanding is lacking, simplicity is harmful, and the thing becomes mere folly. Ephraim, then, was senseless. How, or in what way? He called on the Egyptians, but they went as captives to the Assyrians, because So proved too weak to help. How, then, would it not have been better for him to seek not human help but rather the care that comes from above and cannot be overcome? That is why the God of all said through the voice of Isaiah, “Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help, who trust in horses and chariots.” And he showed that it was not without God that the hand of those who would defend them grew weak, by adding that wherever they commit fornication he will bring them down like sparrows. He casts a net or a snare over them, as it were, and does not let them boast, but brings them down as from on high to the earth, that is, from a very lofty and exalted brow to a pitiable and humble frame of mind, such as befits those who have fallen into the hands of enemies. Then he says, “I will chastise them by the report of their affliction,” wishing, I think, to indicate the following. The rumours of what was to come went ahead of their actual experience of it, and a dreadful report no doubt terrified those in Samaria. So they were being chastised by hearing of the affliction that was all but upon them. If they had been wise, even this would have been enough to bring them to conversion. But being very insensitive to pain, they were not shamed even by the experience itself, for they had a hard, unbreakable mind, gravely sick with disobedience.
“Woe to them, for they leapt away from me; they are wretched, because they acted impiously against me.”

Through these words too he makes it clear to us that their departure from God is the cause of their terrible sufferings. Those who are sick in body would be found responsible for the severity of their diseases if they refused to accept the physicians and the remedies by which their pain could be soothed. In the same way we too, [?] love for God, will do ourselves no small harm. For nothing saves one who offends God. Since, then, they ran away from God, they are for this reason wretched and accursed. And because they acted impiously, at any rate by worshipping falsely named gods and attaching their reverence to them, they will be subject to the “woe.” For “If God shuts a man in, who will open?” as it is written.
“I redeemed them, but they spoke lies against me, and their hearts did not cry out to me, but they wailed on their beds; for grain and wine they cut themselves.”

He again hints that he brings punishments equal in measure to each one’s offences. For they spoke against the God who redeemed them and brought them out of the house of slavery “with a mighty hand and an uplifted arm,” as it is written, and delivered them from the greed of the Egyptians. They spoke against his glory by giving the praise for the benefits they received to unclean demons and to the works of their own hands. So, of course, when they made the calf in the wilderness, they all but insulted their Redeemer in an unholy way and said in their madness, “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt.” It is therefore an insult and a drunken outrage against God, and the plainest slander, to dedicate reverence to carved images and demons, to bring thank offerings to them, and to drag down to them the preeminence of the highest glory. And not only did they speak against God, as I said just now; they also turned away entirely from even so much as thinking that the means of life come to those in the world from him. For “their hearts did not cry out to me,” he says; that is, they asked nothing of me, though [?] they should have been disposed to believe that I am the provider and giver of every good thing. From these words too we will learn that God does not need shouting, but rather a disposition of mind and heart. So they did not cry out to God. Instead they turned aside without restraint to outlandish love of the flesh, so that they even wailed on their beds. The thing is proof of shameful habits, of an unchecked inclination to fornication, and of a mind broken down by pleasures. Only those who have made a practice of forcing what belongs distinctively to men into the habits, postures and voices of women would be fit to slide into so shameful and utterly loathsome a condition. These men are effeminate, very womanish indeed, and have reached the limit of human impurity. As for their cutting themselves for wine and grain, this seems to me to point to the following. Giving thanks to their idols for the good harvests of the fields, I mean the grain and the produce of the vine, they chose to practise the so-called mystery rites. As if possessed and raving, they gashed their chests and both their hands with iron, so that, all but sacrificing their own blood to the carved images there and then, they might be condemned for utter godlessness. Perhaps another prophet is mocking them too when he says, “Sacrifice men, for the calves have run out.” Such things are enough to grieve deeply the God who rules over all. They ought rather to have brought their thank offerings to him, and not foolishly have assigned to wood and stones the glory that befits him.
“They were instructed by me, and I strengthened their arms, and they devised evil things against me. They turned away to nothing; they became like a taut bow.”

He adds another form of their ingratitude, showing them to be unholy and ungrateful. He says: Though they were once no different from irrational beasts and utterly without understanding, I instructed them by the law and made them wise. They knew what was beneficial and the way of righteousness, and were not ignorant of how to achieve every good order, so that they even said, rejoicing in themselves, “Blessed are we, Israel, for what pleases the Lord is known to us.” And my generosity toward them did not stop there. I also made them most valiant and well able to crush anyone who wished to make war on them and resisted them. For they conquered many great nations, and that without toil. But toward me, the God who gave them these things, they became wicked, that is, despisers and apostates; and the way they turned was toward nothing. For an image made by hands from perceptible matter is nothing at all. Now if they had found something better, their transgression might reasonably have some excuse. But such things are nothing at all in comparison with God; they are absurdity and silliness and whatever is close to these. So they have no account of their turning away that has a plausible cause. They turned away to nothing, then, and besides this they became like a taut bow. They did not slacken toward repentance or relax the tension that carried them off to such shame and thoughtlessness.

It should be noted that some translators have rendered this “they became like a bow turned backward,” so that Israel is again understood to have done something of this kind. They ought rather, like a bow, to have been drawn against their enemies and to have shot vigorously at those who set out to rise against them. Instead, without realizing it, they struck themselves bitterly, as it were, with the points of arrows. For when they offended God in the ways already described, what else would they be found doing but arming their own hands against themselves?

The passage may also be understood in another way, if anyone prefers. The God of all drew Israel, as it were, as his own bow, fighting the devil’s tyranny and opposing the deceit of idolatry. For of all the nations throughout the whole world, Israel alone, according to the decree of the law, shook off the worship of idols and devoted itself to the One who is by nature and in truth Master of all. But they turned to the opposite. Those who ought to have done that fought against God for the glory of idols. So they became like a bow turned backward, shooting in the opposite direction.
“Their rulers will fall by the sword because of the lack of discipline of their tongue.”

Wrath, he says, will come not only upon those subject to the leaders; it will also overtake, and very swiftly, those who were accustomed to revel in the highest honours. For they will fall by the sword, and the cause of their suffering will be the licentiousness of their tongue. For it is truly a lack of discipline to say “to the wood, You are my god, and to the stone, You gave birth to me.” Such things could very well be said with regard to Emmanuel too. The scribes and Pharisees moved their undisciplined tongue against him, even though he was instructing and strengthening them, spiritually of course. They took none of this into account and turned away to nothing. For they turned to “teachings, commandments of men.” And they became like a bow turned backward, shooting in an unholy way at their own Master. They ought rather to have fought nobly for him and pressed on to conquer his adversaries, as the genuine disciples among those who believed did.

“This is their contempt in the land of Egypt. Into their bosom, like earth, like an eagle against the house of the Lord, because they [transgressed?] my [covenant] and acted impiously against my law.”

These words are stated very obscurely, because the Hebrew language, I think, causes translators a great deal of difficulty. But we will follow the order of the thoughts and say what comes to mind. “This, then, is their contempt in the land of Egypt.” That is, I always save and instruct them and make them invincible to their adversaries, for “I strengthened them.” Yet they treated me with unholy contempt, assigning worship to demons and putting their confidence in the land of the Egyptians, thinking that help from there would be enough for their prosperity. For this reason their undertaking will be turned back into their bosom, and they will find no good reward for their rash counsel. They will receive their punishment as into their bosom. For he will come, he says, he will come, the one who will ravage them: the tyrant of the Assyrians, with a host of warriors beyond number. And he will come upon them like a whole land, a whole country and homeland, so that one would think the entire land of the Persians and Medes had moved wholesale and come to Samaria; this is what “like earth” means. He will also come like an eagle against the house. That is, swift and terrible, he will fly up against the very temple of God and overrun the kingdom of Judah and Jerusalem, seizing them without toil and carrying them off to his own land. For first the land of the Samaritans was sacked, and with it, of course, Israel. Afterwards that famous city itself was finally taken, over which the prophet Jeremiah lamented, saying, “How the city that was full of peoples sits alone! She who ruled among the provinces has become a tributary.” That the temple was burned along with the city is beyond any dispute. These things will happen to them, he says, because they transgressed the divine covenant and acted impiously against the law that had been spoken. They thought very little of what had been decreed through the all-wise Moses and were eager to live by their own wills, and each made whatever seemed good to him into his own form of worship and his own law.
“They will cry out to me, ‘O God, we have known you.’ For Israel [turned away from?] good things; they pursued an enemy.”

These people cut themselves for grain and wine and kept festivals for unclean demons. They did not cry out to God with their hearts. They did not even acknowledge the one who gives and governs all their gladness, nor honour him with the thanksgiving he was owed, since in the broad ease of their prosperity they ignored him. Yet they will come to know him when they suffer what they must. When their own bad counsel brings them to a bitter and dreadful end, they will at last cry out and call on him, once they have slipped into terrible and incurable disasters. Then, taking the very experience of these terrors as their counsellor, they will accuse themselves of folly and say something like this: “Israel has turned away good things.” They could have had those good things, and in abundance, had they stood firm with God and worked hard to do what pleased him. Instead “they pursued an enemy.” That is, they all but ran to their enemies of their own accord and fell into the hands of those who hated them, because by their apostasies they grieved God, who always saves them and sets them above their adversaries. It is truly very wise and profitable, then, not to wait until we have experienced such terrors. We should rather avert them while they are still far off, and hurry to see what is good for us before they arrive.

They made kings for themselves, but not through me; they ruled, and did not make it known to me. With their silver and their gold they made idols for themselves, so that they might be utterly destroyed.

He disowns the kingship of Jeroboam and of those who reigned after him over Israel in Samaria. Yet he himself had said plainly, “This thing has come from me.” He had also threatened Solomon himself, who followed the views of his foreign wives and impiously dedicated sanctuaries and altars to the gods they worshipped: “I will tear your kingdom apart and give it to your servant.” What, then, shall we say? That the God of all speaks falsely? Far from it! We shall rather turn to thinking rightly, and consider this. It is written, “Will there be evil in a city that the Lord has not done?” By “evil” he means affliction. Some things God brings about by his own will. Others he allows to happen in order to punish certain people [?], even if they are done in some way against his will. And since he often lets something happen for the sake of his providential plan, though he could prevent it, he is said to be the doer of these things as well. Let us take Solomon himself as an example. God granted him to build the stone temple in Jerusalem, and made him wise and distinguished by incomparable understanding. This was the work of God's will. But he permitted Solomon's kingdom to be torn apart. He did not bring matters to this by his own will. He kept silent, as it were, even at what he did not wish, because of his indignation against Solomon. So even though Jeroboam and his successors did reign, it was certainly not with God's consent. Things that happen as punishment, out of anger against certain people, are of a different kind. They should hardly be regarded in the same way as what truly happens according to his will. Therefore “they made kings for themselves, and not through me.” And since “they ruled” as though God did not even know of it (for what happens against his will he seems not even to know), their rule became weak and easily overthrown. It could not resist its enemies or save its subjects. For “through him kings reign, and through him rulers hold the earth.” They were gravely insensible in this. They used what God had given them to grieve him, or rather to destroy their own souls. He taught this when he said, “With their silver and their gold they made idols for themselves, so that they might be utterly destroyed.” They could have used that wealth to win approval by showing pity to their brothers. Instead it became the means by which they offended God. So they foolishly turned the very means of their salvation into the thing by which they were bound to perish.
Cast off your calf, Samaria! My anger is kindled against it. How long will they be unable to be cleansed in Israel? A craftsman made it, and it is not God. Your calf, Samaria, was leading you astray.

He puts it very aptly when he says “cast off,” or literally “wipe off,” as one would a stain, a defilement and the worst kind of uncleanness. That is truly what idolatry is. It makes the human soul loathsome and foul-smelling and hateful to God. So, being compassionate and good, he advises them to change for the better, to turn away his wrath, to curb from now on the causes of what is coming, and by repentance to check [?], even if they have come to their senses late. He says that he was provoked by the calf itself. This shows that, because he loves humankind, he sometimes overlooks the failings that come from human weakness. But he certainly punishes turning away from him, and he cannot bear the defection of those who insult him, I mean by choosing to worship demons. How long will you remain unchanged in your uncleanness? What length of time will be enough for you to put away your folly? You believe that what a craftsman made is God. You regard as venerable and worthy of acceptance something that does you no good at all, but rather carries you off to ruin and destruction. For the calf leads astray, and does nothing else.
For they have sown what is blighted by the wind, and its destruction will await them. It is a sheaf with no strength to make flour, and even if it does make some, strangers will devour it.

He compares them to people who labour at farming to no purpose, and so hints at how fruitless their bad counsel and their zeal for vain things are. When people choose to toil for idols, sometimes worshipping them diligently and honouring them with offerings and sacrifices, they are doing nothing other than gathering up seed ruined by the wind, which cannot benefit the one who labours over it at all. What reward is there for zeal in idolatry? What profit comes from carved images? How can things that are certain to come to ruin bring anyone joy? So those who habitually do such things and devote their zeal to honouring idols are like people who sow wind-blighted seed. They are like a sheaf of ears with no grain in it, useless for making flour. And if something does come of their efforts, that is, even if they seem in some way earnest and sincere in the works of error, even this will pass from them to strangers, and will in no way please God. By “strangers” he means the falsely named gods. Even our earnestness, then, goes entirely unrewarded when it is spent on things that grieve God. Whatever decency we show will be wholly discredited before him, and we will fail in our pursuit of the good.
BY THE SAME AUTHOR, ON THE PROPHET HOSEA: FIFTH VOLUME.

Israel has been swallowed up; now it has become among the nations like something useless, because they themselves went up to the Assyrians. Ephraim has sprung up again by himself; they loved gifts; therefore they will be handed over to the nations.

He says that Israel has been swallowed up, as one who has suffered a pitiful shipwreck, drowned in the waves of his own sins and dashed to pieces, as if on a rock, by the surges of divine wrath. Or, taken another way, he says that he has been swallowed up as if by a terrible and insatiable dragon, Nebuchadnezzar. For another of the holy prophets spoke in just this way, taking on the person of Israel when it had already been captured by the spear and was serving those who had taken it: “He has devoured me, he has torn me apart, a thin darkness has seized me; Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has swallowed me like a dragon; he has filled his belly with my delicacies.” It is also true in another sense, since the many-headed dragon in some way gulps down those who fall away from love for God and makes them his own food; and the voice of the Psalmist says that he has been given as food to the Ethiopian peoples: “For you,” he says, “crushed the head of the dragon; you gave him as food to the Ethiopian peoples.” For those who have a mind that is utterly black and without light within themselves might fittingly be regarded and called Ethiopians, both by us and by God. These people feed the many-headed dragon, and in turn they themselves feed on him.

Israel, then, has been swallowed up and has become among the nations like a useless vessel. For having been carried off to the Assyrians and the Medes, he became entirely useless, perhaps forced to think as they thought. Or else: because he had become a useless vessel, for that very reason he was swallowed up, and leaving the land that bore him he migrated among the nations. The Lord of all says something of this kind also through the voice of Jeremiah concerning one of those who had reigned in Samaria over Israel: “Jeconiah has been dishonored like a vessel for which there is no use, because he has been cast out and thrown into a land he did not know. Land, land, hear the word of the Lord: write this man down as a man banished.” Israel, then, has become useless. For what use to God is a soul that goes astray, loves sin, and runs off readily into anything whatever that is outrageous, and, worst of all evils, turns away from service under God? What, then, is the reason Israel suffers such things? Because they themselves went up to the Assyrians. For he all but says: they have run over to the enemy as deserters. How, or in what way? Fearing the enemy's attack, they did not rather seek God's help with repentance; instead they persuaded them with gifts to keep quiet for a little while. Then he in a way laughs at such a plan as one that would prove vain and useless to them, saying of those of the tribe of Ephraim who had reigned and had sent to the tyrants of the Assyrians: Ephraim has sprung up again by himself.

It is as if he were saying: the one of the tribe of Ephraim who reigned, though he was about to be cut down like a trunk and withered as if by the fire of divine wrath, sprang up again by himself, that is, without me and without my cooperation; he thought, he says, that he would live and send his root down deep and not slip from his own throne. For he bought a temporary and brief postponement of the evil, having loved gifts — not receiving them, but rather giving them. And what came of it? No benefit at all; rather, they will be handed over to the nations, and he would learn from the very things that will happen that no one can spring up again by himself, and that giving gifts to enemies will not profit those who offend God. For they will be subject to punishment, and before long.
Now I will receive them, and they will cease for a little from anointing a king and rulers.

Those of the tribe of Ephraim who reigned over them were responsible, so to speak, for all of Israel's wickedness. For first the accursed Jeroboam became the inventor of the apostasy, setting up golden heifers for them and appointing as priests of the so-called high places, that is, of the precincts on the mountains and hills, men not of the tribe of Levi but rather whoever “filled their hand,” as it is written. Then after him, when the Assyrians were expected, in the time of Menahem's reign, they sent money, persuading them to keep away from the land. For this reason the divine threat was rightly made against the kingdom of the tribe of Ephraim that had arisen over Israel. “For now I will receive them,” he says — not as people of good character, nor as having chosen to live excellently, nor as aspiring to the way of life according to the law, but as a corrector, demanding a penalty and already summoning them to judgment. For in my gentleness, he says, I put off the effects of divine wrath during the time now past, but now I will receive them, so that by experiencing terrible things they may at last learn that they are under a Master and not outside my hand. And by saying “now” he has made it certain that the effects of his wrath are no longer postponed. Received, then, so that they might be disciplined, they will thereafter cease from anointing kings and rulers. For while serving the Assyrians and Medes, what leisure would they have had to carry out the works of apostasy? They spent their time lamenting and bewailing their unexpected calamity. One should know that after Cyrus son of Cambyses released Israel from captivity, they no longer anointed those of the tribe of Ephraim in Samaria, but all came under one yoke, with those of the tribe of Judah reigning in Jerusalem. For they no longer dwelt divided, but all in Jerusalem. The first after the time of the captivity to begin the reign over both — I mean over Israel and Judah, or quite simply over all twelve tribes — was Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, of the tribe of Judah, while Joshua son of Jozadak, the great priest, led the Levitical orders and carried out the ministry of the high priesthood.
Because Ephraim multiplied altars for sins, the altars became beloved; I will write down against him a multitude, and his ordinances. The beloved altars were reckoned to him as foreign.

He explains the reason why he now, fittingly, declares that the kings must fall from their rule. For Ephraim made a great many altars for sins. The word reaches back to Jeroboam, the first to reign from the tribe of Ephraim, and after him to those who followed, who set up altars to demons on every mountain and hill and persuaded the Israelites to sacrifice. Then, though they ought to have been grieved at such outrageous undertakings — for they multiplied altars for sins — they made them, he says, even beloved; and besides this, the beloved altars were reckoned as foreign to him, that is, clearly, to Ephraim. By these he certainly means those in the ancient tabernacle, or rather those standing in the divine temple in Jerusalem. There were two of these: the altar of burnt offerings in the first tabernacle, and the other, the golden altar of incense, in the second and innermost. Many, therefore, are the charges against those who reigned from Ephraim: first, that they multiplied altars for sins; then that they made beloved the very things over which they ought to have mourned and lamented as having given offense; and, what is still greater, that, having sunk into madness, Ephraim made foreign the beloved altars, which he truly ought to have loved and held in every regard. In between he threw in, “I will write down against him a multitude, and his ordinances.” And he implies something like this: the multitude of the altars they made for sins, and his ordinances — that is, again, the sacrifices customary among them, or the times or manners of the sacrifices in which they brought their profane rites (for they cut themselves over grain and wine, and were eager to do other things of this kind) — I will write down against them as sins and as charges.

It is a saving thing, then, to cling to the divine altars, to lay claim to what comes from God, and not to seek what belongs to others, which leads to sin. This is what those do who are not genuine Christians but who, after saving baptism, fall back into pagan customs and observances; to them it is fitting to quote the words of Paul: “You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons.” So too those who join themselves to the unholy heretics and share in their altars; for them, in truth, the beloved altars have become foreign. For they have multiplied for themselves things that lead to sins, sacrificing the Lamb outside the holy and divine court, that is, the Church.
Therefore, if they offer a sacrifice and eat meat, the Lord will not accept them. Now he will remember their injustices and will avenge their sins.

Through these words too he shows very clearly that Ephraim made and multiplied altars for sins. For what they sacrifice, he says, they offer not to God but rather to the precincts of the idols; and even if they keep festival over the sacrifices, filling themselves with food and drink, the matter is nothing to God. For they do not celebrate the festival for him, since the divine and pure nature would in no way accept what is done for the glory of demons; rather it is provoked as having been insulted, and is all but compelled, even against its will, to bring the penalties of wrath upon those who call it to this, and then to come to the remembrance of all, so to speak, of the offenses committed by those who give offense. And when this happens, the anger is sharp, the punishment is close at hand, and no one escapes. “It is a fearful thing, then, to fall into the hands of the living God.” It is more fitting, incomparably better, and the source of every blessing for us, to offer sacrifices to God — spiritual ones, of course — and to keep festivals for him, choosing to live uprightly and striving earnestly not to fall away in anything at all.
But they themselves turned back to Egypt, and among the Assyrians they will eat unclean things.

Again he accuses them as people who choose to live most foolishly and utterly impiously, and who have entirely failed to recognize the path of what is beneficial. For I, he says, threatened that those who had come to such a frame of mind would henceforth fall under my wrath, and that I would avenge their sins and remember all their lawless deeds. And at first the coming events were only expected, while the war was already terrifying Israel and all but falling upon the land. Then, when they ought to have propitiated God with prayers and repentance, learned anew what pleases him, and by turning back to the better way turned aside his wrath, as something very useful and able to deliver them, they turned back to Egypt, calling to their aid “the Egyptian, a man and not God, the flesh of horses,” as it is written. But “a king is not saved by great power, and a giant will not be saved by the greatness of his strength. A horse is a false hope for safety. It is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man. It is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in rulers.” And that such ill-considered counsel turned out, he says, to be of no help to them in their need, they will learn from experience itself. For carried off to the Assyrians and Medes, there they will eat unclean things; that is, they will live having cast off the last remnant of their reverence for the law, eating whatever comes their way without caution.

But someone will perhaps say: How then would this have grieved the Israelites, who had chosen to worship idols? To this we reply that, admittedly, they had gone astray, yet there remained in their minds some small concern for the law, and they had not entirely slipped away from Jewish customs, even while worshipping in the temples of idols. For this reason the blessed prophet Elijah once accused them of limping on two knees, wishing neither to cleave wholly to Baal nor fully to God. So when Israel became captive, he cast off entirely his reverence for the law, following, as of necessity, the customs and laws of those who ruled him. And this, I think, is what Christ himself said: “To everyone who has, more will be given, and he will have abundance; but from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away from him.”

We must not, therefore, despise the divine gifts; rather, we must hold in the highest possible regard whatever we have from God. For the gift will gladly abide with those who take care of it; but if we become careless and slack about it, it will surely fly away.
And Israel forgot the one who made him, and they built sacred precincts; and Judah made walled cities. And I will send fire upon his cities, and it will devour their foundations.

He rebukes both kingdoms, I mean the one in Samaria and that of Judah, that is, the one in Jerusalem. For it is necessary both to observe and to state what both of them did. When the war was expected and the terror was all but at their very gates, those in Samaria and those reigning from the tribe of Judah ought to have sought help from God the Savior; instead they turned to outrageous and useless designs, and though they ought to have appeased him by repentance, they provoked the God who rules all things against themselves still more. For Israel, that is, the ten tribes and those who had taken power over them, brought still more worship to the demons, as though the demons had been offended, or as though they were able to avert the capture and overturn the enemy's ranks; and as if propitiating them and making them favorable, they built precincts, set up altars, and honored them with still more sacrifices. Judah, for his part, made his cities stronger, trusting rather in stones, not in God — even though God clearly says of Jerusalem: “I will be for her, says the Lord, a wall of fire all around, and I will be her glory in her midst.” But the scheme did Israel no good; and God then threatened to send fire upon the cities of Judah, since the Babylonians, who became the servants of his wrath against them, would burn them down. Nothing at all, then, will save the one who offends God. Admittedly it is a loss, and indeed a charge of ignorance — or rather of the most extreme impiety — to trust in the powers of demons; but when God is grieved and withdraws his help, it is no less ignorant to be deluded by earthly aids. Rather, we must ward off his wrath with prayers and repentance; for he is “compassionate and good, and relents over evils,” as it is written.

Do not rejoice, Israel, nor be glad as the peoples are, because you have [?] away from your God; you have loved gifts upon every threshing floor of grain. Threshing floor and winepress did not know them, and the wine deceived them. They did not dwell in the land of the Lord; Ephraim dwelt in Egypt, and among the Assyrians they will eat unclean things. They did not pour out wine to the Lord, and they did not please him; their sacrifices are like bread of mourning to them; all who eat them will be defiled, because their loaves for their souls will not enter into the house of the Lord.

Among the herds of the nations — since they suffer from very great folly, for admittedly they had gone astray — it was the custom, when beginning to work the soil and about to plough the land, to offer sacrifices to the demons and to ask them for good harvests from the fields; and again when reaping, when the season called for it, and also when putting the grapes into the winepresses, they poured libations, sacrificed to the seasons, sang the songs of the winepress, offering thank-offerings, and went on rejoicing and making merry. God accuses the Israelites of doing this. For he clearly insists that he must not rejoice like the rest of the nations. For what reason? Because the nations, having been entirely ignorant of the one who is God by nature and in truth, and having been born rather in error, perhaps have a not implausible excuse in their weakness, or rather their ignorance; but Israel, though trained by the law and knowing the Lord of all, went whoring into apostasy. He would therefore rightly be regarded as liable to a heavier charge, with an accusation of impiety that is hard to escape. For knowing the will of his master, he neglected it and did not do it. He will therefore receive many lashes, while the one who did not know and then did not do it will receive few, according to the Savior's words.

“Do not rejoice, then, as the peoples do,” he says. For they have gone astray from the womb, but you, though trained by the law, have gone whoring away from God. And what form did his whoring take? He loved gifts, he says — not those from God, but rather those from the heifers and Baal, although they give nothing to those who ask. And for what did he seek gifts from them? Upon every threshing floor of grain. For in their impiety and folly they thought fit, as I said, to ask for good harvests from the fields from their empty objects of worship. Did Israel, then, seek gifts from the idols, and did his requests turn out as he prayed? By no means; for threshing floor and winepress did not know them, and the wine deceived them. No one of the more studious doubts that there were famines in Samaria, crop failures, and long droughts. He was thus disappointed in his hope, not receiving what he asked; and besides this, they departed from the holy land itself and went into Egypt, as into a land fortified also by still more gods. For in Egypt there were countless objects of worship, and those who served them were held in remarkable esteem for their powers, as if they could easily accomplish anything by their magical arts. They therefore renounced dwelling in the land chosen by God and took in exchange the land of the idols. But even though they did this, they will go to the Assyrians. They did not pour out wine to the Lord: for having gathered the fruit of the vine into the winepresses, they poured out the firstfruits to the demons, and not to God who gave it. They also offered loaves, as at the firstfruits of the harvest. But the matter will become defilement and profanation for them, he says, and what they bring will be reckoned to them as bread of mourning, that is, as loathsome, profane and hateful. For what reason? The law made unclean anyone who came near a dead body — near either through kinship of blood or through actual touching of the body. So the relatives or friends of the dead were necessarily defiled in their mourning as they attended to the corpse and wished to perform the customary rites for it; and everything they happened to touch was unclean. Bread of mourning, then, is that set before those mourning the dead as food; even to taste it seemed a dreadful thing to those who made a practice of avoiding defilement from a corpse. Foul and to be rejected, therefore, he says, are those loaves which they might bring as at the firstfruits of the harvest, and those who eat them will be defiled. They will serve rather for their souls, that is, as food for themselves; for they will not enter into the house of the Lord. One should know that the law commanded sheaves and bread to be brought as a sacrifice as the firstfruits of the harvest. But Israel transferred what was for the glory of God to the carved images, although God says plainly: “My glory I will not give to another, nor my praises to carved images.” It is necessary, therefore, to ask God for the necessities of life, and to confess him as the giver and supplier of all our fruitfulness, bodily and spiritual. For there is no other besides him who sends rain, as it is written; but by his nod the produce of the seasons springs up in the fields, and we are filled with the blessing from above, feeding on the spiritual bread and having the wine from heaven “that gladdens the heart of man.” If we choose to think in this way, we will dwell in the land. For we will be with God, and among the Assyrians we will not eat unclean things. For “the world-rulers of this age, the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places,” feed those who approach them on uncleanness.
What will you do on the day of the solemn assembly, and on the days of the feast of the Lord?

For since, he says, you have come to such a pitch of evil counsel and impiety, and have become so loathsome and hated, what way will there be to help you? Or by doing or planning what will you escape so terrible and savage a calamity, when my festival is celebrated, as the war consumes those who have grieved me? God, then, calls his own festival the time, clearly, at which Israel would be made to pay the penalty for his offenses against him.

We must not, therefore, simply and thoughtlessly do whatever seems good, delighting in present things and swept away by our desires into offending God; rather, we must look ahead to what is to come and hasten to escape the effects of divine wrath. For in this way we will be wise, and will understand what is beneficial.
Therefore, behold, they will go from the distress of Egypt, and Memphis will receive them, and Machmas will bury them; destruction will inherit their silver; thorns will be in their tents.

When the Babylonians were laying Samaria waste, those who managed to escape barely got away to the land of the Egyptians. And when they took Jerusalem itself as well, in the time of Jeremiah's prophecy, only a handful were left of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin. These too went into Egypt, even though God had warned them through the voice of Jeremiah. He told them plainly that they must not leave the land that bore them and go to the land of the Egyptians, and he threatened that if they did this against his will, they would meet the same fate, or one even more grievous. The text runs as follows: "Thus says the Lord: If you set your face [?] toward Egypt and go in there to dwell, then the sword you fear will find you in Egypt." The Jews had relied on Egyptian help in resisting the Babylonians, and this angered the Babylonians. So after the capture of Jerusalem and Samaria they turned against the Egyptians and defeated them without effort, and the remnant of the Jews then perished together with the Egyptians. Those who managed to escape the distress in Egypt barely got farther on, going into the country of the Arcadians. They settled in Memphis, as though in a very strongly fortified city, and in Machmas, which was surely another city somewhere nearby and more notable than the rest. There they died, evidently after spending a long time there and without being able to return to Judea. The prophet Jeremiah also said this: "Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I set my face to destroy all the remnant who are in Egypt. They will fall by the sword and by famine; they will perish from the least to the greatest, and they will become a reproach, a destruction and a curse. And I will visit those who dwell in the land of Egypt as I visited Jerusalem, with sword and famine and death. None of the remnant of Judah who sojourn in the land of Egypt will be saved to return to the land of Judah, to which they long in their souls to return. They shall not return." Do you hear that they died in Egypt, and that the divine wrath came upon them there too? So when they try to escape the distress in Egypt and come to Memphis as to a notable city, it will receive them, but they will die in Machmas. That is the meaning of "Machmas will bury them." When God is in pursuit, no one will rescue the one in danger. Wherever a person goes, there he will meet his wrath. These, then, are the things he says will happen to them in Egypt.

They had also grieved him with their own wealth, for "they made idols for themselves out of their silver and their gold," he says. So it is just that destruction will inherit it, that is, it will become the portion of the destroyer. By "destruction" he means the Assyrian, who killed and fought savagely and without mercy. And thorns, he says, will spring up in their dwellings. For the cities came to such desolation that they were full of thorns, and this is the sign of a land that no one walks through and that has turned to waste.

So when someone does not use rightly the good things God has given, whether bodily or spiritual, and does not use them for his glory, but thoughtlessly does things that offend him and is caught grieving him, he will go down to destruction. He will become the portion of Satan the plunderer and a lodging place for thorns, that is, for wild and monstrous desires, and he will bear no cultivated fruit in his mind. Heretics above all would suffer this, since they impiously spend their gift of speech on undermining the brothers and "wounding their weak conscience," even though Christ suffered for us.
The days of vengeance have come, the days of your recompense have come, and Israel will be afflicted like the prophet who is out of his mind, the man who bears the Spirit.

The people of Israel had the habit of shaking off the words of the holy prophets and of counting as nothing what came from God, even though he had often foretold that terrible things would befall them. Indeed, the God of all once addressed the prophet Ezekiel, saying, "Son of man, behold, the embittering house of Israel keep saying, 'The vision that this man sees is for many days, and he prophesies of distant times.' Therefore say to them: Thus says Adonai the Lord: None of my words that I speak will be delayed any longer, for I will speak a word and I will do it, says Adonai the Lord." He says something similar here: "The days of vengeance have come." It is as if he were saying: the judgment is near, the contest is already at the very doors, the calamity is close by, and the war is before your eyes. The day of recompense is upon you. And when you are afflicted, O Israel, he says, every false prophet among you will certainly be afflicted along with you and will share the punishment in the same way: the man who is out of his mind, that is, the one who is possessed and raving and has lost his wits, whom you thought to be a bearer of the Spirit. For together with the rest perished the priests of the high places, the servants of the idols, and all who spoke falsely and divined falsely in Israel. Since they pretended to be in a frenzy when they gave their oracles, and feigned prophetic inspiration, he calls such a man "out of his mind."
Because of the multitude of your iniquities, your madness has been multiplied.

By "multitude of iniquity" he means, as it were, the manifold and many-formed worship of Israel. In a word, they had gone astray and were all idolaters. But they divided up the forms of their error among themselves: different people offered rites to different gods and gave false oracles to those who came to them. Some served the heifers, others Chemosh, the idol of Moab, and others Astarte. There were also some who served Baal and the host of heaven. That is why God accused them through the voice of Jeremiah: "For according to the number of your cities were your gods, O Judah." Each of their cities professed to have its own god. He rightly calls this very thing a "multitude of iniquity." For it is truly an injustice and an outrage against God to depart from him and to cling to wood and stone and "to the works of their hands," as it is written. By "madness" he means divination. So, he says, since a multitude of iniquity has been found in you, madness, that is, false divination, has also been multiplied among you, each false diviner presumably having his own method of divining. It is therefore monstrous, lawless and truly profane, and quite enough to grieve and fiercely provoke the God of all, to be fond of clinging to the falsehoods of those who are accustomed to speak "from their own heart," as it is written, "and not from the mouth of the Lord." Christians must therefore guard against this offense. Such a sickness would befit only the servants of demons.
Ephraim is a watchman with God; the prophet is a crooked snare on all his ways.

Divine Scripture is accustomed to call "watchmen" those who stand at the head of the people and are set over them, raised on high because of their rank, so that anyone who wishes to live an upright and blameless life might look to them. Indeed, God once said to the blessed prophet Ezekiel, "Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel; you will hear a word from my mouth and warn them from me." Such watchmen are accustomed not only to set their own life before those under instruction as a pattern of virtue and lawful conduct, but also to introduce what is profitable and to interpret rightly what pleases God. Those who were under good watchmen went straight along the path of what is fitting and were saved. But those who gave the weight of their minds over to wicked and worthless men went on "deceiving and being deceived," with minds banished from all good works and true knowledge. This is what he now accuses those of the tribe of Ephraim, that is, Israel, of having suffered. For he says that a prophet became his watchman along with a god. It is as if he were saying: for each of the falsely named gods there was also a false diviner of its own. For, as I said before, they were divided among a manifold error. Some worshiped Baal, others Chemosh, that is, Baal-Peor. In each sanctuary some image had been fashioned, a statue or carved figure made by hand, and each had its own false prophet in attendance. Among them the method of divination varied, and they belched out to those who came to them whatever they pleased, as though it were useful and necessary. So since the people of Ephraim had for a watchman, along with each of the falsely named gods, a prophet of its own, they then turned without restraint to every shameful thing whatever. This became a crooked [?] for him. For [it was impossible] [?] that those who had slid into such polytheism, so as to have a prophet of their own with each god, could ever be set straight and walk rightly, and moreover that they should take as watchman one who carries them away from piety toward God and throws them into the pits of destruction.

Those who wish to live lawfully must therefore pay attention, not to just any teachers, nor to those who speak from their own heart, but to those whose genuine love for God is attested by the divine grace from above. That is why Christ also says, "Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves." We speak the truth when we say that the inventors and leaders of unholy heresies differ little from wild beasts, "those who devour Israel with open mouth." For they consume, as it were, the souls of the simpler sort, crushing them with the teeth of deceit. Let us too, then, say, "God will break their teeth in their mouth; the Lord has shattered the jaws of the lions. They will be brought to nothing like water running away; he will bend his bow until they grow weak. Like melted wax they will be taken away."
They have fixed madness in the house of the Lord. They were corrupted as in the days of the hill. He will remember his iniquity; he will avenge his sins.

Here too, as usual, by "madness" he means false divination. By "house of the Lord" he means Israel. Indeed, it was said somewhere through the voice of Jeremiah to the synagogue of the Jews, as from the person of God, "Did you call me as a house, and father, and guide of your virginity?" He is therefore astonished at the magnitude of their folly and the excess of their outrageous undertakings. They have gone so far in unholiness, he says, as to fix madness in the house of the Lord, that is, false divination, and to commit what the divine laws forbid. And he says "they have fixed" well.
