For the deed was not dared once and then stopped; the thing of impiety was, as it were, fixed fast and dug in from then on. Israel did not stop having false diviners and false prophets. And since they dared such things, they were rightly made to pay the penalty for what they had done: they were corrupted as in the days of the hill. For he will remember their iniquity and avenge all their sins. Come, let us briefly recall what this "they were corrupted as in the days of the hill" means. Something of the kind is written in the book of Judges. I will run through the whole account as quickly as possible and shorten what is rather long. "In those days," it says, "there was no king in Israel; each man did what was right in his own eyes. And there was a young man from Bethlehem, of the clan of Judah, and he was a Levite, and he sojourned there. And the man went from Bethlehem, the city of Judah, to sojourn wherever he might find a place, and he came to the hill country of Ephraim, to the house of Micah, as he made his way. And Micah said to him, 'Where do you come from?' And the Levite said to him, 'I am from Bethlehem of Judah, and I am going to dwell wherever I may find a place.' And Micah said to him, 'Stay with me, and be a father and a priest to me, and I will give you ten pieces of silver a day, a suit of clothes, and your living.' And the Levite went and began to sojourn with the man. And the young man became to him like one of his sons. And Micah filled the hand of the Levite, and he became his priest, and he was in the house of Micah." Micah, then, was an idolater, yet he hired a man of the blood of Levi, made him the servant of a carved image, and devoted him to the service of idols. And what happened after this? The sacred text goes on thus: "And in those days the tribe of Dan was seeking an inheritance for itself to dwell in, for until that day no inheritance had fallen to it among the tribes of Israel." Then they chose five men and persuaded them to go ahead of them and search out a land that they might take and make their own portion. And they came, it says, "to the hill country of Ephraim, to the house of Micah, and lodged there." While they were in Micah's house they recognized the Levite as one of their own race, because he spoke their language: he spoke as a Hebrew to Hebrews. They asked the reason for his being there and learned how Micah had hired him, though he was of the tribe of Levi, and had appointed him priest of his own objects of worship. They ought to have grieved with him as a captive, deceived and wandering, but instead they at once slid down with him into the snares of deceit and asked him to tell them, by inquiring of the idol, whether their undertaking would turn out as they hoped, I mean the conquest of the land they had come to spy out. And he spoke whatever he pleased as though it came from God. When the men who had been sent had spied out the land, they reported to those who had sent them that it was good and rich and could be taken without sweat. When the people of the tribe of Dan heard this report, six hundred of them went up under arms. They too came as far as Micah's house. "And the five men who had gone to spy out the land of Laish answered," it says, "and said to their brothers, 'Do you know that in this house there are an ephod, teraphim, a carved image and a molten image? Now consider what you will do.'" "Ephod" is interpreted "redemption," and "teraphim" in turn "healer of them." It was an idol that carried the false reputation of being able to heal people, for the children of the Greeks sometimes surround handmade objects with notions of this kind. When the Danites learned this, they took the carved image and persuaded the man of the blood of Levi to leave Micah and follow them. They drew up for battle, won, and took the land in hand, and they built a city which they named Dan, inscribing on it the name of their forefather, for, as I said, they were of the tribe and blood of Dan. They set up the idol in it and offered sacrifices, and so they acquired a god together with the land. To such thoughtlessness had their minds been brought down.

For this reason God was angry from then on, and with good reason, since he had been insulted. Then, when all Israel ought to have regarded the Danites as enemies and bitter foes and called them to account for their impiety toward God, they perhaps even went along with them and thought fit to praise them, as though they had done nothing wrong at all. Come, let us next tell what wages they received for such negligence. While Israel remained without a king, a certain Levite who sojourned on the slopes of the hill country of Ephraim took as his companion a woman from Bethlehem. When the woman ran away to her father, the Levite followed her and persuaded her to return with him and to be at home again. When this had happened, halfway along the road he lodged with the woman in Gibeah, which is interpreted "hill." Gibeah, that is, the hill, was inhabited by men of the tribe of Benjamin. While he was lodging with an old man, lawless men of the tribe of Benjamin came in the middle of the night, as it is written, wanting to force the Levite himself, and others as well, into lewdness. Barely shamed out of the extreme of that outrage, they seized the Levite's concubine and in fact killed her, abusing the woman all night long. He cut the body into pieces and distributed them to the tribes of Israel, making plain the sin of the Benjaminites against strangers and their unbridled lewdness, and that they had imitated the offenses of the Sodomites. At this all Israel gathered in anger and made war on the tribe of Benjamin in Gibeah, that is, on the hill. They destroyed it so thoroughly, populous as it was, that only a very few were saved and barely escaped into the wilderness. And not a few of the fighting men of all Israel perished as well. But God would not have let the Israelites come to blows with one another had the Danites not honored the carved image from Micah's house, while the other tribes unreasonably held their peace. Something similar happened when God was grieved over the golden heifers. The two tribes of Judah and the ten of Ephraim clashed with one another, and as in the days of the [hill?] [?] countless men fell, and the defeated perished together with the victors, because the divine wrath summoned them to it. This happened when Amaziah was reigning over Judah and Joash over Israel. Joash took Jerusalem and went so far as to tear down four hundred cubits of the wall.

Like a grape in the wilderness I found Israel, and like an early fig on a fig tree I saw their fathers. They went in to Baal-Peor and were estranged into shame, and the beloved became like the abhorred.

He now tries to teach that their destruction did not come upon them for nothing, but justly. For I chose them, he says, as if I had found a grape in the wilderness or plucked a ripe fig from a fig tree. I brought them out of the land of the Egyptians, which was wholly given to idolatry and astray, and sick with a great dearth of every good thing. What, then, did the chosen ones do, those snatched out by my hand? They inclined toward Baal-Peor; they departed from their close bond with me into shame. This is the meaning of "we were estranged into shame." And by "shame" he means Baal-Peor, for he had the ugliest form of all the others and was indecent to look at.

Let us, then, love being with God, and honor him as the one who called and chose us, who snatched us, as it were, out of the barren and thorn-bearing land of our state in this world, and who loved us like a grape and an early fig. Let us keep our union with him unbroken, that is, our spiritual union. But if we should turn aside toward what is ugly and grieves him, we will no longer differ in any way from the Gentiles. For we, the beloved, will become like the abhorred, who are justly hated. "For the righteousness of the righteous," it says, "will not deliver him on the day he sins." And the blessed Paul writes very wisely, "So let anyone who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall."
Ephraim has flown away like a bird.

Birds that are not tame or domestic are kept when they are caught, and they delight their owners. But if a chance to escape comes, they leave without delay and fly swiftly back to their accustomed haunts. In the same way Israel had, in a sense, been caught like a bird through Moses and brought to God. He was in a fine state of prosperity, being tutored by the law and enjoying care and protection from above. But he flew back to what he had been at the beginning, all but escaping the hand of the one who had caught him. Or you may understand the saying in another way. Many birds cannot endure the winters of their own region and move to other lands, knowing without being taught what is good for them, as their Maker willed. In the same way Ephraim, fearing the calamities of war, flew off to the Egyptians.
Their glories are from births and birth pangs and conceptions. [?] And even if they rear their children, they will be bereaved of them among men; for indeed woe is theirs [?].

Israel left the land that bore him and ran away to the Egyptians, and begged the ruler of that country to come to his aid. Was this because God was weak and unable to save them? Certainly not. The divine power can do all things, and it was well able to drive off the war of the Assyrians. But those of Ephraim, that is, Israel, came to suffer these things because they abandoned God their Savior, mocked as stale and outworn the idea of taking pride in him and in him alone, and imagined that they would be formidable and unconquerable to their enemies on their own, since they had grown into a great multitude and had numberless children. Their women did bear children according to the promise, as a kind of blessing, for Moses had foretold: "There shall be no one barren or sterile among the sons of Israel." But it was utterly foolish to disregard the help that comes from God because of the number of their bodies. If they had thought rightly, they ought rather to have reflected that with him and through him "one shall chase a thousand, and two shall put ten thousand to flight." So, he says, they take pride not in God but rather in the births, conceptions and labor pains of their women. Let them know, then, that even if they bear sons, even if they toil to bring up children, they will regret laboring in vain. For they will surely and utterly mourn their childlessness, and the Babylonian sword will be enough to consume with ease their entire race. For woe also is upon them. It is as if he were saying: "When God casts woe upon them, who will grant them cheer?" For "if he shuts against a man, who will open?" as it is written. "It is a fearful thing, then, to fall into the hands of the living God." We must soothe him by gentleness when he has been grieved, and seek salvation from him, trusting in nothing else, but rather crying aloud: "I will boast in God my Savior; the Lord God is my strength."
Let my flesh be out from them.

When God threatens, and indeed declares concerning Ephraim, that is, all Israel, that it will perish root and all, that it will mourn its childlessness, and that it will labor in vain at rearing its children, the prophet withdraws himself from the punishment and prays to be outside the wrath, saying: Let my flesh be out from them. You will understand "out from them" as meaning "far away from them." For he says: "May I myself, and my whole race, be outside them and as far from them as possible." For "flesh" sometimes signifies race as well. This is how we shall take what Paul rightly said, for he wrote thus: "Now I am speaking to you Gentiles. Inasmuch as I am an apostle of the Gentiles, I glorify my ministry, if somehow I may provoke my flesh to jealousy and save some of them." It is the custom of the holy prophets, when they often see that the offences of certain people are grievous and intolerable, to set themselves apart from their abomination. So, for instance, when the prophet saw that the Jews had fallen into ever so many charges and had offended God, he says: "O Lord Almighty, I did not sit in their council while they made sport, but I was in awe before your hand; I sat alone, for I was filled with bitterness." We must therefore admire the blessed Paul when he writes to us, saying: "Keep yourself pure, and do not share in other people's sins." And so any devout person might fittingly say of those who offend God and are all but on the point of being punished: Let my flesh be out from them.
Ephraim, as I have seen, set out his children as prey; and Ephraim is to lead out his children to slaughter.

Here again the prophet bewails Ephraim, that is, Israel, and says that he himself has become responsible for his own childlessness and incurable disaster. "For as I have seen, O Master," he says, "both from your words and from the events themselves, Ephraim himself has set out his own children as prey and for slaughter." And so, if he chose to think sensibly, he would not blame others any longer, nor cry out against the divine wrath; he would rather blame his own folly and apostasy. For since he has grieved beyond measure the God who helps and saves him, he has all but handed over his own offspring willingly, with his own hand, to the savagery of the nations, and set them out for deportation and captivity. That is what "as prey" means, and "for slaughter," that is, for butchery. For some of those from Israel the Babylonians killed, and others they carried off to their own land.

So when we sin, if we think rightly, we shall blame ourselves rather than the divine wrath. For we have despised what is fitting and have grown careless about what pleases God. And the insolent and unbridled person, who all but says to the Master of all, "Depart from me; I do not wish to know your ways," must necessarily be punished.
Give them, O Lord — what will you give them? Give them a childless womb and dry breasts.

"If those of Israel," he says, "are going to refuse to know God, and are instead to be carried away toward a useless and profitless hope, imagining that they will overcome their enemies by the number of their children and because their fighting stock is large, and that for this reason they have no need to be helped by your hand, then let their women bear no children at all." That is what the childless womb means. "And even if they do bear, let them not rear them"; that is, let them be consumed before their time, and let the race fall before it reaches maturity. For when the arrogance that is in them because of this has thus been cut away, and their hope in the number of their fighting men has been removed, they will take refuge in your mercy and will acclaim you as Savior and Redeemer. The prophet says these things here too out of love for God. At the same time he seeks both the glory of his own Master and the return of those of Israel's blood, even if it be by necessity, since they do not have it as the fruit of a good choice.

A childless womb and dry breasts would also be fitting, in a spiritual sense, for workers of evil and for everyone who leads astray and carries away from the straight road those who are accustomed to walk uprightly—in faith, I mean—"and to make straight their ways." For if their mind gave birth to nothing, neither a false word nor a spurious doctrine, they would not rear their own children in error—I mean their children by instruction—and the churches of the wicked, having dry breasts, would not become mothers of the deceived.
All their wickedness is in Gilgal, for there I hated them because of the wickedness of their practices. I will cast them out of my house; I will not love them any longer.

Once again the God of all begins to recount their offences, and he recalls Gilgal. This was a city in which handmade idols were worshiped in an especially dreadful and outrageous way. What he says is again something like this: "Those of Israel are abominable in many ways, but one could see the extremity of the wickedness that was in them by considering Gilgal. There I saw all their wickedness; there I hated them"—not because of the place, for that would be foolish, but rather because he loathed what was done in it. "Therefore," he says, "I will turn them out of their home, drive them from my court and cast them out of my household. And having justly hated them, I will hold firm from now on, and I will never change so as to choose to love those who have sinned in such ways."

But someone, I think, will say: "How then did he bring them back to Judea from the land of the Assyrians, or how did he release them from captivity? Was it not because he had changed to gentleness and counted them worthy of mercy and love?" Yes, I too would say that this is true. Admittedly, they received mercy out of his gentleness. But those against whom this word was spoken went away into captivity and died under the punishment, after a long time had passed. Just as, in Egypt, he promised through Moses to bring all those of Israel into the land he had sworn to their fathers, yet some did not enter because they disobeyed, "whose bodies fell in the wilderness," and the land was instead given as an inheritance to those born of them, so you will understand it here too. Those against whom the word was spoken died, but in due time their descendants returned to Judea, when Cyrus at last released them, after they had completed their seventieth year of living in a foreign land.

Those who dared dreadful things against Christ, impieties beyond all words, will also be cast out of the house of God—or rather, they have already been cast out—as will those who loosed a bitter and blasphemous tongue against him, and they will endure a wrath that cannot be revoked. For they are convicted of having raged drunkenly not against one of the prophets, but against the very Master of the prophets. So, even if one passes over in silence the other offences they committed on their own account, one could see their wickedness and the extremity of their depravity in what was done against Christ alone. All their rulers are disobedient. Ephraim is in pain; his roots are dried up; he shall no longer bear fruit. For even if they bear children, I will kill the beloved offspring of their womb. God will reject them, because they did not listen to him, and they will be wanderers among the nations.

He says that not one good person, that is, one who is obedient and submissive, has been found among them: not small, not great, not ruler, not the one under authority and bearing the yoke. For this reason he insists very firmly that they must perish utterly, dug out as it were from the very root, and that they have now become like withered and blighted trees, which need only to be cut down, since they openly confess, as it were, their fruitlessness. That fruitless trees ought to be cut down the Savior himself taught as well, when he ordered the fig tree that bore no fruit to be cut down, as a figure of the synagogue of the Jews: "Why," he says, "should it even use up the ground?" Since Israel has been found fruitless, then, he says, it may fittingly be cut down, for it will yield no fruit. "But even if this should happen," he says, "I will destroy what is born of them." And this is what the beloved offspring of their womb means.

I think it is also necessary to examine closely what the point of this saying is. Why does he say, All their rulers are disobedient? What need was there at all for the submission of the rulers? The saying refers to a certain story from more ancient times. And what that is I will tell in turn.

Israel made a calf in the wilderness while Moses was away, for he had gone up on Mount Sinai to receive the law. Then, when he came down, he was deeply grieved at the sin and broke the calf in pieces, and in a sense he softened the indignant God by his own sincerity and virtue. For he fell down before him and earnestly entreated him, saying: "If you will forgive them their sin, forgive it; but if not, blot me also out of this book of yours that you have written." And God granted the prophet his gentleness toward them all, and indeed said: "I am merciful to them according to your word." Do you see how much the leader's love of God benefited Israel, and how one man was enough to win God over on behalf of all, through submission and obedience? So he fittingly accuses Israel of having turned away entirely, and then of having among its leaders no one to rebuke those who stumble, to draw them away from error, or, that is, able by his own splendor of life and virtue to avert the wrath by appealing to God, as indeed happened in the time of Moses. "Therefore," he says, "they will be thrust out and will be wanderers among the nations." This befell them both then, when they were carried off to the Assyrians, and no less now, when they are loathed for their drunken outrages against Christ. For those of Israel continue throughout the world without hearth or home, strangers everywhere, and without a city. "For I will scatter them to every wind," God said through the holy prophets as well. If, then, we have any care and regard for intimacy with God, let us bow our neck to him, and let us come with good obedience to Christ, who says: "Come to me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you." For in this way we shall be fruitful and unblighted, our root not withering, our fruit not falling to nothing, not wanderers and far from God, but near him and with him, having as our city the one above and in heaven, the mother of the firstborn, the nurse of the saints, the pure dwelling place of the spirits above.

Israel is a vine with fine branches, its fruit abundant. In proportion to the abundance of his fruits he multiplied altars, and in proportion to the good things of his land he built pillars. They divided their hearts; now they will be destroyed. He himself will dig down their altars; their pillars will be brought to wretchedness.

Having said that Ephraim was in pain in his roots, and that he would be fruitless and like those who have never given birth at all, since the savagery of the Assyrians would consume what was born, he must necessarily show also what condition he was in long ago, and that he had been fruitful when he wisely made the life under the law his own. For to the surrounding nations he looked like a beautiful vine with fine branches, and he was rightly admired. Somewhere the blessed David speaks of it in the book of Psalms, addressing God, the Savior of all: "You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out nations and planted it; you made a way before it. It stretched out its branches to the sea, and its shoots to the rivers." It was planted "on a hilltop, in a fertile place," in the words of the prophet. Yet it did not produce grapes but bore thorns instead. For it displayed an iniquity that kept pace, as it were, with the abundance of good things given to it, and matched it—iniquity against God, clearly. For it multiplied altars and built pillars; and the richer it grew in good things from above, the more eager it was for profanation, by worshiping demons, raising altars, and dividing its own heart, as it were, among the error of many gods. "But these things," he says, "will not continue so." Why? For he himself will dig down their altars, and their pillars will be brought to wretchedness—being smashed and pulled down, obviously. You will sensibly refer "he himself" either to God, who holds power over all, or to the person of the Babylonian, as has already been shown many times. For it came about that, along with the cities in Samaria, the temples themselves were burned down and the carved images plundered.

We ought, then, to offer thanksgiving joyfully for whatever we have from God, and not to slip through an excess of good cheer and be carried off somewhere toward what is displeasing to him. Rather we should seek, and hasten very eagerly to achieve, the glories of virtue, not dividing ourselves toward the passions of the world and bowing our neck to Satan. For what Christ said is true: "No one can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will hold fast to one and despise the other." If we are divided, we shall also "be a portion for foxes," in the words of the psalmist, and we shall surely and utterly be in want of the one who knows how to gladden us.
Therefore they will now say, "We have no king, because we did not fear the Lord. And what will the king do for us?" Speaking words, false pretexts, he will make a covenant.

He not only said that their altars would be shaken and their pillars brought to wretchedness, but he adds that they will also repent and lament over their own folly. Having been disappointed in their hope and deceived by the lies of their rulers, they will understand it late and with difficulty. For those among them who occupied the royal thrones said that the golden heifers and the security offered by the other idols would be enough to help them, even if they did not keep the divine law, even if they chose not to do what was commanded through Moses. But experience proved them liars. For they saw those who had long been giving them such assurances and talking so foolishly fall into the hands of their enemies. That is why they say: We have no king, because we did not fear the Lord. "Look, look," they say, "there is no one to help, no one, that is, to stand up against the attacks of the Babylonians. They have all grown weak; our leaders are undone and have fallen. And the cause of the weakness, both theirs and ours, is that we did not fear the Lord. So what benefit is there from our rulers?" he says. "What they offered was nothing but false words and empty covenants," that is, promises. For it is the custom of the divine Scripture to call promises covenants.

It is wise, then, and worthy of all praise, to trust rather in God, and not to be carried away by the words of deceivers into offending God, but sensibly to escape the wrath before experiencing it, and not to lament after suffering, having come late and with difficulty to a useless afterthought.
Judgment will spring up like couch grass on the dry land of the field, against the calf of the house of On.

Couch grass grows in fields, especially in those that are unplowed and lying waste, and it seizes very vigorously upon whatever land happens to be next to it. For it creeps out somehow far and wide, and it is hard for those who wish to stop its constant spread beyond whatever lies beside it to get the better of it. So he says that judgment—clearly from God himself—will spring up like couch grass on the dry land of a field against the calf of the house of On. It is as if he were saying: "A sentence of destruction and a punishing decree will come from me, and it will seize like couch grass upon the calf, that is, upon the objects of worship in the temple of On at Bethel." For that is what "the house of On" signifies. The other translators, for their part, rendered it "the calf of the house of Bethel," whereas the Seventy said "house of On" in place of "house of Bethel." We have already given the reason in what came earlier, but we shall not hesitate to remind you of it. The Egyptians, in their mythmaking, said that Apis was the child of the moon and the offspring of the sun, and "On" is in their usage the sun. And the heifer that Jeroboam made was in the image of the Egyptian Apis. "So, like couch grass," he says, "which seizes upon and overcomes everything that lies beside it, a judgment will come from me against the calf of the house of On," that is, Bethel. For the divine power can always do all things, and nothing will withstand its decrees. "For who will turn back the uplifted hand?" as it is written.
Those who dwell in Samaria will dwell as aliens, for his people mourned over it; and just as they provoked him, they will rejoice over his glory.

See, now he makes plain the judgment that seizes upon the calf and that, like couch grass, naturally spreads out against whomever God wishes. Here too he recalls a story, which we must tell, for in this way and no other shall we understand the prophecy. All idol worshipers had the custom, when times pressed hard and enemies were at hand, of laying hands even on the offerings in their sanctuaries if they ran short of money. Now it is written in the Books of Kingdoms that when the king of Syria was besieging the cities in Samaria, Menahem, who was reigning over Israel at that time, being unable to oppose him with equal forces, sent envoys to Pul, the king of the Assyrians, and persuaded him with gifts to come to his aid and drive off the Syrian. And this was done: for Pul took Damascus by force and slaughtered Ader himself. Now they say that, since a very great weight of gold was demanded, Menahem's affairs were reduced to such necessity that he took away one of the golden heifers and sent it along with the envoys. And Israel mourned when it saw being sent away the heifer it believed to be a god. Yet it comforted itself with cold reasoning, thinking that it would be in greater state and that the Babylonian would set it up in more splendid temples. Besides this, they supposed that it would be worshiped by more nations as well, for the nations of the Persians and Medes are countless. So Menahem sent the heifer as though it were all of solid gold, but Pul took it and smashed it to pieces, for their worship is different and they do not tolerate a heifer. Then, they say, it was found not to be gold, but rather of bronze overlaid with gold. Hence, he says, the Assyrian laughed at Ephraim, that is, at Menahem, who reigned from the tribe of Ephraim, and on top of this he scorned the rash folly of Israel.

Now that we have told the story, that is, the tradition of the Hebrews, come, let us run through the wording as we must, for the construction of the passage is very obscure and extremely difficult. He said, then, that those who dwell in Samaria will dwell as aliens. "Will dwell as aliens" means "will migrate," that is, "those who are now in Samaria will be transported elsewhere"; and he means the calves, that is, the heifers. For they were sent off, as I said, to the Babylonians. And his people mourned over them. Whose people? Clearly that of On, that is, of Apis. "But just as they were seen," he says, "to provoke and dishonor him by sending him to others, so too they will take delight over his glory." For they will suppose that he will be far more renowned, being worshiped by more nations. But they were disappointed in their hope, for he was smashed to pieces and became a laughingstock to the Babylonians. And so their pillar was brought to wretchedness, in the very words of the prophet. They provoked the calf—not that it was truly provoked, for how could senseless matter have suffered this? It means rather that the force of their actions would have angered him, if he really were a god and able to perceive what had befallen him.
For it was carried away from him, and they bound it and took it off to the Assyrians as gifts for King Jareb. Ephraim will receive it as a gift, and Israel will be put to shame by its counsel.

The prophetic word interprets itself for us: what it said obscurely, it now tries to make plain. The calf was carried away from Israel, and they bound it—the passage is speaking with a touch of irony here—and took it off as gifts for King Jareb, that is, “the avenger.” For he was being called in to help, and in a manner of speaking to avenge Samaria as it was being destroyed by the Syrians. Phul, then, will receive the heifer as a gift from Ephraim; and by Ephraim he means the king. But Israel, he says, will be put to shame by its own counsels. For, as I said, because it turned away from the God who has all power and chose instead to worship heifers, it was ridiculous, and was caught out as having fallen into a folly that was old-womanish, insipid and useless. So the prophet, or rather God, speaks the truth when he says through the voice of the saints concerning those who worship the works of their own hands: “See that their heart is ashes, and they go astray.” The passage could also fit those who undermine the correct doctrines of the Church. For just as the shattering of the heifer exposed the folly of Israel, so too their doctrines, shattered by examination and broken to pieces by the power of the truth, will bring shame and confusion on those who put them together, who devised them impiously, and who most thoughtlessly receive them into mind and heart.
Samaria has cast off her king like a twig on the face of the water, and the altars of On will be taken away—sins; thorns and thistles will come up on their altars.

This too, once again, would easily show both the fickleness and the unreasonableness of the ways of those from Israel, that is, of those in Samaria, even toward the very beings they supposed to be gods. And there is nothing surprising in this. For those who impiously outraged the one true God, God by nature, through their apostasies and their running off after every kind of shameful thing—how could they have been loyal toward many falsely named gods made of stone or wood? He says, then, that the calf, which held the rank of both god and king among them, was cast off by those in Samaria; and cast off in such a way that, like a stick that has fallen into the swirling waters, it is carried off wherever those who push it away see fit. And that the sanctuaries will vanish along with the objects of their worship, that the altars will be torn down and the places become places of thorns, when their whole land has been laid waste—how could that be in doubt? He calls the altars the sins of Israel, and very fittingly, since they were impiously set up as a kind of memorial of their ungodliness toward God. And by On, again, he means Apis, that is, the heifers in Bethel and Dan, in whose honor the altars also stood. So whatever God does not establish will in every way and without fail be destroyed. And I take something of this kind to be indicated by what was clearly said through another prophet: “They will build, and I will tear down.”
And they will say to the mountains, “Cover us,” and to the hills, “Fall on us.”

Carved images were worshiped not only in the two cities, I mean Dan and Bethel. There it was the golden heifers; but on the mountains and the hills it was the objects of worship of the surrounding nations: Baal, Baal-peor, Astarte and Chemosh. By these words, then, he indicates that not only will the altars of On, that is, of Apis, or of the heifers, be shaken down, but the sanctuaries on the hills and mountains will in every way and without fail fall as well. For their circumstances will come to such a pitch of misery and terror that they would rather choose to be buried under the very mountains and hills than live to see what they would have to suffer against their will. It should be noted that Christ himself, when he foretold to the Jews the calamities that would be brought on them for their outrages against him, used the same words: “Then you will say,” he says, “to the mountains, ‘Cover us,’ and to the hills, ‘Fall on us.’” For when evils reach their limit and terrors become extreme, they sometimes make death, bitter though it is, seem greatly to be desired by most people. So to the very mountains and hills on which the false worship took place, and on which the crimes of ungodliness against God were dared, they will all but say, he says, “Fall on us, and come before the savagery of the Babylonian sword and the inglorious and unbearable misery of being led away into captivity.”

Since the hills, Israel has sinned; there they stood. War will not overtake them on the hill; it came upon the children of iniquity. And peoples will be gathered against them when they are chastised for their two iniquities.

He says that the apostasy carried on in the mountains and hills was older than the error concerning the heifers. Indeed, it was when the ten tribes took possession of Samaria, having shaken off the yoke of Rehoboam's rule, that Jeroboam brought in the heifers; but while they were still [?], they were practicing the error on the mountains and hills, since Solomon yielded and gave way to his foreign wives, and at that time even set up altars and sanctuaries for the objects of their worship. So from the time the hills and the playthings on them and the false worship were devised, from that time Israel has offended. This too would be no unclear proof of God's gentleness, which does not bring itself to punish the ungodly even over a long time, but rather holds back and waits, perhaps, for those who have gone astray to repent. But they were all the more hard-hearted and were caught suffering from still worse ills. For to the hills they added the inventions concerning the heifers as well. And while they sacrificed to demons on mountains and hills and supposed they were being devout toward vain things, they perhaps imagined to themselves, or rather firmly believed, that they would stand secure in prosperity, would be stronger than their opponents, and could not be taken by their enemies. This is a common sickness among those who go astray.

Indeed, when they went down into Egypt after Jerusalem had been taken by the Babylonian, the prophet Jeremiah advised them to stop sacrificing to idols, so that some mercy might be shown them by the God who is able to save. But they claimed that they had fallen into their troubles for this very reason: that they had stopped being willing to carry out the customary rites, and had been found neglecting the honor due to their vain gods. It is written thus: “Then all the men who knew that their wives burned incense to other gods, and all the women, a great assembly, and all the people living in the land of Egypt, in the land of Pathros, answered Jeremiah, saying, ‘As for the word you have spoken to us in the name of the Lord, we will not listen to it. For we will certainly do every word that goes out of our mouth: we will burn incense to the queen of heaven and pour out drink offerings to her, just as we and our fathers, our kings and our princes did in the cities of Judah and outside Jerusalem. Then we had our fill of bread and were well off, and saw no evil. But since we stopped burning incense to the queen of heaven, we have all been brought low, and have perished by sword and by famine.’” He therefore blames those from Israel both for their foolish talk and for the rottenness of their hope, and says of the hills that there they stood; that is, as they themselves say, or rather think to themselves, by serving the carved images there they had gained secure prosperity and stood firm amid unshakable blessings. And again, as they think, nothing at all that usually brings grief will overtake them on the hill, if they choose to carry out the customary rites for the carved images. But they have been deceived, he says, and their hope has failed. For war has come upon them, since they are children of iniquity, and they will learn by experience itself that their unbridledness is bitter. And who would be the ones through whom their chastisement will come? A vast gathering of enemies. This is what “peoples will be gathered against them” means; and the calamities of war will without fail befall them, when they are chastised for their two iniquities. What these are he showed us more clearly through the voice of Jeremiah, saying: “The heaven was astonished at this and shuddered greatly, says the Lord, for my people have done two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves broken cisterns that will not be able to hold water.”
Ephraim is a trained heifer that loves victory; but I will come upon the beauty of her neck. I will mount Ephraim, and I will pass over Judah in silence.

He likens Ephraim to a calf that is stubborn and extremely unruly, that does not know how to be checked in whatever impulse it may happen to have, or will not put up with being tamed, but is always seeking to win and rushes on after whatever it fancies with unrestrained impulses. But even if he is like this, he says, he will give way, though unwillingly. For he will be broken by the onslaught of calamities, as God yokes him, all but doing it with his own hand, and undoes the beauty of his neck, that is, the part of Israel that is especially rebellious. This was their monarchy, which provoked the peoples under its hand to apostasy. So it will be thrown down, as God bears down on it; for this, I think, is what “I will mount Ephraim” means. And it is in keeping with his providential dealings that he says, “I will pass over Judah in silence,” meaning, “For a little while I will put Judah off, not subjecting him to punishment, not yet bringing on him the effects of my wrath, but rather bearing with him and quietly giving way.” And for what reason? Because Ephraim, that is, the ten tribes, as I said before, had turned wholly to choosing to carry out the works of error; whereas the two tribes in Jerusalem, I mean Judah and Benjamin, were often under upright and devout kings who shook down the playthings of idolatry and persuaded them to live decently and according to the law. Such was Amaziah son of Joash, a devout and righteous man; and likewise Hezekiah, who was admired equally with the one just mentioned, zealous and dear to God. For this reason the ten tribes suffered captivity first; but when the Babylonian marched against Jerusalem, he did no harm, but rather went off to his own land, a terrified fugitive, when one hundred and eighty-five thousand of the Assyrians fell in a single night by the hand of an angel. Since, then, God is forbearing and bears with our weaknesses, let us not grow careless, nor be found slack in doing what pleases him and is dear to him.
Jacob will be strong against him.

I said that the Assyrian, after leading his forces on campaign, uprooting all Samaria and burning both its cities and its temples, afterward besieged Jerusalem, but did not take it at all, since God was its shield; for one hundred and eighty-five thousand were slain by an angel in a single night. This, I believe, is what he now foretells when he says, “Jacob will be strong against him.” Against whom? Clearly, against Rabshakeh, who was going to besiege it. By Jacob he means those of Jacob's blood, I mean Judah and Benjamin. But the phrase could also apply, if one wished, to all Israel.

Again, the sense of the prophecy seems to bring to our minds an older event, as if God were all but fulfilling the promise he made to the inspired Jacob. For when he wrestled with him in the form of a man at night beyond the brook Jabbok, and then, when dawn had come and day was breaking, God wished to depart, saying, “Let me go, for the dawn has come up,” and Jacob said he would not let him go unless he blessed him, he then heard: “For you have been strong with God, and you will be mighty with men.” Perhaps this is what the word of the prophecy is hinting to us in the present passage, in stating very plainly, “Jacob will be strong against him.” Notice the precision of the promise: he does not say that Jacob will overpower the Assyrians, but that he will be strong; for he was strong in God, not through himself.
By the Same Author: On the Prophet Hosea, Volume Six.
Sow for yourselves unto righteousness, gather the vintage for the fruit of life, light for yourselves the light of knowledge; seek the Lord until the fruits of righteousness come to you.

There are always two ways of giving exhortation. Either we explain the punishment that awaits those who choose to be careless, and so we usually frighten people into choosing, with real urgency, to live an upright life; or we announce the honours prepared for the good, and so make those we teach more eager to go on towards the better life, the one most in keeping with the law. The God of all does something like this here. He threatened those who had gone astray with wars and disasters, with being carried off among foreigners, with cities set on fire, and with the savagery of the enemy. Yet he does not stop his exhortation there. See, he helps them once more in another way. He commands them to let go of what is useless, the cause of all their misery, and to choose instead what is most able to help them: to be like farmers, sowing unto righteousness and gathering the vintage for the fruit of life. For as the blessed Paul writes, "Whatever a man sows, that he will also reap." And as it is written, "He who sows what is worthless will reap evil"; but the worker of righteousness will be full of salvation and life, illustrious and worthy to be envied, and he will gather the vintage of the wine "that gladdens the heart of man." Besides this, those who want to win approval must let the light of true knowledge make its home in their mind and heart. Those who worship "the creation rather than the [?]" do not have that light. How then can one rightly be able to sow unto righteousness, and also to gather the vintage for the fruit of life, and to receive the bright light of knowledge? He himself showed us when he added: Seek the Lord until the fruits of righteousness come to you. We seek God not as though in a place, for that would be foolish, since the divine is not in a place. We seek him rather in the disposition of the soul, with a mind eagerly inclined towards everything that pleases him, looking towards a knowledge that is right and polished and open to no reproach from any side. For when we have found him in this way, we shall also be rich in the possession of all other goods. Or does Christ not speak the truth when he says, "Apart from me you can do nothing"? I think that to those accustomed to think rightly this is in no way doubtful. For our possession of every good is with God, and through God, and from God.

One might very reasonably say that the words Sow for yourselves unto righteousness, and what follows, are addressed not only to those who served idols, but also to those who run away from the right faith and attach themselves instead "to spirits of error, in the hypocrisy of demons, seared in their conscience," as the most wise Paul writes. These people do sow, when they devote themselves to the labours of knowledge and of love for learning; but not for works of righteousness. They sow for injustice and ungodliness, "deceiving and being deceived," and "wounding the weak conscience of the brothers, for whom Christ died." So they do not gather the vintage for the fruit of life. How could they? They gather it for punishment and judgment. Indeed Christ said, "Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him to have a great millstone hung around his neck and to be drowned in the depth of the sea." Let them therefore love the truth. This is the light of knowledge; this is how God is sought. From this the fruits of righteousness will spring up for them unto life, and wine will be gathered as well: not bodily wine, but spiritual wine, given through the Spirit, which gladdens both heart and mind.

Why have you passed over ungodliness in silence, and gathered the vintage of its injustices, and eaten false fruit? Because you hoped in your chariots, in the multitude of your power; and destruction will rise up among your people, and all your walled places will be gone.

Again he accuses them, as people who out of a taste for evil chose to keep quiet where they should never have kept quiet, and who very foolishly held their tongues over things that would naturally grieve God greatly. "They ought," he says, "to have thrust away with all their strength the ungodliness committed against me, and to have rebuked those who counselled shameful things; and by doing so they would have come to every good. Instead they kept silent and accepted the ways of error. There was no one among them to stand against those who introduced these novelties, no one to set against them what the law says and to remind them of what had been decreed." For it is written, "You shall have no other gods besides me," and again, "You shall not make for yourself an idol." But they gave very little thought to these things. They kept silent, honouring ungodliness, that is, the [?]. So they have gathered the vintage of the injustice that followed from it; they have eaten false fruit, that is, they have had a [?] and useless hope. For the true fruit, the one that can save and help, is love for God and the glories of righteousness; but false fruit may fittingly be understood as the fruit of ungodliness, for it always leads in the end to what no one would wish for. What, then, was the false fruit that came to them from their ungodliness? He showed it at once, adding: Because you hoped in your chariots, in the multitude of your power; and destruction will rise up among your people, and all your walled places will be gone. "You have acted with no small ungodliness," he says, "worshipping wood and stones and dishonouring the God who alone is God by nature and in truth. Then, when war had been announced and had already come inside your very gates, you did not rather seek help from me. Instead you trusted in your own forces and the multitude of your chariots, and supposed you would overcome the strength of the enemy, thinking that the protection and help of the falsely named gods was enough for you. This will be your false fruit. For there will be destruction upon the peoples, and every splendid and strongly walled city will be shaken to the ground." For whatever God does not uphold will fall, completely and in every way.

Let these words be spoken by us too, or rather by God, to those who are willing to sit at the feet of the unholy heretics and who pretend to be learning the things that lead to life and understanding. These people pass over ungodliness in silence. They put up with hearing blasphemers, although they ought to denounce them as strongly as possible. So they will share in their own bad counsel and will reap the fruits of injustice. For they will eat what is false, receiving a counterfeit knowledge that ought to be thrown away, and being taught perverse things, everything that tries to debase the beauty of the truth. And who could doubt that all their power too will fall, when God overthrows it, and that they will go off into ruin and destruction?
As the ruler Zalmunna from the house of Jerubbaal, in the days of war, dashed the mother to the ground upon her children, so will I do to you, house of Israel, because of your wickedness.

It is written in the book of Judges that at one time Israel turned aside after the Baals. In this way they offended God, and they were handed over into the hands of Midian for seven whole years. They suffered such harsh oppression from their conquerors that they even lived among the rocks, hiding in them and barely keeping themselves alive there, and made the rough terrain their rampart, because they had completely given up on fighting. So it happened at that time that those who fell into the hands of the Midianites were cruelly killed, so that children perished together with their wretched mothers, all mercy having been taken away. Their rulers were Oreb and Zeeb, Zebah and Zalmunna. The disaster went on until God took pity on suffering Israel and raised up Gideon, whom his father and the local people renamed Jerubbaal, for the following reason. God had instructed him through the voice of an angel, and he pulled down the pillar of Baal and cut down its grove, secretly and at night. When the inhabitants of the little town came to the sacred precinct at dawn, eager to perform their usual rites, they saw Baal thrown down and the grove fallen on top of him. They guessed at once that this was Gideon's zeal for God, and they laid the blame for the deed on him. Then they went to his father and said, "Give us your son, so that we may kill him, because he pulled down Baal." To this he replied, "Will you avenge Baal? If he is a god, let him contend with the one who pulled him down." From then on Gideon was renamed Jerubbaal, which means "Let Baal contend."

"Just as Zalmunna," he says, "the leader of the Midianite host, dashed the mother to the ground upon her children from the house of Gideon, that is, Jerubbaal, in the very same way the Assyrian general will wage war against you cruelly and inhumanly and without any pity, and will dash the mother to the ground together with her children." This will happen because of your wickedness. For the God of all, being a just judge, does not punish without cause. But if the offences of those who have offended him stretch on beyond all measure, then he brings upon them, in proportion, the effects of his wrath. If, then, we would beg off his anger, we must first take good care to avoid sinning and, so to speak, whetting the divine and most gentle nature into indignation, or perhaps forcing it to this against its will by the excess of our faults. It should be known that some of the earlier interpreters say it was not Zalmunna, ruler of the Midianites, who dashed the mother to the ground upon her children from the house of Jerubbaal, that is, of Israel (for sometimes the whole people is indicated by its leaders), but rather that Gideon dashed the mother to the ground upon her children in the house of Zalmunna. But I think it better, and more strongly supported by what is fitting, to take it not in this way but in the other. For just as at that time, when Israel had inclined towards the Baals, their children were dashed to the ground together with their mothers by the hand of foreigners, so now too, since Ephraim has turned aside to idolatry, their offspring will again be dashed to the ground together with those who bore them, by barbarians, that is, the Assyrians. So I think the passage will better keep its plausibility, and the likeness drawn, as from an image, from the ancient events to the more recent ones, if the meaning of the text is understood in this way.
At dawn they were cast off; the king of Israel was cast off.

The other translators, and also the Hebrew text, say plainly, "Like the dawn they were cast off," meaning by this that Israel fell away from its intimacy with God as though in a very short time, that is, swiftly and without delay. For the time of dawn is very brief: it comes as soon as the light of day begins to break, yet when the sun has risen and sent out its first ray, it is immediately dissolved and gone. So like the dawn, that is, in a short, brief and very contracted time, they were cast off together with their leaders. Either we shall understand it in this way, or we shall take it in another sense. When God does not yet bring the penalties for human sins, or when he extends his forbearance for a longer time, it is not unfitting to compare him to people asleep at night. Indeed the blessed prophets have cried out to us in many ways, signifying just this. The most wise Jeremiah says, "Do not be like a man asleep, or like a man who cannot save." And the inspired psalmist at one point says, "Awake! Why do you sleep, O Lord, O Lord? Arise, and do not reject us for ever." At another point, seeing him roused to help certain people, he says, "And the Lord awoke as one who sleeps."

So it seems that he calls "dawn" the time when he, as it were, wakes up concerning them, for it is at dawn that we rise from sleep. When God has become wakeful concerning them, and has, so to speak, roused himself at last to examine what they have done, they will be rejected and cast off, even though in the time already past, because of his very great forbearance, he had all but dozed concerning them. He says that the king too was cast off together with the people, because the kingdom of Ephraim was about to be removed from the midst. For, as I said, when they returned to Judea after the time of the captivity, they all came under one king, just as they had been at the beginning, before the times of the conquest. For when all Israel still existed together, kings from the tribe of Judah reigned in Jerusalem.
For Israel was a child, and I loved him, and out of Egypt I called his children. As I called them, so they went away from my presence.

Here the passage seems to be meeting an objection raised by some. Let us imagine someone who thinks this over, or even says it openly: "If those of Israel's blood were going to fall away at some point and go out from God's presence, and become loathsome and hated, why were they called at all in the first place?" To this God, very fittingly, gives a kind of explanation, saying: Israel was a child, and I loved him, and out of Egypt I called his children. "Jacob, who was renamed Israel, was a plain man," he says, "and that is why I loved him." For while they were still in the womb, he says, "I loved Jacob, but Esau I hated." "Since, then, I loved him, I also rescued his children from the oppression of the Egyptians. For I show mercy to thousands of those who love me." What, then, of those who were honoured and chosen for their fathers' sake, who were honoured with the grace of freedom and released from slavery and toil? Did they honour him in return? Did they strive to gladden with their goodwill the God who had shielded them? "Not at all," he says. They ran away from their Master; they went off from the one who had honoured them; they insulted the one who had called them. And in what way did they go off? Was it one by one, a few at a time, slipping away from right thinking and being stolen away by the deceptions of others? Not at all. They broke away in the same way as they had been called, that is, as a whole multitude and by tribes, with all their kin and all their households. For this is how they came out of Egypt at that time. We remember that when Pharaoh reluctantly promised to let Israel go, and wanted to learn who made up the multitude that was departing, saying plainly, "Who exactly are the ones who are going?", Moses answered, "We will go with our young and with our old, with our sons and daughters, and with our sheep and our cattle." So the calling was by whole tribes and as a multitude, by family and by household; and the apostasy was in the same way. He indicates its ugliness most strongly when he says, they went away from my presence. For those whom the Master of all chooses to hate he would not look upon, in the sense of what is sung in the Psalms: Look upon me and have mercy on me. For it is written, "The eyes of the Lord are on the righteous"; and he himself says somewhere, "And upon whom shall I look, but on the one who is humble and quiet, and trembles at my words?"

They sacrificed to the Baals and burned incense to the carved images. And I bound Ephraim's feet together; I took him up on my arm; and they did not know that I heal them. In the destruction of men I stretched them out with the bonds of my love.

He shows that the gentleness within him is boundless and worthy of God. To grant good things to those who already believe and know him and have chosen to worship him alone would have a fitting reason, and the matter would not lie outside what is reasonable; for if one chooses to act rightly, one honours someone who is already one's own and has already come running to one. But to show oneself the giver of every good even to those who are still profane and do not know him would be an excess of love for humanity and a marvel, and truly a proof of a gentleness worthy of God. This is why the Saviour himself, taking pity on our condition and, as God, granting a mercy in no way due to those who love to sin, said at one time, "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick," and at another, "I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." The most wise Paul too greatly marvels at the incomparable forbearance of God, the ruler of all, and says, "Christ came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the first." "They, then," he says, that is, those of Israel, "were going astray in Egypt; they did not yet know me, the true God. Instead they were caught offering sacrifices to the Baals, that is, to the idols, and burning incense to the carved images, that is, to the objects of worship of the local people. But I, since I am kind and good, even though Ephraim (that is, Israel as a whole, indicated here by one tribe) was so perverse, bound his feet together," he says.

What this means he made clear himself, saying: I took him up on my arm. The comparison comes from what is done with infants. Those who take little babies up in their arms, as it were, bind their feet together by bringing the feet together. For, I think, anything that is held curled up must have its thighs and knees drawn in. That is what I bound his feet together means, just as it is written of Abraham that he bound the feet of his son Isaac when he expected to sacrifice him to God. It is necessary to know, though, that the Hebrew version, and the version of the others too, does not have I bound his feet together, but rather, "I became like a nurse to Ephraim." "So I was like this towards them, but they did not know, that is, they did not understand, they did not perceive, that by destroying others I was setting their affairs right." For this is what I heal them in destruction means. The Egyptians were the first to be destroyed, by the ten plagues, when Pharaoh would not let the people go. After the plagues of Egypt the Hittites, Hivites and Amorites, Canaanites and Jebusites perished. Israel conquered them by force and inherited the land of the promise, while God levelled every steep place before them and gave them the power to prevail over their enemies. "So they do not perceive," he says, "that in destroying men of their own kind I was ordering their affairs well." And I stretched them out, that is, I bound them tight and held them together as in bonds of love. If they had been wise, they would surely have noticed and reasoned among themselves why these nations were destroyed by God and we were brought in in their place. For if they had understood in this way that I hate the wicked and take no account of the one who serves demons, they would perhaps have stopped choosing to do the same things.

Those who wish to gladden God, then, need a sober mind and a good heart, and must make the wrath that falls on others an occasion for their own safety. And how terrible a thing ingratitude is, and how one who has fallen into this disease would rightly be punished as though convicted of every kind of wickedness, we can easily see from this: "The ungrateful man," it says, "is like a blasphemer."
And I shall be to them like a man striking him on his cheeks; and I will look upon him, I shall prevail with him.

Since he had said that he loved Ephraim, and took him up on his arm like an infant, and held him tight as with bonds of love, even though Ephraim was still profane and wicked, he therefore says he will also bring him back when he sins. "For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and scourges every son whom he receives." See how he promises that even the manner of his rebuke will not lack a gentleness worthy of God. For he says that his dealings with them will be like slaps on the cheek given by a man's hand. This should be understood as the action of a father, who mixes his anger with mercy and love and strikes softly, as it were, and barely with his hand, so that the child may not be left entirely without rebuke.

And because he loved him, he also promises to look upon him. For he grants his oversight to those he chooses to honour. And he prevails with us, overcoming by his divine skill and power those who choose to suffer from unruliness. For if he does not help us by persuasion, he turns us by necessity to choose to do what is better, and frightens us by afflictions into what is most beneficial to us and necessary for salvation. Let the God of all, then, hear us say, "Lord, in a little affliction your discipline was upon us"—this is the slap—and again, "Discipline us, Lord, but in judgment and not in anger, so that you may not make us few." For to the right-minded, being disciplined is not bitter; but being punished in wrath is terrible and hard to bear, or rather a thing full of destruction.

Ephraim dwelt in the land of Egypt, and Assur himself was his king, because he would not return. And the sword grew weak in his cities, and came to rest in his hands; and they shall eat of their own counsels.

Being cut off from God brings us, in every way and without fail, to the very worst of all evils. This happens when we turn away without restraint and choose to do what is wicked, and in a sense insult him by our disobedience, even though he calls us to salvation. Blessed Paul makes this clear when he says, “See, brothers, that you do not refuse the one who calls”; but it will be no less plain from the passage before us. For the utterly wretched Ephraim, he says, left the land that had borne him and made the land of the Egyptians his own, fearing the disasters of war. He also came under Assur himself and bowed his neck beneath foreign sceptres, for he had slid down into this depth of misery. And if anyone asks the reason, he will hear the one who knows all things saying: “Because he would not return.” For when God offered amnesty and, as it were, commanded him to go back, and so to return to what pleased God, turning away from wickedness and leaping out of the pits of idolatry, he was terribly negligent and would not return. For this reason he was finally captured and came under the hand of those who hated him. For the sword grew weak in his cities and came to rest in his hands; that is, in no city of Ephraim was any man found who was formidable in battle and able to wield the sword. For the hands of those who used to hold it went slack, and were, as it were, unstrung. And since they both planned and did what was evil against themselves, they will eat the fruits of their own bad counsel.

It is a bitter thing, then, to dare to dishonor the Savior by disobedience. Even if some have the chance of escaping their offenses through God's gentleness, negligence does not go unpunished. For we shall dwell in Egypt; that is, we shall be homeless and wanderers in every way and without fail, not by leaving a physical land and moving to another, but by leaving the inheritance of the saints. And we shall also come under Assur, clearly meaning the ruler of this age. We shall lie beneath him as slaves and captives, bowing to his will, because the sword has grown weak among us and come to rest. For it is not, it is not possible for those who love sin to take up “the whole armor of God” and the sword “of the Spirit, which is the word of God.” By “sword” you will understand also the most warlike and God-loving movement, as it were, of our mind. We lead it out against the passions and set it in array against the devil's evil deeds, and so we travel the pious and blameless path and bind upon our own heads the glories of the gospel way of life.
And his people are hanging from his dwelling; and God will be angry at his precious things, and will not exalt him.

The sense of this passage is very hard to express, and the arrangement of the words is rough; those who wish to understand it will need a great deal of clarification. But what it means to show is, in brief, as follows. Ephraim, he says, went off to the Egyptians, and also came under a king, Assur. Then, as though someone were asking, “Why, and in what way, was he allowed to suffer this? How did Israel come to serve foreigners?”, he next sets out the explanations. First he says, “He would not return”: for though gentleness was offered, he was found, he says, negligent and disobedient even in this. Then, “and the sword grew weak in his cities.” For there was, as I said, no one to stand against the Assyrians, or anyone distinguished in tactics, since God was paralyzing their fighting spirit and perhaps shaking even the very strong in battle beforehand with cowardice. But there was another reason too for his falling under Assur. What was it? The people, that is, Ephraim, all but hung from him, namely from Assur, and wished to depart from its own dwelling to the land of the Persians and Medes. We certainly do not say that Ephraim himself would have wished to suffer this. But as far as his offenses went, he all but sought to suffer such terrible things. For when he could have escaped the wrath by choosing to turn to what was better and more fitting, he all but hung from Assur. And leaving the land that bore him, that is, his own dwelling, he foolishly longed to go to Assur's land, even though God had declared that he would certainly bring such things upon him if he would not repent. And since they slid down to this end, God will be angry at his precious things. The precious things, the choice and foremost of the peoples, are clearly the kings and leaders. They too were carried off together with the common crowd, pitiable and enslaved, ranked among captives of war, because they led astray those under their hand and became a snare to those who could have traveled the straight road if they had wished. For the one who leads always goes before those beneath him. So they will be humbled and cast off, though they had enjoyed very great glory; for renown always attends the thrones of kingship. But God would not exalt them, for the kingdom of Ephraim has come to an end, as I have already said many times.

So we who are in Christ must above all guard against the inclination toward what is base, especially when God is reining us in. If we do not do this, we shall willingly place the devil's yoke on ourselves, all but hanging on our love for him and going with all eagerness to come under him from then on and to carry out what pleases him. But if this happens, we shall provoke God, and so we shall be brought low, with a mind that is base and trampled underfoot, since God paralyzes us and will not consent to raise us up by courage for what is good.

What shall I do with you, Ephraim? Shall I shield you, Israel? What shall I do with you? I will make you like Admah and like Zeboiim. My heart is turned within me; my repentance is stirred up. I will not act according to the anger of my wrath; I will not abandon Ephraim to be blotted out, because I am God and not a man, the Holy One in you.

He set out the charges first, showing that the sharpest wrath now had to be brought upon them in every way and without fail, since they had done unholy things and had acted impiously against God beyond all measure, so that no kind of mercy was left for them any longer. But since he is good, the source and origin of gentleness, he checks the impulse. He does not rebuke it, as though it had arisen unreasonably, on the basis of some better reasoning; for the divine and ineffable nature could never miss the thoughts or actions most fitting to it. Rather, out of gentleness he holds back, as it were, what they deserved and prevents what was most fitting for them, namely total destruction and the need to be dug up, as it were, by the very root. That is why he says, “What shall I do with you?” What course, he says, shall I take in settling your affairs? Shall I shield you and defend you again, and make you hard to conquer for those who wish to plot against you? But then how will this come about? For punishment rather than prosperity would be fitting for those who have done terrible things against God. So, giving what is deserved and fixing penalties equal to your offenses, I will make you like Admah and like Zeboiim. These were cities of the region of Sodom, which the fire that came down devoured to their very foundations. But I will not do even this, he says, though it ought justly to happen. I will hold back, for I have changed my mind. I will not give free rein to my wrath; I would not give Ephraim over to utter destruction, though he has become wicked. For what reason? Did they not deserve to suffer it? Yes, he says, but I am God and not a man; that is, I am good and do not let the impulses of anger prevail, for such a passion is human. “Why then do you still punish,” someone says, “if you are God, not ruled by anger but rather following your inborn gentleness?” I punish, he says, because I am not only good, as God, but also holy besides. I hate injustice, I turn away from the defiled, I reject the one hateful to God, I turn the sinner back, I scour away what is profane, so that he may be joined to me again.

So the Prophet helps us when he cries out and says, “Seek the Lord, and while you can find him, call upon him; when he draws near to you, let the ungodly forsake his ways and the lawless man his counsels, and let him turn back to the Lord, and he will find mercy.” For if we set great store by being with God, we must refuse to sin with all our strength and remember him who says, “You shall be holy, because I am holy.”
And I will not enter into a city. I will walk after the Lord.

Sometimes knowledge of the future comes precisely upon the minds of the holy Prophets, as the Holy Spirit flashes the matter upon them like lightning. So, in the middle of their own words, or rather the words that come from above and from God, they sometimes cry out beforehand the words of certain people, whether repenting, giving thanks, or leaping for joy at the things God promises will gladden them. We shall find that something like this happened to blessed Hosea here. For the God of all was promising gentleness and said he would not utterly destroy those who had sinned, because he is God, that is, good, and not a man; for he who is above all creation is not like us. And they, as though recognizing their own offenses and already somehow blushing at this great and unexpected grace, promise to give up the things they had devised, through which they had given offense. And what these things are, God has again made fully clear to us through the prophet himself. For a little earlier, accusing both Judah and Ephraim, he said, “And Israel forgot him who made him and built sacred precincts, and Judah multiplied fortified cities; and I will send fire upon his cities, and it will devour their foundations.” For Ephraim, that is, Israel, built altars and precincts to the idols throughout Samaria and so slid into apostasy. They forgot God and, counting love for him as worth nothing, kept on provoking him. Judah, on the other hand, though they trusted in God and from times long past had been saved by him and through him, provoked him to anger in many other ways, but above all in this one. For when God threatened to send the Assyrian against them to devastate the land, Judah walled up his cities, thinking that even if God did not will it, he would be saved by the strength of his city walls and would get the better of the hand of the one fighting him.

So, since God promises the good things that come from his gentleness even to those who have given grave offense, those who are being saved now say for their part that they will cease from their improper undertakings and plans alike. Let Judah cry out, “I will not enter into a city”; that is, I will make no wall apart from God; I will make my hope in him my security; I will run for refuge to the right hand of the Savior; he alone will suffice for my salvation. I will confess that it is futile and utterly useless to expect that, when war is overrunning the land, I will be saved by entering a city. Therefore I will not enter into a city. And let Israel, that is, Ephraim, in turn cry out something else, namely, “I will walk after the Lord.” I will cease, he says, from the old offenses; from now on I will follow the divine laws; I will make the God of all my guide. And if anyone goes toward what pleases God, he will surely acknowledge him alone, offer worship to him, and bow down to absolutely no one else besides him.

He will roar like a lion, for he himself will roar, and the children of the waters will be amazed; and they will fly like a bird out of Egypt and like a dove out of the land of the Assyrians; and I will restore them to their homes, says the Lord.

When the time had at last come and the period had run its course in which Israel was to be released from captivity, Cyrus son of Cambyses, who had taken power over the Persians and Medes, marched with a vast host and an irresistible force against Babylon itself and the land of the Assyrians, God having roused him to this. Indeed, the prophet Jeremiah, foretelling the capture of Babylon, says about the Medes and Persians, “They will attack you, and Babylon will be taken, and you will not know it; you were found and seized, because you opposed the Lord.” And about Cyrus: “A lion has come up from his lair; destroying nations, he has set out and gone forth from his place to make your land a desolation, and your cities will be torn down so that they are not inhabited.” That it was the God of all who gave Cyrus the power to conquer, the prophet Isaiah will make fully clear when he says, “Thus says the Lord to my anointed, Cyrus, whose right hand I have grasped, that nations may obey before him; and I will break the strength of kings; I will open doors before him, and cities will not be shut. I will go before you and level mountains; I will shatter bronze doors and smash iron bars, and I will give you treasures of darkness, hidden ones; I will open to you unseen ones.” So Cyrus conquered and took the land of the Babylonians by force, and he released Israel; and they returned home and settled in their own land.

The prophet Hosea interprets this story when he says, “He will roar like a lion.” Who will roar? Cyrus, clearly. It is as if he were saying, perhaps, “Terrible and crushing will be the war that Cyrus thunders against the land of the Babylonians.” And when he roars, and as it were shouts against his enemies like a lion, “the children of the waters will be amazed.” He says “will be amazed” in the sense of “will be panic-stricken.” By the children of the waters he means the Babylonians, who, yielding nothing in cowardice to the children of the waters, that is, to the creatures that swim in the waters, namely fish, will be captured, having proved in actual experience to be easily frightened and unmanly. For the race of fish is extremely prone to fear; it flees noises and shrinks even from the shadow of the one hunting it. So when Cyrus roars, he says, and raises some terrible and dreadful war cry against the land of the Babylonians, the children of the waters will be panic-stricken with fear; that is, the Babylonians, who yield nothing to fish in cowardice. Then those who had long ago fled together into Egypt will fly away from it like a bird and a dove, and those caught in the snares of captivity will run away from the land of the Chaldeans. They will return at last and dwell in their own land.

Since, then, we can have good things by bowing the neck of our mind to God and acting under him alone, let us not walk of our own accord toward what grieves us, as if dragging upon ourselves a self-invited impulse of wrath; for we can, as I said, stand secure in prosperity by delighting the Master through a lawful way of life and conduct and through sincerity toward him.
Ephraim has surrounded me with falsehood, and the house of Israel and Judah with impiety.

God is by nature good and compassionate, and striking anyone at all is against his will. Yet he is necessarily summoned to an indignation that aims at conversion when people's offenses go beyond reason and measure. He teaches us this again through the passage before us.
