For he all but says, “As I cast and turned the eye of my divinity here and there, and as it were all around in a circle, the falsehood and impiety of Ephraim and Judah were to be seen everywhere.” By falsehood he means the frivolities of idolatry and the worship of vain things; by impiety, perhaps, the insult against God. For how is it not a terrible and utterly outrageous impiety to shake off the one who is God by nature and in truth and foolishly bow down to wood and stones; that is, to worship the creature rather than the Creator, and to try to crown with the Lord's own exaltation the things he brought into being?
Now God has known them, and they will be called a holy people of God.

The house of Ephraim and Judah, he says, has surrounded me with falsehood and impiety. Even so, I will be kind, bringing upon them a measured stirring of wrath. For I have known them: they could not learn better ways otherwise, unless they also suffered some of the things that cause grief and call one to an awareness of one's sins. So God has known them; that is, he has not been ignorant of the path of conversion that would benefit them. And the thing will not be without profit for them, for the result will be that they are ranked among the holy peoples of God. For once the wickedness in them has been melted away through hardship and afflictions, they will be pure and sanctified. And they will have learned by experience that sincere love toward God will win them every delight and prosperity, just as, of course, the charges of apostasy cast them into the pits of slavery and affliction.
But Ephraim is an evil spirit; he pursued the scorching wind. All day long he multiplied empty and vain things, and he made a covenant with the Assyrians, and he traded oil to Egypt.

The discourse moves again from the common multitude to those from the tribe of Ephraim who reigned over Israel in Samaria. He says they are an evil spirit because their minds were hard to change and they were utterly bent and uncontrollable in their apostasy from God. For he says, “He pursued the scorching wind”; that is, though he could have been under my shade, he went off to the scorching wind like a deserter. By the scorching wind he means the burning of afflictions and the disaster that sets everything ablaze. Indeed, the wise author of Proverbs speaks of troubles figuratively in this way, saying, “An understanding son was saved from the heat; but a lawless son is blasted by the wind at harvest.” So Ephraim, since he is an evil spirit, pursued the scorching wind; that is, he sought it and ran off to it of his own will. But the wise say concerning God, “In his shade I longed to be, and I sat down.” [?] They call the protection of help from God above a shade. But Ephraim did not do this; he sought the scorching wind. How, or in what way? All day long he multiplied empty and vain things; that is, at every season he did and planned cold and useless things. What were these? He made a covenant with the Assyrians. I have already said before, many times, that some of the kings in Samaria and in Jerusalem sometimes tried to buy peace with the Assyrians and security from that quarter with money, and at other times called in the help of the Egyptians. Trading for the promise of their goodwill, they sent the produce of their own land, together, of course, with other things. The land of the Samaritans bears olives, and oil was prized in Egypt, since that land does not produce it. So hope in human beings is empty and vain. Let the one who trusts in God, then, dance in triumph over the one who trusts in human beings, saying that word in the Psalms: “Behold the man who did not make God his helper, but hoped in the abundance of his wealth and grew strong in his vanity. But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God; I have hoped in the mercy of God forever, and to the ages of ages.”

Those who love goodness and wish to live in safety should above all love being under God's shade. They do this by provoking him in no way at all, and by shunning offense against him as they would the very gates of Hades.
And the Lord has a case against Judah, to punish Jacob; according to his ways and according to his practices he will repay him.

Just as, by naming Ephraim, he indicated that we should understand those of the tribe of Ephraim who reigned, so here too, by the name of the reigning tribe, he signifies those of the tribe of Judah who reigned at various times. Having rebuked Ephraim, that is, those of Ephraim who ruled over Israel, calling him an evil spirit and saying that he multiplied empty and vain things by making covenants with the Assyrians and trading oil to Egypt, he now in turn accuses those of Judah. He says very aptly that the God of all will enter into judgment with them, as though avenging Jacob, I mean the Patriarch, who had been wronged in no small way. For those descended from him chose not to think as he did, nor to follow their ancestor's mind, but shook off any wish to imitate him as though it were something utterly outrageous. So he promises to avenge Jacob, whose glory had been wronged by the wickedness of his children, repaying the wrongdoers according to their ways and according to their practices.
In the womb he supplanted his brother, and in his labors he prevailed with God; and he prevailed with an angel and was victorious.

He usefully lists Jacob's achievements and sets them out as a reproof to those who chose to think and act otherwise. For the bad is always exposed in some way by setting the good beside it, and the display of what is praised naturally condemns what is not like it. He tries to show that Jacob was well endowed from his very swaddling clothes, or rather even before he was born, by saying that he took his brother by the heel in the womb. Granted, what happened was the work of divine power, for we certainly do not say that the baby, still an embryo in the womb, took Esau by the heel by its own effort. Rather, God, foreknowing that he would be good, placed in him the success of what took place. So also he said, "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated." This was according to the election of grace: God chose the one who would certainly prove the better, again by foreknowledge. But that was in the womb. When he reached youth, or rather when he was at last counted among men, "in his labors he prevailed with God." For when God, by his providential ordering, sent him into sweat and toil, he did not grow weak, he says. Was it not sweat to leave his father's hearth, to go to Laban, to endure servitude, and to bear the toils of shepherding? How could this be doubtful to anyone? So in his toils he prevailed with God, not as one fighting against God, but rather as one obeying him, and as it were prevailing [?] by fulfilling what he was commanded. Jacob could have grown rich without sweat and prospered by staying at home, but God did not leave him untrained. Instead, on the pretext of his fear of Esau, he had him go to a foreign land and city and made him bear hard toil, so that he might rightly be admired for keeping his love for God genuine even amid afflictions. So in his toils he prevailed with God. But he also "prevailed with an angel," it says, "and was strong." For an angel wrestled with him in the form of God, and at that time his thigh went numb. Yet the godlike Jacob acknowledged the very great grace he had received through the wrestling, for he said, "I have seen God face to face, and my life has been preserved."

The mystery of Christ, then, was shown beforehand through the wrestling with the angel. For the descendants of Jacob were going to contend against Christ, whom the word of the prophets called "the Angel of Great Counsel." Some of them would be struck numb, not accepting the redemption he offers; others would confess that through him and in him they had seen face to face the one God, who is God by nature and in truth. For Emmanuel showed us the Father in himself, saying, "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father." So the manner of the contest prefigured the mystery [?]. Yet God credits what happened to Jacob as an achievement.
They wept and entreated me; they found me in my house, and there it was spoken to him. But the Lord God Almighty will be his memorial.

Again he recalls other stories, showing us Jacob as illustrious and approved in every respect. It is written in Genesis that Jacob's sons Levi and Simeon killed the Shechemites cruelly and inhumanly, inflamed with anger over their sister Dinah, whom Hamor son of Shechem had violated. Blessed Jacob was then terrified, and expecting at any moment to perish together with his children and all his household, he rebuked those who had done it, saying, "You have made me hateful, so that I am odious to the inhabitants of the land, among the Canaanites and the Perizzites. I am few in number, and they will gather against me and cut me down, and I shall be destroyed, I and my house." The young men did not in the least give up their boldness, but retorted, "Should they treat our sister like a harlot?" But since, as I said, the righteous man was greatly afraid, he again fell before God who saves. Then God, who loves the just, promised to free him from his fears, and that before long, saying, "Arise, go up to the place Bethel and dwell there, and make there an altar to the God who appeared to you when you fled from the face of Esau your brother." Then, as blessed Jacob was about to go up to Bethel and enter the house of God (for Bethel is interpreted "house of God"), he called to all his household and to all who were with him: "Put away the foreign gods from among you, purify yourselves, and change your garments; and let us arise and go up to Bethel, and make there an altar to the God who heard me in the day of affliction, who was with me and kept me safe on the way by which I went. And they gave Jacob the foreign gods that were in their hands and the earrings that were in their ears, and Jacob hid them under the terebinth at Shechem, and destroyed them to this day." When this was done, the godlike Jacob was in good hope, for he was completely freed from fear of the Shechemites, as God by his own power calmed those who were bent on making war against him. For the sacred text says next, "And the fear of the Lord came upon the cities around them, and they did not pursue the sons of Israel." And when the altar had been raised at Luz, which is Bethel, "God appeared," it says, "to Jacob and blessed him, and said, I am your God; increase and multiply. Nations and gatherings of nations shall come from you, and kings shall come forth from your loins. And the land which I gave to Abraham and Isaac, I have given it to you, and to your offspring after you I will give this land." These are the stories he recalls for us in the present prophetic oracle.

So Jacob was a heel-grabber from the womb, but you are always tripped by the heel and do not rather trip up sin. He was most industrious, approved in his toils and true to God; but you, luxuriating in your apostasies, behave insolently and have not honored the one who supplies all your happiness. "Your fathers wept and entreated me," he says. For if ever they were in fear of suffering from someone's plotting, they wept and entreated me, since they expected to be saved by me alone. But you fortify cities and think that even if I am unwilling you will perhaps be saved and overcome your adversaries. They "found me in my house." For Jacob went up, as I said, to Bethel, and God appeared to him, and there the promise of blessing was spoken to him, as we have just shown. But you, again, do not seek God in his house; instead you run, and very eagerly, into the precincts of Baal, and you ask for words not from God but for the oracles of demons. The godlike Jacob, on going up to Bethel, that is, to the house of God, did away with the idols; you, on the contrary, set up a carved god in the house of God. For they set up the golden heifer in Bethel, even though Bethel means, as I said, "house of God." That is why God says through Jeremiah about the synagogue of the Jews, "Why has the beloved done an abomination in my house?" that is, an idol. The godlike Jacob commanded those going up to the house of God to purify themselves and even to change their garments; but you are seen to be profane and unclean, and you are not ashamed to go into the divine house with unwashed feet, he says. Since Jacob was such a man, "the Lord Almighty will be his memorial." For he is kept in God's remembrance and has unfading glory, since God glorifies those who love him.

So—for again I will say something necessary for our benefit—the glories of the fathers will condemn us if we do not choose to think as they did and to adorn ourselves with similar ways and pursuits. And we shall be condemned not as having wronged only our own souls, but as having in a sense plotted against the fathers' good name and disgraced our ancestral nobility.
And you shall return in your God; keep mercy and judgment, and draw near to your God continually.

The promise of grace is mixed with threat. For the statement here is that of one threatening rather than purely promising. Yet the threat comes from love, and the oracle is that of one calling to right thinking and to a desire for good order. "The godlike Jacob," he says, "was wise and most excellent, and he had love for God as the fruit of his own disposition. You did not imitate your father. Nevertheless you too shall return in your God"—that is, even if you have faded away, become an apostate and an insolent man, you will still come back, even against your will, to choosing to live rightly. You will come back being disciplined in God, that is, through God. And since good reasoning has not persuaded you to go on the right path and to love thinking as you ought, the scourge will entirely and certainly prevail over you and will swiftly bring you round to choosing and recognizing what is to your advantage. This, then, as I take it, is what the words "And you shall return in your God" would fittingly signify for us, containing, as I said, a threat well mixed with kind promises. Then, as to one already being scourged and actually undergoing the blows, God calls out, "Keep mercy and judgment, and draw near to your God continually." Just as a master might say to a servant being disciplined and actually under the lash, with both forbearance and indignation, "Be sensible and obedient, and do not despise your master's commands," in the same way, I think, the God of all says to Ephraim, who is in a sense being beaten and disciplined by the blows of war, "Keep mercy and judgment, and draw near to your God continually." It is as if he were saying, "Know that you are being struck for this reason: you did not keep or honor what is dear and beloved to me." Mercy signifies love, and love is the fulfilling of the law, for "it does no wrong to a neighbor," in the words of blessed Paul. Judgment signifies right conduct, that is, righteousness and the keeping of the divine will, for the law is called "judgment" in the divinely inspired Scripture. Drawing near to God continually would indicate the mind's genuine longing and inclination toward him, and not being disposed to cling to other gods who are no gods, or perhaps to the creation, that is, to wood and stone. He too will draw near to God and be close to him in disposition who knows how to be distinguished by good deeds and has kept his faith uncorrupted within himself. For sin often comes between and separates us from God. In the same way, clinging to the words of unholy false teachers also drives us away from closeness to him—spiritual closeness, obviously. Those who wish to be near God, then, must reject the things that would put them far away.

Canaan—in his hand is a balance of injustice; he has loved to oppress. And Ephraim said, "But I have become rich; I have found relief for myself." None of his labors will be found for him, because of the injustices by which he sinned.

As far as it depended on God's will, Ephraim would have kept mercy and judgment and drawing near to him continually. But since he slipped from good sense and counted such holy and precious things as nothing, he became equal to the foreign Canaanites, godless and impious, delighting above all in wicked ways and, with a barbarous mind, unrestrainedly overcome by the desire for what belongs to others. Ephraim ought to have been seen as an imitator of his forefather Jacob and to have loved following in the footsteps of his righteousness. But he became a Canaanite, for a balance of injustice was found in his hands, that is, inequity and greed. Like the nations that do not know God, he prized accursed oppression. He did not see fit to consider that he was sinning in doing this, but delighted only in being rich and living in luxury, as though God did not look on, as though he no longer watched over those on earth and justly rebuked those who want to do wrong. It would be clear proof of the utmost folly that Ephraim was eager to grow rich by any means at all, considered the crimes of robbery and violence to be nothing, and then, in his great stupidity, made a boast of the very things he ought rather to have blushed at. For he said, "But I have become rich; I have found relief for myself." What then does God say to this? "None of his labors will be found for him, because of the injustices by which he sinned." Indeed it is true that "wealth unjustly gathered will be vomited up," as it is written. And to those who want to gather from injustice and to grow rich from greed, let someone now call out the words spoken by a holy man: "It would have been better for you to do judgment and fine righteousness." For the divine saying stands before us: "Treasures will not profit the lawless, but righteousness will deliver from death." And as the author of Proverbs says, "Better is a small portion with the fear of the Lord than great treasures without fear." And again the same author: "Better is a little gain with righteousness than much produce with injustice." Our actions and the quality of our deeds sometimes make us worthy of the nobility of the holy fathers, but they also assign us to sinful fathers. For we shall differ in no way from those who have lived in impiety if we imitate what they did. That is why we say Ephraim is called Canaan: he thought as foreigners think. The Canaanites were foreigners and notorious for godlessness. So certain people were reproached and heard, as their audacity deserved, "Offspring of Canaan, and not of Judah."

But I am the Lord your God who brought you up out of the land of Egypt; I will yet make you dwell in tents as on a day of festival. And I will speak to the prophets, and I multiplied visions, and by the hands of the prophets I was represented.

He named Ephraim Canaan, as I said, clearly proving that he had hated mercy and judgment and had chosen instead greed, inequity and every kind of injustice. But see, he now tries to show that Ephraim was not only like this in his dealings with people, but that by his very conduct he also refused to draw near to God. So he accuses him of having failed to recognize his Redeemer, of having insulted with his folly the one who brought him out of the house of slavery with signs and wonders, with great power and with an uplifted arm. "For I," he says, "brought you up out of Egypt." In saying "brought up," he calls to mind everything that was done for them until they entered the land promised to the holy fathers. These things were countless and beyond all wonder. That they had no excuse for forgetting them he showed by adding, "I will yet make you dwell in tents as on a day of festival."

And what does this mean? you will ask again. The law given through Moses commanded that the Feast of Tabernacles be celebrated in the seventh month, on the fifteenth day. The lawgiver himself made clear to us the reason for it, saying about the Feast of Tabernacles in Leviticus: "In the seventh month you shall celebrate it. You shall dwell in tents seven days. Every native in Israel shall dwell in tents, so that your generations may see that I made the sons of Israel dwell in tents when I brought them out of the land of Egypt. I am the Lord your God." So they celebrated the feast in remembrance of the exodus from Egypt. "How then could you forget me," he says, "who brought you out of Egypt, when you still live in tents and make the occasion a festival?" For "I will yet make you dwell in tents as on a day of festival." He says "I will make you dwell" in the sense of "I settle you," that is, "I cause you to dwell in tents" during the days of the festival held for these events. So forgetfulness is inexcusable for you.

"But perhaps you wanted to know something of the future and wished to pry into your own affairs. Why, then, did you have to go to the false seers of Baal, that is, of the falsely named gods, and seek such things from them, instead of wisely remembering that it is I who speak to the prophets and I who have multiplied visions?" That is, every word of prophecy will come from me, and already has, and not from any of the falsely named gods. "For to me alone will belong both knowing what is to come and remembering what is past. But the false seers and false prophets you honored imitated me," he says. This is "by the hands of the prophets I was represented." "You sought to learn the future from them. Then, fabricating my words and imitating the deeds of my prophets, they belched out to you what came from their own hearts." Thus the prophet Jeremiah placed wooden yokes around his neck, God having commanded that this be done. But the false prophet Hananiah, opposing his words, took the yokes and broke them, and said, "Thus says the Lord: I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon." This, as I said, is "by the hands of the prophets I was represented."

The charge against Ephraim, then, is that although he had a clear reminder of the exodus from Egypt in the Feast of Tabernacles, he forgot God, and did not rather seek him as the one who speaks to the prophets and has multiplied visions, but clung instead to the deceptions of the false prophets, who counterfeited God's ways in both word and deed.
If Gilead does not exist, were the rulers who sacrificed in Gilgal then false? And their altars are like tortoises on the dry ground of a field.

In these words he proves that they clung to the false seers and false prophets, going up to Gilead and Gilgal and sacrificing there. He takes these two cities in particular as proof, because in them the error was more outrageous than in the others: every form of piety toward God was neglected, and everything that incited to evil, everything full of folly at its height, was held in esteem. Thus earlier God said about Gilead, "There Gilead despised me, a city working vain things," that is, idols, for its inhabitants were makers of idols; and about the other city, "All their wickedness is in Gilgal, for there I hated them because of the wickedness of their practices." We must also mention something of what happened to the Gileadites, for in this way we will understand the sense of the passage. Pul, king of the Assyrians, was the first to come against Samaria, and he took the two tribes beyond the Jordan as a sort of first spoils, captured all their cities, and Gilead before the others. God alludes to this in passing when he says, "If Gilead does not exist." "If Gilead does not exist," he says, "and is not preserved now—if it has perished and it is no longer possible to prove Ephraim's drunken insolence from it, since it is not now to be seen—were the rulers who sacrificed in Gilgal then also false and not real?" Gilgal is a city beyond the Jordan, in which small and great alike flocked together and devoted themselves to the defilements of idolatry. So if Gilead no longer exists, who would dare to say that the rulers who sacrificed in Gilgal were false and not real? They were not a dream or shadows, nor obscure people, but illustrious and prominent rulers and leaders, setting up lofty and conspicuous altars to the carved images, like the "tortoises" in the fields. By "tortoises" he does not mean the animals—do not think so—but raised mounds of earth that some people make, banking up watercourses into ridges; farmers labor over countless such works. By "rulers who sacrificed" he means either generals and commanders of the troops, or those of the blood of Levi who held the leadership given by the law. For they too fell away along with the others, and not a few of them worshiped the carved images. Thus it is written in Ezekiel: "Therefore thus says the Lord God: No foreigner, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, shall enter my sanctuary, of all the foreigners who are in the midst of the house of Israel; nor the Levites who withdrew from me when Israel went astray, who went astray from me after their own notions; they shall bear their iniquity."
And Jacob withdrew into the plain of Syria, and Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he kept watch.

Here the discourse turns back again to test two things: the integrity and goodness of the forefather, and the perversity and impiety of those descended from him. It marvels, as it were, at how he endured hardship for small things, and then sets this beside the case of the ten tribes to expose how careless they were about the greatest things. For who would not admire Jacob, who bore such bitter and grievous toil, and did not refuse to serve Laban as a hired hand for the sake of wives and marriage? Even though the forefather's wage was very small (it was a marriage, as I said), he still kept watch and kept faith with the one who had promised him the marriage. And he did not labour in his own city or land or home, but as a newcomer, living in a foreign country. Such was Jacob; now let us look at the charges against those who came from Israel. They were not sent off to a foreign land. On the contrary, when they were in the condition of captives taken by the spear, serving the Egyptians and once enduring unpaid sweat, by the power of God they were set free from the land of their oppressors and settled in the land promised to their fathers. What was set before them as a reward for keeping the law was not marriage to a woman, but rather an abundant supply of every good thing: "a land flowing with milk and honey," the ability to crush their adversaries, glory and wealth, and the boasts that come with these — indeed, what was lacking of all that makes for prosperity and luxury? Yet they did not keep it. They transgressed, thinking the keeping of it worth hardly any regard at all. So it is plain that, since they fell short of their fathers' goodness, and that beyond all measure, they will have no share either in the forbearance that was granted to those fathers; for the judge is just.
And by a prophet the Lord brought Israel up out of Egypt, and by a prophet he was preserved.

In these words he makes plain to us why Israel did not keep the commandment laid down for it, and despised God when he said, "You shall have no other gods besides me," and why it would not strive to rival the goodness of its fathers. For he rebukes them because those from Israel came under the rule of men at all, although God [?] them through holy prophets, and nothing was lacking to them for being blessed. For we remember that while the blessed Samuel was still alive and still prophesying, they asked for a king. God was angry at this, and, as one greatly insulted, he was grieved; yet he appointed Saul. So he strongly accuses them because they came under the rule of men at all, not tolerating being ruled by God through prophets. God, he says, saved Israel and brought it out of the house of slavery through the mediation of Moses, who was both a prophet and the first of the prophets. And he not only brought them out of Egypt, he says, but also preserved them; for Israel continued to worship the one who is God by nature and in truth. But once they came under kings, they ran aground and lost their love for God. Solomon was the first to build altars and sacred precincts for the Baals; then after him the accursed Jeroboam made the golden heifers. So he accuses them of not keeping a most excellent arrangement — I mean being ruled by God through prophets — and of preferring [?] instead to fall into the hands of men, which in fact became for them the cause of their apostasy.
Ephraim provoked him to wrath and to anger; and his blood shall be poured out upon him, and the Lord will repay him his reproach, according to the word of Ephraim.

In these words he tries very hard to show us that choosing rather to be under the rule of men was bitter and perilous for those from Israel, and became a cause of their ruin. "See," he says, "Ephraim" — that is, Jeroboam, who was of the tribe of Ephraim — "has provoked me, the Master of all, to wrath and anger, and has stirred me to every kind of indignation, by inventing heifers and conferring my glory on them." Therefore he has become the cause of his own destruction: his blood will come upon him. And since, when he set up the heifers in Bethel and Dan, he proclaimed to those from Israel, "Let it be enough for you to go up to Jerusalem; here are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt," for this reason, he says, and quite rightly, he will pay to me, the judge, the penalty for his reproach. For it is plainly an outrage and an admitted reproach against God to dare to attribute to lifeless matter the splendid and marvellous deeds he has accomplished. So according to the reproach of Ephraim himself — that is, in equal measure to his blasphemies and unholy words — the consequences of wrath will be brought back upon him. For just as, so far as his undertaking and his words could manage it, God was thrust out of the glory that befits him alone, so he too will be thrust out of his own dominion. In due time the kingdom of Ephraim will come to an end. As I have already said, after the return from Babylon no one from the ten tribes ever again reigned in Samaria; instead all were in Jerusalem under a single ruler from the tribe of Judah in each period.

He took his ordinances in Israel and gave them to Baal, and he died. And he went on to sin still more, and they made for themselves a molten image from their silver in the likeness of idols, works of craftsmen completed for them.

Here he accuses not the ten tribes alone but the whole of Israel. He says that, though ordinances had been given them through Moses, by which they were taught how God must be served and how sacrifices were to be offered, they all but dedicated these very things to Baal, that is, to the idols; for sometimes the part stands for the whole. They no longer sacrificed to God; rather, they celebrated their festivals for the works of their own hands and brought them worship, firstfruits, homage, gifts and thank-offerings; and, robbing God of his own glory, they assigned it to carved images. But having done this, he says, Israel died, and again went on to sin. It is as if he were saying: "He was punished for what he did, he was destroyed for his daring, he came to know the indignation of the Master, who brought punishment by blood upon those who went astray; and yet he by no means ceased from his perversity, but would instead be caught in other offences just as bad." For we have read in Numbers that the sons of Israel committed fornication, inflamed with outrageous pleasures, and gave themselves to the women of the Moabites. Then for this they paid the most extreme penalty of all. What is written runs thus: "And Israel settled in Shittim, and the people were defiled by committing fornication with the daughters of Moab. And they invited them to the sacrifices of their idols, and the people ate of their sacrifices and worshipped their idols. And Israel was initiated into the rites of Baal-peor, and the Lord was angry with Israel in his wrath. And the Lord said to Moses, 'Take all the leaders of the people and make an example of them to the Lord before the sun, and the fierce anger of the Lord will turn away from Israel.' And Moses said to the tribes of Israel, 'Each of you kill those of his own household who have been initiated into Baal-peor.'" When this was carried out, no small multitude of those from Israel fell. Notice, then, that in the time of Moses Israel, by offering God's ordinances to idols, died a pitiable death; for the one who had gone astray was slaughtered by the swords of his own kin, not by a foreign hand. Yet he went on to sin, for they made themselves a golden molten image, the work of a craftsman, gods fashioned by the skills of artisans. The text seems almost to smile at their foolishness, for they believed that the things they themselves had made were gods. Let the psalmist, then, cry out over them too: "May all who make them become like them, and all who trust in them."

They say, "Sacrifice men, for the calves have run out." Therefore they shall be like a morning cloud and like the early dew that passes away, and like chaff blown from the threshing floor, and like vapour from a chimney.

He accuses them again: not only did they act impiously, shaping the silver God had given them into the likeness of idols and bestowing the name of divine glory on things made of wood and stone, but they also slid down into such ignorance — or rather such perversity, inhumanity and beastlike savagery, or something even beyond these — that they did not spare even their own children, but slaughtered them to demons. Yet God abhors this thing so much that he would never even tolerate the word itself being spoken to others or heard from anyone. For the Master is not bloodthirsty, nor does he take pleasure in the destruction of human beings — far from it! "For he created all things that they might exist," as it is written, "and the generative forces of the world are wholesome." But since the apostate dragon is both the inventor and the cause of death, he delights in human slaughter. That even the bare mention of this is hateful to God he makes plain when he says, "They say, 'Sacrifice men, for the calves have run out.'" "The word is not mine," he says, "nor would I ever utter such a thing; it is they, the servants of the demons, who say that men must be sacrificed to them." Then he mocks their reasoning and ridicules the undertaking, adding: "For, it seems, they had no calves; that is why they honoured man-slaughter. But suppose," he says, "you went astray and honoured carved and molten gods; why did you also drench their altars with human blood?" We have read in Kings that there was Jonathan son of Ahaz [?], who reigned over Judah. He "walked in the way of the kings of Israel, and burned incense on the high places, and even made his own son pass through the fire," sacrificing to the demons the one born and begotten of him. Since they have done such things, he says, they will be like a morning cloud and like dew, like chaff and like vapour from a chimney — that is, after being seen for a little while they will pass away to destruction and go to nothing. For a morning cloud, that is, a mist, and dew and chaff and vapour from a chimney are easily blown away and are scattered in a very short time, or rather within a single hour. For what substance is there in chaff or dew, or in the vapour that is formed from smoke?
By the same author: On the Prophet Hosea, Volume Seven.
"But I am the Lord your God, who makes the heaven firm and creates the earth, whose hands created all the host of heaven; and I did not show them to you so that you might go after them."

Somehow the ugliness of false belief is always exposed once true knowledge is brought into the open. It is like a light shining out in the night and the darkness, when the word that trains our thoughts toward what is right is present. The Israelites had become filled with the worst folly of all, and the wretchedness of their thinking had reached its very lowest point. They honoured molten images and the work of craftsmen and passed over the One who is truly and by nature God. So he rebukes them by saying that it is he who makes the heaven firm, who also fixed the earth in place, and who is the maker of the stars. He reproaches them because they cast aside, as something stale, the possibility of learning the glory of the Maker through the things that have been made, and instead made those very things the pretext for their own error. Yet these things did not come into being so that they might wrong the divine glory by being taken for gods by those on earth. They came into being so that, as the sacred Scripture says, "from the greatness and beauty of created things" the minds of those who understand might rise by analogy to whatever grasp is possible of the Maker's power and skill. So the Creator did not show us the creation so that it might be worshipped by us. Indeed, he had warned beforehand, saying through Moses: "And do not look up to heaven and see the sun and the moon and the stars and all the array of heaven, and be led astray and worship them and serve them, things which the Lord your God has allotted to all the nations under heaven." But they called gods the things that had been allotted to mark the seasons and set in their places as lights, and they dared to worship them. And seeking things still more shameful than these, the wretches honoured molten images and pieces of wood as gods, worshipping the craft of bronzesmiths and carpenters.

"And I brought you up from the land of Egypt, and you shall know no god but me, and there is no saviour besides me. I shepherded you in the wilderness, in an uninhabited land, according to their pastures."

In these words their insensibility is thoroughly exposed. The ways in which he helped them are set out one after another, showing how great the ingratitude of the Israelites was. He does not rebuke them, I think, as people who did not know. How could they not? He rebukes them as people who, out of very great perversity and a mind sunk into insensibility, had all but fallen into forgetting the things they ought always to have remembered. The accursed Jeroboam set up the heifers for them and said, "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt." And although they knew that this deed had been accomplished for them by God and by no one else, they brought their thank-offerings to handmade heifers, and somehow they persuaded one another to ascribe to these the surpassing greatness of the divine works. So, as though they were drunk on the wine of Sodom, he all but jabs them awake. He says that it is clearly he who brought them out "of the house of slavery," he who commanded through Moses, "You shall have no other gods besides me," and he alone who saves and accomplishes without effort whatever he wishes. It was he who carried them along through the wilderness; in a land that was desert, trackless and waterless, he released springs of water, sent down the manna and gave them the bread of angels from heaven, and like a good shepherd he pastured them in contentment "according to their pastures," that is, at each of their departures. For the Israelites lacked nothing good in the wilderness, even though they were always moving from place to place and camping in a rough and barren land.

We must therefore always remember whatever we have received from God, and make a habit of banishing any forgetfulness of these things as far as possible from our minds. Such forgetfulness brings destruction and provokes to anger God, the giver of all our well-being. For the ungrateful man is like a blasphemer, as someone has wisely said.
"And they were filled to the full, and their hearts were lifted up; for this reason they forgot me."

The most experienced physicians examine the causes of diseases very carefully and hurry to check them with the remedies of their art. In the same way, I think, the God of all looks within, into the mind and the heart, investigates the causes of the passions in us, and then binds up the ailing mind with fitting medicines. So he charges the Israelites with having been carried by too much prosperity into forgetting the One who supplied them with everything needed for life, and who knew how to make splendid whatever seemed splendid. And this although the law had warned beforehand: "Take heed to yourself, lest you forget the Lord your God by not keeping his commandments and his judgements and his ordinances, which I command you today; lest, when you have eaten your fill and built fine houses and lived in them, and your sheep and your cattle have multiplied, and your silver and gold have multiplied, and everything you have has multiplied, your heart be lifted up and you forget the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery; who led you through that great and terrible wilderness, where there were biting serpents and scorpions and thirst, where there was no water." For luxury, and taking pride in honours we did not expect, are always quite able to carry us off into forgetting God and to shake the human mind into every kind of outrageous behaviour. Israel's rebellion will suffice, I think, as proof. It found in the abundance of its prosperity the starting point of this dreadful disease. And since they were stronger than the nations, plainly because God, who is able to do all things, was defending them, they fell sick with arrogance, perhaps crediting the glory of their successes to themselves and not to God who shielded them.

Luxury, then, is a slippery thing and hard to manage, a smooth road, as it were, to falling away from God. Moderate affliction is far better. The voices of the saints will assure us of this. One of them said, "Lord, in affliction we remembered you; in slight affliction your discipline was upon us." The most wise Paul made affliction the root and, as it were, the origin of every good thing for us, saying, "Affliction produces endurance, and endurance proven character, and proven character hope, and hope does not put us to shame." And somewhere the inspired David sings, "It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I might learn your ordinances."

"And I will be to them like a panther and like a leopard along the road [?]; there the cubs of the thicket [?] … [like a bear] in want [?], and I will tear apart the enclosure of their heart, and [?] will devour them [?] … the beasts of the field will tear them apart [?]."

Their broad contentment had become the cause of their destruction and the occasion of their apostasy. For this reason afflictions are now brought upon them, in proportion to their diseases. Bodies that are very sick and already rotting will no longer yield to gentle medicines; they need the knife and the cautery instead. So, since the greatness of God's gentleness had profited the Israelites little, not to say nothing at all, a savagery fit for wild beasts is brought upon them. He compares himself to the most terrible and ravenous of beasts, those most inclined to cruelty. This is not because the divine and ineffable nature could ever be subject to such fits of anger. Rather, he is perhaps teaching once more that the Assyrians will indulge such unmixed anger, and that the Israelites will be captured by men who have become inhuman and hard-hearted, and everything else of that kind. Yet what is done may be regarded as God's doing, since he himself allowed it to happen, letting loose on those who had sinned so savagely the anger that befitted them. "I will find them, then, like a panther and like a leopard," for they will be carried away into the land of the Assyrians. "And I will meet them like a bear in want," that is, one that is perhaps hungry, or else greatly distressed because its cubs have been taken away; for they say that this is when the beast's innate fury reaches its height. "And I will tear apart the enclosure of the heart." By "enclosure" here he means security, and the security of the heart is the courage one may have against enemies. When that has been torn apart, the passions born of cowardice come in, so that people hand the victory to their enemies without a fight. It is as if he were saying, "I will bring them down into utter cowardice," while their adversaries are likened to a hungry beast robbed of its young, I mean the bear. And he showed that even when they have been caught in the bonds of captivity and carried off to the land of the Assyrians they will find no relief from their troubles, but their miseries will follow them there too, when he said, "And the cubs of the thicket will devour them there; the beasts of the field will tear them apart." For he likens the untamed tribes of the Assyrians, so much inclined to savagery, to cubs in the thickets and to wild beasts.

"In your dispersion, O Israel, who will help you? Where is this king of yours? Let him save you in all your cities; let him judge you, he of whom you said, 'Give me a king and a ruler.' And I gave you one in my anger, and I held in my wrath a conspiracy of injustice."

I already said briefly above that God was accusing the Israelites because, for some reason, they chose rather to be yoked to human yokes and rejected God's kingship over them, although he had ruled their forefathers through holy prophets. For he said, "By a prophet the Lord brought Israel up out of Egypt, and by a prophet he was preserved." "But you," he says, "thrust aside life under God and cried out against the blessed Samuel, saying, 'Look, you have grown old, and your sons do not walk in your way. Now appoint a king over us to judge us, like the other nations.' So since you think you planned well when you set up a king over yourself like the other nations, and expected to be saved by him, where is he now? Look, here is the moment to prove himself. Let him fight your war, let him arm himself splendidly, let him save your cities, let him shield those under his hand, let him put his adversaries to flight, let him boldly drive off those who want to ravage your houses and cities."

But perhaps you will say, "Yet it seems that I asked, and that you gave, and in the beginning anointed Saul." "Yes," he says, "but I gave the leader in my anger, and I held in my wrath a conspiracy of injustice," meaning, "since I had been wronged by you." "I was very angry because, as far as your intentions went, I was all but thrust out of the seats of kingship. Still, I appointed him," he says, "though I knew the thing was of no necessary benefit, so that experience of events might fully convince you that in this too your counsel was perverse and useless. For where is he now, or what benefit could come from him any longer to people under attack? But if you had been once more under my care and my hand, you would surely have been seen to prevail over your enemies." So, as it is written, "The salvation of man is vain," and hope in rulers is "a horse that proves false for safety." But God rescues very easily those whom he chooses, and those whom he sees honouring their hope in him.
"Ephraim, his sin is hidden away; pangs as [?] will come upon him. This is your son, the wise one, for he will not stand firm in the crushing of children."

This, I think, is the meaning of "He conceived toil and gave birth to lawlessness." For in the beginning, when Israel wished to complete the sacrifices prescribed by the law and for this reason went up to Jerusalem, Jeroboam devised the golden heifers so that the sceptre would not fall from his hands. And he received the sin into his mind like the sowing of an evil seed, buried and, as it were, hidden away. "But the time of the pangs too will come," he says. This in turn may be understood as the time of war and captivity. For even if these things did not happen to Ephraim himself, they came in due course upon those who descended from him, that is, upon those who succeeded to the rule, because they became imitators of his impiety.

So he addresses the congregation in Samaria and says: Who will save you? Is it this wise son of yours? By saying "this," he either points to whoever was reigning at the time, who also enjoyed a reputation for seeming wise, since this always goes with those in power; or else he hints at something else suited to the time when the word of the prophecy came. For when Ahaz was reigning over Judah in Jerusalem, "in the eleventh year, Hoshea the son of Elah began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and he did what was evil in the sight of the Lord." At that time Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, marched against Samaria. "And Hoshea," it says, "became his servant." The Assyrian was very angry with him for the following reason. He had sent messengers to him demanding tribute and the customary payments. But Hoshea, unwilling to take orders from him, sent envoys to Segor, king of Egypt, asking for his help. Offended at this, Shalmaneser besieged Samaria for three whole years. Then he took Hoshea alive, put him in chains and enrolled him among his slaves, and he deported Israel to the borders of the Persians and the Medes. So the prophetic word seems to point here to Hoshea the son of Elah. It calls him wise not because he was truly intelligent, but somewhat ironically. Among the Israelites he was considered intelligent and thought to have planned very wisely, because he chose to call for help from Egypt for them. But he was caught out in having done and planned things that were feeble and useless. "Who, then," he says, "will rescue you from suffering incurable calamities? This wise son of yours? For he will not stand firm in the crushing of children." That is, he says, when your children are being crushed, he himself will not hold out either, for he will be taken as a slave and a captive together with the rest and will go off to the Assyrians. Wise, then, is the one who sings, "The Lord is my strength and my song." For from him comes all power and all salvation, and there is no saviour besides him.
"From the hand of Hades I will rescue them, from death I will redeem them. Where is your penalty, O death? Where is your sting, O Hades?"

Having spoken in anger to those who had sinned, and having foretold what would come upon them out of his grief, he returns again to a gentleness worthy of God. He makes known that he has not turned away completely from the race on earth, nor given it over to unbridled and endless destruction, but that in due time there will be mercy and a recall, in Christ, to the original state. He adds that he will rescue from the hand of Hades and redeem from death, plainly meaning those who had come under its power through the sin that entered in from outside and through Adam's transgression in the beginning. For this promise in turn was made not to Ephraim alone, that is, not only to those of Israel's blood, but rather to all on earth. As the inspired Paul writes, "God is not of the Jews only, but of the Gentiles also. For he has justified the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith." For he has redeemed us from the hand of Hades, that is, from the tyranny of death, and the means of our redemption is understood to be the death of Christ. For he willingly endured being slain on the cross for us, and he triumphed over the rulers and authorities, nailing to it the bond that stood against us. Then, yes, then "all lawlessness stopped its mouth," and the power of death was abolished, because sin was taken away. For sin is the victory of death and the sting of Hades. This is how the wise Paul too explained it to us, for he said, "The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law." So, since the sin of all has been taken away in Christ, we too may rightly say, "Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O Hades?" "For it is God who justifies; who is it that condemns? It is Christ Jesus who died" for us, or rather who "gave himself as a ransom for all," the One who is worth more than all, through whom and in whom we have gained the riches of returning once more to incorruption.
"Consolation is hidden from my eyes, because he will divide between brothers."

We shall read the first line of this passage as a question, with a pause after it, and it would suggest something like the following to those who have chosen to understand it rightly. "Human nature," he says, "has fallen sick with sin in many forms and has sunk into wrongdoing to no small degree. For this reason it has justly been condemned to death. What, then, will be the means of help for those who have suffered this, or how might they shake off what has befallen them? I myself will consider it; or rather, I have already decided. Or is there anyone among you who has gone so far in madness as to think and say that there is some means of consolation and comfort which the divine and pure mind has not seen? For I am a craftsman, powerless for nothing; I know all things well and accomplish at once whatever I please." And indeed, he says, "this one will divide between brothers." Through these words he foretells to us our Lord Jesus [?]

Christ. For he is the consolation of all, the means of healing. Before eternal ages the Father foreordained him as Saviour and Redeemer for those held fast by death. He said that it is he who divides between brothers. What this means we have heard from Christ himself, the Saviour of us all, when he says, "Do not think that I came to bring peace on earth; I did not come to bring peace, but a sword. For I came to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man's enemies will be those of his own household." And again, foretelling to the holy disciples what would come to pass, he says, "Brother will hand over brother to death," and a father will rise up against his sons. For when he had brought down the devil's tyranny and rescued those who had gone astray from the snares of idolatry, he bound believers so firmly to love for himself that they disregarded natural affection, renounced brothers and fathers, homes and families, and considered that being joined to Christ would suffice them for every kind of happiness. Indeed, the blessed David, speaking as if in the person of those who had achieved this, sings somewhere, "My father and my mother have forsaken me, but the Lord has taken me up."
"The Lord will bring a scorching wind from the wilderness upon him, and it will dry up his veins; it will make his springs desolate. He will dry up his land and all his desirable vessels."

He shifts his words to death itself as their subject, and likens Christ to a south wind, a scorching one, which he says will be brought from the wilderness in due time. Before anything else, we should know that the land of the Jews has a broad and boundless wilderness lying in its southernmost parts. Whenever the wind from there happened to sweep down violently, the people were greatly alarmed, because the land was parched. Some think that even the veins of water in the ground supply their flow more sluggishly and are checked by the onslaught of that violent, fiery wind. So he frames his words from what they knew and had experienced.

The prophetic word, then, told us that Christ would be brought against death like a scorching wind, which will dry up all its springs and veins. He keeps to the figure, and very fittingly, and reveals the mystery by drawing on what usually happens. By the veins and springs of death we mean the ways of [?], or the evil and hostile powers. For it is through them, as it were, that death is supplied with the multitude of those who perish from age to age. In the same way you will understand "his desirable vessels." One might rightly call "vessels" the things that destroy those on earth and that are precious to death: either the evil and hostile powers, or certain unholy people on earth who serve his perversity and bring others to destruction along with themselves. So when the scorching wind blows, he says, the whole land of death will be dried up. Here again the words are framed as a metaphor. It is as if he were saying: "Death used to graze on those on earth as on a field; but the field will be dry, and death will find no pasture." For corruption has been taken away, since Christ set life before all and made incorruption recoverable once more.
"Samaria will be destroyed, because she rose up against her God. They will fall by the sword, and their infants will be dashed to the ground, and their pregnant women will be ripped open."

Having fully completed his discourse on Christ and foretold the mystery of universal redemption, the blessed prophet once more laments the calamities of those who had given offence, and all but mourns over the people in Samaria. For though it was open to them, he says, to enjoy the good things that come from gentleness, and very richly too, they ran of their own accord toward what was to come upon them from wrath. This was because they chose to resist God and to raise their own will against the Master's commands, and so seemed all but to have ranged themselves against him, or even truly to have taken their place among those who oppose him. Therefore, with all mercy withdrawn, they themselves will become the sword's work, and strange forms of inhumanity will be devised against their women and children. For together with their newborn infants, even those not yet called into being and life will suffer an untimely death, and the enemies' sword will come before their emergence through birth. It is bitter, then, to set oneself against God, and truly a cause of destruction; this is seen from experience itself.

Return, O Israel, to the Lord your God, for you have grown weak in your iniquities. Take words with you and return to the Lord your God. Say to him, so that you may not receive iniquity, but may receive good things: “And we will render the fruit of our lips. Assyria shall not save us; we will not mount on horses; no longer will we say ‘Our gods’ to the works of our hands.”

Here again one could hardly admire enough the prophet’s skill and the arrangement of his discourse. It is composed in a manner befitting a holy man, and it is full of instruction in the mysteries from above. He had already foretold the redemption that would come through Christ: that in due time death would lose its strength and the sting of Hades would become powerless; and besides this, that there is no means of comfort or consolation at all that is not known to God. And what then? It was necessary next to counsel them to think and do what leads to salvation, and to hasten, as it were, to bring back to sobriety those who were drunk—not with wine, how could that be? but rather with love of worldly pleasure and a fondness for clinging to the deceits of demons. So that they should not, lulled into carelessness by the promises of kindness and love for humanity, make nothing of the one who knows how to correct them, he usefully brings them back once more to the remembrance of terrible things. He says that Samaria will be destroyed because she rose up against her God, and then adds to this things that clearly have no small power to frighten and grieve those who hear. For he says that infants will be dashed to the ground, and that the mothers themselves will perish together with the unborn, before they have brought from the womb into the light the burden they had so longed for. Having first struck them with terror, he then at the right moment instills into the hearts of those he is admonishing the word that calls to repentance, very aptly urging them that they must turn back and return to God. And by saying, “You have grown weak in your iniquities,” he gives them to understand that their weakness will cease completely and altogether along with their iniquities, and that if the ways of apostasy are removed, the terrible things will depart with them. He also smooths the way of turning back to God. For he says very well that those who have sinned will be in a better state and in God’s favor, not by bringing what comes from wealth, not by dedicating gold, not by choosing to honor him with silver vessels, not by pleasing him with sacrifices of oxen or the slaughter of sheep, but if they offer words and choose to speak well, appeasing the Master of all. For “Take words with you; say to God, so that you may not receive iniquity, but may receive good things”—that is, so that you may not be punished in proportion to your iniquities, but may rather be enriched with abundant supplies of good things; and promise to bring him what comes from the lips, songs of thanksgiving and confession. For such things are the fruits of the tongue. But this above all, he says, cry aloud and promise firmly: that neither will Assyria save us, nor will we mount on horses; nor will we any longer say “Our gods” to the works of our hands. For these were the ways of their apostasy. This is why they stumbled: because they worshiped idols, and, dishonoring the God who always saves, they placed their hope in human help. When the Egyptians made war on them, they called in the Assyrian; and again, when the Assyrians took up arms against Samaria, they hired with money the mounted archers of the Egyptians, that is, men skilled in cavalry warfare. That is why they heard God saying plainly, “Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help, who trust in horses and in chariots”; and they were mocked, quite rightly, for striving to make their defender “an Egyptian, a man and not God, horses that are flesh,” as it is written. So they promise to give up both worshiping idols and setting their hopes on human beings any longer. This is the correction of the faults already committed, and it calls to gentleness the Creator of all, who says through the voice of a prophet, “Turn, turn away from your lawless deeds, O house of Israel, and your iniquities shall not become your punishment.”
He who is in you will have mercy on the orphan.

This is the voice of the prophet urging them to repentance, making plain the Master’s gentleness, and cutting away the hesitation of the one who wishes to repent. “Do not doubt, O Israel,” he says, “that you will obtain what you pray for, if you bring repentance. For the God who is in you knows how to have mercy on orphans and to pity them.” So too the divine David says somewhere, “He will uphold the orphan and the widow,” showing, I think, from a single case—that is, from persons who above all naturally arouse pity—the love for humanity of the divine and ineffable nature. But if someone should wish to ascribe the condition of orphanhood to Israel itself—for it all but fell away from God as Father, although he said plainly, “Israel is my firstborn son”—I for my part would say that this too is a correct understanding.

We must, then, take courage from the fact that the Master of all is good and ready to show love for humanity, and repent without the least hesitation, and by amending ourselves for the better, free ourselves from the charges for the faults already committed.
I will heal their dwellings; I will love them openly, for my anger has turned away from him.

Immediately there is brought in, as a neighbor—indeed almost next door—the word from God, who promises to heal those who have grown weak and to love them openly, that is, to be seen from now on acting avowedly and without concealment in sparing and love, and in bestowing every good thing. He shows besides that his anger against them has ceased, and that he will not withdraw from the love for humanity so dear to him. But here again the passage seems to us to call to mind not only the turning back of those who are of Israel by blood, but rather to bring in along with it the calling of the Gentiles as well; for “not all who are descended from Israel are Israel,” but rather those are reckoned as children who follow “in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had while still uncircumcised.” So the calling of the Gentiles is included as well, and their being made God’s own in Christ through faith and sanctification; and in addition there is indicated the supply of spiritual gifts and the abundance of grace—that is, plainly, the grace in Christ.
I will be like dew to Israel.
Surely enriching and watering the mind of those called to repentance with the consolation from above—that is, plainly, the consolation through the Spirit; for dew comes from above.
He will blossom like a lily.
He will give off, he says, the sweet scent that is in Christ, the fragrance of a holy way of life, and from now on he will be a choice flower.
And he will cast his roots like Lebanon; his branches will spread out.

By this he shows that the mind of believers is not easily shaken, nor, as it were, ready to be overcome by evil spirits. For it will be as secure and firmly fixed as the tree of Lebanon, which sends its root down very deep and spreads out widely in its branches above. For when the root is richly nourished, the shoots that spring from it are surely sturdy as well.
And he will be like a fruitful olive tree.
That is, evergreen and abundant in fruit; for such is that tree.
And his fragrance will be like that of frankincense.

Frankincense is an exceedingly fragrant substance. That is why the law of Moses also prescribed it as sacred to God; for it ordained in many places that the fine flour brought as a sacrifice must be sprinkled with frankincense. So the fruit of those who have been called, he says, will be fragrant and acceptable as a sacrifice to God, who loves virtue.
They will return and sit under his shelter.

They will cease, he says, from their old ways and will return vigorously to the worship of “the living and true God,” and will be under him alone, expecting salvation from their enemies not from another but from him only. The Church from the Gentiles fulfills this well when she says of the Savior of all in the Song of Songs, “In his shade I longed to be, and I sat down.” And to those who are accustomed to do this let the divine David also call out, saying, “The sun shall not burn you by day, nor the moon by night.” God did this for the people of old, when a cloud overshadowed them in the wilderness, gracefully foreshadowing the shelter that is from above and from God. And he says “they will sit” very aptly, so that by this the steadfastness and secure settledness of the resolve of those who return may be understood.
They will live and be drunk with grain.

These are gifts worth receiving for their turning back and their steadfastness. For they will share, he says, in eternal life, and in an abundance of strength—plainly spiritual strength. This, I think, is what “they will be strengthened with grain” means. And it is written, “Bread strengthens the heart of man.” For bodies delight in suitable foods, but the soul of man is braced by the divine word from above. For how can one doubt that whoever turns from error to the knowledge of God, and leaps vigorously up from the pits of wickedness to the desire for virtue, would pass from weakness to strength? Since it is truly the charge of weakness to fall back into carelessness and worldly pleasures and a fondness for clinging to the worship of idols, whereas it is understood as a splendid achievement of spiritual strength to choose eagerly to do good, and besides this to consider nothing better than love for God, and to walk the path that leads to it unfalteringly and with vigorous resolve.
And his memorial will blossom like a vine, like wine of Lebanon for Ephraim.

God says somewhere to the mother of the Jews, that is, the Synagogue, “But I planted you as a fruitful vine, wholly true.” And the divine David also sings of her somewhere: “You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out nations and planted it; you cleared the way before it. It stretched out its branches to the sea, and its shoots to the river.” So Israel was a vine rich in branches; but since it stumbled in many ways, “The Lord tore down its hedge; all who pass along the road have plucked its fruit. A boar from the forest ravaged it, and a wild ass fed on it.” For it was laid open, as it were, to be trampled by those who wished to do it harm, a pasture for swine and wild asses—that is, for pleasures and irrational passions. That is why it withered. Yet its memorial—that is, plainly, Israel’s—blossomed again in Christ. And he says “memorial” because not all believed, but a remnant was preserved, as it were, as a memorial of it. And the grace from God became for Ephraim, that is, for Israel, like wine of Lebanon—that is, fragrant, and yielding little to frankincense in sweetness of scent. Such is the word from Christ, and of it the blessed David says, “Wine gladdens the heart of man”; and the holy word spurs us to hasten very eagerly to partake of it, for it runs thus: “Eat and drink, and be drunk, O neighbors.” For the things that come through Christ never cloy the saints, and taken even to the point of drunkenness they are all the more beneficial.
What has he to do any more with idols?

For if he comes, he says, to be filled with and to share in such venerable goods from above, he will entirely abandon any wish to go astray and to cling to the works of his own hands. For what good thing would he still lack, that he should seek it from another? Or rather, is not such seeking entirely useless for those who have gone astray? For what will lifeless matter bestow on anyone? To such people God rightly said, “Do good or do harm, and we shall know that you are gods.” But handmade things could never harm people—how could they, or by what means? Nor could they give them anything good or beneficial. So let them hear, and very fittingly, “Let the gods who did not make heaven and earth perish from the earth and from under this heaven.” By saying, then, “What has he to do any more with idols?” he indicates a love for God that is fixed and firm.
I humbled him, and I will strengthen him.

I, he says, am able to afflict those whom I see neglecting the ways of true devotion to me; and again I give strength to those who choose to practice virtue and to know him who is God by nature and in truth. So neither was the affliction, that is, Israel’s weakness, the work of those [idols]; nor could the passage back to strength be thought a gift of demons. It is a God-given good, just as the weakness, of course, was the offspring of the movements of his wrath. Wisely, then, and with love for God does the great David sing to us, “The Lord is my strength and my song.”
I am like a dense juniper; from me your fruit has been found.

The juniper is a plant so thick and so luxuriant in foliage that it seems almost a roof made by hand, letting through neither the rays of the sun nor the downpours of rain, even when they beat violently upon the earth. So by saying, “I am like a dense juniper,” he hints that those who have come under God will have a shelter—that is, a protection—that no plot can assail.

And that all the fruitfulness of those who are under God can come about in no other way than in Christ and through Christ, he himself will assure us when he says in the oracles of the Gospel, “Apart from me you can do nothing.” So let him rightly say to each of the believers, however illustrious and admirable he may be and however distinguished for virtue, “From me your fruit has been found.”

Who is wise, and will understand these things? Or who is discerning, and will come to know them? For the ways of the Lord are straight, and the righteous will walk in them, but the ungodly will grow weak in them.

He says very well that whoever understands these things is wise and most discerning. For the comprehension of the divine words does not lie open for anyone who wishes to grasp it at will; indeed, no one could understand “a parable and a dark saying, the words of the wise and their riddles,” as it is written, except through the torch-light from above, as Christ sends down into mind and heart his own grace like a bright ray. And he teaches that to be able to travel the straight path that pleases God is quite free of toil for those who love good order, but is no smooth matter for those not so minded. For the former are braced by their desire and eagerness for every good thing whatever, and are moved to press on in an unchecked course toward the wish to win approval; but the latter, their inclination and leaning toward wickedness and sin would show to be cowardly and unmanly, and not to have from God the ability to achieve virtue, because they did not honor it from the beginning, and their aim was not directed toward it. So if we are sharp-minded and wise, we will ask God for the ability to do what is fitting; and he will surely grant it, since he loves humanity, and will fill us with spiritual strength through Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.
COMMENTARY BY THE SAME AUTHOR ON THE PROPHET JOEL.

The divinely inspired Joel prophesies, it seems, in the same times as those placed before him, I mean Hosea and also Amos. The Hebrews hold that he should be ranked not after Micah but together with those two. As it seems to me, he accuses the people of Israel and raises a very loud outcry against them, because they had now come to such a pitch of arrogance, stupor and insensibility that no evil could check them at all. Nor were they humbled by calamities so frequent, brought on them almost one after another, even though no interval had passed in which any respite from the evil, however brief, appeared to have come. We shall find the blessed prophet Isaiah also going through similar words. For he said: “And the Lord of Hosts was kindled with wrath against his people, and he laid his hand on them and struck them; and the mountains were provoked, and their corpses became like dung in the middle of the road. For all this his anger was not turned away, but his hand is still raised high.” You see how they suffered one thing and then another, and the hand of the one striking stayed raised high, ready at any moment to bring yet other blows on them. Some diseases that are hard to heal need not one incision but several. In the same way the human mind, once it has reached a state of insensibility, needs more frequent blows, which barely bring it back to the point where it can at last learn again to strive after what leads to its benefit. So the blessed prophet Joel, since Israel had remained uncorrected after very many blows, seems to deliver his rebuke wisely, and at the same time to counsel them to let go of their more shameful ways and choose to cross over to what pleases God. He also adds to this the promise of the very dearest things, if they should choose to repent, and he gives them confidence that they will find the Master kind and most gentle. This, then, is the aim of his whole prophecy. We shall speak of each of the following points in turn, following the contemplation of the passages before us.
The word of the Lord that came to Joel the son of Bethuel.

The Prophet says that the word of the Lord came to him so that we may put faith in the prophecy, firmly settled and confident that what has been foretold will in every way and by all means come to fulfillment. The Saviour himself confirms us in this when he says: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away.” For the truth is not a thing that speaks falsely, and whatever God says will certainly come true. For he is the one “who confirms the words of his servant and makes true the counsel of his messengers.” So with great skill and wisdom he asks his hearers for faith, because he is not a false speaker as some are, bringing out what seems good to him from his own heart. Rather, as he has said most clearly, he speaks from the mouth of the Lord in the Spirit. Bethuel is added of necessity, so that no other Joel should be understood besides him. For perhaps many, or rather undoubtedly many, were called by this name, but not all were sons of Bethuel. So, I think, Bethuel has been added for the sake of certainty.

Hear these things, you elders, and give ear, all you who inhabit the land. Has such a thing happened in your days, or in the days of your fathers? Tell your children about it, and let your children tell their children, and their children another generation.

He takes the old men back to the antiquity of times and of memory, and bids them consider when, and upon whom, they have seen such things brought by divine wrath, whether upon their own fathers or upon those still earlier. He said they must reckon whether these accounts are not strange and unheard of, perhaps known to none of the ancients. It is fitting, he says, that the others also understand [?] very well whether such things happened in their time. This will also be the subject of endless tales, reaching not to one generation, nor even to two or three, but piercing through far beyond. We say that brilliant stories are worth hearing for most people, and perhaps also bring delight. In the same way, things that have reached the extreme of calamity and suffering seem somehow worth remembering. For such things too all but force their way past oblivion: though their impact is more burdensome, with very great boldness they claim to be remembered and vie with the glories of the sweetest things. And just as the memory of good things is not without profit, so too, I think, is the memory of grievous and gloomy ones. The first whet the hearers' desire for virtue. The second teach them to refuse the experience of evils before they arrive, and through the very things for which others have been punished they keep people from seeking to be caught in the same.
What the caterpillar left, the locust has eaten; what the locust left, the young locust has eaten; and what the young locust left, the blight has eaten.

The word of the holy Prophets is always somewhat hidden. Because of their hearers' untamed tempers, they are reluctant to utter the gloomiest parts of their message, and they shade them with such obscurity as is allowable. By shaping riddles and parables they do no small good. Sometimes [?] their speech also proceeds through useful examples, such as the passage in the most wise Ezekiel: “The great eagle, with great wings, long in extent and full of talons, which has the design to enter Lebanon, took the choice parts of the cedar, cropped off the tips of its tender shoots, and carried them into the land of Canaan.” For he was elegantly hinting at the ruler of the land of Babylon, who sheared off the choicest of Israel and carried the plunder home. The sacred scripture has told us that there were barren fields, shortages of seasonal crops, and famines, many times harsh and long, in the land of the Jews. For under the pressure of famine some were driven to such straits that an ass's head was bought for fifty shekels. The savagery of the want at such times is shown by the women who quarrelled over their children. When the two had eaten the one child, they asked to go to law before the rulers over the living one.

So if the prophetic word here signifies to us barren fields and ruined crops, even so the matter would be understood as unbearable. To be tormented one after another, without interval, by so many grievous blows: how is that not utterly hard to bear, and not undeserving [?] of being remembered? But if the contemplation carries us to other meanings, shadowed by the more evident ones, then by the caterpillar and locust, the young locust and blight, and the terrible and unbearable harm they cause, the Prophet seems to us to indicate the ravagings at each period and to hint at the forms the captivities took.
