By these the people were consumed and destroyed, for those who carried out the invasions all but ate them up and destroyed them like crops in a field. There were indeed many devastations of the land of the Jews in turn [?]. Sometimes the neighbouring nations made war on it, and sometimes those who reigned over Egypt.

While Rehoboam held the royal dignity in Jerusalem, Shishak king of Egypt came up and took the palace. He emptied all the treasures in it, took the golden spears and the shields that Solomon had made, and went home again glorious and victorious. Hazael the Syrian also dealt them no small blows. Pul king of the Babylonians took the tribes beyond the Jordan. Besides this, Pharaoh Necho king of Egypt, in the reign of Josiah, campaigned against Samaria and put the land under tribute, for he demanded a hundred talents of gold.

So there were very many disasters at various times, but four ravagings were terrible and memorable. When Hoshea son of Elah reigned in Samaria, Shalmaneser the Assyrian came up and deported Israel to the territories of the Persians and Medes. Then, a little later, while Jeremiah was prophesying, Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem by force, and Israel was barely released by Cyrus son of Cambyses when the seventy years were completed. Then in due time came Antiochus, surnamed Epiphanes. He came into Judea, burned the divine temple, seized its vessels, and forced those throughout all Judea to neglect their ancestral customs. It was at that time that the brilliant and admirable achievements of the Maccabees took place. The fourth war to come upon Israel was that of the Romans, when they were also scattered to every wind. So the Prophet seems to wish to convey his meaning to us obscurely and dimly, by such accounts used as examples. By the caterpillar, the locust, the young locust and indeed the blight he indirectly points either to the wars themselves, which followed one upon another, or to the leaders of the armies, whom we have just mentioned.

If anyone should wish to give a more moral interpretation of these things as well, he would not miss what is fitting. Suppose a soul is seen bitten by frequent passions one after another, losing each virtue little by little as it were, and adding one loss to another through carelessness. How is it not true to say of it: What the caterpillar left, the locust has eaten; what the locust left, the young locust has eaten; and what the young locust left, the blight has eaten? For like blight and the other pests, wicked and unclean powers somehow ravage the good things in us. They fall upon the mind and are used to consuming with insatiable teeth. Caution, therefore, is a good thing, and the writer of Proverbs helps us not a little when he says: “If the spirit of the ruler rises against you, do not leave your place, for healing will put an end to great sins.” For passions rebuked at the outset are calmed and checked. But if they are given broad and unchecked progress toward the worse, they seize the whole soul completely and will not endure the reason that would chastise them.
Sober up, you who are drunk with their wine, and weep; lament, all you who drink wine to drunkenness, for gladness and joy have been taken away from your mouth.

Here again, I think, one could see plainly and without effort how very wise the divine Paul was when he called out to those caught in the net of salvation through faith in Christ. At one time he said: “Awake, you sleeper, and rise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.” At another he urged them to love endurance in hardships, and for that reason said: “If you endure discipline, God is treating you as sons; for what son is there whom his father does not discipline?” For God, though he loves humankind, does in a sense strike sinners. He does so not willingly but as one turning them back out of necessity, making the blow a means of helping them. In just the same way, physicians apply even very stinging medicines to the sick, making the pain they must suffer a cure for their disease. See how, having first shown the scourges and revealed beforehand what wrath would bring, he all but “chokes their jaws with bit and bridle,” as it is written. He bids them go forward as human beings should, turning their minds to choose to do what was better and most fitting. For he says: Sober up, you who are drunk with their wine. You hear how he now rebukes them as children out of their senses and already somehow drunk. Had they sobered up at the beginning, the damage from the caterpillar alone would have sufficed as their punishment. But since they remained insensible to the first wrath brought upon them, a second was added, and after that a third, and it advanced even to a fourth. Still, he bids them, even if late, to be roused and sober up, to let go of their love of pleasure, which is a kind of drunkenness of the mind, and their wanton choice to do wrong. He bids them now come to a sense of what has happened, weeping and wailing over their own sins.

We should also know that each of us has, as it were, a particular wine of his own that makes the heart drunk. For we divide up the passions among us, so to speak. One of us has turned without restraint to avarice, while also sick with other things. Another has set his mind on the things of the world and is sick with love of the flesh, wholly given over to luxuries and pleasures. Another has run off into some other sin. We rush toward such loathsome and God-hated passions, some not very eagerly, others with all their impulses, and the bent of their mind goes uncorrected. For this reason the Prophet says: Sober up, you who are drunk with their wine. And he counsels that those who drink wine to drunkenness ought to lament. For, as I said just now, some do not stop their pleasures at satiety and sufficiency but drink, as it were, to drunkenness, stretching beyond all measure. From the mouth of these, he says, gladness and joy have been taken away. For Christ speaks truly when he says that those who mourn now will certainly be comforted. And those used to luxury will have to shed tears, because the end of arrogance will be lamentation and wailing, and it brings down those who love it into the snare of Hades. David too speaks truly when he says to God: “In death there is no one who remembers you; and in Hades who will give you thanks?” And again: “The dead will not praise you, Lord, nor any who go down into Hades; but we the living will bless you, Lord.” But the force of the passage may also be understood in a more earthly way. If the sources of gladness have been consumed by the caterpillar and the other pests, then surely the gladness and joy of those who suffered this will perish together with the good harvests. For people cannot help being gloomy at events that are distressing, that tend to cause grief, and that are quite capable of melting the heart with bitter and unbearable sorrow.

For a nation has come up against my land, strong and without number; its teeth are the teeth of a lion, and its molars those of a lion's whelp. It has made my vine a desolation and my fig trees a wreck; it has searched them out thoroughly and cast them down; it has stripped their branches white.

He wants the tears of repentance to match, in a sense, what had happened, or rather what was expected and about to arrive at any moment. So he describes in detail what will be, all but setting the onset of these gloomy events before their eyes. He gives the stricken a lament and teaches those who are told to mourn a kind of mournful song, persuading them to say: For a nation has come against my land, strong and without number, yielding little to lions and their whelps in the sharpness of its teeth. [?] the matter, then, even if it were perhaps understood of the locust, the young locust and the caterpillar. For it is a thing that cannot be fought, and the onset of such creatures cannot be resisted at all. It is enough to destroy utterly what is in the fields, the crops, I mean, and the grass, to ruin fig trees and vines, and to make the face of the ploughland ugly and unsightly. But if the passage is turned again to the inhumanity of the ravagers and the total desolation of the land, it would suggest nothing other than this: their whole land perished, and those who were prominent among them were consumed, those who surpassed the common herd in glory and wealth. These are to be understood in the place of the fig tree and vine before [?] they withered. The same is understood of actual vines if they happen to fall into the teeth of locusts. Locusts drink up the moisture in the plants and suck out all their life-giving power, and before long they dry them up and so make them look white. So the teeth of the devouring enemies have entirely consumed those who stood in the place of vines or in the form of fig trees, and have reduced them to complete uselessness, either cutting them down with swords or putting them under the yoke of slavery.

If one chose to understand these things spiritually, one might also take them of sinful people. Into their mind and heart the wicked demons are always somehow slipping, like locust, young locust and caterpillar, along with the many-formed and manifold passions themselves. These make them appear useless and most unsightly, stripped of the bloom of piety and with no shoots of righteousness in them. I would say it would befit them to weep unceasingly and lament before God, and to long to obtain forgiveness and help through frequent prayer. In this way they might become, however late and with whatever difficulty, wise and strong, and able to escape what has befallen them. This would happen most of all to those whose mind has ignorantly turned aside to heed people who habitually hold other doctrines and undo the right doctrines of the Church. Of these it might very fittingly be said: Their teeth are the teeth of a lion, and their molars those of a whelp. For that nation is hateful to God, counterfeit and accursed. With words of pretended wisdom it devours and consumes the minds of simpler people, so that no remnant of orthodoxy can be seen in them. These people wither the Master's vineyard, leave the garden bare of figs, and show it stripped and laid waste. “Their judgment is not idle but just,” and it comes in due time.

Those, then, who are used to living with ignorance will be food for locust, young locust and caterpillar. They will be left bare of all beauty, with nothing at all in bloom in them. But the wise and God-loving soul is richly clothed with the doctrines of truth, and its heart all but teems with the fruits of righteousness and is beautifully adorned with flowers. Such a soul will surely say boldly, like the bride we read of in the Song of Songs: “Let my beloved come down into his garden and eat the fruit of his trees.” For sweet, sweet are the fruits of piety and the fruits of true love of learning to Christ the Saviour of us all, who is also our beloved kinsman, since he was born of the holy Virgin.
Lament to me more than a bride girded with sackcloth for the husband of her youth.

He bids them make their repentance, and the mourning that goes with it, nothing incidental, nothing done in passing or simply carelessly. Rather, it should vie hard with the very heaviest of griefs and strive to equal them, so that their sorrows weigh as much as their sins. A newly married girl tends to wail bitterly for a bridegroom who has died and to take the grief of it so sharply that her mind is beyond all admonition, and no way of mourning him seems to her worthy enough. The female sex is admittedly given to tears and mourning, and most of all the woman who sees her young bridegroom, who was a virgin, lying pitiably dead and breathless even in the marriage bed. He says the multitude of the Jews should certainly be like her. They should ward off the wrath with their laments and check the divine movement coming upon them as though unstoppable. And they should be confident that the Master of all is “kind and gentle” and loves humankind, “abounding in mercy and relenting from evils,” as it is written.

Yet the Synagogue of the Jews did not lament the bridegroom from heaven, that is, Christ. For it killed him and treated him with drunken outrage. It is therefore shut out of the divine bridal chambers. It stands outside the sacred marriage and has no share at all in the feast. Henceforth it is disinherited and cast off, as far as possible from the hope of the saints. In its place has been called the new bride without wrinkle, all-pure and wise, the bride from Lebanon, the beautiful dove, that is, the Church from the Gentiles. She confesses the very passion of the Lord and all but weeps over him by suffering with him and mourning, taking up her own cross and following him, and she gladly goes through these things out of love for him. Emmanuel would be understood as her virgin bridegroom. She seemed to have committed adultery and fornication with Satan by going astray, and yet he is her virgin bridegroom because of the regeneration from above. We have been enriched with this regeneration through the Spirit, renouncing the birth of the flesh. For it is written of Christ: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him. But to all who received him, who believe in his name, he gave the power to become children of God, who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God.” So, rejecting birth according to the flesh, we make the spiritual birth our own. In this sense the Church from the Gentiles, that is, those who have believed in Christ, may be understood as a pure and all-holy virgin. The divine Paul writes to them plainly: “For I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ.”

Sacrifice and drink offering have been cut off from the house of the Lord; mourn, you priests who serve the altar. For the plains are wretched; let the land mourn, for the grain is wretched, the wine has dried up, the oil has dwindled. They have dried up.

It is as if he were saying plainly: Thanksgivings have ceased, and there is no longer anyone at all to offer sacrifice, to bring an offering and the firstfruits of the crops — that is, surely, the holy sheaf dedicated to God as firstfruits of the wheat harvest, according to the law of Moses. And there is no one, he says, to set out the first-ripe fruits of the seasons, to go to the house of the Lord, and to raise to God the songs of thanksgiving that it was customary to recite. For this reason he bids the chosen race mourn, I mean the priests. They are not to be troubled for the sake of their dues, but are to grieve deeply for the peoples under their charge, as men appointed to a sacred and renowned ministry, so that they, before all others, may appease the God of all, and imitate the sacred teacher Moses himself, who led Israel and said to God: "I beg you, Lord, this people has sinned a great sin; and if you will forgive them their sin, forgive; but if not, blot me also out of this book of yours that you have written." For the office of priesthood mediates between God and the peoples, and boldness in supplication would befit those appointed to so august a ministry, and quite reasonably so, I think. For they all but consecrate their own life to God on behalf of all, eating the sacrifices offered for sin. The God of all says this too through the voice of Hosea: "They shall eat the sins of my people, and in their iniquities they shall take their souls." That is, when the peoples do wrong, transgressing what the law prescribes, then, he says, then the ministers of the divine altars will take their own souls to God on their behalf. He says "they shall take" instead of "they shall bring" or "offer up"; for what was offered up to God was said to be "taken."

And what is the reason for their mourning? The plains are in distress, he says, and so is the grain, stripped bare by the teeth of the locusts and burned up by the blight as if by fire; for the blight scorches and withers what is in the fields. He says that the earth itself must in a way lament, since its fruits have perished. For the grain is in distress, the wine has dried up, the oil has dwindled, they have dried up. That is, everything that comes from it is gone, including the very things for which it would rightly be greatly admired as the mother and nurse of good fruits.

Let this much be said by us as concerning things perceived by the senses. But every priest who is truly approved will lament those who, out of boundless madness, do not accept the cleansing that comes through faith and have not cared to be sanctified by Christ. For they will remain wholly and utterly bereft of spiritual fruitfulness, and will lack everything that knows how to nourish them and raise them up to spiritual strength, having neither grain nor wine, and deprived of the use of oil. The meaning is mystical. To those who accept the faith Christ will offer himself as the bread of life — for he said, "I am the bread of life" — and as wine that gladdens the heart of man (understand again what I am saying); and he will anoint them with oil, that is, the spiritual and sanctifying oil, understood as participation in the Holy Spirit. But those whose disposition is harsh, bitter and without love for God, whose mind is disobedient and intractable, he will surely leave in want and wholly without share in the good things we have just named. It should be known that the most wise Paul too, serving as a priest of the gospel of Christ among the Gentiles, all but lamented the disobedient of Israel. For he said: "I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart for my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites." Mystical, then, as I said, and hidden is the meaning here.

Lament, you farmers, for your holdings, for the wheat and the barley, because the harvest of the field has perished. The vine has withered, and the fig trees have dwindled; pomegranate and palm and apple and all the trees of the field have withered, because the sons of men have put joy to shame.

The utter ruin of what is in the fields is truly mourning, pain and lament for those who are accustomed to till the soil, and so is being able to gather nothing at all from them, sometimes after long sweat. And then to see what grows in the gardens withered and dead, the choicest of the trees, the vines ruined along with the crops, and even the wild woodland wasting away together with the gardens! For all the trees of the field, he says, have withered, because the sons of men have put joy to shame. "Put joy to shame" means this: the inhabitants of the land turned into a season of shame and disgrace and of reproofs leading to punishment and penalty the very time in which they could have expected to revel in prosperity — gathering in the produce of the fields, filling the storehouses with grain, singing the songs of the winepress as they harvested the grapes, and delighting in their flocks of sheep, with abundant, flowering grass spread out before them.

Here again the text seems to call "farmers," in riddling fashion, those who at that time presided over the ranks of the Jews. He said they must lament, since practically everyone throughout the country, that is, the inhabitants of the land, was about to go to destruction; and these might be understood as the wheat and barley and the fair trees. But we shall apply the force of these ideas more fittingly to the scribes and Pharisees. They held the place of tillers, yet they behaved outrageously toward Christ and killed the heir, so that they might have the garden for themselves and become masters of the vineyard from then on. They all but exulted in the populous multitude of their subjects as in their crops, and were accustomed to pluck the most illustrious among them like a pomegranate or an apple. But the war of the Romans overtook them; it consumed great and small, the illustrious and the notable — understood, as I just said, as fig trees, or perhaps as the vine, the palm, the apple and the trees, or as barley and wheat. For people's ways differ, and the measure of life is not the same for all. Since he had once likened the land of the Jews to a field and called its leaders tillers, the text keeps the metaphor to the end, comparing those under them in various ways to crops and trees.

If anyone thinks that these words must also be carried over into a moral interpretation, he will judge well. For the vine, the fig tree and the other trees that are wont to be crowned with fair fruits are to be likened to the virtues and to the achievements of the mind. If someone is wise and quick-witted and careful to cultivate good things to boast of, he will bear in his mind and heart a garden full of flowers and trees, nurturing within himself virtue in its many forms and every kind of goodness. But if he is lazy and pleasure-loving and strongly inclined toward what is shameful, he will surely lament, as his goodness withers and his mind suffers great barrenness. So the sensible must take care of the good things in their hearts; and these will surely be present if, for their own part, they choose to gladden with their virtues God, the giver of heavenly gifts.

Gird yourselves and beat your breasts, you priests; lament, you who minister at the altar. Go in, sleep in sackcloth, you who minister to God; for sacrifice and libation have been withheld from the house of our God.

By these words too he heightens, as it were, what has happened and sets it amid unbearable terrors, showing that the situation calls for the greatest possible supplication, since even the priests themselves must wail. But the passage also has a certain artfulness. They had most ill-advisedly settled down beside the precincts of idols, and though God was striking them in his anger, they sought help from there. So the God of all usefully assigns to his own ministers the task of leading the supplication and of presiding with endurance over the efforts toward repentance, so that the transgressors might know that unless they chose rather to seek what pleases God and brought their supplications to him, they would not ward off the wrath. He therefore said that those who serve as priests must all but lend the others the labours of supplication: beating of the breast, lament, and putting on sackcloth. By sackcloth is signified the laying aside of luxury and ease, hardship and toil, and the right and blameless practice of a holy life. Then, making the cause of the toil plain, he says that sacrifice and libation have been withheld from the house of God. The saying is pointed. He does not say that sacrifice and libation have been reduced or diminished, but rather that they have been withheld, which signifies complete overthrow. And it is truly a terrible and grievous thing for those who preside over peoples if God is in no way served by those under them.
Sanctify a fast, proclaim a service, gather the elders, all the inhabitants of the land, into the house of our God, and cry out to the Lord earnestly: Alas, alas, for the day!

He again makes clear in what way they ought to carry out their mourning. He shows himself a wise guide for them on the road to repentance, and plainly points out the means by which the God of all might become gentle and kindly. This, I think, was the part of one who wished to check the wrath, remove the grief, restrain the harm, and grant them prosperity once more and joy in good things. He said, therefore, "Sanctify a fast," that is, make a truly all-pure and blameless fast, treating it as an offering, as a kind of sacrifice. For it is not fitting to waste the flesh by abstaining from food while doing, even as we fast, the things by which God would rightly be provoked. If during a time of fasting we do not cease from following our own wills, but goad those under our hand "to strife and quarrels, and strike the lowly with fists," as it is written, we have not yet fasted in holiness and purity; rather, we shall rightly suffer the loss of our labours, since God has cried aloud: "This is not the fast that I have chosen, says the Lord." So we must abstain from wickedness and follow the decrees of the lawgiver with great vigour, directing our hearts toward everything that pleases him and bowing the neck of the mind, singing and saying: "See my lowliness and my toil, and forgive all my sins"; and in addition that prophetic word: "Behold, we will be yours, for you are the Lord our God." For this is a spiritual offering and a pure sacrifice, pleasing to God "more than a young calf," more than a lamb from the flocks, more than a kid from the goats, more than fine flour and frankincense. For "God is well pleased with spiritual sacrifices." And as we sanctify the fast, we shall proclaim a service, that is, the fulfilment of the divine will, which would fittingly be accompanied by uprightness, a teachable character, and readiness for everything that belongs to the principles of piety. And we shall carry out the forms of this service when the members of the council of elders have gathered in the assemblies, and all the inhabitants of the land have flocked together, weeping intensely all day long, firmly convinced that God will wholly and surely have mercy. For he is "long-suffering and abounding in mercy and true," "taking away iniquities and passing over unrighteousness, and not holding on to his anger as a witness," as it is written, "because he delights in mercy."
For the day of the Lord is near, and it will come like misery upon misery. Before your eyes food has been destroyed; gladness and joy have withered from the house of our God as well.

He calls it the day of the Lord, the day in which the effects of wrath would be fulfilled. This was either when the locust was brought upon them, devouring what was in the fields, bringing the terrors of famine and want, and instilling the very dread of death; or when the Babylonians were destroying everything, fastening upon cities and villages, working one evil after another, and constantly heaping misery upon misery on the inhabitants of the land, so that they could not catch their breath even for a moment, nor could any good come in between to give those now unbearably worn down by the frequency of their evils at least some partial and moderate relief. And since the invasion of the locust perhaps happened when the fruits were already ripening, when the crops were all but calling the reaper to themselves and the grape cluster was darkening and longing to be pressed, he says that food was destroyed from them, as if what had come into view were snatched away, though it lay, so to speak, before them and was ready to be enjoyed. He also affirms that gladness and joy have been removed from the house of the Lord. For they used to offer sacrifice, exulting in the abundant fruits of the fields, and practised the customs of rejoicing, offering thank-offerings because they were richly surrounded with the good things of the earth.

We shall find that those who acted outrageously toward Christ suffered something of this kind most of all. For the bread of life had already in some sense come before their eyes — "he who came down from heaven and gives life to the world," "the grain of wheat that fell into the earth" and sprang up many times over, the spiritual wine that knows how to gladden the heart of man. But since they did not cease committing outrage by their disobedience, the spiritual food was taken from before their eyes and, as it were, out of their midst. For participation in every good has departed from them, and gladness and joy have been removed from their house as well. They have been given over to desolation, and the wretches continue "without king or ruler, without sacrifice or altar, without priesthood or manifestations."

In another sense too we say that food and gladness and joy have been removed from before their eyes. For our Lord Jesus Christ said: "Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God." And no one would doubt that the word is the food of the mind. This has been taken away from the multitude of the Jews, for they have come to lack spiritual food: they have not understood the writings of Moses. Indeed, the divine Paul writes: "To this day, when the old covenant is read, a veil lies over their heart." And they have hated the oracles given through Christ. So all spiritual food has been destroyed for them — not that it has itself suffered destruction, but that it no longer lies before those who have suffered this, and, as far as they are concerned, does not exist at all. But our Lord Jesus Christ grants those who believe in him to feast and to revel in the good things from above. For it is written: "The Lord will not starve the soul of the righteous, but he will overturn the life of the ungodly."

Heifers have leapt at their mangers, storehouses have vanished, winepresses have been torn down, for the grain has withered. What shall we store up for ourselves? The herds of cattle have wept, for there was no pasture for them, and the flocks of sheep have vanished.

Divinely inspired Scripture sometimes attributes speech even to irrational animals, skilfully embellishing the nature of things so as to make it graceful and elegant, and portraying events as though in living character, in the way it is fitting to understand them. So what is surprising if it says that heifers leapt about and herds of cattle wept? With famine pressing upon them unbearably, they would perhaps indeed have leapt about and died, had they any perception of what had been brought upon them. He says that the storehouses have vanished and the winepresses have been torn down, perhaps because they were not thought worth any care, since nothing was being gathered from the fields: the sickle for the vine and the cluster lay idle, and the ear of grain, dry perhaps and unripened, drooped in the fields. That is why they say, "What shall we store up for ourselves?" And that, as I said, the plants of the wilderness also perished together with the cultivated fruits he makes plain by saying that even the flocks of sheep have vanished, surely destroyed by famine and deprived of their accustomed and most beloved pasture. This too may be applied wisely to the misfortunes of the Jews, who, as I said, acted outrageously toward Christ, the Saviour of all.

To you, O Lord, I will cry out, for fire has consumed the fair places of the wilderness, and a flame has set all the trees of the field ablaze. And all the beasts of the plain have looked up to you, for the channels of water have dried up, and fire has devoured the fair places of the wilderness.

By "the fair places of the wilderness" he perhaps means what grows of its own accord in untilled plains, and by "the trees of the field" the noble shoots in gardens and orchards, whose nature is to blossom with the abundant fruits of the seasons. These, he says, the grasshopper and the blight have all but devoured in the manner of fire. He makes this prayer to God usefully and most skilfully, teaching that one must by no means seek relief from misfortune from anyone else, but must bring supplications to him alone who is able to save, and who in his anger brings on the things that usually cause grief. For he says one must be well aware that such evils do not happen by chance, but have rather been brought upon them as the result of divine wrath. The God of all himself tells us this through the voice of another prophet: "Shall there be evil in a city which the Lord has not done?" For none of the things that usually harm cities or countries could happen unless God permitted it; for he saves whom he chooses and delivers them from evils. So he persuades them to seek from God release from what has grieved them, casting as far away as possible the notion that their affairs need the hand and help of the falsely named gods. He says that the channels of water have dried up. For when rain does not water the earth, and in addition the blight is sent down, the locust is armed, the grasshopper leaps and the caterpillar creeps, how could there be any doubt that their means of life would vanish entirely into nothing? And when the grass too is destroyed, the cattle must necessarily suffer destruction as well.

I would say that perhaps it would also be fitting for the Jews, when they turn back to God in the last times of the age, to speak such words, afflicted and wailing at their lack of good things. For the good things of the mind have been consumed for them as if by fire, a spiritual locust has devoured them, and the channels of water have dried up. For "he commanded the clouds not to rain rain upon them," as it is written, and they have become an impassable and waterless land that will not be inhabited. But concerning us who have been justified by faith, God proclaimed beforehand, and hinted that the supply of gifts through Christ would be most abundant, saying: "In that day the mountains will drip sweetness, and the hills will flow with milk, and all the channels of Judah will flow with water, and a fountain will come forth from the house of the Lord and water the brook of the rushes." And again elsewhere: "I the Lord God, I the God of Israel, will hear, and I will not forsake them, but I will open rivers on the mountains, and in the midst of the plains turn them into marshes, and the thirsty land into watercourses." Such, then, is our condition. But if they go on to repentance and look up to God, and they too say, "To you, Lord, I will cry out," they will receive the channels of water, and with us they will draw the spiritual water "from the springs of salvation"; they will be given to drink "the torrent of delight" from God the Father, and will have the fountain of life in their hearts. And the fair places of the wilderness will be set before them for their delight, that is, good and abundant pasture, nourishing them into the divine and evangelical knowledge that is understood in Christ.

Sound the trumpet in Zion, proclaim on my holy mountain, and all the inhabitants of the land will be confounded, for the day of the Lord is at hand; for near is a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and mist.

Once again the shape of the war is vividly described for us. And it would be true in both cases, whether one understands it of the locust and the grasshopper, or prefers to take it of the Babylonians themselves. As though the war had already come within the gates and had all but been announced throughout the whole land of Zion, that is, in all Judea, he says that everything will be filled with tumult and terrors. For the day of the Lord is at hand. That is, the matter is no longer merely a prediction; the sufferings are in plain view, and they have come to experience in fact what was long foretold. They would have done far better to choose to turn to better things and to shake off the experience of these evils before they approached and arrived. So he does not allow them to shrink back from repentance, but bids them, letting go of slackness of mind and indolence, to turn briskly to diligence and to resolve to help themselves altogether — running, that is, to God, and wiping out the charges of their former offences by taking up better ways. For this reason he says that the day of the Lord is near, in which they will be as in mist and darkness, dreading the famine brought by the locust, or the misery and onslaught from the Assyrians hanging over them.

Like the dawn a people many and strong will be spread over the mountains; its like has not been from of old, and after it there will be none again until the years of generations upon generations. Before it is a consuming fire, and behind it a blazing flame; the land before it is like a garden of delight, and behind it a plain of destruction, and none escapes it.

By "dawn" he seems to mean either the dew of early morning, which, when it is poured over the mountains, leaves nothing on them unwetted; or else the first rays of the sun, the first gleam of daylight as it breaks, which spreads out over the mountaintops before anywhere else and turns the hills red. In the same way, he says, the strong people will come upon the mountains. This may mean the locusts, or, by a likeness drawn from them, the Assyrian, pictured in a multitude beyond compare. For he says that nothing like it has ever been from of old, nor will there ever be. When locusts swarm, whatever lies in their path is eaten at once, and if anything happens to be left over, it becomes the work of those that follow the first. So he called what goes before it a consuming fire, and what comes after and follows a kindling flame. An army of enemies, I suppose, would do exactly the same. Those marching a little way behind will certainly follow the arrogance and ruthlessness of those who went ahead, and they will treat the land like a garden of delight, stripping it bare and feasting on whatever they find. The statement also holds true if it is applied to the locust itself.

Their appearance is like the appearance of horses, and like horsemen so they will pursue. Like the sound of chariots they will leap upon the mountaintops, like the sound of a flame of fire devouring stubble, and like a people many and strong drawn up for battle.

When the locust and the caterpillar sweep over lands and cities, he says, they will be no less than the most warlike horse. They will leap over the land so that they seem to imitate the clatter of chariots. They spring onto every mountaintop and swoop down on every hill, and they make a sound like a flame burning up stubble. People say that they do not devour what is in the fields without noise: their teeth produce a bleating, harsh sound as they crush whatever they fall upon, like wind fanning a flame. Nor is there anything strange in comparing the locust to a crowd of enemies, for it charges in multitudes and gives little ground to those who fight bravely in battle. It is a voracious thing, and because its numbers are beyond counting it is not easy to defeat; indeed, it is hard even to face. The same could be said of the Assyrians. And if someone wished to apply it to the campaign of the Romans, who like locusts devoured Israel after it had wickedly sinned against our Lord Jesus Christ, that would not be wrong either.
Before its face peoples will be crushed.
For, as I said, an invasion of caterpillar and locust is utterly irresistible and very hard for human beings to overcome.
Every face like the scorching of a pot.
For it is true that through fear and unbearable grief the bloom of the face sometimes withers and darkens into ugliness, as though discolored by the turmoil of the mind.
Like warriors they will run, and like men of war they will climb the walls.
They charge like the most warlike soldiers, they are above hesitation and fear, and they will rise over the very walls, as though practising a bold assault.
And each will go on his own way, and they will not turn aside from their paths, and none will hold back from his brother.

The locust has no king, yet it marches out in good order at a single command. They say that locusts move in ranks and fly as if in formation. They hardly ever stray, but look after one another as if they were brothers, since nature itself governs their care for one another.
Weighed down with their weapons they will march.
By "weapons" I suppose he means their teeth. With these they wage their war and win their victories, as it were in battle: the grass is eaten up, the crops fall, and the plants wither.
And they will fall among their missiles, and they will not make an end.

Locusts do not strike those they make war on with arrowheads, nor do they string a bow. How could they? But they strike them down by destroying their food and by the terror of famine and want. Those who fall into such a calamity will not suffer only the loss of what is in the fields. The army of locusts, that is, the Assyrian himself, will also enter their very houses and cities and harass them terribly. He showed this by saying, "And they will not make an end." It is as if he said, "Even this will not be the limit of the wrath; it will go further still." For he says:

They will seize the city and run upon the walls, they will climb onto the houses, and they will come in through the windows like thieves. Before their face the earth will be thrown into confusion and the heaven will be shaken. The sun and the moon will be darkened, and the stars will not give their light.

You hear that they will swoop down even on the walls themselves. And just as they ravage the grass, they will burst in through the windows like housebreakers, throwing whole populations into confusion and all but turning everything upside down. It will seem as if heaven itself has been shaken, and as if the sun, the moon and indeed the stars have cut off their own light. Here again the language has become hyperbolic, showing that the calamity will be hard to bear and very painful for those who live in the land. Yet the statement is accurate even if it is understood of an army of men that chooses to overrun country and city. Spreading over everything like locusts, such armies ravage the fields and crush the cities as well. They climb over walls and rush into the very houses, rivalling the terrors of an earthquake in their savagery.

And the Lord will utter his voice before his host, for his camp is exceedingly great, for strong are the works of his words. For the day of the Lord is great, great and very manifest; and who will be equal to it?

I have already said that the prophet's aim is to show the calamity as terrible and hard to bear. He wants those who have grieved the Lawgiver by turning aside to wickedness to change course, to choose at last to do what is better and to take wiser counsel. For the extremity of suffering knows very well how to bring people easily, as if by force, to choose from then on to do what pleases the One who is able to save and deliver. So, he says, the Lord will utter his voice before his host, all but commanding it like a general and spurring it on as against enemies. It suits no one better than those who fight in the front rank and are stationed ahead of the rest to rouse the fighting spirit and lead their own camp. By these words he hints that the disasters do not come of their own accord, nor have they simply happened by chance. Rather, they have been brought on by God, who has obviously been grieved and is now justly punishing. He terrifies them by saying that the camp is vast and that the works of his words are strong. It is impossible for whatever God commands to happen not to come to pass completely and in every way. Indeed, he said to one of the holy prophets, Jeremiah, "Are not my words like a blazing fire, says the Lord, and like an axe splitting rock?" For the word of God passes through everything, as it were. Nothing can stand against whatever it speaks to; even what is hard and resistant gives way. It is easily shattered and yields to the Master's will even against its own wish. Great, then, and very manifest is the day, he says, because news of the disasters about to come will spread to all people. And who will be equal to it? That is, no one on earth could be so unyielding and strong as to withstand the divine wrath. Very wise indeed was the inspired David when he cried out to God, "You are terrible, and who will stand against you when you are angry?"

And now the Lord our God says, "Turn to me with all your heart, with fasting and weeping and mourning. Rend your hearts and not your garments, and return to the Lord your God, for he is merciful and compassionate, slow to anger and abounding in mercy, and he relents over evils." Who knows whether he will turn and relent and leave a blessing behind him, a sacrifice and a drink offering for the Lord our God?

From this you can learn very clearly that he told his tale in such lofty terms, and foretold a calamity so harsh and hard to bear, for no other reason than to persuade them at last to come to repentance. He does not allow them to despair. Instead he assures them very clearly that if they choose to think on better things, and at least from now on to set their ways right so as to please God, the effects of his wrath will certainly cease and their affairs will move into a broad place of good order. He makes plain what their turning back and their manner of prayer should be when he says, "And now the Lord our God says, Turn to me with all your heart." Let the past be thrown away, he says, and let what has gone before be sent off into oblivion. Show yourselves better than you were from now on, and appease God with fasting and toil, with mourning and lamentation. For those who choose to do this, a life of comfort and delight will surely follow. Just as ease and a slide into pleasure always end in wailing and punishment, so gentleness and the labours of repentance lead out into the broad place of prosperity. It is profitable, then, to weep over sins and to grieve in a godly way. As the blessed Paul writes, "Godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation and brings no regret." And Christ himself blesses "those who mourn now, for they will be comforted." Our wise Solomon too says something of the kind in a riddle: "It is better to go to a house of mourning than to go to a house of drinking." But we must also consider how great the power of fasting is. It tames the Master, lulls his anger to sleep and overturns punishment. When we afflict ourselves, we strongly move to shame the divine wrath, even when it rages and grows fierce against us, and we easily hold back the hand that is striking us. If it is true that merely by confessing our sins we are justified by the One who has pity on us, how could anyone doubt that by wasting ourselves away with the labours of discipline, as though exacting the penalty from ourselves, we will gain from God the forgiveness of our sins? So he commands them to mourn and to tear themselves, not their clothes at all, but rather, in a spiritual sense, to open up the hard, packed-down heart into which the fear of God does not enter. Paul writes to the Corinthians, "You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections. In return, I speak as to children, open wide your hearts too." So we must widen our hearts for God, as it were, and all but tear open the mind, so that it may receive what is his. To put on a show of grief by tearing one's clothes idly and in vain will do no good to those who choose to do it. But opening the heart and storing in it what pleases God will bring no small gain, for it leads to salvation. He confirms that they will not miss their aim when they make their prayers by saying that the Master of all is loving toward humankind and abounding in mercy, compassionate and good, and relenting over evils. Even if he does choose to afflict sinners, he will be gentle, and not for long, for he turns easily to plans of kindness. This, I say, is what it means to relent over evils. The prophet usefully cuts short the rash thinking of those who have despaired of salvation when he says, "Who knows whether he will relent and leave a blessing behind him?" That is, he will grant to those who turn back a share in blessing, so that they may again offer him a drink offering and a sacrifice and, rejoicing and glad, make their thank offerings.

Blow the trumpet in Zion, sanctify a fast, proclaim a service, gather the people, sanctify an assembly, choose the elders, gather the infants nursing at the breast. Let the bridegroom go out of his chamber and the bride from her bridal room. Between the steps and the altar the priests who minister to the Lord will weep and say, "Spare your people, O Lord, and do not make your inheritance a reproach, for the nations to rule over them, so that they may not say among the nations, 'Where is their God?'"

With these words too he rouses them very effectively to repentance, and he usefully commands them to leave no means of pursuing it untried. They must, he said, use a loud and ringing proclamation to sanctify a fast, proclaim a service, and gather into an assembly those who ought to serve, plainly meaning to serve the God of all whom they have grieved. These would be "young men and maidens, old men together with the young," and newborn babies still at the breast besides. There would be bridegrooms too, and newly married girls, perhaps rushing out of bridal rooms still hung with garlands, turning away from the marriage bed, looking past luxury and drinking and taking up a hard way of life instead. The clapping is put away, and the songs and good wishes that people sometimes offer to the newly married are silent, while the brides lament together with their bridegrooms. What one of our wise men said is true: "Music in mourning is an untimely tale." When the divine wrath hangs over us, then, we must mourn and not be fond of priding ourselves on drinking and luxury. One of the holy prophets makes clear that untimely luxury does not escape blame and punishment when he says of the people of Israel, "And the Lord of hosts called on that day for weeping and mourning, for shaving the head and putting on sackcloth. But they made merry, slaughtering calves and sacrificing sheep, and saying, 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.'" So when wrath hangs over us we must turn to lamentation and tears, and drinking must be cast aside. The prophet says that the holy and chosen race of priests must also join the mourners. At the very steps of the temple, between the steps and the altar, they must wail earnestly, crying out and saying, "Spare your people, O Lord, and do not make your inheritance a reproach, for the nations to rule over them, so that they may not say among the nations, 'Where is their God?'"

But if he were speaking only about the locust, why do they not instead ask to be freed from famine and want? They are terrified of falling into the hands of enemies, and they beg to be spared mockery and reproach. It is likely, then, and I would say it is true, that the invasion of the Assyrians was being described in a hidden way in these riddles about the locust. Yet if someone wishes to understand these things of the locust itself, he would rightly marvel at the wise design of the prophetic oracles. For the very manner of the punishment all but cries out against Israel's folly, and against their weakness as well. They exchanged their God for "gods that are not gods," and abandoning the Creator of all they worshipped Baal. But look: the locust invades them in an unbearable host, the caterpillar arms itself, and they have fallen, getting no help at all from their falsely named gods. If those gods are defeated by caterpillar and locust, what remedy could they still give their worshippers if they had to fight enemies and were besieged by the battle lines of their foes?
BY THE SAME AUTHOR, ON THE SAME PROPHET: SECOND VOLUME.

And the Lord was jealous for his land, and spared his people. And the Lord answered and said to his people: Behold, I am sending you the grain and the wine and the oil, and you shall be filled with them; and I will no longer make you a reproach among the nations, and I will drive the one from the north away from you.

See how mercy follows hard on its heels. Calm, I think, comes quickly after mourning, and the grace of the one who pities comes quickly after the tears of repentance. He not only showed mercy to those who had fared so wretchedly. More than that, he was jealous for them and grew angry with those who had caused them grief, who had also served as the agents of the misery brought upon them. Somewhere the God of all charges the Babylonians with having been harsher than they should have been toward those who had come under the divine wrath. For he said: “I gave them into your hands, but you showed them no mercy.” And indeed he says to the blessed prophet Zechariah as well: “Thus says the Lord: I have been jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion with a great jealousy, and with great anger I am angry with the nations that joined in the attack; for I was angry only a little, but they joined in to do harm.” So, being jealous for his people, he promises to supply them generously with what they need to live. He promises a gladness that somehow matches the calamity that came before, and food in plenty. On top of this he promises security: they will not be handed over to their enemies, nor fall into slavery under them and live out a pitiable and wretched life. He also promises to make the one from the north vanish, that is, the Assyrian, for his country lies further north of them and more toward the sunrise. But if anyone should think that the locusts' invasion also came from the more northern parts of Judea, nothing prevents the passage from being rightly understood that way as well.

Suppose that in some people the goods of the heart and the wealth of spiritual fruitfulness are being destroyed, as though the herd of demons were leaping on them like locusts, and principalities, powers and authorities, evidently the evil ones, were overrunning them. Such a person should mourn, practise repentance and shed tears before God. Then he will at once hear God say, out of his love for humankind: Behold, I give you the grain and the wine and the oil. For God will make that person's heart like land rich in ears of grain, like a garden thick with ripening seed, like a vineyard heavy with clusters, and will anoint it richly with oil, as the Psalms sing: “You have anointed my head with oil.” And he will drive away from him the one from the north, that is, Satan, who chills people and does not let those who fall under him be fervent in spirit. Paul too said that “the love of many will grow cold because lawlessness has multiplied.” But those who know Christ are fervent in spirit, and in no way do they let themselves grow cold and drift toward perverse pleasures, “for they have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.”

And I will drive it out into a waterless land, and I will make its front vanish into the first sea and its rear into the last sea; and its rot shall go up, and its stench shall go up, because it has done great things.

He is still shaping his words as he did at the beginning, as though speaking of the locust and the grub. He says that these will vanish, carried off by God's will perhaps to the very edges of the land of the Jews, and will rot to such a stench that it spreads oppressively to everyone throughout the country. But the passage does not at all spare us from also having to understand these things as referring to the Babylonians. South of Jerusalem a deep desert stretches out, bounded on the east and south by the Indian seas, and on the west and further north by the sea that borders the Palestinians and also washes the shore of Egypt. There, he says, the grub and the locust perish, and their stench becomes unbearable, perhaps the stench of the locust, as I said just now. But the Babylonians were destroyed too, who live in the land further north and lying to the east. As we have often said, they were destroyed in the time of Hezekiah's reign, and the stench of the corpses was unbearable, so that it took the land nearly seven months to be cleansed and rid of the rotting bodies. That, I believe, is what the prophet Ezekiel says. That the land of the Babylonians lies toward the north becomes clear when God, through the voice of the saints, says to those of Israel's blood who had been carried off into captivity: “Oh, oh, flee from the land of the north, says the Lord; escape to Zion, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon.”

Christ has also driven the locust out of us, I mean the spiritual locust, that is, the utterly wicked hordes of demons. He has made them vanish, as though casting them into the depths of the sea, for he shut them up in Hades and in the recesses of the abyss. Their rot and stench then went up, and it has become oppressive and loathsome to us, although long ago it did not seem so. For Satan was always foul-smelling, yet only now, and barely, have we recognized him as such. While we were caught in the bonds of wickedness and had fallen into his hands, we wretches thought him fragrant and lovely. But when Emmanuel appeared to us, crying aloud, “I am a flower of the plain, a lily of the valleys,” then at last, having been called to share in the fragrance that is in him, we condemned the other's foulness.

Take courage, O land; rejoice and be glad, for the Lord has done great things. Take courage, beasts of the plain, for the plains of the wilderness have sprouted, for the tree has borne its fruit, and the vine and the fig tree have yielded their strength. And you children of Zion, rejoice and be glad in the Lord your God, for he has given you food for righteousness, and he will rain on you the early and the late rain, as before; and the threshing floors shall be filled with grain, and the vats shall overflow with wine and oil.

The holy prophets have a habit of moving from particular blessings, given to a few, to blessings that are universal and broader, and these are the blessings that come through Christ. So our discussion turns to them once again. When was the earth granted the right to take courage? When did the Lord do great things among us? Surely it was when the Word, who was God, became man, so that he might flood the whole world under heaven with blessings from above and be found by those who believe in him to be “like a river of peace, like a torrent of delight,” like early and late rain, the giver of all spiritual fruitfulness. Then, yes then, a spiritual grass sprang up even for the very dullest, who are called the beasts of the plain, and that grass is the word of the teachers. Then the plains of the wilderness sprouted. He calls the Church a wilderness, in keeping with what the prophets say of it: “Be glad, thirsty wilderness; let it exult and blossom like a lily.” Its plains would be those who lead the peoples and know how to instruct them. Their minds, as it were, teem with divine and heavenly gifts and are in full bloom. They are sweetly fragrant with the flowers of doctrine and crowned, so to speak, with fresh green grass. These nourish the minds of those who have become like beasts, so that they too may rise to an understanding fit for human beings. He also said that the tree has borne its fruit, and that the vine and the fig tree have yielded their own strength. By this I think he means the solid teaching of the teachers, which has sweetness in it and also the power to gladden, and so he likens it to the fruits of the fig and the vine. It would be quite fitting for those who are still duller of mind and slow like cattle to graze on the more lowly kind of learning, which grows, like grass in form and in nature, among those who teach elementary things. But those who are already perfect should have the fruit that is understood on high and blossoms, as it were, on beautiful trees, that is, the teaching about the holy and consubstantial Trinity, or moral instruction, as contemplations set on a height. That is why he calls the first group beasts and calls the more perfect children of Zion, and commands them to rejoice in the Lord their God. For Christ is our whole delight. From him and through him comes every fullness of blessings, and the abundant supply of heavenly gifts to those who love him. These gifts are understood under the images of early and late fruits, of grain filling the threshing floor, of wine overflowing the vat, and of oil gushing over. We should also know that the promise is true in the sense of a mystical fulfilment. For we have been given, in the image of rain, the living water of holy baptism; in the image of grain, the bread of life; and in the image of wine, the blood. The use of oil has been added as well, which helps bring to perfection those who have been justified in Christ through holy baptism.

And I will repay you for the years that the locust and the grub and the blight and the caterpillar have eaten, my great power, which I sent against you; and you shall eat and be filled, and you shall praise the name of the Lord your God, who has done wonders among you.

As far as the interpretation suited to the historical account goes, he promises a generosity fully equal in strength and measure to the locusts' earlier invasions, and he says that the food set before them will be more plentiful than the suffering they endured at that time.

But if the words of the prophecy are understood spiritually, we say this. Satan had, as it were, devoured us. The accursed spirits had played the part of the caterpillar and the locust, and indeed of the blight, and had ruined us beyond endurance through many kinds of passions. So we remained dry and fruitless, naked and stripped of every good. We had no moral virtue in our minds and were not illumined by the contemplation of doctrine. We were wasted, as if by famine, and in short we were deprived of all fruitfulness. But we have been enriched by Christ with the ability to take courage, for we have conquered the world with him, and “he has given us power to tread on serpents and scorpions.” Then, yes then, we received the spiritual rains, early and late, by which I mean the instruction of the law and the exhortation of the Gospel. Then we also flourished anew in righteousness and bore the fruits of life. Then we ate and were filled, and we glorify Christ our Savior as Master, proclaiming him a worker of wonders who bestows on those who love him things beyond words and beyond hope. Besides him we have come to know no other at all. We have been taught to say with a good mind: “Lord, besides you we know no other; we name your name.” But see how the God of all all but laughs at human affairs and mocks them, when he calls the caterpillar his great power and says that he sent it against them. We certainly do not say that the caterpillar is truly a power of God, let alone a great one. Rather, it is as if he were saying to those who could not bear the punishment it brought: “O you fearsome and arrogant people, who think nothing of offending me! I am not seen sending fire down on you from heaven. I did not let loose thunder or hail, or bring on you anything else that is lofty and most fitting to the glory of God. A wretched swarm of the most paltry worms rose up against the land, and it threw you into confusion. You have lamented and you have perished. Perhaps the caterpillar is very great; I shall count it as my own great power.” So the words are spoken with irony, as if with a laugh. God is all but jeering at those who are used to despising him, as if to say that if he chose to punish them, even a caterpillar would be enough, instead of a great and invincible force.

So let the heretics not laugh too broadly or babble against the glory of the Only-begotten, on the grounds that the caterpillar too was called a great power. And if he too is called the power of God, let him not be ranked as equal with the worm. For the wretches have dared to sink even to such miserable thoughts.

And my people shall never be put to shame. And you shall know that I am in the midst of Israel, and that I am the Lord your God, and there is no other besides me; and all my people shall never again be put to shame.

He clearly promises the manner of the economy in the flesh. He will live among those on earth, lowering himself in self-emptying and becoming like us, that is, a man. For it was then that he came to be in the midst of Israel, and we escaped disgrace and were set free from shame, since death had fallen, sin had been destroyed and true knowledge had been brought in. For we no longer worship “the creature rather than the Creator,” and we have accepted no other God whatever besides him. Accordingly we have been enriched, in sure hope, with life and glory and a way of life in holiness and piety that lasts for long ages.

And it shall come to pass after these things that I will pour out of my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions; and on my male slaves and on my female slaves too, in those days, I will pour out of my Spirit.

See, he clearly promises to grant the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, that is, an abundant supply of it. It will not be given selectively, to one prophet or perhaps two, but to absolutely all who are worthy to receive it. We say that this was fulfilled when Christ had been raised and had destroyed the power of death. For he placed in the holy disciples, as it were, the firstfruits of this venerable and admirable grace when he breathed on them and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit.” It was necessary, truly necessary, that those who were to be the Church's guides into the mysteries and the teachers of the world under the sun should be adorned with the gift of the Holy Spirit before all others. Since they had become a kind of firstfruits of those called through faith to sanctification, they had to be gilded with divine and heavenly grace. Then, in the days of Pentecost, when the disciples were gathered in one house and were offering their usual prayers to God, there came “suddenly from heaven a sound like a violent rushing wind, and behold, tongues as of fire appeared to them, divided, and one rested on each of them, and they began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance.” They spoke out in prophecy, that is, they understood and declared the testimonies about Christ given through the holy prophets. These were the things likely to persuade their hearers thoroughly and lead them readily to obedience: that the time of God's good pleasure had now arrived, and that what had long ago been foretold about Christ through the law and the prophets had now come to fulfilment. So they prophesied, speaking in every tongue, and God had foretold this too through the voice of the saints. For it is written: “With other tongues and with the lips of others I will speak to this people, and even so they will not believe.” The inspired Paul understood this and said that speaking in many tongues was given as a sign to the Jews. Paul also makes clear that, after the Holy Spirit came down from heaven, very many were filled with the spirit of prophecy, when he writes: “Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others weigh what is said. If a revelation is made to another who is sitting there, let the first be silent. For you can all prophesy one by one.” Long ago, when Israel went astray through great perversity, God said: “Behold, I am bringing a famine on the land, not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord; and they shall run about from east to west seeking the word of the Lord, and they shall not find it.” And to the blessed Ezekiel he said: “I will bind your tongue, and you shall be mute, and you shall not be to them a man who rebukes, for they are a rebellious house.” But now, in the words of the psalmist, “God is the Lord, and he has shone upon us.” For our Lord Jesus Christ has shone upon us, forgiving offences, releasing us from charges and stopping the mouth of sin. So the outpouring of the Holy Spirit has now been given. God is gladdening human nature, crowning it with the glory it had from above in the beginning, and in his goodness bringing it back to what it was at first, before sin had entered. For we shall find that Adam was not without the prophetic Spirit before he transgressed the divine commandment. He was still standing, as it were, firmly established, and adorned with the goods of his nature. Indeed, when God had fashioned the woman and brought her to him, Adam had heard from no one who she was, where she came from or how she had come into being. Yet he exclaimed at once: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called woman” (or, in the version of the Hebrews, “she-man”) “because she was taken out of her man.” But the grace given to humankind fell idle. Yet it was renewed in Christ, who is the second Adam. How was it renewed? Insofar as the Son is God and from God by nature, for he was truly begotten of God the Father, the Spirit is his own, in him and from him, just as is understood of God the Father himself. But insofar as he became man and appeared as one like us, he is said to have the Spirit as something received from outside. Indeed, the Spirit came down on him in the form of a dove when he had become like us, as I said, and was being baptized as one of us, in keeping with the economy. It was then that his own Spirit is said to have been given to him from above, because of his humanity, and this is the self-emptying. This, and nothing else, is how one should understand the words: “though he was rich, he became poor for our sake, so that we might become rich through his poverty.” For the Spirit was given to Adam in the beginning, as I said, but it did not remain in human nature. For human nature turned aside to wrongdoing, slipped into sin and fell sick with every kind of impurity.

But the Only-begotten, as I said, though rich became poor, and as a man he received along with us his own Spirit as if it came from outside. And “it remained on him,” as the blessed John the Evangelist said. He did this so that the Spirit might from then on dwell in us too, and remain there, since it had already remained in the second firstfruits of our race, that is, in Christ. That is why he has been called the second Adam. Through him we have been refashioned into something incomparably better, and we richly gain rebirth through the Spirit. We no longer have the first birth, I mean the birth according to the flesh, which leads to corruption and sin, for, as it is written, “the mind of the flesh is death.” We have instead the second birth, from above, from God through the Spirit, if it is indeed true that “we were born not of blood, nor of the will of man, but of God.” It was necessary, then, truly necessary, that those counted among the children of God should also be enriched with the grace of the Holy Spirit. Christ accomplished this too for us, and the inspired Peter confirms it when he says: “Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this which you see and hear.” As man he receives from the Father what is his by nature. But he pours it out richly on us because he is God by nature, even though he became flesh. And he pours it out on all flesh. This clearly means that he pours it out not only on those of the circumcision but on all without exception who are called through faith, even if they come from the error of the Greeks, whether small or great, slaves or free, barbarians or Scythians. For the grace of salvation in Christ is offered to those throughout the whole world under heaven, since he himself is “the expectation of the nations.”

If some people, speaking without restraint, should say that cattle too are called "flesh," they are talking nonsense, for they have surely heard by now that the aim of the prophecy concerns the human race alone, and that "God does not care about oxen," as the wise Paul also said. He says that sons and daughters will prophesy, and by this he shows how abundant grace is and how it reaches [?] to all. For the female sex would not be rejected by God if it eagerly did what pleases him and chose to think rightly. Nor would it be left without honour or without a share in sanctification if it won approval through faith and through goodness in its works. How could it be? For it too has been counted worthy of grace and mercies, it receives "the pledge of the Spirit" from God, and it is reckoned among the children. He says, then, that the old men will dream dreams and the young men will see visions. By "old age" he means, I think, the age that excels and stands out in the measure of its virtue. It is grey-haired, as it were, with splendid achievements, distinguished and admired for the most perfect wisdom. Such was the divine Paul, who in his sleep saw a man from Macedonia pleading with him and saying, "Cross over into Macedonia and help us"; for so it is written in the Acts of the wise apostles. And Ananias, one of those proven in faith, saw a vision about the blessed Paul himself. For when Paul came to Damascus, after Christ had appeared to him on the road and the flash of light had taken away his sight, he was healed through Christ. Again it is written thus: "Now there was a disciple in Damascus named Ananias, and the Lord said to him in a vision, 'Ananias.' And he said, 'Here I am.' And the Lord said to him, 'Get up and go to the street called Straight, and in the house of Judas look for a man of Tarsus named Saul.'" Do you hear how he spoke to Ananias in a vision? For Ananias was perhaps vigorous in faith and a young man in disposition. His mind was bursting with vigour for the good, and he was unbreakable in strength, clearly spiritual strength. But it was in sleep that the Macedonian seemed to bring his petitions to the blessed Paul, for Paul was an old man in mind, aged in understanding, and full of the wisdom from above. The wise John also addresses those sanctified in Christ through faith: "I write to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning. I write to you, young men, because you are strong and have overcome the evil one." So he promises the outpouring of the Holy Spirit to those who serve him. And who, again, would these be? Surely those who bow the neck of their mind to the decrees of the gospel, who have departed from worship in types and have given up pagan deception, as the one speaking says [?].

And I will show wonders in the heaven above and signs on the earth below: blood and fire and vapour of smoke. The sun will be turned into darkness and the moon into blood, before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes.

At the impious acts of the Jews, namely those committed against Christ, the very nature of the elements was distressed. Creation lamented, as it were, seeing its own Master insulted. The divine temple, as though grieving along with the mourners, tore itself, for it is written, "The curtain of the temple was torn from top to bottom." The sun cut off its own brilliance, drew in its rays and would no longer deign to shine on those on earth, for there was darkness from the sixth hour until the ninth hour, and the rocks were split. Perhaps something unusual also happened to the disk of the moon, so that it too seemed to have been turned into blood. The holy evangelists pass over this in silence, yet the prophecy gives sufficient warrant for believing it. At the Creator's command signs appeared not in the sun alone. Rather, the whole of creation passed, as it were, into a state that was unlovely and unaccustomed to it. This becomes clear when God says through Isaiah, "And I will clothe the heaven with darkness, and make its covering like sackcloth." When he says "heaven," he surely means everything in heaven, which is clothed with darkness as with sackcloth, mourning and grieving and, as it were, crying aloud by its appearance. These, then, I would call the signs in heaven. The signs on earth, blood and fire and vapour of smoke, indicate, I think, the calamities of the Jews, which the most grievous war heaped on them at the hands of the Romans. For their whole country was spattered with blood. The famous temple itself was to be burned along with the cities, and houses shaken to the ground were to smoke. These things would befall the Jews before the great and manifest day, on which the divine judgment seat will be set before all and Christ will give to each according to his works. He made this clear by saying, "before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes." We should also note that when the wise apostles asked the Lord himself about the consummation of the age and the destruction of Jerusalem, he mixed the signs together, so that perhaps it would remain unknown which of them would happen when.

And it shall be that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved; for on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be one who is saved, as the Lord has said, and those who bring good news, whom the Lord has called.

He says, then, that because of the unholy deeds of the Jews there will certainly be signs and wonders in heaven and on earth. Yet even so the gifts of God's gentleness will be set before them: salvation through faith, justification in Christ, the pledge of the Spirit, sanctification, and the hope of the kingdom of heaven. God bears no grudge and forgives them even their crimes against Christ. So it was that the divine Peter vehemently accused the crowds of the Jews, crying out plainly that they had killed the Saviour and Redeemer of all by hanging him on a tree, and that they "denied the Holy and Righteous One and asked for a murderer to be granted to them." But he added, "And now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did your rulers. Repent, therefore, and let each of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit; for the promises are for you and for your children." So, he says, even if signs and wonders occur, everyone who acknowledges as Master the Lord of heaven and earth will be saved. The word of salvation was to be spoken first in Jerusalem itself, the city that killed the Lord, and from there carried to all the nations by the holy apostles. This becomes clear when the Prophet says, "On Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be one who is saved, and one who brings good news, whom the Lord has called." For, as the divine Paul writes, "no one takes the honour for himself, but only when called by God." So the blessed disciples were called, chosen out of all, and they did not come forward to be apostles of their own accord. They were not like that crazed Pharisee, or rather lawyer, who thrust himself into the glories of discipleship and came forward saying, "Lord, I will follow you wherever you go." That man was pestering the Saviour idly and had not come even remotely near the practices of the gospel. For this reason the Saviour himself pushed him away, saying, "Foxes have holes, and the birds of the sky have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head." But to those who were fit for the apostleship he called out, "Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men." Matthew he raised up from the very workshops of greed and commanded him to follow. By his own will he called those who were likely to be most capable of carrying out what pleased him, and doing it with great vigour, even though the inventor and father of lawlessness snatched away the betrayer.

For behold, in those days and at that time, when I bring back the captives of Judah and Jerusalem, I will gather all the nations and bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat. There I will enter into judgment with them on behalf of my people and my inheritance Israel, who were scattered among the nations. For they divided up my land and cast lots for my people; they gave the boys to prostitutes, and they sold the girls for wine and drank.

After the ten tribes broke away from the kingdom of Rehoboam, and they and all Israel were divided into Ephraim and Judah, the blessed prophets arose. They spoke about both, while the whole kingdom continued until the times of the captivity. After the return from there to Jerusalem, and the homecoming that took place in stages, Haggai and Zechariah, and Malachi too, prophesied to Israel.
