Ezra also appears to have foretold a few of the events of that time that took place in his own days. The present passage, then, recalls an event not from the time of the ancient prophets but from when the people returned to Judea, after Cyrus had at last released them. What this event worth hearing was, and what actually happened, we shall tell as best we can, bringing forward the writing of Ezra as proof.

When those of Israel had just returned to Judea and had gained relief from tribute and the toils of slavery, they turned to carelessness. They were not reliable in practising and guarding what had been decreed through Moses. The law forbids anyone to sleep with the daughters of foreigners, yet they cared little for the oracles God had given them and had relations with foreign women. Ezra was deeply distressed at this. He tore his garment, lamented over those of Israel, and urged them to rid themselves of the foreign women. They were persuaded to do so. Perhaps they feared the effects of wrath, and they took the experience of past events as their teacher about what would happen to them if they did not choose to honour the law. But when the multitude of foreign women had been cast out and had left Jerusalem, the surrounding nations were inevitably embittered to anger, since they had been greatly insulted by this. Besides this, they were perhaps also reasoning among themselves about something else. Since the Israelites were rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem and were eager to raise the divine temple itself, the nations were inflamed to anger by the darts of envy and tried to stop them. They were thinking, as is likely, that if Israel returned to its former power, with walled cities and with the God of all as its defender, worshipped in the temple according to the ancient customs, it would prevail again and become unbearable to everyone around. It would impose tribute on some of its neighbours, and if any should choose even belatedly to stand up to it, they would certainly be conquered and their lands laid waste. For this reason they arranged for certain people to hinder the Israelites from the building work on the temple itself and on the walls. But their effort was useless, because God widened the path of the Israelites' undertakings. So they armed themselves and wanted to make war. But they were defeated and fell, because God defended Israel. Those assembled for this purpose gathered in the valley of Jehoshaphat. This place lies not many stades from Jerusalem, on its eastern side, and they say it is bare and suitable for cavalry. Some of the more powerful envied those of Israel who were raising the divine temple, but they achieved nothing. The blessed Ezra will teach us this when he says: "In the times of Artaxerxes king of the Persians, Belemus, Mithridates, Tabellius, Rathumus, Beeltethmus, and Geeltethmus the scribe, and the rest of their associates, who lived in Samaria and the other places, wrote against those living in Judea and Jerusalem." The gist of their letter was this: Jerusalem was a city of unbreakable strength that in no way yielded to the kings of other lands. Rather, it rose up in revolt with great vigour, and if it returned to its ancient state it would heap up troubles even for the successive rulers of Babylon. But, as I said, those who wrote such things achieved nothing at all. Some of the people in Samaria also urged those who had come back from Babylon to let them work and build together with them. They refused, and for this reason they suffered no little hardship, holding out against their plots. For again it is written thus in Ezra: "And the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin heard that the children of the exile were building a house for the Lord God of Israel. They came to Zerubbabel and to the heads of the families and said to them, 'We will build with you, for we seek your God just as you do, and we have been sacrificing to him since the days of Sarsathus king of Assyria, who brought us here.' And Zerubbabel and Jeshua and the rest of the heads of the families of Israel said to them, 'It is not for you and us together to build a house for our God; we ourselves together will build for the Lord our God, as Cyrus king of the Persians commanded us.' And the people of the land kept weakening the hands of the people of Judah and hindering them from building, and they hired people against them, plotting to frustrate their purpose." They plotted, but this attempt of theirs was fruitless too. When their secret plotting proved feeble, all the surrounding nations went out to make open war, and they were defeated and fell. You may learn this from the following as well, for he writes thus again in the second book: "And it came to pass that when Sanballat and Tobiah and the Arabs and the Ammonites heard that the walls of Jerusalem were rising, and that the breaches had begun to be closed up, it seemed very bad to them. They all gathered together to come out and fight against Jerusalem. And we prayed," he says, "to the Lord our God, and set guards against them day and night because of them. And Judah said, 'The strength of the enemies has been crushed, and so has the great crowd.'" The valley is not mentioned in these passages, but tradition hands this down to us as well. The prophecy, which names for us the very site of the war, is also sufficient warrant for believing it. We say, then, that he is recalling this history when he says he will gather all the nations into the valley of Jehoshaphat. Clearly he will not bring them against their will; he will simply not stop them when they wish to come. He will contend with them for Israel and for his inheritance, which they divided up. They did this, it seems, by plundering what the Babylonians had left and joining in the attack in the time of misery. They gave boys to prostitutes and exposed girls to unaccustomed prostitution, trafficking, as it were, in other people's licentiousness, and then spent the wages from it on luxury and drunkenness. And we say that something similar has happened in our own case, when we consider the redemption through Christ. We were captives living under a tyrant, the bitter Satan, I mean, and he rescued us. He brought us back, as it were, into a holy land: into the gospel way of life, into a most teachable disposition, into a walled city, the spiritual Jerusalem, "which is the Church of the living God." There he prepared us to be built up as precious stones "into a holy temple, into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit." But the unholy multitude of demons was inflamed by the pangs of envy, and so were those who fight against the doctrines of the truth. They have made many assaults on the saints, but did them no harm, because God shielded them and Christ encouraged them, saying, "In the world you will have tribulation, but take courage: I have overcome the world."

Among the Jews there is a rotten old wives' tale that in time God's judgment on all will take place in the valley of Jehoshaphat, after the dead come back to life. They think that people throughout the whole world will render account there for what was done to them. This notion of theirs deserves [?] to be laughed at, since the inspired Scripture says that the prophecy has already been fulfilled, and that the surrounding nations were punished by God when the war took place in the valley of Jehoshaphat. For, as I said, they leapt on the remnant of Israel, even though Israel had already endured the greatest misery, having been handed over to the Babylonians.

And what are you to me, Tyre and Sidon and all Galilee of the foreigners? Are you paying me back a recompense? Or do you bear a grudge against me? Swiftly and speedily I will return your recompense on your own heads, because you took my silver and my gold and carried my choice and beautiful things into your temples. And you sold the sons of Judah and the sons of Israel to the sons of the Greeks, in order to drive them far from their own borders.

Every nation, then, gathered against Israel: Moabites, Idumeans, Jebusites, Ammonites and the rest. But I think the people of Damascus and Tyre, and those called the Philistines as far as Gath itself, which is also called "Gath of the foreigners," took the lead in planning and in action. That is why the God of all says to them, "And what are you to me, Tyre and Sidon and all Galilee of the foreigners?" He means: "What grounds do you have for your savagery? Israel was already wretched and heavily burdened by the calamities brought by the Babylonians, yet you wickedly pile more on it. You attack it bitterly and, as it were, mock me, who perhaps save and defend it, and you dare to speak against me as enemies do, or rather you have already acted as they do. So before long you will receive your recompense. It will come on your own head, for you will pay the penalty to me, who will contend with you in the valley of Jehoshaphat." He charges them with plundering the choice things of the temple, carrying off its golden vessels, and dedicating them to the honour of their own gods. This is an unbearable and bitter thing, and quite capable of grieving God. For he said, "I will not give my glory to another, nor my praises to carved images." To adorn the temples of idols with offerings dedicated to God is nothing other than practically crying aloud that the God of all comes second, while the idols hold first place and know how to save their own worshippers. "And it is not enough for your impiety," he says, "to have stripped my temple of its divine offerings: you have also sold the sons of Judah and the sons of Israel to the sons of the Greeks." Something like this probably happened, with some of the Israelites being carried off into the lands of the nations, sold off perhaps by the Tyrians, or by others whose pursuit was trade and whose practice was love of gain.

The passage would also fit, it seems to me, the leaders of unholy heresies. They all but snatch away the sons of the Church and sell them off to the wisdom of the Greeks, so that, filled with convoluted notions, they become bitter disputers, or rather disobedient and wicked men who pervert what is right. Yet they ought to live with simplicity and meditate on the unadulterated word of truth. So the heresiarchs cause those they have deceived to end up outside their own borders. The borders, and as it were the land, of the children of the Church are the knowledge of the truth and a leaning toward correctness in everything that has been carefully examined. Those may rightly be called God's gold and silver vessels and his choice things who are truly adorned with faith, gilded with the glories that come from good works, and gleaming with the beauty of godliness. But if any of these splendid people are caught in the snares of deception, the inventors of the deception will certainly hear: "You took my silver and my gold and carried my choice things into your temples." This is a terrible charge and hard to escape. For "by sinning against the brothers, for whom Christ died," they wrong Christ himself, and to him they will certainly pay the penalty for their offences against him.

Behold, I am rousing them from the place where you sold them, and I will return your recompense on your own heads. I will sell your sons and your daughters into the hands of the sons of Judah, and they will sell them into captivity to a nation far away; for the Lord has spoken.

He says most plainly that the schemes of the Tyrians, and the devices their perversity invented against those of Israel, will come to nothing. The calamity will turn back, as it were, on those who did the wrong, and they will be caught in the same evils, as an evenly balanced penalty all but falls on the heads of those who committed these unholy offences. They captured the people of Judah and handed them to slave-dealers, telling them to carry them off to a distant nation. In the same way, he says, their own children will be sold off by the hand of the Jews. And he confirms that these things will certainly happen by saying, "For the Lord has spoken." Nothing whatever that is spoken by
God goes unfulfilled. Indeed Christ said, "Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away."

That is the historical sense. But if someone chooses to look closely at the spiritual sense and to be filled with its hidden meanings, he will see that here too the children of the Greeks, puffed up with their supposed wisdom, and the heretics as well, who claim some standing for themselves through intricate devices of deceit, carry off some of the simpler people from the right and blameless faith they have received from God. They bind them, as it were, in the snares of deceit, take them as spoils of war, and carry them as far as possible from the bounds of the truth. But the God of all makes their wickedness come to nothing. He releases those who were deceived, and he hands over to the people of Judah the sons of the deceivers, that is, their sons by discipleship. The people of Judah here would again be the divine disciples and all who speak the mystery of Christ. They free these people from their error and carry them off into a good and lovely servitude, namely servitude under Christ. They seize them like captives and bring them over to their own habit and mind, which is as far as possible from that of the others. For a great gap can be seen between the mind of the saints and the mind of such people. Christ too is said to have taken captive those who were brought over from the deception of the Greeks to the knowledge of the One who is God by nature. For blessed David said, "You ascended on high, you led captivity captive, you received gifts among men."

Proclaim this among the nations: sanctify war, rouse the warriors; draw near and go up, all you men of war. Beat your plowshares into swords and your sickles into spears; let the weak say, "I am strong." Gather together and come in, all you nations round about, and assemble there; let the meek be a warrior. Let him rouse himself, and let all the nations go up to the valley of Jehoshaphat, for there I will sit to judge all the nations round about.

He has threatened the nations with calamities that turn back on themselves and with a penalty matching their unholy deeds. Now he turns his words to his own worshipers. He commands them to be not in the least cowardly or unmanly but vigorous. They are to make what amounts to a ringing proclamation, to gather the nations for battle at once, and to hurry to rouse them for it, even if those nations should happen to prefer a quiet and unwarlike life. In this he was making them as bold as possible and persuading them to take courage in him, since with him as their shield they would prove stronger than their enemies. "Proclaim this, then, among the nations," he says, "and sanctify war." And what does "sanctify" mean here? "Consecrate it to me, in a sense. For I will be the warrior, and what is done will be for my glory, since those who transferred my glory to wood and stones will die." Whatever is said to be sanctified is always offered for the glory of God. That is why he says, "Sanctify war, rouse the warriors," and also, he says, call out: "Draw near, all you men of war." Let the farmer leave off the cares and pursuits dearest to him. Let him reforge the plowshare into a sword and the sickle into spears. For this is not the time for farming but for paying the penalty to the God who was dishonored. And if anyone is weak, he says, let him not use his feebleness as an excuse. Let him lie, if he likes, and claim that he is able, but let him not keep far from arms. "Gather, then, all of you," he says, "who are around Judea, and let the meek be a warrior." That is, even if someone is slow to anger, let him too be a warrior. It is as if he were saying: with no one at all left behind, whether he is a farmer, or cowardly and unmanly (for this is the "weak"), or meek and unwarlike, let him be sharpened for battle. "For I will excuse no one, and I will judge them all in the valley of Jehoshaphat." "I will judge" means, "I will be a mighty judge, subjecting to punishments and penalties those who plundered my land, divided Israel by lot, gave the boys to prostitutes, sold the girls, and drank them away like wine."

Our Lord Jesus Christ might in turn call out such things to the enemies of the Church. Even if they should come in full force and make war on the saints with all their power, they will certainly fall, because he shields the saints. He overthrows the enemies, but walls in his own worshipers with faith, hope and love, and with the good gifts of his own gentleness.

Send forth the sickles, for the vintage has come; go in, tread, for the winepress is full; the vats overflow, for their wickedness has multiplied. Sounds have resounded in the valley of judgment, for the day of the Lord is near in the valley of judgment. The sun and the moon will be darkened, and the stars will withdraw their light. And the Lord will cry out from Zion and will utter his voice from Jerusalem, and heaven and earth will be shaken.

He had commanded that the nations bordering the land of the Jews (I mean the Arabs and Tyrians, the Gittites and Philistines, the Moabites and Idumeans, the Ammonites and Girgashites) be gathered, as if by a trumpet, to the valley of Jehoshaphat, since they were about to die and pay bitter penalties to the Judge. Now he spurs on the people of Israel to an irresistible eagerness and a formidable strength, and in a way bids them leap upon the gathered nations. He says they must show themselves most courageous, manly and vigorous. They must not be terrified by the fears of war, nor behave at all as men going into battle. Rather, they must count the matter a delight, reckon it among their joys, and rejoice like those who gather the rich fruit of the vines. That is why he says, "Send forth the sickles, for the vintage has come." He uses "send forth" for "put forth and stretch out," as grape-harvesters do, for the enemies will lie ready for slaughter, prepared to be cut down. Let the enemy be cut off, he says, like a cluster from the vine, and let him be trodden as in winepresses, lying in heaps underfoot. For he says, "Go in, tread, for the winepress is full." That is, the multitude of the nations has been brought together for destruction, and nothing prevents them from lying under your feet. "The vats overflow": by this he signifies how abundant are those gathered to be trampled. For when grapes are plentiful, the wine often overflows even the presses themselves. So by saying, "The vats overflow," he indicates the multitude of those lying underfoot.

"Sounds have resounded in the valley of judgment." What does this mean? It is the custom of the holy prophets to announce what is to come, and sometimes to be inside the very visions of the events, so that they seem already to see what is happening and to hear voices. So the divine prophet Jeremiah, when he foretold what would happen to the Jews, and that Nebuchadnezzar, once set in motion for war, would destroy them utterly, was caught up into the joyless sight of the war itself. As though he had actually seen a countless multitude of corpses, he said, "Woe is me, for my soul faints because of the slain." Blessed Joel, I think, had a similar experience and perhaps heard the uproar of battle in his ears; that is why he says, "Sounds have resounded in the valley of judgment." He calls the place of battle the "valley of judgment" because the nations were gathered in it for no other purpose than to pay bitter penalties. By "resounding sounds" he means here either the wails of those who fall or the war cries of the victors. For in wars it happens that the fallen groan, while the conquerors exult over those who lie dead and boast loudly.

He says that the sun and moon will be darkened and that the stars themselves will be without light. This is not at all because the elements will suffer this very thing at that time. It is because war produces darkness and casts a kind of mist over the eyes of the defeated. For the fear of death always darkens, the magnitude of an unexpected calamity dulls the mind, and excessive suffering blackens the heart as if with gloom. He says that the Lord will cry out, as one who is with Israel and fights at its side, and like a general urging the people of Israel on against the enemy. But the saying that the Lord will cry out from Zion would fit the time of the resurrection best of all. For, as the divine Paul says, "The Lord himself will descend from heaven with a word of command, with the voice of an archangel and with the trumpet of God, and the dead in Christ will be raised incorruptible." The law of Moses also prefigured this, for it commanded the people of Israel to blow the trumpet at the new moon. The new moon may be understood as a type, and a very apt one [?], of the age to come, which is new after the first. And the trumpet is a type of the ringing sound of the archangel's voice, the trumpet from God, which will raise all who lie in the earth with an extraordinary and vocal sound. We should also note that when the Lord himself performed the miracle of Lazarus, he went to the tomb and, as the Evangelist says, cried out with a loud voice, "Lazarus, come out." How is this to be understood, when God says through the prophet, "He will not quarrel or cry out, nor will his voice be heard outside"? The Savior's use of a loud voice when he raised Lazarus was therefore a sign of the ringing trumpet and of its sound at the end of time, the sound from heaven, I mean.

But the Lord will spare his people, and the Lord will strengthen the sons of Israel. And you will know that I am the Lord your God, who dwells in Zion, on my holy mountain; and Jerusalem will be holy, and foreigners will no longer pass through it.

When the people of Israel were charged with apostasy, when they worshiped the golden heifers and impiously said, "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt," they were weak and easily captured and lay before their enemies as the readiest prey. That is why they were sent into captivity. But once they had received mercy and settled again in their own land, as God relaxed his anger, they became invincible and unrivaled against their enemies from then on. They prevailed without effort, even though all the nations had gathered for battle. So he says that from their victory over their adversaries they will know that he is among them and that from now on he rests in Zion as a holy city. That is why he says he will spare his own peoples and make them most valiant, and that they will learn, as I just said, that he is with them. He says that Jerusalem will be holy, entirely freed from its ancient godlessness. It will no longer offer its forms of worship to falsely named gods, and false divination and sorcery will no longer be honored in it. Instead a lawful life will prevail, and the best practices will be pursued eagerly among its people. Since it will be in this state and has chosen to live this way, he says that none of the nations will pass through it. That is, it will not be easy for anyone to overcome, nor will it be seized in passing by whoever wishes, as before. Rather, it will be secure, and very well fortified by my powers and aid.

The matter also holds true if it is understood of the Church of Christ itself. For he cares for his own worshipers and makes them stronger than their enemies. They are strong and most valiant and full of spiritual vigor, since they know and believe that God is in them through the Spirit. For he dwells in our hearts through faith, and as John the Evangelist says, "By this we know that he is in us, by the Spirit whom he has given us." The spiritual Jerusalem, that is, the Church, where the ranks of the saints are found, is holy in the true sense. They are not a thoroughfare for foreigners, for "those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires." They remember one of the wise, who said, "If the spirit of the ruler rises against you, do not leave your place, for healing will put an end to great sins." For their heart is secure. It is not a road for unclean spirits to walk or ride over. It does not yield easily to the assaults of the passions. It is not defiled by the false doctrines of those who teach otherwise, nor shaken by the deceits of their own thoughts. Rather, it is firm and well fortified with towers by the doctrines of the truth.

And on that day the mountains will drip sweetness, and the hills will flow with milk, and all the channels of Judah will flow with water, and a fountain will come forth from the house of the Lord and will water the torrent of the rushes.

Jerusalem has now been shown to be holy and is no longer passable to foreigners, because the Lord of all dwells in it, spares his own people, strengthens them, and makes them stronger than their opponents. Then, he says, at that very time, the mountains will drip sweetness, the hills will flow with milk, and the channels of Judah will pour out their own stream. By "channels" I think he means the outflows of springs, or, put another way, what might be called water conduits. The mountains may be understood as those who have been raised to the height of virtue and surpass the measure of others in the glories of a virtuous life. They are the conspicuous and illustrious, such as the disciples were, and before all the others the Baptist, of whom the Savior says, "Among those born of women there has not arisen one greater than John the Baptist." These great and most renowned men will drip sweetness. They will speak about the Savior as though spreading honey on their words, so that everyone who shares in them cries out for joy, "How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!" For the word of the saints is always sweet to those who love to please God. Such men, then, may be understood as mountains, and very fittingly. The hills, we say, are those who fall a little short of the eminence of the first and sit somewhat below the measure of their way of life, yet who themselves stand high and rise far above the rest. These pour the spiritual, pure milk into the souls of those who have just believed, supplying food suited to infants. For solid food belongs to the mature, while milk is most suitable for infants. We do not say that the measure of their understanding consists only in being able to pour milk for infants. They are quite capable, if they choose, of giving heartier food to those whose condition is firmer, but they remember the sacred scripture that says, "Know well the souls of your flock." Thus the divine disciples, although Christ had given us countless commandments, wrote by way of accommodation to those who had believed from among the Gentiles that they must abstain "from fornication, from what is strangled, and from blood. For it seemed good," it says, "to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you no greater burden." Do you hear how suited to infants the command is, given like milk to those whose condition is weaker? Spiritual water too will be abundant for those "planted in the house of the Lord," so that "they may flourish in the courts of our God," watered by divine streams and enriched by words from above, from heaven. He suggests this by saying that all the channels of Judah will flow with water. For the blessed disciples too confessed that they were comforted by God. The first outflows of spiritual waters would surely be the supplies of good things that God gives to the saints through the Spirit. The second outflows, as it were, are the words that come to us from the saints and fill us with spiritual gifts. And what could the fountain coming forth from the house of the Lord be but Christ? For this is what the blessed psalmist called him when he said to the Father and God in heaven, "How you have multiplied your mercy, O God! The sons of men will hope in the shelter of your wings. They will be drunk with the richness of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight, for with you is the fountain of life." So Christ is both the fountain of life and the torrent. As for the torrent of the rushes, the prophet is referring to a certain torrent-bed along which many rushes grow. It is said to be the same as the Brook of the Cedars, where, the Evangelist says, our Lord Jesus Christ was found when the traitor disciple came looking for him with the cohort.

It is a fine interpretation, too, if we compare the Church to the torrent of the rushes. Our Lord Jesus Christ "has turned toward it like a river of peace," and he always flows beside it, so to speak, watering the evergreen rushes, that is, the souls of the saints. For the rush always loves water and is always green. And if the rush is seen to have a sharp point, that too would fit well. For the virtue of the saints is not entirely without a sting. They love meekness, yet along with this they are also warriors.

Egypt will become a desolation, and Idumea will become a plain of desolation, because of the wrongs done to the sons of Judah, because they shed innocent blood in their land. But Judea will be inhabited forever, and Jerusalem for generations of generations. I will avenge their blood and will not leave it unpunished, and the Lord will dwell in Zion.

As far as the historical sense is concerned, the land of the Egyptians paid the penalty: it was stripped of its kingdom when Cambyses, the son of Cyrus, overthrew it. And Idumea suffered desolation, as the events themselves bear witness.

Yet in these words the prophetic discourse seems to hint at a hidden dispensation, which the Only-begotten fulfilled when he became man. For divine Scripture has always somehow made a practice of likening the herds of demons, and those who always oppose the saints, to the worst idolaters and to those most given over to idolatry. So he says that every enemy will perish, and he compares them to Egyptians and Idumeans. For Christ's promise is secure, when he says of the Church that "the gates of Hades will not prevail against it." The evil powers, and all who dare to do the same things they do, were certainly going to be made to pay the penalty for the wrongs they had committed against human beings. These include those who lead people away into the deception of the Greeks, and those who turn them toward a debased mind by being eager to teach perverse things. He makes this clear by saying that those who made war on Zion will be destroyed for this reason: because they shed innocent blood and intolerably wronged the sons of Judah, that is, the saints, who are children of confession. For "Judah" is interpreted as "confession." Blessed David also says somewhere of those who were impiously slain, "For he who avenges their blood has remembered; he has not forgotten the cry of the poor." And to Satan, who is depicted, as in an image, in Assyria, he says, "As a garment soaked in blood will not be clean, so you too will not be clean, because you defiled my land and destroyed my people; you will not remain forever." So he says that those who made war on Zion will go down to destruction, but that Judea will be inhabited forever and Jerusalem for generations of generations. He does not mean the Jerusalem that was sacked and burned, if indeed the Lord and God, being truth itself, cannot speak falsely. He means rather the spiritual Jerusalem, the heavenly Jerusalem, the divine Zion above, the glorious and beautiful city "whose craftsman and maker and builder is God." May we too arrive there through Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, forever. Amen.
Commentary of Cyril, Archbishop of Alexandria, on the Prophet Amos. Volume One.

Amos was a goatherd, a man brought up in the customs and ways of shepherds. He spent his time in the desert to the south of the land of the Jews. This desert reaches as far as the shores of the Indian sea and stretches into the land of the Persians. Countless barbarian tribes graze their herds in it, and it is very well suited to feeding flocks of sheep, because it is rich in pasture, broad, and covered with every kind of grass. Amos came from the village of Tekoa, which lies at the very foot of the desert. Because he was a good man who practised every virtue, the spirit of prophecy soon enriched him. He prophesied not in Jerusalem but at first while he was still among the flocks themselves, busy with the cares that custom and practice had made his own, and afterwards also when he had come to Bethel itself. For Tekoa was not under the kingdom of Judah but rather under that of Ephraim. You will see without any effort that what we say about these matters is true, and his own words will fully convince you. For he prophesied in Bethel, as I said, declaring that the altars of laughter would be destroyed and the rites of Israel laid waste, and adding to this, "And I will rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword." The priest of Bethel, who was Amaziah, gnashed his teeth at the prophet. Then he sent word to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying, "Amos is conspiring against you in the midst of the house of Israel; the land cannot bear all his words. For this is what Amos says: Jeroboam shall die by the sword, and Israel shall be led away captive from its land." And Amaziah said to Amos, "Seer, go, flee to the land of Judah and live there, and prophesy there. But never again prophesy at Bethel, for it is the king's sanctuary and the king's house." And Amos answered Amaziah, "I was no prophet, nor a prophet's son; I was a goatherd and a dresser of sycamore figs. The Lord took me from the sheep, and the Lord said to me, Go, prophesy to my people Israel." So he was taken from the flocks, and he prophesied in Bethel, where the first Jeroboam, the son of Nebat, had set up the golden heifer. I think it also useful to point out that Amos the father of Isaiah was a different man. As we take up the text before us, we shall make clear, as far as we can, what his words were and what they concerned.
The words of Amos, which came to him in Akkarim, from Tekoa, which he saw concerning Jerusalem.

He says that these are the words of the prophecy of Amos of Tekoa, which came to him in Akkarim. It should be noted that the Hebrew text does not have this phrase "in Akkarim" at all; it says only, "The words of Amos from Tekoa." The other translators put "among the cattle-breeders" in place of "in Akkarim." So he is saying that these are the words of Amos of Tekoa, which came to him while he was still tending flocks, in the very sheepfolds. He says that he did not so much hear the words concerning Jerusalem as see them. For God made things plain to the holy prophets together with the revelations, setting the events before them almost as though they were present, so that the words seemed in a way to have already become visible, since the sight of what was to come ran alongside whatever God was saying. But one point deserves inquiry. How could anyone suppose that the words concerned Jerusalem alone, when God, through the voice of this same prophet, accuses both Judah and Israel? For he said again, "This is what the Lord says: For three transgressions of the sons of Judah, and for four, I will not turn them back, because they have rejected the law of the Lord and have not kept his commandments. Their vain idols, which they made and which their fathers followed, have led them astray. And I will send fire upon Judah, and it shall devour the foundations of Jerusalem." And right after this: "This is what the Lord says: For three transgressions of Israel, and for four, I will not turn him back." Having then set out the ways in which they sinned, he threatened them with terrible things, and his word carries the fullest possible rebuke against both. How then can the words be understood as concerning Jerusalem, when God says, "I will send fire upon Judah, and it shall devour the foundations of Jerusalem"? Come, let us consider how this may be answered. We say, then, that the holy prophets have the habit sometimes of calling the two tribes in Jerusalem, Judah and Benjamin, "Israel" in a distinct sense, and at other times of giving the name "Israel," or else "Ephraim," to the other ten tribes in Samaria; but very often they make no distinction. Since all of them are of the blood of Israel, they call the twelve tribes by that name as well. And if they wish to denote for us the whole synagogue of the Jews together, we shall find them using the name of Jerusalem no longer in a restricted sense.

So the words of the prophecy of Amos concern the whole multitude of the Jews, both those in Jerusalem and those in Samaria. We must also explain how they can concern them, and the answer is twofold. First, he has introduced the God of all recounting the sins of the synagogue of the Jews and announcing beforehand what would come upon them; and to this he added the good things that would come from his gentleness: in due time they would be spared to a very great degree and restored to their original state. For Amos himself said again, speaking as in the person of God, "Yet I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob, says the Lord. For behold, I am giving the command, and I will winnow the house of Israel among all the nations, as grain is winnowed with a winnowing fan, and not a fragment shall fall to the ground." He also, as he must, foretells the redemption that was to come through Christ: that they would pass over to renewal and would live in well-being under the compassion of God. He spoke thus again: "On that day I will raise up the tent of David that has fallen, and I will rebuild its ruins, and raise up what was torn down, and rebuild it as in the days of old." So the words do concern Jerusalem. They may reasonably be understood as concerning it in another way too. Syria and the kings of Damascus, and not a few of the neighbouring nations, ravaged the land of the Jews. One after another they rose up against it and laid it waste, plundering and carrying off, and acting with unrestrained fury, so that the people were brought to the depths of misery. Against all those who had devastated the land the prophet has introduced God threatening desolation, and he said that they would pay the penalty for their unholy deeds. So the words of Amos concern Jerusalem, that is, the whole synagogue of the Jews. We shall see this clearly by examining the dates of the prophecy, for the text continues:
In the days of Uzziah king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel, two years before the earthquake.

But someone will say, I suppose, "What benefit does it bring to readers to have to investigate, and in such fine detail, the dates of the reigns of the kings just named, Uzziah, that is, and Jeroboam?" To this we reply that the matter is necessary, for it carries within itself, so to speak, the whole setting of the prophecy. He threatens Syria and Damascus and the barbarians living around Judaea with destruction, uprisings and burnings, and this is where his divine oracles begin. So we must learn the reasons why the dates of the reigns were added: what each king accomplished and how much, how each lived, and what is worth hearing about them both. Israel and Judah had fallen away into apostasy and were being chastened in many ways. At one time the rulers of Damascus and of the Syrians overran and besieged them and plundered their lands. At another time the Moabites and Idumaeans, the Gerhesenes [?] and Elamites, the people of Ashdod and the inhabitants of Ekron, maltreated Samaria and the kingdom of Judah as well, with unbridled impulses and insatiable greed, raging in the utmost fury. Indeed we shall find that they did this in various ways, as for instance when Ahab was reigning in Samaria and over Israel. It is written thus in the third book of Kingdoms: "And the son of Hadad gathered all his army and went up and besieged Samaria, and thirty-two kings were with him, and all his horses and chariots; and they went up and besieged Samaria and made war against it." Notice that the king of Damascus, that is, Hadad, took as his allies against Israel thirty-two other rulers of the neighbouring nations, and so made war on the land. In the time of Joash king of Judah, too, Hazael the Syrian made war on Jerusalem. It is written again in the fourth book of Kingdoms: "Then Hazael king of Syria went up and fought against Gath and took it. And Hazael set his face to go up against Jerusalem. And Joash king of Judah took all the holy things that his fathers Jehoshaphat and Jehoram and Ahaziah, the kings of Judah, had consecrated, and his own holy things, and all the gold that was found in the treasuries of the house of the Lord and of the king's house, and sent them to Hazael king of Syria; and he went away from Jerusalem." They did such things by the wrath of God, because Israel had given offence by turning away so far and being so dreadfully infatuated with the worship of idols. Yet when the foreigners won, they outraged the glory of God. For the wretches thought among themselves that the hand that defended Israel had grown weak, and they dared to behave insolently toward the glory of God. Indeed, when the Syrians were beaten during Hadad's brief siege of Samaria, they made an excuse for their cowardice, saying falsely, "The God of Israel is a God of the mountains and not a God of the valleys." For they thought that the Israelites had won because God was able to save only on the mountains or on the hills. "We were defeated," they say, "because the God of Israel is a God of the mountains; but if we meet them in battle on the open plains, we shall certainly overcome them, since the God of Israel is powerless in the valleys." These are the charges of pagan madness, and the dreadful loose talk of those who do not know the One who is truly and by nature God. So God, who is almighty, was angry with the foreigners, and with very good reason, because when they defeated Israel, as I said, they offered thank-offerings to their own gods, and in their folly thought they had prevailed over God himself. As time went on after the reign of Ahab, and after certain other kings in between, one after another, a second Jeroboam, distinct from the first who was the son of Nebat, was declared king over Israel in Samaria. He bore the same name as the first and shared his mind and his impiety. Yet in the time of his reign God, who loves to show compassion, at last took pity on Israel, worn down by unbearable misery, and freed them from their troubles by the hand of Jeroboam, although he was wicked and a thorough apostate. He showed such courage against the foreigners that he recovered cities they had torn away in the times of earlier kings and brought them back under his own sceptre, and he did very great harm to those who had once been the victors. For it is written of him in the fourth book of Kingdoms: "In the fifteenth year of Amaziah son of Joash king of Judah, Jeroboam son of Joash began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned forty-one years. And he did what was evil in the sight of the Lord; he did not turn aside from all the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who made Israel sin. He restored the border of Israel from the entrance of Hamath to the sea of the Arabah, according to the word of the Lord God of Israel, which he spoke by the hand of his servant Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet from Gath-hepher. For the Lord saw that the affliction of Israel was very bitter, and that they were very few, hemmed in, diminished and forsaken, and there was no one to help Israel. And the Lord had not said that he would blot out the seed of Israel from under heaven, and he saved them by the hand of Jeroboam son of Joash. Now the rest of the acts of Jeroboam, and all that he did, and his mighty deeds, how he fought, and how he restored Damascus and Hamath to Judah in Israel, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?" See, he says plainly that the Israelites had been crushed, since there was no one to save them, so that they were very few and scattered, but that they were saved from the hand of Jeroboam. He has put "from the hand" in place of "by the hand." For it was not Jeroboam who was crushing Israel; on the contrary, he fought for Israel and shielded it. He brought back Damascus, recovered the territory of Israel, and performed many mighty deeds. While Jeroboam was reigning, Azariah, also called Uzziah, was anointed king over Judah in Jerusalem. He was no less a heavy burden on the nations, and pressed hard and vigorously upon those who had ravaged Judaea. He was a pious and God-loving man. But when he had overcome his enemies, God granting him the victory, he fell sick with arrogance, and on his own initiative set about acting as a priest to God as well. He even dared to go up to the divine altar itself and offer incense. But God at once rebuked him. He was marked with leprosy, a terrible and incurable disease, so that, being unclean according to the law, he would be sent out of Jerusalem and would stop serving God as a priest, stop the sacred ministry he had unlawfully taken upon himself, and stop defiling the divine temple. Holy Scripture speaks of him thus in the fourth book of Kingdoms: "In the twenty-seventh year of Jeroboam king of Israel, Azariah son of Amaziah began to reign as king of Judah. He was sixteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem; his mother's name was Jecoliah of Jerusalem. And he did what was right in the eyes of the Lord, according to all that his father Amaziah had done. Only he did not remove the high places, for the people still sacrificed and burned incense on the high places. And the Lord struck the king, and he was a leper until the day of his death." This is in the Kingdoms; but in the second book of Chronicles there is a more detailed account of these things. It reads as follows: "And all the people of the land took Uzziah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in place of his father Amaziah. He built Elath and restored it to Judah after the king slept with his fathers. Uzziah was sixteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem; his mother's name was Jecoliah of Jerusalem. And he did what was right in the sight of the Lord, according to all that his father Amaziah had done. And he sought the Lord in the days of Zechariah, who had understanding in the fear of the Lord; in his days he sought the Lord, and the Lord prospered him. And he went out and made war against the Philistines, and broke down the walls of Gath and the walls of Jamnia and the walls of Ashdod, and he built cities of Ashdod; and the Lord strengthened him among the Philistines, against the Philistines and against the Arabs who live on the rock, and against the Minaeans. And the Minaeans gave gifts to Uzziah, and his fame spread as far as the entrance of Egypt, for he grew exceedingly strong." Then it says of him next: "He acted wrongly against the Lord his God, and went into the temple of the Lord to burn incense on the altar of incense. And Azariah the priest went in after him, and with him eighty priests of the Lord, valiant men. And they withstood King Uzziah and said to him, It is not for you, Uzziah, to burn incense to the Lord, but for the priests, the sons of Aaron, who are consecrated to burn incense. Go out of the sanctuary, for you have turned away from the Lord, and this will bring you no glory from the Lord God. And Uzziah was angry, and in his hand was the censer for burning incense in the temple. And while he was angry with the priests, leprosy broke out on his forehead in the presence of the priests in the house of the Lord, beside the altar of incense. And the chief priest and the priests turned toward him, and behold, he was leprous on his forehead, and they hurried him out from there; and he himself hastened to go out, because the Lord had rebuked him."

This is enough about Uzziah's becoming a leper. Holy Scripture has taught us sufficiently that he was a powerful man, that he campaigned against the lands of the Philistines, and that he grew so strong that he built cities among them, imposed tribute on them, and brought them under his own sceptre, even though they had once been very proud. So, since the prophetic word has introduced at its outset the desolation that was to come upon the foreigners, it was necessary to mention the reigns of Uzziah and Jeroboam, for it was through them that the foreigners were defeated, as we have already said. We know, of course, that Damascus was also set on fire by the hand of the Assyrians, and that the foreign nations were laid waste no less. But since those events came later than these, we must connect what happened to the foreigners with the times of Jeroboam and Uzziah, and no less with the Assyrian rulers themselves. And since the prophet added, "two years before the earthquake," we have had to mention Uzziah's leprosy as well. For when he dared to act as priest against the law, he was struck with leprosy as God's rebuke, and Jerusalem was shaken by an earthquake; by this too God clearly signalled his wrath to the people of that time.
And he said: The Lord has uttered his voice from Zion, and from Jerusalem he has given forth his voice; and the pastures of the shepherds have mourned, and the top of Carmel has withered.

In these words the whole aim of the prophecy shines through for us, and the meaning of the passage may fairly be understood as a kind of summary of the entire oracle, a sort of preface shrouded in much obscurity. The saying is framed as a comparison and a metaphor, drawn from what naturally happens to well-wooded mountaintops, and at times also to the open plains. Mountains, though thick with forests and trees, and plains covered with abundant, luxuriant grass, wither unexpectedly when something blights them, perhaps a pestilence or some other sickness carried in the air. Human affairs decline in the same way: bitter and unbearable calamities sometimes fall upon cities and lands, destroying and ruining small and great alike. For whom would an enemy's sword spare, or, let us say, a pestilence, which mows down utterly both the man who is conspicuous for wealth, glory and power and the man who is obscure and despised? So the prophet's language here is especially fitting to what he was used to. For he was, as I said, a goatherd, and he has drawn his figure from the way the pastures of flocks are often blighted.

What, then, is the truer meaning of these words? The Lord, he says, uttered his voice from Zion, as from his own place, and from Jerusalem, as from the city allotted to him. The incorporeal is not, of course, in a place; but because that famous temple stood in Jerusalem, the spot seemed in some way to be his own, at least in the view of the people of old, who still had small thoughts about God. In place of "uttered his voice," the Hebrew text has "roared," that is, "bellowed," in the manner of lions. When this happened, he says, the pastures of the flocks mourned. By the pasture of the flocks he means the nations of the foreigners, laid down, as it were, beneath their own rulers as beneath shepherds, who lead and drive the peoples under their hand toward whatever they please. They mourned, then; that is, they fell into dejection and every kind of misery, for mourning is made over the dead. The cause of their calamity was that God roared against them and, as it were, threatened them with destruction. "For the lion will roar," he says, "and who will not be afraid?" Yet not only did the pastures of the flocks mourn; besides this, the summit of Carmel also withered. By the summit of Carmel he means Jerusalem. Carmel is a mountain lying in the land of the Jews, on which Elijah the Tishbite also lived, and the whole land of the Jews is often signified by the name of Carmel. An example is what God said to the children of Israel through the voice of another prophet: "And I brought you into Carmel to eat its good things and its fruits, and you came in and defiled my land, and made my inheritance an abomination." Since, then, Jerusalem was reckoned more distinguished and illustrious than the other cities of Judea, he calls it the summit of Carmel: exalted in glory, standing out in eminence, conspicuous above the rest, because it had the divine temple and the kings who reigned at various times from the tribe of Judah. It is the custom of the holy prophets to hide their words, by a wise design, in obscurity, because of the unbridled impulses of their hearers. For these, carried away to great audacity, would not have put up with them if they had spoken openly; they rebuked the holy prophets and said, "Rather, speak to us and announce to us another deception."

And the Lord said: For three impieties of Damascus, and for four, I will not turn away from it, because they sawed with iron saws the women with child of those in Gilead. And I will send fire upon the house of Hazael, and it shall devour the foundations of the son of Ader. And I will break the bars of Damascus, and I will utterly destroy the inhabitants from the plain of On, and I will cut down a tribe from the men of Haran, and the chosen people of Syria shall be taken captive, says the Lord.

The inspired Moses marvels at God as good and long-suffering, and with very good reason. When Israel made the calf in the wilderness and foolishly said, "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt," they inevitably gave offense. But when God threatened to destroy them once and for all, and then Moses fell down and entreated him, and actually persuaded the Creator to remit the penalty from those who had sinned, he offered up songs of thanksgiving, saying: "The Lord God is compassionate and merciful, long-suffering and abounding in mercy and true, keeping righteousness and mercy for thousands, taking away iniquities and injustices and sins; and he will not clear the guilty, bringing the sins of the fathers upon the children and upon the children's children, to the third and fourth generation." The Jewish masses did not understand this rightly. They thought God so harsh and unrelenting and so long in his anger as to visit the fathers' offenses on their children's children. Indeed, mocking this very thing, they used to say, "The fathers ate sour grapes, and the children's teeth were set on edge." That is why God says to the prophet Ezekiel: "Son of man, what is this proverb of yours in Israel, when you say, 'The fathers ate sour grapes, and the children's teeth were set on edge'? As I live, says the Lord, this proverb shall no longer be spoken in Israel. For all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son, they are mine. The soul that sins, it shall die. The son shall not bear the sin of his father, nor shall the father bear the sin of his son." For how could the Lord of all still be long-suffering and abounding in mercy and true if he does not forgive sins and clear the guilty, but rather prolongs his indignation to the third and fourth generation? What, then, is the explanation? He is, as I said, long-suffering and incomparably good, and he does not at once bring punishment on those who have sinned. He postpones it, even to a second generation, so that perhaps repentance, coming in between, might check his wrath. But if this should not happen, and the third and fourth from the first are caught in the same evils or even worse, and are found to be imitators of their ancestors' impiety, then at last he brings on the penalties, having granted the family forbearance enough for what was already past. This is what it means to bring the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation. So then, he says, after being patient with Damascus so many times, should I not now at last be angry, and with every reason, at three and four sins? What have they done? Many other things too; but they will pay the penalty for their excessive cruelty. For I will turn away from them, because they sawed with iron saws the women with child of those in Gilead. Gilead is a small town of Judea lying on the border of the Philistines. The Syrians seized it and destroyed it utterly, cutting the pregnant women with iron saws, and together with the infants wasting away the unformed fetuses of the women. By iron saws he means the wheels of wagons, with which the Syrians are accustomed to thresh the threshing floor. Indeed, through the voice of Isaiah he says somewhere to the synagogue of the Jews, "Behold, I have made you like the wheels of a wagon, threshing, new, shaped like a saw." It is as though he were saying to Damascus: I will determine your punishment, because you threshed and crushed those in Gilead, so as not to spare even those still in the womb, to whom mercy from everyone is due and given. That some from Damascus treated those of Israel cruelly and savagely you may learn without effort by attending to the words of the prophet Elisha. He came to Damascus, and when he met Hazael while Ader was still ill, "the man of God wept," it says, "and Hazael said, 'Why does my lord weep?' And he said, 'Because I know all the evils you will do to the children of Israel: you will send their strongholds up in fire, and you will kill their chosen men with the sword, and you will dash their infants to pieces, and you will rip open their women with child.'" Since Damascus did these things against Gilead, or rather against the whole land of the Jews, he threatens to burn the house of Hazael and Ader and to break the bars of Damascus. These things were carried out partly, and at various times, by Uzziah and Jeroboam, for they too took Syria and conquered it by force; and, as time went on, by the king of the Assyrians as well. Then he says, And I will utterly destroy the inhabitants from the plain of On. The prophets call Bethel "On," the place where the accursed Jeroboam set up the golden heifer; and from that time on they were accustomed to call every land given to idolatry by this name. So those who dwell in the land and plain of On, that is, of vanities, which means idols (for this is how the other translators rendered it), I will destroy and utterly exterminate, he says; and I will cut down no less the tribe from the men of Haran, which is no doubt some small town near Damascus, whose inhabitants were very warlike. He says that the chosen people of Syria will also be taken captive. By "chosen" he means either the very famous people, or the mercenaries gathered by them as auxiliaries, for, as I said, when they campaigned against the land of the Jews they hired the neighboring foreigners; or else "called in" means one summoned from outside, a settler. For it should be known that in place of "people of Syria" the Hebrew text says "of Cyrene"; for the Syrians are colonists of the Cyrenians. We recall too that, as is written again in the Fourth Book of Kingdoms, when Ahaz was reigning in Jerusalem, Pekah and Rezin, the kings of Syria and Damascus, came against Jerusalem, ravaging the cities of Judah under her. Since Ahaz, who reigned over Judah, was in unbearable fear, he hired Tiglath-Pileser the Assyrian with money to help him. "And the king of the Assyrians listened to him," it says, "and the king of the Assyrians went up to Damascus and took it, and carried it away captive, and put Rezin to death."

Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of Gaza, and for four, I will not turn away from them, because they took captive the captivity of Solomon, to shut them up in Idumea. And I will send fire upon the walls of Gaza, and it shall devour its foundations. And I will utterly destroy the inhabitants from Azotus, and a tribe shall be removed from Ashkelon, and I will bring my hand upon Ekron, and the remnant of the foreigners shall perish, says the Lord.

I think it necessary, before anything else, to say this: neither the Hebrew text nor that of the other translators mentions Solomon. The Hebrew says, "because they took them captive in a captivity," while the others added, in place of "of Solomon," "complete," that is, "entire." We, however, shall necessarily follow the text of the Seventy as well. Gaza, then, is accused (this is a city of the Philistines, which is now Palestine) of having taken captive the captivity of Solomon, to shut them up in Idumea. If we understand it as the other interpreters rendered it, they did not make an ordinary raid on Judea, but took a large number of captives and handed them over into the power of the Idumeans. The Idumeans were descended from the blood of Esau, yet they were always hostile toward those of Israel; and by cooperating with them and taking up arms alongside them, the people of Gaza, Azotus and Ashkelon, those of the place called Ekron, and certain others of the foreigners, brought it about that the cities of Judea were taken by force. But if, following the text of the Seventy, we say that they took captive the captivity of Solomon, we must surely understand it in this way. Solomon was a very powerful and mighty king, and he so prevailed over the surrounding nations that he built many cities among them and settled Israel in them, Hiram having given them to him. It is written thus in the Second Book of Chronicles: "And it came to pass after twenty years, in which Solomon built the house of the Lord and his own house, that the cities which Hiram had given to Solomon, Solomon built them and settled the children of Israel there. And Solomon came to Hamath-zobah and prevailed over it, and he built Tadmor in the wilderness, and he built all the fortified cities in Hamath." And again, after other things: "And whatever Solomon desired to build in Jerusalem and in Lebanon and in all his kingdom. All the people left of the Hittite and the Amorite and the Perizzite and the Hivite and the Jebusite, who are not of Israel, were of their sons who were left after them in the land, whom the children of Israel did not destroy, and Solomon made them tributaries to this day." So the people of Gaza and Azotus and the rest, joining forces with those from Idumea, took these cities, which were called Solomon's, so that they no longer lay under the kingdom of Judah but were assigned, as it were, to the unholy leaders of the Moabites. For this reason he says that Gaza, together with the others, will be consumed by fire, that the people of Azotus and the tribe of Ashkelon will be utterly destroyed, and that Ekron will come under the hand of the one who strikes; and that the remnant of the foreigners will certainly perish along with them. For in all likelihood some of the neighboring barbarians served as mercenaries and had been called in as auxiliaries.

So it is evident that it is a grievous thing, and full of every danger, to join forces with the wicked, to be eager to take up arms against those beloved by God, and to persecute the saints. For even if they sometimes suffer because of their faults, being disciplined by God, he will not altogether disregard those who belong to him; and having disciplined them for their good, he will bring destruction on the vessels of wrath, that is, on those who rushed upon them with unbridled fury. This accords entirely with what was well said to Babylon concerning the children of Israel: "I gave them into your hands, but you showed them no mercy." For excessive harshness in inflicting torments, on the part of those appointed to carry this out, is utterly out of keeping with God even when he is angry.

Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of Tyre, and for four, I will not turn away from it, because they shut up the captivity of Solomon in Idumea and did not remember the covenant of brothers. And I will send fire upon the walls of Tyre, and it shall devour its foundations.

The Tyrians, in turn, in addition to those of Damascus, and indeed the people of Azotus, Gaza and Ashkelon, and those of Ekron, overleaping the forbearance befitting God, and in a way outdoing them in the excess of their impieties, will fall under his wrath, according to the sense of the oracle, and will suffer the most extreme punishment of all. The charge against them is that they shut up the captivity of Solomon in Idumea, forgetting even the covenant of brothers. What the captivity of Solomon is, our discussion has sufficiently shown; but how it was shut up in Idumea, and by the Tyrians at that, must now be explained. They enslaved a countless multitude of those from Judah and Israel and sold them to the Idumeans. These treated their brothers by blood, free from the beginning, as spoils of war, oppressed them under the bitter yoke of slavery, and forced them to live by the laws of the Greeks, the wretches all but mocking the glory of God, as if he had neither preserved for them the freedom inherited from their fathers nor been able to grant them a prosperous and happy state. Indeed the God of all, through the voice of another prophet, speaks of those who shut up the captivity of Solomon in Idumea, accusing them in no measured terms: "And what are you to me, Tyre and Sidon and all Galilee of the foreigners? Are you paying me back a recompense, or do you bear a grudge against me? Swiftly and speedily I will return your recompense upon your heads, because you took my silver and my gold, and carried my choice and beautiful things into your temples, and sold the sons of Judah and the sons of Israel to the sons of the Greeks, in order to drive them out of their borders." The border of those of Israel is, as it were, bodily the land of Judea and spiritually the law; and they were put outside both, being sold away abroad to the sons of the Greeks. The Tyrians did this together with the others, forgetting even the covenant of brothers.

This too may be understood by us in three ways. Let us say who the brothers are and what the covenant is, being guided to our understanding of the point by the sacred Scriptures. Hiram, who reigned over the Tyrians in his time, was among the very dearest friends of the inspired David; and after him he became beloved of Solomon, so that he made a pact of unity of heart with him, cooperated with him in everything, and contributed the needed care when he was completing the divine temple. He brought very many gifts, and himself gained even greater and richer ones in return. So either he means that the Tyrians made war on Israel, forgetting the covenant of those who were brothers through love and had come together in such affection and fondness that they seemed to be of one blood; or else that the Idumeans, descended from Esau, were brothers to those of Israel, yet made war on them with no regard for the covenant of brothers. For Esau was at first hostile to Jacob and acted as an enemy, grieved over the birthright; but when Jacob in time departed from the household of Laban and wished to return home with his wives and children, Esau met him as a brother. They embraced one another and clung to each other, spoke as befits friends, and, trampling down their old quarrel, made covenants of harmony and peace. That was how things stood with them. But the Tyrians, forgetting the covenant of brothers, set the peoples against each other and persuaded the Idumeans to hold as slaves those who were their own blood and brothers, making the Idumeans, by their collusion, far stronger than those who had formerly prevailed over them. Or someone might say this applies to the Moabites, who were of the blood of Lot: that the Tyrians violated a covenant of brothers, clearly meaning the one between Abraham and Lot. For when the shepherds of the two quarreled, "Abram said to Lot," it says, "'Let there be no strife between me and you, and between my shepherds and your shepherds, for we are brothers.'" For this reason, then, he says that the city will justly be burned and shaken from its very foundations. For the saying "You shall not follow the majority in wickedness" is useful in every case.
Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of Idumea, and for four, I will not turn away from them, because they pursued their brother with the sword.

The discourse now passes to the Idumean himself, that is, to the descendants of Esau, and says that they too will very surely fall under the consequences of wrath. For they made war on Israel, who was their brother, and did not shrink from raising a bold and savage sword against their near kin and blood relations. They cared nothing for the law of nature and had no regard for anything humane; rather, they were accustomed to outdo even outsiders and the bitterest enemies in hostility toward their brothers, and perhaps even prided themselves greatly on this. So let them hear from us too: "Why do you boast in wickedness, O mighty man?" And of them it might very fittingly be said, "Whose glory is in their shame." For honoring with an utterly wicked judgment the very things they would have done better to keep as far away from as possible, they will hear again: "Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness, who call bitter sweet and sweet bitter."
And he destroyed the womb upon the earth.

The list of the Edomites' crimes is a useful one. The prophet goes back to Esau himself and shows that they are of base birth, sprung from an unholy father. Here, I think, we can see what Isaiah hints at indirectly: "For from the seed of serpents will come the offspring of asps." He tells us, then, that Esau, who had become their forefather, all but ravaged the blessings that had come to him from the womb and from his birth. He threw the dignity of the birthright down to the ground, valuing it at almost nothing for the sake of bodily food. He asked for a stew of lentils, and when he received it he gave away nature's gift. "For this reason," it says, "his name was called Edom," which means "earthy." From this, I think, his descendants were afterwards called Edomites. So he ravaged the dignity of birth and womb "upon the earth," it says; that is, he exchanged it for an earthly thing. The same charges would apply to those who put the enjoyment of fleshly things before spiritual ones. They choose the temporary over the eternal and the things that are shaken over the things that are not. They despise the glory that comes from God and, most foolishly, prefer what is splendid among human beings, though such things pass their owners by like shadows. Very usefully, then, does the divine Paul cry out: "Let no one be sexually immoral or godless like Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal."

And he seized his shuddering as a testimony. Again the prophet recalls another matter that can expose the Edomite as always perverse and wicked, and as especially hostile and warlike toward his own blood. It is written in Numbers: "And Moses sent messengers from Kadesh to the king of Edom, saying, 'Thus says your brother Israel: You know all the hardship that has come upon us. Our fathers went down into Egypt, and we lived in Egypt many days, and the Egyptians mistreated us and our fathers. And we cried out to the Lord, and the Lord heard our voice, and sent an angel and brought us out of Egypt. And now we are at Kadesh, a city on the edge of your territory. We will pass through your land. We will not go through fields or vineyards, nor will we drink water from your cisterns. We will travel by the King's Highway. We will not turn aside to the right or to the left until we have passed through your territory.' And Edom said to him, 'You shall not pass through me; otherwise I will come out to meet you in battle.' And the sons of Israel said to him, 'We will pass along by the mountain. And if I and my cattle drink any of your water, I will pay you for it. It is nothing; we will pass along by the mountain.' But he said, 'You shall not pass through me.' And Edom came out to meet them with a great multitude and a strong hand. So Edom refused to let Israel pass through his territory, and Israel turned away from him." Notice again here how terrible, beyond all words, are the charges of heartlessness. Israel was not asking Edom for free water, yet Edom took up arms and drew up his ranks. He begrudged them even passage, and he was shown to have gone so far in perversity that, had Israel not turned aside, he would not have spared even their lives. So "he seized his shuddering as a testimony." The Israelites begged off and drew back, fearing to make war, so that they would not seem to disregard their love for their brothers. But Edom made their drawing back, that is, their fear of doing this, which the prophet indicates by the word "shuddering," the pretext for a kind of harsh warning to them. He plainly threatened that if Israel would not keep away from the territory that belonged to him, he would come out against them and make war. Edom, then, was without love for his kin and fully guilty of the crime of hating his brother. For this reason God rightly loathed him. "For God is love," in the words of John, "and whoever abides in love abides in God." So whoever chooses to live without love is not in God. How could he be? Rather, he will be left outside any closeness to God.
And he kept his fury for victory. And I will send fire upon Teman, and it shall devour the foundations of its walls.

This is the third offense of Esau's descendants. "His fury," that is, his fierce impulse toward hatred and unholiness, "he kept for victory," that is, to the utmost and for all time. He never stopped his unholy undertakings, even though, as I said before, Esau himself had left that old unholiness behind. He no longer wanted to murder Jacob, and he changed instead to gentleness and brotherly love. When Jacob was returning from Laban's house, Esau embraced him with tears; tears tend somehow to flow at times of great joy too. But his descendants were very harsh, and in the perversity of their ways they outdid even their ancestor's wickedness. But it is true, always and in every way, that "the ways of those who bear grudges lead to death." That is why he says, I will send fire upon Teman (this was the chief city of Edom), and it shall devour the foundations of its walls. It was burned when its enemies conquered it, and Teman perished together with the other cities.

So hating one's brothers, rising up against one's own blood, or against those gathered into unity and one-mindedness by spiritual kinship, will end in fire and flames. But those who glory in love are free of such evils.

Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of the sons of Ammon, and for four, I will not turn away from them, because they ripped open the pregnant women of Gilead, in order to [?enlarge] their borders. And I will kindle fire upon the walls of Rabbah, and it shall devour its foundations with shouting in the day of war, and it shall be shaken in the day of its destruction. And their kings shall go into captivity, their priests and their rulers together, says the Lord.

The savagery of the Ammonites, like that of the Damascenes, is recorded too. They also killed the pregnant women of Gilead. They were not helping anyone else, nor lending their anger to foreigners; they did it for their own sake, to widen their dominion and stretch the borders of their kingdom far, once the whole land of the Jews had been laid waste and the people of Israel utterly overthrown. They acted as though God had grown feeble and was truly too weak, the God who had promised to save them and to make them invincible to anyone who wished to make war on them. So these too, when they had captured the cities, dared to laugh at the God who protected Israel, and they offered thanksgivings and victory songs to their falsely named gods. That is why he says that Rabbah will be burned; this too was the chief city of the land of the Ammonites. He says it will perish "with shouting," that is, as the Babylonians raised the war cry over it, as is the custom of war. They took it with their whole army when Nebuchadnezzar overran the land of the Ammonites. And the subjects, he says, will go into captivity together with their rulers, and those whose lot it was to serve as priests will go with their own gods, getting no help from them at all. For what could a deaf image do, or how could it be of any use to anyone?

Those who stand at the head of heresies are also like those who rip open pregnant women in order to enlarge their borders. To appear as the leaders of many, they force wretched souls, and by the deceptions of their words they make them miscarry their faith, unripe, as it were, and not brought to term. They speak perverse things to them and pour out what comes "from their own hearts, and not from the mouth of the Lord." For no one says "Jesus is Lord" except in the Holy Spirit, and no one says "Jesus is accursed" except in Beelzebul.

Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of Moab, and for four, I will not turn away from him, because they burned the bones of the king of Edom to lime. And I will send fire upon Moab, and it shall devour the foundations of its cities. And Moab shall die in helplessness, with shouting and with the sound of the trumpet. And I will destroy the judge from it, and I will kill all its rulers with him, says the Lord.

The Moabites, in turn, committed such great impiety that they too went beyond the gentleness and forbearance that belong to the God of all. The charge against them is a sin against a dead man: I mean the burning of the bones of the king of Edom, burned so thoroughly as to be reduced to dust and lime. What, then, is the charge? Hatred, inhumanity, and unbridled savagery against the people of Israel. One could say that the bones of the king mentioned were burned for no other reason than because of the Israelites alone. The story is clear, but I will tell it briefly. In the Second Book of Kings it is written: "And after Ahab died, the king of Moab rebelled against the king of Israel. And King Joram went out of Samaria on that day and mustered Israel. And he went and sent to Jehoshaphat king of Judah, saying, 'The king of Moab has rebelled against me. Will you go with me to war against Moab?' And he said, 'I will go up. I am as you are, my people as your people, my horses as your horses.' And he said, 'By which way shall I go up?' And he said, 'By the way of the wilderness of Edom.' So the king of Israel went, and the king of Judah and the king of Edom, and they made a circuit of seven days' journey; and there was no water for the army or for the animals that followed them." Notice, then, how the king of Edom, that is, of Idumea, took up arms together with the other kings. When they were short of water, they sent for the blessed prophet Elisha and begged that God would grant what they needed. When this was done, the Moabites were defeated. For it is written further on: "And Israel rose up and struck Moab, and they fled before them. And they went in, advancing and striking Moab, and they tore down the cities; and on every good plot of land each man threw his stone and filled it, and they stopped up every spring of water and felled every good tree, until only the stones of the wall were left, torn down." The Moabites, then, bore a grudge because the Israelites had once defeated them with the help and leadership of the king of Edom. Since they had no other way to hurt him once he was dead, they committed an outrage against his remains. They consumed them with fire and did not spare even his bones, consigning the man who had once been Israel's ally to the same fate as the Israelites, as though he were destroyed along with them.
