So he says that their cities will be burned and that they themselves will perish "in helplessness": not wasting away from disease or worn down by ordinary illnesses, but "with shouting and with the sound of the trumpet," that is, as in war and battle. He threatens too that its judges and rulers and all its leaders will perish together with their subjects. For they were the ones who led in counsel and in action, and they were surely the ones who introduced the whole impiety to the others.

Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of the sons of Judah, and for four, I will not turn away from them, because they rejected the law of the Lord and did not keep his commandments, and their vain idols, which they made, led them astray, the ones their fathers followed after. And I will send fire upon Judah, and it shall devour the foundations of Jerusalem.

Added to the lawless nations is the one who was trained by the law, that is, Judah; for the Judge shows no partiality. That God always bore with Judah's offenses and endured them for a long time is shown by the fact that he was moved to act only at the third sin, and indeed the fourth. Yet surely, one would think, it was right to show more abundant gentleness to the other nations, since they did not have the divine law, and to grant them a generous length of pardon, while demanding punishment from Israel for its negligence at once, since Israel had been raised on the divine commandments and was not ignorant of the path to its own good. But God bore even with those who knew the law as if they did not know it. When, however, he saw that they had at last been carried away to the very limit of wickedness and perverse thinking, he says that he will then let loose the fire upon Jerusalem itself and consume that splendid and renowned city down to its very foundations. The charges against Israel are very many, but above all God blames them for following the errors of their fathers. Their fathers, while still under the yoke of Egyptian greed and brought up in the customs and laws of the Egyptians, gave worship to a calf. But these, who had escaped that utterly wretched slavery and had been trained in many ways by the divine commandments to know clearly what pleases God, were caught going backward. They were dragged down into their fathers' error, perhaps even fearing, as something unseemly, not to be seen involved in the same evils. For they too worshiped the golden heifers. The cause of such impiety in them was that they rejected the law of the Lord and were unwilling to keep his commandments.

So as long as we keep the law and love God and are eager to observe what has been commanded, we will be found wise and quick of understanding, skilled in every virtue; and what good thing of this kind will we not be found rich in? But if we lean toward negligence and disregard the divine laws, we will be carried about by every wind, deprived of the best mind and understanding. We will become "a portion for foxes," as the unclean spirits drag us this way and that. Rightly and wisely, then, does the divine David sing of every righteous man: "The law of his God is in his heart, and his steps will not slip."

[?] and for four, I will not turn away from him, because they sold the righteous for silver, and the poor for the sake of sandals that tread upon the dust of the earth.

He does not leave Israel, that is, the tribes in Samaria, unaccountable; rather, he subjects them to punishment. That they too, by sinning without restraint, had all but used up the calm forbearance that God owes to the weak is shown by his turning away at three and four sins. Those who suffer this must necessarily fall into terrible things and come into every evil. That is why the divine David, fearing this and knowing that it brings destruction, pleaded, saying, "Do not turn your face away from me, and do not turn aside in anger from your servant." For wrath surely follows, and somehow goes hand in hand with, his turning away. What the charges against Israel are, he states clearly. They sold, he says, the righteous for silver and the poor for sandals. That is, they could not bear to speak what was right and just, or to judge each case that came before them in keeping with the law. If it happened that a righteous man, self-controlled and fair, modest and unassuming (for such a man may be understood as both righteous and poor, that is, poor in spirit), was brought to judgment by one of the more powerful, he was sold to his enemies. And this although the law had clearly declared, "You shall not show partiality in judgment," and again, "You shall not kill the innocent and righteous." For whoever has been entrusted with judging is surely appointed in the place of God, to whom alone judging properly belongs. "For there is one lawgiver and judge," in the words of the saint. So whoever falsifies the case of the righteous and looks to a person's standing surely insults the divine dignity and offends God, who says, "Judge with righteous judgment, and each of you show mercy and compassion to your neighbor." He accuses them, then, of selling the righteous and poor man to his enemies, and of being in the habit of doing this for small and utterly paltry gains, which would scarcely be enough for those who received them to buy a pair of sandals. Far better would it have been for them to choose to honor what is right and what pleases God, and so rather to be filled to overflowing with the honors that come from him, and indeed to possess the wealth that comes from a good reputation. "For a good name," it says, "is to be chosen rather than great riches." And we should know that through Isaiah too he says something similar to the mother of the Jews, that is, Jerusalem: "Your silver is counterfeit; your merchants mix the wine with water; your rulers are disobedient, partners of thieves, loving bribes, chasing after rewards, not judging for orphans and paying no attention to the widow's case." And again through Jeremiah: "Her leaders judged for bribes." Everywhere, then, it is accursed not to give a judgment that is right and blameless, but one that is oppressive and tainted by unfairness.
And they struck the heads of the poor with their fists.

He clearly charges and accuses them of oppression and greed, as unholy and pitiless people. Those whom it would have been better to think worthy of care, to choose to honor, and to win over to affection with loving help and kind words [?], they were in the habit of wronging instead, wearing down with unbearable and bitter griefs those weighed down by poverty. But our Lord Jesus Christ counts what is done to them as done to himself. For he says, "Inasmuch as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me." So we will offend God greatly if we take advantage of the weak and "strike the lowly with fists," as it is written, and embitter with distress those burdened by poverty, when we ought instead to stretch out to them a loving hand. "For poverty," it says, "humbles a man, but the hands of the strong make rich." And the disciple of Christ writes somewhere: "Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained by the world."
And they turned aside the way of the lowly.

You can understand this in two ways. Either he means that they were arrogant and reached such a degree of God-hated boastfulness that they rejected even their brothers unless they were surrounded by wealth and had splendid possessions, and that they hated, as it were, to walk the same way as those who had not much cultivated the passion of avarice, who are the lowly, since they reject the pointless turmoil of life. Or he means that, having become teachers and leaders of peoples, they turn aside the way of the weaker, that is, of the lowly. These are clearly people who do not have from their own resources an exact knowledge of what is good for them, but rather depend on the words of those who guide them. Such people are a very great multitude. Some live quite simply and without fuss, but they hang on the words and teaching of their instructors, and whatever way they learn is good, they love dearly. So the wise and God-loving among those whose lot it is to lead show them the straight path; walking along it above all, they succeed in living a life pleasing to God. But those who care little for the divine law turn aside the way of the lowly, causing them to end up outside what is reasonable and truly fitting. This is just what Jeroboam did when he persuaded the people to worship the heifers made by hand, and turned them away from the straight and good way, I mean from cleaving to the one who is God and Lord by nature and in truth. They turn aside the way of the lowly who do not hesitate to say to someone childish in mind, "Come with us, share in unjust bloodshed." They also turn aside the way of the lowly who bend the correctness of the Church's doctrines toward their own opinions and persuade the minds of the simpler to walk a crooked and twisted path. For with them nothing is right; instead there are distorted and ugly little phrases and contrived arguments full of both impiety and ignorance.

And a son and his father went in to the same girl, so as to profane the name of their God. Again he accuses them of hot and unchecked pleasures, and by this one offense he has shown that they had thrown away all decency. It would have been far better to master their passions and rise above monstrous and loathsome pleasure, to cut off their desires, knowing how to rebuke the wishes of the flesh and persuading the law that rages in our members to grow quiet. But they fell far behind such splendid virtue and were, it seems, even overcome by the passions of the flesh.

How, then, is it not wise, even among shameful things, at least to choose the lesser evil, and to recognize that it is among the most monstrous things of all for a son to leap into his father's bed, or for a father to make a habit of raging wickedly after the very bed of his son? How is it not wise to see that they chose to commit a dreadful deed, one that nature knows to be shameful even without the law given through Moses, and that it sees fit to condemn with stirrings of anger? Reuben, at any rate, gave no small offense when he wronged his father's bed. The inspired Paul was also deeply indignant over a deed of this kind committed by certain people, namely the Corinthians. He wrote to them, saying, "It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and immorality of a kind not found even among the Gentiles, that a man has his father's wife." But he did not stop his indignation there; he handed the man who had done it over "to Satan for the destruction of the flesh." Those who are guilty of such sins therefore profane the name of their God. We do not mean that they inflicted profanation and impurity on the divine nature. How could they, or by what means? Rather, they cause the God of all to be reviled as the ruler of profane peoples. Indeed, he said somewhere to the Jews, "Because of you my name is continually blasphemed among the Gentiles." Just as those who live rightly are said to sanctify God, so those who practice an impure and inglorious way of life may be understood to profane him.
And binding their garments with cords, they made curtains beside the altar, and they drank wine gained by extortion in the house of their God.

Our Lord Jesus Christ taught that the divine temples must be maintained for no other purpose than for the God of all to be glorified in them and given the worship that befits him. So he once rebuked the Jewish merchants, who were bringing sheep, oxen and doves into the temple. Indeed, "having made a whip of cords, he drove them all out of the temple, saying, It is written, My house shall be called a house of prayer." And the sacred text noted that "the disciples remembered that it was written, Zeal for your house will consume me." The inspired Paul also rebuked some who were in the habit of daring such things. He writes, "Do you not have houses to eat and drink in? Or do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing?" So it is plainly harmful in every way to dare to misuse the houses of God as though they were common places, each belonging privately to someone. For where could the reverence due to God still be kept, if we indulge the pleasures of the flesh before his eyes? And in the places where we ought to be seen shining with dignity, should we be laughed at there as people slipping into unseemliness and wanting to do what is not permitted? He does not leave those who do this unblamed, and quite rightly. For they did not keep the altar free of hangings stretched around it, he says; instead they lay down under them and dared to get drunk and carry out the works of pleasure, so that they would hear God saying plainly, "And I am a witness, says the Lord." What outrage would a drunken man refrain from, when his mind is deranged and he is easily led to any evil whatever? The God of all oversees even "the things in darkness," as it is written, and nothing at all is hidden from his sight. Yet what we do in churches above all seems to be done almost in his presence and before his very eyes. And if getting drunk at all is truly utterly shameful and incurs the severest condemnation under the law, how is it not beyond all words that look upon wickedness for such people to be seen in the very churches? And it is more grievous still if the means for their luxury were gathered from unjust and wicked gains. Those who do this will hear God saying plainly, "Is my house a den of robbers?" So the faults of others will be of great benefit to us, and through the things by which others gave offense we shall become better, if we reject what they did. For the self-controlled will rightly be safer if they wish to live lawfully and do not choose to imitate the wicked. Now if this is said to Judah, that is, to the two tribes in Jerusalem, "Binding their garments with cords, they made curtains beside the [?]," then the passage may rightly bear the interpretation we have just given. But if the offense is also charged against Israel, I would say that it was not in the house of the one who is God by nature and in truth, nor beside his altar, that tents were woven from the hangings, that is, that the deeds of drunkenness were done. It was in the house of their god, meaning Baal or some other of the beings that human invention has fashioned into the form of an idol. How, then, could it still be counted as a charge against Israel to get drunk with wine and weave tents in what was perhaps a house of idols, beside the profane altar itself? It is because they honored these things, and made the temples of their supposed gods into workshops of drunkenness and of every shameful pleasure, although they ought rather to have longed to worship God purely and with complete chastity, to enter the house that is truly holy, and to regard the altar as sacred. But they were eager to count as nothing things so sacred and so worthy of admiration, and they honored things far more shameful. They even dared to behave drunkenly toward their own gods, trampling the divine dignity underfoot in every way and fearlessly insulting the glory that befits the one God who is God by nature. For when they had conferred that glory on the falsely named gods, they could not bring themselves to hold it in any regard.
But I removed the Amorite from before them, whose height was like the height of a cedar, and he was strong as an oak; and I withered his fruit from above and his roots from beneath.

Next he shows how wickedly insolent they were, how they chose contempt, and how, in their utter folly and thoughtlessness, they chose to grieve the one they ought rather to have gladdened with songs of thanksgiving and with obedience in everything. Out of the great perversity of their character, they even drove the benefits they had received into oblivion. "For I," he says, "removed the Amorite from before them." That is: I destroyed the barbarian nations, which are perhaps signified by the single name of the Amorite, since he was harsh and very mighty. I made it possible to conquer one so huge and unbreakable that he seemed somehow to have risen to the height of a cedar and to rival the power of the sturdiest oak. "For it was no one else," he says, "but I alone who withered him and struck him down to the roots, and very nearly dried up his fruit as well." Since he has spoken as if of a tree, the passage fittingly keeps to the figure and says that the damage struck at his root, and in this way his fruit too was destroyed. For a tree in the forest would die in no other way than this. No one would doubt that the Amorites and Hivites, Girgashites, Perizzites and Jebusites were destroyed when the Israelites made war on them, with God clearly fighting alongside them.

How bitter, then, it is to despise Christ, who has given us power "to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy," and who overthrows and subjects to us even those who are stronger. "For our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against the principalities, against the powers, against the world rulers of the darkness of this age, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places." And we have prevailed over all of these in Christ. If we are going to grieve our own Savior and Redeemer by turning aside to idleness, I know that we shall have no argument or excuse that could rescue us from punishment and fire.
And I brought you up out of the land of Egypt, and led you about in the wilderness forty years, to inherit the land of the Amorites.

He clearly explains what he has said and, as if the discourse were turning back, briefly sets out everything from beginning to end. "I rescued them from slavery," he says, "and freed them from the greed of the Egyptians. I fed them in the wilderness, sending down manna to them from above, making springs of water gush up in a manner worthy of God, and granting them unexpected streams bursting from the flinty rock. And the toil of the journey was not for small ends, but so that they might inherit the land of the Amorites that had been promised to their fathers. But they slid into such perversity that perhaps they do not even recognize my love and kindness toward them."

We, then, who are in Christ through faith must remember that we too have been freed from slavery. As if out of Egypt, we have crossed over into the wilderness, that is, into a broad and truly most pure way of life, unmixed with what is worse: I mean the life of the Gospel. We have been enriched with the bread from heaven that gives life to the world. For we are strengthened in Christ, and we have as springs of pure water the writings of the holy apostles. That is what the prophet Isaiah called them, saying, "And draw water with joy from the springs of salvation." And what could the springs of salvation be, if not surely those who pour forth for us the saving and life-giving word, who proclaim the good news of the mystery of Christ, and who initiate the whole world under heaven into it?

And I took some of your sons to be prophets, and some of your young men for consecration. Is this not so, sons of Israel? says the Lord. But you made the consecrated drink wine, and you commanded the prophets, saying, You shall not prophesy.

On top of every other evil, it is a great ground for reproach and condemnation that God should, as it were, be repaid with ingratitude, when he distributes to us everything that brings glory and sustains life. Although there were many nations throughout the world, he chose Israel alone, and God called and raised it to such a height of glory that some who loved a pure and most law-abiding life were adorned with the dignity of prophecy, and the young men among them, that is, those of sturdier mind and possessing spiritual vigor, were taken for consecration. For under the law some were consecrated, those called Nazirites, who let the hair of their heads grow for the Lord. They refused wine and whatever comes from it (I mean vinegar, grapes, raisins and grape seeds), and kept well away from dead bodies. The meaning of these things is deep. In any case, God honored them, as I said, raising some of them to be prophets and to be consecrated in a figurative way. But they outrageously rejected so splendid and desirable a glory, and made the consecrated drink wine, that is, those who had taken a vow of consecration upon themselves. For they persuaded them to despise consecration itself, no doubt saying that the law of God was nothing at all, and that it was useless for people to want to be consecrated and to fulfil what was prescribed for it. For even if the law was in shadows, it was not entirely without the teachings of the truth; the form of godliness gleams through the types. And to rebuke even the holy prophets themselves is the mark of people who utterly shake off the word of God, who will not tolerate being taught, and who do not know that they had been honored, since men from among them had been taken into converse, as it were, with God. In the middle he adds a question, saying, "Is this not so, sons of Israel? says the Lord." He means: Will you accuse even facts so evident of being false? Will God need witnesses to convict you, when you have chosen to slander things so plain? We must therefore be consecrated and attend upon God with a steadfast mind, refusing to admit the opinions of the wicked. "For bad company corrupts good morals," and the words of pleasure lovers carry us away from consecration and from all goodness. Let us rather devote ourselves to the voices of those who speak of God, to whom the Savior himself bears witness when he says, "It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you."
Therefore, behold, I roll beneath you, as a wagon full of straw is rolled.

The ancients were accustomed to carry the produce of the fields, and whatever fills the threshing floor, in wagons, and the practice survives to this day among those who live in the lands of both East and West. The wheels roll together with the axles, the timbers grinding out a heavy, harsh sound, as though crying out under the loads laid on them. "So I myself too," says the Lord of all, "will be like the roller under the wagon," that is, the axle. For the axle, as I said, rolls the wheels along with it, since they are fixed and fitted to it. "I will cry out, as it were, against the ungodly, no longer able to bear the heavy weight of their offenses. 'For they rejected the law of the Lord and did not keep his commandments, but their vain things, which their fathers made, led them astray,' and they forgot me, who brought them out of the land of Egypt, who removed the Amorite from before them, who took some of their sons to be prophets and some of their young men for consecration. I honored them, but they sank into such folly as 'to bind their garments with cords and make curtains beside the altar, and to drink wine gained by extortion in the house of their God,' and to make 'the consecrated drink wine, and to command the prophets, saying, You shall not prophesy.' So, weighed down as it were by such impieties of yours, like an axle under a wagon full of straw and sheaves, I will raise a very great outcry." What harm will follow from this, or what sufferings will befall them in turn, he makes clear at once in what follows.

But this much must be said: it is truly a terrible thing to provoke God, and to sink so far into wickedness that our sin becomes unbearable to him, even though by nature he is kind, good and exceedingly gentle. Above all, then, we must refuse to make a habit of offending him. And if we should suffer some human failing, we must not be seen to put off repentance, nor allow our sins to grow. Instead, practicing a sobriety fitting for saints, we must rein them in and hasten to bring the ailing mind back to what is better. In this way God will be patient with us, and since he is good, he will grant mercy.

And flight shall perish from the runner, and the strong shall not keep hold of his strength, and the warrior shall not save his life, and the archer shall not stand his ground, and the swift of foot shall not escape, nor shall the horseman save his life. And he will find his heart under domination; the naked shall pursue on that day, says the Lord.

Nothing, he says, will save those who have offended in the days of wrath. Swiftness of foot will not deliver the fastest runner from disaster, nor bodily strength the robust man, nor experience of war the man who knows tactics, who has trained to shoot arrows with great skill and is admired for it. The speed of horses will be useless to those who ride them, and so will knowledge of cavalry warfare itself. But each of these, he says, will find his own heart under domination, that is, overpowered by fear and surrendering victory without a fight to those who wish to ravage them. For at that time there will be such cowardice among the Israelites, and such power among the Babylonians, that even the naked man will be able to pursue, that is, to overpower men in armor, even if one of the Babylonians has no breastplate; and the unarmed and unequipped man will be able to pursue men in full armor.

So when God shakes those he has chosen to punish into weakness, nothing can help them. I think this is what the voice of the psalmist tells us in other words: "He will take no pleasure in the strength of the horse, nor does he delight in the legs of a man"; and again, "A horse is a false hope for salvation, and by the greatness of its power it will not be saved." Such things are utterly useless if God does not fight alongside. For he is the Lord of hosts, who gives strength to the weak and saps the strength of those who have grieved him. With him "one will pursue a thousand, and two will put ten thousand to flight." But a great and countless multitude will be destroyed when perhaps only two or three stand against it, if God does not come to its aid.
BY THE SAME AUTHOR: ON THE SAME PROPHET, SECOND BOOK.

Hear this word that the Lord has spoken against you, house of Israel, and against every tribe that I brought up out of the land of Egypt, saying: You alone have I known out of all the tribes of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your sins.

This word should be understood as spoken against all Israel. Judah and Ephraim are no longer treated separately; the whole race is gathered, as it were, into one, since every tribe of Israel was brought up out of Egypt. So he has commanded them to hear what comes from God, and no one is left out. And what was it they were to hear? "Countless," he says, "are the cities and lands under all of heaven, and those who live in them are past numbering. Yet out of them all I made you of Israel my chosen. I made myself plain to you through many wonders. I rescued you from a bitter and unbearable slavery. I made you envied and thrice blessed. I trained you by the law in what pleases me. I walled you about with my help. I brought you into the land promised to your fathers. But you alone," he says, "of all who were counted worthy of so splendid a grace, have never stopped grieving me, and you have offended in many different ways. For this reason I will now call you to account for your madness. I will no longer put up with your sinning, or with a bent toward sin that goes unchecked."

So from now on, to despise God and disregard the Master's will brings destruction on anyone who has come to know him, or who has been known by him in the sense of spiritual intimacy. Indeed, the most wise Paul writes to those who had been called from the gentiles through faith and who then grew sick with weakness and were eager, as it were, to go backward: "But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you turn back to the weak and beggarly elemental spirits of the world, to which you want to be enslaved all over again?" The Creator certainly knew them before they believed, for he is ignorant of nothing whatever that exists. But in these passages, as I said, "knowledge" may very well signify spiritual intimacy.
Will two walk together at all unless they know each other?

The riddle is deep and the saying obscure; still, I will explain it as best I can. He was accusing Israel because "they commanded the prophets, saying, You shall not prophesy." We must also say why they so recklessly rebuked the voices of the saints. The prophets announced the grim things that wrath would bring, things that were likely to make sinners better than they had been, perhaps through fear of what the prophecies foretold. So those who were used to leading the minds of the common herd where they ought not to go, and to leading astray the people under their yoke, set about opposing the prophets and working against them. They rebuked the prophets, but they welcomed those who had gone astray as though these were walking the straight path. That is why God says through the voice of Isaiah: "My people, those who call you blessed lead you astray and throw the path of your feet into confusion." Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, also rebuked the prophet Amos, saying: "Seer, go, depart into the land of Judah, live there and prophesy there; but you shall never again prophesy at Bethel." Those who opposed the prophets, out of great perversity and terrible obstinacy, made up a plausible excuse for their opposition, saying: "The Lord has not sent you." So he accuses them because they claimed that his prophets did not deliver words from above and from God. They thought instead that the prophets were spewing out their own opinions, and saying things that went against the will of the Lord of all. That is why he says: "O foolish and senseless people, will any of you become friends and walk the same path of life without having known themselves, that is, one another? That is, unless they have seen that they are alike in character and of one mind?" For "every living creature loves its like, and a man will cling to one like himself." "And if this is true, how could I, who am holy, have received the prophets into friendship and love, as it were, unless they too had become holy? How, then, can you persecute the saints, to whom I have entrusted my own words, and whom I accepted as good, since they walk the same road of will as I do? For whatever I want is also what they want. So to rebuke the prophets is nothing other than to direct your reproach at me." The Savior said something similar to the holy disciples: "Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me." And he commanded those who were driven out to wipe off even the dust of their feet, saying: "It will be more bearable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment than for that city." So we must welcome those who serve as God's ambassadors and convey his will to us, as the divine Paul did when he wrote: "So we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were appealing through us; we beg you on Christ's behalf, be reconciled to God."
Will a lion roar from his thicket when he has no prey? Will a young lion cry out from his den at all unless he has seized something?

Those who study the habits of wild beasts say that the lion, when it is short of food, roams with great vigor over mountains, glens and thickets, turning its eyes this way and that and looking to seize one of the animals that graze in the woods. When it spots something fit to eat and comes close, it makes its attack with a terrible, harsh roar. And when food is being brought back to the cubs and comes near the den, they too leap up, seize it with a cry and tear it apart. "Why, then," he says, "do you blame God because he utters threats before the terrors arrive? And why do you gnash your teeth at the prophets themselves, because they too have cried out against your impiety? I am like a lion," he says, "which is used to roaring before it takes its prey, all but announcing its attack in advance. And the cubs, which is what the prophets are, imitate my habit, for they have cried out, as I said, against those who are used to impiety." The beast's warning roar is not entirely without profit to the animals in the mountains, since it may frighten them into flight before they are caught. In the same way, the threat and warning that comes before the terrors is extremely useful to sinners, moving them to repentance and to escape from what hangs over them. God, then, compares himself to a lion that does not leap on anyone or bring the effects of wrath upon them without first making his threat plain. He does this so that by repenting they may be saved, receiving the warning of what is to come, before the terrors strike, like a medicine for their salvation.
Will a bird fall to the ground without a fowler? Will a trap be sprung on the ground without catching something?

This saying, too, is framed as a comparison. Fowlers very skilfully bring down the sparrows perched in trees, and others crush whatever they catch in traps. Here the saying seems to hint, through the sparrows, at those who are used to thinking lofty thoughts: people arrogant in mind and with their heads in the air, who cannot bear to keep company with the lowly. Through the creatures caught in traps it hints at lovers of earthly things, who seek only what is fleshly and fattening. God in turn compares himself to a fowler and a trap. He brings the proud down to the ground, and he crushes and catches, as it were, for punishment those whose minds are set only on the things of earth. The people of Israel were arrogant: they despised God, thrust the prophets aside and dishonored the law. And they were no less very greedy about worldly affairs and sought only earthly things. Overcome by their outrageous desires, they would not accept the word of God, but worked against those who called them to virtue. For they said to the holy prophets: "Speak to us instead, and announce to us another deception." "If, then," he says, "it is I who bring down the proud like a fowler, and who, like a trap, crush the one who clings greedily to the things of the world like a fox or a mouse, why do you persecute the saints for nothing? They bring you nothing but words, while it is I who carry out what wrath has laid upon the impious."
Will a trumpet sound in a city and the people not be afraid? Will there be evil in a city that the Lord has not done?

"It is I," he says, "who bring the effects of wrath; the prophets serve as go-betweens for words alone. They convey to you whatever I command them through the Spirit. But perhaps you make light of it, and sometimes you are deeply vexed even at the mere words they speak. Tell me, what benefit at all do you get from them? What fear has entered you? What change for the better have you made? If a trumpet sounds in a city to announce that enemies have set out and a war is coming, who is so callous as not to be thoroughly afraid of the evils to come? My trumpets have never stopped announcing in advance what is to come. Yet you get no benefit at all. When you learn that enemies will ravage you, you look down so haughtily on the terrors in store that you perhaps even laugh at the warning as an idle thing, and you even shout that familiar saying so common among the senseless: 'The vision this man sees is for many days off, and he prophesies about distant times.' Why, then, do you find those who sound the trumpet, so to speak, so burdensome, if you think their words are nothing? But perhaps you will say that the outcome of events grieves you not a little. Will there, then, be affliction in a city that the Lord has not done?" It is as if he said: "Is there anyone among human beings able to afflict a city with diseases, sieges, ruined crops or anything else of the kind? If no human being could do such things, and they lie instead in the authority and power of God, why are you angry with those who announce them in advance? You ought rather to repent, and by turning in that direction to appease the one who has been grieved, who has the power to afflict those who have sinned." So here we shall understand the "evil" that comes upon cities from God not as wickedness (God forbid!), but rather as affliction: that is, the anger and stirring against anyone at all that he might hang over sinners to persuade them to turn to better ways. For it is written: "With bit and bridle you will hold in the jaws of those who do not come near to you." Since he is good, and "wants all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth," he in some way forces them toward what is better by the effects of his wrath. At times he forcefully moves by terrors and threats those whom reason and guidance toward what is good for them do not persuade.
For the Lord God will do nothing without revealing his instruction to his servants the prophets. A lion will roar, and who will not be afraid? The Lord God has spoken, and who will not prophesy?

"It is not the prophets," he says, "who bring the effects of wrath. How could they? They are human beings with the same nature as you. But God has honored them by letting them learn everything he means to carry out and to bring upon cities and lands, whether good things or things that bring grief. But perhaps you will answer: 'Let them learn, if he likes; let them be enriched by you with knowledge of what is to come; let every mystery be made plain to them. But let them speak to no one, and let them not ring anything in the ears of those who shake them off.'" What, then, is God's reply to this? "A lion will roar, and who will not be afraid?" "If," he says, "no one could be so hard and proud as not to be seized with terror when the lion roars, the mightiest of beasts, how could the prophets fail to fear the one who gave the command, when God, who is beyond all things, speaks and orders them to announce what they learn? They are not, like you, scornful and unyielding, setting at nothing what the Lord of all has willed." So he protects the saints in every way, and wards off from the prophets the harm done by those who choose to do evil. This was nothing other than to count them worthy of proper care. For to do away with the doctors would be nothing other than to leave the sick without help. He also proclaims this in advance through the voice of the blessed David, saying: "Do not touch my anointed ones, and do my prophets no harm." And somewhere he says to them: "Whoever touches you will be like one who touches the pupil of his own eye." For whoever gnashes his teeth at the heads of the saints, attacks them in an unholy way, and does not shrink from doing them some outrageous harm will do great wrong to his own soul.

Proclaim it to the lands among the Assyrians and to the lands of Egypt, and say: Gather on the mountain of Samaria, and see the many marvels in her midst and the oppression within her. And she did not know what would come before her, says the Lord, those who store up injustice and misery in their lands. Therefore thus says the Lord God: Tyre, your land round about shall be made desolate, and he will bring down your strength from you, and your lands will be plundered.

Once again he threatens to bring upon them what was fitting for people to endure and suffer who had sunk so far into wickedness that they sprang away from God, rebuked the prophets and wholly disregarded what had been decreed through Moses. It should be noted that here again the Hebrew edition and the text of the Seventy disagree. The Hebrews have rendered it: "Proclaim to the lands among the Azotians and to the lands of Egypt"; but the Seventy: "Proclaim to the lands among the Assyrians and to the lands of Egypt." Azotus is a neighbor of the land of the Jews and borders on it, while the land of the Assyrians, that is, of the Persians and Medes, is very far away, lying, as it were, at the very ends of the east. We say, then, that it makes no difference whether they are called Azotians or Assyrians. In either case the word of divinely inspired Scripture will prove true, as we shall indeed show in explaining the passage. What it points to recalls history recorded in the Second Book of Kings and in the Second Book of Chronicles. But I shall tell the story very briefly, so as not to seem long-winded to those who already know it.

In his time Manasseh reigned in Jerusalem. He was the son of Hezekiah, but very different in character and as far as possible from his father's piety. He became a wicked man, ready for every kind of outrage, abominable, an idolater, and devoted beyond measure to the deceptions of demons. He built altars and sacred precincts to Baal, worshiped the whole host of heaven, and passed his own children through the fire. He gathered augurs and those whose business is lying: people who think they know something that matters but do not, and who instead speak what comes from their own hearts. Perhaps there was no form of the very worst wickedness that he did not willingly pursue. While he was reigning, God said through the voice of the prophets about Jerusalem and the whole land of the Jews: "Behold, I am bringing evils upon this people, so that both ears of everyone who hears of them will ring." When Manasseh died, his son Amon succeeded to the sceptre. He fell short of his father's wickedness in nothing, for he honored everything his father had honored. He lived only two years. Then after him his son Josiah was anointed king, a wise and shrewd man, and one of the most God-loving of all. The man of God had proclaimed his coming when he went to Bethel, while Jeroboam was standing at the altar and inaugurating the feast for the heifers. For he said: "Altar, altar, thus says the Lord: Behold, a son is born to the house of David, Josiah is his name, and he will sacrifice upon you the priests of the high places who sacrifice upon you, and he will burn human bones upon you." When Josiah became king, he tore down the precincts of the idols, demolished the altars, destroyed the sacred groves, burned the chariot of the sun, slaughtered the priests of the high places in Bethel, burned human bones on the altar of the heifers, and drove out the soothsayers (I mean the false prophets, false diviners and ventriloquists). He ordered that what had been decreed through the all-wise Moses should prevail and have force in Israel. Under him they sacrificed the lamb and celebrated the Passover in Jerusalem. Because he was good and sincere toward God, he sent to Huldah the prophetess, wanting to find out whether the Lord of all would cease from his wrath, whether Israel would enjoy prosperity, and whether what had been foretold against it through the voice of the prophets would now come to nothing. She said to them: "Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Tell the man who sent you to me: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I am bringing evils upon this place and upon all who live in it, all the words of the book that the king of Judah has read, because they have forsaken me and burned incense to other gods, so as to provoke me to anger with the works of their hands. My wrath will be kindled against this place and will not be quenched. And to the king of Judah, who sent you to inquire of the Lord, you shall say this: Thus says the Lord God of Israel: As for the words you have heard: because your heart was softened and you humbled yourself before the Lord when you heard what I spoke against this place and its inhabitants, that it would become a desolation and a curse, and because you tore your clothes and wept before me, I too have heard, says the Lord. It will not be so. Behold, I will gather you to your fathers, and you will be gathered to your grave in peace, and your eyes will not see any of the evils that I am bringing upon this place and upon those who live in it."

And the promise was fulfilled. The Lord of all held back his wrath for the length of Josiah's reign, which was thirty-one years. Toward the end of it, Pharaoh Necho, the ruler of Egypt, marched against the land of the Babylonians and set out from his own country with his whole army. Josiah suspected that he might have come to ravage Judea, so he armed himself for war and meant to confront him. But Necho told him to withdraw, saying that he was hurrying to the river Euphrates and heading for the country of the Assyrians. When even after this Josiah needlessly drew up his forces against him, he was struck down in the battle. He died, and his own men carried him home to Jerusalem, and his son Jehoahaz was anointed king. He had barely completed his third month when Pharaoh Necho removed him from the throne, bound him and kept him under guard in Egypt. Only for a great deal of money did Necho reluctantly agree to let Eliakim, also called Jehoiakim, who was another son of Josiah, reign in Jerusalem. He oppressed Israel (I mean both those in Samaria and those in Jerusalem) so heavily that he imposed tributes on everyone throughout the land and demanded taxes from all. Such was the state of affairs, with Jehoiakim governing the kingdom, when Nebuchadnezzar came up. He so completely mastered Jerusalem that he made Jehoiakim his slave, exacted tribute from him too, and simply ravaged the whole city. Nor did God stop measuring out calamity at this point to those who had done unholy things; he added something else, grievous and most oppressive. From all the surrounding country and land, I mean from the Syrians, Tyrians and Azotians, the Idumeans and Moabites, bands of raiders swept out from place to place and plundered the land of the Jews. For it is written thus in Chronicles: "Then the land began to be taxed, to give the silver at Pharaoh's command, and each man was required, according to his means, to give silver and gold to the king of the land, to give it to Pharaoh Necho. Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Zechora, daughter of Neriah of Ramah. He did evil in the sight of the Lord, according to all that his fathers had done. In his days Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came into the land, and Jehoiakim served him for three years, and then rebelled against him. And the Lord sent against them the Chaldeans, and raiding bands of the Syrians, and raiding bands of the Moabites and of the sons of Ammon and of Samaria."
All these things Israel came to suffer because it had outraged the glory of God and had been corrupted so far, in unholy fashion, as to want to worship "the works of its own hands," as it is written.

Now that we have told the history at sufficient length, come, let us go over the text briefly and say what is fitting. "Proclaim to the regions among the Assyrians and to the regions of Egypt, and say: Gather on the mountain of Samaria, and see many wonders in its midst and the oppression within it." He all but says: Let someone announce it with all speed to the Egyptians and Assyrians, and let them overrun in strength the mountains of Samaria, that is, the country itself, for they say it is mountainous. And when they come, they will see in it many wonders and an unexpected oppression. For those who once were conquerors, he says, will be pitiable and counted among slaves; those who raised their brows haughtily over practically every nation will lie wretched and cast down under the feet of their enemies, and will endure such oppression that they will count it a blessing merely to be saved, to live in slavery, and to pay tribute to the victors. "But Samaria did not know," he says, "what will be before her," that is, what will befall her. Then where now are "those who store up injustice and misery in their lands"? For what did greed profit them, he says, and their heaping up of sins, because they did not wish to know the things of God? Will the calamity of the impious, then, stop at the invasion of the Assyrians and Egyptians? Not at all, he says. "Therefore thus says the Lord God: Tyre and round about, your land shall be made desolate, and he shall bring down your strength from you, and your regions shall be plundered." You may understand the words "Tyre and round about" somewhat as follows. From Tyre, he says, and from the land round about and neighboring, your country will be made desolate, as the robber bands, as I said, overrun it. For then they will bring down your strength; that is, all your power will be shattered, and, broken, will all but lose its vigor. So if perhaps the Hebrew edition says, "Proclaim to the regions in Ashdod," while that of the Seventy has "among the Assyrians," the statement will be true in both cases. For it was not only the Assyrians who plundered, but also Syrians and the people of Ashdod, rushing out in great numbers and wronging Israel in the manner of brigands.

Thus says the Lord: As when the shepherd pulls two legs or the lobe of an ear out of the lion's mouth, so shall the sons of Israel who dwell in Samaria be pulled out, those over against the tribe, and in Damascus.

Observe it everywhere, and you will greatly admire the sobriety of the prophecy. Since Israel did not perish entirely, but "the remnant" was saved, as Isaiah puts it, he always joins to his predictions of evils the mercy that springs from gentleness, so that Truth itself might not seem to speak falsely. Just as, he says, when a lion has eaten its fill and devoured at once the animal it seized, scarcely a few remains are left, perhaps two legs or part of an ear, and the herdsmen gather these up weeping, so it will be with the sons of Israel in Samaria and with those who dwell in Damascus, those "over against the tribe," that is, those who were hostile to the tribe of Judah and always opposed it. For the inhabitants of Samaria were taken by force and sacked by their enemies, and since the war consumed practically all of them, very few were barely saved, and only remnants of the dead remained in the land. Or again, in another sense, they were pulled out as from a lion's mouth: carried off into the land of the Assyrians, and released from captivity in due time, for not all returned, but only a very few remnants of those who had been carried away. That the Assyrian Tiglath-pileser in his day destroyed Damascus and deported its people to his own land is plain to everyone, I think. For as is written in 2 Kings, he was once called in to help by Uzziah king of Judah, when Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, and Rezin king of Syria were at war with him. And when he arrived, he killed Rezin and captured Damascus itself.

If someone should choose to apply the sense of this passage to all humanity as well, he will not miss the mark. For he will understand quite rightly, if he reflects that Satan, like some savage beast, seized and devoured those on earth, but "the good shepherd, who lays down his life for the sheep" appeared and came to our aid, and pulled us out, both those still left among the living and those already dead. For as the blessed psalmist says, "The Lord has shattered the molars of the lions," and as Paul says, "He died and lived again, so that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living."

Hear, you priests, and bear witness to the house of Jacob, says the Lord God the Almighty: on the day when I punish Israel's ungodliness upon him, I will also take vengeance on the altars of Bethel, and the horns of the altar will be broken off and fall to the ground. I will throw into confusion and strike the house with wings all around, together with the summer house, and the houses of ivory will perish, and many other houses will be added, says the Lord.

He returns again to a vivid account of what will happen to the impious, often expanding on the same theme for the benefit of his hearers. That is why, I think, the divine Paul too, understanding that the practice is not without profit, writes to some: "To say the same things to you is no trouble to me, and for you it is a safeguard." He commands those serving as priests, then, to raise their voice aloft, as it were, and testify to Israel, and to foretell clearly to them each of the things that were about to happen. Whom, then, shall we understand, or say, to be those commanded to cry out so piercingly? The priests of the heifers, or those of the idols in some other sanctuary? But I think that unlikely, for they would not have proclaimed the evils coming upon themselves and upon the others whom they had led astray. Who, then, are the priests commanded to do this? Those of the blood of Levi. For not all of them slid into error with those who had gone astray in Samaria, nor would they consent to worship idols; instead they fled the land of the Samaritans and went back to Jerusalem. It is written of them as follows in 2 Chronicles. The account concerns Jeroboam; then, describing the strength he had, it says: "And Judah and Benjamin were his. And the Levites and the priests who were in all Israel gathered to him from all their borders. For the Levites left the dwellings of their possession and went to Judah, to Jerusalem, because Jeroboam and his sons had cast them out from ministering to the Lord. And he appointed for himself priests for the high places and for the idols and the vain things and the calves that Jeroboam had made. And he cast out from the tribes of Israel those who set their heart to seek the Lord, the God of Israel, and they came to Jerusalem to sacrifice to the Lord, the God of their fathers. And they strengthened the kingdom of Judah."

Since those of whom the passage speaks were grieved not a little, having been driven from their kindred, their inheritances, and the ministry itself (for Jeroboam had cast them out), he fittingly commanded them above all to proclaim the destruction of the idols and of Samaria, as though consoling them and teaching them that those who had chosen to set their minds on the things of God and had loved the Lord of all would not perish with the others but would remain outside the wrath. For when, he says, I bring their sins upon those of Israel, then I will also take vengeance on the altars of Bethel; for their horns will be broken off and fall to the ground. Will the sack of Samaria, then, go only this far, and will it be enough for those commanded to ravage it merely to pull down sanctuaries and demolish altars? Not at all; for "I will throw into confusion and strike," he says, "the house with wings all around, together with the summer house." What this means is something like the following. The people of Samaria, living in great luxury and enjoying the ample means that come from wealth, built themselves winter houses and summer houses. The winter house he calls "winged all around," as being girded on every side with wings, that is, walls, so that it might be all but impervious to the onslaughts of winter; the summer house is the one left open and exposed to the gentle breezes of the winds. So together with the demolished altars, he says, I will throw into confusion and strike both winter and summer houses; and the houses of ivory too will perish. We remember that Ahab, when he reigned in Samaria, built such a house for himself. "And many others will be added," he says, that is, the houses of the lowly and more obscure, the poor and the common folk. So the whole of Samaria perished, every house shaken to the ground.

What, then, shall we learn from this in turn, we who have chosen to think rightly? That worldly splendor will profit its possessors nothing, neither wealth nor glory nor anything else that serves luxury, if love for God is absent and righteousness is in no way honored among us. "For treasures will not profit the lawless," as it is written, "but righteousness delivers from death." It would be far better, then, to love righteousness, to store up treasure in heaven, to long for the dwellings above, and to make it our habit to cling to our hope in God. For the things of this world are small and fleeting, and have no firm footing to make them secure; but that other good endures forever, is kept safe, and accompanies us through the endless ages.

Hear this word, you heifers of Bashan on the mountain of Samaria, who oppress the poor and trample the needy, who say to their lords, "Give us, that we may drink." The Lord swears by his holy things: Behold, days are coming upon you, and they will take you with weapons, and those with you, fiery pests, [?] into cauldrons, and you will be carried out naked, [?] a woman and her husband facing one another, and you will be cast out onto Mount Remman, says the Lord God.

Out of very great arrogance and luxury, the more prominent people of Samaria, who surpassed all the rest in abundance of wealth, built themselves, as I said just now, splendid and extremely costly houses suited to the seasons, winter, I mean, and summer; and the oracle foretold that these would perish utterly and completely. It is these very masters of the houses, then, those who made it their business to fatten themselves on fading luxuries, that he calls "heifers of Bashan." Bashan is a country of rich pasture and abundant flowers, exceedingly well suited to fattening generously whatever grazes there. So, since they lived in great comfort, were excellently fed, and made luxury their whole pursuit, God likens them to heifers from Bashan. He accuses them of oppressing the poor and all but crushing the needy under their own feet: "For the poor are the pasture of the rich," as it is written. And by adding "who say to their lords, 'Give us, that we may drink,'" he showed them to be insubordinate, unwilling to yield even to those who ruled over them, so far as royal honor was concerned, but rather, out of boundless arrogance, assigning even to their own lords the status of servants. For to dare to say to those who are preeminent and set above them, "Give us, that we may drink," is the mark of people who would rather be served than serve. What, then, will happen to those who have gone so far in folly? The Lord swears, he says, by his holy things, that is, by his holy places, or rather his mysteries, which again are himself, for he has no one greater to swear by, that times and days will come when the fear of suffering will drive even you, who live so luxuriously, are so pampered, and are so used to indulgence, into the toils of war and into arms. Yet even so equipped and armed, he says, they will take you, together with your dearest ones, your wives, and your flatterers, who were always at your side, applauding you with every possible acclamation and calling you thrice-blessed; for that is what the tribe of flatterers always cries out to those who feed them. But those men will be burned, for they were pests, approving of nothing else and admiring the shameful and the lovers of sin. And you, stripped of glory, as far as can be from all luxury, and as though divested of your former prosperity, will be carried off as slaves and captives, and you will be cast, he says, onto Mount Remman. It belongs to Armenia, lying at the farthest edges of the land of the Persians, for these countries border and adjoin one another. One can see from this, then, how the pursuit of luxury comes to a bitter end for those who indulge in it, as the Savior says: "Blessed are those who mourn now, for they shall be comforted." For luxury ends, as I said, in tears, but the end of toil is rest. And someone will bear witness to this, saying that the fruit of good toils is glorious.

It is not implausible to take the "heifers of Bashan" to be the women of Samaria, who, wantoning and fattening themselves in luxury, delicacies, and ornaments to beautify themselves, and in the bloom of their bodies, overpowered the poor and trampled the needy, all but inflaming toward outlandish pleasures those who are weak in this regard and poor in the spiritual sense, who, lacking the wealth of strength from above, have hearts easily shattered by the assaults of the passions. These heifers, then, say to their lords, "Give us, that we may drink." For women who play the courtesan are always showing themselves off, and with excessive wantonness they all but wear out those they have captivated; and even if they have them as masters, yet seeing them [?] by their voluptuousness, they persuade them to do whatever seems best to themselves. But you, he says, O heifers, they will take with weapons; that is, not acting the part of lovers, who persuade you with flattery and court you with endearments because they are utterly overcome by their pleasure in you, but cruelly, savagely, and by the law of war; and they will burn up the pampered lovers who are with you. And you, stripped of those outlandish adornments, will be carried off to Mount Remman.
You went into Bethel and acted lawlessly, and at Gilgal you multiplied ungodliness.

He immediately sets the offenses beside the punishments, and usefully places a vivid exposure of their impious deeds next to his account of the terrible things to come, so that no one might find fault with God or accuse him of hanging a harsher penalty than was fitting over those of Israel. Such and such things will come upon you, he says. And as for the reason, he cries it out openly: You went into Bethel and acted lawlessly, where the God-hated Jeroboam set up the golden heifer; there you will be caught transgressing terribly and outrageously. For I legislated through the all-wise Moses: "You shall not make for yourself gods of gold and gods of silver," and "You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve." But you, he says, scoffing at my law, have worshiped the works of your own hands; and seeing a golden heifer, lifeless matter, you persisted in it, when the inventor of the error said, "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt." And you committed the very greatest impiety at Gilgal. This is a city beyond the streams of the Jordan, which had fallen terribly into apostasy. Indeed the God of all said of it: "All their wickedness is in Gilgal, for there I hated them because of the wickedness of their practices." So then, as the author of Proverbs says, "A man's ways are before the eyes of God, and he watches all his paths." He welcomes those who take care to walk uprightly, but shakes off the one who walks outside the straight way and is eager to go where he ought not.

And you brought your sacrifices in the morning, your tithes for the three days; and they read a law from outside, and called for professions. Proclaim, then, that the sons of Israel have loved these things, says the Lord God.

It is truly most dreadful, and has reached the very height of impiety, to dare to counterfeit the glory of God and to attach to the honors paid to idols what befits him and him alone. For those accustomed to do this, as far as lies in their power, cast down the divine and supreme nature from the thrones that are fitting to it alone, banish it from its sacred seats, and enthrone the unclean demons there in its place.

We shall find the senseless Israel caught in charges as dreadful as these. For the God of all legislated through Moses, on the one hand, that they were to sacrifice two lambs every day in the holy tabernacle, one in the morning and the other in the evening, signifying, as in riddles and types, the continual and unceasing fragrance of the Church, the spiritual fragrance, clearly. And he further legislated: "Three times a year every male of yours shall appear before me." And at these three times appointed by the law they brought tithes, firstfruits of the fields, sacrifices, and thank offerings. For it is written: "You shall not appear before me empty." But they transferred what had been so rightly ordained through the all-wise Moses to the glory of idols, offering their sacrifices in the morning in the idols' sanctuaries, and bringing their tithes there "for the three days" as well. By "the three days" he means the three days of the year on which, as I said, every male had to come before God. Nor did the impiety of those of Israel stop there, but "they read a law from outside," that is, they honored the law of foreigners, holding the law from God in very little account. For they offered sacrifices in the sanctuaries of idols at fixed times and gave the greatest attention to the feasts customary among them. Or else he means this: what was ordained for my glory they have assigned to outsiders, and they have dedicated my law to idols, offering them the morning sacrifices and dedicating the tithes to them at the three days. "And they called for professions." "Called" signifies that they vowed, that is, made promises; and "professions" are the voluntary offerings under the law, whatever someone might bring to God of his own free will. Then he cries out to the priests, "Proclaim" and "testify," that "the sons of Israel loved these things"; that is, they did not merely dare it once but even loved it, plainly hating the things of God. For one must be single-minded. To limp, and to hurry to walk both ways at once, would bring great reproach before God, and the Savior himself will bear witness, saying: "No one can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will hold to the one and despise the other." It is a most grievous thing to divert elsewhere what belongs to the glory of God, and to deem others worthy of the honor that befits him. For the things of God are his own and set apart, and would befit no one else but him alone.

And I will give you aching of teeth in all your cities, and lack of bread in all your places; yet you did not return to me, says the Lord. And I withheld the rain from you three months before the vintage; and I will send rain on one city, but on another city I will not send rain; one portion will be rained on, and the portion on which I do not send rain will dry up. And two and three cities will gather into one city to drink water, and they will not be satisfied; and even so you did not return to me, says the Lord.

Again, as part of God's plan, the word meets those who are in the habit of finding fault, and who out of very great folly babble most thoughtlessly against the gentleness that is in God. Some might perhaps ask: why does he bring so savage and utterly unbearable a punishment on the people of Israel, though God is by nature good? In a way, then, he offers a defense through these words, and shows that they had by now made themselves liable to severe wrath. At the same time he shows that at first he strikes sinners more gently. He does not demand penalties. Out of his innate love for humanity he turns them back to himself, and as it were "with scourge and toil" moves them to choose to do what is better. For when they had come to the state I have described, and had committed impieties that could no longer be borne, he disciplined them with dullness of teeth, and also with lack of bread, that is, with famine. And you did not return to me, says the Lord. I withheld the rain from you three months before the vintage. Or, as the Hebrews have rendered it more fittingly, three months before the harvest, when the crops most need watering, and need it greatly, if they are to ripen. And there was, he says, such a scarcity of water that, by the power and decree of God who knows all things, rain fell on one city while the other withered. And again, two and three cities gathered into one and were still thirsty. And you did not return to me, says the Lord. These things happened to the people of Israel both historically and spiritually. For as the Savior's disciple has said, Elijah "was a man of like nature with us, and he prayed earnestly that it might not rain on the earth, and it did not rain for three years and six months." And so harsh a famine came upon Samaria that a donkey's head was sold for many denarii. In the times of Jeremiah's prophecy too the God of all withheld the rain. And so he spoke these words about the drought: "Judea has mourned, and her gates have been emptied, and they have been darkened upon the earth, and the cry of Jerusalem has gone up. And their nobles sent their young men for water; they came to the wells and found no water; they brought their vessels back empty. And the works of the land failed, because there was no rain. The farmers were put to shame; they uncovered their heads. And the deer in the field gave birth and abandoned their young, because there was no grass. Wild asses stood on the glens, they drew in the wind; their eyes failed, because there was no fodder, on account of a people's iniquity." Since, then, the people of Israel had been so grossly impious, God withheld the rain, and sent dullness of teeth and lack of bread into all his cities.

But, as I said just now, they suffered this in a spiritual sense as well. For bodies made from earth, food and drink are the produce of the earth and water that the senses perceive. But the human soul is nourished on divine and heavenly words. Its spiritual stream, the spring that waters it spiritually, is the divinely inspired Scripture, which speaks the mystery of Christ. Now teeth that have been dulled are rather feeble at chewing anything or grinding food fine. In the same way, the human mind that has slipped into weakness and suffered the infirmity of sluggishness cannot attain spiritual knowledge or digest any of the more subtle contemplations. So the heart of Israel grew fat, for it did not understand the mystery of Christ at all. This is why they have suffered a lack of spiritual bread and a scarcity of water. For they do not have the Word who nourishes: the Word who came down from heaven and gives life to the world, who waters souls with the grace of the Spirit, the living spring, the Son from God the Father, the consolation proclaimed through the law and the prophets. For as the prophet Isaiah says, "He commanded the clouds not to rain rain upon it."

I struck you with burning fever and with jaundice. You multiplied your gardens; the caterpillar devoured your vineyards and your fig orchards and your olive groves; and even so you did not return to me, says the Lord. I sent death among you on the way of Egypt, and I killed your young men with the sword, together with the capture of your horses, and in my wrath I brought up your camps in fire; and even so you did not return to me, says the Lord.

Some people feel no pain at what comes upon them from wrath. They are deeply complacent, and they sink still further into indifference, so that they do not even think the need to repent worth considering. For such people no single way of being struck will suffice. They need more blows, each worse than the last, and increasing so as to cause still greater distress. For the people of Israel, then, being disciplined with lack of bread and drink was perhaps too small a thing to bring about their amendment. So something still more grievous was added: sickness of their very bodies, such as comes with fever and jaundice. We will find this said again through the voice of Jeremiah. For he said, "Thus says the Lord: Behold, I am bringing sickness upon this people, and fathers and sons together will sicken in it; a neighbor and his fellow will perish." They were also slaves to shameful gain and intent above all on the love of profit. For this reason, as they multiplied gardens and vineyards, fig orchards and olive groves, God struck these too. Grieved by this in no small degree, they would likely return to a sober mind and choose what was beneficial rather than what was worse. So he heaped these blows upon them, that being struck from every side they might be saved. And since this too was a small thing, something greater was added. "For when," he says, "you dishonored my hand, and all but declared that God, who is all-powerful, was weak, and you made the journey to the Egyptians, preferring 'the flesh of horses' to my care and setting 'an Egyptian man' above me, then indeed," he says, "the most warlike part of your race was consumed by the sword of the Babylonians." And all your horsemen were taken captive, for God unnerved even men who knew how to win renown and were well practiced in victory in battle. But you will also understand I sent death among you on the way of Egypt in another way. When Josiah was reigning over Judah, Pharaoh Neco, the tyrant of the Egyptians, marched against Babylon. Since he had to pass through the land of the Jews, Josiah supposed that the march on Babylon was a pretext and that the Egyptian had armed himself against him, and so he unreasonably went out to meet him. There Israel fell. So he says, I sent death among you on the way of Egypt, that is, as the Egyptians were passing through. Then also I brought up your camps in fire, meaning, "I razed to their foundations your walled cities with their many fine towers." He said this also at the beginning: "And Ephraim went to the Assyrians, and Judah multiplied walled cities; and I will send fire into his cities, and it will devour their foundations." So, he says, I shook your strongest camps from their very foundations, and even so you did not return to me, says the Lord.
I overthrew you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you became like a firebrand snatched out of the fire; and even so you did not return to me, says the Lord.

"Seeing no amendment in you," he says, "I added to the torments things harsher still, and made my indignation against you hotter." For I overthrew you as Sodom and Gomorrah, and you did not return. Here he seems to point to the final sack, which took place in the times of Jeremiah at the hand of Nebuchadnezzar. He took all Judea, and burned Jerusalem itself and the cities and villages around it. He tore down the divine temple itself, made captives of those who had survived the war, and returned home in splendor and victory together with his prisoners. They scarcely returned to Judea, and only when seventy years had passed. For Cyrus, as I said, took Babylon and released from captivity those of Israel who were left and had been preserved. This is why, he says, you became like a firebrand snatched out of the fire: like a half-burned brand, still surviving in a few remnants. When God disciplines, then, complacency is a bitter thing. For those who shake off all feeling it will also be the cause of evils more grievous still, since it follows that they will go on without end choosing to do and to think what is unlawful. Consider those who check the diseases of the body and have trained their skill in healing. They cleanse the wounds that have lost their feeling with hot and sharp medicines, and by thinning out the thick impurity in them they make them yield to the remedies of their art. In the same way God, who knows all things, burdens those who are unfeeling toward small blows with blows that are harsher still. Anyone who is wise and shrewd would reasonably beg to be spared their onset before he experiences them.
Therefore thus will I do to you, Israel.

"For," he says, "I did this, and added that, and brought on almost every kind of torment and hardship, and I saw that you remained insensitive and learned it from experience itself. For this reason I will do so to you." How "so"? "I was not content with the first blows. I added as well an overthrow like that of Sodom." For this was the last blow, as I said, that the divine wrath brought upon them.
But because I will do so to you, prepare to call upon your God, Israel.

"But if," he says, "you wish to learn the reason why I will do so to you, you will surely find it out, for I all but cry out to you while you are being struck and say, Prepare to call upon your God, Israel." Prepare means "Be eager. Be ready and willing to call upon, not the alien and falsely named god, but your God, Israel." That is, the God whom you have come to know through experience itself to be God by nature and in truth, not one devised by someone's skill, as are, of course, the things made of wood or stone.

For behold, I am the one who strengthens the thunder and creates the wind and announces his anointed to men, who makes the dawn and the mist, and treads upon the heights of the earth: the Lord God Almighty is his name.

When something is compared with what is superior, its lower rank is easily exposed. Some people, out of very great stupidity, supposed that the idols were gods and deserved worship. So that the powerlessness of the idols may be made plain to them, the God of all helpfully makes himself manifest to us. He presents himself as Maker and Creator of all things, as holding authority over our affairs, as in a sense the helmsman of human life, as being beyond every height and every eminence, and as a kind of steward of the whole creation. For it is God's nature to be beyond all things. He surpasses the measure of everything that has come into being, not by any height of place, but by the eminence of his glory and by incomparable power.

"Call upon your God, then, Israel," he says, "recognizing his authority and the supremacy of his almighty power. For I am the one, and no other, who strengthens the thunder": that is, who covers the sky with clouds and sends down rains. "And creates wind": that is again, the maker of winds. "And who announces his anointed to men." It is as if he said, "By me kings reign, and by me tyrants rule the earth." For by "anointed" here he means not Emmanuel but rather one anointed as king. Likewise the "spirit" he creates is not the divine and Holy Spirit, even if some who have made a practice of distorting what is right rave otherwise. It is this wind of the air and of the world, of which the Savior himself also says, "The wind blows where it wills, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes; so it is with everyone who has been born of the Spirit." "I, then," he says, "am the one who gathers clouds and strengthens thunder and 'brings the winds out of their storehouses,' who makes manifest whomever I wish to take pride in the seats of kingship." So the King of those who reign and Lord of those who rule, who is God by nature, is himself the one who makes the dawn, that is, day or light. He himself is the one who makes the mist, that is, darkness or night. He himself is the one who treads upon the heights of the earth, greater than and above everything lofty and high. And he bears a name that is fitting and wholly suited to his own glory: Lord Almighty.

See, then, how much gentleness and love for humanity the God of all shows us. For having held his threat over them, and having foretold some things as already done and others as yet to come, he calls them to knowledge. He initiates into the mysteries the one who has turned aside, and brings back to understanding the one who has slipped through ignorance. And to those who did not know the one who is Master by nature and in truth, he makes himself plain by his power to accomplish all things and to rule over the universe. This was the work of one who brings people to their senses "with toil and scourge," all but disciplining them into conversion even against their will, and helpfully bringing upon them the things through which they could be expected to learn to think better.

Hear this word of the Lord, which I take up over you as a lament. The house of Israel has fallen; it will never rise again. The virgin of Israel has stumbled on her own land; there is no one to raise her up.

The blessed prophets learned beforehand the evils that were to come upon certain people. Filled with fear at this, and grieving exceedingly over them as over brothers, they sometimes make their rebukes more heated.
