They all but bite out of love, and by foretelling what is about to happen they rouse their hearers to sobriety. The Prophet does something of this kind now. He speaks as if in his own person, yet he speaks not from his own mind but as from divine oracles. This is why he says Hear this word of the Lord, which I take up over you as a lament. "For the God of all has spoken in me," he says, "and I have composed a lament over you who desert him." What, then, is the mournful song? What is the lamentation? Over what would I shed my tears? Over a terrible calamity, past all correction. The house of Israel has fallen. For it stood firm while God was honored and loved, but now it has fallen, because the madness of those who go astray has provoked him. Then who will raise up one who falls at God's decree? The virgin has stumbled, meaning, she has committed fornication. Who is she? Surely Israel once again, that is, the synagogue of the Jews, to whom God said, "Did you not call me house, and father, and guide of your virginity?" So she who had God as the guide of her virginity has stumbled on her own land. That is, she has committed fornication, and her sin admits no excuse. She did once commit fornication in Egypt. But she was then in a land not her own, subject to the laws of those in power, and perhaps she was forced against her will into their customs, driven as if by necessity from the piety of her ancestors. Now, however, she is a harlot with no one pushing her to it. She is on her own land, where the law is her tutor, leading her to the knowledge of the one who is God by nature and in truth. The road to every good thing lies open and free, and no one hinders her at all. What defense, then, could still be found for her? She committed fornication not under compulsion (how could she?) but of her own free will. This is why she lies dashed to the ground, and there is no one to raise her up. Let us too, then, say very fittingly to God who is all-powerful: "You are fearsome, and who will stand against you in your wrath?"

The multitude of the Jews has also fallen in another way. Their outrage against Christ has driven them to destruction, and they now lie with no one to help them. Yet they wait once more for the grace of the one who pities, I mean Christ. For she too will be called to knowledge through faith in the last times of the age.
For thus says the Lord: The city from which a thousand went out, a hundred will be left; and from the city from which a hundred went out, ten will be left for the house of Israel.

Here he makes very clear the manner in which she will fall. "The cities," he says, "will be left empty of men, for war will consume their inhabitants and bring them to such misery that barely a tenth part of them will remain." They provoked God by offering their tithes to the unclean demons for the three days. So they themselves will scarcely survive, as a tenth part. God all but weighs their offense in the balance and brings upon their impieties a penalty of equal weight.
It is a fearful thing, then, to be disciplined in anger. This is why the prophet entreated God, saying, "Discipline us, Lord, but in judgment and not in anger, so that you may not make us few."

For thus says the Lord to the house of Israel: Seek me and you will live. Do not seek Bethel, and do not go into Gilgal, and do not go up to the Well of the Oath; for Gilgal will surely be taken captive, and Bethel will be as though it did not exist. Seek the Lord and live, lest the house of Joseph blaze up like fire and it devour it, and there be no one to quench it for the house of Israel.

Once again he does not let those who have sinned slip into despair, though they are caught in terrible and unbearable offenses. He holds out what God offers and draws them like fish in a net toward repentance. And here too he has had to bring in God promising to forgive them the charges against them and to free them from punishment and from the fears it brings. For the Creator is good by nature, "long-suffering and abounding in mercy and relenting over evils," as it is written. As he himself says through the voice of Ezekiel, "He does not desire the death of the one who dies so much as that he turn from his evil way and live." "If, then, you value life highly, and the thing seems to you worth gaining, cease from your delusion, leap away from your long ignorance, and seek me," he says. That is, "Worship me, who am God by nature, the giver of life, who am able to save those who revere me and to set them beyond all evil." "But you must," he says, "first wash yourselves. Drive the filth of apostasy out of your souls, thoroughly melt away beforehand the stain of having gone astray, and so cleave at last to God, who is wholly good."

He made clear what those who chose to repent had to do, saying, Do not seek Bethel, and do not go into Gilgal, and do not go up to the Well of the Oath. By the Well of the Oath he means Gerar, a city of the Philistines, that is, of the Palestinians. For the godly Abraham and Abimelech swore oaths to each other and made a treaty of peace at the well, and so the city was thereafter renamed the Well of the Oath. Gilgal, then, and Bethel, and Gerar too, were cities deeply given over to impiety, setting error in many forms before those they deceived. He commanded that they must stay away from these, and he wove a threat into his word, so as to drive them from every side toward what was beneficial. For Bethel and the rest, he says, will be gone. One will go captive to its enemies; the other will be burned down so completely that it will seem never to have existed at all. "So let God be sought," he says, "that you may live, before the house of Joseph blazes up, and it devours it, and there is no one to quench it." By "blaze up" he means being set on fire. By "the house of Joseph" he names Ephraim, that is, the people in Samaria, for Ephraim and Manasseh were descended from Joseph. When he calls them Israel, we understand that his descendants are called after their father. So too if he happens to say Joseph, you will understand it in the same way.
Repentance, then, is a good thing. It drives away penalties and checks what wrath would bring. It sets those who practice it beyond the reach of the Master's anger, and frees us from every calamity.
It is the Lord who executes judgment on high, and he has set righteousness on the earth;

who makes all things and transforms them, who turns shadow into morning and darkens day into night; who summons the water of the sea and pours it out on the face of the earth: the Lord God Almighty is his name; who brings ruin upon strength and misery upon the fortress.

This passage leads into the mysteries. It is especially fitting for those who are called to the knowledge of God and are eager to come to the light of the truth. The Prophet's aim is to teach those who have gone astray. First, he teaches that power over all things belongs to God, that the whole universe is steered by his will, and that the all-blessed multitude of the angels is subject to the law of righteousness. Then he teaches that it follows, altogether and of necessity, that those who live on the earth are also yoked to the laws of his righteousness. If what is higher in creation serves God, and the holy multitude of spirits on high submits to him with fear, how or on what grounds could something so inferior in nature and glory escape blame when it veers into unruliness? I mean the human being, who comes from the earth and returns to the earth. So, he says, the Lord of all is the one who makes judgment on high. It is as if he said: "He is the one who gives the spirits on high and above the pattern of the righteousness that befits them"; for by "judgment" he means righteousness. He himself has also set righteousness on the earth. That is, he has laid down laws for those on the earth as well, by which it would befit them to live, if they care about being well and living well, and about sharing in his gentleness and love for humanity. He is almighty and all-powerful, as God is. Nothing at all is impossible for him. The very nature of the elements yields to him, and things change according to his good pleasure. He demonstrates this by taking as examples the turning of shadow into morning and, in turn, the darkening of day into night. He adds to these that he calls water up from the sea, high and aloft, by an ineffable power, and lets it fall sweet on those who live on the earth, so that at the bidding of the Ruler it passes into a state contrary to its nature. He says that shadow is turned into morning, meaning that the night, or the darkness, passes over into day. As the blessed Moses writes, "Darkness was" in the beginning "over the abyss", which is the shadow. But "God said," he says, "and there was light." In this way, we say, the shadow, that is, the darkness, was turned into morning, that is, into day. But once day had come, night took hold again, and this is the darkening of day into night. So the Prophet helps those who have gone astray by showing that the God who is God by nature and in truth is not lifeless matter. Nor is he on a level with the golden heifers, or like any of the gods invented by human skill. Rather, he is King and Lawgiver of the spirits above and likewise of those on earth, Master of the elements, who bends the nature of things to his good pleasure. For this reason, and quite rightly, he says that the name that befits him is "the Lord God Almighty." Since he is these things by nature and in truth, he apportions ruin upon strength and brings misery upon the stronghold. He lays hold of the proud, he says, and deals out crushing blows to those who shake off his yoke. And if anyone in his folly perhaps imagines that he is strong and great, on him too he brings misery. This was a subtle hint that if they chose to be careless, to remain in their guilt of arrogance, and to think highly of themselves, they would fall into utter misery and in the end be justly shattered by the hand of the One who rules all. "For the Lord," it says, "opposes the proud," as it is written. He regards the boastful, the disobedient and the intractable as his enemies, but he looks "upon the one who is humble and quiet and trembles at" his "words." This is a good thing, and truly worth striving for, at least for those who have chosen to live in the best way.
They hated the one who reproves in the gates, and they abhorred a holy word.

Once again the discourse keeps to its proper sequence. The inspired Prophet had called God almighty and all-powerful, and had added that "he apportions ruin upon strength and brings misery upon the stronghold." Now, of necessity, he lists the charges and brings into the open the reasons why he deals out ruin and misery to some. Otherwise someone might think that God pours out his wrath excessively on those who sin only a little. They hated, he says, those who corrected them. They set at nought those who reproved them and who were accustomed to set them right toward what pleases God. They counted as abominable every holy word, meaning one that calls and spurs them on to holiness and sanctification. You should understand "in the gates" to mean clearly, openly and boldly. He seems here to be recalling their senseless contempt for the prophets and the law, and their turning away from them. The prophets reproved them, coming to them without concealment. And the law was a holy word, because it is a guide to God and to righteousness, a tutor leading to godliness, and it points to the One who is God by nature and in truth. That is why the blessed Paul too called the commandment given through Moses "holy and just and good." So the most shameful of diseases is to shake off advice, to hate reproof and to pretend not even to know the divine law. It is, as it were, the root and source of the passions in the soul. Whoever has sunk to this level of wickedness will surely be like a ship without rudders and with no one at the helm. Such a ship is carried about by every wind and rushes heedlessly wherever it is driven, staggering almost as if drunk, until it becomes a plaything of the waves. But our wise David calls the righteous man blessed, saying, "The law of his God is in his heart, and his steps will not slip"; for the law sets a person straight toward what pleases God.
Therefore, because they struck the heads of the poor with their fists, and
you accepted choice gifts from them, you have built houses of hewn stone, but you shall not live in them; and you have planted desirable vineyards, but you shall not drink their wine.

It is true that to hold back from what is good is, in every case and without exception, the origin of wickedness. Turning away from what is useful and naturally beneficial makes us stumble, almost of necessity, into what is not. Just as darkness follows immediately on the track and at the heels of light once the light has been driven away, so the departure of virtue is followed by the inrush of wickedness. Since, then, they hated "the one who reproves in the gates" and "abhorred a holy word," they slid down into sin of many kinds and turned to greed. They practised oppression, which God hates above all, and struck "the lowly with their fists" and beat the heads of the poor. These were no doubt the powerful, who surpassed everyone else in glory and wealth. They plundered under the name of gifts, taking from unwilling people the most valuable things they owned. Yet he usefully shows that greed brings no profit to those accustomed to do such things. Being overcome by shameful gain ends in grief, and its outcome is punishment. They will not enjoy the houses they built with such zeal and lavish care. Their labour in the fields will be in vain. Their enjoyment of the things they loved will vanish in an unexpected way, though these were the things for whose sake their greed arose and the passion of avarice crept in. How, then, could the attitude that one must be greedy fail to appear futile and profitless to anyone? It is wise, then, to bear in mind what the author of Proverbs says: "Better a small income with righteousness than abundant produce with injustice." Paul too calls greed idolatry, and quite rightly. The thing is in fact godlessness. Those who trample on the law of love toward their brothers, which is also the fulfilment of the law, are placed on a level with those who have not acknowledged the One who is God by nature. Whoever does not know the law denies the Lawgiver. Christ himself also made us more self-controlled and raised us above unjust love of money when he said, "For what will a man profit if he gains the whole world but forfeits his soul? Or what will a man give in exchange for his soul?" "For treasures will not profit the lawless," as it is written, "but righteousness will deliver from death."

For I know your many impieties, and your sins are mighty. You trample the righteous, take payoffs, and turn aside the poor in the gates. Therefore the one who understands will keep silent at that time, for it is an evil time.

He is trying to teach that God does not punish offenders for small faults or for just any transgressions. Rather, he bears patiently with moderate failings, and only in the end moves against unbridled inclinations toward wickedness. He says that the people in Samaria will lose their houses, and their vineyards too, and, I think, everything that can gladden them and keep them in prosperity. Their sins had become terrible and great and no longer bearable. They oppressed the righteous. This means either, perhaps, a righteous man, or else that, intent on unholiness, they saw fit to care little for right and just judgment. This is a kind of oppression, a greedy and reckless overriding of what the law ordains. They also took payoffs, that is, returns and rewards for unjust judgments, and besides this they turned aside the poor in the gates. What does this mean? He may mean that they treated as people to be shunned those who urged them to be moderate and gave them open counsel about this. Or he may mean that they dared to pervert justice for the poor, and not in secret. Far from it! They did not try to disguise their impiety cleverly, but did it as if in the gates, that is, openly and in the sight of many. They no longer blushed at all, and they showed no reverence for the divine law. They had already dragged the times down to such a depth of wickedness and evil that even the wise, and those able to understand how affairs are managed, thought it better neither to reprove any longer nor to correct those who had chosen impiety. For those who were reproved had become like people without ears. They leapt like dogs at those who wanted to help them, and treated those who urged them toward what is best as enemies. They rebuked the holy prophets, and saw to it that they suffered troubles whenever they came forward to deliver the words from above. Indeed, when the prophet Jeremiah announced the message from God, Zedekiah at one time put him in chains, and at another had him let down into a cistern, wanting to drown him in the mire at its bottom.

So it is necessary to repent while our faults are still small, and not to provoke God by adding greater ones, almost forcing him to act against his will. If sins become mighty and very many, then he will certainly repay them and bring the flames of his indignation upon us. By mighty sins we mean those that are terrible and unbearable, for "not every sin leads to death," in the most wise words of John. Yet no sin can overcome the love for humanity of God, to whom be glory for ever. Amen.
BY THE SAME AUTHOR, ON THE SAME PROPHET: THIRD VOLUME.

Seek what is good and not what is evil, so that you may live; and so the Lord God Almighty will be with you, just as you have said, "We have hated what is evil and loved what is good." And restore justice in the gates, so that the Lord God Almighty may have mercy on the remnant of Joseph.

I have said many times already that there was not one captivity but several, at different times and in stages. Pul the Assyrian came first into Samaria, uprooted the two tribes beyond the Jordan and the cities there, and went away. After him Shalmaneser, though he did not take all of Samaria, carried off a part of it to his own land along with the captives. God did this by his providential ordering, disciplining Israel, which had turned aside, "with pain and the scourge," and moving them toward thinking and doing what was better and more fitting. It came about, then, that those who had managed to escape the wars we have just described, now somehow changing their minds, repented of the things in which they had been deceived. They recognized and confessed that the effects of divine wrath had been brought upon them because they had committed many grievous sins, and then they all but promised God to amend their ways, saying, "We have hated what is evil and loved what is good." "So then, just as you have said," he says, "seek what is good and not what is evil, so that you may gain well-being, living and being kept safe, and so that the Lord God, who has authority over all things, may be with you." And restore justice in the gates, that is, be upright judges: do not record an unjust verdict against the weaker, do not falsify the cause of the righteous, do not strike the poor with your fist, do not turn aside the way of the lowly, so that God may then have mercy on those of Joseph who were left after the captivities that had already taken place. Here again he means Ephraim, that is, the ten tribes. For as I said before, since Ephraim was descended from Joseph, he is designated by his father's name.

We must therefore think rightly and set our own minds straight, so as to think what pleases God, to achieve virtue, to hold fast to the ways of righteousness, and to be wise guardians of uprightness. For in this way we shall have the God of all with us and fighting for us.

Therefore thus says the Lord God Almighty: In every square there will be lamentation, and in every street they will say, "Woe, woe!" The farmer will be summoned to mourning and lamentation, and to those who know how to wail; and in every road there will be lamentation, because I will pass through your midst, says the Lord.

"Having tasted the evils of war," he says, "and having been grieved not a little by what had already happened, you promised to hate what is evil and to love what is good. But no sooner were you barely and briefly freed from the terrors of that time than you slid back into carelessness, and you were plainly no less attached to your old evils. For this reason, then, the cities will be full of wailing and lamentation, there will be beating of breasts and tears everywhere, and people will go looking for those who know how to mourn. And since the townspeople will not be enough for you for this, the farmer too will be brought in, to sound a country song for you and to bewail the misfortunes of the fallen in the rhythms of the countryside." For "I will pass through your midst," he says, meaning that he now looks upon their sins and no longer stands far off from those who have committed intolerable impieties. For as long as God does not yet discipline, he seems in a way not even to be present; but when he brings on the effects of his wrath, he is all but there in person and hurls down the punishments. So too angels came to Sodom to burn up the ungodly, as though they had stood apart for as long as there was no punishing. Thus "I will pass through your midst" signifies visitation, and the arrival of the time when punishment must fall.

Woe to those who long for the day of the Lord! Why should this day of the Lord be yours? It is darkness and not light. It is as when a man flees from a lion and a bear falls upon him; and he dashes into his house and leans his hands against the wall, and a snake bites him. Is not the day of the Lord darkness and not light, and gloom with no brightness in it?

When the holy prophets foretold to them what was to come, and that they would fall into bitter and incurable misfortunes, they, having turned without restraint to the works of error, laughed and grew insolent. At times they said that the prophecies would be postponed to some distant time; at other times, utterly dismissive, they dared to say, in the words of Jeremiah, "Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come!" For they thought that the prophets were lying and filling them with empty fears; or that even if some war really did come against them, they would prove stronger than the enemy's hand, opposing it with a hard and formidable strength and zeal. For it is true, as it is written, that "when the ungodly man comes into the depth of evils, he becomes contemptuous." But people of such a disposition, like wounds past hope, all but cry out that they need fire and the knife, and they are in desire of such things. For in a way they thirst for punishment, even if they do not actually say so.

"Woe, then," he says, "to those who desire and await nothing other than the day of punishment." He calls it the Lord's day as well, because it is brought on by God. "Why, then," he says, "should it be yours, when it is darkness and not light, filled as it is with the greatest calamity?" For no one, he says, could slip out of it, nor could anyone get clear of the evil; rather, whoever escapes the one will be caught by the other, and the second will meet those who have evaded the first. This is what it means to escape from the mouth of a lion and fall upon a bear. And even if someone should think, he says, that he has perhaps reached safety and has rushed into his house, he will meet death there, falling unexpectedly victim to a snake's bite. For when God drives someone into destruction and suffering, who will save him? Who will help him and free him from the penalty? Or what way could there be by which someone might pass through and get clear of the evils? None at all. For, as it is written, "Who will turn back the uplifted hand?" and "If he shuts a man in, who will open?"

I have hated, I have rejected your feasts, and I will take no pleasure in the smell of your festal assemblies. For even if you bring me your whole burnt offerings and sacrifices, I will not accept them, and I will not look upon your appearances with peace offerings.

This saying would fit those of Judah and Benjamin above all. For the tribes in Samaria, wholly given over to the worship of idols, were found to be very careless and to have badly neglected the laws given through Moses. But those in Jerusalem, while they sacrificed to Baal on the high places and poured libations to the host of heaven, also pretended to care about showing reverence for the law and to be eager to carry out sacrifices and feasts. But that the Creator of all hated these things he made plain through the voice of Isaiah as well, saying: "Hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom; give heed to the law of God, you people of Gomorrah. What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me? says the Lord. I am full of burnt offerings of rams, and I do not want the fat of lambs and the blood of bulls and goats, not even if you come to appear before me; for who has required these things from your hands? You shall no longer trample my court. If you bring fine flour, it is futile; incense is an abomination to me. Your new moons and sabbaths and the great day I cannot endure; your fasting and idleness and your feasts my soul hates. You have become a surfeit to me." We say that the present passage depends on this sense. For he says, "I have hated and rejected your feasts, and I would not approve your sacrifices, nor would I ever count your whole burnt offerings and your presentations for peace offerings as a fragrant aroma." These are kinds of sacrifices, distinguished by their occasions and each having its own form. For the whole burnt offering is one thing, the sacrifice another, and the appearance with the peace offering another, that is, coming into the sight of God and bringing the sacrifices for the peace offering.

But while what we have just said would rightly apply to the Jews, who practiced the utmost impiety, God accepts, very gladly, and welcomes the sacrifices of those who are in the faith: the spiritual whole burnt offering, the appearances at the feasts. For the sweet fragrance we give off is not our own, but that of him who is in us through the Spirit, I mean Christ. The rejection of sacrifice would also fit, and very rightly, the unholy heretics, who cannot say, as those genuine in faith can, "We are the fragrance of Christ to God." For their odor is in Beelzebul, if indeed it is true that "no one says 'Jesus is accursed' except in Beelzebul." Blaspheming recklessly, the wretches, and slandering the glory of the Only-begotten, they carry about a mind drunk not with spiritual fragrance but rather with filth.
Take away from me the noise of your songs, and I will not listen to the psalm of your instruments. And judgment will roll on like water, and righteousness like an impassable torrent.

Along with the feasts and the useless sacrifices, God dismisses the praises made with instruments. He does not assign to lifeless materials the duty of glorifying him, but rather transfers the share in so splendid an honor to those who raise their voices from a pure mind; for such praise is beautiful and pleasing to the Master of all. And he does very well to call the Jews' praises, devised from who knows where (the instrumental ones, as I just said), a "noise of songs": a superfluous and idle sound, as it were, giving out a melody without meaning and without force. That these too were inventions of Jewish folly he showed by saying "the psalm of your instruments"; he all but says, "Not mine," for the practice lies outside the law, and Moses said nothing about such things. "So," he says, "I will not be appeased, nor will you ward off the charges with the pleasant sounds of instruments. Rather, my judgment will roll on like water, and the righteousness that comes from me," that is, the just sentence now passed against you, "will be like an impassable torrent," sweeping away whatever lies in its path and sparing nothing. For torrents burst violently down from the mountains. So too the divine verdict, if it should come against anyone, will be irresistible water and an unopposable torrent [?], and nothing else.

Everywhere, then, repentance proves useful and necessary, as does warding off wrath by turning back to what is better: not sending up to God a wholly useless and indistinct sound, but from a good mind singing out a song that is truly wise and well measured. For he says, "Offer a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High; and call upon me in the day of your affliction, and I will deliver you, and you will glorify me."

Did you offer me slaughtered victims and sacrifices for forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel? says the Lord. And you took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Raiphan, their images, which you made for yourselves. And I will deport you beyond Damascus, says the Lord; the Lord God Almighty is his name.

In the passage just interpreted, it was God who said to those of Israel's blood: "I have hated, I have rejected your feasts, and I will take no pleasure in the smell of your festal assemblies. For even if you bring me your whole burnt offerings and sacrifices, I will not accept them, and I will not look upon your appearances with peace offerings." He wished to make it plain that he had saved Israel out of his own gentleness, granting mercy to the children in memory of their fathers, and not treating the matter as repayment for sacrifices or, as it were, as wages. So he must point out that they spent no few years in the wilderness. The manna was their food; they journeyed with a cloud overshadowing them by day and a pillar of fire by night. The ark led the way as a figure of God, going before them and searching out a place of rest for them. And they lacked none of the necessities, for water burst forth for them unexpectedly and their enemies fell. While all this was happening, they received the laws about the sacrifices, but everywhere, and perhaps with each of the ordinances, they heard, "When the Lord your God brings you into the land that he swore to your fathers to give you," you shall do this and that, and you shall also offer sacrifices. So during the forty years in which they were in the wilderness they offered sacrifices of their own accord, but none was required of necessity; rather, the matter was put off for them until they should enter the land promised to their fathers. That is why he says, "Did you offer me slaughtered victims and sacrifices in the wilderness for forty years, O house of Israel? says the Lord." Yet they were kept safe then even without sacrifices, as he says again through another prophet: "No incense bought with silver was for me, no sheep of your whole burnt offering was for me, nor did I weary you with frankincense." But they, with no excuse for their apostasy, were fickle in those days, and dishonoring the one who is God by nature and in truth, they took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Raiphan. What this means we must now examine.

Now the divine Moses had gone up the mountain to receive the law, but those of Israel's [?] blood rose up against Aaron, saying, "Make us gods who will go before us; for as for this Moses, the man who brought us out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him." So they made a calf in the wilderness. The calf was the visible idol, common, as it were, to all; but many other things were also done by each individually. For having once turned back to their old error and leapt away from piety toward God, each one made whatever object of worship he saw fit and fashioned it for himself, according to the custom they had long kept in Egypt; and they were especially devoted to the worship of the stars. "And how could this be made evident?" someone may ask. It takes little effort for those who wish to prove it, for we shall learn it from the sacred writings themselves.

The divine Moses was indignant and cried out against Aaron, and then fell down before God, saying, "I beseech you, Lord: this people has sinned a great sin, for they have made for themselves gods of gold," even though what had been fashioned was a calf. But he was well aware that others had made carved images as well. And the blessed Stephen, when he was once accused before the leaders of the Jews of blasphemies against God and Moses, repelled the slanders with a fitting defense, and then went on to show that in their savage impiety and their outrages against Christ they were imitating the wickedness and hardness of heart of their own fathers. He clearly recalls the making of the calf in the wilderness, and says of the all-wise Moses: "This is the one who was in the assembly in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai, and with our fathers; who received living oracles to give to us. Our fathers would not obey him, but thrust him aside and in their hearts turned back to Egypt, saying to Aaron, 'Make us gods who will go before us; for as for this Moses who brought us out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.' And they made a calf in the wilderness in those days, and offered sacrifice to the idol, and rejoiced in the works of their hands. But God turned away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: 'Did you offer me slaughtered victims and sacrifices in the wilderness for forty years, O house of Israel? says the Lord. And you took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Raiphan, the images that you made in order to worship them; and I will deport you beyond Babylon.'" Observe, then, that the divine Stephen too, a man full of the Holy Spirit, has testified that they made a calf and also turned to the worship of the host of heaven; and he recalls the Prophet's words as well. From this we can understand that besides the calf they also took up the tent of Moloch. For they made a tent and set up an idol in it, and called it Moloch, or Molchom. This was an idol of the Moabites, which had a translucent and remarkable stone at the very top of its forehead, as a figure of the morning star. Moloch is interpreted "their king," for that is how Aquila and Theodotion rendered it; but what was fashioned was an image of the morning star. "You took up, then," he says, "the tent of Moloch," that is, of your king. And who was this king? "The star of your god Raiphan." Raiphan is interpreted "darkening" or "blinding." They worshiped the morning star because it rises before the sun's brilliance and brings the beginning of day to those on earth; but to those who worshiped it, it became Raiphan, that is, darkening or blinding. This is not at all because the star itself worked blindness in them, but because their worship of it became for them the cause of darkening. "And since," he says, "you have emulated the madness of the Moabites and of neighboring Damascus, for this reason you will go off beyond Damascus, and to those who lie still farther away," I mean the Babylonians. For the version of the Seventy says "beyond Damascus," whereas the divine Stephen said "Babylon." What, then, shall we say to this? The blessed Stephen spoke according to the version of the Hebrews. For it seems that among them the land of the Babylonians is what is called "beyond Damascus." Since the kingdom of the Damascenes, that is, of the Syrians, perhaps stretched as far as the borders of the cities toward the dawn and the sunrise, the region and land of the Babylonians lay immediately next to it.
Woe to those who despise Zion, and to those who trust in the mountain of Samaria!

Here again the word pronounces wretched not only those of Ephraim, that is, the tribes in Samaria, but also those of Judah and Benjamin. Having first shown that those who came before them had an unsound and ever-wavering mind (for they made a calf and took up the tent of Moloch), he now proves that they take after their fathers, and that by following in the footsteps of their ancestors' impiety they provoke the Master of all against themselves. He says that those of Judah and Benjamin despise Zion. For though they remained in Jerusalem and had the divine temple, they made nothing of reverence and love for God, but, as the sacred scripture says, "They burned incense on the high places, under oak and poplar and every shady tree." They also worshiped the host of heaven. Indeed, the God of all, grieved not a little, said to Jeremiah: "As for you, do not pray for this people, and do not ask that they be shown mercy, and do not come to me about them with petition and prayer, for I will not listen to you." Then he adds the reason for turning away from them, saying: "Or do you not see what these people are doing in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem? Their sons gather wood, and their fathers kindle the fire, and their women knead dough to make cakes for the host of heaven; and they have poured out libations to foreign gods to provoke me to anger." So those in Jerusalem despised Zion. Fittingly, therefore, he brought the woe upon them.

Such a saying would also fit those who trust in the mountain of Samaria, that is, those who lived in Samaria and trusted in themselves. For they thought that even without God they would get the better of their enemies, would be well established in prosperity, and that every one of their pleasures would rest on an unshakable foundation.

It is bitter, then, and truly something to pray against, to slide so far into folly as to dare to make nothing of love for God, to be devoted to wrongdoing and to do what is unlawful, and to grieve him, while thinking that any good thing will be ours without his giving it. For "every good gift and every perfect present is from above, coming down from the Father of lights." It is good, therefore, to cleave to him and to make him our hope and our helper. Those too despise Zion, that is, the Church, who stand at the head of unholy doctrines, who have grown bold in their own eloquence and are accustomed to pride themselves on the inventions of their unholy syllogisms and on worldly wisdom. The woe would fit them even before all the others.

They have gathered in the harvest of the firstfruits of the nations, and they themselves have entered in. O house of Israel, cross over, all of you, and see, and go from there to Hamath the Great, and go down to Gath of the Philistines, the strongest of all these kingdoms, and see whether their borders are greater than your borders.

He shows that they are ungrateful and have chosen to forget his generosity. Yet they ought always to give him the fullest possible thanks and to raise songs of gratitude, because he not only rescued them, against all expectation, when they were weighed down under a harsh and unbearable slavery, but also brought them into the land that he swore to their fathers. And he brought them in after cutting down many nations that were hard to defeat and well practiced in winning battles. So blessed David too says somewhere to God about those of Israel's blood: "You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out nations and planted it." So they are reproached, and very rightly, as thoroughly ungrateful, grieving their Benefactor by running off into every kind of outrage. For they gleaned, he says, the first of the nations, and made those nations' land their own inheritance, while God shook down those who opposed them and with unspeakable power broke the strength of those who rose against them. But they had inherited a rich land, good for pasture, drunk with every good thing, better and wider than other countries. He commands them to learn this by inquiring into the domains, or kingdoms, of their neighbors and of those still farther off. "Go," he says, "to Hamath Rabbah and to Gath of the foreigners"; for these were the kingdoms with the most conspicuous glory. "And there inquire," he says, "whether their borders are greater than your borders." Now there were many kingdoms of the nations, each in its own region: that of the Moabites, that of the Idumeans, that of the sons of Ammon. But there was nothing great about them. Those of the Damascenes and the Palestinians were more brilliant than the rest. There were two cities under the kingdom of Damascus, lying to the east, that bore the name Hamath. One of them was wider and greater, and the other was the lesser. "Rabbah" means "greater" or "broader." Go, then, to Hamath Rabbah, that is, to the greater and wider Hamath; for, as I said, it shared its name with another city, and was the greater of the two. They say that this broad Hamath is the present Antioch, and that the lesser and narrower one is its neighbor on the border, Epiphania; for Antiochus surnamed Epiphanes named the one Antioch and the other Epiphania to his own glory. Gath was at that time the most brilliant city of what is now Palestine. In it remained the Anakim and those called the Philistines, since the sons of Israel did not destroy them at that time. That is why he says of it, "to Gath of the foreigners." Go, then, he says, to Hamath Rabbah and to Gath of the foreigners, and examine closely whether it is not rather you who inhabit the wider country, better and more excellent than all others.

One must also know that the Hebrew text puts Calneh first [?]. For it says, "Go to Calneh and to Hamath and to Gath." Calneh is under the kingdom of the Persians and is now called Lysippon. And since the Hebrew edition also mentions the kingdom of the Persians, we say that this is why blessed Stephen, instead of "I will deport you beyond Damascus," said "beyond Babylon."

So the charge against those of Israel is ingratitude. They had inherited a land so rich, so good for tillage and so broad, yet they did not rather offer their thanks to God. Instead some despised Zion, and others, trusting in the mountain of Samaria, took no account of the reverence owed to him.

The words "Go to Hamath Rabbah and to Gath of the foreigners, and see whether their borders are greater than your borders" are useful too, it seems, for those who after coming to faith have admired the wisdom of the Greeks so much as to think their opinions better than ours, and for those who are inclined to seek out and attach themselves to people who counterfeit the truth and undermine the correctness of the Church's doctrines. For the divinely inspired Scripture is wider than the narrow chatter of the Greeks. It proclaims the light of truth, brings in the knowledge of beneficial doctrines, and lifts the minds of believers up to everything that deserves praise.

Again, the teaching about the truth is broader than the narrowness of the heretics. Those who fight against it all but drown as they float on cold and murky reasonings. But those who speak in defense of the doctrines of piety and gaze around at the shining beauty of the truth run out into a broad sea of contemplation, "taking every thought captive to the obedience of Christ." They dart this way and that, and gather very skillfully from the inspired Scripture whatever leads to true knowledge. So when the Corinthians chose to depart from "the holy commandment delivered to them" and foolishly attached themselves to those who were in the habit of teaching other doctrines, the divine Paul writes to them: "Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians; our heart is opened wide. You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections. In return, and I speak as to children, open wide your hearts too. Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers."
Woe to those who long for the evil day, who draw near and lay hold of false sabbaths.

He had said, "Woe to those who despise Zion, and to those who trust in the mountain of Samaria." Since he mentioned two groups, I mean those who despise Zion and those who trust in the mountain of Samaria, we had to examine the meaning of these ideas, and we applied the charge of despising Zion to those of Judah and Benjamin, and that of trusting in the mountain of Samaria to those of Ephraim. Now the discourse goes back, as it were, and lists the charges against both again, bringing the woe upon them. It is the custom of divine Scripture to put the word "woe" with the nominative case, for example: "Woe, those who desire the day of the Lord," and again, "Woe, those who rise early in the morning and pursue strong drink." Woe, then, he says, to those who long for the evil day, that is, to those in Jerusalem. For to refuse to repent, and to refuse to take in the fear of what had been foretold, is practically to desire to fall into the day of destruction. It is as if someone were to say of a person fond of sin, "He wants to die." Of course that person does not wish to suffer this. How could he? But insofar as he has come to want to do, and to do unceasingly, things at odds with the laws, he all but loves the punishment and penalty that are always somehow owed to lovers of sin. So by refusing to repent they all but desire to fall into the evil day and to be caught in the calamities already foretold, they who draw near and lay hold of false sabbaths. For the temple was still standing, and the altars in it. They offered God the sacrifices prescribed by the law, and they kept the rest on the sabbaths, but not at all strictly. They did it very carelessly and quite lazily. Indeed, he accused them through the voice of the prophets of not having kept the sabbaths. Woe, then, he says, to those who pretend to draw near to God by pretending still to honor the ordinances of Moses, and who lay hold of false sabbaths. Do you see how he has denounced them for not keeping the rest proper to sabbath observance rightly or attentively?

There is another way to take it, for I think something more essential must also be said on this. The sabbaths among the Jews are false, since the law is a shadow and the things given through Moses are, in truth, a type. A type is not the truth; it rather offers an outline of the truth. That is why the divine Paul writes to the Hebrews and says about the people of old, "So then, a sabbath rest remains for the people of God." For Joshua did not give them rest, and they did not enter God's rest. But we keep the sabbath spiritually in Christ, ceasing from sin and departing from it, and leaving off every perishable and earthly concern. For as blessed Paul writes, "Whoever has entered his rest has also rested from all his works, just as God did from his own."

Those who sleep on beds of ivory and live in luxury on their couches, and eat kids from the flocks and suckling calves from the midst of the herd; who clap along to the sound of the instruments, who reckoned these things as lasting and not as fleeting; who drink strained wine and anoint themselves with the finest perfumes, and were not grieved at the ruin of Joseph.

Again, woe in common to those who sleep on beds of ivory and are in the habit of doing this and that. He strongly accuses those in Samaria who were most prominent in reputation and raised above the rest by abundant wealth. They were all but drunk from their excessive prosperity and so carried away by the extent of their luxury that they did not see [?] any of the dangers at all, nor did they think that the God of all would ever be provoked against people of that kind and bring punishment on lovers of sin. He describes precisely their slackness and their abandonment to luxury. They had, he says, beds of ivory and costly, soft couches; choice lambs and suckling calves for food; songs and melodies, and everything that goes with luxury by way of instruments; revels and applause; and, worse still, they reckoned such evils as lasting and not as fleeting. For such things always fly past, and worldly deception has no stability. It dissolves like a shadow, and "the form of this world is passing away," as it is written; and luxury ends altogether with the dead. In the case of those in Samaria, though, the sense of these words might also be understood another way. Since they were about to be captured, and before long, he calls the things they had devised for their luxury, perishable as they were, fleeting and not lasting, since they were on the point of passing away. So they clap to the instruments, drinking wine with a fine bouquet, perhaps, very carefully strained; they anoint themselves with perfume, blending the choicest ingredients; and they took no account whatever of the fact that Joseph was about to be crushed. For, as I said just now, although they knew in advance of the calamity that was all but upon them, the capture of Samaria, and the ruin that would come on the descendants of Joseph, they did not give up their accustomed luxury.

It is truly a terrible thing for those whose lot is to rule over countries or cities or peoples to be overcome by bodily luxury. They ought rather to practice the sobriety their office requires and look carefully to what is beneficial, to steer those under them straight toward what is fitting, and to appease God by every means when he has been grieved. How, then, is it not utter madness to slide into luxury and to regard nothing as better than profane love of the flesh? It is perhaps of such people that he says through the voice of the saints, "O shepherds who scatter and destroy the sheep of the pasture!" That the flock will be endangered by the negligence of the shepherds becomes clear when God again says plainly, "For the shepherds have acted foolishly and have not sought the Lord; therefore the whole flock has not understood, and they have been scattered."
Therefore they shall now go into captivity at the head of the mighty, and the neighing of horses shall be taken away from Ephraim.

For since, he says, they have lived in luxury and abandoned their love for God, and have also trusted in the mountain of Samaria (that is, the leaders put on airs over those in Samaria, as if they commanded a countless multitude and had a warrior people beyond number), for this reason, he says, the time of captivity will come upon all of them. It will surely come, and very swiftly, but it will take the more powerful as its first spoils. For when enemies sack a city they always run to the houses of the more distinguished to plunder what is in them.

The notables in Samaria were in the habit of riding choice horses, and these, as one would expect, went through the middle of the broad streets, neighing in an intelligent, clever way, as if they had been trained to it; for the animal is always ready, somehow, to learn good order and to take in the skill that suits it. This too, he says, will cease. For the neighing will be taken away from the horses of Ephraim. It is as if he said: The arrogance of the elite in Samaria will cease, and they will stop, even against their will, making splendid processions, with the horses beneath them neighing. These horses, decked out in bright trappings, perhaps even recognize their rider, and all but snort with pride at carrying a rider so revered and admired. But you can learn from this, too, that sobriety is safe for leaders, while a fondness for being puffed up does them harm. For the effects of wrath will fall on them before all others. They will be driven from all their glory, and they too will lie fallen along with the rest, under a bitter and grievous sentence; and they will have to answer for having not only destroyed themselves but also drawn others into their own lawlessness.
For the Lord has sworn by himself: "Because I abhor all the insolence of Jacob, and I have hated his lands."

He shows that the wrath cannot be changed by showing that God has sworn that he hates the insolence of Jacob. We certainly do not say that the divine word is here denouncing our forefather Jacob. It would be utterly foolish to understand it that way, since God both loved Jacob from the womb and chose him while he was still an unborn child. Here again "Jacob" means those descended from Jacob, whose accursed arrogance he says he has hated; for divine Scripture habitually calls haughtiness "insolence." Is it not, after all, haughtiness to push aside reverence for God, to give to idols the glory that belongs above all to him, and besides this not even to deign to listen to what he chooses to make known through the holy prophets, but to treat his threat as a plaything, and, emboldened by a multitude of allies, to disregard completely his forbearance and help? How then can this be in doubt?

So the Lord of all, he says, has sworn by himself, and by himself because "he had no one greater by whom to swear." And what did he swear? "I abhor all the insolence of Jacob," that is, the haughtiness of Jacob, "and I have hated all his lands." For there was no one in them who fulfilled the divine will, no one who offered him reverence and was distinguished by the glories of righteousness. God would not have turned away if there had been some among them, even a handful, who cared about pleasing him. Indeed he said through the voice of Jeremiah, "Run through the streets of Jerusalem, and look, and search in her squares, to see whether you can find a man, whether there is one who does justice and loves faithfulness, and I will be merciful to her, says the Lord." But since the lands of Jacob had come to be without any good and God-loving man, they were given over to desolation, and the cities perished together with their inhabitants. Great, then, is the need for saints. For they save cities and deliver lands from impending calamity. By the brightness of their lives they check the wrath, boiling though it is, and bring it to slacken, and they rein in, as it were, the movements of divine anger as they rush upon people.

And I will take away a city with all who dwell in it. And if ten men are left in one house, they too shall die. And the remnant shall be left, and their kinsmen shall take them and force themselves to carry their bones out of the house. And he shall say to those in charge of the house, "Is there still anyone with you?" And he shall say, "No one any more." And he shall say, "Hush, so as not to name the name of the Lord."

For since he has hated their lands and loathes all the insolence of Jacob, that is, their boastfulness, he says for this reason that their cities will perish together with all their people. He explains in detail how each thing will happen to those who have committed those offenses. "For I will take away," he says, "whatever city I wish, and remove it, as it were, from the midst, together with its inhabitants. And even if some ten members of one household should happen to escape the enemies' sword and slip into hiding places in the innermost parts of the house, they will die, afraid perhaps to peep out even a little from the hiding places they are in."

Famine, then, he says, will take over from the hand of the one who strikes, and will kill those in hiding. When the enemies have withdrawn, some of their kin, by blood or by affection, will come "and force themselves to carry out their bones." Whom will they have to force as they gather up the remains of the dead? Themselves, obviously. For it is truly burdensome and hard to bear to handle bodies already decaying and rotten, and I think those who venture such a task would need a nose with no nostrils, since nothing could be worse than so dreadful a stench. So they will force themselves, showing compassion to the departed who perished from famine by thinking them worthy of burial and a shroud. Those who do this, he says, will then ask the one who knows the house whether there might be anyone else besides them, either perhaps still alive and lying hidden in the recesses, or already dead and stinking. And he answers, "No one any more." This is nothing other than clear proof of complete desolation.
But if those in charge of the house say this, he says, they will hear in reply from the one asking the question, "Hush, so as not to name the name of the Lord."

What this means must be considered. Some think and say that when those in charge of the house are about to swear, the questioners silence them so that they will not swear by the name of the Lord. And they add that the minds of those of Ephraim had slid into such utter hatred of God that they would not even put up with anyone who chose to name the God of all. But I think such an explanation is quite unsound and inelegant. That those of Ephraim had turned away completely from love for God, no one would doubt. But once they had come under blows and the scourge, they would surely have been more likely to be somewhat afraid and to turn at last to wanting what was more needful, rather than, on the contrary, growing so savagely bold against piety toward God. And I might add this to what has been said: what need was there for those in charge of the house, when asked whether anyone was hidden with them, perhaps still alive or already dead, to add an oath that no one was with them any longer?

What, then, does "he will say, Hush, so as not to name the name of the Lord" mean? We say that those of Israel's blood were accustomed to call reviling and blasphemy against God by this expression, which has its origin in the commandments of the law. For it is written in Leviticus that two men fought with each other in the assembly, and then one of the combatants, the son of the Egyptian woman, blasphemed, and he died by stoning. God immediately laid down a law about this, saying, "Whoever curses his God shall bear his sin; and whoever names the name of the Lord shall surely be put to death." So "to name the name of the Lord" means to blaspheme, expressed in the sacred writings in reverent words. Many people, when they are in grief, are in the habit of sometimes hurling ill-omened words against God. So when the one in charge of the house reports that there is no longer anyone with him, having suffered something of that incurable calamity, the other, he says, will stop his mouth so that he does not name the name of the Lord, that is, so that he does not say anything ill-omened against God. This shows that he did not bring the scourge on them at random, and that he punishes not in vain but for a useful and necessary purpose. For it is possible, and quite easy, to see from what happened that the blow suffered by the victims turned those still living and left behind to reverence, and made them afraid to offend God any further, even by grieving him with mere words, although long before they had been accustomed to do even this without restraint, and to add to their words outrages in their very deeds. So it is far better for those who are truly good and sensible to go in pursuit of what is beneficial before the blow and the scourge, and to forestall the experience of the movements of wrath by departing from wickedness and choosing to accomplish what truly pleases the all-holy God.
For behold, the Lord commands, and he will strike the great house with shattering and the small house with cracks.

He clearly threatened that cities would be captured, or rather destroyed, together with their inhabitants. And he makes it very plain that the thing comes from God and will not happen by chance, by saying that he gives the command to those able to lay waste, and that they readily do whatever the divine anger decrees. By the great house and the small one he perhaps means Ephraim and Judah. For Ephraim was populous, being counted as ten tribes, and so it is also a great house. Judah was smaller, consisting of two; for Judah was in Jerusalem together with the tribe of Benjamin.

It follows that we should understand that what is shattered undergoes a complete collapse, while what is cracked may reasonably be understood as suffering in part. And it happened that the house of Ephraim, that is, Israel, endured complete capture and a disaster of war that was hard to heal, while Judah suffered only in part, as with a small crack. So the judge is just and impartial. He weighs, as he sees fit, the charges against cities or countries, and brings on each, in due proportion, a blow that can do it good. Let us not, then, despise God, knowing the almighty power of his supreme hand; for to understand this is a most excellent thing.
Will horses give chase over rocks? Will they keep quiet among mares? For you have turned judgment into wrath, and the fruit of righteousness into bitterness.

He has said that it was he himself who gave the command to strike "the great house with crushing blows and the small house with breaches," even if this was done through the hand of the Assyrians. Now he again persuades us of this when he says, Will horses give chase over rocks? It is as if he were saying plainly: "The horse is a proud animal, and one of the swiftest of all. But the ground that suits it for running is not rocky and full of mounds; it is bare and smooth. How, then, have the Assyrians overrun you, though you were long a very rugged and, as it were, rocky people, never once trodden down by any enemy? It was God, who had been dishonored, who made the hard and impassable places easy for the invaders to walk and ride over." And just as stallions in heat, he says, would not stop, spurred on by the goads of nature when mares are near and leaping upon them, so the enemies would not rest, but would launch a most fiery and unstoppable attack on those who had acted impiously. And what is the cause of this? You, and no one else. For you have twisted my just judgment concerning you, he says, into wrath; and instead of bearing the fruits of righteousness, you have driven the very source of all your good cheer to anger, committing impieties that deserve bitterness. The God of all had pity on Israel when it suffered in Egypt, but they never stopped provoking him. And this, I think, is what is meant by you have turned judgment into wrath.

Ingratitude, then, is a most terrible charge, and it is punished, and very justly. When we ought rather to be calming him still further with words of praise and gladdening him with voices of thanksgiving, how will it not bring us every kind of evil if we foolishly provoke him?

You who rejoice over no good word, who say, "Have we not gained horns by our own strength?" For behold, I am raising up against you a nation, O house of Israel, and they will crush you so that you cannot enter Hamath, nor reach as far as the torrent of the west.

"You have turned judgment into wrath," he says, "and the fruit of righteousness into bitterness"—you who think so highly of yourselves and raise your brows haughtily against God, you who rejoice in a rotten and senseless word. For you have said that it was not I who supplied the strength that is in you and the power to crush your enemies; instead, you credited your boasts to your own might and dared even to say, Have we not gained horns by our own strength? It was as if they had been caught in the presumption of saying foolishly, "We ourselves hold sway and will overcome our enemies. Even if God should not choose to shield us, we have prevailed, and we ought to pride ourselves on such brilliant achievements, giving God no credit at all." Such a deranged way of thinking and speaking is arrogance and an outrage against God. But the divine David was wise indeed, ascribing the glory to God who rules over all and saying, "For you are the boast of their strength." And again: "Through you we will gore our enemies, and in your name we will bring to nothing those who rise up against us. For I will not trust in my bow, and my sword will not save me." All strength comes from him, and nothing worth hearing of could come from us unless he is with us and leads us. For "the Lord crushes wars," as it is written.

"But since," he says, "you are caught having fallen into such boasting and unbridled talk, behold, I am bringing a nation upon you"—clearly that of the Assyrians—and they will crush you so that you cannot enter Hamath, nor reach as far as the torrent of the west. Hamath is one of the cities to the east, which at that time lay under the kingdom of Damascus; but it has now been renamed, as I said, Antioch, that is, Epiphania. By the torrent of the west he means the river of the Egyptians, since Egypt lies to the west of the land of the Jews. Now the people of Israel were accustomed, whenever a war was about to fall upon them, sometimes to ask for help from Damascus and the Syrians, and sometimes to take refuge in the land of the Egyptians. That is why he says that he is raising up a nation against them, and that they will come in strength and inflict such distress on them that they will no longer be able to enter Hamath or reach the torrent of the west—that is, they will not be able to call on the forces of Damascus or of the Egyptians for help. For "when God shuts, who will open?" as it is written. What way of escape will there be when the Almighty is driving them toward destruction?

Thus the Lord showed me: and behold, a brood of locusts coming in the early morning, and behold, one caterpillar, Gog the king. And it shall be, when it has finished devouring the grass of the land, that I said, "Lord, Lord, be merciful! Who will raise up Jacob? For he is very few." "Repent, O Lord, over this." "And this shall not be," says the Lord.

God reveals to the Prophet what nation will be brought against the people of Israel and what kind of harm will come upon them. He adapts himself to the Prophet's way of life, and teaches him what is going to happen through things he knows well. To shepherds the locust and the caterpillar always seem most terrible, and truly are, for when the grass has been stripped bare by them, the flocks must then perish. So God signifies the calamities of the war to the Prophet as to a shepherd. In the form of a locust he signifies the Assyrian, as in a countless multitude, all but devouring and consuming the land. He calls it early morning, as though it fell like dew and poured down over the land like snowflakes. But there was also, he says, one caterpillar, and this was Gog the king. Then, when God says, And it shall be, when it has finished devouring the grass of the land—that is, when it has devoured and consumed the multitude like a herd, namely the one in Samaria and in the cities of Judea—and was about to add something further, the Prophet interrupts and begs him to cease from his anger, saying, Lord, be merciful! Who will raise up Israel? For he is very few. "For if you mean," he says, "to hand Israel over to the enemies to be devoured in the way I have seen, he will be utterly few." To this God replies, And this shall not be, says the Lord. "I would not relent," he says, "nor give way; I would by no means stop chastening the impious."

We must inquire, then, who this Gog is. We say that the blessed prophet Ezekiel also writes a lament over him, at God's command. We think he is Sennacherib, at the time when, as Rabshakeh was mocking God, "an angel of the Lord went out and struck down in a single night one hundred and eighty-five thousand from the camp of the Assyrians." I must recall what was written about him through the voice of Ezekiel. It runs as follows: "Thus says the Lord, the Lord, to Gog: You are the one of whom I spoke in former days by the hand of my servants the prophets of Israel, in those days and years, that I would bring you against them." Do you hear how he says it is this man, and no other, whom he threatened through the holy prophets to bring against the people of Israel? And that he paid the penalty for his unbridled tongue, and, though he expected to prevail, was unexpectedly destroyed and fell in the land of Israel, he immediately indicates again, saying, "And you, son of man, prophesy against Gog and say: Thus says the Lord, the Lord: Behold, I am against you, Gog, prince of Rosh, Meshech and Tubal. I will gather you and lead you and bring you up from the farthest north, and I will bring you onto the mountains of Israel. I will destroy your bow from your left hand and your arrows from your right hand, and I will throw you down on the mountains of Israel. You will fall, you and all who are with you, and the nations with you will be given to multitudes of birds; I have given you to every bird and to all the beasts of the field to be devoured. You will fall on the face of the field, for I have spoken, says the Lord, the Lord." And after other things, again: "And it shall be on that day that I will give Gog a renowned place, a tomb in Israel, the common grave of those who came against it, near the sea; and they will build a wall around the mouth of the ravine, and there they will bury Gog and all his multitude, and it will then be called the common grave of Gog. And the house of Israel will bury them, so that the land may be cleansed in seven months; all the people of the land will bury them, and it will be a renowned day for them, the day on which I was glorified, says the Lord, the Lord." For when the Assyrians, who are signified by Gog, had fallen, the multitude of Israel presumably buried the dead, so that the unbearable plague of so dreadful a stench might not defile the cities and the countryside.

Thus the Lord showed me: and behold, the Lord called for judgment by fire, and it devoured the great deep, and it devoured the portion. And I said, "Lord, Lord, cease, I pray! Who will raise up Jacob? For he is very few. Repent, O Lord, over this." "And this shall not be," says the Lord.

He has seen Gog, that is, the Assyrian, as a locust and a caterpillar; this same one he names judgment by fire. For it was not enough for the Babylonians to consume Ephraim with the sword; they also set fire to a great many of the cities in Samaria. So the judgment, he says—that is, the punishment by fire—has devoured the great deep, namely Ephraim, called a deep because of its great and countless multitude. And no less has it devoured the small portion, that is, Judah and Benjamin. For after burning no small number of the cities of Judea, the boastful Rabshakeh then laid siege to Jerusalem itself. When the Prophet again pleads and tries to persuade the God of all to repent, that is, to change his mind, the Master of all says, This shall not be. What, then, do we learn from this in turn? That sins beyond all measure fiercely provoke God, even though he knows how to be very long-suffering, and render the prayers of the saints all but ineffective. Indeed, he said to the prophet Jeremiah concerning the people of Israel, "As for you, do not pray for this people, and do not ask that they be shown mercy, and do not come to me on their behalf, for I will not listen to you."

Thus the Lord showed me: and behold, a man standing on a wall of adamant, and in his hand was adamant. And the Lord said to me, "What do you see, Amos?" And I said, "Adamant." And the Lord said to me, "Behold, I am setting adamant in the midst of my people Israel; I will no longer pass him by. And the altars of laughter shall be made to vanish, and the rites of Israel shall be laid waste, and I will rise up against the house of Jeroboam with the sword."

Having shown the Prophet the Assyrian, that is, Gog, as a locust, as a caterpillar, and as judgment by fire, God now shows himself standing on a wall of adamant, so that by this he may be understood as standing, so to speak, on unbreakable power and possessing an unshakable security in his own goods. For the divine is all-powerful and has a firmly fixed foundation, since it knows no change but is beyond alteration, and, as I said, it is always and forever firmly established in its own goods.

He is seen, then, standing on a wall of adamant. Among stones, adamant is unbreakable and invincible: it neither yields to things that are hard and accustomed to resist, nor allows other materials to overpower the strength within it, and it is even, perhaps, accustomed to disregard the full force of fire. Since the one standing on the wall was holding adamant in his hand, he asked the Prophet, What do you see, Amos? And when the Prophet understood and said what it was—for he said, Adamant—he clearly declared that he would set it in the midst of Israel. By adamant you will understand either the Assyrian, as harsh and unbreakable and appointed for this purpose by God—for the Lord of hosts empowers whomever he may choose—or else the unbreakable and all-powerful Word of God, which cannot be turned back empty, that is, be shown to be ineffective. For whatever God utters will certainly run its course to the end, with nothing opposing it. So also our Lord Jesus Christ says, "Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away." He said that he would not pass Israel by, that is, he would exact punishment for the wicked offenses they had committed against him; he would no longer be patient, but would hand them over to those called against them, together with their shrines, altars and idols. For the altars of laughter, he says, shall be made to vanish. The making of any idol is truly a laughingstock, but I think that Baal-Peor might properly and specifically be understood as the laughingstock, because of the very ugliness of its form. He ridicules all idol-making by means of this one, the most shameful of all. So the altars will be torn down, he says, and the rites of Israel will be removed along with them—that is, the toys of idolatry, the profane and loathsome mysteries. And he has plainly declared that Jeroboam, distinguished as he was by the glories of kingship, will go off to destruction together with his own gods. It must be remembered that the one now being spoken of is different from the first: the one was the son of Nebat, the other the son of Joash.

These things, for the present, would fit the account of the history. But the adamant will show us the true one, Christ, the Lord of hosts, whose strength is invincible and unconquerable, who shatters his enemies and defeats those who oppose him, and is broken by no one. He has been set as a chosen stone in the midst of the people. For "he appeared on earth and lived among men." That is why he was called by the voice of the angel "Emmanuel, which means, God with us." For he came to be with us when he became like us. Having been set among us, then, by God the Father as an adamant stone, he shook the tyranny of the devil and truly made the altars of laughter vanish. For as soon as Emmanuel shone forth and spread the light of true knowledge over all those under heaven, he showed himself to us as the image and likeness of the Father. Then, then indeed, the darkness of the ancient deceit was driven away, profane and God-hated idolatry was removed, and the very ruler of the deceit, that is, Satan, fell.

And Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying, "Amos is making conspiracies against you in the midst of the house of Israel; the land cannot bear all his words. For thus says Amos: 'Jeroboam shall die by the sword, and Israel shall be led away captive from its land.'"

Falsehood is always helpless on its own, and the feet of deceit stand on rotten ground. That is why it is laughable: it can barely be kept standing by help from outside. Such was the idolatry of Israel. The things they worshiped were the playthings of drunkards: golden calves, "the work of a craftsman, and molten images," as it is written, the art of a human hand and the inventions of unholy undertakings. Now the blessed prophets call those held captive by deceit back to sobriety; but the servants of idols, as though their whole stage set were being torn down, are exceedingly vexed, try to frighten people with terrors, and lament the sobering up of the deceived. For they know that a quick and wakeful mind easily sees the profanity of their worship. So the profane Amaziah was terrified that those who had been persuaded to worship the golden calves might be carried by the Prophet's words into good knowledge, and that he himself would lose his priestly office, while the images in the shrines would perish together with the shrines. That is why he tries to stir up Jeroboam, saying that Amos was all but rising in revolt against his kingdom and was now daring to utter a grievous and intolerable word: that the king himself would die by the sword, and that Israel too would go into captivity.

The wretched Jews did something similar when they concocted their false accusations against Christ. Since he was astonishing Judea with his miracles and calling all to himself, the miserable men, having let the flames of envy take hold of their minds, brought him before Pilate and said, "If you do not kill this man, you are no friend of Caesar." In the same way, the outrages against the saints committed by all who fight against godliness always come by similar devices, since falsehood everywhere suffers from feebleness.

And Amaziah said to Amos, "Seer, go, withdraw to the land of Judah, and live there, and prophesy there. But at Bethel you shall prophesy no more, for it is the king's sanctuary, and it is a royal house."

Now he is plainly shameless, and sets the display of his own malice against the divine words. They used to call prophets seers; but he did not deign to honor him even with the name of prophet, and as though he were slandering him as one of the false diviners, he ordered him to withdraw to the land of Judah. By adding Live there, he is all but saying: "If you are after shameful gain and seek to scrape together a living by chanting little spells over people, leave Samaria and speak to the people of the tribe of Judah, and you shall not prophesy at Bethel, for it is the king's sanctuary." By sanctuary he means a votive offering, or rather the place of a votive offering, for it was there that the first Jeroboam set up the golden calf. And as if turning the Prophet's offense into one against the honor of the ruler, he says, It is a royal house. "But you are throwing the king's affairs into confusion and stirring up unrest, recklessly opposing the will of those in power." See, then, clearly how true is what God said to Israel: "You gave the consecrated ones wine to drink, and you commanded the prophets, saying, 'Do not prophesy.'"

And Amos answered and said to Amaziah, "I was not a prophet, nor a prophet's son, but I was a goatherd, scraping sycamore figs [?]. And the Lord took me from the flock, and the Lord said to me, 'Go, prophesy to my people Israel.' And now hear the word of the Lord. You say, 'Do not prophesy against my people Israel, and do not stir up a crowd against the house [?].' Therefore thus says the Lord: 'Your wife shall play the harlot in the city, and your sons and your daughters shall fall by the sword, and your land shall be measured out with a line, and you shall die in an unclean land, and Israel shall be led away captive from its land.'"

When those who practice wickedness heap insults on the upright, they accuse them of their own habits; and in bringing up the ugliness of their own faults, they think they are abusing them, without realizing that they are all but painting themselves on a tablet and showing others what sort of people they are. We shall find that this is just what has now happened to the deranged Amaziah. For though he was a false prophet who attended the altars of idols, collecting the joints and leftovers of the sacrificial victims and unrestrainedly overcome by the desire for shameful gain, he reproached Amos and said that he ought to leave Samaria and withdraw, if he wished, to the land of Judah, and live there.
