"For there," he says, "you will easily speak your falsehoods, and by deceiving many you will scrape together a living and find your livelihood more readily." For Live there suggests some such meaning, as I have already said. But since the Prophet had no such aim and did not look to gain, but rather submitted to the Master's will, he fulfills the ministry fitting for a prophet and tries to teach him, and very gently, saying that he was neither a prophet nor a prophet's son—meaning, of course, by discipleship, that is, in the spirit, as Elisha was the son of Elijah—but that he was a goatherd, living a rustic, simple and harmless life, having very little for food and content with what came from the fields, things no one would even buy. These were sycamore figs. For those who tend flocks have leisure; they take refuge in the shade of trees, and, all but making light of the reproach of idleness, they nip off fruit and satisfy the needs of the belly as best they can. "But while I was in this state," he says, "God made me a prophet as he saw fit, and commanded me to declare to those of the blood of Israel what is coming upon them and will very soon be present. But you set your own wishes against the commands from above and order me to be silent." That is why, then, Thus says the Lord: Your wife shall play the harlot in the city—clearly by falling victim to the outrages of the enemy and being forced to endure the unbridled lust of those who hold her. And your children will be destroyed, becoming the work of the sword. And besides this, your land shall be measured out with a line, that is, it will be subject to tribute and will pay taxes to the conqueror. "And in addition to this," he says, "you, who now think you live in a holy land, Bethel, and possess the king's sanctuary, will go away captive and die amid your misfortunes, never to return—for how could you, or from where?—remaining a corpse in a foreign and unclean land of enemies. And Israel too will go off into captivity, Israel which has chosen you as its prophet and overseer of holy things." It is a grievous thing, then, to oppose the divine will, and to rush rashly into rebuking even the saints at times, when they are interpreting what pleases God—the saints to whom he has said, "And whoever touches you will be like one who touches the apple of his eye."

Notice how the saints share one admirable aim: to serve the words of God without holding back, and to count human things as nothing, even if some people bring wars and afflictions upon them. Blessed Amos paid no attention at all to Amaziah's crudeness. Far from falling silent, he boldly pronounced sentence against him. And when the scribes and Pharisees once ordered the divine disciples to be silent, they said plainly: "Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge; for we cannot help speaking about what we have seen and heard."

Thus the Lord showed me, and behold, a fowler's vessel. And he said, "What do you see, Amos?" And I said, "A fowler's vessel." And the Lord said to me, "The end has come upon my people Israel; I will no longer pass them by. And the panelled ceilings of the temple will wail on that day," says the Lord. "Many are the fallen in every place; I will cast silence upon them."

Now the Prophet's account flows on again, as it were, along its course. The matters introduced earlier have received a sufficient explanation, and the sequence of visions moves on to its proper goal. He saw the multitude of the Assyrians as a morning brood of locusts, and with them Gog, that is, Sennacherib, depicted in the form of a locust. This is because the creature leaps powerfully far from the ground, and the boastful man is somewhat like that: he is always leaping up toward the heights and refuses to live among the lowly. He also saw judgment summoned as in fire, and the adamant set in the midst of Israel by the one standing upon the wall of adamant. And what comes next? It was the fowler's vessel. What I said at the beginning I will say again: since the Prophet had been raised in a rather rustic way, God reveals mysteries to him chiefly through things done in the fields. Fowlers, and the creatures they hunt, namely birds, would surely suit not so much townsmen as those whose occupation and way of life are bound up with the fields and what is in them. The force of the visions hinted in a riddle that the choice race in Samaria would be caught for slaughter, in every way and without fail, as if by the hand of practised fowlers, together with the common flock. I mean the race of the boastful, who had made it their practice to soar on high like birds. For what he saw was a fowler's vessel. Therefore the God of all says that the end has come upon my people Israel, and that he will no longer pass over their offences. He also made clear that the temple itself, the one at Bethel that held the golden calf, would be burned down, when he said that the panelled ceilings of the temple will wail on that day. By "panelled ceilings" he usually means the roof, or the parts around it, which had been very artfully decorated by the skill of the carpenters, as in the Song of Songs: "Our beams are cedars, our panelled ceilings cypresses." He says that the panelled ceilings will wail, not uttering an articulate voice, but rather a sound like crashing and the creaking of timbers as they break apart. And since, he says, many are the fallen in every place, I will cast silence upon them. For when every place has been reduced to desolation and has no inhabitants, there will be a great silence, that is, stillness, as in deserted and trackless lands. So the God of all will in no way be at a loss if he chooses to discipline those who have sinned. He has many and various ways of punishing. No one will withstand him when he brings punishments on the one who provokes him. Yet the one who shakes off his wrath through repentance will escape, for he turns the Master, who is good and full of compassion, toward gentleness on his own behalf.
BY THE SAME AUTHOR, ON THE SAME PROPHET: FOURTH BOOK.

Hear these things, you who crush the poor in the morning and oppress the needy from the land, who say, “When will the month pass, so that we may sell, and the sabbaths, so that we may open our storehouses, to make the measure small and the weights large, and to make an unjust balance, to buy the poor for silver and the lowly for sandals, and trade in every kind of produce?”

One of the Pharisees once asked our Lord Jesus Christ which commandment he considered the first and great one in the law. He answered that the first commandment is, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your strength,” and that the second, close to it, is, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” One may also see the divine Paul himself all but making every kind of virtue depend on love. He dared to say that it is greater than faith and hope, and he plainly declared that whoever does not have it is nothing, even if he sets out his possessions for those in need, even if he hands over his very body to his persecutors to be burned. So everything in us that is great and worth hearing of will certainly come from love toward God and toward our brothers. But if someone is carried wholly outside the laws of love, and is seen to have no share in its flowers, he will be entirely useless, and might reasonably be thought to be caught fast in every kind of wickedness. For wherever the good is not practiced, there wrongdoing will surely flourish.

See, then, how the whole discourse is arranged. He first accused Ephraim, that is, Israel, of godlessness. He showed him to be a worshiper of heifers, without love for the one God who is God by nature, since he loved to devote himself to the works of his own hands. Now he goes on to show that Ephraim is truly impious toward his own brothers as well, and has utterly cast aside love of neighbor. He makes the reproof general and very clear, and though he is still brief, he lists the charges. That is why he says, “Hear these things, you who crush the poor in the morning and oppress the needy from the land.” It is as if he said, “My word is addressed to you, whose eager concern is, so to speak, to wipe the weak and poor off the earth and to oppress them in the morning.” For those who love the gentleness that pleases God offer up thanksgiving to God as day dawns. They worship, they pray, and they turn their efforts to whatever is praiseworthy. But those who look only to oppressing others, and who think nothing equals the need to get more, make it their eager business to leap out of bed as soon as dawn begins, to go off to their accustomed wickedness and to take advantage of whomever they can. They all but blame the night as it comes on, because it does not give them time enough for their greed. These are the ones who say, “When will the month pass, so that we may sell?” This is the prayer of moneylenders and [?] petty profiteers, shameful and grimy-fisted people who always thirst for the end of the month. Collecting little upon little, they want to make their trading bigger, and by impiously amassing interest upon interest they crush the weaker, although the law plainly says, “If you lend money to your neighbor, you shall not press him; you shall not lay interest upon him.” So some say, “When will the month pass, so that we may sell?” Others, held fast by the same or even worse sicknesses, and mastered by shameful gain, say in turn, “When will the sabbaths pass, so that we may open our storehouses, to make the measure small and the weights large, and to make an unjust balance?” We must now explain what this means, and what sabbaths they long to see pass so that they may open their storehouses, make the measure small and make the weights large.

It is written in Deuteronomy: “Every seven years you shall make a release, and this is the ordinance of the release: you shall release every private debt that your neighbor owes you, and you shall not demand it of your brother, because a release has been proclaimed to the Lord your God. Of the foreigner you may demand whatever of yours he has; but to your brother you shall grant release of your debt.” And again, a little later: “If there is a needy man among you, one of your brothers, in one of your cities in the land that the Lord your God is giving you, you shall not turn away your heart, nor shut your hand against your brother who is in need. You shall freely open your hands to him, and you shall lend him whatever he needs, as much as he lacks.” And he adds this further charge: “Take heed to yourself that there be no hidden word in your heart, a lawless thought, saying, ‘The seventh year, the year of release, is drawing near,’ and your eye be evil toward your brother who is in need, and you give him nothing, and he cry out against you to the Lord, and it be a great sin in you.” The law, then, commanded that debts be cancelled in what were, as it were, sabbath years, for it ordered this to be done in the seventh year. It also warned in advance that one must not act wickedly but should rather lend to those in need, even if the year of release seemed close at hand. Yet those who had many and abundant stores held back their hand. They were eager to wait until the sabbath of years, which was already at the doors, had passed, and only then would they lend, so that the debt would not fall within the time of release. These are the ones who say, “When will the sabbaths pass?” (clearly, the sabbaths of years) “so that we may open our storehouses.” Nor did their impiety stop there. Pouncing heartlessly on the poverty of those who had fallen on hard times, they gave with small measures, and took back in return with weights that were not equal but larger, and far heavier than the first, although God says through the all-wise Moses: “You shall not have in your bag two kinds of weights, a large and a small. You shall not have in your house two kinds of measures, a large and a small. You shall have a true and just weight, and you shall have a true and just measure, so that you may live long on the land that the Lord your God is giving you as an inheritance. For everyone who does this, everyone who acts unjustly, is an abomination to the Lord your God.” But they had no regard for justice. Looking only to their love of gain, they crushed the poor, all but taking possession of the wretched as property and treating them like sandals. For, as it is written, “The poor are the pasture of the rich.” But the writer of Proverbs helps us greatly when he says, “Let a man’s heart devise just things, so that his steps may be directed by God. For a man’s ways are before the eyes of God, and he watches over all his paths.” Since God oversees us, then, and closely examines everything we do, those who are truly good and sensible must make their paths straight and hold nothing equal to love toward God and toward the brothers. Love toward God has genuineness and incorruptness in faith, while love toward the brothers is bound up with the glories of righteousness. For it is true that “love does no wrong to a neighbor.” And I say that those who have chosen to win good repute and to live a life wholly in keeping with the law must put on “heartfelt compassion,” utterly despise accursed love of gain, and set out what they have as common property for those in need. Whoever keeps the law of love in this way will be illustrious and worthy of emulation before God and men. For it is written, “He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever and ever.”

The Lord swears by the pride of Jacob: “None of your works shall ever be forgotten. And shall not the land be shaken at these things, and everyone who dwells in it mourn? Destruction will rise up like a river, and go down like the river of Egypt.”

God charges those of Jacob with arrogance. They cast aside the divine laws, utterly disregarded the Master’s will, and trampled underfoot even love toward their brothers. So he swears by the pride of Jacob. Of course we do not say that the God of all takes the arrogance of certain people as the thing he swears by. Rather, he swears against it, that is, he fixes for it the penalty it deserves. And what does he swear, after all? That he will no longer overlook their offenses or bear with them to the very end. For this, I think, is what “ever” means here: running on to the very end and to final victory. Then he says that once forgetfulness has been taken away (I mean forgetfulness of their unholy offenses), how could the land not be filled with turmoil as enemies overrun it, and the people themselves mourn, having suffered a terrible calamity from which there is hardly any escape? And what is this calamity? Destruction, he says, will be brought up upon them like the river of Egypt, covering everything and flooding the whole land of Samaria with many irresistible streams. It will also go down, sweeping away everything in its path in the same way, and sparing nothing whatever. For Sennacherib came up against them with armies of countless thousands, like a river flooding the land and bringing everything under its power. Then he went back again to his own land, dragging with him a vast and countless host of captives.

So when we despise God, we shall find the hostile powers ranged against us. We shall fall into turmoil and grief, in a sense plundered by them, and sink as of necessity into a slave’s bondage. For they will come against us like irresistible water, sweeping us away to ruin and drowning us in destruction. But if we wish to please God, “rivers will not overwhelm us,” as it is written, nor “will the deep swallow us up,” nor could “a tempest drown us.” For then, having bravely escaped the greed of the demons and caring very little for their malice, we shall say with joy, “If the Lord had not been among us (let Israel now say), if the Lord had not been among us when men rose up against us, then they would have swallowed us alive.” And again, “Our soul has passed through a torrent; indeed our soul has passed through the irresistible water.” The water of the devil’s malice, that is, the flood that comes through the passions, may be irresistible and beyond the power of our minds to withstand, but in Christ we shall be able. For we shall pass through his perverse onslaught as through a torrent.

“And it shall come to pass on that day,” says the Lord God, “that the sun will set at noon, and the light will be darkened over the earth in broad daylight. I will turn your feasts into mourning and all your songs into lamentation. I will bring sackcloth upon every waist and baldness upon every head. I will make Jacob like the mourning for a beloved one, and those with him like a day of anguish.”

This passage is pregnant with a twofold meaning. For it is the constant custom of the holy prophets, especially at the end of their own discourses, to make mention of Christ and to give an account of the mystery concerning him, though it is still shadowed by obscurities. Come, then, let us look to both meanings and say what is fitting. We shall first set out the meaning that follows from what has already been said, and then apply the sense of the words to an interpretation concerning Christ. On that day, then, when destruction sweeps over the whole land of the Samaritans like the river of Egypt, a terrible and deep darkness will be poured over virtually all who live in it, as though the sun were setting, and at noon at that. Of course we do not say that the light of the sun actually set. Rather, the calamity of the war became like darkness to those who lived in Samaria. For great and overwhelming grief, when it arises, muddies the mind; things that happen against all hope and expectation darken the heart; and the bitterness of sorrowful events creates a kind of mist and fog in the hearts of those who suffer them.

So they will see darkness, he says, even if the sun happens to stand at noon. And those who once held splendid feasts, always making use of strings and lyres and the sweetest of songs, will give up such pursuits. Instead they will wail, will practice songs of lamentation, and will take on the garb of mourners, by which I mean sackcloth and baldness. It was [?] to shave the head completely bare; indeed, the divine Job cut off his hair when his children perished. “I will make Jacob,” he says, “like the mourning for a beloved one.” That is, those who see him will grieve over him as a mother or father grieves over an only and beloved child lying dead. “And those with him like a day of anguish”: that is, their neighbors, Judah and Benjamin, who worshiped idols together with Ephraim and so were with him in this sense, will be found as people having a day of anguish, as though in labor pains. I mean the pangs that come from terror, grief and toil. For after ravaging Samaria, Sennacherib took all their cities. Then he sent Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem, and he threatened terrible things against those on the wall. He so crushed the people of Jerusalem with despondency that they expected to perish at any moment along with those in Samaria. Then King Hezekiah too, deeply dejected, sent messengers to the prophet Isaiah, saying, “This day is a day of affliction and reproach and rebuke and wrath, for the pangs have come upon the woman in labor, but she has no strength to give birth.” So by “a day of anguish” he means toils and dejection like the pains of labor. The people of Jerusalem, then, were in a day of anguish, expecting to perish, since they had been with Ephraim, I mean in his way of idolatry.

These things I have said as fitting and appropriate to those who at that time provoked the Master of all against themselves. But one could apply them no less to those who acted impiously against Emmanuel himself at the time of the incarnation. For they are “those who crush the poor in the morning,” that is, those who shunned the choice to live by the law, and pressed on toward nothing else, perhaps, than corrupting justice, daring to treat as nothing what is so clearly laid down in the divine commandments, and taking advantage without restraint of any of the weaker they pleased. They would also be the ones “who say, ‘When will the month pass, so that we may sell, and the sabbaths, so that we may open our storehouses, to make the measure small and the weight large, and to make an unjust balance?’” For that the scribes and Pharisees were exceedingly fond of money and greedy for shameful gain we can learn in many ways if we fix our minds on the Gospel writings. Christ advised those who love the gentleness that pleases God to show themselves above shameful gain and to be free of all love of profit, and he urged them to go further still, to help the needy and to give away their possessions. But what does the Evangelist say? “The scribes and Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all this, and they sneered at him.” So it could fittingly be said of them too: “The Lord swears by the pride of Jacob: none of your works shall ever be forgotten.” For it was truly arrogance for them to disregard the divine laws and, what is more grievous still, to go on to commit outrage against Christ himself. That is why their offenses will never pass into oblivion. Instead destruction has come up upon them like a flooding river: the Roman war. And when they handed over the Master of all to the cross, the sun set upon them and the light was darkened, for “there was darkness from the sixth hour until the ninth hour.” This was a clear sign to the Jews that the souls of those who crucified him had been darkened in a spiritual sense. For “a hardening has come upon Israel in part,” and as the divine Paul writes, “To this day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart.” Blessed David too, out of love for God, called down a curse on them, saying, “Let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see, and bend their backs continually.” That they mourned, turning their feasts as it were into gloom, becomes clear when Christ himself says to the women weeping over him as he was being led away to the cross, “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children.” For they mourned as they perished together with the city and with the divine temple itself, when the Romans set everything on fire. “I will make him,” he says (clearly meaning Emmanuel), “like the mourning for a beloved one, and those with him like a day of anguish.” For when Jesus was crucified, those who had believed in him mourned, and women stood far off lamenting: Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James, and some others with them. Creation itself mourned its own Master. The sun was darkened, the rocks were split, and the temple itself took on the garb of mourners, as its veil was torn from top to bottom. God hinted at something of this kind to us through the voice of Isaiah, saying, “I will clothe the heaven with darkness, and make sackcloth its covering.” So the mourning over him was as for a beloved one. And those with him, that is, the disciples, were brought into a day of anguish. For how can anyone doubt that they too mourned? It was while they were in anguish that the women brought them news of Christ’s resurrection, and only then did they barely lift up their heads and run to the tomb. And perhaps it is to these very women, who brought the good news of the resurrection, that the prophet Isaiah says in the Spirit, “Women coming from the sight, come here; for it is not a people that has understanding” (meaning, clearly, the people of the Jews); “therefore he who made them will not have compassion on them, and he who formed them will not show them mercy.”

“Behold, days are coming,” says the Lord, “when I will send a famine on the land: not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord. The waters will be shaken as far as the sea, and from the north to the east they will run about seeking the word of the Lord, and they will not find it.”

It is written, “Lord, in affliction we remembered you; in small affliction your discipline came to us.” The divine David also knew that affliction is an excellent and truly beneficial thing. So at one time he said, “In my affliction I called upon the Lord,” and at another, “It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I might learn your statutes.” For afflictions make us more self-controlled and drag us out of the snares of idleness. They persuade us to love the ways of gentleness, and they bring the harsh and unruly, as if by necessity and fear, under the yoke of holiness and obedience.

When Samaria has been ravaged, he says, and the Babylonian is burning its cities, some at that time may choose to learn what the will of God is, and what they must do or say to obtain his mercy and escape his wrath. But there will be no one to teach them, he says. “For I will bring upon them a famine of the words that come from God, so that no prophet at all will be found, even if they run from west to east, even if from south to north.” Similar to this is what God said to blessed Ezekiel: “I will bind your tongue and you shall be mute, and you shall not be to them a man who reproves, for they are a rebellious house.” For those who have once spurned the word that comes from God would rightly be unable to receive it, even if they later wanted it of their own accord. By waters being shaken he means the countless multitude of the Jews, thrown into turmoil and now like the waves of the sea, which are tossed in every direction by the blasts of the winds.

It can also be taken in another way. After Christ was crucified, the wretched Jews suffered a famine of the words that come from God. For there is no longer any prophet among them, no exact teacher who knows how to refine the coarseness of the Mosaic history and bring to light the mysteries buried in its letter. They did not accept Christ when he said, “I am the bread of life, which came down from heaven and gives life to the world.” That is why they heard him say long ago through the voice of Isaiah, “Behold, those who serve me will eat, but you will be hungry; behold, those who serve me will drink, but you will be thirsty.” For it is true that “The Lord will never let the soul of the righteous starve, but he will overturn the life of the ungodly,” since he does not let down to them the divine word that nourishes the mind toward the desire for virtue. For as the Savior himself said, “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.”

On that day the beautiful virgins and the young men will faint with thirst, those who swear by the propitiation of Samaria, and who say, “As your god lives, Dan,” and “As your god lives, Beersheba.” They will fall and never rise again.

The passage suggests that their sons and daughters will be carried off by enemies. That is what the virgins and the young men stand for, since we shall find that those used to carrying people off into captivity are especially eager for people of that age. But the passage also seems to hint to us at something else, among things hidden. There were certain virgins who sat in the precincts of the idols, and with them lads, that is, boys not yet grown, through whom those more curious about sorcery thought they learned things from the demons. They called the demons down upon these undefiled bodies, as it were, and arranged for them to give answers in secret whisperings. And they say that even to this day some [?] who wish to commit impiety practise divination in the same way as they did. So Israel will lack not only the word from God through the holy prophets, which is useful and necessary for correction, but also the word of the false prophets, that is, of the demons, which they used to deliver to certain people through virgins and boys. He indicates this by saying, "In that day the fair virgins will fail." It is as if he were saying: "Your fair virgins too will perish together with the rest." And along with the girls the passage also mocks the lads who swear by the propitiation of Samaria. For it was perhaps their custom to like swearing by the gods in Samaria, that is, the heifers. Perhaps laughing God to scorn, they attached what belongs to him to the carved images, saying, "As your god lives, O Dan, and as your god lives, O Beersheba." These are cities of Judea, lying at the very extremities of the country and, as it were, marking out the extent of the land from the south to the sea. It is as if those who swore were saying, "As the god of the land of the Jews lives," that is, the calf; for the middle is included by naming the extremities, and so a picture of the whole is woven. He says that the virgins and the young men will faint with thirst, since they are no longer supplied with the lying utterances of the demons, because they themselves have become the work of a foreign hand: they have either fallen by the sword or endured an inglorious and grievous captivity.

When Christ was crucified and had set for the Jews, they were deprived not only of the sun of this world and of perceptible light, but also of the spiritual radiance and the enlightenment that comes through the Spirit. For they are without the divine word and the consolation from above. Their virgins have fainted together with their young men, that is, the fair and esteemed souls, whose purity is signified by the virgin and whose vigor and great strength are signified by the young man. For who among them is holy, since the law can perfect nothing and is not sufficient for their righteousness? And in which of them could there be spiritual vigor and a strong mind, when they have not known the brilliant achievements of the gospel way of life? Are they not all sluggish, steeped in sins, and slack of mind? How then can this be in doubt? So they have fainted with thirst, and it was not to them that it was said, "Draw water with joy from the springs of salvation." Rather, "he commanded the clouds not to rain upon them," because they did not obey Christ himself when he cried out, "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink." Having forsaken him, though he is the spring of life, "they dug broken cisterns that will not be able to hold water." For they have given heed to teachings and commandments of men, which cannot give drink unto life or keep those who use them safe unto salvation.

I saw the Lord standing over the altar, and he said, "Strike upon the altar, and the gateways will be shaken; and cut into the heads of all; and those of them who are left I will kill with the sword."

The blessed prophets, whose mind's eye is brightened by the torchlight of the Spirit, receive not only knowledge of what is to come; at times they also see the spectacle of the events themselves, as though painted on a tablet. They are themselves astounded, and they persuade their hearers to share their feelings, striving very earnestly to make clear the meaning of the visions. Thus blessed Amos said, "And the Lord said to me, 'The end has come upon my people Israel; I will no longer pass them by; and the panelled ceilings of the temple will wail in that day, says the Lord. Many are the fallen in every place; I will cast silence upon them.'" But see, he has beheld what was foretold actually being carried out in events, just as the prediction said. For he says he saw the Lord himself standing at the altar, as if beginning the overthrow and commanding that it take place. God stands over the altar, not to pay it honor; it would be foolish to understand it that way. If it is utterly absurd to think and say that God pays reverence and honor to the altars of idols, how could he have honored the altar of the heifers? No, he stood over it as one about to pull it down and bring it to the ground. This is why he all but commanded the prophet to begin the overthrow, saying, "Strike upon the altar, and let the gateways be shaken," he says, "and let the temple now reel, as though about to fall at any moment." "And cut into the heads of all": that is, begin with the most prominent among them, and strike the leaders, who are placed in the rank of head over the others. The rest will perish along with them without distinction and will share the calamities of those set over them, they too becoming the work of the sword. Like this is what God said through Ezekiel to the six men who came from the gate facing north and, carrying their axes, followed the man girded with the long robe. God had said to them, "Go into the city after him, and strike, and do not spare, and have no pity. Kill old man and young man, infants and women, to utter destruction; but do not come near any on whom is the mark; and begin from my holy places." Do you see how he made the leaders the first fruits of his wrath, that is, those who seemed venerable and holy, perhaps because they had attained the glory of the priestly ministry or had been made illustrious by other honors? For such people are like heads over the rest.

This is what happened also to those who acted outrageously against our Lord Jesus Christ. The wretched people cared little for the law and the prophets and did not receive Christ, who is the end of the law and the prophets. Though they knew clearly that he was the heir, they cast him out of the vineyard and at last crucified him. So they were handed over to the Roman generals for desolation. That renowned temple was burned, the altar in it was pulled down, the gateways were shaken, and the leaders perished together with the common herd; for the war spared none of them.

So too with each believer. He may be a temple of God, since he has God dwelling within him, or he may be thought of as an altar, since he offers his own way of life to God as a sacred service. But if he then turns aside to sloth and provokes God, he will come to nothing and suffer a most terrible overthrow. For the Master shows no partiality, and "the righteousness of the righteous will not deliver him on the day he goes astray," as it is written.

None of them who flees will escape, and none of them who tries to save himself will be saved. If they dig down into Hades, from there my hand will drag them up; and if they go up into heaven, from there I will bring them down. If they hide on the top of Carmel, from there I will search them out and take them; and if they sink out of my sight into the depths of the sea, there I will command the serpent, and it will bite them. And if they go into captivity before the face of their enemies, there I will command the sword, and it will kill them. And I will fix my eyes upon them for evil and not for good.

Perhaps at this point it will be fitting to say to those who hear these things what blessed David sang to God: "Where shall I go from your Spirit? And where shall I flee from your face? If I go up into heaven, you are there; if I go down into Hades, you are present. If I take up my wings at dawn and settle at the farthest parts of the sea, even there your hand will guide me, and your right hand will hold me." For the divine is all-seeing, and all-powerful besides, and no one can escape that sleepless eye. For he said, "I am a God who is near, and not a God far off. Will anything be hidden from me?" No one could ever get out from under the calamity cast upon him by divine decree, as it were; for "his lofty hand, who will turn it back?" as it is written. What device will help us? What means at all will come to our aid, when God decrees that we must suffer? Counsel and deliberation and every kind of contrivance are entirely useless to those who have fallen under divine wrath, and he makes this clear by saying that no one could escape even if he were hidden in Hades itself (the expression is hyperbolic). Even if he were to fly up to heaven, or cross over to the top of Carmel, wherever he went he would be caught. Even if he were in the sea, he would fall upon the serpent, or, according to the Hebrew version, he would be handed over to the sea monster. Even if he were among his enemies [?], a captive from then on and wretchedly held fast under the yokes of slavery, this too, he says, will be a small thing and not punishment enough for him; for the terror of the sword will also be raised against him. And the God of all, he says, will not cease to fix his eye upon them. That is a sign of anger and threat; for we ourselves sometimes fix our eyes on those who grieve us, looking at them grimly and without a smile. But since God also watches over the good and the righteous, he makes clear the difference in his watching by saying "for evil and not for good." For he will look upon them, he says, not to bestow any good thing, but so that the penalty and punishment he has decreed may remain unshaken and, as it were, fixed fast upon them.

This is what the wretched multitude of the Jews also suffered, who called down the righteous blood upon their own head. For when they were urging Pilate to crucify Christ, they said, "His blood be on us and on our children." So they perished with their whole households, and their cities were taken along with the men themselves, so that perhaps no one was able to escape. What kinds of things they suffered, and how many, the long histories of those who have written about such matters relate.
And the Lord, the Lord God Almighty, is he who touches the earth and shakes it; and all who dwell in it will mourn, and its end will rise like a river and go down like the river of Egypt.

Out of love the prophet does not let his hearers disbelieve what is said, as though it would not come to pass. In this he was persuading them rather to choose to learn what is better and to treat what is profitable with reverence, so that God might cease from his wrath, rein in the calamity, and receive them when they repent. For he always takes pity on those who are willing to turn back. He teaches, then, that God is all-powerful and quite able to bring the end upon those he spoke of. For he says, "the Lord, the Lord God Almighty, who touches the earth and shakes it." It is as if he were saying: Do not think that the one you have grieved is like you. For the Master is not as a man; he is the Lord of hosts himself, who lays his own hand on the land (that of the Samaritans, clearly) and shakes it. He does not make it undergo an ordinary tremor; he shakes the whole of it with war and incurable calamities and makes it quake. That is why he says, "Everyone who dwells in it will mourn, and like the river of Egypt the end will rise," covering and submerging everything; and in the same way it will subside, dragging down and carrying away everything again. We have said that he likens Sennacherib, the multitude of the Assyrians, and the war they raised against Samaria to the streams of rivers.

So for those who offend and grieve God there will be no way of escape; the hand that strikes is all-powerful and hard to elude, and those it has once seized will find no help or comfort: "For if he shuts a man in, who will open?" as it is written. It is surely far better to turn away his wrath by hastening back to what seems good and dear to him. This would come about, and quite rightly, if we forget what lies behind, eagerly flee from evil, and make ourselves illustrious by advancing in virtue. For then we shall swim safely through the effects of his anger, and we shall easily move the Creator, who is good by nature, to see fit, I mean, to watch over us kindly and most gently.
He who builds his ascent into heaven, and founds his promise upon the earth; who calls the water of the sea and pours it out upon the face of the earth: the Lord God Almighty is his name.

With still more words he frightens those who desert God and drives them toward what is better. He skillfully expounds the supremacy and the all-powerfulness of the divine nature, and he tries to assure them that God will fulfil his own words completely and in every way, with nothing to hinder him. "For he who touches the earth," he says, "and shakes it" (in the senses we have just explained), he it is who builds his ascent into heaven. He all but says: "He who has all authority, so that he treads upon the heavens themselves and holds power over all things, so that even the creation above and in the heavens, that is, the blessed multitude of the holy angels, lies subject beneath him." By "heavens" we mean the angels who dwell in heaven. We should know that the divine Jacob too saw this matter in a figure. For there was a ladder reaching from earth to heaven, and "the Lord," it says, "stood firmly upon it," and he saw the angels ascending and descending by it. This, I think, is what "he who builds his ascent into heaven" means.

Moreover, he says, whatever he promises to those on earth is entirely unshaken and firm and, as it were, founded on a foundation. For the Lord of hosts will in no way fail, nor could any word of his fall to the ground. And the Savior confirms us in this, saying, "Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away." He it is who also draws up the water of the sea by ineffable powers and rains upon the earth; that is, again, he governs human affairs, and he is so mighty that he easily transforms the natures of created things into whatever he chooses. And his name is Lord God, and Almighty besides. This should not be understood as a mere name, as it might be in the case of a man, but as rightly derived from the truth itself. For he is so named, both by us and by the holy angels, because he is Lord by his very essence and holds power over all things. The prophet's aim, then, is to use every possible means, as best he can, to strike terror into those who have been deceived and to persuade them thoroughly that they must quickly turn back, as it were, regard righteousness as a splendid thing, and once again choose piety toward God, vigorously checking their inclination toward what is more shameful by the terrors of what is to come. And this, I think, is what David rightly said to the Master of all: "With bit and bridle you would constrain the jaws of those who do not draw near to you."

It could also be said of Christ, and very fittingly: "He who builds his ascent into heaven." For he himself is from above and from heaven, since he was begotten by nature as God from God. That is why he also said, "I am from above." And the wise John bore witness of him, saying, "He who comes from above is above all." Having by his very essence the ascent into the heavens (for, as I said, it lay open to him as God), he made it passable for those on earth. For "as a forerunner on our behalf" he ascended to the Father, and, as the divine Paul writes, "he opened for us a new and living way." As man he appeared "on our behalf before the face of God" the Father, who also "raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places." For since Christ ascended, he built his own ascent for us too, if blessed Paul speaks the truth when he says, "For this we declare to you by a word of the Lord, that we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will by no means go before those who have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a word of command, with the voice of an archangel and with the trumpet of God, and the dead in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord." So he ascended as man, in order that the ascent which befits him alone, since he is God and from God, he might make passable for us believers too. He also founds his own promise upon the earth. For he has never spoken falsely; rather, he will bring to completion whatever he promises to accomplish for us. For he said, "It is to your advantage that I go away; for if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but when I go, I will send him to you." That is why he commanded the holy apostles "not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, which they had heard from him." And he poured out his grace on them richly. That is why they became "witnesses of his glory both in Jerusalem and in Judea" and in all the earth. In another way too we shall find his promise founded: for we have believed that he will raise us from the dead, make us superior to corruption, "transform the body of our lowliness to be conformed to the body of his glory," and receive us as sharers in his kingdom. He it is who calls the water of the sea and pours it out upon the face of the earth; that is, he changes what is bitter, unacceptable, and unfit for use into what is beneficial. For "the letter" of the law "kills," as the most wise Paul says, and the shadow in itself is useless. Yet for us who understand it, it has become extremely useful for understanding the things concerning Christ, and it has proved to be a kind of spiritual rain, watering in a way the whole earth beneath heaven. For it is true that the law, which was formerly bitter and unbearable to the people of old, has become for us a tutor leading to the mystery of Christ, so that we can bear fruit in it, refining the thickness of the shadow into truth. We shall take what was said, then, as an illustration, bringing forward as proof the water of Marah too. It was bitter, but it was made sweet when God showed a piece of wood to the blessed Moses and commanded him to throw it into the waters. That wood was an image and type of the precious cross, through which the law became sweet and, as it were, very good to drink, although the history contains what is bitter. For "the letter kills," as I said, or rather as the wise Paul has written for us.

"Are you not like the sons of the Ethiopians to me, O sons of Israel?" says the Lord. "Did I not bring Israel up out of the land of Egypt, and the Philistines out of Cappadocia, and the Syrians out of the pit? Behold, the eyes of the Lord God are upon the kingdom of the sinners, and I will remove it from the face of the earth."

The people of Israel always held their noses high. They talked endlessly about the noble descent they had from their fathers, and with mouths opened wide they kept saying, “We have Abraham as our father.” But they heard Christ answer them: “If you were children of Abraham, you would be doing the works of Abraham.” “For not all who are descended from Israel are Israel, and not all are children because they are the seed of Abraham.” It is likeness in works that rightly gives someone the power to boast splendidly in the fame of his fathers. They also gave themselves airs over all the other nations by saying that God had chosen them out of all the nations, had delivered [?] them from the land of Egypt and had brought them into the land of promise. What they said is true. But they, of all people, owed their benefactor fitting returns to gladden him. Instead they were caught in many ways insulting him outrageously, through complete apostasy and through turning aside to wickedness. And in the end the wretches reached such a pitch of madness that they thought it was enough for their welfare and their glory that they had sprung from the root of Abraham and had been brought from the land of Egypt into the land of promise. They had sunk into indolence and refused to be godly, so to make them understand that such boasts did them no good, he had to say: Shall I not regard you just as I regard the sons of the Ethiopians, who do not have Abraham as their root, even if you happen to have noble descent from your fathers? For the Divine is entirely impartial and shows no favoritism, and it takes no account of a fleshly nobility that lacks good deeds. Spiritual nobility, however, it counts worthy of all honor, and so too the nobility that goes with a love of being adorned with splendid achievements. You also think it something great and exceptional that you moved from Egypt to another land. Well then, he says, what of it? What benefit will it bring you? Others have this too, and they received it from me. For I brought over the foreigners, that is, the Philistines (this is how the Hebrews interpreted it), from Cappadocia. And the Syrians, meaning plainly all who were then under the kingdom of Damascus, I brought up out of the pit.

It should be noted that where we read “pit” the Hebrews have rendered “Cyrene.” So the Philistines were colonists from the Cappadocians, and the Syrians from the Cyrenaeans. He called Cyrene a “pit,” even though it is very elevated and lies high up, because it lies as though in a deep gulf. For practically the whole land of Libya has gulfs along the sea that open outward. So, he says, I look on all people equally, and my aim is to cut off from the earth every kingdom of sinners. Fleshly distinction, then, would do its owners no good. For with God nobility means a good character that is strongly drawn to the desire for virtue and is practiced in emulating the piety of its forebears.

Yet I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob, says the Lord. For behold, I am giving the command, and I will winnow the house of Israel among all the nations, as grain is winnowed with a winnowing fan, and no fragment shall fall to the ground. All the sinners of my people shall die by the sword, those who say, “Disaster shall not come near, nor shall it come upon us.”

Once again a remnant has been preserved for Israel “for the sake of the fathers.” For they will not suffer total destruction, he says, and the race descended from Jacob will not vanish completely. They will be scattered as though by a winnowing fan, he says, and dispersed among all the nations. Yet no fragment shall fall to the ground. That is, the race of Jacob will not fall in such a way as to come to complete ruin, but will be saved in the part that has received mercy. For at that time some were brought back from captivity. It has also been saved through Christ, since a good number of the Jews have believed. And in the last times the remnant will also be saved, once the flock of the gentiles has been called in first. Someone might then say, “If Jacob is saved after all, against whom are the threats directed?” He usefully answers this. The wrath, he says, will not fall indiscriminately on everyone alike, and the effects of his anger will not strike without distinction. Rather, it will fall on those who have committed unbearable offenses. This is the meaning of: All the sinners of my people shall die by the sword, those who say, “Disaster shall not come near, nor shall it come upon us.” For some had become so deranged that they thought even the holy prophets were lying, and they kept saying that none of the things foretold would come to pass. The wise Jeremiah will also bear witness to this, when he says to God, “Behold, they say to me, ‘Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come!’” So people of this mind commit a twofold offense: they provoked him in many ways, and they also thought that the truth was telling lies.

We shall also find that at the time of his coming the teachers of the Jews paid no heed to the words of our Savior. That is why they heard, “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! You have taken away the key of knowledge. You do not enter yourselves, and you do not let those who are entering go in.” And again: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! You travel around sea and land to make a single proselyte, and when he has become one, you make him twice as much a son of Gehenna as yourselves.” So they were justly not reckoned as children. Having slipped from the nobility of their fathers, they were enrolled as if among the sons of the Ethiopians. They were also consumed by the sword, and they paid the Judge a penalty equal in weight to their own folly.

On that day I will raise up the tent of David that has fallen. I will rebuild its fallen parts and raise up its ruins, and I will rebuild it as in the days of old, so that the rest of humankind may seek out [the Lord], and all the nations upon whom my name has been called, says the Lord who does these things.

He promised that he would not utterly destroy the race descended from Jacob. They would indeed be scattered, in a sense, as by a winnowing fan. They would become strangers and sojourners, driven from their homeland and their houses and living in a barbarian and foreign land. Yet they would not be crushed completely, and they would not go off to total destruction. That is why he says that he will raise up the tent of David even though it has fallen, and will restore its ruins as in the days of old, that is, for many long days. This, he says, will be a sign and an assurance to the other nations, both neighboring and far away, that they must now turn to God and choose to seek him, for they will surely have marveled at God's gentleness and at the greatness of his strength. So when he speaks of the tent of David, he means the race of the Jews, that is, the house descended from Jacob. It should be noted that when Cyrus released them from captivity, they returned to Judea and rebuilt the temple. They fortified the desolate cities with towers, built houses in them and lived there in safety. They did endure wars waged by certain rulers, I mean Antiochus and Hadrian, for example, but they were never again taken captive, nor were they laid waste as they had been by the Babylonians.

So much, then, for the historical sense. The deeper and truer sense, however, would be found in Christ. For he came back to life from the dead when God the Father raised up his tent that had fallen into death, that is, his flesh taken from the earth. Then and only then did all things human rise up to their original form, and all our ruins were brought to a new appearance. For according to the Scriptures, “If anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation”; for we have been raised together with him. Death tore down the tents of all, but God the Father rebuilt them in Christ. This will be ours not for a limited time but for the days of eternity. For the good of incorruption cannot be taken from us, and death will no longer have power over those who have been saved in Christ. Then and only then did the rest of humankind too, after the believers from Israel, come to know the one who is God by nature and in truth, and they left behind that ancient and profane error. For Christ could not be proved false when he said, “Unless the grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.” And again: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all people to myself.” So on that day, the day on which I raise up the ruined and fallen tent of David, all the nations will be called, and my name will be upon them. He has given full assurance that what was foretold will in every way and without fail be fulfilled, by adding: says the Lord God who does these things. For if he is truly Lord and God, he will in every way and without fail do these things as well, since nothing is beyond his power. For he does “great and unsearchable things, glorious and marvelous, beyond number.”

Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when the threshing will overtake the vintage, and the grapes will ripen at sowing time. The mountains will drip sweetness, and all the hills will be thickly planted. I will turn back the captivity of my people Israel. They will rebuild the ruined cities and live in them; they will plant vineyards and drink their wine; they will plant gardens and eat their fruit. I will plant them in their own land, and they will never again be uprooted from the land that I have given them, says the Lord God Almighty.

He has clearly explained the very thing I spoke of. Someone might choose to give a plain, historical account. He will then say that the return was clearly promised to those who had endured captivity, and that they would possess their own land and rebuild cities and houses. Having at last come into a happy state of prosperity, they would gather the good things of the fields and devote themselves to farming with gladness and joy. Their labor of gathering in the sweetest produce would never cease: the good things of the threshing floor would get in the way of their vintage, and the vintage in its turn would stretch into the season for sowing. The farmer would go straight from the winepress, the pruning hook and the grape clusters to plow the fields of the plain, and after washing off the dust of the threshing floor he would turn to the cares of the winepresses.

But if we wish to approach the contemplation of these words in a more subtle and spiritual way, it would be fitting to understand them as follows. As I said, Christ came back to life, for the Father raised up the tent of David and rebuilt its ruins. Since then, an abundant and generous share of spiritual good things has come to all people, Greeks and Jews alike. For “God is one, who has justified the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith.” So the very great abundance of spiritual fruits supplied to believers is aptly signified by the earthly fruits. For there will be plenty of grain and wine, he says. Let us now take the grain to mean strength, clearly spiritual strength, for it is written, “And bread strengthens the human heart.” This bread is surely spiritual, divine and from above. Let us take the wine to mean gladness, for again it says, “And wine gladdens the human heart,” and we “rejoice in hope,” as the blessed Paul says. The mountains also drip sweetness. By mountains here he seems to mean the churches of Christ. He calls them so because of the loftiness of their doctrines and their surpassing piety toward God. He also calls them so because mountains are seen covered with all kinds of plants, while the churches of Christ have countless heads of saints, like cedars and the tallest trees, planted beside the channels of spiritual waters. On the most thickly wooded mountains, swarms of bees fly about and make sweet and precious honey. In the same way, in the churches those who are more eminent than the rest and more mature in virtue and understanding gather the sweet honey of the teaching about Christ, and they all but drip it into the hearts of others too. This, I think, is how the mountains will drip sweetness. He also said that the hills will be thickly planted. The hills are, as it were, those of second rank, who fall short in virtue of those who are especially distinguished in it. For there are degrees of holiness and righteousness in the churches, and, as Paul says, each has them according to the grace given to him by God, who distributes such gifts. These too, he says, will be thickly planted, that is, flourishing and fruitful, their minds richly covered in leaf with the right teaching of divine doctrine. No one could doubt that the God of all has turned back our captivity. For Christ proclaimed “release to the captives” and rescued the whole world under heaven from the devil's greed. Then and only then did we become like farmers, tending the fruitfulness of the mind. We planted gardens and vineyards, and we shall eat their fruit. For we shall receive the rewards of our labors, and we shall also harvest the fruits of goodness. Our dwelling with God will be unshaken, and no one could drive out those who have entered the inheritance he has once given. He makes this clear when he says: I will plant them in their own land, which I have given them, says the Lord God. “For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable,” and we shall be securely established in every good thing, with Christ himself as our guide and the leader of our festival. Through him and with him be glory and might to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.
END OF THE COMMENTARY ON THE PROPHET AMOS.
COMMENTARY BY THE SAME AUTHOR ON THE PROPHET OBADIAH

Obadiah, in turn, prophesies, it seems, in the same times as Joel. He all but shared the vision with him, and the account is divided between them. The inspired Joel, at the very end of his prophecy, says: "Egypt shall become a desolation, and Idumea a plain of desolation, because of the wrongs done to the sons of Judah, since they shed righteous blood in their land." Obadiah, for his part, recounts in detail how and in what way the desolation of Idumea will come about in its time. Readers of this book will benefit from learning precisely, before anything else, who Idumea is, what happened to it, and why it was made to suffer the calamities that come from divine wrath. So come, let us speak of these things as best we can and set them out clearly for those eager to learn. The Idumeans, then, are called so, and are, the descendants of Esau. He was named Edom, that is, "earthy," because he sold his birthright: he cared nothing for the honor due to him from it and chose instead a single serving of food, and a very cheap one at that. For this reason his descendants were called Idumeans. The land of the Idumeans is called both Seir and Teman. It is called Seir because its inhabitants are said to be hairy, and Esau too was hairy, for he was covered with hair; "Ser" is interpreted as "hairiness" or "hairy." There was also a mountain in that land called Seir. It is called Teman, again, because it lies farthest to the south, for in the Hebrew language Teman means "south." Some think it was called Teman for another reason as well. They say that in time a son, Eliphaz, was born to Esau, and from Eliphaz came Teman, after whom the land of Teman is named. That is enough about Idumea and its inhabitants. They perished for the following reason. When Jerusalem was besieged by Nebuchadnezzar and had come to the very extremity of evils, countless people were falling, consumed by the swords of the nations. Some barely escaped and made their way to the lands of the neighboring nations. Most of those from Israel went down to Idumea, which bordered on them, thinking that the Idumeans would share their grief as brothers, remember their kinship by blood, and grant help to those who had suffered so miserably. But the Idumeans, though they ought to have pitied them as brothers, received them into their land and then slaughtered them. Like brigands they prowled about the exits of Idumea and seized them while they were confused and cowering. They were so inhuman as to surpass even the savagery of the Babylonians. For, as I said, they set upon people who were already perishing, mocking them and making the calamities of their own kin an occasion for festivity. At that time the Jews were carried off to the land of the Persians and Medes. But when the seventy years were completed and God took pity on them, they were brought back to Judea and set about rebuilding the city itself and raising up the temple in it once more. Yet the Idumeans, their brothers and neighbors, were again gnawed by envy and wanted to stop these undertakings. They gathered the like-minded barbarians who lived round about and actually went out to battle. They fell and perished in the valley of Jehoshaphat, for God was defending those of Israel. And since the Idumeans had been more oppressive than the foreigners, those of Israel overran their land and killed its inhabitants, searching the clefts of the rocks, the caves and the holes in the ground, and slaughtering whomever they found.

"The vision of Obadiah. Thus says the Lord God to Idumea: I have heard a report from the Lord, and he has sent out a siege among the nations: Arise, and let us rise up against her for war." In these words he explains to us the whole purpose of his prophecy, that is, of his vision, and makes clear what it looks toward. He seeks to assure us that his vision concerns what is about to happen to Idumea. He confirms his hearers in faith and tries to persuade them that what is spoken will come to pass in every way and without fail, saying that the words are not his own at all, but rather God's. He says, then, that he heard a report from God against Idumea. And what this should be taken to mean he made clear at once by adding that "he has sent out a siege among the nations." Which nations? Those of Idumea. For he says that the siege, that is, the investment or blockade, has been sent against them, as the divine judgment forces them by necessity to suffer desolation.

Or it may be taken another way: he has commanded the nations around Idumea to lay the siege. He did not command them in so many words, but stirred them up, as God does, and sharpened them against the Idumeans. Persuaded by the divine prompting, these nations all but cry out eagerly to one another: "Arise, and let us rise up against her for war." For the surrounding nations also joined in the invasion alongside those of Israel who were ravaging Idumea.

"Behold, I have made you least among the nations; you are utterly dishonored. The pride of your heart has lifted you up, you who dwell in the clefts of the rocks, who make his dwelling on high, saying in his heart, 'Who will bring me down to the ground?' Though you soar like an eagle and set your nest among the stars, from there I will bring you down, says the Lord."

He says that Edom has been made least among the nations and dishonored because they became very few in number when compared with the multitude of those attacking them; for, as I said, a great many were sharpened against them. Or he says they became the least because the war consumed them and reduced their race to a very few. The prophetic word hints to us that the Idumean, out of great folly, was puffed up with empty conceit. He thought his enemies would find him hard to capture, not because of any strength of his own or skill in war, but because the roughness and inaccessibility of his land would be enough to keep them safe. For everywhere there were ridges, rocky peaks overhanging fearfully, wild hills and lofty mountains. Why then, he says, do you vainly boast against the hand of those who attack you? Even if you dwell in a land that is largely impassable and raised on high, even if you became an eagle, as it were, with its nest in the air (the language, again, is hyperbolic), you will still be hurled down from there, as God drags you down; for nothing at all is impossible for him.

"If thieves had come to you, or robbers by night, where would you have been cast away? Would they not have stolen only enough for themselves? And if grape-gatherers had come to you, would they not have left gleanings? How Esau has been searched out, and his hidden things seized!"

We have already said that the men of other races who invaded and attacked alongside those of Israel searched the ravines of the mountains, the caves, the clefts in the rocks and the thickets, and slaughtered the Idumeans, so that very few, or none at all, managed to escape. So the word mocks them and speaks, as it were, with irony, saying: If you had experienced a robbers' raid, and bands of thieves had descended on you, would they not have been content to take what would likely satisfy them? And if some people had stripped you like a vine, would not the gleanings have escaped the eye of the harvesters, sharp as it is? But this was bound to happen to them even against their will. For thieves, fear always urges flight and getting away unnoticed, and whatever they can snatch of what lies to hand seems enough to please them. For grape-gatherers, the leaves always get in the way of their search, covering and concealing whatever can escape notice. But you, he says, O Esau, that is, O Idumean of Esau's blood, have suffered worse: your hidden things were seized, no one escaped, and flight was useless, as was the very ruggedness of the terrain.

"They sent you out as far as your borders; all the men of your covenant opposed you; your men of peace prevailed against you; those who ate with you laid snares beneath you; there is no understanding in them. In that day, says the Lord, I will destroy the wise from Idumea and understanding from Mount Esau. And your warriors from Teman shall be dismayed, so that every man may be cut off from Mount Esau, because of the slaughter and the impiety against your brother Jacob. Shame shall cover you, and you shall be cut off forever, from the day you stood opposite him, on the day when foreigners were taking his forces captive, and strangers entered his gates and cast lots over Jerusalem, and you were like one of them."

When those of Esau's blood wanted to stop those of Israel from building the temple and rebuilding the walls of the holy city, they made pacts of common purpose with the surrounding nations, as we have already said. But when their own land came to be captured as those of Israel campaigned against it, then even those who had formerly been their true friends, fellow conspirators and comrades in arms became more oppressive than all the rest, ravaging the land and fighting. So the war, he says, sent you out as far as your borders, that is, caused you to vanish, for that is the meaning of "sent out." It did not merely break into parts of your land, but took the whole of it by force and brought it to desolation right up to its very borders. And they opposed you, he says, and fought against you, those who might very well have been expected, by your hopes at least, even to grieve with you in your suffering. But those from whom you expected to be saved laid snares beneath you. In "There is no understanding in him" a meaning such as this is conveyed. They used to call "wise" and "understanding" the false prophets and charlatans, the deceivers and augurs, and those who pour out false little tales about the stars, people who have reached such a pitch of nonsense as to suppose foolishly that from the stars they can obtain knowledge of the future. Those devoted to the worship of idols were greatly excited by such things. The Idumeans too suffered from this sickness along with the others. When the war was about to be declared, they considered how things would turn out. Gathering those who were wise in these matters, they ordered them to declare which way the war would go for them. These, as is likely, foretold victory for them. But they were captured and fell, their art having failed them, and the wretches were shown to be utterly without understanding and to have spoken falsely. That the men of Teman, though formerly bold (and these again are the Idumeans), would become cowardly and full of fear, he indicated by adding: "Your warriors from Teman shall be dismayed, so that every man may be cut off from Mount Esau," that is, until those of Idumea perish down to the last one. He then sets out plainly the cause of the calamity brought upon them: "because of the slaughter and the impiety against your brother." Since you killed, he says, the one closely related to you by blood, that is, Jacob, or rather those descended from Jacob, you will be consumed by war and utterly destroyed, full of shame and disgrace. That what befell them would never be undone, and that they would remain in such terrible calamities, he declared by saying: "And you shall be cut off forever." In "from the day" he recalls the time when the Babylonians had captured Judea, were plundering its goods and were dividing by lot what had been gathered from Jerusalem. The Idumeans themselves then lay in wait for the fugitives and slaughtered them, and as it were worked together with the foreigners who were carrying off the descendants of Jacob into captivity. So they were caught gloating over the calamities of their brothers and yielding little to the Babylonians in savagery.

"And do not look upon the day of your brother in the day of strangers, and do not rejoice over the sons of Judah in the day of their destruction, and do not speak boastfully in the day of affliction, nor enter the gates of peoples in the day of their sufferings; nor look upon their gathering, you too, in the day of their ruin, nor join in the attack on their forces in the day of their destruction; do not stand at their crossings to destroy those of them who escape, nor shut in those of them who flee in the day of affliction."

Once more he enumerates the crimes of the Idumeans, showing that they had been harsh and pitiless. The passage is framed as though God were calling out to them while they are already being struck and tormented, and were reproaching them for the kind of sin they had committed. "To look upon" means to laugh at and gloat over brothers in distress, and to make the calamities of others an occasion for delight, even though divine Scripture says that one must not smile at all at those who suffer. In "do not rejoice" and what follows, he again enumerates the crimes of the Idumean, showing him to have been harsh and pitiless, and that toward his brothers. Do not, he says, rush inside the gates yourself just like the Assyrians, not lending a helping hand as to brothers, but rather intending to ravage. And do not look upon a gathering being miserably destroyed; nor add to the burden of those already sorely weighed down by you; nor be a snare to the fugitives, watching the crossings and setting nooses, so that no one caught by your lack of natural affection may be saved, even if he has escaped the sword of the enemies. Throughout, the passage accuses the Idumeans of inhumanity, so that the divine judgment may in turn be seen to be truly holy and beyond reproach, since those who committed such offenses are punished justly.

"For the day of the Lord is near upon all the nations. As you have done, so shall it be done to you; your recompense shall be returned upon your own head. For as you drank upon my holy mountain, all the nations shall drink wine; they shall drink and go down, and they shall be as though they had never been. But on Mount Zion there shall be salvation, and it shall be holy."

Again he foretells the time of the war, when the neighboring nations, gathered together with the Idumeans in the valley of Jehoshaphat, paid a bitter penalty. He calls it the day of the Lord, for it was God who handed over to those of [?] the people who had wickedly wronged them. That they will be punished by a holy judgment he makes clear when he says: "As you have done, so shall it be done to you." For the divine nature weighs the faults of each, and in every case brings a penalty equal to the offenses of which each is found guilty. In "for as you drank" he indicates something like this. It is perhaps customary for those who have conquered their enemies to boast over the vanquished, to hold feasts and drinking parties, to raise shouts of victory and to carry out the works of drunkenness. Just as you mocked, he says, and capered in triumph over those of Israel, drinking and dancing and making the calamities of your brothers an occasion for festivity, so all the nations will drink and dance in triumph over you. And they will go down against you, that is, they will overrun your land. And you yourself will be counted among those who do not exist; for you will be destroyed so completely that it will seem you never existed at all. The divinely inspired Scripture calls the Church "Mount Zion"; for it is truly lofty and truly a watchtower, and holy besides, since it is the house and city of the all-holy God.

"And the house of Jacob shall take possession of those who took possession of them; and the house of Jacob shall be a fire, and the house of Joseph a flame, and the house of Esau stubble; and they shall be kindled among them and devour them, and there shall be no fire-bearer left to the house of Esau, for the Lord has spoken. And those in the Negeb [?] Mount Esau, and those [?] the foreigners; and they shall take possession of Mount Ephraim and the plain of Samaria, and Benjamin, and Gilead."

The senseless Idumean thought he would have the house of Jacob, that is, those of Jacob's seed, as his allotted portion, and he actually divided up their land among his people after helping to ravage it. But for them, he says, the situation will be unexpectedly reversed: they will become the allotted portion of those from Jacob. They will be consumed like stubble by a flame. For the whole of Jacob will be a fire, and the house of Joseph will yield nothing to the power of a flame. So they will be devoured entirely, so that not a single fire-bearer could be found from a whole tribe or nation. The passage seems to say "fire-bearer" in keeping with the figure, since it called the house of Jacob a fire and Joseph a flame. By the house of Jacob may be understood those of Judah and Benjamin, and by the house of Joseph those in Samaria, that is, the ten tribes, whose kings in their time came from the tribe of Ephraim; and Manasseh and Ephraim were both descended from Joseph. In "those in the Negeb shall take possession" the following is meant. When the Babylonians left their homeland and marched against Jerusalem, with Nebuchadnezzar rousing them to battle, it necessarily followed that the whole land of the Jews was ravaged and reduced to such misery that it lay utterly desolate and was seen stripped of its inhabitants. But when God took pity on them, loosed the bonds of captivity and they were brought back to their own land, he says that they would expand so greatly and grow into so populous a multitude as even to occupy the lands of the neighboring nations, since Judea, naturally, would be too cramped for them. This would be a very clear sign of blessing from God. For "those in the Negeb," he says, that is, those toward the south (for Negeb is interpreted as "south"), will take Mount Esau, that is, Idumea, as their allotted portion. Since it lies to the south, those who live in the southern parts of Judea will certainly occupy it, as it neighbors and borders on them. And those in the Shephelah, that is, in the lowland (this too is a part of the land of the Jews, lying somewhat farther north), will take possession of the foreigners. By these he means the Philistines, that is, the Palestinians. They will equally hold Mount Ephraim, Samaria, Benjamin and Gilead. These were the allotments distributed to the tribes of Israel long ago, when Joshua, Moses' successor, was their commander. But since they had been laid waste by the Assyrians, by the kings Pul and Shalmaneser, even before Nebuchadnezzar arrived, he says that these too will be inhabited and will shake off the desolation that befell them long ago.

"And this is the dominion of the exiles for the sons of Israel: the land of the Canaanites as far as Zarephath; and the exiles of Jerusalem as far as Ephratha; and they shall take possession of the cities of the Negeb. And men who have been saved shall go up from Mount Zion to take vengeance on Mount Esau, and the kingdom shall be the Lord's."

By "the exiles" he here means those of Jerusalem, or rather of all Judea, who had been deported to Babylon. He says that their dominion will be the allotted territory that will be under their hand and authority, just as one might perhaps speak of a ruler and say "the dominion of so-and-so." So, he says, those who were formerly deported will have as their dominion and allotment the land of the Canaanites (by which he means Arabia), and as far as Zarephath, which belongs to the territory of Sidon, so that by this you may understand Phoenicia. And it will extend, he says, even to Ephratha, or, as the other translators have rendered it, as far as the Bosporus, that is, the most southerly parts of the east. They will also bring under their control the cities of the Negeb, that is, of the south. By these words the passage seems to indicate to us the nations of India, for the Indians and their lands are the most southerly.
