It is as though one were to say: Everything will be full of them, to the south, to the north, to the east and to the west, and they will hold every city and land without exception. In "And men shall go up" he in a way sums up the purpose of the prophecy. For the inhabitants of Zion, he says, saved by God and having burst the bonds of captivity, will in time go up and take vengeance on the mountain of [?]. For, as I said, they fought against the Idumeans after the time of the captivity. And the God of all reigned over them, although he had long rejected them and had departed from Judea because of their apostasy; for they had worshiped idols and the golden heifers. But when they returned, he received them again and reigned over them. For the Master loves humankind and is kind, and is easily reconciled with those who offend him, if only we show some small turning toward him. To him be glory forever. Amen.
COMMENTARY BY THE SAME AUTHOR ON THE PROPHET JONAH

The divinely inspired Jonah was born of his father Amittai, but he came from Gath-hepher. This was a small town in the land of the Jews, or most likely a village. He seems to have delivered the words of his prophecy at the same time as those before him, I mean Hosea, Micah and the rest. Anyone can see that he gave a great many oracles to the people of the Jews. He conveyed words from above, from God, and clearly foretold what was to come. Yet no other written record of his prophecy exists besides this one. But divinely inspired Scripture testifies that he kept foretelling to the flocks of the Jews what would happen in their times. In the fourth book of Kingdoms the sacred text speaks about Jeroboam. This is not the Jeroboam at the beginning, the son of Nebat, who made Israel sin, as it is written, by persuading them to worship the golden calves. It is another Jeroboam, who came many generations later. The text makes clear what the blessed Jonah foretold, saying: "He restored the border of Israel from the entrance of Hamath to the sea of the Arabah, according to the word of the Lord, the God of Israel, which he spoke by the hand of his servant Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet from Gath-hepher. For the Lord saw the affliction of Israel, which was very bitter: they were very few, hard pressed, reduced and forsaken, and there was no one to help Israel. And the Lord had not said that he would blot out their seed from under heaven, and he saved them from the hand of Jeroboam son of Joash." It says "from the hand" instead of "by the hand." For Jeroboam son of Joash, as I said, made war on the foreigners. He brought back under his own rule cities of the land of the Jews that had been plundered, and he helped the Israelites in no small measure. God was shielding them and wished to save them, even though they had reached the end of the worst misery of all. So the blessed Jonah received other prophetic words at various times as well. But what is recorded about him here was recorded usefully and by divine design. The matter is well worth hearing, I mean his preaching to the Ninevites and what he suffered in between. In a way it also sketches, as in shadows, the mystery of our Saviour's incarnation. Indeed, Christ himself said when speaking to the Jews: "An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah the prophet. For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea monster three days and nights, so too the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights."

So the mystery of Christ is depicted for us, and in a way given shape, in the story of the divinely inspired Jonah. But I think I must say this to those who will read this work. Spiritual contemplation often takes a person set before us as a figure of Christ, the Saviour of us all. When it does, the wise and learned interpreter must judge which features should be set aside as useless for the purpose at hand. He must also judge which are useful and necessary, and best suited to benefit the hearers. Take, for example, the blessed Moses. He presented Israel to God at the foot of Mount Sinai and became a mediator between God and men. The Israelites were afraid and begged him, saying, "You speak to us, and let not God speak to us, lest we die." God the Father himself taught that this clearly prefigured the mediation through Christ, when he said: "They have rightly said all that they have spoken. I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers." This means one who would mediate, present the human race to God, and announce the ineffable will of God the Father to people throughout the whole earth. "For I will put my words in his mouth, and he will speak to them everything I command." So the divinely inspired Moses was taken as a type of Christ. But we will not attach everything about Moses to Christ as well, or we will be caught doing and saying something absurd. Moses admitted that he was weak of voice, slow of tongue and unfit for the mission. He said: "I am weak of voice and slow of tongue. I have not been eloquent before yesterday or the day before, nor since you began to speak to your servant." And he pleaded: "I beg you, Lord, choose someone else who is able, whom you will send." But Christ is not slow of tongue or weak of voice as Moses was. Rather, he himself is the great trumpet. This is the name the blessed prophet Isaiah gave him when he said, "And on that day they will blow the great trumpet." For the Saviour's word is proclaimed everywhere and has been heard throughout all that lies under heaven. Knowing this, the blessed David said: "The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken and summoned the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting."

So Moses mediates as a type of Christ, but when he is slow of speech he no longer shows the type in himself. The blessed Aaron, too, was taken as a figure of Emmanuel. He was crowned with the glories of the high priesthood, entered the Holy of Holies, and wore that glorious and admirable vestment. But again, we will not ascribe everything about him to Christ, for he was not entirely blameless. He was once rebuked for speaking against Moses together with Miriam. He was also to blame in another way, when Israel made the calf in the wilderness. So not everything in the letter and in the types is useful for spiritual contemplation. When the figure of someone who represents Christ to us in himself is brought forward, we will rightly pass over the merely human features. We will dwell only on what is necessary, and in every case turn what is beneficial toward the purpose at hand. This is how we will understand the divinely inspired Jonah too, for he gives shape, as it were, to the mystery of Christ for us.

However, not everything that happened to him should be considered useful and necessary for this purpose. For instance, he was sent to preach to the Ninevites, but he tried to flee from the presence of God and is seen shrinking from the mission. The Son, too, was sent by God the Father to preach to the nations, but he was not unwilling to serve. Nor did he try to flee from the presence of God the Father. The prophet urged those on board, saying, "Pick me up and throw me into the sea, and the sea will grow calm for you." He was swallowed by the sea monster and given up again on the third day. After this he went to Nineveh and fulfilled his ministry. But he was greatly grieved when God took pity on the people of Nineveh. Christ, too, willingly underwent death. He remained in the heart of the earth three days and three nights and came back to life. After this he went away into Galilee and ordered the preaching to the nations to begin. He commanded the disciples to make disciples of "all the nations, and to baptize them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." But [?] he did not grieve at seeing them saved through repentance, as the blessed Jonah certainly did. So if we do not turn every part of the story toward the purpose of spiritual contemplation, let no one find fault. Bees fly over meadows and flowers and always gather what is useful for building their honeycombs. In the same way, the wise interpreter searches the holy and divinely inspired Scripture. He always gathers and puts together whatever helps to explain the mysteries of Christ, and so he will produce a well-shaped account that is beyond reproach. Let us begin our exposition here, then.
And the word of the Lord came to Jonah son of Amittai, saying: Arise and go to Nineveh, the great city, and preach in it, for the cry of its wickedness has come up to me.

When we consider Jonah's prophetic ministry and mission, we might very fittingly quote at this point what is proclaimed through the voice of the blessed Paul: "Or is God the God of the Jews only? Is he not the God of the Gentiles too? Yes, of the Gentiles too, since God is one, and he will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith." The divinely inspired Peter himself also proclaimed this to us from experience, saying: "Truly I perceive that God shows no partiality, but in every nation whoever fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him." For he himself created earth and heaven and all that is in them. In the beginning he made man in his own image and likeness. His purpose was that man, devoted to the pursuit of virtue, might live gloriously in holiness and blessedness and have a rich share in God's gifts. Then man was led astray into sin, deceived by the devil's wiles, and for this reason he became accursed and subject to corruption. Christ, then, was foreordained and foreknown before the foundation of the world for the restoration of all things. For God the Father was pleased "to sum up all things in him, things in heaven and things on earth." Such achievements were reserved for the Only-Begotten when he became like us and shone upon the world in the flesh. Yet even before the time of his coming, God considered it necessary to care for those who had gone astray. He granted his visitation to those who had slipped through ignorance, and he wished to make this certain through actual events as well. That is why he commanded the blessed prophet to go to Nineveh. Nineveh is a famous city lying toward the east, and, as the prophet Jeremiah says, "It is a land of carved images." There were very many cities bordering on the land of the Jews, and they were devoted to the worship of idols. "Tyre and Sidon and all Galilee of the foreigners" were devoted to the works of their own hands. Among them were shrines, altars and sacred precincts of countless demons.

Tell me, then: why does he pass over the neighbouring cities and send the prophet to Nineveh, which lay farthest away? As I have already said, its people were above all a savage multitude who had given themselves without restraint to the belief that they must worship the sun, the stars and fire. Beyond all reason, the city was carried away into sorcery hateful to God. For it is said of it through the voice of Jeremiah: "A beautiful and charming harlot, mistress of sorceries." I think, then, that God, who knows all things, wished to show even the people of old, for their benefit, a further truth. Even those who have strayed very far and are caught in the snares of error will in due time be drawn in the net to the knowledge of the truth. This holds even if they are exceedingly fierce and hard and have gone very far in unruliness. For the word of God has power enough to nourish the mind and persuade it to learn the things that make one wise. You will hear him saying to Jeremiah at one time, "Behold, I have put my words in your mouth as fire, and this people as wood, and it will devour them." At another time he says, "Are not my words like a blazing fire, says the Lord, and like an axe that splits rock?" So the divinely inspired Jonah was not sent to the Ninevites in vain. He was sent so that there might be an advance demonstration of the gentleness in God, which would in due time be granted even to those who had gone astray through ignorance. At the same time, what was done served to condemn Israel. Israel was exposed as hard to lead, disobedient, and caring little for God's laws. A single prophet preached to the Ninevites, and they were at once transformed and chose to repent, even though they were deeply sick with error. The Israelites, however, ignored Moses and the prophets. They even despised Christ, the Saviour of us all, although he added wonders to his teachings. Through these wonders they could reasonably, and very easily, have been persuaded that he was God by nature and had become man. He came to save all that is under heaven, and them before all others. Christ himself will make clear that this would very rightly serve to convict the Israelites, when he says: "The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, because they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here." But how is Christ greater than Jonah? Jonah only threatened the Ninevites with destruction. Our Lord Jesus Christ, however, astonished people with ineffable wonders and was marvelled at, and a miracle that accompanies the word always draws people to faith. So it was by a most wise design that the blessed Jonah was sent to proclaim to those living in Nineveh that the cry of their wickedness had gone up to the God of all. God is ignorant of nothing whatever. But when he is moved to deal with the offences some have committed, he then says that the outcry from their deeds has come up to him. For as God he is the judge of all. In the same way, Abel's blood is said to have cried out against Cain's murder, and the savagery of the cities of Sodom against their shameful deeds.

And Jonah arose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord. He went down to Joppa and found a ship going to Tarshish, and he paid his fare and went on board, to sail with them to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord.

Joppa is a city of Palestine lying right on the sea. It is a convenient port for people from Judea setting out by sea, especially to cities toward the east. So the prophet goes down and finds a ship setting sail for Tarshish, since that was presumably the ship's planned course. He paid the fare and sailed off with the others. By Tarshish he means the place now called Tarsi, or Tarsus. Some think it refers to a city among the Ethiopians and Indians, and admittedly there is a Tarshish among them. In fact, the whole land of the Indians is signified by "Tarshish." But I do not think the text means that here. Anyone wishing to sail to the nations of India would naturally not sail from Joppa but rather by way of the Red Sea. Perhaps someone might suppose that the prophet wanted to escape through Persia and Assyria to the innermost Ethiopians. But I think that is utterly foolish. So, as I said, by Tarshish he seems to mean present-day Tarsus. This is a city of the Cilicians that drinks the waters of the Cydnus and lies right at the foothills of the Taurus, a huge mountain of the Cilicians. At any rate, the prophet sets sail, and the purpose of his journey is to flee from the presence of God. Here we cannot leave the statement unexamined, or rather the manner of the flight. I think that to decline the mission and, as it were, to shrink from the ministry is what "fleeing from the presence of God" means.

But why he goes to Tarshish, and with what in mind, I cannot understand. Perhaps one might consider this: his conception of God was somewhat limited, as was also the case with the saints of earlier times. For some thought that the power of the God of all was bound to the land of the Jews alone. They thought he was confined there, as it were, and absent from the rest of the earth. Indeed, the divinely inspired Jacob once left his father's home and hurried to Laban in Mesopotamia. He camped for the night in a certain place, put a stone under his head as usual, and went to sleep. Then he saw the ladder reaching from earth to heaven, with the angels of God going up and down on it and the Lord standing above it. And when he rose up he said, "God is in this place, and I did not know it." So I think the blessed prophet had considered something of this kind. That is why he slipped away from Judea and departed for the Greek cities. As for the reason he shrank back and did not choose to fulfil the ministry eagerly, we will learn it from his own words. He did later go and preach. But when the prophecy did not come to pass, he was deeply grieved and said: "O Lord, were these not my words while I was still in my own land? That is why I hurried to flee to Tarshish, because I knew that you are merciful, patient and abounding in mercy, and that you relent from sending disaster. And now, Master and Lord, take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live." As a prophet, he was not ignorant of how his ministry would turn out. But he was afraid of what might happen when the things he proclaimed were not fulfilled. The Ninevites might fail to recognize the kindness of the God who had pitied them. They might then do away with him and kill him as a charlatan, a deceiver and a liar who had persuaded them to toil for nothing. For barbarians are always prone to anger and very quick to turn savage, even when they have no reasonable excuse for their fury.

And the Lord stirred up a great wind on the sea, and a great storm arose on the sea, and the ship was in danger of breaking apart. The sailors were afraid, and each of them cried out to his own god. They threw the cargo that was in the ship into the sea to lighten it for themselves.

A storm rises against the ship, as God arranges it and churns up the sea with savage blasts of wind. Fear falls on the seafarers, and now their very lives are at stake. The vessel was presumably creaking and all but threatening that it was about to break apart. The crew resorts to the usual remedies and unloads the ship, so that it might ride high above the waves and be carried more easily on the water. A clear proof of how severe the storm was is that even the sailors were struck with fear. They begged their own gods most earnestly to come and save them, as if they had already given up hope of being saved.

But Jonah had gone down into the hold of the ship and was sleeping and snoring. The captain came to him and said to him, "Why are you snoring? Get up and call on your god, so that God may save us and we may not perish."

Prophetic watchfulness would hardly be suited to laziness in prayer while dangers hang overhead. Nor would it be suited to lying idle when the time and the situation call for effort, when it would be more fitting to appease the God of all. From this we may understand that the sleep came before the storm. Going down into the very hold of the ship is the mark of someone accustomed to deep quiet. For the saints always love and eagerly seek to withdraw from turmoil, keep away from crowds and live alone. As the divinely inspired prophet Jeremiah says, "It is good for a man when he bears a yoke from his youth. He will sit alone, because he has taken it upon himself." And again he cried out about the multitude of the disobedient: "Lord Almighty, I did not sit in the company of those who make merry, but I stood in awe before your hand. I sat alone, because I was filled with bitterness." Sitting alone, I think, signifies the quiet life. It means being free from the cares and anxieties of this life, and not mixing with others who have prized a life of pleasure and the flesh. So the prophet dozes off, not neglecting what was fitting, but, as I have already said, before the onset of the storm. The captain, however, prods him awake, telling him that he must call upon his God. For people in danger are always annoyed when others seem to be above fear and give way to idleness at the wrong time.
And each one said to his neighbour, "Come, let us cast lots and find out on whose account this evil has come upon us." So they cast lots, and the lot fell on Jonah.

The seafarers devise something very curious, unusual and strange: they hurry to find out by lot the one with whom God is displeased. But this too is arranged for a good purpose. It exposes the man who thought he could flee from the presence of God, for the lot falls on him, and he is seen to be convicted by the event itself. He was presumably afraid to condemn his own scheme too readily. So for those who wish to observe it, this saying is good and wise: "Do not be ashamed to confess your sins."

And they said to him, "Tell us on whose account this evil has come upon us. What is your occupation? Where do you come from and where are you going? From what country and from what people are you?" And he said to them, "I am a servant of the Lord, and I worship the Lord, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land." The men were seized with great fear and said to him, "What is this that you have done?" For the men knew that he was fleeing from the presence of the Lord, because he had told them.

Their questions serve a purpose. They have already found the one responsible by lot, but they cannot yet see clearly what kind of offense he has committed. Since they were idolaters, they told him to say what his occupation was, what his country and city were, and from what people he came. They wanted, I think, to learn which god he had offended. For each of those on board had his own god; there was not one God of all. They thought that if they appeased the demon who had been offended by him, they would ward off the harm the storm threatened. But when the prophet named himself a servant of God, who fashioned earth and heaven, and said that he worshipped him, they understood at once that he had fled from the presence of God. How did they understand this? Because Jews were not permitted to separate themselves from the land allotted to them, or to visit foreigners, or to enter cities given to idolatry. Among them such a thing was a disgrace, and it did not escape suspicion of apostasy. It was even thought to be outside the law and to deserve blame and punishment. And indeed our Lord Jesus Christ clearly affirmed that they would fall away from his salvation (I mean the salvation that comes by faith) unless they chose to lay hold of him while he was still present and living in the world. For he said: "I am with you a little while longer, and then I go to him who sent me. You will seek me and will not find me, and where I am, you cannot come." But they, taking it as a reproach that Jews should go off to the Gentiles, said in their ignorance: "Where is this man about to go, that we will not find him? Is he about to go to the Dispersion among the Greeks and teach the Greeks?" To them it was something outlandish and out of the ordinary, as far as possible from their own customs, and so they treated mixing with the peoples of the Greeks as a disgrace. So, since he had not stayed within the borders of Judea but was sailing with them to Tarshish, the sailors grew suspicious. They concluded that he was perhaps renouncing life under the law and had given himself over to the customs of the Greeks, and so had planned his flight as if from the presence of God.

And they said to him, "What shall we do to you, so that the sea will calm down for us?" For the sea was running high and stirring up still more of a storm. And Jonah said to them, "Pick me up and throw me into the sea, and the sea will calm down for you; for I know that it is because of me that this great storm has come upon you."

They fear the sea raging against them beyond endurance, yet they dread the God of the Hebrews no less. Though they were foreigners, they were not ignorant of his power and glory. And since he said he was a servant of God, they are at a loss, and their opinions are divided. They shrink from killing him, wary of the wrath of the all-powerful God. But as the sea kept leaping upon them as fiercely as before, they had to look to their own safety. So they beg him to tell them what they should do so that the storm would be lulled, the waves would subside, and they would escape the deadly danger. What then does the prophet do? He confesses his offense. Having offended, he is ashamed, and he condemns his own bad decision: "Pick me up," he says, "and throw me into the sea." He all but said that they ought to exact from him the penalty for shrinking from his mission. For he knew that the storm would somehow make its peace with the ship if it got the one it was seeking, and that the sea would leave off its battle once it had the offender.

And the men strained hard to get back to land, and could not, because the sea was running high and rising still more against them. And they cried out to the Lord and said, "By no means, Lord! Do not let us perish for this man's life, and do not lay innocent blood upon us; for you, Lord, have done as you wished." And they took Jonah and threw him into the sea, and the sea ceased from its raging.

The prophet had passed sentence of death on himself and thought it right to end their fear at the cost of his own life. But they were still very much afraid and reluctant to shed blood. They wanted to save him, since he was a servant of God, and to put him ashore alive, thinking that this was a better way to rid themselves of the wrath. So they strained to run the ship aground. But their efforts could not succeed, for the wind raised the waves against them beyond all resistance and swept down on the vessel with fiercer blasts. So at last they try to appease God with prayer and beg him to forgive them. They did not want to kill; they were yielding to his judgments, and in the end they were forced to give Jonah to the sea. And give him they did. The sea, once it had received him, made its peace, though barely. It spread out in calm and gave the sailors hope of being saved. The events themselves showed that it yields to the divine will in everything and swiftly carries out the Master's commands.
And the men feared the Lord with a great fear, and they offered a sacrifice to the Lord and made vows.

They have gained a great deal. They believe that the one who is by nature God is one, although they had been divided by outlandish error and thought that there were countless gods throughout the world. So they sacrifice to the one who alone is God by nature and truly. They abandon their own gods and say goodbye to those that deceit had honored, which steal the glory due to God. They also make vows, though they were used to doing this to the demons of the sea. For the children of the Greeks think that power over the sea also belongs to a certain Poseidon. Everything they have is myth, trickery and dreadful madness. But we glorify the one who is by nature God, and we say to him truly: "You rule the might of the sea, and you calm the surging of its waves. Yours are the [heavens?], and yours is the earth; you founded the world and all that fills it."
And the Lord commanded a great sea monster to swallow Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the sea monster three days and three nights.

God commands the sea monster simply by willing it. When he wills that something be accomplished, that is law and fulfilment, and it has the force of law. For we do not say that the God of all gave orders to the sea monster as he does to us, or to the holy angels, somehow sounding in the mind what is to be done and placing in hearts the knowledge of what he wills. It is utterly foolish, and not far from madness, to think that the God of all deals with beasts in any such way. Rather, whenever he is said to command irrational animals, or the elements, or any part of creation, we say that his good pleasure is law and command. For all things yield to his will. The manner of their obedience is wholly beyond our telling, but he knows it perfectly. So Jonah is swallowed by the sea monster without suffering any harm, and he was inside it three days and three nights.

Perhaps the matter may seem to some rather unseemly and beyond what reason finds fitting. Above all, those who do not know the one who is by nature and truly God, but are devoted to the deceits of demons, will refuse to believe it. They will say: "How could he have been kept safe inside a sea monster? How was he not destroyed when he was swallowed? How did he endure the heat inside it? Surrounded by so much fluid, I mean the fluid in the belly, how did he survive? Or rather, how was he not stewed and consumed like food? For flesh is very weak and all too ready to decay." We reply that what happened may rightly be considered truly marvelous, beyond reason and ordinary experience. But if God is said to have accomplished it, who will still stand against it [?]? For the divine is all-powerful. It easily reshapes the natures of things into whatever it chooses, and nothing resists its ineffable will. What is by nature corruptible would become superior even to corruption if he willed it; and what is firm and unshakable and beyond the reach of the laws of corruption would easily suffer corruption. For, I think, the nature of existing things is whatever seems good to the Creator. But this too should be noted: the children of the Greeks, in composing their own myths, say that Heracles, the son of Alcmene and Zeus, was swallowed by a sea monster and then given back again from its inner heat with his head made bald, having lost nothing but his hair. Lycophron, one of their select writers, mentions the story. He says of him: "the lion of the three nights, whom once Triton's jagged-toothed hound devoured in its jaws."

But we do not draw our confidence in divine things from the tales told among them. We have recalled this for a useful purpose, to refute the unbelievers, since even their own accounts do not reject stories of this kind. And since I think it necessary also to support this marvelous event with things that still happen by the will of God, come, let us point out that the embryo in the womb also floats in natural fluid and is buried, as it were, in the belly of the woman carrying it. It cannot breathe, and yet even so it lives and is preserved, marvelously nursed by the will of God. But no reasoning can reach such things, and the things of God cannot be grasped by anyone. "For who has known the mind [of the Lord?]," as it is written? Or who could know the ways of marvels? Or what mind would not be surpassed by things that outrun the power of reason? It is dangerous, then, to disbelieve, even when God does something far beyond reason. Instead let us accept it as true and set aside untimely scrutiny.

Since the blessed prophet has been taken as a type of the ministry we understand to be in Christ, I must add the following. The whole earth was in danger, and human affairs were tossed by the storm. The waves of sin were all but leaping upon it, a terrible and unbearable pleasure was flooding all around, corruption was rising like a swell, and savage winds were bursting upon it, I mean the devil and the evil powers under him and with him. While we were in this state, the Creator took pity. God the Father sent us his Son from heaven. He came to be in the flesh and arrived on the endangered, storm-tossed earth, and he gave himself up to death of his own will, so that he might still the storm, so that the sea might calm down, the waves be lulled and the swell subside. For we have been saved by the death of Christ. The winter is past, the rain has gone, the waves have been smoothed, the violence of the winds is broken, a deep calm now lies spread out, and we enjoy spiritual fair weather, because Christ suffered for us. You will find something like this in the Gospels. Once the apostles' boat was crossing the Sea of Tiberias. Then a violent wind fell upon the waters, and they were tossed beyond endurance. Facing deadly danger, they woke Christ, who was with them, asleep, crying out plainly, "Master, save us; we are perishing!" And he, it says, awoke and rebuked the sea, saying with authority, "Silence! Be still!" and he saved the disciples. What happened was a type of what befell human nature. For through him, as I said, we have been set free from death, corruption, sin and the passions. The old storm has been driven away, and our condition has changed to calm.
And Jonah prayed to the Lord his God from the belly of the sea monster, and said: "I cried out in my distress to the Lord my God, and he heard me. From the belly of Hades you heard my cry, my voice."

He has suffered no harm. He is using the sea monster like a house. He is in his right mind, and neither his body nor his mind has been injured in any way, and so he perceives that he has been helped. He knows that God has been gracious to him. He knows too that what happened came from his shrinking from his ministry. So he turns to prayer and lifts up prayers of thanksgiving. At the same time he confesses the glory of the one who saves, marvels at his authority and proclaims his gentleness. For he said that his prayer had been received, and he understood this, I think, through the prophetic Spirit. "From the belly of Hades" means, so to speak, from the stomach of the sea monster. He aptly likens the beast to Hades and death, since it knows how to kill and savagely gulp down whatever it catches.
"You cast me into the depths of the heart of the sea, and rivers surrounded me; all your surges and your waves passed over me. And I said, 'I have been driven away from your sight.'"

He describes what happened in many ways, lifting up the grace he received, so to speak, and bearing witness that the divine will can easily save from every evil. He says that he was in the very depths of the sea and in a turmoil of many waters, which flooded over him like river currents, and that he sank so low in misfortune that he finally thought God's eyes had turned away from him completely, and he came to despair of being saved. It is an utterly dreadful thing, a thing that brings ruin, to be out of God's sight. That is why the divine David pleaded, saying, "Do not turn your face away from me, and do not turn aside in anger from your servant." Suffering the divine wrath must surely follow such turning away. Or rather, the anger rises first and comes before the turning away. "Shall I look again toward your holy temple?" He knows that he has been preserved by God's power, and that he has survived and been saved because he was granted help from above, and this inside a sea monster, in a beast's belly, marvelously and beyond reason. Yet he doubts, naturally enough, whether he will be given up and come out into the light again. To enter the divine temple itself and offer songs of praise to the God who saved him is something he longs for intensely and prays for earnestly. He prays to obtain this grace, and so, as I said, he bears witness that God can accomplish all things.

"Water poured around me up to my soul; the deepest abyss surrounded me; my head sank into the clefts of the mountains. I went down into the earth, whose bars hold fast forever. Yet let my life come up from corruption to you, Lord my God."

Since God had saved him by his ineffable power, he wanted to send up still more splendid songs of thanksgiving. He recounts in full what happened. He explains in detail the misfortune that had trapped him, and then proclaims how he was saved. Being a prophet, he knew that he had been in the sea, in a vast abyss, and in the clefts of the mountains, since the sea monster was very likely diving among rocks and undersea caves. He says that he went down into the earth whose bars hold fast forever, that is, Hades. He does not mean that he was actually there, for we will not find that he died. He means that the greatness of the danger and the weight of what befell him were no less than if he had died and come to Hades itself, from which no one could leave and from which no one once caught could ever return. This, I think, is what the bars holding fast forever signify: they are unbreakable and have never yet been overcome or loosened by anyone. But that he did not die, but survived inside the sea monster, as I said, and was in it without suffering anything that leads to death or decay, is easily shown by the fact that he was hoping to be saved again. That is why he says, "Let my life come up from corruption, Lord my God." For he prays to be given up into the light and to be brought up from the sea monster's stomach as if from Hades.
"When my soul was failing within me, I remembered the Lord; and may my prayer come to you, to your holy temple."

For those who want to win approval, toil is not without profit, and affliction should not be thought a burden. The blessed David will testify to this, saying, "In affliction I called upon the Lord"; and another of the holy prophets says, "Lord, in affliction we remembered you." The divine Paul, too, was strongly inclined to welcome and praise affliction, meaning, of course, the affliction that comes for the sake of virtue. For he said: "Affliction produces endurance, endurance produces proven character, proven character produces hope, and hope does not put us to shame." So when the prophet's soul was failing, that is, when it was enduring the ordeal that brought him into danger and to the brink, once again he did something profitable. He did not, as some do, slip at once into despondency and rail against the divine judgments; he remembered the one who saves. He cried out to him and thirsted for his help. Knowing his gentleness and his surpassing strength, he made his supplications to him, begging that his life be rescued from death and corruption. It is a great and admirable thing, then, not to lose heart in hardship, but rather to appease the Master with entreaties and supplications, and to ask him to put off the evil and bring the misfortune to an end.

"Those who cling to [?] and false things have forsaken their mercy. But I will sacrifice to you with a voice of praise and thanksgiving; what I have vowed I will pay to you for my salvation, to the Lord."

"For others," he says, "do not know you, the Master of all, the Creator. Then they are caught in the snares of vanity and give their worship to falsely named gods. They chase flying birds, that is, the hope they place in those gods, and they herd the winds. They do not ask you for mercy, and they have never come to have any such hope. But I am not like them. How could I be? I know you as my helper, good and compassionate. Therefore with my voice and my prayer I will give thanks to you," he says, "and I will offer my songs like the most fragrant incense. I will bring you sacrifices of thanksgiving, spiritual ones, clearly: songs of praise and blessings. And I will fulfil, and most eagerly, my vows for my salvation, that is, whatever brings about my salvation and benefits my soul." This meant obedience in everything that pleases God, and the fulfilment of his prophetic ministry, with all reluctance and faintheartedness removed.

The prophet, then, prays while he is inside the sea monster. The type is human, but the true image of the matter, that is, Christ, appeared before the precious cross, when his suffering was all but upon him, saying to the Father in heaven, "If it is possible, let this cup pass from me." He became very fearful and was in distress. Whether he also said some human word when he had come to the regions beneath the earth, he himself would know; it is hazardous to say. But we shall find the divine Peter applying to him the words spoken through David: "For this reason you will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor will you let your holy one see corruption." For his flesh did not see corruption. He came to life on the third day, since it was not possible that he, who is life by nature, should be held by the bonds of death.
And the sea monster was commanded, and it cast Jonah out onto the dry land.

The sea monster is commanded again. It is moved by a divine and ineffable power of God to do what pleases him, and so it releases the prophet from its insides. His suffering had not been without profit. Rather, experience had sharpened him, and he had learned clearly how dangerous it is to oppose the Master's decrees.
And the word of the Lord came to Jonah a second time, saying, "Arise and go to Nineveh, the great city, and proclaim in it the proclamation I spoke to you before."

Now that Jonah was showing warmer eagerness, God again tells him to go to Nineveh and to use the same proclamation that had been given him at the beginning. That was: "For the cry of its wickedness has come up to me." I have already spoken about what concerns Christ, but I will speak of it again without hesitation. For it is written: "To repeat the same things is no trouble to me, and for you it is a safeguard." Before the precious cross, then, we shall find Christ still holding back in some way, I mean from setting forth the word of the gospel's divine oracles to the Gentiles as well. Indeed, he says most plainly, "I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." And he commanded the holy disciples themselves: "Do not go on the road to the Gentiles, and do not enter a Samaritan town; go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." But he was "in the heart of the earth three days and three nights." He came "to the springs of the sea and walked in the tracks of the abyss." He sank, as it were, into the clefts of the mountains and went down into the earth whose bars hold fast forever. Then he despoiled Hades, preached to the spirits there, threw open the gates that could not be moved, and came to life again. For his life came up from corruption, and so he was seen first of all by the women who were looking for him in the garden. Then he greeted them and told them to announce to the holy disciples that he was going ahead of them into Galilee. From then on his word went out to the Gentiles as well, through the blessed apostles. Then he preached to those who had gone astray, according to the [former?] proclamation. For he did not [?] instruct Israel with one set of commandments before his death and the Gentiles with another set afterwards. The gospel is one for all. The knowledge of the divine disciples is surely one as well, and it is no different for those from Israel and for us from the Gentiles, who have been called through faith to sanctification.

And Jonah arose and went to Nineveh, as the Lord had spoken. Now Nineveh was a city great in God's sight, about a three days' journey across. And Jonah began to go into the city, about a day's journey, and he proclaimed and said, "Three more days, and Nineveh will be overthrown."

The prophet is sent, and, girded with irresistible eagerness, he sets about what must be done. He enters, and with great vigour, into foreign Nineveh, to serve the divine commands. The city was wide and stretched to such a size that anyone who chose to go all the way round it would need a journey of three days, yet he passes through it in a single day; or, as others think, after covering a day's journey within it, he delivered the message of the divine proclamation. The prophet must surely have been a marvel: a Hebrew man, come from a foreign land and probably known to no one there, walking through the middle of the city, crying aloud and saying, "Yet three days, and Nineveh will be overthrown." Here again, look at this point and examine it closely. The God of all had commanded him to proclaim concerning Nineveh "that the cry of its wickedness has come up to me"; but the prophet, once he was in the city, cried, "Yet three days, and Nineveh…" What then shall we say? Does he speak falsely? Has he spoken things from his own heart, and not rather from the mouth of the Lord, as some claim? That is not what we say. We say rather that the prophets often indicate the manner of their mission, but they do not by any means pass on to us all the words that came to them from God, nor indeed all the words they spoke to God. That the Master said to him, "Arise and go to Nineveh and proclaim in it that the cry of its wickedness has come up to me," we heard clearly at the very beginning of the prophecy; but that Jonah himself said anything to God, we were not told. Yet we shall find him saying, "O Lord, were these not my words while I was still in my own land? That is why I hastened to flee to Tarshish, because I knew that you are merciful and compassionate." Do you see that most of it has been passed over in silence, and that things were said unrecorded both by God and likewise to God through the prophet's voice? It follows, then, that we should affirm that the words of the saints are true, for those who are rich in the Spirit of truth will hardly speak falsely.
And the men of Nineveh believed God, and made a proclamation, and put on sackcloth, from the least of them to the greatest.

The statement is emphatic. Those of Nineveh believed, it says; that is, the people of a city always condemned for every kind of outrage, where there was a great and countless swarm of idols, temples beyond number, and zeal for forbidden rites. Sorcery and false divination were what they held in honour; the man who turned a prying eye on the stars was thought exceedingly wise, and the man ready for any outrage whatever reached the height of renown. Yet they believed God, from the least to the greatest; that is, the eminent and the obscure, the illustrious and the despised, those awash in the luxuries of wealth and those drunk with the burden of poverty. All had a single aim: to be persuaded by the prophet's words. Great is the wonder, and very great the praise due to those who believed. For they follow at once and without delay the one who calls them to better things, and they bow a tender neck to the divine proclamation; and this when the one calling them to repentance was a foreigner, a single man, and not long known to them.

So much for the Ninevites. But senseless Israel disobeys the law, laughs at the writings of Moses, and counts the words of the prophets as nothing. And why do I say this? It even became the murderer of the Lord, refusing to obey even Christ himself, the Saviour of us all. So the Ninevites were in a better state, and the God of all showed this to be true when he spoke in this way to the blessed prophet Ezekiel: "Son of man, go, enter the house of Israel; not to many peoples of strange speech or strange tongue, nor heavy of tongue, whose words you would not understand. Had I sent you to such as these, they would have listened to you. But the house of Israel will not be willing to listen to you, because they do not wish to listen to me; for the whole house of Israel is contentious and hard of heart." Those of strange tongue, deep of lip and harsh of speech, that is, the Ninevites, honoured the oracle and turned to repentance without delay; but contentious Israel did not honour, as I said, even the very Master of the law and the prophets.

And the word reached the king of Nineveh, and he rose from his throne, took off his robe, put on sackcloth, and sat on ashes. And it was proclaimed and spoken in Nineveh by the king and by his nobles, saying, "Let neither people nor beasts nor oxen nor sheep taste anything; let them not graze, nor drink water." And people and beasts put on sackcloth, and they cried earnestly to God, and each turned from his evil way and from the injustice that was in their hands, saying, "Who knows whether God will repent and turn from the wrath of his anger, so that we do not perish?"

He heightens still further the praise of their obedience and marvels all the more at the readiness to obey of those called to repentance. Since they had given heed to the prophet's words, even the one honoured with the sceptre and crowned with the highest glories at once withdrew from the royal throne, bade farewell to the robes befitting him, stripped off the purple and put on sackcloth; that is, he put on the garb of mourning. And sitting down on ashes, he gave the signal to the others that they too must fast and, appeasing God with unceasing prayers, beg for mercy. The Ninevites were very wise, joining to their fasting a turning away from wickedness; for this alone would be the true and blameless way of repentance. Israel, however, lacked skill in these matters and sometimes displayed a most senseless and profane fast, and so God commanded the prophet to raise his voice on high and announce to them, "I have not chosen this fast, says the Lord." And he himself made known the reason, adding at once: "For on the days of your fasts you pursue your own wishes, and you goad all who are under your hand; you fast for lawsuits and quarrels, and you strike the lowly with your fists. Why do you fast for me as you do today, so that your voice is heard in an outcry? This is not the fast I have chosen, nor such a day for a person to humble his soul." So the Ninevites were better, offering God a pure and blameless fast. For the sacred text has testified that each turned from his evil way and from the injustice that was in their hands. What they did was done with reason and understanding, for they believed that God would repent and turn away the effects of his wrath. It says "will repent" in place of "will change his counsel": if he sees them pass over from wickedness to the good, he too will move over to the calm and kindness that are dearest to him. For he is good by nature. Yet he brings punishments on those who offend, and on those who have swerved uncontrollably into unbridled ways he brings the effects of his wrath like a kind of bridle, checking them as a whole and turning them to obedience. Observe how the Ninevites say, "Who knows whether God will repent and turn from the wrath of his anger, so that we do not perish?" whereas wise Israel, taught by the law that the Master is kind and gentle, cannot bring itself to think this way. In their ignorance they used to say, "Our errors and our iniquities are upon us, and we waste away in them; how then shall we live?" Yet they heard God saying plainly, "Turn, turn back from your evil way; why will you die, O house of Israel?" This is just what the Ninevites did, averting the wrath that hung over them by turning swiftly to better things. They even ordered that the beasts should grieve along with the people, deprived of food and drink and, as it were, forced to mourn. This was an extravagant act, not something that had to be done, nor as though God required this hardship of the beasts. The sacred text has recorded this too, showing, as I said, the extravagance of the Ninevites' repentance. I know, of course, that some are embarrassed by this and say that "beasts" must be understood as the most irrational among men. That is true, and it would on occasion be well for some to understand it in this way. But for the sense of the present passage the other view would perhaps fit better: namely, that the extravagance of the repentance is indicated by the hardship being imposed even on the beasts themselves.
And God saw their works, that they had turned from their evil ways; and God repented of the evil that he had said he would do to them, and he did not do it.

The Master is swift to mercy and saves those who repent. He releases them at once from their old charges, and when their sin has ceased, he too relaxes his wrath and changes his counsel to kindness. When he sees them changed toward the good, he passes over to gentleness, postpones the overthrow, and judges them worthy to be spared. For he speaks truly when he says, "Why will you die, O house of Israel? says the Lord. For I do not desire the death of the one who dies, says the Lord Adonai, so much as that he should turn from his way and his soul should live." When it says "evil," do not understand wickedness, but rather the wrath that inflicts harm. For our God, who loves virtue, is no worker of evils.

And Jonah was grieved with great grief and was confounded; and he prayed to the Lord and said, "O Lord, were these not my words while I was still in my own land? That is why I hastened to flee to Tarshish, because I knew that you are merciful and compassionate, long-suffering and abounding in mercy, and that you repent of evils. And now, Master, Lord, take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live."

God had taken pity on those who were warding off his wrath by repentance. The appointed time had now run its course, after which the foretold event might have been expected to happen, and yet none of the things expected had taken place. So the blessed Jonah was deeply grieved, not because the city had escaped destruction, for that would be the mark of a wicked and envious man and in no way befitting a saint, but because he seemed a liar and a buffoon, who had alarmed them for nothing and spoken from [?] his own mind and not at all from the mouth of the Lord, as it is written. Some others, however, think that the prophet was grieved over certain other, hidden thoughts. Since he knew, they say, that once the flock from the nations was called Israel would surely fall away from its hope in God, the time for this having now arrived, he was deeply downcast, all but mourning for his own kin by blood as though they had already perished. But he himself steers us away from this interpretation by saying very plainly that he had fled to Tarshish and was caught shirking his mission because he knew clearly that the Master is kind and compassionate and repents of evils. "Since you were such," he says, "why did you command me to proclaim the overthrow to them in vain?" And he loses heart, as a human being would, affirming that he had used these very words even in the land of the Jews; and now he begs to die, and all but raises no small outcry against the divine plan. But this is a dangerous thing and unworthy of a holy mind. If no one with any sense would reproach physicians of the body for altering their remedies to suit the wounds better, how could anyone reasonably cry out against God, who knows all things and devises for our minds the cure that is always fitting and truly most useful? For he is a physician of spirits, calming the savagery of the passions within us sometimes by hardships, and sometimes again by the blessings of his gentleness.

And the Lord said to Jonah, "Are you deeply grieved?" And Jonah went out of the city and sat down opposite the city, and made himself a booth there, and sat under it in the shade until he should see what would become of the city.

He does not let the prophet's mind be choked by despondency, but strengthens it as one would something weak; and very kindly, yet to good purpose, he reproaches him for having been grieved. For the question "Are you deeply grieved?" would, I think, imply nothing else at all; he all but rebukes him for grieving and for not understanding the purpose of the divine judgments. Now when the days had passed, as I said just now, after which what had been announced might have been expected to come to pass, and the wrath was still idle, he understands that God has shown mercy, yet he has not entirely given up hope. He thinks that a postponement of the calamity has been granted them because they chose to repent, but that some of the effects of wrath would surely still come, since the hardships of repentance they had shown were not equal to their offences. For what good would three days' sweat do people buried in every kind of outrage and held fast in such terrible transgressions? Turning these things over in his mind, as is likely, he left the city and waits to see what will happen to them; for he expected that it would perhaps collapse in an earthquake, or be burned up with fire like Sodom. A dwelling is improvised for him, and what he made was a booth.
And the Lord God commanded a gourd, and it came up over Jonah's head, to be a shade above his head, to shade him from his distress; and Jonah rejoiced over the gourd with great joy.

Again God gives a command, this time to the gourd, just as he did to the sea monster; that is, by merely nodding and willing it. At once it springs up, fair and in full bloom, immediately covers the whole booth, and, shading it very well, as it were anoints him with good cheer. The prophet rejoices greatly over it and is truly delighted, as though over some great and precious thing. Observe, then, from this too how his mind inclines toward simplicity. He was grieved with great grief because the prophecy had not been fulfilled for him; and then again he rejoiced with great joy over a vegetable, a mere plant.

A guileless mind is very easily moved both to grief and to delight. You will see the truth of this if you look at the ways of infants, who are often distressed over nothing and weep bitterly over little things, and then again are glad, shifting all at once from grief to joy, sometimes charmed once more by some little thing. Just as in human bodies those that are not usually very robust fall easily when someone pushes them, even if he does not push hard but touches them, as it were, with a gentler hand, so too the mind free of cunning is easily carried away by anything at all that naturally delights or grieves it.

And the Lord commanded a morning worm on the next day, and it struck the gourd, and it withered. And as soon as the sun rose, the Lord God commanded a scorching, burning wind, and the sun beat down on Jonah's head; and he lost heart and gave up on his life, and said, "It is better for me to die than to live."

By "morning worm" it means the caterpillar, because it takes the beginning of its existence from the dew that falls toward dawn. God gives his command to it, and indeed to the scorching wind as well, in the same sense in which he would be understood to have commanded the gourd itself and the sea monster, as we have already said. The gourd withers unexpectedly. The scorching wind strikes hard and pours burning glare on him in his distress, finding him without shade, so that his despondency grew all the greater. And he had now sunk so low in spirit that he made death itself the object of his prayers.
And the Lord said to Jonah, "Are you deeply grieved over the gourd?" And he said, "I am deeply grieved, even to death."

Observe again how the God of all, out of his boundless love for humankind, all but plays with the guileless souls of the saints, and falls short in nothing of the tender affection of fathers. The gourd gives shade, and the prophet delights in it greatly; afterward the caterpillar, by design, attacks it, and the scorching wind strikes, showing him how very useful and necessary the shade was for his benefit, so that he might be all the more pained at being deprived of what was best. Then, grieving over a small thing, and grieving terribly at that, over the gourd, I mean, he would no longer find fault with God's love for humankind if God should choose to grant forbearance and gentleness to the most renowned of cities, filled with a countless multitude of inhabitants. So God skilfully asks whether he is deeply grieved, and over a mere plant at that. Jonah admits it, and this then became a kind of defence for God, the lover of humankind.

And the Lord said, "You had pity on the gourd, for which you did not labour and which you did not raise, which came into being in a night and perished in a night. And shall I not spare Nineveh, the great city, in which live more than a hundred and twenty thousand people who do not know their right hand from their left, and many cattle?"

O incomparable gentleness, beyond all understanding! What words could suffice us to sing its praise? With what kind of mouth shall we offer songs of thanksgiving to the one who is compassionate and good? For he removes our iniquities far from us, and as a father has pity on his sons, so the Lord has had pity on those who fear him, for he knows how we were formed. See how he shows that Jonah is grieving out of season and over the wrong things, when he ought, as befits a saint, to applaud the Master and praise him as good. "If you," he says, "are gloomy, or rather are brought to the depths of grief, because the gourd plant has withered on you, which sprang up in a single night and perished in the same way, how could I disregard a populous city in which there are more than a hundred and twenty thousand people who, because of their time of life and their age, cannot tell which is their right hand and which their left?" For even these things are indistinguishable to those who are still infants, and it was fitting to grant his love to them before all others, since they had committed no sin; for of what transgressions could one be guilty who does not yet know his own hands? And if he also mentions the cattle and judges them worthy to be spared, this too comes from his love of goodness. For if "a righteous man has pity on the lives of his cattle," and this too is to his credit, what is surprising if the Creator of all himself also bestows forbearance and compassion on them?

In this way Christ saved all, giving himself as a ransom for small and great, wise and unwise, rich and poor, Jew and Greek. To him it might fitly be said, "People and beasts you will save, O Lord, as you have multiplied your mercy, O God. And the children of men will hope under the shelter of your wings." To him be glory and might, with the Father who is without beginning and the all-holy, good and life-giving Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.
END OF JONAH.
Commentary on the Prophet Micah by Our Father among the Saints, Cyril. First Volume.

All the holy prophets share one aim, and it is dear to God: to persuade Israel to break away resolutely from its wish to go astray, to choose instead to serve the living and true God, and to glory in the boasts of righteousness, casting as far away as possible the reproach that wrongdoing brings. Many prophets came one after another, with God, so to speak, testifying in advance and clearly proclaiming through a great many mouths that if they did not choose to live rightly, and did not make it their great concern to return at last to better ways, they would be passing sentence on themselves. They would bring on themselves a self-invited destruction, and would trace the causes of their suffering back to their own choices. If the words of the holy prophets keep returning to the same themes, let no one find fault with them and accuse them of repeating themselves. Rather, let him clearly consider this: there must never be a time when there were none able to set sinners right. No one with sense would find fault with the fact that at every period there are physicians who check the same afflictions in us with the remedies suited to them. In the same way, I think, no one could reasonably reproach the holy prophets if they appear to go over the same matters and the same words. For it was one Lord who spoke to them all, and who at every time showed those going astray people who knew how to lead them back, as it were, onto a straight road. All of them foretell wars, captivities, the desolation of cities, toils, mourning, laments for the dead, the miseries of the captives, the cruelty of the plunderers. In short, one may see their accounts passing through every kind of savagery, because this was necessary for the good of those going astray. For sometimes terrors check even someone who has swerved without restraint into apostasy and sin.

The blessed Micah, then, also prophesies in the times of the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah. While Jotham was reigning, Pekah son of Remaliah and Rezin king of Syria marched against Jerusalem. When Jotham died, Ahaz succeeded to the throne. As the war dragged on, he hired the Assyrian with money and begged him for help, since he was unable to stand against the forces of the invaders. The Assyrian came, took Damascus and killed Rezin. Then, at that period, while Jeroboam son of Joash was reigning in Samaria, and after him Azariah, and third Menahem, Pul king of the Assyrians came up. Only with great difficulty, and with a great deal of money, was he persuaded to return to his own land. After Pul, Tiglath-pileser the Assyrian marched against the land of the Jews and depopulated a great many cities of Samaria, adding to them all Galilee as far as Naphtali. These things were set out in detail when we composed our commentary on the blessed prophet Hosea. We have had to mention them again now because the dates of Micah's prophecy are also given. The attentive and studious hearer needed to know why the kings who reigned in Jerusalem, Jotham and Ahaz, are named. The period of the prophecy extends as far as the reign of Hezekiah. In his time Sennacherib, he too a king of the Assyrians, took the land of the Samaritans by force and ravaged the cities of the Philistines, that is, of the Palestinians. Then he took Lachish, a city of the kingdom of Judah, and from there he sent Rabshakeh to besiege Jerusalem. Rabshakeh paid the penalty for his arrogance and for the blasphemous tongue he wagged against God, when a hundred and eighty-five thousand of the Assyrian army died in a single night. So, it says, the word of the Lord came to Micah the son of Morathi.
And the word of the Lord came to Micah the son of Morathi, in the days of Jotham and Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.

Again, one should know that the Hebrews have written "the Morathite" instead of "son of Morathi," so that he is identified not by his father but by a place. They say that Morathi was a village or small town in the land of the Jews. The other translators also agree with this rendering. So Morathi would not be the prophet's father. Rather, as I said, he is identified by a place, as a Morathite. Now we must look closely at the words that came to him.
Concerning the things he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem.

He beheld what was to come as in a vision. The evils were all but present, even at the doors. He did not merely gain knowledge of them; as far as they came into his sight, in a vision I mean, he dreaded their outcome. So of necessity he speaks his words about Samaria and Jerusalem.
Hear words, all you peoples, and let the earth and all who are in it pay attention. The Lord God shall be among you for a witness [?], the Lord from his holy house.

He commands them to make themselves ready to obey, and all but to incline their ear and understand precisely the force of the divine oracles. He then assures them that this message does not come from human opinion or wishes but from God himself, the ruler of all, by adding that the Lord will be among you for a witness. He all but says: "Even if I, Micah, am the one who speaks, even if I perhaps act as a mediator, being a man, it is the God of all himself who testifies to you, and I lend my own voice to the Master's decrees. So he himself will be a witness to you. For him you built this renowned and splendid temple; for him you set up the divine altar; to him the law taught you to pay reverence. He has always spoken from his own house to the holy prophets, and before all the others to the blessed Moses, who set up that ancient tabernacle in the wilderness." For he spoke from above the mercy seat, and, as the sacred writing says, "Moses spoke, and God answered him with a voice." And now, he says, he testifies to you from his house. So hear, you peoples, and let the earth too pay attention. Similar to this is what is said through the voice of Isaiah: "Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken." The Most High does not, of course, dwell in temples of stone or in sanctuaries made by hands. But since we say that holy houses are raised for the glory of God, we believe for this reason that the God of all does not disdain to dwell in them, even though he fills the heavens and the earth and all that lies beneath.

One might also fittingly apply these words to Christ. He calls to salvation not only the peoples who were of Abraham's blood but the whole earth. For he testified, as it were, through the voice of David, saying: "Hear this, all you nations; give ear, all you who inhabit the world." And how can anyone doubt that the Word came down to us from heaven as from his own house, one very dear to him? There is nothing strange in calling heaven the house of God. The divinely inspired Scriptures call even the earthly Zion, which is also taken as a type of the Church, his house and his city. For the divine David sings somewhere: "Glorious things have been spoken of you, O city of God." So the Church would be both city and house of Christ, who fills all things by the nature of his Godhead.

For behold, the Lord is going out from his place, and he will tread upon the heights of the earth. The mountains will be shaken beneath him, and the valleys will melt like wax before fire, and like water rushing down a slope.

Such a passage is very obscure and full of riddles. Still, we must say this: even if things about God are expressed in words drawn from our own condition, someone skilled in these matters, who knows how to understand "a parable and a dark saying, the words of the wise and their riddles," will understand them precisely, and in the way that best befits the divine and ineffable nature. For the voice of the saints speaks of its being seated, its thrones and its rising, and indeed of ways and journeys, and of other small and human things besides. But, as I just said, the good and sound-minded would rightly understand such matters subtly and with refinement. For these expressions arise by likeness and by metaphor from our own condition. So when you hear the prophet saying, "For behold, the Lord is going out from his place, and he will tread upon the heights of the earth," and then adding that the mountains will be shaken and the valleys will melt, at that point rise a little above things perceived by the senses and climb in contemplation to refined thoughts. You will understand here a going out of God as from his own place: a movement, as it were, out of rest, toward certain things that are about to be done. He all but says: "He who was long patient has now been stirred. He will no longer care to remain at rest toward those who have offended him. In a way he has set aside the gentleness so dear to him, and now he will bring on the punishments." For he will tread upon the heights of the earth, that is, he will now trample those in very lofty positions. By these we are to understand the kings in Samaria and in Jerusalem. The mountains too will be shaken, that is, those who tower over others and stand very high in glory will be removed from their dignities, for such people may very well be compared to mountains. And the valleys will melt like wax. These are the lowly and the downtrodden, who rank as the common herd. Yet they are very hard and cannot bear to yield to the divine decrees. So, coming up against the fire of divine wrath, they will melt like wax. And they will become like water rushing down a slope, that is, darting downhill in a swift and unchecked course. For, as I said before, the kings of the Assyrians savagely ravaged both Samaria and the kingdom of Judah. They deported some of the kings and killed all the leaders, and they carried off the mass of the common people to their own land, sweeping them along like water coming down a slope [?]. This was the water rushing down a slope and running from Samaria to the land of the Persians and the Medes.

The Word of God too went out from his place. For, being God by nature, he became man. In this, I mean, he seems in some way to have undergone a movement, though he knows no change but rather stands firm in his own nature and remains steadfast as God. He also trod upon the heights of the earth: he shook the mountains, melted the valleys, and made them flow like water rushing down a slope. The heights of the earth might be understood as the spiritual powers that exalt themselves over all, the spiritual forces of wickedness. The shaken mountains are the demons, thrust out of their rule over us. For they have been cast out, and we are now called to be subject to the one who is God by nature and in truth. The valleys, again, are the common herd of the demons, lowly and downtrodden, melted like wax and flowing like water into the depths of Hades. For the evil spirits came to Christ and "begged him not to command them to depart into the abyss." Others had already been sent away before them, and those who were left shuddered at the prospect. But someone may wish to understand the heights, the mountains and the valleys as the leaders of the Jews, and indeed the populace under them, who were thrust out of their own rule because of their outrage against Christ. They melted like wax, meeting the calamities of the war with the Romans as if meeting a flame. "They came to nothing like water that runs away; like wax that melts they were taken away," in the words of the psalmist. Whoever understands it this way will not stray from the proper aim.
All these things are because of the impiety of Jacob, and because of the sin of the house of Israel.

He has said that the God of all will tread upon the heights of the earth, that the mountains will be shaken by him, and that the valleys will melt and run down like wax and water. Then he adds: "All these things are because of the impiety of Jacob." Notice how he speaks hidden mysteries and does not let the meaning of the passage stop at things perceived by the senses. He knows how to describe indirectly the calamities about to come upon those in Samaria and in Jerusalem. For what terror would there be in the shaking of mountains, and how would it grieve those in Samaria, or the others? And in what way would valleys melt, or become like water rushing down a slope? But, as I said, he knows how to signify fittingly what would happen to those of Israel. Therefore he goes on, of necessity, to give the grounds for the punishments. He is not, I think, speaking to them as if they did not know, but rather reproving them and turning them firmly toward choosing to think what is profitable and more fitting. He said, then, "All these things are because of the impiety of Jacob, and because of the sin of the house of Israel," so that the whole race of Israel may be understood to have offended against both God and men. For he seems to call offenses against God "impiety," and offenses against brothers and kinsmen "sin."
What is the impiety of Jacob? Is it not Samaria? And what is the sin of the house of Judah? Is it not Jerusalem?

By "Jacob" he means those descended from Jacob, Ephraim I mean, the people in Samaria, and he makes their crimes plain. He says that Samaria is the very form of impiety. We certainly do not say that he blames the land itself; it would be utterly senseless to think so. By "Samaria" he means what belonged to Samaria: the heifers, for example, Chemosh and Baal, and the things done there against certain people through the greed of those in power. For he said: "They struck the heads of the poor with their fists, and turned aside the way of the lowly." And besides, they said: "When will the new month be over, so that we may sell, and the sabbaths, so that we may open our storehouses, to make the measure small and the weight large, and to make the scales dishonest?" He says that Jerusalem too became the sin of Judah. Again, if we think rightly, we shall by no means blame the city itself here. Rather, we shall consider that the things done in it became sin for Judah. God somewhere blamed the drunken outrages of the Jews and said plainly: "For your gods, O Judah, were as many as your cities, and you set up altars to burn incense to Baal as many as the streets of Jerusalem. Why do you speak to me? You have all acted lawlessly, and you have all been impious toward me, says the Lord Almighty." He also rebukes them through the voice of Isaiah, saying: "How has the faithful city Zion become a harlot! She was full of justice; righteousness lodged in her, but now murderers. Your silver is worthless; your merchants mix the wine with water. Your rulers are disobedient, companions of thieves, loving bribes, chasing after rewards, not giving judgment for orphans, and paying no heed to the widow's cause." So it was what was impiously done in Jerusalem, not the city itself, that became sin for Judah.

We must, then, love God, and do so with all our soul and heart. We must shake off sloth in doing good, and in no way harm our neighbor but rather win him over with kindnesses. We must flee from what is evil and devote ourselves instead to the boasts of righteousness. But if we grow careless about things so sacred and choose to despise them, he will bring on us the effects of his wrath. He will punish us in fire and melt us like wax, and he will scatter us like water, no longer counting us worthy of his forbearance and love.

And I will make Samaria like a watchman's hut in a field, and like a planted vineyard. I will drag her stones down into a chasm and lay bare her foundations. They will cut to pieces all her carved images, and burn all her wages with fire, and I will bring all her idols to destruction.

He now describes clearly what the sufferings of those who have offended in this way will be. For Samaria, he says, will be like a watchman's hut in a field and like a planted vineyard. Some people guard what grows in the fields. They weave huts and sit in them, and so they drive off all harm from the crops. But when the fruit has been gathered, the watchmen end their labors and go back home, pulling down the huts themselves. We shall find that Samaria suffered this. She offended beyond measure, or rather she acted impiously against the God of all himself, paying reverence to the works of her own hands. So she was overturned and fell, abandoned perhaps even by those who had long been appointed to guard her, I mean the holy powers and angels. The blessed prophet Isaiah also said something like this about her: "The daughter of Zion will be left like a booth in a vineyard and like a watchman's hut in a cucumber field." How was she left? As I said, the rational host of the orders above, which had attended and protected her, departed. She will be, then, like a watchman's hut in a field and like a planted vineyard. It is as if he said: "Stripped of cities and houses, she will take on the appearance of fields." Or, if you like, you may understand it another way. Those who plant vineyards take the ground best suited to them and break it up with plowing, turning it over and over. He threatens that the land of the Samaritans will suffer this: it will all but become plowland, once its cities and houses, as I said, have been removed. That is why he says: "I will drag her stones down into a chasm and lay bare her foundations." He says that something laughable will happen as well. Those whom they expected to be their saviors, as gods, will perish together with those who used to worship them. Her wages will be burned, and all her idols, he says, will go to destruction. The "wages" burned along with the idols perhaps mean the votive offerings. For they brought to the sanctuaries, for the glory of the idols, offerings set aside from their own wealth. To beings neither accustomed nor able to help anyone, they dedicated their thank-offerings as a kind of wage and repayment for what they thought they had received from them. We remember that through the voice of Hosea too he accused the synagogue of the Jews, saying: "And she did not know that it was I who gave her the grain and the wine and the oil, and multiplied silver and gold for her; but she made things of silver and gold for Baal." So the votive offerings are plain. Senseless Israel reckoned its prosperity as wages and repayment for its zeal in going astray.
