You will understand this no less from God saying again: "And I will destroy her vine and her fig trees, of which she said, 'These are my wages, which my lovers gave me.'" For, as I said, she thought that by the will of the idols she abounded in wealth, lived in luxury and prospered. Blind, then, is the mind of those who go astray. Had Israel not been ignorant of the one who is God by nature, it would have paid reverence to him and not to any others. It would have offered its prayers of thanksgiving to him, and confessed him as the giver and dispenser of every good. Had it resolved to think in this way, it would not have become like a watchman's hut in a field, nor like a planted vineyard. Instead it would have gone on being called blessed in unshaken prosperity, walled about by favors from above, admired for its good cheer.
For she gathered from the wages of harlotry, and from the wages of harlotry she amassed.

Here again the passage laughs them to scorn and mocks the ignorance of the Jews with heavy irony. It exposes the madness of their folly and brings clearly to light what lies hidden in their mind and heart. "Yes indeed," it says, "Israel was right and just to dedicate thank-offerings to stones, so full of understanding, so grateful and wise! He recognized those who honored him, the providers of his prosperity, who gathered wealth for him and made him live in comfort." For he thinks that prosperity is the wage of his spiritual harlotry. Since he has sacrificed to idols and worships wood and stones, he thinks he will lack nothing he prays for. He gathered, as it says, and grew rich from the wages of harlotry. He amassed and collected, and his contentment cannot be shaken. So we shall take the force of these words as spoken ironically and mockingly, with a threat woven in.

Because of this she will beat her breast and wail. She will go barefoot and naked. She will lament like dragons and mourn like the daughters of sirens. For her wound has prevailed, because it has come as far as Judah and has reached the gate of my people, as far as Jerusalem.

For since, he says, she spent her life in error and never stopped grieving her own Master, but dedicated to the carved images the thank-offerings for the things in which she prospers and is praised, and has now gone this far in impiety, for this reason she will beat her breast and lament. And she will not grieve over others, perhaps, that is, over strangers, shedding a tear out of love, as it were. She will be struck down by her own calamities. Nakedness and going barefoot show the appearance of captives. So too the blessed prophet Isaiah, pointing to the captivity that was soon to come upon them, went about Jerusalem "naked and barefoot," because God commanded this to be done. In her own sufferings, then, she will imitate the mourning of dragons and the wailing of sirens. For some say that when a dragon is struck, then, at that very moment of danger, it laments, and shows this by beating the ground with its tail, and it usually makes no small noise. The Greeks and their followers say that sirens are winged creatures that know how to sing and can enchant their hearers with the fine rhythms of their songs. But divinely inspired Scripture uses the name sirens for the most talkative of the small birds, those that usually sing sweetly, or sometimes for the nightingales themselves, which brood along the inlets of the sea. Then, when the nest is carried off by the waves, they sing a mournful song and in a way lament the loss of their brood. In the same way, he said, Samaria will lament the destruction of her own children. For her blow has overpowered her, he says, and it has reached as far as Judah, even up to the gates of Jerusalem. Here the passage seems to us to hint at the war waged by Sennacherib. He took all of Samaria, laid Judea waste, and besieged Jerusalem. He came right up to its gates and threatened to burn it, but he could not do so, because God was defending it, in the time of Hezekiah's reign.

So when we abandon the one who is Master by nature and in truth and eagerly attach ourselves to the unclean demons, then we will by all means and in every way lament ourselves, groaning over our own folly. We will be stripped of his grace and help, and we will live a shameful and graceless life, for that is what going barefoot signifies. We will also lie open to the blows of Satan, and nothing will any longer prevent us from falling into every evil.
You who are in Gath, do not boast; you Enakim, do not build up mockery out of a house; sprinkle earth over yourselves as the mockery against you.

The passage is veiled, and the sense of these words, and of those that follow, is very hard to grasp. Nevertheless I will try to explain it as far as I can. When the war was overrunning the cities of Samaria, and other cities under the scepter of Judah and Benjamin were also being taken, the foreigners who lived nearby, the nations that bordered the land of the Jews and were its neighbors, laughed loudly and jeered at Israel, as though it had gained no benefit from God. For they thought that the hand of the one who saves must have proved feeble and grown weak against the onslaughts of the ravagers. But they would have done better to recognize that because the Israelites chose to grieve the one who saves and offended God, they had experienced terrible things and had been handed over into the hands of their enemies. It was absurd for those nations to suppose among themselves that they had remained in good fortune by the power of their own objects of worship, while Israel had perished and been destroyed through the weakness of the one who saves. For this reason God handed over to Sennacherib for desolation the very cities of the neighboring peoples as well. Indeed, Rabshakeh, speaking to those on the wall of Jerusalem, mentioned these very cities when he said: "Where is the god of Hamath and Arpad? Where is the god of the city of Sepharvaim? Was he able to deliver Samaria from my hand? Which of all the gods of these nations has delivered his land from my hand?" Now Gath belongs to those called the Philistines, and is a chief city of Palestine. Enakim, likewise, is a small town lying on the outer edges of Judea, toward the southern desert. It was subject to the scepter of Judah, yet it no longer shared the outlook of the Jews but was rather attached to the neighboring nations, I mean the Moabites and the Idumeans. So, he says, you inhabitants of Gath, you inhabitants of Enakim, do not make the misfortunes of others an excuse for a festival. Do not boast because of these things, and do not laugh loudly, he says, just because the house next to you, that is, the house of Israel, has been laid waste, all but dancing over those who have perished. Do not build mockery out of a house. Rather, since you too are going to suffer worse things, sprinkle on yourselves, like earth, the mockery that is going to come upon you, and lament your own misfortunes. For the Babylonians will dance over you, and your enemies will smile at you as you perish miserably. It is wise, then, to remember the one who says: "If your enemy falls, do not rejoice over him, for the Lord will see, and it will not please him, and he will turn his anger away from him."

Those who do not know Christ do the same. For sometimes, when the churches are persecuted and the saints in them are being tested, at that very moment they most of all marvel at their own gods. But their laughter ends in tears, as Christ makes the hardships easy, calms what has been stirred up, drives away the cause of grief, and widens joy and gladness for the saints. For the end of labors is glory and delight. And I think the blessed David says something of this kind to the God of all: "We went through fire and water, and you brought us out into refreshment."
She who dwells well in her cities; she who dwells in Sennaar did not come out to mourn the house next to her; she will receive from you a painful blow.

The Seventy rendered this as Sennaar, but Aquila said Senan, and Symmachus "she who is strong," which is perhaps what Senan suggests. If it is understood as Sennaar, we say that it is a broad territory, inhabited city by city and village by village by foreigners, but lying on the borders of Judea. If it is understood as Senan, it denotes a splendid and famous city of Egypt. And how could anyone doubt that it is strong, since the land is rich and thick with crops? So he says that Sennaar, or Senan, is the one that dwells well in her cities. But the word will turn against those who dwell in them. She did not weep over those nearby who perished pitiably and wretchedly. She did not come out to mourn the house next to her, that is, she did not lament her neighbors. As I said, Sennaar is near Judea, and so is Senan, that is, the Egyptian city. When Israel was falling and being sacked, she did not grieve for it. She mocked it instead and rejoiced over it, just like the people of Gath and Enakim. What then, Israel? Will the neighboring nations laugh with impunity, and will God tolerate them doing this? Will he endure having his glory laughed at by his enemies? By no means, he says. She will receive from you, or because of you, a painful blow; that is, she too will be laid waste together with the others. And indeed Sennaar was sacked, and so was Egypt, when Sennacherib overran it. So even the one who stands firm must fear falling. He must cast far away from himself any smiling at those who have suffered, and rather "weep with those who weep." He must not look down with contempt on the misfortunes of others, but rather fear falling into the same.
Who has begun to turn to good things, she who dwells in pains? For evils have come down from the Lord upon the gates of Jerusalem. A noise of chariots and horsemen.

You people of Gath, he says, you inhabitants of Enakim, you inhabitants of Sennaar or Senan, you were not struck by the misfortunes of your neighbors. Instead, Israel's falling and perishing became an occasion of laughter for you, Israel which was once terrible and unbearable to you. You thought that God, who saves them, had become weak, while your handmade idols were strong and had reached such a pitch of power that they could save your cities without effort. Come, then, let us look at the facts and see who is God by nature and in truth, who is all-powerful and grants irresistible help to whomever he chooses. For the cities of Israel, he says, were taken and sacked, and so were your own cities, and you endured what was, so to speak, a common misfortune. Which city, then, while it was in pains and in fear of the worst (for that is what "dwelling in pains" means), unexpectedly turned toward good things, that is, toward gladness and prosperity? Was it one of yours? By no means, he says. It was my Jerusalem. For evils came down upon it from the Lord; that is, I grieved and disciplined them, and I brought the Assyrian against them, and the affliction that came upon them arose from my anger. Yet it was quenched and undone, as my hand prevailed and wondrously rescued those who revere my might. For the trouble halted at the gates. We know that Rabshakeh came to Jerusalem with a large force of cavalry and all but laid hold of its very gates, but he never took it, for the Assyrian was destroyed in a single night. The people in Jerusalem had been lamenting as if they were about to die at any moment, and they spent the night weeping without sleep. But when dawn broke, the marvel was seen: countless corpses lay on the ground. So those who had been wondrously granted victory and saved through God leapt for joy and said: "Weeping will lodge for the evening, but in the morning comes gladness." Do you see, then, how Jerusalem first and alone among the cities began to turn toward good things, even though she dwelt in pains? For God will not utterly abandon his own. He disciplines them in due measure and then saves them again, and he takes no small care for the glory that befits him, even if we offend. For he said somewhere through one of the prophets: "I am not doing this for your sake, says the Lord, but for the sake of my name."
She who dwells in Lachish, she is the beginning of sin for the daughter of Zion, for in you were found the impieties of Israel.

Lachish, again, is a city subject to the scepter of Judah, a neighbor bordering the Philistines. It too was extraordinarily harsh and idolatrous. It shunned piety toward God and reverence for the law, and it made it a point of the highest importance to love wandering into error and to bring other cities to ruin with it. This was perhaps the first of the cities under the scepter of Judah and Benjamin that Sennacherib captured, and from there he sent Rabshakeh to Jerusalem. So Lachish, he says, which once dwelt well and was securely established, became the beginning of sin for Zion, that is, for Jerusalem. For the impieties of Israel were found in it, that is, the handmade idols and no small crowd of falsely named gods.

What, then, does the passage mean to show? In a way it makes a defense to the foreign peoples and tries to persuade them to understand from now on that God who saves had not become weak. Rather, because the cities of Judah acted impiously toward him, they were handed over to their enemies. For Lachish, he says, became the beginning of sin for Zion, and was the first to be given over to Sennacherib as the occasion of the apostasy. Israel perished, then, as one can see from Lachish, not because God had fallen sick with weakness (far from it!), but rather because Israel had fallen sick with error and had senselessly devoted itself to the worship of idols.

Therefore you will give those who are being sent away as far as the inheritance of Gath, vain houses; they came to nothing for the kings of Israel, until they bring in the heirs. She who dwells in Lachish, the inheritance will come as far as Adullam.

When Israel fell under the onslaughts of wrath and was paying the penalty for its offenses against God, the people of Gath and Enakim dared to sneer at God's glory. For, as I have already said, they thought that he had not saved his own because he was defeated by the hand of the Assyrians. God then wanted to persuade them otherwise, and to show from the case of Lachish that the Israelites had been handed over to their enemies because many impieties of Israel had been found among them, and because they had become the beginning of sin for the daughter of Zion, that is, for Jerusalem. When God said this, the blessed prophet understood very well what was meant, before anyone else. He accepts the words and, all but crowning them as true with his own vote, immediately cries out: "Therefore you will give those who are being sent away as far as the inheritance of Gath, vain houses." Yes, Master, he says, they will go to their enemies and be sent away by you, leaving the land that bore them and moving to the land of the Assyrians. And not only those in Samaria, he says, but those in Gath [?] as well. For the former became apostates and insolent, refusing to follow your decrees, while the latter, mocking those who had fared wretchedly, made what had happened an occasion to disparage your glory. So you yourself will give those who are being sent away as far as the inheritance of Gath, vain houses. Both the house of Ephraim and the houses of the people of Gath are vain houses, because they would not consent to honor God but gave their worship to carved images, and because they thought only of the things of the flesh and, attached to earthly things, took no account of virtue. Then, in the middle of this, the blessed prophet in a way cries out in indignation and all but wrings his hands, as he calls to mind what had been done in Samaria in various times. He reflects on the arrogance of the kings, and on how the offenses by which Israel sinned were the unholy deeds of their own perversity. For the heifers were their invention, as were the sanctuaries of the other idols, and they never stopped provoking the Creator in every way. So the prophet, in distress, says: "They came to nothing for the kings of Israel, until they bring in the heirs." It is as if he were saying: the kings did not cease from their zeal for vanities until they fell into such wretchedness that the inheritance allotted to them by God became the portion of others. And since the Assyrians were going to rule over the whole land of the Jews, he takes two cities lying at the far edges of the whole country, I mean Lachish and Adullam, which Rehoboam built, and he says: "She who dwells in Lachish, the inheritance will come as far as Adullam." For the enemy will inherit Lachish, though it was very well walled (that is what "dwelling" means), and it will stretch, he says, as far as Adullam.

So if someone chooses to be wise and docile, and hates to set himself against the divine will, he will enjoy long prosperity and will rest securely in his own inheritance. For he will be full of good hope and will shine together with the saints in due time. But if he shows himself harsh and unmanageable and does not yield to the divine laws, he will certainly be driven out from the hope of the saints and will lose the inheritance that is with God. He will even become the portion of his enemies, as is sung in the Psalms about certain people: "They will be portions for foxes," that is, a portion for wicked, cunning and malicious powers.
Glory of the daughter of Israel, shave your head and cut your hair for your delicate children; make your widowhood broad like an eagle's, for they have been carried away from you into captivity.

It is as if he were saying again: O daughter of Jerusalem, once thrice-blessed, you who were allotted glory so very renowned and illustrious, Jerusalem, or rather Samaria, your delicate children are gone, and the multitude that once lived in luxury has perished, splendid and soft-living, the multitude that slept "on beds of ivory and lived luxuriously on their couches; that ate kids from the flocks and suckling calves from the midst of the herds; that clapped to the sound of the instruments; that regarded these things as lasting and not as fleeting; that drank strained wine and anointed themselves with the finest perfumes." Strip yourself, then, daughter of Jerusalem; that is, lay aside your glory and show yourself bare of that former prosperity. Then, wailing loudly and beyond the usual measure, and striving to imitate the deep grief of eagles, lament your children, for they will go off as captives, and you will be a widow, left alone. Those who are wise in these matters, and who study the nature of birds as closely as possible, say that the eagle is a creature that loves its young and laments terribly when its chicks fall from the nest or are carried off by someone. That this bird does not lack a disposition to love its offspring the divine Moses will also persuade us, when he says about God and those of Israel's blood: "As an eagle shelters its nest and yearns over its young, it spread its wings and received them and took them up on its back." You see how he said that the eagle yearns over its own chicks and loves to keep them under its wings, overshadowing its offspring out of great love. "Make your widowhood broad," then, he says, "like an eagle's."

One might rightly apply this also, not only to the more ancient peoples of the Jews, but also to those who lived at the time of our Savior's coming. For when they handed him over to the cross, they fell into terrible and inescapable calamities, and they were scattered to every wind, enduring the sufferings of captivity, so to speak, in another way.

They took to devising troubles and working evils on their beds, and at daybreak they carried them out, for they did not lift up their hands to God. They coveted fields and plundered orphans, and oppressed households, and they plundered a man and his house, a man and his inheritance.

When the God of all speaks at length about the punishment of certain people, so that no one may think him harsh or prone to anger, but rather a just Judge who weighs each person's faults rightly and repays sinners according to their works, he immediately sets out the charges and lays bare the magnitude of their impiety. They have become wicked in their ways, he says, and have reached such a pitch of perversity that they plot by night and make it their leisure occupation to devise troubles, that is, to contrive ruin against certain people, and to work evils, that is, again, to devise pretexts [?] by which they might be able to harm those weaker than themselves. Then, when they ought to have changed their minds and chosen to do what is better, they gave their own deliberations no time at all, but at dawn they carried their plans through to the end, when they ought rather to have lifted up their hands to God, since a morning sacrifice was offered according to the law. Their plans by night and their leisurely deliberations were these: coveting others' fields, overturning households, acts of oppression and greed, the plundering of a man and of his inheritance. For this reason they were justly sent away as vain houses, since they did not know how to think what is pleasing to God.

It is better, then, incomparably better, to rise far above such things, to depart from all wickedness, to cast greed as far away as possible, and, not longing for superfluities, to seek food and clothing and whatever suffices the temperate for living. "For those who want to be rich fall into many foolish and harmful desires, which plunge people into ruin and destruction." Besides this, it is harmful to spend the leisure of the night on schemes that lead to sin. It is good rather to imitate the blessed psalmist, who says to the God of all: "At midnight I rose to give thanks to you for your righteous judgments." And again: "O God, my God, I seek you at dawn; my soul thirsts for you, how often my flesh longs for you." And again: "When I remembered you on my bed, at dawn I meditated on you."
Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I am devising evils against this tribe, from which you will not lift your necks, and you will not walk upright all at once, for it is an evil time.

Since they themselves devised troubles and worked evils against others, pushing aside the lifting up of their hands to God as unprofitable and useless, for this reason, he says, I too will devise evils against every tribe of this kind; that is, I will consider what evils, or rather incurable calamities, they should be subjected to. And what is brought upon them, he says, will be so hard to bear and so heavy that those who suffer it will be like people bent over, and in a way they will be bowed down, terribly and unbearably weighed down. For it will be an evil time, he says, in which the effects of wrath will hang over them. And this, I think, is what someone wisely sings: "For my iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden they have weighed heavily upon me." But our Lord Jesus Christ called those who were weighed down in this way to lay aside what hung over them, saying: "Come to me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." Those who honored the one who called them by faith shook off the burden. But the scribes and Pharisees, who had grieved him by their disobedience, and the rest of the crowd with them, have remained toiling and oppressed, and very rightly so; they could never walk upright. Knowing this, the divine David cried out to God: "Let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see, and bend their back continually." So that, not seeing the things above, and unable to lift the eye of the mind toward the hope of the saints and the beautiful city in heaven, they may look only at the things on earth, all but bent over, fixing their insolent and God-hating mind on what is temporary and fleshly.

On that day a parable will be taken up against you, and a lament will be sung in a dirge, saying: We have been utterly wretched; the portion of my people has been measured out with a line, and there was no one to hinder it so as to turn it back.

He says that two things will happen at the same time: a byword and a lament. The byword seems to mean that the talk about them, or concerning them, will be in everyone's mouth, so to speak. Extraordinary calamities are always remembered, and the report of such things travels through cities and countries and darts to the ends of the whole earth. The lament means the tears and the wailing over them that others might perhaps raise, or else that they themselves would raise among themselves as they bewail their own sufferings. Accordingly he says, "We have suffered utter misery." And he makes clear what kind of misery is meant when he says, "The portion of my people has been measured out with a line, and there was no one to prevent it, so as to turn it back." The lot, he says, that was assigned to my own beloved people (plainly Israel) has been measured out by enemies; that is, it has been made subject to tributes and taxes, for whatever is measured falls under tribute and taxes. Then, once this had happened and come about beyond all expectation, there was no one to prevent it. Where then, he says, are the heifers, Chemosh, Dagon, Baal-peor, Baal, and the many handmade images of every kind in the sacred precincts of Samaria? They have fallen silent. They did not stand against those who were dividing the land; they did not help their own worshipers; they did not bring down wrath on those who were measuring the land. He says something similar about the people of Israel through the voice of Jeremiah: "And in the time of their troubles they will say, 'Arise and save us.' And where are your gods which you made for yourself? Will they arise and save you in the time of your affliction?" But how could they save others, when they would easily suffer whatever anyone chose to do to them? For they are, they truly are, the works of human hands: silver and gold, stone and wood, dumb and senseless matter. So let the divine David sing: "May all who make them become like them, and all who trust in them."
Your fields have been measured out; therefore you will have no one to cast a line by lot.

He makes plain the force of what has been said. You have been disinherited, he says: what is yours has been measured out to others, and you are not permitted to measure out your own. We shall find that the arrogant Jews also suffered this at the time of Christ's coming. Because they behaved outrageously toward Christ, they slipped from the lots assigned to them. Israel was the firstborn, and the most wise Paul says that theirs are the promises, theirs the fathers, and from them, according to the flesh, comes Christ. But Israel has fallen from that hope and from all the glory that went with it, and the multitude of the gentiles has entered in and gone up into its lot in its place. For the promises have become theirs, Christ is theirs, the fathers are theirs; they are called children of Abraham because they follow "in the footsteps of the faith" he had "in uncircumcision." "For not all who are descended from Israel are Israel, nor are all children because they are Abraham's seed; but the children of the promise are counted as seed." Accordingly the divine John too, bringing down the haughtiness of the Jews and their great conceit, says: "Bear fruits worthy of repentance, and do not presume to say within yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father'; for I tell you that God is able from these stones to raise up children to Abraham." So senseless Israel has fallen from the inheritance, while the flock from the gentiles has sprung up, as it were, in its place, and to them Christ allots the glorious and precious portion of the good things from above. For they have become fellow citizens of the saints and members of God's household, and of one body with Christ. Made radiant by their union with him through the Spirit, they will live the truly longed-for life in holiness, sanctification and incorruption.

Do not weep with tears in the assembly of the Lord, and do not let your eyes shed tears over this; for he will not drive away reproaches who says, "The house of Jacob has provoked the Spirit of the Lord." Are these his practices?

Does he then bar Israel from choosing to repent? Tell me, does God hold back his gentleness toward them even if they want to learn what is most fitting for them and are already in some way doing what pleases him? That is not what he says. Rather, it is the habit of some people, when one of the wise happens to reprove them for their sins, to measure their repentance by tears alone. They confess the sin and seek forgiveness by this and this alone, yet they do not go on to give up the evils they have set before themselves. Some of the people of Israel did this, so that at times they did not even spare their garments. But what does he say who sees into the heart and the inmost being? "Return to me with all your heart, with fasting and weeping and mourning, and rend your hearts and not your garments." Those who merely pour tears from their eyes and put on a show of fair words, yet do not give up their own desires, would not make the Judge kindly and gentle toward them. He teaches this when he says, "Do not weep with tears in the assembly of the Lord." Do not make God's temple a house of mourning, he says. Do not weep over this so as to seem to have wept merely in God's house, for such a thing is wholly useless. And let no one say, "The house of Jacob has provoked the Spirit of the Lord." For no one would in the least wipe away the reproaches for his sins, even if he chose to use such fine words. "Are these his practices?" And what are these practices, he says? "They took to devising troubles and working evils on their beds, and at daybreak they carried them out, and they did not lift up their hands to the Lord. They coveted fields and plundered orphans, and oppressed households, and plundered a man and his house, a man and his inheritance." If these are his practices, then, he says, how could he ward off the reproaches by merely pouring out tears, confessing and saying, "The house of Jacob has provoked the Spirit of the Lord"?

So those who have chosen to repent must rid themselves of the charges of wickedness, and only then weep and confess to God, once they have already come to value doing good. For God will not look simply at tears or at fine words, but at character and conduct. Weeping will be of profit to people, he says, then and only then, when good conduct is seen to come in along with the overthrow of wickedness. For when sin is done away with in us, virtue springs up in its place.
Are not his words good with him, and have they not gone upright? And formerly my people stood up in enmity against his peace.

Again he accuses them of habitually speaking very fine words while having a mind at odds with those words. Their words are upright, he says, and exceedingly good: they confess their offenses and call God kind and good. Yet they mock him in many ways and have never stopped provoking him by their deeds. One can see that they have become their own enemies and are driving away their own peace. For my people itself, he says, has risen up as an enemy against its own peace. They could have lived in comfort and luxury, secure in glory and firmly grounded in contentment, had they honored God; but they willingly slipped into apostasy. So, having thrown away a life of peace, they stir up a war against their own heads, a war they invited upon themselves. Yet it is not altogether unprofitable for sinners to speak well to God, if one chooses to blush for one's own faults, and we will show this from the divinely inspired Scripture itself. For it is written in the second book of Chronicles about Rehoboam: "And it came to pass, when the kingdom of Rehoboam had been established and had become strong, that he forsook the commandments of the Lord, and all Israel with him." Then Shishak, the tyrant of the Egyptians, armed himself against Jerusalem and marched out of his own land with his whole army. After this "Shemaiah the prophet came to Rehoboam and to the rulers of Judah who had gathered at Jerusalem for fear of Shishak, and said to them, 'Thus says the Lord: You have forsaken me, and I will forsake you into the hand of Shishak.' And the rulers of Israel and the king were ashamed," it says, "and said, 'The Lord is righteous.' And when the Lord saw that they were ashamed, the word of the Lord came to Shemaiah, saying, 'They are ashamed; I will not destroy them.'" Again it says: "And when he was ashamed, the wrath of the Lord turned away from him, and not to utter destruction; for in Judah too," it says, "there were good words." You see, then, that it is not unprofitable to have good words on one's tongue, if shame goes with them and one blushes for one's wrongdoing. Nevertheless, as Paul says, "The kingdom of God is not in word but in power," and Christ himself said openly somewhere, "Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father in heaven." So, as I said just now, it is pointless to speak well of God when deeds worthy of praise do not go along with it.
They stripped off his skin, to take away hope, the crushing of war.

Again he brings the charges for the destruction of the flock against those whose lot it was to lead. They were well able to instruct the people and bring them onto the straight and unswerving path: to cling with all their love to piety toward God, and to reject devotion to carved images as useless and a cause of ruin and put it as far away as possible. Instead they themselves became destroyers and corrupters. They turned the minds of those in their charge to the very opposite, persuading them to depart from God and to delight instead in the ways of error. For this reason, having offended God, they also slipped from their hope in him. Had they kept that hope, nothing would have stopped them from crushing their enemies. So he speaks as of a sheep, saying that they stripped off his skin, to take away hope, the crushing of war. It is as if he were saying: "They have left him naked of the clothing that hope provides; they have, as it were, unclothed him of my care and help, and so they have made him vulnerable and easy to capture." For their hope in God was taken from them, and this was what crushed war for them. Skin is a secure covering for the irrational animals, since bare flesh is extremely vulnerable. In the same way the power of hope in God is a secure covering for us too, a kind of skin, as it were. If we have it, and grieve God in no way, we will prevail over our enemies and overcome every war, both of the flesh and of the spirit. As it is written, we will tread "on the asp and the basilisk, and trample the lion and the dragon"; and we will sing with confidence, "O Lord God of hosts, blessed is the one who hopes in you."
Therefore the leaders of my people will be cast out of their houses of luxury; because of their evil practices they were driven out.

For, he says, there were those who could have benefited the people under their yoke by instruction and admonition: the guides and fathers, the shepherds and overseers. Yet they stripped off his skin and took away the hope in God through which it was easy to crush every war. Therefore, justly, they will let go of the good things at home; deprived of what was dearest to them and fallen from delight and luxury, they will go off to their enemies and pay a bitter reckoning for their indolence and wickedness. That no one else caused their suffering, but rather they caused it themselves, he makes clear when he says, "Because of their evil practices they were driven out." For as it is written, "Not unjustly are nets spread for winged creatures; for those who share in bloodshed store up evils for themselves."

So we will wrong ourselves if we choose to do what is not lawful, and we too are sent out of houses of luxury. For those who offend God will not see the dwelling places above in heaven; they will have no share in the hope of the saints and in eternal delight. But the wise and good, who are inclined toward everything praiseworthy, will not be among them. How could they be? Instead they will have as their city the Church in heaven, and will live in the dwelling places above, delighting in heavenly good things.
Draw near to the everlasting mountains. Arise and go, for this is not your rest.

The word is still addressed to those whose lot it was to lead. He speaks ironically and, as it were, in character, presenting what is grievous as though it were useful. He all but says: "O leaders of the peoples, perhaps you find it burdensome and wearisome to live in luxury at home, to have your native land, to remain in peace, and to lead a life befitting free people. Since this, it seems, is what you think good, go off to your enemies, hurry away to the land of the Persians and Armenians. Draw near to the everlasting mountains." He means the mountains of Ararat. They are called everlasting either because the people were to spend long ages among them, or because they have been famous from of old, perhaps because the ark came to rest on them.

The word would also apply to the Jews at the time of Christ's coming, who followed the opinions of the scribes and Pharisees and did not accept the faith. For the leading men among them were, as it were, mountains: conspicuous, lifted high by the boasts of the priesthood, and arrived at the summit of glory. But those things were temporary. The shadow has ceased, the worship in types has grown old, so to speak, and the priestly race of that time has become idle. For the everlasting mountains have now been revealed: that is, the heralds and ministers of the new covenant, who proclaim the mystery of Christ, renowned and most illustrious, distinguished by the heights of virtue. God calls them mountains through another prophet as well, saying, "And the mountains shall drip sweetness, and all the hills shall be planted." For the word of those who speak of God is exceedingly sweet, sweeter than honey itself to those who truly love God. They might fittingly say to Christ, the Savior of us all, "How sweet are your words to my throat, more than honey and the comb to my mouth!" So if those who have not yet believed draw near to these spiritual mountains (in a spiritual relationship, clearly), they will find rest. They will at once be relieved of the burden of the sin that has fallen on them, though they have no rest in life under the law, if indeed it is true that "the letter kills, but the spirit gives life." Let the Jews, then, hear from us as well: "Arise and go, for this is not your rest." Since you do not find rest in the law, go and pass over through faith to the teachings of Christ.
Because of uncleanness you have been destroyed with destruction.

By uncleanness he means the infamous defilement of outlandish and abominable idolatry, for it is truly shameful and foul-smelling. Another kind of filth and uncleanness is to cheat one's brothers, to seize what belongs to others as plunder, and to wrong many people in any other way. Because of this uncleanness, he says, you have perished, wretchedly destroyed with a destruction that leads to death.

Those who fight against faith in Christ have also perished, and for no other reason than because of uncleanness. Christ himself makes this plain to us when he says to the disbelieving Jews, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you believe that I am he, you will die in your sins." Is this not the same as "Because of uncleanness you have been destroyed with destruction"? For they did not wash away their offenses, and they were not freed from their ancient charges so as to share in the salvation that comes from Christ, as those who received the faith did.
You were pursued when no one was pursuing.

You have brought on yourselves a captivity of your own choosing, he says, that is, flight into foreign lands, and clearly to enemies as well. No one was pressing or compelling them; they themselves chose, and very eagerly, to do the things for which they would inevitably be punished against their will. So the throngs of the Jews were pursued when no one was pursuing. They could have gone on prospering and enjoying every good thing by honoring Christ, but they slipped into apostasy and offended in many ways: disobeying, insulting, and what outrageous thing did they not do and say?

So when no one is pursuing us, we shall pursue ourselves. And since we have brought incurable evils upon our own souls, we shall no longer impiously blame God, the giver of all things, but rather ourselves, if we are of sound mind and understanding.
A spirit has set up falsehood; it has dripped for you into wine and strong drink.

Some people in Samaria haunted the precincts of the idols and practiced divination in many ways. Pretending to have exact knowledge of the future, they told those who came to them whatever was pleasing and agreeable, seeking paltry and contemptible little gains and selling lying words for a few obols, or "for a piece of bread," as it is written. This above all corrupted and destroyed Israel. So he says that an evil spirit set up Falsehood as a snare for Ephraim. Like some deadly poison, it dripped the demonic error into wine, and showed him all but drunk, lurching without restraint toward every most shameful thing.

The evil one, the apostate dragon, also dripped into the Pharisees false opinion about Christ and outlandish error. At one time they said, "If this man were from God, he would not break the Sabbath." At another they dared to call him a Samaritan, and even a drunkard. And if it is true that no one says "Jesus is accursed" except by Beelzebul, how can it not be easy to see that a spirit set up falsehood among them above all? It dripped into their mind and heart the drunkenness of error, and for this they justly perished, as they leapt on him like wild beasts and resorted to every insolence and blasphemy.
And it will be from the drop of this people. Jacob will surely be gathered together with all; I will surely receive the remnant of Israel; I will bring about their turning away all together.

Wickedness advances toward growth little by little; it blossoms first among a few, but somehow always lays hold of still more and spreads beyond its original measure. Anyone can see that what I say is true by considering carefully what happened to Ephraim. First Jeroboam and some who shared his views set up the heifers in the sacred precincts, worshiped them, and listened to the words of unholy false diviners, that is, false prophets. Then, as the evil crept on and kept adding new things to the first, all Israel was at last brought together and ran together toward a single aim. It was held fast by the offense, no longer in part, but in its entirety and completely. So, he says, from the drop that the word of the false diviners dripped upon them (for very many in Ephraim were in the habit of doing this), the whole of Jacob will be gathered together; that is, it will be brought together into one mind, and the disease will spread over all. "But I will not bring the penalties for this upon them piecemeal; rather I will wait for those who will be added to the ones already corrupted." This is the meaning of "I will surely receive the remnant of Israel": then, and only then, "I will turn away from them all at once."

This would also show the forbearance that is in God. He does not punish at once, but kindly defers, waiting for those who go astray to amend and return. But if this does not happen, and the sickness instead appears to be growing, then at last, hardly and reluctantly, he turns away. And suffering will certainly follow his turning away for those to whom it happens. Accordingly the divine David sings, "Do not turn your face away from me, and do not turn aside in anger from your servant." It should be noted that Beelzebul dripped, as it were, into the scribes and Pharisees the false and ill-omened opinion about Christ. The disease spread over all, as it were, and the rest of the multitude ran along with the deceptions of their leaders. So, having incurred a single sentence (I mean that of condemnation and turning away), they paid penalties equal to their sins.

Like sheep in affliction, like a flock in the midst of its fold, they will leap out from among men through the breach; they broke through before them, and passed through a gate, and went out through it; and the king went out before them, and the Lord will lead them.

The holy prophets often see in their visions the very things they foretell as coming to pass in their own time. They all but see as present and already happening events that will come about only many ages later. So the blessed prophet Isaiah, telling of Christ, all but sees him being led away to his saving passion, and says, “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb silent before its shearer.” And as though looking at the marks of the nails, he asks, addressing perhaps our Lord Jesus Christ himself, “What are these wounds between your hands?” And he said, “Those with which I was wounded in the house of my beloved.” Likewise the inspired Jeremiah, foretelling the war that would come upon Jerusalem, and seeing a great multitude of the Jews already lying dead (in his prophetic visions, of course), laments and says, “Woe is me, for my soul faints over the slain.” In the same way the blessed prophet Micah seems somehow to see the tumult that will come upon the cities of Samaria. Many are already terrified; others are fleeing and racing over walls and ditches. The very ranks of the enemy are bursting through gates and pouring in through them, their commanders with them, while God all but shields them and whets [?] for blood, as one who has been grieved. So, he says, they will be terrified, as a sheep might be when it happens to be in distress, or a whole flock. If a flock were lying down in some place and then people tried to seize it, one would see the animals leaping up and down, and wherever a breach opened, going through it and fleeing. So too, he says, will it be with those against whom the Babylonians’ war advances. The enemy will break through the gates while they look on, that is, “before their face,” and will go in and out through them. That is, they will pass into the cities effortlessly and without any fear, having the Lord of all himself as their leader. For the conquest of Israel was not the work of their own strength; rather it was the nod and decree of God, who handed Israel over. We say that these things also befell those who acted outrageously against Emmanuel himself. For their cities and villages were sacked when Vespasian and Titus conquered them at that time and carried out the divine wrath upon them.

And he will say: Hear these things, you rulers of the house of Jacob and remnant of Israel. Is it not for you to know judgment? You who hate what is good and seek what is evil, who tear their skins from them and their flesh from their bones. Just as they devoured the flesh of my people, and flayed their skins from their bones, and broke their bones, and cut them up like flesh for a cauldron and like meat for a pot, so they will cry out to the Lord, and he will not hear them. He will turn his face away from them at that time, because they acted wickedly against them in their practices.

He who opens the gates to those who make war on Israel, who smooths every path for them and levels every obstacle so that they can then advance with great ease and seize their opponents without a struggle, is the Lord who leads them. He himself will also speak to the rulers and to the remnant of the people. The prophet has put “will say” in place of “will further address.” He charges those who hold office with negligence: having neglected those under their hand, they have become their ruin and destruction. To those who are subject to them, however, and who have been deceived by the perverseness of those in power, he gives to understand that punishment is being brought on the wrongdoers because of the offenses committed against them. For the Creator of all cares even for those who go astray, he who created man “for good works, which he prepared beforehand,” as the inspired Paul writes, “that we should walk in them.” What, then, does he say? “Is it not for you to know judgment?” By “judgment” he means the holy and blameless sentence passed upon them, that is, their condemnation. Here it would be fitting to understand knowing the judgment not as a matter of learning alone. For what harm would that do to those who had committed those offenses? Or how would it have grieved the ungodly? Rather, it is knowing through actually experiencing what was going to happen. For when habitual offenders pay the penalty to those who punish them, then indeed they are said to learn both the supremacy of the authority vested in those punishers and the power of their sovereign judgments. “It is therefore necessary,” he says, “that you above all learn the judgment through what is going to happen: you who are always inclined to what is base and eagerly shun the good; you who make a savage and untamed assault on my sheep and yield nothing to the cruelest of wild beasts; who flay the sheep, tear their flesh, cut them up unsparingly, and, as it were, boil them in a pot.” By these words he signifies every kind of greed, insatiability and [?]. “Since they have done these things,” he says, “they too will cry out. I would not count them worthy of my care, nor, if they should cry out asking for mercy, would I grant it. For they too dealt villainously with those who were subject to them and brought upon them every kind of wickedness, bitter and unholy schemes and deeds.”

One might quite rightly apply such words to the scribes and Pharisees as well. They led the people and presided over the flocks, yet they savagely fell upon those who believed in Christ, together with the common people, as though upon so many sheep. They all but flayed the saints, cut them to pieces and devoured them, differing in nothing from savage beasts. Therefore they also heard God declaring beforehand through the voice of Isaiah: “When you stretch out your hands to me, I will turn my eyes away from you; and if you multiply your prayer, I will not listen to you; for your hands are full of blood.”
BY THE SAME AUTHOR, ON THE SAME PROPHET: SECOND VOLUME.
Thus says the Lord concerning the prophets who lead my people astray, who bite with their teeth and proclaim peace to him; and when nothing was put into their mouth, they raised war against him.

He bitterly accused the people of Israel of having brought ruin on themselves by their own choice, of throwing themselves into evils they had invited, and of being much given to idleness. He added that they had also been greatly wronged, since the wicked and unclean spirit was always deceiving and misleading them. He spoke thus: "Draw near to the everlasting mountains; arise and go, for this is not your rest. Because of uncleanness you have been utterly destroyed. You were pursued when no one pursued you. A spirit has set up a lie; it has dripped for you into wine and drunkenness." For this reason he passed heavy sentence on those whose lot it was to lead. Now he usefully turns his words to the false prophets and diviners among them. These all but dripped into them, like wine, the things that come from the wicked and unclean spirit, that is, lies and deceptions, and so the people were wrapped as if in drunkenness and lost their sober reason. For the false prophets bit them and did them great wrong, persuading them to hold to their own words rather than to the words that come from God through the holy prophets. And they lied, saying that the people would live out their lives in peace and prosperity, and that nothing at all of the things that bring grief would trouble them. But this word of theirs was not from God, for unclean tongues would never have been granted to speak things so glorious and so worth accepting. And since they had persuaded the people to heed them, they raised up war against them. They did not themselves stir up the Assyrians to this; how could they? Rather, they sharpened the holy wrath against them. Because the people heeded those men, the evils of war were justly brought upon them.

This charge is indeed most true and most fitting for the chief priests and Pharisees. By following them the wretched multitude of the Jews perished and was destroyed, for it became impious and a murderer of the Lord.
Therefore you shall have night instead of vision, and darkness instead of divination; the sun shall set upon the prophets, and the day shall grow dark over them.

For since, he says, you dripped falsehood into wine and drunkenness for the people, and bit them like wild beasts while you announced the good news of peace, and you lied to them and so brought them to be caught in the calamities of war, night and darkness will justly come upon you. This will happen even though you pretend to see and, as you think of yourselves, have practiced divination excellently and truthfully. For the sun will set for you, and the very light of day will grow dark. Of course we do not mean that the sun really withdrew its rays from them, or that the light of dawn was darkened. We mean that the greatness of the calamity was to them like darkness and a lightless night, a setting of the sun's ray and a shrinking of the light. And what of such things did not befall them? For terrible and extraordinary evils make the mind drunk, muddy the heart, and fill it with darkness.

One might truly say that for the Jewish multitudes who behaved outrageously toward Christ, the spiritual sun then set. God no longer shone upon them, and the spiritual day no longer dawned for them. Instead their hardening spread over them like night. For they have been hardened, as Paul says, and "whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart." "For claiming to be wise, they became fools, and their senseless heart was darkened." Christ himself foretold that they would suffer these things, saying, "While you have the light, walk in the light, so that darkness may not overtake you." But since they did not accept the divine light, that is, Christ, they were overtaken by darkness, and they had night instead of vision, as the Prophet said.

This same thing will happen also to the inventors of heresies. They pretend to see and insist that they can clearly understand the mystery of Christ, but the wretches speak falsely. They all but drip the harms of deceit into the hearts of the simpler, and then carry them away from the doctrines of truth. For them, then, there will be night and darkness instead of vision, for they will depart into the outer darkness, "sinning against the brethren and wounding their weak conscience, for whom Christ died."
And those who see dreams shall be put to shame, and the diviners shall be laughed to scorn, and all of them shall speak against them, because there will be no one to listen to them.

They had divined that there would be abundant peace, and with their worthless little dreams they swept along those who came to them. They led them to believe that everything would go smoothly for them and that what they prayed for would come to pass. But experience showed the outcome of events to be at odds with what they had said, and the people's hopes turned out the very opposite in every respect. So the false prophets were then necessarily condemned as liars, buffoons and impostors, and they sank into such disrepute that no one would heed them. How, indeed, or why should anyone? They spoke pleasant things, but they plunged those they had deceived into unexpected calamity, as far as could be from what had been hoped.
Unless I fill with strength in the Spirit of the Lord, and with judgment and might, to declare to Jacob his impieties and to Israel his sins.

He shows that those whose reputation for prophecy is counterfeit must, in every way and without exception, speak falsely. For how could anyone speak the truth who does not speak in God, who is the truth? Concerning Cain, Christ said somewhere, "He was a murderer from the beginning, and did not stand in the truth, because he is a liar, as is also his father." He gives him as father the one who invented falsehood, that is, Satan. And who can doubt that those who speak from a diabolical spirit, saying what belongs to it, must lie? Those, however, who speak through God speak excellently and truly in every way and without exception, for they have the truth within themselves. So how could the word of prophecy among some not prove false, he says, unless through my Spirit I were to fill certain people with power and righteousness, that is, judgment, so that they might rise up fearlessly and boldly against sinners and convict them? For I think that those who speak the things of God need very great and noble courage. At times they rebuke whole peoples, and indeed kings and those in high places, who gnash their teeth most of all at those who want to correct them, and find the word of those who would help them unbearable. The blessed prophets toiled, or rather were in danger, and were put to death in many ways, falling at various times victim to the unholy anger of those they were instructing. The divinely inspired disciples too were scourged. For being full of power and judgment and righteousness, they brought the flocks of the Jews to God through faith in Christ. But they rejoiced when they were mistreated, and went out from the councils delighted that they had been dishonored for the sake of the Name. For they knew that, having suffered with Christ, they will also reign with him.
Hear these things, you leaders of the house of Jacob and you remnant of the house of Israel, who abhor judgment and pervert all that is right, who build Zion with blood and Jerusalem with iniquities.

The Creator is exceedingly good, and he was not ignorant of how great the evils were that would befall them. So he goes about it in every way and brings in every kind of exhortation and threat, so that perhaps the sinners might be persuaded and choose to repent. They would then unlearn their shameful ways and choose to do the things by which they could most likely escape the effects of wrath without trouble. But the studious and learned reader must know that, while the word of the prophets is continuous in the books and writings, it was given at various times and piecemeal. So even if they sometimes seem to say the same things, one must remember that they did not say such things at one time, as I said, nor to the same people. Often long intervals came between, and they spoke to different people at different times. For everyone needed to know what would happen, and the prediction of a common calamity had to be made to those throughout the whole land. To you, then, he says, is this word, you who have come to such stupefaction that you abhor judgment, that is, righteousness, and declare perverse the law that guides rightly to the knowledge of the good. To you who perhaps think that by bloodshed and the shedding of innocent blood you restore Zion and make Jerusalem glorious and renowned. But it would have been better for them to realize that they were rather overturning it, though they had been appointed for building up and restoring it, since they presided over the flocks as priests and guardians of the law appointed by God.

And they truly destroyed Zion with blood. For they killed the prophets, and to them they added even the Lord of all, I mean Christ. Though they were the builders of Zion, they rejected him, even though God says plainly, "Behold, I lay in the foundations of Zion a chosen stone, a precious cornerstone, and whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame." But, as I said, the builders of Zion rejected the chosen and precious stone; yet it has been set as the head of the corner. For Christ has become king over us and over those of the circumcision. He created them "into one new man, making peace through the cross," joining them together as if into a corner in oneness of soul in the Spirit. For it is written, "The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and one soul." And since they have been conformed through sanctification and faith to the most precious cornerstone, the divinely inspired Peter fittingly and wisely writes to them, "You also, like living stones, are being built up as a spiritual house," "into a holy temple, into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit." For Christ has made his dwelling in the hearts of believers. And concerning them he says somewhere through the prophet's voice, "For I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people."

Her leaders judged for bribes, and her priests answered for hire, and her prophets divined for silver; and they leaned upon the Lord, saying, "Is not the Lord among us? No evil shall come upon us." Therefore because of you Zion shall be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem shall be like a watchman's hut in an orchard, and the mountain of the house like a grove in a thicket.

Unjust judgment and bribery are a loathsome thing, among those most hateful to the all-holy God. For it is written, "The ways of one who unjustly takes gifts into his bosom do not prosper." Some are so overcome by accursed greed and shameful petty profits that they think it nothing to pervert justice and sell the truth. Those who get dust in their eyes find their power of sight weakened; in the same way these people let blindness into their minds and no longer see. "For gifts blind the eyes of the wise," as it is written, "and corrupt righteous words." And those who pervert justice wrong the pure beauty of God's own prerogatives. For judging belongs to God alone, and the blessed Moses knew this when he said, "You shall not show partiality in judgment, for the judgment is God's." The one who makes a practice of judging unjustly all but lays hands on the divine and supreme thrones. Let him know that he has offended against the ineffable glory itself, which knows how to judge rightly and justly. For judgment belongs to God, as I said. Besides this, it is utterly dreadful to make piety a means of gain and to treat the things of God as a source of profit. Notice how he does not leave unblamed the prophet or priest who wants to work for hire and promises to speak to those who come to him, provided they choose to bring fees and gifts. But I think that here again the word is speaking of false prophets. It is not speaking at all of those who truly serve as priests according to the law, but of those who made a habit of creeping into such honors and acquiring a purchased reputation for themselves. For a holy prophet, or a true priest, would never have made his own soul guilty of such faults.

Then, while committing such offenses, he says, they leaned upon the Lord, saying, "Is not the Lord among us? No evil shall come upon us." The God of all was admittedly in Israel. He rescued them from their misery in Egypt, brought them into the land of promise, and made them stronger and mightier than their enemies. But surely they ought to have realized that, since they were offending grievously and stood condemned for such outrageous deeds, God would not bear to be with them. For the holy has nothing in common with the profane, and the pure cannot be joined to the filthy. They thought vain things, supposing that even if they were workers of wickedness, even if they chose to do things worse than any evil, God would still be with them all the same. Therefore, he says, they will learn from the very events that are about to happen. For Zion shall be plowed, and the renowned Jerusalem shall be like a watchman's hut in an orchard, that is, desolate and overthrown. And the very mountain of the house, that is, the temple that stands on the high hill, shall become a grove in a thicket. It is as if he said, a lair of wild beasts and dens of serpents. For just as wild beasts and the untamed kinds of reptiles live in mountains and thickets, so too they live in desolate places, and wherever many ruins are to be seen.

These things happened to the Jewish multitudes when they behaved outrageously toward Emmanuel himself. For then, at that very time, they perished utterly, and not one stone remained upon another, according to the word of the Savior himself. And Zion, once venerable and admirable, has since been shown to be plowland fit for farmers. But we must know that God will be among us too, not if we have faith alone, nor if we merely rest on him because of it, but if good repute from works is added to faith. "For faith without works is dead," as it is written. But when works go hand in hand with the good things [?], then indeed God will be with us. He will readily give us strength, count us as friends, gladden us as his true children, and deliver us from every evil.

And in the last days the mountain of the Lord shall be manifest, established on the tops of the mountains, and it shall be lifted up above the hills; and peoples shall hasten to it, and many nations shall go to it and say, "Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and they will show us his way, and we will walk in his paths."

In these words we can now see clearly the prediction of the Church from the Gentiles. Israel according to the flesh had been, as it were, removed from the midst. The sacrifices under the law had ceased, and the priesthood descended from the blood of Levi had fallen silent. The renowned temple itself had been burned, and Jerusalem destroyed. Then Christ revealed the Church from the Gentiles, and that in the last time, that is, at the consummation of this age, for it was then, in our times, that it came to be. So he calls the Church a mountain, the Church which is the house of the living God. He calls it high because there is nothing at all lowly in it. The knowledge of the doctrines about God is lifted on high, and the very life of those who have been justified in Christ and sanctified in the Spirit has its dwelling on high. For in them there is nothing groveling or trodden underfoot in their way of life, as one may certainly see among those of the circumcision. For they were overcome by love of the flesh and by shameful gains, they were caught committing unjust murders, and they were guilty of a great many other offenses. "But those who belong to Jesus Christ," as the divine Paul says, "have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires." They have so hated being rich that one may hear them cry out boldly, "If we have food and clothing, with these we shall be content. But those who wish to be rich fall into temptation and snares and many senseless and harmful desires, which plunge people into ruin and destruction." And they have so far withdrawn from murder that they turn the other cheek also to those who strike them on the right. The Church might also be understood as a mountain in another way, when compared with the doctrines of the Greeks. For the Greeks teach, most senselessly, that one must worship stones and wood and creation itself. The Church, however, makes plainly known the One who is God by nature and in truth, who fashioned this universe, holds it together in its well-being, and as God is Lord of all.

He says that the mountain of the Lord is lifted above mountains and hills and is established, meaning by this that it stands in full view, as it were. For what lies on a mountain can be seen from all around and is very easy to see, and is perhaps unknown to no one, even to those who live farthest away. The word of prophecy has clearly declared that the nations would hasten to it with great eagerness, and the outcome of events has itself borne witness to this and shown it to be true. For peoples shall hasten to it, he says, clearly meaning to the Master of the house, that is, Christ. And what will they say? "Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of our God, and they will show us his way, and we will walk in it." You hear how eagerly they urge one another on, and rightly and sensibly they say, "Let us go up." For I would say that, aware how low and abject the doctrines of the Greeks are, they say "Let us go up" because they are now leaping on high, as far as their thoughts about the One who is God by nature and in truth are concerned. They long for righteousness, and they thirst to learn the way of the Lord, and indeed they promise to walk in his paths, and with great zeal. And who would teach them such things? Clearly the Savior's disciples, who were entrusted with the divine preaching, to whom Christ said, "Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you."
For out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. And he shall judge among many peoples and rebuke strong nations, even to a distant land.

The countless and innumerable flocks of the nations make their way to the mountain of the Lord, that is, the Church. They long to learn the way of the Lord and eagerly promise to walk in it. Here they state the reason why they no longer [?] wish, as it were, to be initiated into the law and to run after Judaism. For before the coming of our Savior, while the customs under the law still stood, some of those who had gone astray would come over. They bade farewell to the evils of idolatry, had their flesh circumcised, and earnestly sought to live by the customs and laws of the Jews. Such converts among them were beyond number. Indeed, when Solomon planned to build the temple in Jerusalem, he appointed one hundred and fifty thousand stonecutters and laborers from among the proselytes, for so it is written in Chronicles. What took place was a type of a mystery. For those who were to build a temple to God, true and visible to all, that is, the Church, would not be Jews but rather people from the Gentiles. They carry within them the Jew who is one inwardly, and they have a circumcision that is not in the flesh but in the spirit.

So before the Savior's coming some of the idolaters came over and lived by the laws of the Jews. But now that the mountain of the Lord, truly visible to all, has been revealed, they come rather to it, rejoicing and saying, "For out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem." They seem to want to show, and perhaps to cry out plainly, that Zion will be left without even the law itself, and Jerusalem stripped of the divine words. For in a way the law has departed from them, and with it the word of God spoken through angels. The shadow has been done away with, what was in types has ceased, the sacrifices too have been abolished, and everything given through Moses has in a way come to an end, so far as the letter is concerned, I mean. They all but prophesy and foretell that Christ was to judge and convict many nations. How he would judge and convict them, and in what manner, needs to be explained. He persuades them to abstain from the ways of error and shows them clearly that they are hastening to destruction unless they choose to live rightly and wipe away the charges of their former offenses. In this way he will, in a certain sense, judge and convict not just one nation but nations as far as a distant land, that is, to the ends of the earth under heaven. For the saving word is celebrated everywhere. "For this gospel," he says, "will be preached in the whole world."

The prophetic word also seems to hint to us at another mystery, a subtle and hidden one. It relates, as it were, how those from the Gentiles would be received, and how, having abandoned that ancient error, they will at last walk to the mountain of the Lord, that is, the Church. For from the Zion above, it says, and from the spiritual Jerusalem, the law and the word of the Lord will go forth. The Word of God has come down to us from heaven, and he has become for us both law and lawgiver; and he will judge between many peoples, and will convict strong nations as far as a distant land. What "he will judge and will convict" might mean, I will say as far as it comes to mind. Satan had tyrannized over all, and together with the evil powers that were with him he waged war on the whole world under the sun; laying the yoke of his greed on everyone, he lured the race on earth away from God. But "God the Lord has shone upon us," as it is written. The good shepherd at last appeared on earth: he rescued the deceived from that one's greed, condemned the deceivers, and convicted the wrongdoers, that is, "the rulers, the authorities, the world-rulers of this age, the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places." Christ himself makes this plain to us when he says, "Now is the judgment of this age; now the ruler of this world will be cast out. And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all to myself." For he has given judgment for many and countless peoples, clearly for those who had been wronged, and he has justified them in mercy and faith. He has cast out the ruler of this age and driven him from his rule over us, convicting him as unjust, as unholy, as a murderer, as one who had greedily seized the world under heaven. And the other nations of demons were surely convicted along with him, those once fearsome and strong, which did not haunt a single city but were scattered as far as a distant land, that is, to the ends of the world under heaven. They had, as it were, divided up the earth among themselves, and there was no one at all who had not felt their perversity.

And they will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears [?] into sickles, and nation will no longer lift up sword against nation, and they will no longer learn to make war. And each will rest under his vine, and each under his fig tree, and there will be no one to make them afraid, for the mouth of the Lord Almighty has spoken these things.

In Christ all things have become new, and Paul speaks the truth when he says that "in Christ there is a new creation, and the old things have passed away." For the very state of affairs has changed for the better. It no longer labors with wars and battles, whose assault on everyone is truly hard to bear and utterly grievous. When the prophet says that the instruments of war are reshaped for the work of farmers, that each person rests under his own fig tree and indeed his own vine, and that there is no one to frighten them, what else could he be suggesting to us than that there will be a deep and unbroken peace, a time without war? This was fulfilled in the time of the Lord's coming. Indeed Christ himself said, "My peace I give to you, my peace I leave with you."

But when, and how, did peace come about in the world as well? When the dominion of the Romans, that most glorious empire, at last prevailed over the world under heaven, all the nations were brought together and came under one yoke. They ceased from war with one another and turned to the works of peace, clearly to farming, and each people lives securely in its own cities. Before the hand of the Romans held sway over them, there were wars everywhere, and whole countries and cities were uprooted. Anyone who wished was free to ravage whomever he chose and to carry off the goods of others as a conqueror. The people of every country and city had to be well equipped with the gear of war, to drill in tactics, and to defend themselves and their children. But once the power of the Roman empire was firmly established, such things ceased, and the implements of war became mattocks and sickles and indeed plows, and from then on they were refashioned into other such things.

If anyone should choose to approach the passage spiritually as well, he will understand that since Christ awards us peace out of his own gentleness, and abolishes the rulers who of old fought against those who wished to live godly lives, we have ceased to be afraid. We are now beyond the reach of assault and battle; we have turned to cultivating spiritual things and gather the fruits of righteousness, and from now on we rest under fig tree and vine. The fig tree will be a symbol of sweetness, and the vine of spiritual gladness. For the Savior's word is very sweet, and it knows how to gladden the human heart, as it is written. Sweet, too, and full of gladness is the hope for the future with which we have been enriched in Christ.
For all the peoples will walk, each in its own way [?], but we will walk in the name of the Lord our God forever and beyond.

Those who have made it their aim to go up to the mountain of the Lord, and who wish to learn his paths, promise to be obedient and embrace the glories of the life in Christ. By these words they show us very clearly that they will lay claim with all their strength to the pursuits of godliness. For, they say, let each person in every [?] and city walk whatever path he himself chooses, and live as seems good to him or as he has judged to be right. But our concern is Christ: we will make his decrees our straight path, and we will walk alongside him, as it were, not only in this present and passing age but far beyond it. And the saying is true. Those who now suffer with him will be with him forever, will be glorified with him, and will reign with him. Those make Christ their concern who put nothing before their love for him. They give up the vain distractions of the world and seek instead righteousness and what pleases him and to excel in virtue, as the divine Paul did. He writes, at any rate, "I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me." And again, "For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified."

In that day, says the Lord, I will gather her who is crushed, and I will receive her who has been driven out, and those whom I drove away. I will make her who is crushed into a remnant, and her who was driven out into a strong nation, and the Lord will reign over them on Mount Zion from now on and forever.

He goes on to show that Israel would by no means slip entirely away from hope. She was crushed and became an outcast, that is, she was rejected because of her very great impiety. She fought against God and worshiped idols; she was loathsome and profane, and she bore no small guilt for bloodshed. They killed the prophets, and then at last they crucified the very Savior and Redeemer of all. Yet she has been shown mercy for the sake of the fathers: the remnant has been saved and has become a great nation. And it is true, and quite reasonable, that the holy multitude of those justified in Christ may be understood as a very great nation. Its distinguishing marks, the things for which it deserves to be admired, are the goods of the mind and the glories of the heart: sanctification, hope in Christ, sincerity in faith, admirable virtue, praiseworthy endurance, and being ruled and shepherded by Christ himself and having him as teacher. "For one is our teacher, the Christ." And when the dead are raised, "we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord." By Mount Zion he means the Jerusalem above, the mother of the firstborn, where we will be with Christ himself.
And you, murky tower of the flock, daughter of Zion: upon you [?] the first dominion shall enter, the kingdom of Babylon, upon the daughter of Jerusalem.
