He announces the gifts of his gentleness to those who have suffered, and he has said that in due time he will receive her who is crushed and make her a great nation. In the meantime, however, he lays blame, and he reproaches her, to her benefit, for having become utterly wretched, crushed and rejected. For as the blessed Paul said, "Godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation and brings no regret." So he strikes her out of love, and because, though she could have avoided experiencing any of the things that grieved her, she came to this by her own free inclination. He calls Zion, that is, Jerusalem itself, a murky tower of the flock, speaking as it were with feeling, almost groaning over her: "O Zion, that is, Jerusalem, wretched daughter, O wretched and lightless dwelling of my sheep, you will surely lie exposed to your enemies, even against your will. For it will come, it will come upon you before long, the foremost and mightiest of the kingdoms on earth, that is, the kingdom of the Babylonians." He calls Zion, or Jerusalem, a murky tower and a dark dwelling because all who were in her walked as if in darkness. They would not make the law of God a lamp and a light, so to speak, or receive in their minds the illumination that comes from him. Only in this way, and in no other, could they have traveled a road without straying, kept clear of pits, leapt over sin, and avoided stumbling into the evils that befall people along the way.

Let us too, then, sing to God, saying, "Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death, lest my enemy ever say, I have prevailed against him." For when we are illumined by divine light and have received into our minds the radiance of the wisdom that comes from above and from God, the enemy will never capture us. We will escape what comes from divine wrath and enjoy the good cheer that comes from above, and in Christ we will surely prosper.

And now, why have you come to know evils? Was there no king for you? Or has your counsel perished, that pangs have seized you like a woman in labor? Be in labor, and be brave, and draw near, daughter, like a woman giving birth, for now you shall go out from the city and encamp in the plain, and you shall come as far as Babylon. From there the Lord your God will rescue you, and from there he will redeem you from the hand of your enemies.

"The first dominion," he says, "will come upon you." But what, then, is the reason you are being shattered by such dreadful evils? To "know evils" is to fall into evils, that is, into the things that usually cause harm; I mean the calamities of war. Was there no king for you, then? Or have you not practiced taking wise counsel and making the best plans for yourself? Again he strikes at her subtly and reproaches her indirectly, as utterly foolish and as one who did not shrink from offending God. How so, I will explain briefly.

In the beginning the God of all reigned over the people of Israel, with the all-wise Moses as mediator. After him he reigned through Joshua son of Nun, who took over the command; then through the judges appointed from time to time; and after them through blessed Samuel. While their affairs stood thus and were in the very best order, the wretches devised bitter things against themselves. Shaking off, as it were, the yoke of God's kingship, they came to blessed Samuel and said, "Look, you have grown old, and your sons do not walk in your way. Now appoint for us a king to judge us, like the other nations." "And the word was evil in Samuel's eyes," it says, "when they said, Give us a king to judge us. And Samuel prayed to the Lord, and the Lord said to Samuel, Listen to the voice of the people in whatever they say to you, for it is not you they have rejected, but me they have rejected from reigning over them." Then blessed Samuel declared to them the rights of the king, alarmed them greatly with many terrors, and tried very forcefully to turn them from such unsound and unholy schemes. Yet they pressed on no less, saying, "No, but there shall be a king over us, and we too shall be like the other nations, and our king shall judge us, and go out before us, and fight our war." So he brings those ancient and perilous counsels back to their memory, and as it were speaks ironically of what happened, saying, "How have you come to know evils? Was there no king for you? Or has your counsel perished?" Did you not ask for a king, he says, saying, He will go "before us, and will fight our war"? Surely that was good counsel you took! See, the outcome has shown your counsel to be excellent and necessary! You cast off the yoke of God's kingship: see, pangs have seized you like a woman in labor. "Be in labor, then, and be brave, daughter of Zion." Again the words are spoken with feeling. "O good daughter," he says, "be patient in your pangs, endure your griefs, draw near to giving birth," that is, you will not be far from what you expect. Like a woman already in labor you will wail with pain; leaving your well-towered cities, you will encamp in the plain, that is, he says, you will lodge in deserts; and you will come to Babylon itself. Yet he does not leave her entirely without comfort, for he at once added that she will escape and be brought back again, since God will take pity on her.

It is best, then, to remain under God and be ruled by him, to make him our strength, defender and helper, to bow the neck of the soul to him alone, to live by his will, and to hold what seems good to him worthy of every regard. If we do not do this, we will be wholly and certainly under spiritual Babylonians, I mean the opposing and unclean powers, and under the first dominion, that is, Satan. Cast out, as it were, from the holy city "whose builder and maker is God," we will dwell in the city of the Babylonians. For we will live in confusion and tumult, amid the many distractions of this present life; and Babylon means "confusion."

And now many nations have gathered against you, who say, "We shall rejoice, and our eyes shall look upon Zion." But they did not know the thought of the Lord, nor did they understand his counsel, that he has gathered them like sheaves on the threshing floor. Arise and thresh them, daughter of Zion, for I will make your horns iron and your hooves bronze; and you shall grind many peoples to pieces, and you shall dedicate their multitude to the Lord, and their strength to the Lord of all the earth.

We have already said many times that while Hezekiah held the kingship in Jerusalem, Sennacherib ravaged Samaria and took many cities of Judea along with it. Then he sent Rabshakeh from Lachish, who babbled no small amount of insolence against the divine glory; and it was then that one hundred and eighty-five thousand Assyrians perished in a single night by the hand of an angel. Here again he mentions this history. Many nations, he says, have gathered against you, all but frolicking, ready to dance over you as you were about to fall. Yet they did not know what God had purposed. They have been brought together as onto a threshing floor, and like sheaves they will lie beneath your feet. Arise, then, and thresh them, for you will have horns of iron and hooves of bronze; that is, you will be hard to overcome and invincible to your enemies, and you will all but trample those who resist you. Since he has mentioned a threshing floor and sheaves, he has kept the metaphor consistent and speaks of horns and hooves as though of a young bull. But since they were not destroyed and did not fall by human hand, but lay dead as the work of divine wrath, do not, he says, claim the glory for these things yourself, but rather dedicate to the Lord of all the earth both the multitude itself and the strength of those who perished.

This, then, is the meaning according to history. But the sudden turns of the prophetic proclamations may perhaps trouble some readers. For just now we heard him say, "Upon you will come and enter the first dominion, the kingdom of the Babylonians," and the manner of the captivity was described to us; and then at once we see her saved and trampling her enemies. We need, then, to distinguish the times clearly, for in this way our understanding of what is said will be clear and free of confusion. While Hezekiah was king, Sennacherib came up against Jerusalem. After Hezekiah's death there were four other kings, and fifth came Jeconiah. It was then that Nebuchadnezzar took all Judea and Jerusalem itself, and carried off all Israel into captivity. The blessed prophet Jeremiah records the history of these events clearly for us.
Now the daughter of Ephraim shall be hemmed in by a barricade; he has laid siege against you; with a rod they shall strike the tribes of Israel on the cheek.

Many peoples and many nations will gather against Zion; and then, having expected to dance over her and laugh at her, they were threshed and crushed, as God threw them down like sheaves before the feet of the victors. But Samaria was taken and perished, consumed by war. Concerning her he says that she will be hemmed in and held fast, clearly because God decreed that she should come under siege and must suffer. He calls Samaria, that is, the multitude in Samaria, the daughter of Ephraim. For the one entrusted with kingship seems in a sense to stand in the place of a father to those subject to him, and it was men from Ephraim who reigned over Samaria. So, he says, Samaria will surely be surrounded and encircled, as it were, by the hosts of her enemies, who will all but strike her on the cheek, not slapping her with hands that show restraint, but crushing her with rods and violently maltreating her. By these words he signifies that, in addition to the disgrace, the toil of captivity will be hard to bear. Blows on the cheek are an unmistakable sign of disgrace; and if they are understood to be given with a rod, they will surely bring suffering as well, the kind of treatment fit for a slave. So, he says, Samaria, ruled by men of the tribe of Ephraim, will be dishonored and will live amid torments and toils.

But the hand of the striker will be idle, and we will never taste torment, if with all our strength we refuse to provoke the Lord of all to anger against us by doing what is unlawful and by eagerly pursuing what he hates. If instead we honor him with uprightness, we will enjoy prosperity and live a life that is truly splendid and worth attaining.

And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrathah, are very few to be among the thousands of Judah; from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, and his goings forth are from the beginning, from the days of eternity.

In these words the prophetic word brings us the good news that our affairs will return to how they were at the beginning. It recalls very clearly the recapitulation said to have taken place in Christ. For what is in him is a new creation, as it is written, and "the old things have passed away, and through him new things have come into being," since he transforms what is human and renews it once more to well-being. For he has reigned, and he has once again made his rule over all a thing to be desired. The universal truth is also signified through particular dealings of God. As I said, Israel was ruled in the beginning by God, with holy men as intermediaries. Then not long afterward, falling sick with folly, they scorned life under God and honored human powers instead. Indeed they asked for Saul as king over them. Then they gave great offense, for the God of all, grieved, said to blessed Samuel, "It is not you they have rejected, but me they have rejected from reigning over them." Experience itself has shown that this thing brought them no benefit at all, but was rather bitter, harmful and ruinous; how could anyone doubt it? For because of it they fell into dreadful and inescapable evils. So, bringing Israel back, as it were, to its original state, I mean to being ruled by God himself, he proclaimed beforehand Christ, who would come from Bethlehem to be their Savior and Redeemer.

And it would not be off the mark if someone chose to take the statement in a general sense. For since we on earth fell away from God's kingship, fashioning a foreign yoke for ourselves and taking as master one who is not master by nature, but rather a braggart and an apostate, I mean Satan, we came into every kind of evil. But, as I said just now, God the Father was pleased "to sum up all things in Christ, things in the heavens and things on earth," and "he rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, in the light."

So he addresses Bethlehem, that is, the house of Ephrathah. The region is called Ephrathah, and Bethlehem is the small town, that is, the village in that region. Jesse and David came from there, and so did the holy Virgin herself, who bore for us the divine infant, her own son Jesus, "whose rule was upon his shoulder, and his name is called Angel of Great Counsel" (Isa. 9:6). For he has reigned through the cross. Since he became "obedient unto death, even death on a cross," therefore, as the divine Paul says, "God also highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus Christ every knee should bend, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father. Amen." "O Bethlehem," he says, "house of Ephrathah, though you are too small to be among the thousands of Judah." That is: countless are the splendid and great cities of Judea, brimming with a populous throng of inhabitants; but even though very few indeed dwell in you and occupy you, you will become the nurse and will be called the city of him who reigns over Israel. He is the good shepherd, so good that he lays down his very life for the sheep, and he will rule over all Israel. And this does not mean only those of Israel by blood, but also those of the promise, promised beforehand to Abraham. For God said to him somewhere, "In Isaac shall your seed be called," and "in Isaac" means "by promise." So the promise is sure not only to those of Israel by blood, "but also to those who walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had while uncircumcised." For these are Israel, because "the children of the promise are counted as seed." It is as if he were saying, "He will rule over everyone who believes in him and joins himself to me through him." For we have been brought to the Father through the Son, and he himself will bear witness, saying, "No one comes to the Father except through me." So Christ was shown forth from Bethlehem, the good shepherd "who pastures us among gardens and lilies." He sets before us the fragrance of the gospel oracles and offers his own ripe flowers, as it were, to those who wish to pluck them and be filled spiritually with their fragrance. For he said, "I am the flower of the plain, the lily of the valleys." And he says that his goings forth are from the beginning and from the days of eternity. Either he means the pre-eternal existence of the Word, for he is, truly he is, coeternal with his own Begetter and is himself the maker of the ages. Or else he means that, although he became man in the last time of the age, the mystery concerning him had been determined beforehand in the foreknowledge of the Father, even before the foundation of the ages. So by "going forth" he means either the timeless begetting of the Son from God the Father into his own existence, or else his manifestation that would take place in time, when he became flesh. Yet from the beginning and from the days of eternity he had been predetermined and appointed by the Father as Savior and Redeemer, for the Father knew what would befall the human race in the meantime because of the transgression in Adam.
Therefore you will give them up until the time of her who is in labor. She will give birth, and the rest of their brothers will return to the sons of Israel.

The Prophet seems to have pondered this within himself, and perhaps reasoned and said: "God will not speak falsely; he will surely accomplish what he has promised. And if Israel has such bright hopes, and the leader will be born to them and will rule and deliver them from every evil, why will they be taken captive at all?" Then, having considered the time of the promise and understanding that it had not yet come, he in a way answers himself, saying: "Since the time of the promise is still far off, and they are caught up in no small offenses and never cease from wrongdoing, therefore you will give them up, that is, you will hand them over to their enemies, O Master, until the time of her who gives birth": until, he says, that divine infant is brought forth from a virgin's womb. For then there will be the most complete redemption, and they will be securely established in prosperity, lacking nothing at all that makes for gladness. While the Prophet was pondering these things, as I said, and as it were whispering them to himself, God answers him: "She will give birth," and calls him to firm faith. Similar to this is what was said to the prophet Habakkuk: "Yet a little while, and he who is coming will come and will not delay." For he will certainly be born, he says, without fail, and the remnant of their brothers will return to the sons of Israel. For not a few of the Jews accepted faith in Christ, the blessed disciples first of all; but those who outraged him by their disobedience slipped away from the hope. Yet in the last times they will be added to the others, and, as if returning from a retreat, they will at last run back with difficulty to what it would have been better to come to at the beginning.

And he will stand and see, and the Lord will shepherd his flock in strength, and they will dwell in the glory of the name of the Lord their God; for now he will be magnified to the ends of the earth. And this will be the peace.

He says "he will stand" in place of "he will preside over them." The shepherd will tend his own sheep in person. He will not entrust the guiding of them to someone else, as he once did to blessed Moses, but will do it himself, by himself. For it is true that "not an elder, not an angel, but the Lord himself saved us." And he will shepherd us in strength, setting us above all sweat and toil. For he will stand in front of us, as it were, and save us all together. He will not allow false shepherds to do wrong by deceit, or wild beasts to spring upon the flocks. Nor will he permit the wicked and hostile powers to act insolently against the believers and get the better of the sanctified, as they certainly did in former times. Rather, he grants them "to tread upon the asp and the basilisk, and to trample the lion and the dragon." For through him we have become glorious; we have been lifted up on high, bright and conspicuous, and have reached to the ends of the world under heaven. For he is our strength and power, he is the mediator and reconciler, he is our peace. As it is written, he broke down "the dividing wall of partition, abolished the law of commandments expressed in ordinances, and created the two peoples into one new man, making peace," binding them tightly into unity with the bonds of love. So Peace is a fitting and true name for him, even though he is called Christ.

When the Assyrian comes upon your land, and when he sets foot in your country, then seven shepherds and eight bites of men will be raised up against him, and they will shepherd Assur with the sword, and the land of Nimrod in its trench. And he will deliver you from Assur when he comes upon your land and when he sets foot within your borders.

The Hebrew text of the present passage begins with "And this will be the peace, when the Assyrian comes upon your land and when he sets foot in your country." For this, he says, will be the manner of the peace, if Assur should wish to overrun your land and country. In interpreting the verses, however, we will say that the discourse once again leaves sensible and more obvious matters behind and rises, as it were, on high, carrying us subtly from a visible image to things that happen spiritually. For here by "the Assyrian" he no longer means the man from Babylon. Rather, he signifies the inventor of sin, I mean Satan, or, to put it simply, the savage and warlike multitude of demons, which rises up spiritually against every saint and wages war on the holy city, the spiritual Zion, "which is the church of the living God." It is a type, a close likeness as it were, of the Jerusalem that is understood to be above and heavenly. So too the divine psalmist made mention of it, saying, "Glorious things have been spoken of you, O city of God." For Christ dwells in the Church and has made it his own city, as it were, although by the nature of his divinity he fills all things. This city of God, then, is a kind of land and country for those who have been sanctified and enriched with unity with God in the Spirit. So when, he says, the Assyrian comes upon your land, that is, if the barbarous and hostile powers should fight against the saints, they will not find them bereft of protectors. For seven shepherds and eight bites of men will rise up against them. The meaning of the prophecy seems to be that through the times, that is, through the numbers seven and eight, it indicates the saints: those before the advent, and those who lived at the time of it and after it. For before the advent, under the law of Moses, the Sabbath rest on the seventh day was honored, and it was still the time of the shadow. At that time the band of the holy prophets also appeared, guiding people toward piety and the knowledge of Christ. But when the Only-begotten finally appeared, endured the cross for the life of all, and came back to life on the eighth day, having despoiled Hades, he then commanded the holy apostles to make disciples of "all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and to teach them to keep all that he had commanded them." These, then, he calls the eight bites of men, counting from the time of the resurrection, and so indicating those who lived at that time and after it.

So when, he says, the Assyrian comes, or a foreigner and barbarian, then he will come up against seven shepherds and eight bites. For we shall find the saints who lived in the time of the law, whom he calls the seven shepherds. Besides these we shall find the apostles and evangelists, and the teachers of the churches in each generation, always fighting and standing firm against all the deceits of demons, and setting their own vigilance, as it were, against the perversities of the evil one. For they keep safe those who dwell in the holy country and land, walling them about with admonitions and securing them with instruction in everything that is best. That the choir of saints would in some way lay plots against Satan and devour him spiritually with bites, God again made plain through the voice of a saint, saying of him: "Woe to him who multiplies for himself what is not his own (how long?), and makes his yoke heavy and stout! For suddenly those who bite him will rise up, and those who plot against you will awaken, and you will become plunder for them. Because you plundered many nations, all the peoples who are left will plunder you." Do you hear him say that the one who multiplies for himself what is not his own, that is, Satan, will be bitten and plundered? Then he calls those who plunder him "those who are left," that is, those from the remnant, namely those from Jacob. But even if some Assyrian should come, he says, that is, a man of other opinions who has gone astray, who lacks the faith that runs straight but limps, as it were, and is broken in mind, they set against him too the power of the truth. Exposing the [?] of his rottenness, they snuff him out like a wolf, all but biting him, and make him keep far away from the flock of spiritual sheep and be driven out even against his will. These seven shepherds, then, who are also understood as eight bites, will shepherd Assur with the sword. He says "they will shepherd" in place of "they will pursue." Since he had mentioned shepherds, he kept the metaphor fitting by saying "they will shepherd."

And what sword may reasonably be understood here, the sword the saints customarily use? The psalmist will make it clear when he says of them, "And two-edged swords in their hands, to execute vengeance on the nations and rebukes among the peoples." For "the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword." Paul too, arming the spiritual soldier in Christ, gives him "the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God." That the divine and all-powerful sword, that is, the Word of God, pursues Assur, the prophet Isaiah will persuade us no less, when he says, "And it shall be in that day that God will bring his holy sword, the great and the strong, upon the dragon, the crooked serpent, and will slay the dragon." And again: "And it shall be, when the Lord has finished doing all things on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, that he will bring it upon the great mind, the ruler of the Assyrians, and upon the lofty glory of his eyes. For he said, By strength I will do it, and by the wisdom of understanding I will remove the boundaries of nations, and I will plunder their strength, and I will shake inhabited cities." With this sword, then, they will shepherd Assur, and all the land of Nimrod in its trench. What he means by this is the following. He calls the country of the Assyrians, that is, Babylon, the land of Nimrod; around it, they say, a deep trench had been dug. And he calls it the land of Nimrod because Nimrod was the beginning and origin of the Babylonians and the father of the race. It is written of him in Genesis as follows: "The sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan. And Cush fathered Nimrod; he was the first to be a giant on the earth. He was a giant hunter before the Lord God; therefore they will say, Like Nimrod, a giant hunter before the Lord. And the beginning of his kingdom was Babylon and Erech and Accad and Calneh in the land of Shinar." The tower was raised in Calneh (this is a Persian district), as divine Scripture also says. So by the land of Nimrod he means Babylon, which is girdled by a trench, as I said just now. In this way, then, he says, they will shepherd Assur and all the land of Nimrod, so that they stay within the trench. They will no longer spread out over cities and countries but stay at home, as it were, frightened and trembling. This, indeed, is what we shall find the hosts of demons have suffered through Christ. For they no longer lord it arrogantly over the world under the sun, as they did before the advent. They stay, as it were, where they are, checked by the vigilance and good counsel of the saints and shut out from the land of the saints. And so the saints, living a quiet and peaceful life, are able to accomplish what pleases God and are made radiant through the good order most dear to him.

And the remnant of Jacob will be among the nations, in the midst of many peoples, like dew falling from the Lord and like lambs on the grass, so that no one may gather or stand against them among the sons of men.

I have already said many times that the remnant of Israel has been saved, and that the race descended from Jacob has not perished entirely. For not a few of them believed in Christ and were enriched with salvation through faith even before the others, I mean those from the nations. And from this part that was left and saved through faith came the divine disciples themselves, and those who contended alongside them and suffered with them in the gospel of Christ. These, then, he says, have been saved among the nations like dew poured down on the fields, relieving the scorching heat of the devil's perversity. In gardens or fields, if the blazing ray of the sun falls on grasses and lilies, it makes them droop into unsightliness and seem already, in a way, to have withered. So too the inventor of sin, when he inflames the human mind with worldly pleasures, withers it in a way and makes it look very unsightly. But the Word of God revives it, as dew revives a flower or grass. And so, he says, those from Jacob will be among the nations, watering the souls of those who are persuaded with words of piety as if with dew, and richly fattening them with the teachings of the gospel. And they will frolic like lambs at pasture, that is, they will find very abundant and plentiful pasture. For the nations were somehow always readier to be led, and much more inclined to believe in Christ and, I would add, to choose a life incomparably better than their former one. Lambs, when abundant and flowering grass lies before them, revel and skip about. In the same way, I think, the minds of teachers take delight and pleasure in the docility of those they instruct and the ready obedience of those they initiate.

Indeed, our Lord Jesus Christ made the ready obedience of the Samaritan woman his own food, as it were, food fitting for him. For he said to the holy apostles, "I have food to eat that you do not know about." Then, to explain this, he added, "My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to complete his work." So the work of God is food and delight to the saints. They will frolic, then, he says, as if cropping grass, that is, flowering pasture. Those from Jacob will, as it were, feed upon the believers from the nations, and they will find the road of the preaching so widened that no one can gather and stand against them, that is, neither assemble nor resist them. For that is what "stand against" means: if any among the sons of men should choose to harm them. For many schemes and attempts have been devised against them by many people, yet they suffered no harm. God calmed the fury of the powerful, surrounded his own as with the shield of his favor, and wondrously rescued and preserved them from every trial.

And the remnant of Jacob will be among the nations, in the midst of many peoples, like a lion among the beasts in the forest and like a young lion among flocks of sheep, which, when it passes through, singles out its prey and seizes it, and there is no one to rescue. Your hand will be lifted up against those who afflict you, and all your enemies will be utterly destroyed.

Stories that are good and worth hearing do not become tiresome even if they are told in the same words; rather, they carry great charm. So the remnant of Jacob, he says, will be like dew among the nations. That is, those from Jacob who were saved through faith in Christ and were appointed heralds and ministers of the gospel oracles will be like dew, and they will graze like lambs frolicking in fine and plentiful grass. No less will they be like a lion among the beasts of the forest, roaring deep and terribly and striking unbearable fear even into those far away. And they will be like lion cubs among the flocks, rising up nobly and springing upon whatever they choose, while no one resists them or is able to rescue what has been seized. For our Lord Jesus Christ said to the holy disciples, "Behold, I send you out as sheep in the midst of wolves," that is, gentle and humble. It is as if he said: "Even if some in the world should be ready to kill, falling nothing short of the savagery of wolves, I myself by my own strength will shatter the hearts of those who make war on you. I will make them cowardly and unmanly, and I will create great reverence for you." So they prevailed over their enemies and conquered their opponents. They became fearsome to the wolves, though they were ranked as sheep. They escaped the plots against them, "dangers from robbers," as blessed Paul writes, "dangers from my own people, dangers among false brothers." The flocks of the nations were carried off as if by lions, and Satan, who had pastured them on his own wishes to their destruction, could not defend them or wrest from the apostles' hands what had been taken for salvation. This, then, was what was said to him through the voice of Habakkuk: "Woe to him who multiplies for himself what is not his own (how long?), and makes his yoke heavy and stout! For suddenly those who bite him will rise up, and those who plot against you will awaken, and you will become plunder for them. Because you plundered many nations, all the peoples who are left will plunder you." For the eight bit him and, like cubs, carried off what he had gathered together. For he had gathered to himself what was not his own: man belongs to God, or rather all things do, and nothing at all belongs to Satan. And he was plundered by the peoples who were left, that is, those from the remnant; here again you should think of the ministers of the gospel oracles. Then the Lord, who strengthens and sustains them, says to them, "Your hand will be lifted up against those who afflict you, and all your enemies will be utterly destroyed." For, as I said, they conquered in Christ. They rose above every plot, shone in the world, and prevailed over their enemies, winning for God those who were lost.

And it shall be in that day, says the Lord, that I will destroy your horses from your midst and ruin your chariots. I will destroy the cities of your land and tear down all your strongholds. I will take your sorceries out of your hands, and there will be no soothsayers among you. I will destroy your carved images and your sacred pillars from your midst, and you will never again bow down to the works of your hands. I will cut down the groves from your midst and wipe out your cities. And in anger and wrath I will execute vengeance on the nations, because they did not listen.

The discourse turns back again to grim matters. For the moment it leaves off the splendid and admirable accounts concerning Christ, links these words, as it were, to what came before, and shows what will happen as a result of wrath. He said, then: "And you, parched tower of the flock, daughter of Zion, upon you it will come, and the first dominion, the kingdom of Babylon, will enter." Then, he says, then indeed your cavalry will be gone, and the arrogance of chariots will perish along with them. The cities will be laid waste, and you will be stripped of your very fortifications, that is, your walls, for the Babylonians burned the cities with their inhabitants inside. The practices of your folly, sorceries and false divinations, and the very workshops of deception, meaning the sacred precincts together with the idols, will be utterly destroyed, and the groves will fall from their foundations. And what follows from this? The punishment will be notorious, and the manner of the penalty will not escape the notice of the neighbouring nations. They will know that the people suffered all this because they did not listen, that is, on the charge of disobedience. Wisdom too says something like this to those whose bent toward disobedience is unbridled: "Because I stretched out my words and you did not heed, but made my counsels void and did not heed my words, I in turn will laugh at your destruction and rejoice over you when ruin comes upon you, when sudden confusion overtakes you and overthrow arrives like a whirlwind." The fruits of turning away are "wrath and fury, affliction and distress" upon everyone who habitually refuses to listen. So when God calls us to what is good for us, we must follow him promptly and without any delay, and do what pleases him. To choose to be slow and lazy in doing good will bring us great loss and plunge us into bitter toil. But see how God does good even when he exacts the penalty for sins. He frees Israel from profane and abominable idolatry and from unholy undertakings: sorcery and false divination, altars, precincts, sacrifices, and the worship of the works of their own hands. So being disciplined is not without profit, "provided it be in judgment and not in wrath," as the prophet says.

If anyone should say that these things happened to the Jewish people for their drunken outrages against Christ, he will not miss the mark, for the idea is plausible in itself. It is true that their cities have been made desolate, and their whole fighting class perished, consumed by the hands of the Romans. Perhaps they were also called to account for that ancient idolatry, if some among them still wished to worship the creation and practised sorcery. These things somehow always tend to accompany those who have chosen idolatry, and among such people none of the most outlandish abominations is held in ill repute.

Chapter 6. Hear now what the Lord has said: Arise, plead your case before the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice. Hear, you hills, the judgment of the Lord, and you ravines, foundations of the earth; for the Lord has a case against his people, and he will argue it out with Israel.

The word is meant to shame them, and it virtually cries out against the insensibility of the Jews, if they set at nought even the divine words, which came gently and mildly, as from a father showing his children the genuineness of his love and leaving them no excuse for their unruliness. It is the custom of God, who loves goodness, sometimes to frighten sinners beforehand by foretelling terrible things. Yet he does not leave them unsoftened and harsh, as people who have given up hope; along with what is about to happen he brings in a word of encouragement, and keeps open for them, as it were, a way of escape, should they choose to run back to repentance. This is what he does now once more, out of his innate gentleness. Hear, then, he says, what the Lord has said. And what has he commanded me? Arise and plead before the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice. This resembles what was said through Isaiah: "Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken." For perhaps by mountains and hills he means the spiritual powers who watch over this universe according to God's will, driving off the encroachments of the demons from those on earth. These, above all and before all others, recognize the surpassing greatness of God's gentleness, and they have learned how much care he takes for us from what they do on our behalf in obedience to his laws. That is why he commands that the judgment take place before them. But the prophetic word probably suggests something else to us as well. The Israelites used to go up onto the mountains and hills and offer rites and sacrifices there to demons "under oak and poplar." For this reason the judgment is now [?] before the hills that had shared in the sin, where the charges against the accused were plain to see. It is also likely that by hills and foundations of the earth he means those who stand above the common crowd in glory and surpass it in honour, and who most of all became for those under them both a road and a snare leading to destruction. For he says to them somewhere: "The judgment is against you, because you have become a snare to the watchtower, and like a net spread over Tabor." You, then, he says, who stand above the rest, you foundations of the earth, that is, you on whom the affairs of others rest, hear the judgment of the Lord of all against you.

But the one who thinks rightly sings and says to the Master of all, "Do not enter into judgment with your servant." For he who knows all things will certainly prevail; no one will boast of having a pure heart, nor could anyone be clean from sins. It is therefore a terrible thing indeed to be judged against God.

It should be noted that the version of the Seventy has "ravines," while the Hebrew speaks of hills and foundations of the earth. This is so that we may understand by the hills that the leaders of the peoples are raised on high, as it were, and rise above and surpass the measure of others, and that these same people are foundations. For those who lead countries or cities are conspicuous in glory and raised up high, and in the same way they would also be foundations of the earth, that is, they serve as a kind of support and base for affairs. The affairs of others depend on them and are, as it were, settled upon them, as I said just now.

O my people, what have I done to you, or how have I grieved you, or how have I troubled you? Answer me. For I brought you up out of the land of Egypt and redeemed you from the house of slavery, and I sent before you Moses and Aaron and Miriam.

God pleads his case through the voice of the Prophet. He shows that those who acted impiously toward him had no excuse for their apostasy, that their audacity went beyond all reason, or rather beyond all madness, and that the magnitude of their insensibility was unusual and strange, perhaps even to the most ungrateful. Tell me, he says, what was your pretext for the impieties committed against me? What at all in my decrees was hard to bear or burdensome? Or what was [?] contrary to right reason in my freeing you from bitter slavery and mightily bringing you out from the clay, the brickmaking and the sweat they cost? Did I offend those on whom I had shown mercy, when I armed [?] even creation itself on my own account against the Egyptians who wronged them, and [?] gave you my own tutor, I mean Moses, who led you to glorious understanding and showed you clearly what pleases God, so that you might live a splendid life without wavering and reach the height of prosperity and glory? He will perhaps make no small outcry about the priesthood as well: For I anointed Aaron and appointed him to mediate between God and you, and to appease God with sacrifices offered in type. Are you vexed at this too? And what should I say of Miriam, who mocked the Egyptians as they perished and led the women in the dance? For as she beat the timbrel she saw horse and rider drowned in the waters. But perhaps to you even victory is something to be wished away, and the works of God count for nothing, though he let you pass through the midst of the waves and made the sea savage against your enemies. So he makes his reproaches with feeling, rousing them to remember the benefits they had received, and in a way chiding them gracefully for having let slip into forgetfulness things it would have been better always to remember, and for not gladdening their Benefactor in return by obeying him in everything whatsoever.

The Saviour has also brought us out of a spiritual Egypt, that is, out of darkness and the tyranny of demons. He rescued us from clay and brickmaking, meaning fleshly passions and impure love of pleasure. He brought us across the sea too, the distractions of this world, and very nearly delivered us from the bitter waves of the dangers in them, and he engraved the divine laws on our minds. He also appointed as priest Jesus, "the author and perfecter" of our salvation. And he sent forth, as it were, a Miriam as well, clearly the Church, which raises a splendid shout of triumph over the plotting of our enemies and ascribes the glory to the God who saved us. For in the churches there are always hymns and thanksgivings, praises and proclamations of God's glory. We must therefore be on our guard, lest laziness somehow bring us under the charges laid against the Jews, and lest we consider burdensome what pleases God. For as blessed John says, "His commandments are not heavy"; and Christ himself says, "For my yoke is kind, and my burden is light." Let us then offer what pleases God, since nothing that comes from him is burdensome; everything is kind and altogether easy to put in order for those who have chosen to live in the best way.
My people, remember what Balak king of Moab plotted against you, and what Balaam son of Beor answered him, from the Reeds to Gilgal, so that the righteousness of the Lord may be known.

He calls them to account again for outrageously insulting his sovereignty, though they could name nothing for which they might plausibly have turned to apostasy because they had been justly aggrieved. For I counted you worthy, he says, of so much forbearance and love from me that I would not allow you to be cursed, not even so far as a thought in someone's mind. The accursed Balak, tyrant of the Moabites, hired Balaam, the sorcerer and augur, and urged him to curse Israel. But the God of all brought about something strange and beyond nature, turning the false prophet's tongue to blessing. When Balak complained of this and blamed the augur, he immediately took him off to other hills. Then he ordered altars to be raised and sacrifices offered on them, supposing, perhaps, that God was not able to act in every place. But Balaam blessed everywhere, though he went round from the place called the Reeds, a region of Moab, as far as Mount Gilgal. Remember, then, what Balak plotted and what Balaam answered. For I cut short even the curses against you, and did not permit the augur to grieve you even so far as words. But you forgot even this, and ascribed the glory that belongs to me to lifeless matter, crying out to the golden calves and saying, "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt."

So, since God bestows good things on us out of love, enriches us with the utmost generosity, subdues our enemies and frustrates the schemes against us, what should we do, who have chosen to think rightly, if not surely that which will make us too be seen as dear to God? That means following his will and accomplishing thoroughly what pleases him, and, having come almost near to him by the disposition of our mind, saying the words in the Psalms: "My soul has clung close behind you."
BOOK TWO.
BY THE SAME AUTHOR, ON THE SAME PROPHET: THIRD BOOK.

With what shall I lay hold of the Lord? Shall I take hold of God Most High? Shall I lay hold of him with whole burnt offerings, with year-old calves? Will the Lord accept me with thousands of rams, or with tens of thousands of fat goats? Shall I give my firstborn for ungodliness, the fruit of my womb for the sin of my soul? Has it not been declared to you, O man, what is good? Or what does the Lord require of you, but to do justice and to love mercy and to be ready to walk with the Lord your God?

God has shown that the apostasy of those of Israel is without excuse. He has, in a manner, brought them to trial and clearly convicted them: he himself had done them good in countless ways, while they, driven to boundless insensibility, had grieved their Savior not a little. At once the figure of the penitent is brought in, weeping, as it were, over the sins already committed, and seeking to learn by what means he might ward off the charges and hold fast to the pursuits most dear to God. So he says: With what shall I lay hold of the Lord? For what shall I offer, he says, and what is left for me to do, I who have given such offense? Shall I then be clean if I sacrifice calves, young and tender? Will God commend me if I choose to offer whole burnt offerings? Shall I find him—that is, shall I come near him and be received into spiritual intimacy—even if I offer up a great multitude of flocks? Or, passing those by, shall I lay hands on the fruits of my own womb? Shall I please him, then, by slaughtering to him the choicest of my children, that is, the firstborn?

While someone is, as it were, deliberating and saying these things, the prophet answers in turn and says in the Spirit: The matter is not obscure, nor is it won with sweat. Surely you know the good will of God; you have heard what seems good to him and is dear to him. Why then do you hesitate, O man? For what else does the God of all seek from you, except only to do justice and to love mercy and to be ready to walk with the Lord your God? Now to do justice is to accomplish and fulfill righteousness, for justice is righteousness. To love mercy carries the glories of mutual love and is rich in the glory of love toward the brethren. And to be ready to walk with the Lord your God signifies being obedient and tractable in every respect. The blessed Paul said that we too must put on "the breastplate of righteousness, and shoe our feet with the readiness of the gospel of peace," that is, of Christ; and he further commands, saying, "Put on hearts of compassion." And indeed the Savior himself says, "Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful." These are a sacrifice dear and acceptable to God, a fragrance of spiritual whole burnt offerings, surpassing blood and smoke and frankincense. For those things were in types, but these give off to God the fragrance of the truth itself, as he also says through another prophet: "I desire mercy and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than whole burnt offerings." Observe how the figure of the penitent had in mind fulfilling the sacrifices according to the law. But God shows beforehand that the law is powerless and incapable of cleansing away sin, while the power of the way of life in Christ is far better and incomparably superior. So he treats the things of the law as unacceptable, as it were, and says that what God wills is to do justice and to love mercy and to be ready to walk with him. And these are the glories of life in Christ.
The voice of the Lord shall be called upon the city, and he will save those who fear his name.

In another way, too, he makes it plain that there is no fruit in offering by means of blood, while the power of spiritual worship would profit one not a little. Here he has put "voice" in place of "name," that is, invocation. It is as if he were saying: If the name of God is pronounced over the city, it will be saved altogether and in every way. For do not think, O man, he says, that I take delight in sacrifices of blood, or that I consider a city ungodly and lawless if it does not bring calves for whole burnt offering. No, I would not save a city in danger at all for having chosen to sacrifice oxen, even if it drenched the altar with the slaughter of sheep and chose to bring whole flocks of rams. Rather, it will suffice for its salvation that the name of God be called upon it. For she is wholly mine who honors my sovereignty, and who without delay chooses to do and to think what pleases me. Then I will save those who fear me. So when we are called God's, then we also fear him and are saved by him; and this may rightly be understood as the power of spiritual worship. The God of all said something similar through the voice of David as well: "Hear, O my people, and I will speak to you; O Israel, and I will testify to you: I am God, your God. I will not rebuke you for your sacrifices; your whole burnt offerings are before me continually." Then, adding that he will not eat the flesh of bulls nor drink the blood of goats, he says again: "Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High; and call upon me in the day of your affliction, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me."
Hear, O tribe! And what will adorn the city? Will fire, and a house of the lawless treasuring up treasures of lawlessness, and injustice with insolence?

For those of the blood of Israel settled the land of the Jews, and Samaria as well, by tribes and clans, when Joshua, surnamed the son of Nun, allotted them the land of promise. So God speaks not to one tribe but, as it were, to all, or to each, since the word is fitting both to each in particular and to all together. Hear, then, every tribe: a city over which the name of God is pronounced is saved. For he will in no way neglect those who fear him, but will be an impregnable wall to them, an ornament and a glory to those who wish to accomplish what is pleasing to God. But if you wish, he says, to see the opposite as well: what will adorn a city? A house of the lawless, or injustice with insolence? If a city, he says, falls into the hands of its enemies because of much sin and is consumed by fire, will it be seemly and beautiful? Would a house of the lawless, treasuring up treasures of injustice, make it splendid and most renowned, and will injustice with insolence benefit it? But no one accustomed to think rightly would doubt that such things bring disgrace. For a city would not be captured and consumed by fire unless it had certainly given offense through much sin. Why then, he says, have you let go of the things by which a city is saved and beautified, and made your aim instead the things whose nature is to ruin it? Why have you honored the things that would make it appear ugly and unlovely, with wicked inhabitants who love money, who are unjust and treasure up lawlessness?

And shall the lawless be justified by the balance, and deceitful weights in the bag, by which they filled their wealth with ungodliness? And its inhabitants spoke lies, and their tongue was exalted in their mouth.

Do you think, he says, that the lawless will be justified by the balance? That is, if I test and, as it were, weigh the life of each, do you believe that I, the lover of virtue, would ever consent to pass a verdict of righteousness upon the unjust? And as for those with deceitful weights in the bag—that is, those who wish to grow rich through greed, inequity, and an outrageous love of gain—have you supposed that they can escape the wrath? For from such gains they filled their wealth with ungodliness. And they have become liars and boasters as well. For the love of lying always goes along with the lovers of inequity, with those overcome by shameful gains and the love of gain; and boastfulness and arrogance go along with those who have already grown rich.

The inventors of unholy doctrines also have deceitful weights in their bags, those "who pervert all that is right," who steal upon the minds of the simpler with deceits and tricks, and grow rich by ensnaring many. But the wealth they gather for themselves is full of ungodliness, and admittedly they speak nothing true, only things counterfeit and false, colored over, as it were, with the subtleties of deceit. Such people also exalt their own tongue, "speaking injustice against God," as it is written, and "uttering the swelling words of vanity." To them it is fitting to say: "Hear, O tribe! And what will adorn the city? Will fire, or a house of the lawless treasuring up treasures of lawlessness, and injustice with insolence?" For the fire of punishment will be for them not an adornment but a retribution. And since they have become houses treasuring up lawlessness, they will become a curse and suffer retribution, and will fall into every evil.

And I will begin to strike you, and I will destroy you in your sins. You shall eat and not be satisfied, and I will drive you out within yourself; and you shall take hold, yet you shall not be saved, and as many as are saved shall be given over to the sword. You shall sow and not reap; you shall press the olive and not anoint yourself with oil, and the wine, and you shall not drink it; and the statutes of my people shall be destroyed. And you kept the ordinances of Zambri and all the works of the house of Ahab, and you walked in their counsels, so that I might give you over to destruction and its inhabitants to hissing; and you shall bear the reproaches of peoples.

For since they have become houses of the ungodly, treasuring up lawlessness and gathering wealth from injustices, he next threatens retribution. He says that the onset of what is expected to come has in a way already been set down at the beginning, so that destruction will come upon them in proportion to their offenses. He usefully strikes them with terror, and by the fears of what is to come, as if with a bridle, all but turns them around, so that they may choose to do better things and appease God by a change of course. He enumerates the blows, as it were, and sets them before their eyes. For he says that they will be punished with famine and with lack of necessities, that they will be destroyed among themselves, and that they will be overtaken and will no longer escape at all. And even if some should manage to flee the immediate harm, these too will be captured, and before long, and will become the work of another's sword. He seems to show us the following by this. Very many wars were stirred up against those of Israel, that is, against all Judah, though not always by enemies; they also took up arms against one another, so that at one time Ephraim, that is, the ten tribes, rose up against Judah, and at another the people of Jerusalem itself marched against Ephraim. And cities beyond counting perished, so that they were often driven out among themselves; and being thus pursued from their cities, they reached others, but were captured there too in time, perhaps even by the Persians and Medes themselves. This, I think, is the meaning of: I will drive you out within yourself, and you shall take hold, yet you shall not be saved, and as many as are saved shall be given over to the sword. Next he makes clear by what follows that, deprived also of the good harvest of the fields and wasted by lack of necessities, they will live wretchedly and pay the penalty for their unholy deeds. For you shall sow, he says, and not reap—God, I think, destroying the crops. And you shall press the olive yourself (for the land of the Samaritans bears olives), but you will be so lacking in oil, he says, that even if you wished, you would perhaps not manage to find any for anointing. And though your land is very rich in vines and abounds greatly in wine, so that you even distribute it to other cities, you would not find any to drink yourself. The statutes, too, will lie idle, he says, the ones you established for the idols when you brought them the produce of your abundant harvest. For what dedication of firstfruits will there be any longer, if all your fruit has perished and everything in the fields has been ruined? Or what thank-offerings will you bring, and for what, in all reason, you who are falling wretchedly and being consumed?

Then, teaching that no one else could be thought to have caused his misfortune, but that he will be captured having wronged himself by imitating the ways of those who were most impious, he goes on to say: And you kept the ordinances of Zambri and all the works of the house of Ahab, and you walked in their counsels, so that I might give you over to destruction. Zambri became king over Israel, and he is the father of Ahab; but, as the sacred text says, he walked "in the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat," who made Israel sin, "and he did evil beyond all who were before him." Therefore he was also consumed by fire, having himself set fire to his own house over himself; for so it is written. And by the "house" of Ahab he seems to mean Jezebel; murders and plunder and persecutions of the saints were her practices. These, then, are the things you have kept, he says, so that I may justly destroy you and make you a laughingstock and a reproach to others.

Let us apply such a word to the enemies of the truth as well. Trusting in their own eloquence and gathering heaps of wretched notions, they grow rich, as it were, from injustice, collecting for themselves what is not theirs; they are accustomed to ravage the flocks of the simpler like enemies and to carry them off into outlandish error. Let them hear, then, God saying: And I will begin to strike you, and I will destroy you for your sins. You shall eat and not be satisfied. For though they come upon the divine Scriptures, they are not filled with the doctrines of the truth; though they seem to eat, they waste away with hunger. Though they think they are reaching the way of salvation, they will not find it; sowing, as they suppose, they will find no reward for their labors; and pressing the spiritual olive—that is, the sacred text—they will be far from the spiritual gladness that comes by the grace of the Spirit. For they have kept the ordinances of Zambri and all the works of the house of Ahab; that is, they have done evil, been greedy, and carried out persecutions against the saints. They will therefore come to destruction, and will meet an end that is truly shameful and accursed.
Chapter 7. Woe is me! For I have become like one gathering straw at harvest, and like a gleaning at the vintage, when there is no cluster to eat the firstfruits.

Out of love the prophet laments over Israel, as being about to go down very soon to destruction and to be reduced at last to such a number that very few would be left, and those barely. They would be like the ears that fall off, which the hands of the reapers pass by; these are few and are seldom caught by those who gather the straw. They would be no less like the so-called gleanings, which the pruning knives of the vintagers have passed over. I think he also hints by this at how hard the saints were to find, since at that time they were a small remnant, found only as one might find a single ear in a reaped field, or, among the first clusters of grapes, the later after-growths. For when the air grows warm, the first and early cluster bursts forth from the branches; but as the season advances, sometimes a spurious second crop of clusters follows after them. These are hard for the vintagers to find, because they easily escape notice amid so much foliage and consist of only a few grapes. Those who follow the vintagers gather them not without sweat, peering into the vines more carefully. So the prophetic word seems here to lament to us the scarcity of the upright. And how can anyone doubt that this—I mean the lack of saints—became a loss for those of Israel? For the Master, being a lover of humankind, sometimes cares for lands and cities and remits very many charges if even five saints are barely found in them. Even the cities of the Sodomites would once have been saved, with God taking pity out of regard for the saints, though very few, and checking his wrath.

Alas, my soul! For the godly man has perished from the earth, and there is none among men who does right. They all go to law for blood; each one afflicts his neighbor with affliction; they make their hands ready for evil. The ruler asks, and the judge has spoken peaceable words; it is the desire of his soul.

The word, as it seems to us, is exact. For the prophet laments that there is no godly man in the whole land—clearly the land of the Jews—though it once flourished with very many heads of saints whose glory was radiant. This is why God also says through the voice of Isaiah: "How has the faithful city Zion become a harlot, she that was full of judgment, in which righteousness lodged—but now murderers!" For what was most grievous of all, and what drove them to the height of wickedness, was going to law over blood and murdering savagely, and casting aside doing good as something utterly stale, so that they made it a necessary pursuit to keep their hands ready only for harming others. For among those who live this way, [?] the ways of freedom have been discredited. Was it, then, that the subject part was sick in these matters, while the ruling part was strong and the judging part healthy? Not at all, he says; for the ruler asks and the judge has spoken peaceable words. Many of those appointed to office have often been unholy and exceedingly greedy, readily selling their judgments to those who wish to corrupt them. But even if they have already inclined toward being seen to be overcome by gains and bribery, they somehow hold back and hasten to adorn their ways with a good reputation. But to come to such wretchedness of mind and such shameful ways as all but to stretch out the hand, and, if one does not receive, to corrupt the cause of justice in judging and shamelessly to threaten—how would this not be beyond all abomination? The word is therefore emphatic, as though crying out against greed: The ruler asks and the judge has spoken peaceable words.

Would anyone, then, blame one who brings into peace those divided by disagreement? How then would it be true that "Blessed are the peacemakers," and what would their reward be? No, the glories that come from this are kept safe for the arbiters of peace. Yet one who judges rightly interprets what seems good to the divine law: he will reprove the wrongdoers and will certainly plead for the wronged. But when we speak peaceable words to wrongdoers, without reproving them as sinners, then indeed we clearly set aside the will of the Lawgiver. For he said: "The priest's mouth will guard judgment, and they will seek the law from his mouth." It somehow always goes along with those accustomed to taking bribes that they can neither judge rightly nor reprove sinners boldly, but rather counsel what makes for peace, even if they thereby bring the greatest injury upon some through greed. And making clear the cause of the disease, the prophet says: It is the desire of his soul; for perhaps, he says, even what was outrageously done pleases him. How then will he rebuke the wrongdoers? For how could he still censure what he has praised? Greed, then, and oppressing others is a truly unholy and harmful thing.

Accursed besides this is being overcome by shameful gains, and coming to such folly as to disregard henceforth the ways that lead to uprightness, and not to count impartial judgment as of much worth, but rather to side with those accustomed to do wrong, sharing their impiety with them and thus partaking in the sins of others. And that one who plunges himself into such terrible offenses will in every way be subject to wrath and punishment—how could anyone doubt it, if he chose to think rightly?
And I will take away their good things like a moth that devours, and like one walking by a measuring rule, as in a day of watching.

He threatened to bring a twofold kind of punishment upon them. For he said: "And I will begin to strike you, and I will destroy you for your sins. You shall eat and shall not be satisfied, and I will thrust you out within yourself; and you shall take hold, and shall not be rescued." And he added further: "You shall sow and shall not reap; you shall press the olive and shall not anoint yourself with oil; and wine, and you shall not drink it." That the abundant fruitfulness of their fields would vanish, that even the necessities of life would fail them, and that they would be crushed by the lack of what they most needed, he teaches by saying that like a moth he would consume all their good things, that is, the things in which they might be expected to take no small delight, and through which they possessed a broad prosperity. And that they were going to be struck and destroyed and thrust out, as it were even within themselves, that is, to perish together with one another, and to be pitifully driven out of their own houses and cities, he makes clear by saying: And walking along a line, as on the day of the watchtower. "For I will take away their good things," he says, "and not only as a moth devouring them, but also walking along a line, as on the day of the watchtower." This little phrase is altogether hard to grasp, but for my part I think we could not understand it in any other way unless the histories that bear on it were first set out clearly, which is what I shall now attempt to do.

Gibeah, then, is a village, or rather a small town, in Judea, lying on a hill. It was allotted as an inheritance to the tribe of Benjamin, and it is also called "the hill" and "the watchtower." We remember that a Levite, as is written in the Book of Judges, when his concubine had been outraged by men of the tribe of Benjamin in that very place, Gibeah, cut her body into twelve pieces and sent them to all the tribes, making the crime of the Benjamites plain to everyone. After that it came about that the [?] rose up in war against the tribe of Benjamin. At first the Benjamites were victorious, but later the other tribes destroyed them utterly. The prophet Hosea also recalls this history, for he says: "They have fixed madness in the house of the Lord; they were corrupted as in the days of the hill." That is, since they fixed idolatry and false divination in the house of the Lord (for this is what "madness" signifies here), for that very reason they were also destroyed as in the days of the hill, that is, of Gibeah. That the hill, or Gibeah, is also called "the watchtower" you will learn clearly from what is written in the First Book of Kings. Asa reigned over Jerusalem and Baasha over Samaria at the same time. Since they were split by discord, and in their anger against one another armed themselves for war, "Baasha king of Israel," it says, "went up against Judah and built Ramah, so that no one might go out or come in to Asa king of Judah." But when Hadad's son was overrunning the land of Samaria, Baasha withdrew from Ramah to resist the enemy. Asa then marched out of Jerusalem, and when he had come to Ramah, "he gave orders," it says, "to all Judah at Enakim, and they took away the stones of Ramah and its timbers with which Baasha had built, and with them King Asa built every hill of Benjamin and the watchtower." So Gibeah was called both "the hill" and "the watchtower"; for this is how the name Gibeah is interpreted, because it is raised up high and lies on a hill and a lookout.

"I will begin, then, to strike you, and I will destroy you for your sins," and in no other way than in that very manner of the day of the watchtower. For I will walk as though along a line, and I will turn aside neither to the right nor to the left as I go along the road of judgment against you.

The prophetic word seems again to hint at something like this to us. Micah prophesied in the days of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah. Jotham was a pious man, but Ahaz was loathsome and hateful, and among those most notorious for impiety. While he was reigning, Pekah son of Remaliah, who was then king of Samaria, made war on Judah with Rezin king of Damascus as his ally, and killed a great many in a single day. For this is what is written about Ahaz in Second Chronicles: "And the Lord his God delivered him into the hand of the king of Syria, and he struck him and carried away from them a great number of captives and brought them to Damascus. And he also delivered him into the hands of the king of Israel, who struck him with a great slaughter. And Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, killed in Judah in one day a hundred and twenty thousand mighty men of valor, because they had forsaken the Lord their God."

We must recognize, then, that when we offend God we will at once be in want of every good thing, and a terrible famine of divine and spiritual goods will waste us away, and we will consume one another as if biting each other. For Christ does not grant his own peace to those who do not love him. This is seen happening above all among the enemies of the truth: among them no spiritual gift can be found, but rather devouring of one another and fighting, strife and contentiousness and schisms. Of them God would say: "For I have taken away my peace from this people, and they shall die a grievous death." He does not distribute strength and unity of heart to them — how could he? — but to those who revere what is his, in whom the blessing of peace may fittingly settle: those who honor the power of the truth, who will not tolerate being split off into outlandish and rash opinions, but who are eager only to marvel at the beauty of the truth.
Woe, woe! Your punishments have come; now will be their weeping.

Do you hear how he even imitates the voices of mourners, who no longer expect calamity but are already, as it were, in the midst of it, and wail like women? "Your punishments have come," he says, that is, the time of judgment is here, the war is at hand, the suffering is at the door. By adding, Now will be their weeping, he showed clearly that what the prophecy foretells is not to be postponed for long but lies, as it were, before their eyes. For right after Jotham came Ahaz, wicked and apostate, the slaughterer of his own children, whom he offered on the altars of demons. In his time "a hundred and twenty thousand in one day" of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin fell. But we must recognize that at that same time Israel too paid the penalty. For while Pekah was reigning, Tiglath-pileser king of the Assyrians went up against Samaria and destroyed a great many of its cities; he also captured Damascus and killed Rezin himself. So it happened at one and the same time that Judah and Benjamin were consumed by the ten tribes in Samaria, and that those in Samaria themselves suffered from the Babylonian what they had done. You see, then, how, as if running along the line of wrath, the line of the time of the hill or watchtower, he punished those who had sinned.

Now these things "happened to the ancients as types, but they were written for our admonition," so that by always steering clear of being caught in similar offenses we may continue in well-being, having the God of all as gracious, as our friend and our protector. And it would be very fitting for us ourselves to say, so to speak, of those who pervert what is right and undermine the faith of simpler people: Woe, woe! Your punishments have come; now will be their weeping. For "by sinning against the brothers and wounding their weak conscience, they sin against Christ." And that they will certainly and in every way have to answer to the Judge, and "will eat the fruits of their own impiety," how can anyone doubt? "For because they wronged the simple, they shall be slain, and inquiry shall destroy the ungodly," as it is written.

Do not trust in friends, and do not hope in leaders; guard yourself against her who shares your bed, so as not to confide anything to her. For a son dishonors his father, a daughter will rise up against her mother, a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man's enemies are all the men of his own house.

The people of Israel sinned in many ways and provoked the Lord of all to anger against themselves. Then they learned beforehand through the holy prophets that they would be caught in inescapable evils unless they chose to appease the Lord by reasonable conduct. They ought to have chosen to think rightly and to win back him whom they had grieved by turning back to better ways. But this the wretches did not do — how could they? Instead they slid into such folly as to think and believe that they would escape the divine wrath and very easily prevail in any war if they had the help of the neighboring nations and the alliances and promises of their rulers. That they had put their confidence in cold and empty deceptions, and that their hope would be entirely useless, the prophet tries to teach them, saying: Do not trust in friends, and do not hope in leaders; for that is a precarious and entirely useless thing. For when the Babylonian came to ravage Samaria, then indeed the leaders of the neighboring nations, though they had promised them as much help as could be, had no small struggles of their own on their hands; they counted it welcome merely to save themselves, and the duty of giving help perhaps never so much as entered their minds. "Do not, then, trust in friends, and do not hope in leaders. But know," he says, "that when God sets his wrath in motion against you, not even the law of nature itself and the power of innate affection will grant you goodwill, even though those people are your near kin by blood. A wife will then disregard her husband, sons will rise up against their fathers, and daughters too against their mothers. For he who engraved the laws of affection on nature," he says, "could easily change them and turn them to indifference."

Yet the indifference of which we are speaking here should not be understood as of one and the same kind, but as twofold and different. Some offend against the laws of affection by impiously attacking their parents; others do the same thing while pleasing God and saving their own souls. Indeed the Savior said: "Do you think that I came to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but rather division. For from now on there will be five in one house divided, three against two and two against three [?]. They will be divided, father against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law." By a right judgment, then, let us crown so splendid a lack of affection. For it brings a person close to God, even if it cuts some off from their kinship according to the flesh, so that they may sing very fittingly what was said through the voice of David: "For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the Lord has taken me up."
But I will look to the Lord; I will wait for God my Savior; my God will hear me.

These words would be very fitting for Zion as she repents and foresees the end that would come in due time to the toils of her captivity. For Cyrus took the land of the Babylonians, and he released Israel, now barely a remnant, and ordered them to go home together with the sacred vessels and rebuild the temple in Jerusalem. Then, as if escaping from darkness and unbreakable chains, they came into the light, God having pity on them, and somehow rose again into the freedom that had been most fitting for them from of old, released and rejoicing. "I, then," she says, "will look to the Lord" — very late indeed, and only after experiencing what she ought to have prayed to be spared. Still, she says that she will have her hope in God and wait for the salvation that comes from him, and that she is firmly convinced that, because he loves humankind, he will hear her laments and accept her prayers. The beginning of salvation, I think, may be understood as this: first to withdraw the mind from the old deceit, then to choose to think rightly, and to believe that the Lord of all is himself the provider and ruler of salvation, and not to assign so exceptional a good either to human help or, most senselessly and ignorantly, to expect it as the gift of the utterly powerless multitude of idols.

For long ago they used to go down to the Egyptians, and go off to the Assyrians as well, buying alliances and help from both for countless sums of money. They also approached lifeless idols, offering sacrifices and presenting prayers on their own behalf as well. But now they say that they will look to the Lord and wait for him, that is, they will expect salvation and grace from him, and that they will be heard by him, plainly because they are offering their supplications to him and no longer to others. This was the act of Zion coming to her senses, as I said, and now looking to what was needful: shaking off that old error, changing her mind toward better things, and choosing to do what is profitable.

Do not rejoice over me, my enemy, because I have fallen; I shall rise again. For though I sit in darkness, the Lord will give me light. I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him, until he justifies my cause; and he will execute judgment for me and bring me out into the light, and I shall see his righteousness.

Zion's speech here seems to me most gracefully composed. It is addressed to the harsh, insolent and boastful city, clearly the city of the Babylonians, which was in a way mocking the land of the Jews as a land laid waste. "Do not exult over me," she says, "as though I were fallen. For you did not conquer by being stronger yourself; what threw me down was my weakness, my offending God, and that is why I lie fallen. But a time will come when I shall rise again, even though I have been in darkness, 'saying to the wood, You are my God, and to the stone, You gave me birth,' and uttering that saying about the heifers. For I said, I said it out of madness: 'These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt.'
