Nevertheless I shall come into the light; I shall recognize the Lord, the one who saves, the helper, the giver of strength. I shall bear what has befallen me and endure these terrible things, and I shall by no means cry out against God as though he were unjust, but rather I shall hold that he passed a right sentence on me, even if he has sent me into captivity. For I have sinned, and I bear what comes from his wrath until he justifies my cause" — that is, until, having measured out a punishment equal to her offenses, he then has pity, and makes bright her who was long darkened by the mist of error, and prepares her, through knowing the one who is true God by nature, to be herself, as it were, in the light. "And he would rightly be admired," she says, "for displaying in me the purity of his own righteousness. For just as he punished me not unjustly when I sinned, so by the same reasoning he will count me worthy of his care and have pity on me as I lie fallen, now that I have suffered and repent."

So the Lord of all is good. To those who turn to him he grants his mercy without delay, and he gladdens them very richly with the blessings of his gentleness, forgiving their past failings without holding a grudge.

And my enemy will see, and will be clothed with shame, she who says to me, "Where is the Lord your God?" My eyes will look upon her; now she will be trampled down like mud in the streets. A day of the plastering of brick: that day will be your blotting out.

Taken, yes, taken was the land of the Jews, and in due time Israel was carried off as a spoil of war to Babylon and the Medes. This was not because the conqueror prevailed over them by his own strength, but rather because God, who had kept Israel safe, turned away from him as a sinner and, as it were, delivered him into the hands of his enemies. For he had chosen to worship lifeless idols and to shake off the law laid down long before through Moses; in short, he had turned aside to every kind of outlandish thing and left no form of wickedness unpracticed. Then the Babylonians, having taken them and ascribing their victory to their own strength, behaved arrogantly even toward the divine glory itself, and supposed that they would hold Judea even if the God of all chose to save its people. Having the sinners in their power, they tormented them with terrible and unbearable toils, laying a harsh servitude upon them. Indeed God said somewhere through the voice of Jeremiah to the unholy multitude of the Assyrians, that is, to Babylon: "Behold, I am against you, insolent one." And again, concerning the Israelites themselves: "I gave them into your hands, but you showed them no mercy; on the old man you made your yoke very heavy, and you said, I shall be ruler forever." For there was no mercy among them, no sparing of age, no respect for old age, no compassion in their hearts. For this reason they themselves were justly given into the hands of the Persians and Medes, under the command of Cyrus, who took Babylon. And perhaps it is about them that the prophet Jeremiah says somewhere: "They will set upon you, and Babylon will be taken, and you will not know it; you were found and caught, because you opposed the Lord. The Lord has opened his storehouse and brought out the weapons of his wrath." By the weapons of his wrath he means those who sacked her. So it came about that the land of the Babylonians was taken by Cyrus and Israel was released from captivity. That is why the redeemed say: My enemy will see and will be clothed with shame. For when she sees her own children lying on the ground, having perished pitifully and unexpectedly, and those whom she held in her power, how will she not be wholly clothed with shame, though she once said, Where is the Lord your God? "For I shall look upon her like mud in the streets, thrown down and trampled under the feet of her enemies." Then the word turns to Babylon herself and says: That day will be your blotting out, meaning: the time when you come under the feet of your enemies, when Cyrus, that is, tramples and crushes the boastful and insolent city like mud.

As far as understanding these things historically is concerned, our discussion has been carried out quite sufficiently and well. But one could no less apply them to the spiritual Zion, that is, to the Church, which prevails over her enemies, tramples on those who persecute her, and mocks the feebleness of those who are always making war on her, even if they sometimes seem to gain the upper hand and prevail. For very many impiously gnash their teeth at her, sharpen their anger, and contrive every kind of plot. On the one hand there are the children of the Greeks, who fight hard for their own senseless inventions and champion the deceit of idols in general. On the other hand there are the heretics, who are especially murderous toward the saints, and who perhaps rage more savagely against those who have chosen to think rightly than those who have not accepted the faith at all. For when almighty God at times trains the saints, lets them fall into trials, and tests his genuine worshipers as if in fire, the wretches raise their haughty brows against them, and seeing them all but in distress they cry out [?], "Where is the Lord your God?" But the wise, all-pure and holy virgin, who has neither spot nor wrinkle, would rightly say: "But I will look to the Lord; I will wait for God my Savior; my God will hear me." And that she will trample her opponents like mud in the streets, and that those who are always tempting her will never be able to gloat over her at all, even if she is somehow shaken, how can anyone doubt? "For she has been founded upon the rock," and her support is Christ, an unshakable foundation and lasting security, Savior and Redeemer.

I think that a human soul could also say, "Do not rejoice over me, my enemy, because I have fallen," and the words that go with it: a soul that has sinned and been condemned, but is now somehow turning toward the need to repent and is waiting for the grace of salvation through Christ. For it will say to sin, which ruled it like a tyrant, as to an enemy: "Do not rejoice over me. I admit that I have fallen. I set aside what pleased God and let my mind sink into the love of worldly pleasures. Yet I am not far from hope that I will also rise again, even if I have somehow been in mist and darkness. For I too will find Christ as light, and the Sun of righteousness, rising in my mind, will show me made white." "I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him." "For even if I have been away from his presence for a little while," it says, "and have been given over to a debased mind, I will still become wise. Having justly suffered rejection, I will recognize the judgment, and I will say that it was rightly done, for I was not punished for nothing. And since I have paid the most fitting penalty, 'I will see his righteousness.'" And what could the righteousness of God the Father be, if not Christ? For this is what God the Father calls him for us, when he says, "My righteousness draws near quickly, and my mercy is to be revealed." Then, as one would expect, such a soul, reflecting on the grace of righteousness in Christ and the overthrow of sin, will cry out wisely and shrewdly: And my enemy will see, and she will be clothed with shame, she who says to me, "Where is the Lord your God?" My eyes will look upon her. Now she will be trampled like mud in the streets. A day for plastering brick: that day will be your blotting out. For since Christ has come among us, justifying sinners by faith, the mouth of lawlessness has been stopped, and so has its inventor been put to shame. He has been driven out and has lost his rule over us, and sin from now on is trampled like mud in the streets, laid, as it were, under the feet of the saints. The day of Christ has also become her blotting out. On that day he shows everyone who comes to him clean of their old charges through holy baptism, seals them with the Spirit for sanctification, and enrolls them among the children of God.

And that day will thrust aside ordinances. Your cities will be leveled and divided up by the Assyrians, and your fortified cities divided up from Tyre to the river, from sea to sea, and from mountain to mountain. And the land will be made desolate together with those who live in it, because of the fruit of their deeds.

The figure of Zion has been placed in between, that is, of Jerusalem, now already turning in some way to repentance and setting her hope on God. She is confident that she will be redeemed and will see the city of the Babylonians trampled, though in its arrogance it says to her, "Where is the Lord your God?" The sense of the present words, however, should be applied not to the verses in between but to those a little above. We will briefly recall what these were. He commanded them not to trust in friends and not to put their hope in leaders. He made clear that a wife would disregard her husband, a child would despise his father, and daughters would cast aside the respect owed to mothers, driven to this by the terrors of war. For wherever the fear of suffering is seen to sweep over everyone alike, there each person will surely care more for his own life, and the life of another will be utterly neglected.

So at that time, he says, that is, on that day when sons grow careless of their love for their fathers and daughters of theirs for their mothers, the ordinances will be thrust aside. That is, even the sense of what is proper will lose its force. A father will have no leisure to reproach his son for neglecting even the laws of nature, nor will a grieving mother impose the due rebukes on her daughter, since another care hangs over them, or rather destruction and the worst of evils. For the cities will go to ruin, to division and overthrow. Some will march against one city, others against its neighbor, others against the one on its border. They will overrun the whole land from mountain to mountain, from east to west and from north to south, so that the whole land, simply put, is laid waste to its very ends, from Tyre to the river and from mountain to mountain. It is also likely that here again ordinances means the festivals customarily held in the precincts of the idols, that is, the sacrifices. For when their cities have been destroyed and their houses and everything in them plundered, who will still carry out the customary rites and bring worship to the idols' shrines and temples?

The passage could also apply, and very fittingly, if one chose, to the heterodox themselves, those who fancy themselves wise and pervert the right doctrines of the Church. For they have been captured like cities and divided up by the enemies, clearly by the world rulers of this age. And they have become portions for foxes, as it is written, having divided among themselves impiety, the various kinds of blasphemy, and the denunciation of the truth. The same thing happened to the people of the Jews when they impiously outraged Emmanuel. They cast him out of the vineyard, as it is written, and handed him over to the cross, even though they said and recognized that he was the heir. Therefore they were sacked and perished ingloriously, for no other reason than the fruit of their deeds. For when they ought to have admired the Creator for his love for the world, because "he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life," this they did not do. How could they? Instead, puffed up with arrogance, they killed the Master, repaying him evil for good, as it is written, and impiously practicing every kind of ungodliness. So let them hear: "Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame that you have kindled," and also, "You will eat the fruit of your own deeds."

Shepherd your people with your rod, your tribe, the sheep of your inheritance, who dwell alone in a forest in the midst of Carmel. They will graze in Bashan and Gilead as in the days of old. And as in the days when you came out of Egypt, you will see wonders.

The passage again connects with the verses placed in between, and turns toward what is good. It urges them toward better things through the hope of the blessings understood to be in Christ, and very effectively moves them to choose to live rightly. For by foretelling grim events it greatly alarmed those who easily drift into carelessness, but then it restores them, skillfully inserting a note of gladness, so that those to whom the admonition is addressed may not despair and rush headlong over the rocks, never turning back and without restraint. For it is written, "When the ungodly man comes into the depth of evils, he becomes contemptuous." So either the person of God the Father himself has been introduced, saying to the Son, Shepherd your people with your rod, your tribe, the sheep of your inheritance, or else it is once more the prophetic voice, crying out, as it were, to Emmanuel that he must shepherd his own people or portion with his rod. The people of Christ, and indeed the sheep of his pasture, may be understood as both those of the circumcision who believed and those called to sanctification from the multitude of the nations. For he created the two peoples into one new man, making peace, and reconciled both through his body into spiritual unity. Christ himself said, "And I have other sheep" (clearly meaning those of the circumcision), "and I must bring them also, and there will be one flock, one shepherd."

The people of Christ, then, his tribe and sheep and inheritance, are those justified "not by works of the law" but rather through faith. For the former were under a curse, as blessed Paul says, while the latter could truthfully say of themselves, "We are blessed by the Lord, who made heaven and earth. God is the Lord, and he has shone upon us." Christ shepherds his own with a rod, not striking terror with an iron one and shattering them like a potter's vessel, as the Psalmist says, but turning them back gently. Like a good shepherd, he checks with moderate fears the impulses of believers toward carelessness. For this is what the Master of all says somewhere, framing the word about the Son as though addressed to David: "If his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments, if they profane my statutes and do not keep my commandments, I will punish their lawless deeds with the rod and their wrongdoing with scourges, but I will not withdraw my mercy from them." So he shatters, as if striking with the iron rod, the one who is unbridled, disobedient and arrogant, and who does not accept the faith. But he trains believers kindly and pastures them among the lilies, that is, in the God-inspired Scripture, making plain through the Spirit to the more discerning what is hidden in it, so that they may "attain to the perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ," with minds rich and well nourished, delighting in spiritual delicacies.

And we who are chosen and set apart dwell alone, having withdrawn from the others, who think only of earthly things, who have prized the possession of what is temporary, and who, bound by the pleasures of the flesh, have fallen headlong into every sort of outrage. So, keeping our minds at rest and freeing them from the vain and loathsome tumult, we have placed ourselves outside, as it were. We live a holy and admirable life and are alone, just as, of course, the prophet Jeremiah was. For he said, "Lord Almighty, I did not sit in the company of those who make merry, but I was in awe before your hand. I sat alone, because I was filled with bitterness." We dwell alone, as in a forest and on a mountain. By the forest, rich in trees and flowers, you should understand our twofold instruction, the moral and the doctrinal, I mean; and by the mountain, what is lofty and raised up, so to speak. For nothing that we pursue in our philosophy and count worthy of earnest study in the Church is lowly. That such pasture is rich and abundant he again indicates through more tangible examples, saying that those trained under Christ will graze in Bashan and Gilead. These regions pour forth abundant and luxuriant pasture for the flocks and are richly crowned with every kind of grass. So let us rise wisely from bodily things that lie within the senses to spiritual things, and consider the inner and hidden meaning: the mind of the saints, delighting in the insights of the God-inspired Scripture, glories in them and is filled as if with richness, sharing abundantly, as I said, in practical and contemplative virtue. And this not for some brief and limited time but, as the Prophet says, as in the days of old, that is, for a long and endless time. For the things that delight the flesh fall and wither with it, and like shadows that ride past, they shrink away after a short while. But the sharing in heavenly and spiritual goods stretches out through long ages, for the possession of such things cannot be lost.

He said, You will see wonders as in the days when you came out of the land of Egypt. For just as the God of all, when freeing Israel from slavery in Egypt, tormented with various punishments those who wanted to exploit them and were wearing them down with clay and brickmaking, so too the Savior, setting us believers free from the devil's hand and from spiritual slavery, bound the strong man, as he himself says, and cast out the ruler of this age. And just as Pharaoh was drowned and perished together with his own shield-bearers, so again Satan, together with the unclean spirits, has all but been sunk beneath the waters, [?] in chains of darkness … they were baptized in the cloud and in the sea; so we too have been baptized into Christ. For he is the spiritual cloud, which waters everything under the sun with the gospel preaching as with showers. And just as he sent down manna for them in the desert, so he gives himself to us as food, "the living bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world." They were brought into a land perceived by the senses, but we inherit the city above, the heavenly Jerusalem, the Church of the firstborn. And the Savior says that this is the land he also promised to the meek. So through the likeness of what happened long ago to Israel, you will clearly learn the power of what Christ has accomplished in us.

Since we must provide our hearers with what serves their benefit from every side, let us take another path as well and speak on the basis of the meaning of the names. Carmel means "knowledge of circumcision," Bashan "shame," and Gilead "transfer of the covenant." And on these points especially the interpretation is very persuasive. So when Christ shepherds us, we will be in the knowledge of circumcision, clearly the circumcision understood in the Spirit. For we have been circumcised with a circumcision not made with hands, and we carry within us the Jew who is one inwardly, whereas Israel according to the flesh has only the circumcision perceived by the senses and in the letter, and by no means the circumcision of the heart through the Spirit. This is the true circumcision, which makes those who receive it known to God. That is why the prophetic word said to us, "Be circumcised to God, and circumcise your hardness of heart, men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem." So we will be in Carmel when Christ shepherds us, that is, in the knowledge of circumcision. And we will be no less in Bashan, that is, in shame and abashment: not convicted because of sin, but repenting precisely because we have done wrong, and coming at last to an awareness of the sins committed in ignorance. And this is a road to salvation. For it is clear proof of the utmost insensibility when some choose to live with a hard and shameless heart, as it were, and do not blush in the least at their own failings, and perhaps even remain ignorant of their sins. So those who are in the knowledge of the spiritual and divine circumcision will blush at their own failings, and having become aware of what wrongdoing is, they will surely move on to what is most fitting for them. Such people will also be in Gilead, in the change of the legislation, that is, of the covenant. For having come under Christ, we will no longer conduct our lives according to the law, but will live rather according to the gospel. Passing beyond the grossness of the letter, we will offer God spiritual worship, and moving on to what is incomparably better, we will exchange the types for the truth.

The nations will see and be ashamed of all their strength. They will put their hands over their mouths; their ears will be deafened. They will lick dust like snakes crawling on the ground; they will be confounded in their confinement.

By nations here he means the loathsome and unclean hordes of demons. When they see those in Christ called to justification, to sanctification, to redemption, to adoption as sons, to incorruption, to glory, to an unconstrained and free life, then, yes, then they will be utterly put to shame, thrust out of their dominion and seeing their own strength collapse and fail. For our Lord Jesus Christ has given us power "to tread on snakes and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy." So those who once conquered will lie under the feet of the believers, sick with weakness and stripped of their strength through Christ. They will put their hands over their mouths, no longer allowed to accuse sinners. For "it is God who justifies; who is to condemn?" as it is written. And blessed David said somewhere, "All lawlessness will stop its mouth." So those who are clever at bringing charges will fall silent, he says, and not willingly, and as if struck by thunder, clearly by the wonder done for us, they will be deafened. For what has been done for us is an astonishing thing to hear, a great and truly extraordinary thunderclap, if it is true that "while we were still sinners, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly," so that we who were once held fast by terrible and unbearable failings might now be sanctified, "not by works of righteousness that we have done" but by mercy and grace; so that we who were once in grief and as far as possible from all hope might now be loved, radiant and admired, "heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ." So they will be deafened, he says, as though thunderstruck at God's gentleness toward us and the surpassing greatness of his unexpected kindness. They will lick dust, crawling on the ground like snakes; that is, they will not find food. For it is the habit of snakes, when they lack food, sometimes to knead the dust with their tongues and take whatever comes their way as food. He says that the unclean demons will be in the same want. For those who once used to feast and swallow down all the people of the earth wholesale will no longer find anyone who will put up with this, because all have been saved by Christ and have now come to such spiritual strength that they no longer endure those old bites, but rather tread on the asp and the basilisk, as it is written. Not only will they lick the ground, but they will also be confounded in their confinement; that is, gripped by weakness and grief, and besieged, as it were, by the power of the one who crushes them, I mean Christ, they will be in no small terror.

It is likely that the confinement here also hints at something else. For when the Only-begotten became one of us, he did countless marvelous works, but more numerous, I think, than those seen were those not seen. For he commanded the unclean spirits to go down to Hades and be shut up from then on in the abyss, so as to rid the earth of the most savage beasts. We have seen an image of this in the older writings. For when Joshua the son of Nun took the lands of the nations, he shut up five kings in a cave and rolled a stone over its mouth, prefiguring in himself, as I said, the power of the Savior's saving dispensation. And indeed the demons "begged him not to command them to go into the abyss." So he says they will be confounded in their confinement, that is, shut up from now on in Hades and cast into Tartarus in chains of darkness, so that, as I said, the human race may at last be rid of those savage and untamed beasts.

They will be astonished at the Lord our God, and they will be afraid of you. Who is a God like you, taking away lawless deeds and passing over wrongs for the remnant of his inheritance? He has not held on to his anger as a testimony, because he delights in mercy. He will turn again and have compassion on us; he will sink our wrongs and cast all our sins into the depths of the sea. He will give truth to Jacob and mercy to Abraham, as he swore to our fathers in the days of old.

For the mystery of Christ truly is cause for amazement, and the surpassing greatness of his gentleness toward us lies beyond any word that knows how to marvel. Indeed, the inspired Habakkuk, struck with wonder at the manner of the Incarnation, cried out plainly: “Lord, I have heard the report of you and was afraid; Lord, I considered your works and was amazed.” For though the Only-begotten was in the form of God the Father and in equality with him, and was rich as God, he became poor for our sake, so that we might become rich through his poverty: so that he might save what was lost, strengthen what had grown weak, bind up what was broken, give life to what had perished, cleanse what was filthy, free from punishment what had been condemned, declare blessed what was accursed, and adorn with the honor of adoption what was by nature a slave. So let him hear from all: “Who is a God like you?” That is, good and bearing no grudge, forgiving offenses to the remnant of his inheritance. And the remnant of his inheritance may be understood as those from Israel who believed, while the rest of the multitude, of course, was destroyed because they did not believe. For Christ said somewhere, “Whoever believes in the Son is not condemned; but whoever does not believe is condemned already, because he has not believed in the name of the Son of God.” So he leaps over sins and passes by offenses, and he did not keep his anger as a testimony. “As a testimony” stands for “to the end,” or “forever.” For we were cast out in Adam, but we were received back in Christ; he cursed us in the one, but blessed us again in the other. “For just as,” it says, “by the trespass of the one the many died,” so too by the righteous act of the one the many will live. So he ceased from his anger, because he delights in mercy; and at the time when all are turned back, that is, at the Incarnation, he will plunge the sins of all as if into the sea. And since he promised the holy patriarchs, Abraham, I mean, and Jacob, that he would multiply their offspring like the stars of heaven, he will give them, it says, what was promised. For they will be called fathers of many nations, since their children are counted not only among those of Israel's blood but also among the children of the promise. These are the ones who come by faith from what is called the uncircumcision, blended in some way into spiritual unity with those who come from the law and circumcision. For it is written, “Not all who are descended from Israel are Israel; but the children of the promise are counted as offspring.” For “those who are of faith are blessed together with faithful Abraham.” And the manner of the blessing may be understood as the grace that is in Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
ON THE PROPHET NAHUM. BOOK ONE.

Each of the holy prophets was called at various times for some useful and necessary purpose, to serve the divine will and to carry the voices from above across to human beings. Some, to frighten Israel when it sinned, foretold the disasters that would come upon them, and openly threatened that unless they chose to do what pleases God they would fall into terrible and inescapable evils. Others brought forward the very things that had already happened, grieved with those who had suffered, and wisely persuaded them to be willing to live more fittingly, and so to ward off the wrath from then on. Still others nourish Israel in its suffering with good hope, and led them to be confident that, although they had fared wretchedly because of their own sins, they would prosper again when their affairs were restored to their former state by the mercy, grace and power of God, who easily reshapes all things into whatever he wishes. We shall find that the aim of the work now before us is something of this kind.

The land of the Jews had been captured. Those who had grieved God by their outrageous apostasies were carried off as prisoners of war into the land of the Persians and Medes, though he had always protected them, fought on their behalf and made them stronger than their opponents. Those who had already suffered this remained in the grip of the evils of captivity and lived in a misery hard to bear. Those who had barely managed to escape the snares and the savagery of the Babylonians lived in unceasing fear and deep suspicion that they too might somehow fall into the same evils or even worse ones, since God Almighty was angry with them and had not yet relaxed his indignation. Their fear had already gone so far that they scattered into the lands of the neighbouring nations and all but served others as hired labourers, and these were foreigners and idolaters. This did them no small harm, for they learned to live by those peoples' customs, and each of them, among whatever people they found themselves, gave that people's object of reverence the rank of God. That is why the God of all himself, when Jerusalem had been burned in its time by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, commanded the survivors not to go down into Egypt, but rather to settle at home and hold fast to their ancestral worship, since he would be their helper. So the Prophet receives from God the vision against Nineveh. He received it so that those of Israel, holding the hope of returning in due time, would not go on in utter despondency. The captives were rather to reject despair, devote themselves constantly to prayer, and choose to worship the one who is able to set them free and has the power to redeem them. Those living in Judea, for their part, were no longer to mingle with the lands of the nations. Nineveh was the foremost city of the Assyrians. The Prophet foretells that it will fall and that the whole country will be ravaged along with it. This was indeed fulfilled when Cyrus, the son of Cambyses and Mandane, armed the Persians, Medes, Elamites and certain other nations together against Nineveh. He took it by force, released Israel from captivity, and commanded them to go home together with the sacred vessels. This, then, is the aim of the work before us; what follows we shall add part by part, as far as we can. The oracle concerning Nineveh. The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite. He first defines the aim of the prophecy and usefully makes clear what it looks to and where. Then he makes plain who is speaking and where he comes from. He says “the oracle,” that is, the prophecy that has been received and is set before us in hand. It is to be understood as concerning no one else but Nineveh; in other words, let the oracle of the prophecy be understood as Nineveh. The book is entitled The Vision of Nahum of Elkosh. This is surely some village in the land of the Jews. For we shall take “the Elkoshite” as indicating not his father but rather his place. We say this because we have the tradition from written sources.

God is jealous, and the Lord avenges; the Lord avenges with wrath. The Lord takes vengeance on his adversaries, and he himself destroys his enemies. The Lord is long-suffering, and great is his strength, and he will by no means acquit.

The passage is deep and not easy to grasp, except for those who are willing to examine its contents very closely. If it is understood as addressed to the Jews, we shall find consolation in it, fittingly blended with moderate rebuke. But if someone thinks it was composed and spoken against Nineveh, the mind will turn to another line of contemplation, and the passage gives those who suffered devastation the hope of recovering once more and makes that hope firm. So we shall make the aim of the meaning clear in both cases, as far as we can. The Jews kicked away their love for God and took no account whatever of genuine piety toward him. They leapt down into polytheism, strange error and a life outside the law. They built altars and set up sanctuaries to the works of their own hands. They offered rites and sacrifices to Astarte, to Chemosh, to Baal of Peor and to the golden heifers, and, more senseless still, they dedicated songs of thanksgiving to them. For the wretches said in their madness, “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt.” But by such terrible impieties they failed to notice that they were sharpening against themselves the God who had long protected and saved them. They had become his enemies and were placed in the ranks of his foes, because they gave themselves over to gods that are not gods by nature. Yet Moses had long ago cried out about God that he is jealous, that he is like a consuming fire, and that he would not tolerate those who chose to grieve him. For he declared beforehand: “They provoked me to jealousy with what is no god; they angered me with their idols. And I will provoke them to jealousy with what is no nation; with a foolish nation I will anger them.” Having given offence in so many ways, they naturally perished. This is what the Prophet now says to the peoples of the Jews, who were all but chafing at what had happened, and he rebukes and consoles them at once. “Yes,” he says, “you are grieved because you have suffered desolation unexpectedly and have been driven from your homes, your country and your cities, though you always used to conquer your opponents; and now you have fallen even under the feet of your enemies. Then how could you not have realized before you learned it by experience that God is jealous, and the Lord avenges with wrath, taking vengeance on his adversaries and destroying his enemies? And if we too have been destroyed,” he says, “removed from the midst and placed under the hand of our foes, it is because we set ourselves up as enemies, waged an unholy war against the Almighty, and went after everything that displeases him.” “But,” you will say, “the Master is long-suffering.” Yes, I agree, for he is so by nature. Yet he will by no means acquit; that is, he will not entirely release from guilt and punishment those who have offended him, and who do so unceasingly and beyond all measure. For out of his innate gentleness he postpones his wrath and sometimes bears with sinners, waiting for their repentance. But those who delay and hold back for a long time he finally punishes and subjects to penalties as hardened. This is how the passage will stand for us and how it should be understood if it looks to the Jews. But if it is directed against Nineveh, we shall understand it differently.

The Assyrians took the land of the Jews because God granted them victory, since those of Israel were caught in a great many sins. But the Assyrians were savage, boastful and utterly boorish in mind, and they never stopped all but striking at God's very glory with harsh and accursed words. For they thought they had conquered even without his consent, and that they had overpowered both the Jews and the hand that defended them. Rabshakeh, indeed, used blasphemous language. He said to those on the wall of Jerusalem things that would befit only the unholy, unbridled talk of those who do not know the one who is God by nature and in truth. But he paid the penalty for his arrogance at once. Shalmaneser's men, however, took the cities in Samaria and burned others besides, and then they boasted over those they had captured and were insolent toward the divine glory. So the Prophet consoles the peoples of the Jews, who were in no small distress. He teaches that the God of all will in every way and without fail bring punishment on those who made war on them, saying: God is jealous, and the Lord avenges with wrath, taking vengeance on his adversaries, and he himself destroys his enemies. The Lord is long-suffering, and great is his strength. “For he will surely prevail,” he says, “since his power is invincible, and he will overpower those who have grieved him. Even if he is long-suffering and for a while seems to put up with evil, in the end he will not acquit, for he is jealous.” We shall also find that the God of all himself was deeply moved by what those of Israel suffered through the cruelty of the Babylonians. For through the voice of Jeremiah he said to the multitude or city of the Babylonians, “I gave them into your hands, but you showed them no mercy.” And again through the voice of Zechariah he says, “I have been jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion with great jealousy, and I am very angry with the nations that joined in the attack, because I was only a little angry, but they joined in to do harm.”

The words God is jealous and what follows might also fittingly apply to those who are unwilling to walk the gentle, God-loving path and have turned aside instead to a life according to the flesh. That he will take vengeance and subject the unruly and wicked to punishments and penalties, how can anyone doubt, if it is true that “we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or bad”?

The passage might no less fittingly apply to the leaders of the Jews, I mean the scribes and Pharisees. By rejecting faith in Christ they were caught destroying both themselves and others. For they held hostile thoughts and waged war against the Only-begotten's dispensation in the flesh. They took away the key of knowledge, as he himself says, and neither entered themselves nor allowed others to enter. So even if he is long-suffering, he will by no means acquit those who have waged war against the true faith.
The Lord's way is in utter destruction and in earthquake, and clouds are the dust of his feet.

The Prophet is about to foretell the capture of Nineveh to console those who had suffered, and to show those who had been wronged that God will shake it to its foundations. So he usefully describes first the all-mightiness of the divine nature. When it chooses to accomplish anything at all, nothing opposes it; rather, everything will easily follow, and its will prevails, even if some earthly matter seems hard to accomplish for us and those like us. For the Jews thought the Babylonians would be extremely hard to conquer, and that they had gained so invincible a hand that even God, if he wished, would be powerless against these enemies. I think what the Babylonians had cruelly and savagely dared throughout the whole land of the Jews drove them to this despondency. So he wanted them to know that the Babylonians would lie fallen without any effort once God roused his wrath against them, and that they would be captured, and very easily. Therefore he necessarily says: The Lord's way is in utter destruction and in earthquake, and clouds are the dust of his feet. “For if he should form a plan against anyone,” he says (for this is what the way means), “he will certainly overrun them as in an earthquake.” Earthquake and utter destruction are irresistible things and wholly inescapable, and so are clouds flying like dust and covering the sky. The Prophet seems to be reminding them of the flood that came upon the whole human race in Noah's time. For then God went forth, as it were, with utter destruction and with an earthquake against all. He raised up clouds, opened the floodgates of heaven, as the sacred writing says, and deluged everything under heaven with unrestrained rain. “So then,” he says, “how could he who easily prevailed against the whole earth, and with a single decree destroyed everyone on it, be powerless against one nation, the Babylonian?” He says, in a manner most fitting for God, Clouds are the dust of his feet. Just as it is easy for a human being to stir up soil and dust with his foot, so, I think, it is easy for God, who has authority over all things, to cover the sky with storm and clouds.

If it is proper to search out the hidden meaning of these words as well, I shall think it necessary to say this. We say that the Only-begotten Word of God made the way of his dispensation in the flesh, that is, its fulfilment, with utter destruction and with earthquake. For when he became one of us, he destroyed and shook “the principalities and powers and the world rulers of this age.” He drove them from their tyranny over us, scared them away from that ancient strength of theirs, and overthrew the very power of death and, besides it, sin. And clouds also became the dust of his feet. For as dust flies ahead of someone walking, so the spiritual clouds, that is, the blessed prophets, went ahead of the Only-begotten's dispensation in the flesh. Their language was rather obscure and not very clear, yet with their life-giving proclamations they watered the minds of those able to understand.
Threatening the sea and drying it up, and making all the rivers desolate.

He builds his account from things they knew and had experienced, not from events too far in the past. When God their protector brought Israel out from the impiety and unbearable greed of the Egyptians, he led them through the middle of the sea and commanded them to walk as if on dry land; “for the waters stood firm like a wall,” as it is written. So he threatened the sea, and it could be crossed like dry land. But if someone wishes to link the earlier words, I mean “The Lord's way is in utter destruction and in earthquake,” with the thoughts on these events, he will judge rightly in this way too. For the Lord of all had, as it were, utterly destroyed and shaken the land of the Egyptians through the signs done there and the death of the firstborn. They perished in a single night, and everything was filled with lamentation and wailing, as he said. Then he led Israel through the middle of the sea, while the cloud from heaven hung over them.

The blessed David said something like this too. He sings thus: “O God, when you went out before your people, when you marched through the wilderness, the earth shook, and the heavens poured down rain.” I think that by the earth that shook he means the land of the Egyptians. That a cloud also hung over them, going before the sons of Israel, is clear to everyone. But the inspired Paul will also confirm it when he says that the fathers of Israel were all baptized “in the cloud and in the sea.”

To the drying up of the sea the Prophet added the desolation of the rivers, recalling another miracle. When they were being brought into the land of promise, with Joshua leading them after Moses, the Jordan again stood still in its place. God Almighty halted the downward rush of its streams by ineffable commands and bonds. The blessed David also counts these things as the greatest of wonders when he says: “Come and see the works of God, how awesome he is in his counsels toward the sons of men. He turns the sea into dry land; they will pass through the river on foot.” For again they crossed the Jordan on foot. And when he says that all the rivers are dried up, he bids us be convinced that what happened in one case will happen in all, if God so consents.

Some think the meaning of these words can be approached in another way as well. “If the Master of all should choose to make an assault on Nineveh,” they say, “he will certainly do it with utter destruction and with earthquake, for he will destroy it and shake it easily. It is broad, and like a sea it surges against the other nations with wars, but he will dry it up without delay. And even if its [?] rise up like torrents,” they say, “they will in every way and without fail be made desolate.” We say that the sea and the rivers that flood and drown are no less the wicked and hostile powers, and above all Satan. But Christ dried up all their power, and though it was once invincible, he laid it beneath the feet of those who worship him.

Bashan has dwindled, and Carmel, and the blossoms of Lebanon have failed. The mountains quaked because of him, and the hills were shaken, and the whole earth was upheaved before his face, and all who dwell in it.

The passage at once moves on to further proofs, bearing witness that the divine nature is all-mighty and invincible in its authority. The region of Bashan is flourishing and fertile. Carmel and Lebanon are mountains, one of Phoenicia and the other of Judea. Both are very well wooded and thick with spreading forests. But all these, I mean Bashan and the country lying beside the mountains, were inhabited by fearsome and most warlike races and by sons of giants, as it is written. Yet with God protecting them, the sons of Israel destroyed and conquered these peoples and inherited their land. So it is as though he were saying again: “The lands that once teemed with fearsome and most valiant men, and that were thick, as it were, with forests of the many warriors in them, are gone and ravaged; they have been emptied of their inhabitants.” This, I think, is what he means when he says that they have dwindled.

Then how could the famous Nineveh not be captured if God consents? Besides Bashan and Carmel, the blossoms of Lebanon have also failed. Lebanon, as I said, is a mountain of Phoenicia, and by it he means the whole region lying below and around it. So by the blossoms of Lebanon he means those who reigned over Damascus and Phoenicia at various times. They too were given into the hands of the sons of Israel. For they too were conquered from time to time, although they had a very large force and were puffed up by fearsome and formidable allies. Going through the books of Kings, we shall find that the kingdom of the Damascenes was ravaged at times by those who reigned from the tribe of Judah. So the blossoms of Lebanon have failed. That is, the choicest part of Phoenicia, or Lebanon, has many times been destroyed and perished, meaning those who held power there.

“And why do I say this,” he says, “when, if God so wills, even the mountains themselves could very easily be shaken, the hills will be moved, and the whole earth with those who dwell in it will be upheaved? That is, it will pass into nonexistence and will once more be as though it did not exist.” For he who made it in the beginning will surely also blot it out easily, and great things are nothing at all to him. The blessed David also seems to have thought and spoken in harmony with these words: “What ails you, O sea, that you fled? And you, O Jordan, that you turned back? You mountains, that you skipped like rams, and you hills, like lambs of the flock? At the presence of the Lord the earth was shaken.”

For, as he already said, “His way is in earthquake.” If one chose to measure the divine and ineffable glory, the whole earth would be nothing, and the things in it would be worth very little account. The prophet Isaiah will bear witness to this, saying: “If all the nations are like a drop from a bucket, and were counted as the tipping of a scale, they will also be counted as spittle. Lebanon is not enough for burning, and all the four-footed beasts are not enough for a whole burnt offering, and all the nations are as nothing and were counted as nothing. To whom have you likened the Lord, and with what likeness have you compared him?”

Others again think it right that such things were said of Nineveh itself in a figurative way. They take it to be compared to Bashan as an excellent and famous land, and to Carmel and Lebanon as notable and highly conspicuous mountains; and Nineveh was indeed marvellous and notable. He says it has dwindled because it was about to be ravaged very soon, together with those who flourished in it, that is, its leaders and generals and the more distinguished among its other peoples. Since he had mentioned mountains and a well-wooded land, namely Bashan, he kept the figure up throughout the passage. By what is richest and blossoming he meant those who were perhaps more distinguished in wealth, or outstanding in bodily strength, or raised above others by some other kind of eminence.

Anyone who considers what the Jews dared to do against Christ, and the desolation brought on them, their complete shattering and destruction after he came back to life and ascended into heaven, could fittingly apply these words to them as well. Bashan, Carmel and Lebanon may fittingly be understood as Judea. It is Bashan because it was called a land flowing with milk and honey, a land of grain, oil and vineyards. It is Carmel and Lebanon because it was raised high in glory, became conspicuous and seen from all around, and delighted in those who lived in it as if in endless forests. But he says that it has dwindled. For they were consumed by the hand of the Romans; as if they had fallen among fierce and very strong woodcutters, they fell like trees. The blessed prophet Isaiah hints at something of this kind when he says, as if to Jerusalem: "Open your doors, O Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars. Let the pine wail, because the cedar has fallen, because the great ones have suffered greatly. Wail, you oaks of Bashan, because the dense forest has been torn down." And somewhere else he says more clearly: "And there will be the mourning [?] ... being exceedingly [?], they were shattered together with their evils, and they paid the penalty for their drunken outrage against Christ.

In another way, too, our Lord Jesus Christ shattered for our sake "the principalities and authorities and the world rulers of the darkness of this age, and the spiritual forces of wickedness," so that he might deliver us and save us. Knowing this, the blessed David sings: "You are fearsome, and who will withstand you once your anger is roused? From heaven you made judgment heard; the earth feared and was still when God arose to judgment, to save all the meek of the earth." And he has given us power "to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy." For he broke the principalities and shattered like rocks the arrogance of the unholy spirits. When he was angry for our sake and on our behalf against those who had wronged us, they had to give way, even against their will.

The Lord is good to those who wait for him in the day of affliction, and he knows those who revere him. And with a flood of his passage he will make a full end; darkness will pursue those who rise up against him and his enemies.

He admonishes usefully and with great skill. He does not cut off the hope of prosperity, since he said that the Lord will be good to those who wait for him; yet he does not release them into an unbridled and dissolute life either. Rather he moves them toward good order and toward choosing to live lawfully, by saying in turn that if he makes against anyone that passage which is understood as a flood, he will make it like a kind of earthquake. Just as the rush of many irresistible waters, pouring down a steep slope, is something terrible and quite impossible to escape, so if the effects of divine wrath sweep down on any people, they will utterly destroy all those against whom they go and are borne.

He says that his enemies will be pursued and overtaken by darkness. And surely not altogether the darkness of night, but, I think, another kind: darkness in the mind, understood as a form of suffering. For relentless misfortune and bitter, unexpected suffering can darken the human mind, as happened to those of earlier times when they were carried off into captivity and their land was captured. That is why God, comparing such evils to wine and drunkenness, said very aptly to the blessed Jeremiah: "Take this cup of unmixed wine from my hand, and you shall make all the nations to whom I send you drink it; and they will drink and vomit and go mad before the sword that I am sending among them." And also through the voice of Isaiah he says to her: "For you have drunk the cup of falling, the bowl of wrath, and drained it." So he says that those who are hostile to God will be overtaken by drunkenness and darkness, and so he frightens them very effectively into choosing to think what it would have been better for them to know and do.

The God of all has also advanced against the Jews with a flood of his passage, and he has made a full end of them, exacting the penalty for what they did to Christ. They have come into darkness as well and, utterly without a share in the divine light, the wretches remain foolish and blind. For they would not follow Christ when he called out, "While you have the light, walk in the light, so that darkness may not overtake you." And since they were disobedient and unruly, from then on, as the prophet says, "While they waited for light, darkness came upon them; they waited for brightness, and walked in the gloom." For they became enemies of the divine light and rose up impiously against the glory of Christ.
What are you plotting against the Lord? He himself will make a full end; he will not take vengeance twice at the same time in affliction.

I said at the beginning that after Shalmaneser king of the Assyrians had sacked Samaria and laid waste along with it other cities and villages under the rule of Judah, those who survived the war were in unbearable terror and were fleeing to the lands of the neighboring nations. For they naturally supposed that they would meet the same evils a second time when the Babylonians returned against them. So God gave them the comfort they needed through the voice of the Prophet, promising these two things: that he would in due time have mercy on those already overtaken by the war and suffering unbearable calamities, and free them from the bonds of captivity; and that he would hand Nineveh over to desolation and destruction.

So, lest they expect to meet the same evils again and readily take flight from Judea to foreign peoples, he all but questions them, asking what they are plotting and what they have decided to think about the Lord. "Do you suppose," he says, "that the Master of all is harsh and given to wrath, so that he would demand a double penalty for the same offenses? You are far wide of the mark. If you add none of those things that are outside the law and provoke the Lawgiver to anger, neither will he inflict a second blow. He has afflicted you sufficiently for the impieties in which you were caught. Stop sinning, and he will check his anger. He has disciplined you enough; from now on he will have mercy on you if you choose to live soberly." The word is therefore mixed, and its exhortation is blended. At one and the same time it persuades them to choose sincerely to do what pleases God, and it gives those who choose to do this the confidence that he will be good to them and will not let loose his wrath on them unbridled, as they imagined. Notice how the word has again preserved the remnant for Israel. For he declared plainly beforehand that God will not make a full end of them, saying as a question, What are you plotting against the Lord? Will he himself make a full end? He means that he will not make a full end, nor will he shake Israel from its foundations and hand it over to total destruction. He will spare them for the sake of the fathers, and in due time they will be saved, entering after the Gentiles, through faith in Christ, into sanctification and kinship with God through the Son in the Spirit.

For to their foundations they will be laid bare, and like entwining bindweed they will be devoured, and like stubble full of dryness. From you will come forth a scheme against the Lord, plotting evil, hostile things.

Having shown at length that the God of all has the power to accomplish everything with ease, and that nothing at all is beyond him, he now turns his words to Nineveh itself. He says that even if she reaches such splendor that she looks equal to the most richly wooded of mountains, I mean Lebanon and Carmel, covered with many and countless peoples as with foliage, and even if she falls nothing short of Bashan, still a time will come when she will be utterly laid waste. This, I think, is what being laid bare to the foundation means, since the word keeps up the figure of mountains and land, of trees and timber. He says she will be devoured, as though the Persians and Medes grazed her down; for these took Nineveh under the command of Cyrus. He compares the multitude of the Assyrians to bindweed, for they inhabited Nineveh. And what reason could there be for this comparison? Bindweed is an ivy-like plant; it always creeps upward, sends out thin tendrils, and clutches the plants standing near it, so that even the tallest trees are often choked by it. The Assyrians did the same: they were always leaping upon lands and cities, as it were choking and weighing them down with the grip of their wars and their unbearable tyranny. He said she would be burned up, like stubble full of dryness; and stubble is most readily consumed by fire. Then, as Nineveh is being set on fire, suffering the effects of wrath and being laid waste, the Prophet adds his comment and makes plain the cause of her suffering such things, saying: From you will come forth a scheme against the Lord, plotting evil, hostile things. "You will be laid out for desolation," he says, "you will be like barren ground, and you will be burned up with fire, because you will devise against God terrible, arrogant and hostile things. For the God of all, in punishing Israel for its offenses, made it easy to capture and brought it under your feet. But you will not see it that way; you will think rather that you took Judea even against his will." We shall find that this is just how the boastfulness of Rabshakeh stood, when he mocked the glory of God, saying to those sitting on the wall: "Do not let Hezekiah deceive you with words, which will not be able to rescue you; and do not let Hezekiah tell you, 'God will rescue Jerusalem from my hand.'" To such utterly senseless and truly unholy loose talk God replied, through the voice of Isaiah as well, saying: "Will the axe be glorified without the one who cuts with it, or the saw be exalted without the one who draws it?" For just as an axe, however sharp and well forged, could do nothing in cutting down trees unless someone wielded it against something by his own strength, and just as a saw will accomplish nothing of its proper work if no one draws it down or up, so too the strength of the kingdom, or rather of the army, of the Ninevites would not have overcome Samaria, had not the divine wrath brought it against cities and villages, using it like a tool, which is moved by another and is useful when taken up for service, but could do nothing on its own. So Nineveh is punished because she devised evil things against God, and things contrary to the true nature of the matter. For the God of all handed Israel over because it had sinned; it was not that she captured it while God was defending them and still wished to save them.
Thus says the Lord, who rules over many waters: Even so they will be dispersed, and the report of you will not be heard any more.

The word, then, is addressed to Nineveh, the arrogant and God-fighting city. By waters here he means the countless multitudes in lands, cities and nations, which pour down easily like rivers or the sea upon whomever God chooses. For he is the one who rules over them, as Creator, as Lord and God of all, as the one who steers by his own nod the things he has made and turns the inclination of everyone's heart toward what seems good to him, and thus [?] ... Now this was Cyrus, son of Cambyses. And he gives him commands, not by speaking to him as to a saint and prophet, but by putting his own will into his mind and making him a servant of what pleased him, even though he was profane and an idolater. For just as he commanded the sea monster to swallow Jonah, and the gourd to spring up over his head and shade him, and the worm at dawn to strike the gourd, so we say he also gave commands to Cyrus.

So much for the historical sense. But God the Father might also proclaim to Jerusalem, which became the murderer of the Lord, that is, to the land of the Jews: "For to their foundations it will be laid bare, and like entwining bindweed it will be devoured, and like stubble full of dryness. From you will come forth a scheme against the Lord, plotting evil, hostile things." For it has been burned up and laid bare, and consumed like dry stubble. For they dared to devise evil against the Lord, and even to use an unbridled tongue: at one time they called him a Samaritan, a drunkard and born of fornication; at another they said that "he leads the crowd astray," though he had been sent by God the Father for this very reason, to free what had gone astray from its straying, to bring back to God what had bolted from him, to lead back through faith what had slipped in many ways into apostasy, to enlighten what was in darkness and to bind up what was broken. But since he did not destroy Israel completely, and the remnant has been preserved for it, as I have said many times already (for not a few from among the Jews have believed, and glorify Christ together with the Gentiles), let those of the circumcision according to the flesh hear: I will break his rod from off you and burst your bonds, and the Lord will give commands concerning you. How can we avoid saying what rod he means, or what bonds at all? They were subject as if to a kind of scepter, burdened by the madness and savagery of the scribes and Pharisees, and, all but held in bonds by their commandments, they did not accept the faith. But the rod, that is, that rule, has been taken away, the bonds have been burst, and from then on they have run to Christ with a free mind, all but urging one another on headlong and repeating what is said through the Psalmist's lyre: "Let us burst their bonds asunder and cast their yoke from us." And let those from the Gentiles hear no less than they: And now I will break his rod from off you and burst your bonds, and the Lord will give commands concerning you. For of old, yoked under the scepter of the devil and bound tight with the bonds of worldly pleasures, they worshiped "the creature rather than the Creator." They did not know the one who is God by nature and in truth, and, differing little from irrational beasts, they were slaves to the pleasures of the flesh and lived a pitiable and most irrational life. But they too have been set free, since Christ broke that ancient rod and burst the bonds, dragged them out of sin, moved them from error to the knowledge of God, justified them by faith, and from then on gives commands concerning them, clearly to the holy angels. For it is written: "He who dwells in the help of the Most High will lodge in the shelter of the God of heaven." For he will command the holy angels to guard us in all our ways and bear us up in their hands, lest we strike our foot against a stone. And it is true that "the angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him and will deliver them."
No more of your name will be sown.

It is as if he were saying: "You will not be scattered among all the nations, nor be a captive of war and a wanderer far from the land that bore you, enduring a most grievous servitude in enemy cities, scattered pitiably, miserably and wretchedly." It should be noted that the prophet Nahum lived before the second captivity in Babylon, and that after these words of the Prophet Judah was captured, went into captivity and was enslaved to the Assyrians. For while Hezekiah was reigning in Jerusalem, Sennacherib campaigned against Samaria, laid waste its cities and burned others as well, and sent Rabshakeh from Lachish, who let loose his boorish tongue against God; then one hundred and eighty-five thousand of the Assyrian army fell by the hand of an angel. After the reign of Hezekiah, when no little time had passed, and Zedekiah son of Josiah was reigning, Nebuchadnezzar first laid waste all Judea and then besieged Jerusalem; then he took the holy city by force, burned that renowned temple, deported Judah, and added them to those carried off from Samaria by Sennacherib. Does the God of all, then, break his promise when he says through the Prophet to those of Israel's blood, No more of your name will be sown? And how is it not ignorant, or rather the very height of all evil, to suppose that God speaks falsely? The divine nature does not err in speech; far from it. He will prove true in this way. Having first mentioned the release that came in due time, when Cyrus took over the power of the Persians, he then says that after this Israel would no longer be a wanderer and an exile. For they were called back to their own land, returned to Judea, and lived there securely. Wars were indeed waged against them by Antiochus, surnamed Epiphanes, and by certain others after him; yet they did not go off into captivity, but, as I said, lived securely in the land that bore them.

So the words No more of your name will be sown may be understood of Israel according to the flesh. But the spiritual Israel will also hear them, and quite fittingly, that is, those who see God with the eyes of the mind and stand in awe of the glory of the Only-begotten: No more of your name will be sown. For before the faith they were under the hands of enemies, having bent the neck of their mind under the yoke of Satan and the evil powers with him, and bound by the evils of love of the flesh. But now the greed of those who once ruled has been removed; sin has been shaken and has fallen with them; the power of the passions has been taken away. For Christ released us and gathered us through faith into sanctification, though we had been scattered in many ways into manifold and dissolute passions and into countless gods. But we shall no longer be scattered; we shall remain wholly in Christ, having one faith, one baptism, and one Lord, Savior and Redeemer, and through him we are bound to God the Father in spiritual unity.
From the house of your god I will destroy the carved images, and the molten images I will make your grave.

Israel gave no small offense when it turned aside into apostasy, impiously abandoning the God who had saved it and devoting itself to the worship of idols. That is why it was taken captive and went off to its enemies, and so was carried away to Nineveh. Those who were left in Jerusalem were no less careless about the love of God and unsteady in piety, shunning what pleased God and shaking off the yoke of his service, while still sacrificing to Baal, to Astarte and to the host of heaven. But when threats came through the holy prophets, God declaring plainly that Jerusalem would be destroyed and that its inhabitants too would certainly go, together with the others, as captives into the hands of foreigners, some of those who reigned in it came to their senses in due time; they pulled down sacred precincts, overturned altars, and consumed the carved images with fire. Josiah distinguished himself in this above all the rest. The man of God spoke about him once when Jeroboam son of Nebat, who made Israel sin, was sacrificing. Jeroboam was standing by the golden heifers to offer sacrifices, and the man of God said to the altar by the word of the Lord: "Altar, altar, thus says the Lord: Behold, a son is born to the house of David, Josiah by name, and he will sacrifice upon you the priests of the high places who offer sacrifice upon you, and he will burn human bones upon you." That what was foretold came to fulfillment the holy scripture plainly testifies. For it is written thus about Josiah in the Fourth Book of Kingdoms: "And the king commanded Hilkiah the high priest, and the priests of the second order, and the keepers of the threshold, to bring out of the house of the Lord all the vessels made for Baal and for the grove and for all the host of heaven; and he burned them outside Jerusalem in Sademoth of Kedron, and carried their dust to Bethel. And he burned the chomarim, whom the kings of Judah had appointed, and who burned incense on the high places and in the cities of Judah and in the places around Jerusalem; and those who burned incense to Baal and to the grove and to the sun and to the moon and to the mazouroth and to all the host of heaven. And he brought the grove out of the house of the Lord, outside Jerusalem, to the brook of Kedron, and burned them at the brook of Kedron, and ground them to dust, and threw their dust into the grave of the sons of the people." Do you see, then, how for some people the molten images became a kind of grave, and how the carved images were destroyed out of the house of the Lord?

Another scripture will also confirm what we have said on this point. For it says this in the Second Book of Chronicles: "In the eighth year of his reign" — clearly that of Josiah — "while he was still a boy, he began to seek the Lord, the God of David his father; and in the twelfth year of his reign he began to purge Judah and Jerusalem of the high places and the groves and the molten images. And they tore down before him the altars of the Baals and the high places that stood on them; and he cut down the groves and the carved images, and the molten images he smashed and ground to powder and scattered over the graves of those who had sacrificed to them. And he burned the bones of priests upon the altars, and purged Judah and Jerusalem." So they perished, as I said, along with their sanctuaries and altars, and were all but buried together with their molten images, just as the Prophet said. It should be noted that Nahum prophesied around the time of Hezekiah. Then from Hezekiah came Manasseh, who reigned fifty-five years; Manasseh's son was Amon, who lived barely two years; and after him came Josiah, in whose time the things of the prophecy were fulfilled, as our discussion has just shown.
For behold, swift upon the mountains are the feet of one who brings good news and proclaims peace.

The sons of Israel, having been taken captive, were living in Babylon; yet they were in hope of being brought back again in due time, and of returning before long to the noble estate that had been theirs from of old and from their fathers, since the holy prophets had promised this, with God speaking through them. The time of their hope was when the kingdom of Cyrus was about to take Nineveh by force, and this too Isaiah had foretold to them. For he said: "Thus says the Lord God to my anointed, Cyrus, whose right hand I have grasped, that nations may obey before him; and I will break the strength of kings; I will open doors before him, and cities shall not be shut. I will go before you and level mountains; I will shatter doors of bronze and break bars of iron." And again, a little later: "He will build the city of Jerusalem and will bring back the captivity of my people, not for ransom nor for gifts, says the Lord of hosts." So then, he says, a messenger will come to those of Israel [?], announcing the expedition of Cyrus, when they shook off the yoke of captivity and broke the rod of their masters, and, having burst the bonds of a slavery they were not used to, came home again and were saved.

But if someone should choose to apply the sense of these words to the preaching of the holy Baptist, he too would take the right course. For John made his abode in the desert, and, as though crying aloud upon the mountains, he proclaimed the good news of peace, that is, of Christ. Beautiful, then, and swift are the feet of him who says, "Prepare the way of the Lord, make straight the paths of our God."
Celebrate your feasts, O Judah, pay your vows; for they shall no more go on into old age.

The law had commanded that sacrifice must not be offered outside the holy and divine court, but "in the place which the Lord your God chooses for his name to be called upon there." So those of Israel, being in a foreign land and dwelling in the country of the Persians and Medes, remained wholly idle and inactive with regard to their customary observances: they did not keep the usual feasts, nor offer sacrifices, nor firstfruits, nor thank offerings according to the law, nor slay the lamb in the new month; perhaps they even shrank from offering mere doxologies. We say this because the divine David speaks as if in the person of the people in Babylon: "By the river of Babylon, there we sat down and wept, when we remembered Zion. On the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments." And further: "How shall we sing the Lord's song in a foreign land?" For since they were, as I said, outside the holy land, outside the temple and the tabernacle, and did not have the sacred place, they were of necessity inactive with regard to what the law required. But when at last the time of their release appeared, someone fittingly addresses them — either the messenger of peace, whose feet are swift, or the Prophet himself — telling them that they may now keep their feasts, raise songs of thanksgiving, and fully discharge what they had vowed, that is, what they had promised. He also announces the destruction of their enemies, which is all but at hand. For they shall no more, he says, go on into old age; that is, they will not remain for long periods of time any longer, nor will they enjoy a prosperity that grows old, that is, one without end. For it will cease and come to an end, cut short.

But let the spiritual Judah hear such words in a still more fitting sense. "For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is circumcision that which is outward in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter; his praise is not from men but from God." Such a one, then, will celebrate splendidly, having his faith firmly established — faith in Christ, clearly — sanctified by the Spirit and distinguished by the grace of adoption. He will offer God spiritual sacrifices, dedicating himself as a fragrant offering and practicing every form of virtue: self-control, temperance, courage, endurance, love, hope, love of the poor, kindness, long-suffering; "for with such sacrifices God is well pleased." And let the spiritual Judah know, concerning every enemy and those who once held sway over him, that they shall no more go on into old age; that is, they will be removed from the scene, sent, clearly, to punishment. This Christ indeed fulfilled when he commanded the unclean spirits to depart into the abyss, and granted to those who love him to rise up against their enemies, to stand like men against the passions, to crush sin, and "to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy." It is finished, it is taken away; for there has come up one who breathes into your face, rescuing you from affliction.

Since it was now settled, and would come to pass in every way and without fail, that Nineveh must perish, he says she "is finished," meaning by this that she has, as it were, come to her end. And moreover that she "is taken away," that is, cut off altogether and utterly destroyed. And he says very aptly "has come up" of Cyrus, conveying with emphasis, I think, something like what the prophet Jeremiah also said of him when he foretold what would befall Nineveh in due time: "A lion has come up from his den; destroying nations, he has set out and gone forth from his place, to make your land a desolation; and your cities shall be laid waste, so that they are not inhabited." For he sprang upon Nineveh like a wild beast and devoured those within it. But while to them he was a terrible and implacable enemy, unrelenting in his wrath, to those of Israel he was one who breathes into the face and rescues from affliction: that is, he freed them from a slavery they were not used to, released them from their bonds, and recovered them from captivity, by sending them home and commanding them to rebuild the divine temple.

He says "breathing into the face" with reference to Jewish tradition and custom. We shall find such things mentioned here and there in the divinely inspired Scriptures; for instance, the Jews thought it necessary to tear their garments at blasphemies against God. Caiaphas, indeed, when Christ said that he was the Son of God, tore his robe, crying out and saying, "He has blasphemed!" The divine disciples Paul and Barnabas did this too. They were in Lycaonia, and when they freed one of the sick from his affliction, and the thing seemed marvellous to those who saw it, the witnesses of the divine sign wanted to offer sacrifice to them. For they said, "The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men"; and they called Barnabas Zeus, and Paul [?], "because," it says, "he was the chief speaker." And since what was being done was a kind of blasphemy, they tore their garments, still following Jewish traditions and unwritten customs. But this custom has been censured as not coming from the law and as wholly useless. Indeed, the God of all said to the Jews, who invented such practices and strayed far from true piety: "Turn to me with all your heart, with fasting and weeping and mourning; and tear your hearts and not your garments." Just as, then, it was the custom for some to tear their clothing when someone had blasphemed, so too it was customary to breathe into the face of those who were sick in any way at all. This was done especially, and quite extravagantly, by those who were accustomed to perform exorcisms and who pretended to free sufferers from spirits and pains with curious incantations. So the Prophet takes his illustration from their custom and says: "There has come up one breathing into your face" — Cyrus, clearly — "and rescuing you from affliction." For, as I said, some pretended to be able to accomplish this by breathing on others.

It is wise and true to say that the power of the devil, and that of the sin which tyrannized over us, has been curtailed; death has been captured, as it were, and corruption taken away altogether. For Christ has come up from Hades and come back to life, he who breathed into the face of the holy apostles and said, "Receive the Holy Spirit." For in this way we have been freed from every evil, and, having become partakers of the Holy Spirit, we are restored to the original beauty of our nature and spiritually re-stamped into the first image. For our Lord Jesus Christ is formed in us through the Spirit.
Watch the road, grip your loins, be exceedingly strong in your might; for the Lord has turned away the outrage of Jacob, as the outrage of Israel.

Since they are about to set out at once for Judea and to go home, he necessarily calls out to them that they must now survey the road and grip their loins; that is, be ready and fit for the toils of the journey, stand like men against all sluggishness, and show themselves equal to the long distances, bringing unconquerable eagerness to the task. A sign of readiness is to have the loins, so to speak, neat and girded. Indeed, our Lord Jesus Christ says to the holy apostles, or rather to all who believe in him, "Let your loins be girded." For this is the garb of a traveller, and it is especially fitting for those who preach the divine gospel and have their feet most ready for this. So when he says "grip your loins," it is as if he said, "Be prepared and ready, as it were, for departure." For the Lord, he says, has turned away the outrage of Jacob, as the outrage of Israel.
