Notice again that a distinction has necessarily been introduced here. By Jacob he means those who dwelt in Samaria, that is, the ten tribes, who were ruled by kings from the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, who were descended from Joseph, who was a son of Jacob; while by Israel he means those in Jerusalem, I mean Judah and Benjamin. Now when Sennacherib had sacked Samaria, Jerusalem was not taken, because God at that time defended it and destroyed the Assyrian by the hand of an angel. But Cyrus released not only the captives from Samaria who had been carried off to Nineveh, but also those from Jerusalem, after Nebuchadnezzar had taken the country. So the Prophet necessarily says that the Lord has turned away the outrage of Jacob as the outrage of Israel. By "outrage" he means their slavery, or servitude. And that God will release them all, not protecting some while leaving others to be worn down by their hardships, he teaches by saying this: he has turned away the outrage of Jacob, just as that of Israel too is turned away. For all of them together, as we said, hastened back to Judea, having shaken off the harms of captivity.

I for my part say that it is necessary, and very fitting, that those who have been redeemed in Christ should resolve to live no longer heedlessly, but rather to look carefully for the road of the way of life that pleases God, to walk the good path, and to grip their loins; that is, to show themselves superior to the belly and to the love of pleasure, "and to make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires," and to stand like men against the passions and all sluggishness. For in this way they will come to the holy city, the heavenly Jerusalem, and there they will offer spiritual sacrifices to God; and having shaken off the yoke of their ancient slavery, they will live a glorious and free life, released from all wickedness.

For they have shaken them out completely, and their branches too. They have destroyed the weapons of their power from among men, mighty men mocking in fire. The reins of their chariots in the day of his preparation; and the horsemen shall be thrown into confusion in the roads, and the chariots shall be thrown together and entangled in the broad streets. Their appearance is like torches of fire and like lightning flashing to and fro.

When God, who knows all things, sounded in the ears of the holy prophets the things that would happen in due time, they necessarily proclaimed them beforehand as seemed good to him. And very often they found themselves in the very sight of the events. So they were struck with awe, and spoke about them as if they saw them all but fulfilled. Something of this kind the Prophet seems to experience now with regard to the inhabitants of Nineveh and those who fought alongside Cyrus: they have shaken them out, he says, and their branches too. The expression is drawn from what commonly happens to vines. For the cluster is shaken and sheds its grapes when a very violent wind strikes it, or a scorching heat burns it, or some other harm of whatever kind befalls it, so that the branch itself is laid bare along with the fruit, stripped even of its blossom. In this way, then, they shook them off like vines. Their weapons too have been destroyed, that is, their power; for weapons sometimes signify power. And he says that men who were formidable horsemen and skilled in chariot warfare fell into utterly unbearable terror, so that they turned to flight, became entangled with one another, and were smashed as they crashed together; and they imagined that the ranks of the enemy were bearing down on them in such a way as to be no less than torches, or to burn them up just like lightning darting along its swift and unstoppable course.
And their nobles shall remember, and shall flee by day, and shall grow weak in their march; and they shall hasten to the walls and shall prepare their defences.

When the war bears down heavily upon them, even the mightiest along with the rest, they will call to mind, he says, what they did when they took Judea, or rather the outrageous things they said, the wretches, uttering blasphemous words and, as it were, slinging stones at the glory of God with their unbridled mouths. Then, brought to remember these things, they will know at last that they have God as their enemy, who lays them beneath the feet of those who make war on them, even though they were once very formidable and well practised in making an assault that was hard to withstand against whomever they attacked. And if they turn to flight, they will find escape hard, and growing weak in their marches they will shift to other plans: they will see to their walls and set guards upon them. By these things he shows that they are at a loss on every side and do not know at all what they ought to do, because their minds have been darkened; and that, all but drunk as if with wine from their unmixed calamities, they lament the failure of their safety and are tossed about everywhere, readily shifting from these plans to those, and from those to others, and getting nothing but useless toil from it all. And when he says, "and they shall flee by day," he means this, I think: though they were formidable, as I said, hard to overcome and fierce, they will at last sink to such cowardice as to choose to flee openly and to do so now without concealment, although formerly they would not tolerate being accused of it even on mere suspicion.

The wicked powers, too, have been defeated by the majesty of Christ; unable to resist his divine commands, given clearly on our behalf, they were broken by terror and truly fled, no longer kept safe by any security. For when God brings his judgments, who could escape? Or what means will help those who have offended him?
The gates of the cities were opened, and the palaces fell, and the store was laid bare; and she went up, and her maidservants were led away like doves, moaning in their hearts.

So the nobles, he says, finding flight impossible, will hasten to the walls and prepare their defences. But their planning will be of no use to them, since God opens the gates of the cities to their adversaries and hands over the palaces, that is, the houses of the kings, and uncovers what was hidden in them, and sets out the store before them for plunder. By "store" he means the wealth gathered, clearly, by plunder and greed at the expense of others. Then again, as if he were witnessing what was going to happen, he sees them already being dragged off into captivity, both the ruling city — I mean Nineveh — and the cities under her and around her, which he also calls maidservants because they were yoked under her and subject to her, and perhaps served her. He says that they moan like doves in their hearts, that is, not openly but secretly. For it is this bird's way to moan something heavy and grievous within its heart. And it is not at all unlikely that something of this kind happens to those who have fallen into the hands of enemies and are then dragged off into captivity. For they bewail their own misfortune while all but stifling their laments within themselves, since sometimes they are not free even to weep.

And Nineveh, her waters are like a pool of water; and they fled and did not stand, and there was no one to look back. They plundered the silver, they plundered the gold, and there was no end to her adornment; she is weighed down above all her desirable vessels.

He likens Nineveh to a pool that is full and overflowing, because of the vast multitude living in her and the countless peoples of the nations who poured in to her aid. He is, as it were, astonished at those who flee, or better, he mocks them, because, though very many and beyond counting, they sank into cowardice, even though in the past they had been confident against any war because of their numerous forces and had lifted their brows high in their pride. But there was the God of all, who weighed down their minds with cowardice, brought them down to faintheartedness, and paralyzed their fighting spirit. For it is true that "A king is not saved by his great power, and a giant will not be saved by the greatness of his strength"; rather, it is the Lord of all who saves whomever he chooses, and very easily. Then what does the prophet say? They plundered the silver and they plundered the gold — this was the store — and there was no end to their adornment. He seems also to refer here to the Indian gems, over which especially, he says, she was weighed down with grief, though she was also downcast over her other vessels. For it was the custom of the Assyrians, that is, the Ninevites, to collect gems in great quantities and with much zeal, and to adorn themselves like girls, so that even in battle itself they were eager for splendid adornment and to be seen decked out as with flowers. The Prophet goes into great detail here, and with a purpose: in his words he depicts them now falling, now entangled with one another, at a loss for a way to flee, with useless defences, and now plundered, in order to cut short the griefs of those in captivity, skilfully charming them by foretelling such things, and bringing them to good cheer with the most delightful narratives.

Satan too has been plundered, first by Christ the Savior, and then after him by the holy apostles, of whom the prophet Jeremiah also says somewhere: "For suddenly those who bite him will rise up, and those who plot against you will awake, and you will become plunder for them." Christ too introduced this account, in the form of a parable, in his gospel preaching, for he said: "Or how can anyone enter the strong man's house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man? Then he will plunder his goods." For those who worshipped Satan, the choice and precious vessels in his possession, have run to the faith, since Christ, the Savior of us all, has brought them over to godliness, and the holy apostles themselves have persuaded them to take this path.
A shaking out, and a shaking up, and a tossing out; and breaking of heart, and loosening of knees, and pangs in every loin; and the faces of all are like a scorched pot.

He is saying that they will be crushed with every kind of crushing. For what else could being shaken out, shaken up and even tossed about suggest to us but this? Whatever is shaken and shaken up is scattered in every direction. He says that there will also follow a breaking of heart, clearly because God shatters them into cowardice. There will be a loosening of the knees, that is, weakness and paralysis of the body, and on top of these, pangs like those of childbirth, clearly the pangs that come from distress. For how could those who had sunk to every sort of thing that habitually grieves God not fall into such evils? Besides these, he insists, there will also be "And the face of all like the scorching of a pot." For the faces of the despondent always grow dark somehow, and the onset of terror cruelly robs the eyes of their brightness. We say truly that such things happened also to Satan himself, who ruled over us as a tyrant, and to the evil powers with him. For since they were cast out of that ancient honor and glory, how could they possibly escape suffering such things altogether and in every way?

Where is the dwelling of the lions, and the pasture that belongs to the cubs? Where did the lion go to enter there, the lion's cub, with no one to frighten him? The lion seized enough for his cubs and strangled prey for his lions, and he filled his den with game and his dwelling with plunder.

He calls Nineveh the dwelling of lions. For those who reigned there at various times, Pul, Shalmaneser, Sennacherib and indeed Nebuchadnezzar, lived in it and made it a splendid and admirable residence and a secure royal seat. These were the kings who made war on Judea. I do not think the words "Where is" are those of someone asking a question, for I think we must reject so simple-minded a reading. Rather, they are the words of someone mocking, who shows by this that the city has perished utterly, so that not even the place where it once stood can be seen any longer. For it has been brought to an end and removed, as he himself says. Where then, he says, is the dwelling of the lions, that is, Nineveh? And where is the pasture of the cubs? By cubs, I think, he means those who acted under the great king, held their positions under him, and enjoyed honor and glory at his side: satraps, I mean, and generals. Their pasture is his name for those under their hand, who had been subjugated, who paid tribute and supplied them with a store of money. For as it is written, "The poor are the pasture of the rich." So since Nineveh has been completely removed, together with all the surrounding country, where, he says, is the lodging of the lions? Where is the pasture of the cubs? He shows that Nineveh had become, as it were, a secure stronghold for those who reigned at various times when he says, "Where the lion's cub went to enter there, and there was no one to frighten him." For the city's wall was impregnable, superbly built with works of extraordinary magnificence. Nebuchadnezzar ravaged all Samaria, and Judea itself, and the holy city, I mean Jerusalem, and carried off those of Israel's blood to his own land. He extended his power so far over those he had once captured that he made some his subjects and kept them in chains, gave others away as favors or sold them, and filled his own country and city with captives of the spear. That is why he says, "The lion seized enough for his cubs and strangled prey for his lions, and he filled his den with game and his dwelling with plunder." Again the saying is drawn from what happens in nature. Wild beasts simply seize whatever crosses their path, eat their fill, and then feed their cubs with the rest, sharing with them the fruit of their own labors.

Such things might also be said of Satan himself, since Christ destroyed him and his works and removed his prey from the earth. For he crushed the jaw-teeth of the lions, as the psalmist says: "The Lord has shattered the jaw-teeth of the lions."

Behold, I am against you, says the Lord Almighty, and I will burn up your multitude in smoke, and the sword will devour your lions, and I will destroy your prey from the earth, and your deeds will no longer be heard.

God sets himself against them and rises up in person, driving them to despair of being saved. For when God wills to do harm, who is left to save? Or who will hold back the Lord of hosts when he wishes to lay waste? As it is written, "For who will turn back the high hand?" He says that he will burn up her multitude in smoke, and again he means us to picture something like this. When beekeepers want to dig the honeycombs out of the hives, they light a fire and drive off the bees with smoke, so that the bees will not swarm around them, fight, and wound them with their stings. Something like this happened to those who were called in to help Nineveh in its danger. They went off and ran away, because the war assailed them like smoke, terrified them into cowardice and filled them with unbearable fears. By lions he means the most valiant and bold, who perhaps dared to resist. But they too became the work of Cyrus's sword. Since the passage had brought lions to mind, he necessarily adds that their prey will also be destroyed, so that nothing of theirs is worth hearing about any longer. For it was their custom to fall on cities and countries, to spring like wild beasts on whomever they happened to choose, and to do countless such things, so that the calamities of their victims became a song and a lament for many. So he says that their prey will be destroyed. For how could they hunt anyone down any longer, or whom? The common herd had been terrified and had fled as if from smoke, and the most warlike had fallen, those who used to fall on their opponents like lions.

The God of all has also risen up against the Jews who killed the Lord, so that the multitude of the common herd was scattered to every wind, and those more prominent than the rest perished with the many, like savage beasts. For their impiety against Christ, the Savior of all, was past bearing.
O city of blood, wholly false, full of injustice!

He called it a city of blood, for those who reigned in Nineveh were quick to murder and very bloodthirsty. Its people were warlike in other ways too, always eager to launch savage attacks on whomever they marched against. He calls it false because it was full of idols, and in their case above all the falsehood needs no proof. For the gods made by hand bear false names and steal the glory of the Godhead: "Silver and gold," as it is written, "the works of human hands." The wise Jeremiah too somewhere called it a land of carved images. "False" might also be understood another way, if falsehood is taken to mean villainy, deceit and the fraud that God hates, which clearly run together with injustice. For where there is fraud and deceit, injustice will surely follow.

Jerusalem too, which killed the Lord, is a city of blood, false and full of injustice. For we remember Christ saying, "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to her." And somewhere he also said through the voice of the prophets, "Woe to them, for they have sprung away from me! Wretched are they, for they have acted impiously against me. I redeemed them, but they spoke lies against me." For they spoke against Christ's glory, at one time saying that he cast out demons by Beelzebul, at another calling him a drunkard, and a Samaritan besides, and things far more shameful. Only their unbridled mouths could fittingly babble the things they actually dared to say.

Prey will not be groped for. The sound of whips, the sound of rattling wheels, of a galloping horse, of a bounding chariot, of a horseman mounting, of a flashing sword, of gleaming weapons, of a multitude of wounded, of a heavy fall! There was no end to her nations, and they will grow weak in their bodies from the multitude of their fornication.

Again the saying is drawn from what happens in nature. Bird-catchers cover thick, leafy bushes with nets and often catch the birds hidden underneath by groping with their hands. This is their craft. So no longer, he says, will they grope for prey. That is, they will no longer hunt as some did of old, snatching other people's goods for themselves, nor will they be a snare and a noose for the weak, since another worry has fallen upon them and the struggle for their very lives hangs over them. For there will be in her the sound of whips. Here again the Prophet seems to me to describe the tumult of war clearly, as though it lay before his eyes. He sees the city ringing, as it were, with the hoofbeats of horses and clattering with chariot wheels, those who are laying it waste flashing in brilliant armor, the dead beyond number, and the houses in it shaken down. For he also mentions a heavy fall. He is astonished that the multitude of nations gathered in it was so very great, and yet all of them were unmanly, extraordinarily feeble and very easily given to cowardice. He at once gives the reason, saying that they will grow weak in their bodies from the multitude of their fornication. For since they had become base and wicked in their ways, idolaters besides, and had turned aside into error beyond measure, they will justly be weak and terrified, unable to bear even speaking of resistance, or even merely thinking of it.
A harlot, beautiful and charming, a mistress of sorceries, who sells nations by her fornication and tribes by her sorceries.

Praise for shameful things makes the charges heavier, as if someone chose to say of a person that he is a skilled thief, a brave robber, a talented sorcerer. So if it is said of Nineveh, "a harlot, beautiful and charming," this will not be to her praise, far from it. It will rather make the denunciation harsher. For courtesans are thought to cultivate charm most of all when they appear glib and smooth-spoken. Such was Nineveh too: skilled, and well able to win over cities and countries and to persuade them to think what she approved and liked. These things were sorceries, false divinations, profane rites and the games of idols. She reached such a pitch of folly that she counted it a mark of renown even to be thought a mistress of sorceries, and boasted of things so shameful and deserving of the utmost outcry. Some of her people were accustomed to sell nations and countries by their sorceries. How, or in what way, we will explain as best we can. When the Assyrians wished to make war and took up arms against others, it was their custom to hasten first to learn the future through the arts of the magi. And the magi, courting honors from the king, would bid him triumph in every war, and falsely claimed that by their practices they had unnerved his opponents in advance. This is the kind of thing that Balak, the king of the Moabites, wanted to do. For he hired the accursed Balaam and even brought him up a mountain, saying, "Come, curse Israel for me." For they thought events would follow the curses of the magi. So in these words he calls the art of sorcery and magic fornication, by which those who were wise in these things sold nations and tribes, always promising victory to those who brought them fees.

Behold, I am against you, says the Lord God Almighty, and I will uncover your hinder parts over your face, and I will show the nations your shame and the kingdoms your dishonor. I will cast abomination upon you according to your uncleannesses, and I will make you an example.

Again he indicates that her reckoning is not with a human being, nor is the war a human one. Rather, the Lord of hosts has grown angry with her and raises up the Persians and Medes against her. And who can march out against God, who has authority over all and holds power over the universe, if he chooses to make war on anyone? Then he says, "And I will uncover your hinder parts over your face." Again the saying is framed as if about a courtesan, who, as far as her face and outward adornment go, seems lovely to those who see her. But if she is stripped and her finery removed, she will surely be disgraced by her naked body, openly revealing the unloveliness of her parts. So I will uncover your hinder parts, he says, that is, all that is unseemly in you, and above all I will display it to you. For what else could "over your face" suggest to us but this? And he said expressly that he would also uncover her dishonor to nations and kingdoms. For Nineveh seemed beautiful and lovely, seizing rule and dominion over all through the arts of the magi, very strong, and winning victory over everyone without a battle. But when she was captured and fell, she appeared unsightly and unattractive to those who knew her. From then on they thought her loathsome, having surely judged that she had boasted greatly over nothing and had trusted in vain in the help of the magi, or rather in their trickery and deceits. And he affirmed that she will be made an example, since people would sometimes say, when a city or country perished, "It has been sacked and has fallen, just like wretched Nineveh."

As I said, the God of all also made war on the Synagogue of the Jews in due time and exacted punishment for its impiety against Christ, exposing her naked and unseemly and wholly deprived of the covering from above. He foretold this through the voice of Hosea, saying, "Therefore I will turn back and take away my grain in its season and my wine in its time, and I will take away my garments and my linen, so that they do not cover her shame. And now I will uncover her uncleanness before her lovers, and no one shall deliver her out of my hand." For the church from the Gentiles will give glory, saying, "Let my soul rejoice in the Lord, for he has clothed me with a garment of salvation and a tunic of gladness." But the Synagogue, as I said, is seen from now on to be naked, unseemly and unlovely, lacking the covering of divine gifts. She has become an example and utterly loathsome, sick with every kind of worldly uncleanness.
And everyone who sees you will go down from you and say, "Wretched Nineveh! Who will mourn for her? Where shall I seek comfort for her?"

If anyone, he says, who knew your power in former times should see you fallen and desolate, he will lament loudly and hurry away, saying, "Who will mourn for her?" He says such things as though there were no one, that is, no one left, who could even so much as lament. And he very wisely added to this, "Where shall I seek comfort for her?" The sense of these words is something like this. When war and battle are waged against cities or countries, sometimes one part is harmed while another is saved and perhaps escapes the victors, and this is a comfort to the inhabitants. Either the whole has not been burned and some part has remained unsacked, or some have fallen but another multitude has been saved. But in the case of Nineveh, where could anyone find comfort? Or what could console her? For the whole city was captured, the whole was sacked, and everyone in it has perished. "Who will mourn for her?" might also be understood another way. It is like saying, "Who will be so skilled in laments and funeral songs as to say anything worthy of what has happened, and to shed tears enough for such sufferings?"

Prepare a portion, tune the string, prepare a portion, Amon, you who dwell among rivers! Water surrounds her; her dominion is the sea, and water is her walls. Ethiopia is her strength, and Egypt, and there is no end to your flight, and the Libyans became her helpers. Yet she too will go into exile as a captive, and they will dash her infants to the ground at the head of all her streets, and they will cast lots for all her glorious things, and all her great men will be bound in fetters.

The sense of these words is very obscure, and cannot be understood unless the history they contain is first related. It is as follows. Israel turned to apostasy, worshiped idols and provoked the God of all against itself by countless impieties, and so Nebuchadnezzar armed himself against Judea and Jerusalem, roused to this by divine wrath. Then the people of Israel ought to have ceased from the impiety in their hands, given up their desire to worship other gods, overturned the altars, burned the sacred precincts and smashed the molten images, and with earnest repentance and humility appeased God and called on him for help. But this the wretches did not do. Instead they thought that with the help of human reinforcements they would prove stronger than the Babylonians and prevail over their enemies, even if God should not choose to save them. Accordingly they hired many of the neighboring nations, and also sent embassies to the Egyptians and to the city called On, or Amon, which is now Alexandria. These promised to fight alongside them and claimed they could easily drive off the Babylonians, and so they gave the people of Israel occasion to think that even if God did not save them, they would be able to manage by themselves, needing no one. But when Nebuchadnezzar had taken Judea, with God shielding him and laying his opponents low before him, he next advanced against the land of the Egyptians, sent by divine wrath, and took all of it, including On itself, or Amon, for that, as I said, was at one time the name of Alexandria. Beyond the other cities of Egypt this city was especially splendid, an inviolable and secure stronghold, because it was girded on all sides by waters. On its northern side it had the sea, and on its southern side a broad and long expanse that was like a second sea, I mean Lake Mareotis, and it was fortified by other rivers too and by surrounding marshes. The inhabitants of neighboring Libya also came to its aid. Libya extends as far as the land of the Ethiopians toward the west and south, and these people are the Garamantes, who live beyond the land of the Africans. Some of the Ethiopians toward the east and south also took up arms with them, whose innermost city is Meroe and who inhabit a wild and black land.

But let our account of the history stand thus, and let us now go on to explain the sense of the words. Prepare a portion, he says, as if he were saying, "O wretched Nineveh, prepare a portion for yourself! For since you have grown very proud, and think that you will be altogether and in every way impregnable because you are enclosed by great walls and have countless allies willing to fight beside you, which of the countries you sacked do you wish to be like? And yet they too," he says, "were as well equipped as any could be to be hard to capture and impregnable." Tune the string: that is, you too become a song and a melody for cities and countries, suffering at the hands of the Persians and Medes the same things you yourself did to others. Prepare a portion, Amon: let Amon, he says, be your portion and lot. What you did to her, you too must suffer. And who was Amon, who dwells among rivers? She was the city superbly walled by sea and rivers, who boasted in the help of the Egyptians and the arrows of the Ethiopians, and who had the most valiant multitude of the Libyans on her side. Yet even with such a position, such strength and such outside help, she went into exile and became a captive. Her infants were dashed to the ground, her distinguished men were assigned by lot, the more glorious of them became the portions of the victors, and they were bound in fetters. So just as you took Amon, which was impregnable as far as help and position went, since it was God who handed her over, so you too will surely be given into the hands of your enemies, however proudly you raise your brow over your multitude of warriors and your walls. For I am against you, and no one will turn back my hand.
You too will be made drunk and will be overlooked, and you will not seek a standing-place for yourself from your enemies [?].

For just as Amon, he says, suffered misery when she endured the darts of your savagery and the calamities of your assault, so you too will grow dizzy and be as if drunk, with no place to stand. That is, you will be shaken and will fall at the hands of your enemies, deprived of watchful care from above. For those whom God watches over he surely pities, and he makes them stand firm in the things they pray for.

Jerusalem, which fought against God, has likewise been made drunk. She cannot be sober, because she is not illumined by divine light and will not listen to Christ when he says, "I am the light of the world," and again, "While you have the light, walk in the light, so that darkness may not overtake you." Drunkenness, darkness in the mind and night in the heart might be understood as ignorance of what is truly beneficial and the inability to see the way of salvation from any quarter. And that she has been shaken and has no firm footing for the works of righteousness, how or on what grounds could anyone doubt? For she has fallen away from the foundation of all things and does not have the unbreakable foundation, that is, Christ. She has been overlooked and handed over to her enemies, perhaps to the Romans, or else to those who will drag her down into every kind of passion, I mean the unclean spirits. Christ, then, and faith in him, will free us from every evil, make us stronger than the malice of our enemies, and set us in the sight of God. For he will never overlook those who love him.
All your fortresses are fig trees with watchmen. If they are shaken, they will fall into the mouth of the one who eats.

Ripe figs drop off easily if the tree is shaken. They all but leap down into the hand of the one shaking it, and come of their own accord to those who want to eat. Cyrus attacked Nineveh and was already besieging it, setting siege engines, that is, battering rams, against its walls, while its defenders kept watch on the battlements. Then the attackers shot arrows at them and easily brought them down to the ground. So the prophet takes his comparison from what naturally happens with ripe figs. That is why he says: All your fortresses, that is, the walls, are fig trees with watchmen, who drop into the hand of anyone who wants to eat, and very easily, if someone merely shakes the tree.

So too every soul that falls away from help from above, and is deprived of it, will be easy prey, readily captured, and taken without any sweat by Satan, who devours. For it is written: “His food is choice.”
Behold, your people within you are like women; the gates of your land will be thrown wide open to your enemies; fire will devour your bars.

He shows that their hope is vain. They thought they would never be captured, since they had gathered a countless multitude of allies to fight beside them and lived in a city fortified with unbreakable walls and towers. But he clearly foretold that even these things would be utterly useless to them. He said that the defenders would sink into such cowardice that they would differ in no way from weak women, and that the gates would be thrown open, obviously as the enemy forced their way in. For it is true that “Unless the Lord guards a city, the watchman has stayed awake in vain.”

We must therefore have our security from above. We must trust very little in ourselves and much more in God who saves. We must not boast in human help, nor suppose that we can slip out of the way of wrath if God is provoked. For no one will rescue from turmoil and evils the person with whom the Lord of all is angry. Very wise, then, was the divine David when he sang and said: “I will not hope in my bow, and my arm will not save me.” And again in his own words: “For in God I will do valiantly.”
Draw water for yourself for the siege.

They say that Cyrus and his men were ravaging the lands around Nineveh and had already cut off all its sources of help. The Ninevites, now fearing the sack of their city, cut up the country around it with many long trenches and made it hard for the enemy to cross. They diverted rivers, filled the trenches with water, and turned the ground into marshland. But the attackers proved stronger than even these measures, or rather the will of God, who was handing the city over, did. So he shows that this effort too will come to nothing for them when he says: Draw water for yourself for the siege. Some think that the water drawn in here means the gathering or multitude of the nations called in to help. Taken this way too, the interpretation is not off the mark, for in many places the multitude of the nations is called waters.
Strengthen your fortresses; go into the clay and tread it among the straw; make yourself stronger than brick.

God would not urge such things. But since he knew beforehand exactly what would happen, he laughs at their plans, and through these words he shows that, as I said just now, all their effort will be in vain. When the walls needed battlements or some other repair, they made bricks, out of clay of course, but very strong ones, for baked brick is indispensable for building and does not easily crumble. So he says: Tread among the straw, and make bricks too. Become as bold and unyielding in battle as the brick itself. Even so you will be easily taken. You will be anything but unbreakable, and very easy prey for those who know how to batter walls down and whose onslaught is mightier than your hardness.
There fire will devour you, the sword will destroy you; it will devour you like a locust, and you will be weighed down like a grasshopper.

You should understand “there” as meaning “then,” for we will take the word as referring to time and not to place. He says: Even if you do these things and make bricks, you will still be consumed as if by fire, and the enemy will feed on you and your land like a locust. You will be fettered by sluggishness and slow to flee, like a grasshopper weighed down. For they say that when hail falls and rain pours down, the grasshopper cannot fly, because its wings are soaked. So once again he hints, from what happens to grasshoppers, that the Ninevites will have no way to flee.

You have multiplied your trading beyond the stars of heaven; the grasshopper set out and flew away. Your mixed host leapt away like a young locust, like a locust that has settled on a hedge on a day of frost: the sun rose, and it sprang away, and no one knew its place.

By “trading” here he seems to mean not trade for money, for gain and profit, but rather the business of gathering and assembling the nations. As I said, they hired the neighboring nations, all but trafficking in men who were going to die, and gathering for battle men who were very soon to perish. These were very many, beyond counting, and so they are compared to the multitude of the stars. But he says: Even if they have gathered and run together, they will be terrified by the war and run off again like a grasshopper and like a young locust. This is a kind of small locust. When it lands on hedges or garden walls while there is frost, as I said, and rain is falling, it shuts itself up and stays still, robbed of flight by the force of the moisture. But when the sun rises and sends its warm rays on them, they leave quickly and fly off as they usually do. So, he says, will your mixed host be. They will fly off and run home again, leaving your hope empty. Then, as the prophet says, “It is good,” and true, “to trust in the Lord rather than to trust in man.”
Woe to them! Your shepherds have slumbered; the Assyrian king has put your mighty men to sleep; your people have gone off to the mountains, and there was no one to receive them.

He calls the crowds wretched, because they have slipped into such cowardice and fear that they lose heart at the mere onset of war, leap up to the mountaintops, and make the rough terrain a kind of rampart against the danger. Then he gives the reason for their timidity, and in a fitting way he describes the destruction of those whose lot it was to lead them. He speaks figuratively, saying “they slumbered” instead of “they have been sacked and have perished, and have become helpless in the arts of generalship.” He also says that those in power and authority, the leaders of the people, and those who held the high and illustrious offices have been put to sleep. They suffered this slumber at the hands of the Assyrian king, that is, one whose descent was from among them, for Cyrus was native to the region and of Persian blood. The prophetic word as it were pretends to lament, or rather it mocks those who are so quick to panic. For he says: Your people have gone off to the mountains, and there was no one to receive them. That is, there was no one to rally them to courage, to cut short the cowardice of those fleeing, and to rein in the feeble multitude of deserters who had thrown away their shields. For the men who used to do this, the masters of the art of war, had already perished.

One might also, and quite fittingly, apply the words “Woe to them! Your shepherds have slumbered; the Assyrian king has put your mighty men to sleep” to the herd of the Jews. For truly woe to those who killed the very Savior and Redeemer of all, and who impiously added to the blood of the saints even the blood of the Lord himself. This happened to them because their leadership, those placed in the rank of shepherds, slumbered deeply into evil counsel. I mean the scribes and Pharisees, and those crowned with the dignities of the priesthood, whom the Assyrian king, that is, Satan, put to sleep in a spiritual sense. For the kingdom of the Babylonians is often taken to represent him. How can anyone doubt that their shepherds and rulers slumbered, when the divinely inspired Scripture, from beginning to end, lays the destruction of the peoples at their door? For it is written: “O shepherds who scatter and destroy the sheep of the pasture!” And again: “The priests did not say, Where is the Lord? Those who handled the law did not know me, the shepherds acted impiously against me, and the prophets prophesied by Baal.” And Isaiah also says: “How has the faithful city Zion, full of justice, become a harlot? Righteousness lodged in her, but now murderers. Your silver is worthless; your innkeepers mix the wine with water; your rulers are disobedient, companions of thieves, loving bribes, chasing after rewards, not defending the orphan and not heeding the widow's cause.”
There is no healing for your bruise; your wound has festered.

When people happen to suffer some misfortune, if it comes in measure and not utterly beyond what is fitting, those who have suffered it still have good hope. They can expect to recover, as from an illness, and live in health again, and to move on to prosperity once their affairs take a turn for the better. But when their affairs have reached the very limit of misery, then the calamity is surely hard to escape, or rather completely inescapable. This is what Nineveh suffered, and so he says that she has been crushed and has perished. Her hope of being healed has been destroyed along with her, and the evil, so to speak, festers miserably and calls for the final cut of the knife.

It is true to say that Jerusalem, the slayer of the Lord, also came to this state. She was often struck when enemies overran her, but healing followed, because God took pity on them and, as it were, soothed the blow that had fallen on them. But since they behaved outrageously toward the Lord of all, she was crushed and fell, and there was no healing, in the words of the prophet, and the inflammation of what befell them has remained unsoothed. That is why the blessed prophets compared her to Babylon and said: “We treated Babylon, and she was not healed. Let us abandon her and go each to his own land, for her judgment has reached to heaven and risen up to the stars.” Her judgment reached to heaven, and her offense was raised on high. For, as I said, they outraged not simply one of the saints, but the Lord of the saints.
All who hear the news of you will rejoice and clap their hands over you; for upon whom has your wickedness not come continually?

That God's verdict in overthrowing the Babylonian empire was just will be clearly attested by the fact that no one at all grieves over her. Instead, they clap and rejoice and smile at her as she lies fallen, because they had endured unbearable calamities and extortion from her and had experienced everything most apt to cause sorrow. For she was a burden to all and hard to bear, and even those far away felt the malice that was in her.

I would say that the inventor of sin too, that is, Satan, might fittingly hear these words now that he has been overthrown by Christ and driven from his tyranny over us. For he spread the net of his malice everywhere, dragged the whole world under heaven into error, and bound it in the snares of destruction. All who hear the news of you will rejoice and clap their hands over you; for upon whom has your wickedness not come continually?
Our Father among the Saints, Cyril, on the Prophet Habakkuk. Volume One.

The form of the present prophecy has been composed for us very wisely and skilfully, and yet we shall find it full of a divine ordering such as befits the saints. To the saints themselves it is right to say aloud, "It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you." Those who wish to understand it need no small sharpness of mind, since one can see that the aim of the prophecy is in labour with a twofold meaning, spiritual and historical at once. So it will help if I first set out the parts of the prophecy, gathering them together briefly, and say why it was given. That way the minds of those who read it will move along easily and find no uphill climb.

Israel was grieved beyond measure at what the prophets had foretold. They had already been proclaiming that in due time Israel would be taken captive, fall into the hands of enemies and lie under the yoke of an unaccustomed slavery. This blessed Habakkuk tries to teach that such things will befall them in due time by the just verdict of God, who rules over all, and for good reasons. They had prized a life outside the law and utterly perverse, and had turned to every kind of falsehood. In this way they kept on provoking the pure Mind against themselves, until at last their affairs sank to this depth of misery. He makes this plain by denouncing those who had chosen to live impiously, setting this out as a kind of prelude and premise of the whole prophecy. Then he brings in God, threatening the despisers with the onslaught of the Babylonians.

But he was not meant to appear only as a foreteller of gloomy things, of the things most apt to cause grief. He was not to come forward simply to announce the most shameful of all the evils that would in time befall them. He also had to foretell, for their benefit, something that would lead to healing, and to proclaim in advance the things through which the sufferers might be expected to breathe again. So he cried out against the very cruelty of the Babylonians. He calls them despisers, since they burned the divine temple itself, sacked the holy city and showed no respect for the sacred vessels. "For why," he says, "do you look upon despisers? Will you keep silent while the ungodly swallows up the righteous?" Then he added, and very clearly, the capture of Babylon itself, and how in due time those who had suffered would be set free from their unaccustomed slavery through Cyrus. From this partial redemption the discourse moves aptly to the universal and most general one. That is the redemption accomplished through Christ for all who have been redeemed through faith, who have laid aside the yoke of sin and escaped a bitter and savage master, Satan.

Here you have the aim of the whole prophecy gathered together briefly. Now we shall speak, taking up each part in turn as far as we can.

The oracle that Habakkuk the prophet saw. By "oracle" he means here the receiving of the vision, that is, of foreknowledge, which a person may receive when God gives it. For, as it is written, it is he who multiplied visions, and he who has spoken to the prophets. Through the Holy Spirit he reveals to them beforehand the things to come and sets them before their eyes almost as if they were already present. The prophets did not set out to speak things from their own hearts. Rather, they carry across to us the words that come from God. Habakkuk makes this clear from the start by calling himself a prophet, showing that he is full of the grace that belongs to this office.
How long, Lord, shall I cry out, and you will not hear? Shall I shout to you when I am wronged, and you will not save?

The prophet takes on the role of someone who is being defrauded and is enduring the intolerable insolence and drunken violence of habitual wrongdoers. Yet very skilfully he bears witness to God's love for humanity, which is beyond words. He shows that God is extremely forbearing, even though he is known to hate the wicked. He shows clearly that God does not bring punishment on sinners at once. He says that God's silence and long-suffering had gone so far that an outcry was now needed. Some people had made their greed against others unbearable and were letting loose their insolence on the weaker as if it had no bridle. By the very words in which he complains of God's forbearance, he bears witness to God's love for humanity, which goes beyond all measure. "How long, Lord," he says, "shall I cry out, and you will not hear? Shall I shout to you when I am wronged, and you will not save?" And this is said of a God who has threatened many bitter punishments against those who choose to break the law.
Why have you shown me toils and troubles to look upon, misery and ungodliness?

From this too you can learn how the saints hate evil, for they call the troubles of others their own. So the most wise Paul says, "Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?" He has also commanded us "to weep with those who weep," showing that sympathy and love for one another are most fitting for saints. The prophet says that God showed him toils and troubles, meaning clearly the troubles of those who were wronged, and ungodliness, meaning that of habitual wrongdoers. He does not mean that God arranged for him to suffer. He means that God was patient with the evildoers, and for such a long time, when he could have released the prophet from life so that he would not have to watch such outrageous deeds. In such bitter despondency it is the way of the saints to seek to depart. So the blessed Jonah says, "And now, Lord, take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live." And the most wise Paul writes that it is "better to depart and be with Christ." For those who wish to live holy lives, it is a laying aside of toil to be freed at last from the affairs of this world and released, as it were, from the grievous cares of this life.

Judgment has gone against me, and the judge takes bribes. Therefore the law is scattered, and judgment is not carried through to the end, because the ungodly oppresses the righteous. For this reason judgment will go forth perverted.

He shows that nothing personal moves him to lose heart. Rather, as a holy man who loves justice, he is distressed to see people disregarding the divine commandment. These are not just ordinary people, but men made illustrious with the highest honours, set over peoples and appointed to the rank of judges. He shows this plainly when he says that upright verdicts have been undone, even though the law clearly declared, "You shall not show partiality in judgment, for the judgment is God's." Judging, then, is a great thing. The judge who cannot be bribed and will not allow the verdict of justice to be twisted becomes a wise imitator of God's own supremacy and glory. But the bribe-taker is extremely insolent and sets himself against the very dignity of God. He counterfeits the beauty of truth and makes a practice of twisting what is straight. He calls "evil good and good evil," and impiously reckons "darkness as light and light as darkness."

So the prophet shows that the whole law is trampled underfoot at once in this one most excellent and glorious commandment. For if someone has missed the mark in the chief point of what is right, how could he be trusted in what is greater? The prophet presents himself as a witness who has seen this greed for himself. Since right judgment has been neglected, he says, the law is therefore weak, and judgments are not carried out uprightly as seems good to you, the Master, and the ungodly oppresses the righteous.

God brought this charge against the synagogue of the Jews through the voices of other prophets too. He said, "Her leaders judged for bribes." And again he spoke to her through Isaiah: "Your silver is worthless. Your merchants mix the wine with water. Your rulers are disobedient, companions of thieves, loving gifts, chasing after rewards. They do not judge for the orphan, and they pay no heed to the widow's case." Here the prophet Habakkuk seems to want to fulfil the saying in the book of Proverbs: "What your eyes have seen, speak." He goes on to show that his outcry against God's calm was entirely reasonable. God is forbearing as befits him, for God is good. Yet as far as human understanding could tell, he was stretching his forbearance beyond all measure.

In the case of Christ too, judgment went forth perverted and the law was scattered. It would have been better to honour him as God, and as a worker of miracles because he was God. Instead the teachers of the Jews never stopped slandering him. They tried every means with their unbridled tongues, and there was no outrage they did not dare to say against him. At one time they held that he cast out demons by Beelzebul. At another they called him a drunkard and said he had a demon. Then, when they ought to have called him the Saviour and Redeemer of all, the wretches impiously killed him, passing a perverted verdict on him, even though the law had clearly declared, "You shall not kill the innocent and the righteous."

Christ also accused them in another way, saying that they would not think what was right and just. They kept silent and, as it were, shut the eye of the mind to whatever Moses might say, even though he set aside the Sabbath law. But they pounced, and very bitterly, on whatever divine works Christ himself did on the Sabbath. For he said, "I did one work, and you all marvel. Moses gave you circumcision, not that it comes from Moses but from the fathers, and you circumcise a man on the Sabbath. If a man receives circumcision on the Sabbath so that the law of Moses is not broken, are you angry with me because I made a whole man well on the Sabbath? Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment."
Look, you despisers, and see, and marvel at marvels, and vanish. For I am doing a work in your days that you will not believe if someone tells it to you.

The prophet had cried out against the greed of the lawless and all but complained of God's delay in putting up with them, for a righteous soul that loves virtue is something that hates evil. Now the God of all tells the habitual despisers to see and look, and to marvel at the things that are fit to be marvelled at. These were the things hanging over them, as it were, and just about to happen. Their attack was something to pray against and their onset something to dread. He usefully commanded them to look at these things in advance, since they were quite capable of destroying those they were seen to come against. He calls them marvellous because they were unexpected and beyond hope, unbearable, able to stun by their sheer dreadfulness, and perhaps even past belief. For evils of great magnitude are always apt to come very close to being disbelieved, especially when they are seen happening to people who never expected to suffer.

Who would ever have thought that beloved Israel, the firstborn among children, would come to such misery? For Israel's sake Egypt perished and countless nations fell: Canaanites and Amorites, Hivites, Perizzites and Jebusites. Who would have thought that they would be uprooted from their whole land and endure an inglorious and unbearable slavery, wandering in a foreign land after the assaults of war? No words would be enough to describe each of these assaults in detail. There were burnings and slaughters of men. Women were dragged away and infants were dashed to the ground. As the prophet Jeremiah says, "The hands of compassionate women boiled their own children." The holy things themselves were plundered. Of all the evils that reach the very limit, there was none the captors did not commit. These things, then, were incredible and almost implausible to recount, because the perpetrators' cruelty was so extreme. That is why he says that he will do a work in their days that they will not believe, if someone should happen to describe it to them. By saying "in your days," he let them understand that no long time would pass in between. The war was, as it were, at the door, immediate and close at hand, and justice was not far off.
For behold, I am raising up the Chaldeans, the warriors, the swift and bitter nation, which marches across the breadth of the earth to take possession of dwellings that are not its own.

He showed at once what the thing was that would not be believed if it were told. He threatened to let loose the Babylonians on them, a warlike and utterly savage race. In cruelty it yields nothing to untamed wild beasts, and it was notorious for its constant unrestrained frenzies. He called it swift because they are mostly horsemen. He called it bitter because it is fierce and extremely harsh, cunning in tactics and well practised in generalship. When strength runs together with good judgment to meet the needs of war, I think it will most easily accomplish whatever the warriors resolve, and it will easily overcome those who are eager to resist. It was the custom of the Babylonians neither to stay always at home nor merely to beat back those who attacked them in self-defence. Instead they spread out, as it were, over the whole earth, laid waste the lands of others and liked to take as their portion what in no way belonged to them. So he rightly says, "the nation that marches across the breadth of the earth to take dwellings that are not its own." For, as I said, it loves to rage against the lands of others and always to enlarge its own empire.

The Jews suffered something of this kind after they killed the Lord. They could have lived in their own land at ease, with no one oppressing them. Instead they were handed over to conquerors and brought under tributes and taxes. They were placed under the sceptres of those who were always enlarging their rule and had conquered all that is under heaven. For they shook off the rule of Christ and said outright, "We have no king but Caesar."

It should also be understood that if a human soul sets the divine laws at nothing, it will be under bitter tyrants, the unclean demons. It will be a slave to wicked powers that always thirst to take possession of dwellings that are not their own. For a human being belongs to God, since God dwells among the saints and makes his home in the souls of the holy.
He is terrible and renowned. His judgment will come from himself, and his oracle will go forth from himself.

The discourse now moves to the leader of the nation, that is, the tyrant of the Babylonians. This was perhaps Nebuchadnezzar, who took Judea, burned the divine temple itself and carried Judah off captive to his own land. He says that this man is terrible because of his cruelty, his lack of restraint in anger, his untamed mind and his deafness to justice. He calls him renowned because he was ambitious, boastful and an insatiable lover of glory. Those who ruled over Babylon were always arrogant and extremely vainglorious.

These rulers took the lead in every decision and every undertaking. They simply ordered their subjects to carry out whatever seemed good to them. That is why he says, "His judgment will come from himself." In other words, he rushes on his own impulses toward whatever stirs him, and out of great haughtiness he will not put up with the opinions of others, even if he orders something impossible. For the counsels of the Persians are arrogant.

It was also their custom to seek omens about battles beforehand and to try to learn in advance by the magic art how the matter in hand would turn out. So he said again, "His oracle will go forth from himself." By "oracle" he means the divination. He will not send to other nations or lands for those skilled in divination, he says, but rather has them living alongside him. They are always lying and know nothing of the truth, but they always egg him on and are in the habit of predicting that he will win. The Babylonian empire took great pride in this. Indeed, when Balak, king of the Moabites, planned to curse the Israelites and sought knowledge of what was to come, he sent for Balaam from Mesopotamia. He thought that the magi of the Babylonians were clever and precise, and fully able to accomplish anything at all through the magic art.

If you like, we may also take the meaning of the passage another way. Having marked out the tyrant of the Babylonians and said that he is terrible and renowned, he immediately added, "His judgment will come from himself, and his oracle will go forth from himself." We may understand it something like this. God, the Master of all, had resolved to punish Israel, which had chosen to live shamefully and basely. This judgment upon Israel, he says, will be carried out by him, the Babylonian. It is as if he were saying: "He will be the instrument of my wrath, and through him I will punish you. And the oracle concerning you, that is, whatever plan and purpose I may form, will again go forth from him, that is, will be carried out. For he will bring to completion whatever comes from my counsel and purpose."
And his horses will spring faster than leopards and be fiercer than the wolves of Arabia. His horsemen will ride out and charge from afar, and they will swoop like an eagle eager to eat.

Again he terrifies them with the sheer extent of the terrors and tries to teach them that the host of their enemies is dreadful and cannot be broken. He drives them toward repentance, so that they may learn what it would have been better for them to be seen doing. He declares again that the Babylonians are very light of foot, bold and ready to dare anything. They are no different from wild beasts and, as it were, swoop down on anyone who can be caught. He likens their horses to leopards, for the leopard is a great leaper and very nimble at pouncing on what it is chasing. He likens the men to the wolves of Arabia, which are said to be the most savage of all and to dart in at full speed when they launch an attack on whatever they choose. And he says that they resemble not only wolves but also eagles, which rush without delay upon dead bodies and swoop down on them, as I said.

The mind of the Jews too became easy to capture, and their heart was, as it were, trampled by horses, that is, easily overrun. It was overrun by the passions of the flesh, by the unclean spirits themselves and, besides these, by the mighty assaults of the Romans. For they had offended him who says, "And I will be to them, says the Lord, a wall of fire all around, and I will be the glory in her midst." Every mind, I think, is easily captured and very easily overthrown when it is deprived of strength from above. For all our strength and security come from God, as it is written: "In him we shall do valiantly, and he will bring to nothing those who afflict us."
An end will come upon the ungodly, who stand against him with their faces set in opposition.

This is the end of what was foretold and the crowning point of the evils. The Chaldeans will come, he says. They will be of this kind, they will do this, and they will add that as well. And the sum of it all is that the ungodly will perish utterly, with their whole households, together with their cities and villages. God will show them no pity at all, but will abandon to desolation, as it were, those who have impiously resisted his will. They have, as it were, confronted him face to face, rising openly against him and clearly setting their own will against what God wishes.

The synagogue of the Jews too has, in a sense, been brought to its end. It holds views opposed to Christ and fights against the Master's teachings. It does this openly and shamelessly, setting its face against him. It has done and said, so to speak, the most outrageous of all evils. It even nailed him to the tree and slanders the resurrection. They not only killed the Saviour and Redeemer of all. When Christ had risen, they also gave money to Pilate's soldiers to say that he had not come back to life at all, but that his disciples had secretly stolen him away.
And he will gather captives like sand. He will make sport of kings, and tyrants will be his playthings. He will mock every stronghold, heap up earth against it and take it.

The holy prophets had foretold to the people of the Jews, again and again, what would happen to them, and had all but chanted these evils over them like a spell. Yet they slid into such ignorance and such unholy reasoning that they flared up in boldness and anger and raised their brows high. At times they thought they would very easily overcome their enemies by their own numbers. At other times they gathered the surrounding kingdoms to help them, confident that these might hand them victory over the invaders, perhaps without even a battle. They grew careless of their ancestral customs and no longer sought help from God and from above. Instead they went begging, so to speak, for help from the neighbouring nations: now the Egyptians, now the Syrians, and indeed the Tyrians. They rested their hope on these as though on unshakable prosperity, and went on living in luxury and good cheer. Now he explains again that such reasoning was utterly foolish, and that things would not turn out for them that way. For when the Babylonian comes, he says, even if he finds the race of Israel as numerous as the sands, he will still carry the inhabitants of Judea back home as captives of his spear. Even if they have countless defenders, and very valiant ones, he will easily get the better of these too. "And he will make sport of kings, and tyrants will be his playthings." For he carried Jeconiah away to Babylon in chains, along with not a few other local rulers, who became a laughingstock to their captors. He will so lord it over the cities, even the best-fortified, that he will count the capture of each one a mere game. He will also raise siege mounds. In this way he took Tyre, although it stretched far out from the mainland into the sea like an island.

Satan too took Israel captive when it disobeyed Christ. All its leaders became his sport, those who prided themselves on the glory of the priesthood. I think it not unfitting to call them tyrants as well, since they were set over peoples and held great glory and power over them. But they would not have become the playthings of the devil's perversity if they had followed the Saviour's commandments and kept the faith and the sanctification that comes through the Spirit. For then the Saviour of all, who puts every enemy under his feet, would have said to them too: "Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy."
Then he will change his spirit, and pass through, and make propitiation.

The race of Israel will not perish entirely, nor be overlooked forever. A time of prosperity is yet in store for them, and release from their incurable misfortune, when they have been brought back home and the yoke of slavery has been broken off. He lets us understand this when he says that the Lord of all will come to a change of spirit, that is, will reconsider and take a different counsel. We do not mean that God will condemn the counsel he had already formed against them, as though it had not been rightly made at the time. We mean rather that once he has exacted sufficient justice and inflicted punishment in proportion to their offences, he will turn to mercy. He will let his anger pass and will be gracious to those who have suffered. This, I think, is what "he will make propitiation" means.
This is the strength of my God. Are you not from the beginning, O Lord, my holy God? And we shall not die.

God has promised to have compassion on them and has foretold that their gloomy circumstances will change for the better. So the Prophet all but leaps for joy. He says that it belongs to no one else to bring Israel back, to free it from bonds and slavery, and to have mercy on it when it lies crushed. It belongs to God alone, who can accomplish all things with ease, who smooths what is rough and, as it were, levels what is high and steep. Every saint might say to him: "You can do all things, and nothing is impossible for you." Then the Prophet says, "Are you not from the beginning, O Lord, my holy God? And we shall not die." He means: even if Israel has been deceived and carried off into error and strange false worship, you are still the God of all. Long ago too, being holy, you had compassion on those who sinned and preserved them from destruction, and you did not let Israel perish entirely. So there is good hope that it will be saved and that its sorrows will pass, since you have compassion and accomplish things beyond words. The saints rejoiced when they learned of Israel's salvation in the last times, and they offered prayers and raised their voices in thanksgiving and song. So blessed David, foreseeing through the Spirit the gentleness that would be shown to them, and all but seeing them released from the bonds of captivity, sings and says: "You have been gracious, O Lord, to your land; you have turned back the captivity of Jacob. You have forgiven the iniquities of your people; you have covered all their sins."
O Lord, you have appointed him for judgment, and he has formed me to reprove his discipline. Your eye is pure, so that it does not look on evil, and you cannot look upon toils.

These again are the Prophet's words. But it is very unclear whom he means when he says that someone has been appointed by God for judgment. Since we must look closely into the sense of what is said, let us consider the following. Suppose it is said of the king of the Babylonians that he has been appointed by God for judgment. Then we say that he was appointed to carry out the judgment that had gone forth from above against the people of Israel: the devastation, the captivity, the burning of the cities, in short the ravaging of Judea. Suppose instead we apply the meaning to Israel. Then again we say that Israel too has been appointed by God for judgment, and by "for judgment" we mean "for condemnation." Indeed, our Lord Jesus Christ also said somewhere about the Jews, "For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind." By "for judgment" he means "for condemnation." Israel, then, has been condemned for doing wrong, for neglecting the laws, and for grieving the Lord of all in no small measure. "And me," he says, meaning the Prophet, "he formed." That is, he made me and prepared me to reprove the discipline he had decreed against Israel. For the war was brought on Israel as discipline and a scourge. What happened was a form of punishment, not simply an undertaking of the Babylonians. Someone might ask, he says, "Why has the Babylonian been made the punisher?", that is, why has Israel been given over to condemnation and suffering? The answer he will hear is this: the Master's eye is pure. He would never consent to be a spectator of wicked and unholy deeds, nor would he look upon the toils that injustice and greed bring upon the weaker. For he always turns his eye away from those who make a habit of such things. When that happens, terrible things will certainly follow, and whoever suffers that turning away will be in the direst evils. Knowing this, the divine David pleaded: "Do not turn your face away from me, and do not turn aside in anger from your servant." For the effects of wrath will surely follow when God turns away.

Why do you look upon those who despise? Will you keep silent while the ungodly man swallows up the righteous? And will you make human beings like the fish of the sea, and like the creeping things that have no leader?

The Prophet had just declared that the eye of the Godhead is pure. It would never look upon those who do evil, nor look with favour on those who have chosen greed and weave pains for the weaker. At once he is carried away into thoughts something like these. The utterly savage horde of the Babylonians had inflicted countless terrible and grievous evils on the people of the Jews. They had carried their ferocity to such a pitch of cruelty that they did not even spare the divine precincts. Along with Jerusalem they burned the famous temple as well, carried off the ministers of the divine altars together with the common crowd, and profaned the holy things, as it is written. Then, once they were back home, they lived on in good cheer, holding wealth gained by plunder. They paid no penalty for the crimes they had impiously committed. They feared no enemies and no terrors of war. Instead they rose up against everyone, easily mastering whatever they chose, prospering exceedingly, and exulting in the calamities of those who had perished. They counted as grounds for boasting their uncontrolled anger, their unbridled greed, and their supremacy over all.

So the Prophet is astonished to see them spreading themselves in luxury. He now reaches into the divine judgments, trying to inquire into things beyond anyone's search and out of reach of every mind. He prays to learn what reason there could be for such long forbearance on the part of God, who can do all things. Why would God sometimes cast a gentle and kindly eye even on those so used to contempt and so set on living impiously? Why would he keep silent and bear with it when an ungodly man has all but devoured the gentle and righteous? From this, he says, comes the following. Punishment does not follow hard on the heels of offenders; rather, God's wrath has been put off. For that reason the people of the earth have slid into planning, and even attempting, to feed on the weaker as fish do, and to gulp one another down, as it were, with mouths that have no door and are never filled. They lead a life so harsh, unsociable and rough that they differ little from the reptiles in the mountains and in holes. These, because of their great savagery and excessive bitterness, cannot be tamed and do not imitate the ways of other animals. Other animals sometimes graze in herds under one leader who excels and is placed at the head of the herd, and they can be seen moving as if under a general's command. The Babylonians too are unsociable and unapproachable to others, bitter, venomous, full of destruction, swallowing the weaker with gaping jaws.

It is not implausible to think that the Prophet's words were also spoken against the devil and the wicked powers with him. For they are truly despisers. They likewise shake off the fear of God and reach the full measure of every baseness and perversity, although God shows great forbearance. And once we had fallen under them, we wretches devoured one another. For we did not have as our leader the arbiter of peace, that is, Christ, the Lord of earth and heaven and of all things. So we became like fish, utterly irrational and entirely voiceless. There was no word of piety among us, no voice glorifying God. Instead we killed one another and lived the most irrational of lives, going on in the world just like fish. Each one's mind was so bitter that we seemed already to have turned completely into wild beasts. In anger and bitterness we either equalled venomous creatures or were even striving to outdo them.

He has drawn up destruction with a hook, and dragged it in his casting-net, and gathered it in his dragnets. Because of this he will be glad, and his heart will rejoice. Because of this he will sacrifice to his dragnet and burn incense to his casting-net, for by them he has made his portion rich and his food choice. Therefore he will cast his net, and he will not refrain from slaying nations continually.

Having mentioned fish, he lingers on the figure and speaks as if of a seafarer, that is, a fisherman. Fishermen go about their craft in many ways. Sometimes they catch fish with hooks and haul them up leaping from the waves on their lines. Sometimes they fence them in with dragnets and draw them in great numbers, or they cover them with other kinds of nets. When things go well and many have been gathered, they rejoice in their craft and all but sacrifice to their nets, since the nets have provided them with a very rich portion. The Prophet says that Nebuchadnezzar did something of this kind. As if with a hook and dragnets and his casting-net, he surrounded Israel itself and other nations along with it and brought them into his own land. He set them before his own soldiers as a kind of feast and told them to enjoy it, so that the captives became the lot and very rich portion of those who had taken them. This is why he says that perhaps "he will sacrifice to his dragnet and burn incense to his casting-net." That is, he will offer thank-offerings to the forces with which he netted the nations, and Israel besides. And since the business turned out so very successfully for him, he says, he will not hold back from slaying nations, seizing tribes, bringing lands under his rule, and showing no mercy to anyone at all.

Satan too has done this against the whole human race, and especially against Israel. He has caught everyone as if in one net and one dragnet, I mean the net of sin. But he has caught Israel in particular because of its impiety toward Christ. For "his food," it says, "is choice." And the Jews were chosen above all others, even in their way of life. For it says: "When the Most High divided the nations, when he scattered the sons of Adam, he set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God. And his people Jacob became the Lord's portion, Israel the measured lot of his inheritance." Israel, then, was chosen above the others. It was like the firstborn among children. It came from a holy root, I mean that of the fathers. It had the law as its tutor, and it was called to the knowledge of the one who alone is God by nature and in truth. Yet even with such glory and grace, it too was caught along with the others. The others became the devil's portion because they had gone astray. But these knew the One who is God by nature, and yet they impiously killed the Son begotten of him by nature, who had come in human form and in a likeness like ours. For that reason they are bound in his dragnets. And the devil's aim is to destroy utterly everyone on earth and to spare no one. "I will stand at my watch and climb up on a rock, and I will keep watch to see what he will say within me, and what I shall answer when I am reproved." In these words a prophetic mystery is explained to us. The saints have a custom when they wish to learn the things of God and to receive knowledge of what is to come as he sounds into their mind and heart. They remove their mind as far as possible from distractions and cares and every worldly concern. Having kept it at leisure and at rest in this way, they then climb up, as it were, onto some hill or lookout or rock, to contemplate whatever the Lord of knowledge chooses to make plain to them. For he loathes a low and grovelling mind. He looks for hearts that can fly on high and are lifted above earthly affairs and passing desires. For it is written: "For the mighty ones of the earth belong to God; they have been greatly exalted." And again: "The young of the vulture fly to the heights." For the mind of the saints has moved far away from earthly habits and from things of a more earthly kind. "I will stand, then, at my watch," he says. That is: I will again practise my usual, habitual watchfulness. I will purify my mind and free it from worldly care. I will fly up as if onto a rock, that is, to a most steadfast and, as it were, lofty security of thought. Once there, I will look out with the mind as if from a mountain peak to see what words may come to me from God. I will also see what I myself should say if God wishes to reprove me for speaking rashly when I said: "Why do you look upon those who despise? Will you keep silent while the ungodly man swallows up the righteous?"

And the Lord answered me and said: Write the vision plainly on a tablet, so that whoever reads it may pursue it. For the vision is still for an appointed time, and it will rise at the end, and not in vain.

He orders that the vision, that is, the revelation of what is to come, be committed to writing. For the matter is worth hearing and is among the most marvellous things of all. And writings raised to such distinction tend always to be honoured with long and unending remembrance. "Write the vision, then, O Prophet," he says, "so that people in later times may know what was foretold. When they come upon your words, let them pursue them," that is, let them desire to understand their meaning, "and so believe that the prediction will certainly come true."
