For the vision is for appointed times, that is, it is subject to postponement and delay, and a short time will pass in between. Yet it will come to fulfilment in truth, before long, and not in vain. For the Truth will never speak falsely, and nothing it has said could ever prove empty or vain.
If he delays, wait for him, for the one who is coming will come and will not tarry. If he draws back, my soul takes no pleasure in him. But the righteous shall live by faith.

He names no one clearly, but says, "Wait for him." That is: expect him even if he delays, and do not let your hope in him falter. Keep it firm and well grounded, even if some length of time passes in between. It seems, then, that the God of all sounded into the Prophet's mind and revealed to him in a mystery that the one foretold would certainly come. But he told him to wait for him because of the interval of delay, as I said just now. For if the one who has believed shows any drawing back or hesitation, "I would take no pleasure in him," he says. I would see him held fast by the charges against his soul, and I would not pardon such a person. Instead I will count him faithless and hateful. But whoever bears witness to the truth of my words will surely have a share in life. This is the reward of those who honour God, a fine payment for their goodwill. As far as the historical sense goes, it was Cyrus son of Cambyses of whom he says, "If he delays, wait for him." For he did indeed take Babylon, and laid waste the other cities along with it.

As for the mystical sense and the spiritual interpretation, I would say that the meaning of these words may fittingly be understood of Christ, the Saviour of all. For he is "the one who is, who was, and who is coming," and the words of the holy prophets foretold that he would be present in due time. The sacred writing also clearly foretold that when he came he would overthrow the devil's power and drive the unholy and profane horde of demons away from their rapacious rule over us. And the actual outcome of events will come forward as its own witness. But the prediction was "for an appointed time." For the Only-begotten shone forth in the last days of the present age. Whoever drew back and most foolishly rejected faith in him offended God and was left without a taste of the heavenly good things. He was driven out from the holy company of the saints, as the prophet says: "like the wild tamarisk in the desert, which will not see when good things come." But whoever rises above hesitation and drawing back, and makes love and faith toward him dwell in mind and heart, receives a recompense for that disposition. As a choice reward he receives endless life, the putting away of offences, and sanctification through the Spirit. For we have been justified "not by works of the law," as it is written, but through faith in Christ. And "the law brings about wrath," for it summons transgressors to judgment; but grace removes wrath by cancelling the charges.
But the conceited and contemptuous man, the boaster, will accomplish nothing.

Having announced beforehand that the one foretold would come at the appointed times, to put an end to gloom and free the broken from every hardship, he now turns to the one who had laid waste and had inflicted on them all every kind of inhumanity and beastlike savagery. Historically, the profane enemy of God, Nebuchadnezzar, is meant here; in the spiritual sense, again, Satan. He calls him arrogant, contemptuous and boastful, and very fittingly. For this is his nature, whether one takes the force of the words to refer to Satan himself or applies them to the Babylonian. By “arrogant” he means one who is full of conceit or else a fool; by “contemptuous” and “boastful,” again, one who out of enormous haughtiness and empty puffing-up will not so much as consider the incomparable supremacy of God, who is able to do all things. Such a man, he says, “shall accomplish nothing”: the outcome of his affairs will certainly not turn out as he intends; he will not revel forever, nor grow ever greater, nor live in shining glory. And what blessed David said in his psalm is true: “I saw the ungodly exalted beyond measure and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was not; and I sought him, and his place was not found.” For pride always slides toward humiliation, while a measured mind is crowned with the highest honours. The Savior's disciple assures us of this when he writes, “Let the lowly brother boast in his exaltation, and the rich in his humiliation, because like the flower of the grass he will pass away.”
“He has enlarged his soul like Hades, and he is like death, never satisfied; and he will gather to himself all the nations and receive to himself all the peoples.”

God agrees with the Prophet and shows that he speaks the truth, setting the seal of truth by his own words on the charges against both the devil and Nebuchadnezzar. For the Prophet said, “He drew up the whole with a hook, and dragged it in his net, and gathered it in his dragnets”; but the God of all raises the charges to a still greater and truer level and now compares him to Hades and to death. For death and Hades are insatiable things. And it is true that, as far as the Babylonian was concerned, all the nations would have been gathered under him. Such evils may fittingly be understood as charges against Persian ambition too. For to them the whole world under heaven was small, and all the races of mankind would not have sufficed to be their slaves.

The inventor of sin himself, that is, Satan, would also be found guilty, since he strives to bring practically the whole earth under himself and, like Hades, swallows down those who perish through his perversities. He himself said somewhere, “I will seize the whole world in my hand like a nest, and I will take it up like abandoned eggs, and there is no one who will escape me or contradict me.” For the beast is insatiable and untamed and full of boastfulness, truly vile and a hater of mankind.

“Shall not all these take up a parable against him, and a riddle to tell about him? And they will say, ‘Woe to him who multiplies for himself what is not his own—how long?—and who makes his collar heavy, heavily.’”

He has clearly declared that his power is not unshakable, nor will he forever revel in the multitude of those he has gathered; rather, he will certainly slip from rule and glory, and once fallen he will become a song on the lips of many. For he said that they would take up a parable about him, that is, a riddle and a popular saying on the tongues of many. And what is it? “Woe to him who multiplies for himself what is not his own and makes his collar heavy, heavily”—that is, who keeps making the punishment for his impieties ever more burdensome upon himself, destroying nations and sweeping up whole countries, constantly pouncing on those who have nothing to do with him, forcibly subjecting them to his own sceptre, and holding countless peoples in his grasp. In the middle he has exclaimed, “How long?”, showing him to be insatiable in greed, unbridled in cruelty, and not hating to set a limit to his injustice. The tyrants of Babylon were indeed insatiable, terrible in cruelty, and accustomed to daring the most shameful things of all.

Satan too is like this, always gathering what is not his own and laying an ever heavier punishment on himself. It was said to him somewhere, “Just as a garment soaked in blood will not be clean, so neither will you be clean, because you have destroyed my land and killed my people; you shall not remain for all time.” For what peoples has he not destroyed? Or what nations has he spared? What of the most abominable things would he not be found to have dared? The “woe” will therefore justly follow him, and he will become a parable, once his rule is overthrown and his greed against all is banished. The wise Jeremiah hints at this again, saying of him, “The partridge called out; it gathered what it did not hatch, making its wealth without judgment; in the middle of its days they will abandon it, and at its end it will be a fool.” This happened historically. The Babylonian captured Judea, and Samaria as well, and uprooting other countries along with them, he carried them off to his own land. But when Cyrus marched the Persians and Medes against the land of the Babylonians, those who had been gathered departed again; those who had been held in the bonds of captivity all but flew home. So too those from the nations have abandoned their service under the devil, and leaving desolate the one who long ago called them and summoned them to himself, they have run to Christ. For he gathered what was not his own, but Christ received what is his own. For as God he is Lord of all.
“For suddenly those who bite him will rise up, and those who plot against you will wake from their stupor, and you will be plunder for them.”

He says that unexpectedly there will rise up against him those who, as it were, bite and devour him and consume his power with the assaults of war. These were, of course, Cyrus and the Persians, Medes and Elamites with him, who, as though shaking sleep from their eyes and sobering up from drunkenness, will at last overcome their old fears, take up battle against him, and overrun him completely. Then, plotting against him in many ways, they will easily overcome him, plundering the property of the Chaldeans and pillaging the land of the Babylonians. We will find that the accursed Satan has suffered this too. For he gathered all the nations to himself, spreading out the net of polytheistic error and entangling them in the snares of sin. But those who bite him have risen up, that is, the heralds of the gospel's divine commands, tearing his body as if with teeth—his body being, of course, those who have chosen to think as he does. For just as “he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit,” so he who is joined to the devil is one body with him. Those who plot against him, then, will wake up. For understanding that he has now been placed under the feet of the saints, since Christ clearly says, “Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy,” they will seize those who think as he does and easily bring them over to the knowledge of the truth, teaching them who is God by nature and in truth, and expounding the mystery of Christ, who is seen to have been the first to plunder him. We can hear him saying, “Or how can anyone enter the strong man's house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man? And then he will plunder his goods.” As soon as he was born of the holy Virgin, he began to plunder his goods. For the Magi came from the East, “saying, ‘Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? For we have seen his star in the East and have come to worship him.’” And indeed they worshipped him, honoured him with gifts, and became the first fruits of the church of the Gentiles; and though they were the devil's vessels, and of all his members by far the most prized, they ran to Christ. That he was going to plunder the strong man's goods, the prophet Isaiah also foretold enigmatically, for he said this about him: “For before the child knows how to call father or mother, the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria before the king of the Assyrians.” The sense of the passage seems to hint at an historical event, for Samaria had been laid waste both by the king of Damascus and by the ruler of the Assyrians. Yet it also suggests a spiritual mystery: the prophetic word has indicated to us that the Savior's power will easily despoil those who had laid waste his people. “Because you have despoiled many nations, all the remaining peoples will despoil you, because of the blood of men and the ungodliness of the land and of the city and of all who dwell in it.”

The saying is true, whichever of the two it is again taken to refer to. The Babylonian laid waste many nations; Satan did the same. Therefore they have suffered being caught in the same [?]: the affairs of the Chaldeans were laid waste by Cyrus, and Satan by the saints. The charges against both are equal, their offences akin, and their savagery and cruelty toward all, as it were, of one family. For they destroyed countries and cities, the one in the flesh, the other spiritually, using sin as a sharp dart. And he says very aptly that all the remaining peoples will despoil him: since the Babylonian had destroyed nearly everyone, he says that those who managed to escape will become his bitterest enemies and, though few, will easily overpower him, since God grants them victory and allows them to succeed in everything. The matter would be understood as true even if it is applied to the enemy of all, I mean Satan. For he seized and laid waste all who are on the earth and bound them under the yoke of sin. But he himself was plundered by the remaining peoples, that is, by those justified in faith through Christ and sanctified in the Spirit. For the remnant of Israel has been saved, and the divine disciples, who came from them, became the first fruits of those who plundered the accursed one. Then after them, even now, those who lead the peoples [?] continue to plunder him, rightly dividing the word of truth and bringing those who were under his yoke onto the path of godliness.

“O he who covets an evil covetousness for his house, to set his nest on high, to be drawn out of the hand of evils! You have devised shame for your house; you have finished off many peoples, and your soul has sinned.” The word rebukes the Babylonian again, who wanted to build up his own empire out of greed against all, raising his house on high and habitually gilding it and fortifying it strongly with excesses beyond all measure, so as perhaps to be readily able to be drawn out of the hand of evils, that is, always to escape whatever misfortunes might befall him. For the Babylonians always aimed to surround themselves with great numbers of defenders and to have countless men skilled in tactics and equipped in the art of war, so that they could without effort repel the harm coming from those who attacked them. But he showed that the affair would turn to his shame and disgrace, his hope collapsing into its opposite, by saying, “You have devised shame for your house.” You have finished off, that is, brought to an end, many peoples, destroying them utterly. And since your soul has sinned, you will pay a bitter penalty: you who were once splendid and set your nest on high will unexpectedly be found pitiable, cast down and under the feet of your enemies.

The saying would also especially fit Satan himself and the inventors of heresies, who, overcome by love of power and of seeming to lead many, have finished off many peoples and have truly procured an evil covetousness for their own houses. They have set their nests on high, “uttering swelling words of vanity” and belching out against the divine glory things that would suit only their own tongues and minds. Their souls have therefore sinned, for they have committed outrage against the Savior of all himself, Christ, “by sinning against the brethren and wounding their weak conscience,” as it is written.
“For the stone will cry out from the wall, and the beetle from the wood will utter them.”

Holy Scripture often gives voices even to things lifeless and without sense, not as though they could perhaps say anything, but as though the facts themselves all but cry aloud. So blessed Isaiah says, “Be ashamed, Sidon, said the sea”; and David, “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands.” For creation itself, by the very things for which it is admired as well made, proclaims the glory of its Maker. So the voices lie in the facts, even if no words are spoken. You will understand something of this kind here too. He says that a stone from the wall and a beetle from the wood will cry out against the Babylonian. How so, we shall explain. When the Babylonian invaded the cities of Judea, and others as well, he burned down all the houses in them. Then, inevitably, stones were shattered and walls shaken down, and along with them fell timbers and roofs which, from their great age, harboured little beetles, that is, woodworms. In this way, he says, the ruins will cry out against his cruelty. These, as I said, were stones scattered about and lying in the middle of the streets, and timbers half-burned, which by their worm-eaten state bore witness to the antiquity of the cities. So it is a charge against the Babylonian that he burned down cities so old and ancient and demolished houses, after killing, of course, those who lived in them.

It should be noted that instead of “beetle,” other translators have rendered it “a tie-beam of wood.” From this one may conclude that perhaps in those times they called the girders of houses and the interlacing or joining of the timbers in them “beetles,” because they hold up the roof laid on them as if on many feet.
“Woe to him who builds a city with blood and establishes a city in iniquities! These things are not from the Lord Almighty; and many peoples have perished in fire, and many nations have lost heart.”

He bewails the Babylonian again, because he strove to raise high his own glory and the splendour of his empire, not from the things he ought to have, but from those he least should have. For he ought not to have been famous for destroying many peoples, but rather to have adorned himself with a different kind of ornament and to be seen shining with the glories of righteousness. But he dismissed this as useless and ordered his city with blood and iniquities. That the empire of the Chaldeans was most cruel, pouncing like a beast on absolutely every city and country and committing evils beyond all words, would be plain to all who have read the divine Scripture. “But these things are not from the Lord Almighty.” For no, it is impossible to say that evils of this kind came from above; nor could priding oneself on such things be thought a gift of God. They will therefore not stand firm, or rather they will not escape punishment. For what the divine and pure Mind cannot praise, it certainly punishes as unfitting. For how is it not utterly abominable and unholy that many peoples should perish in fire and many nations lose heart—that is, that splendid cities should be burned down together with their inhabitants, and whole nations and tribes give up in their misfortunes?

One might fittingly apply this also to the leaders of the Jews, who killed all the holy prophets and yet thought they were doing Jerusalem no small service, building it with blood and with greed against all. Some they insulted, some they killed, some they stoned, and last of all they added the Son to the others; and the law was their pretext for this madness. For they pretended to be distressed that the commandment given through Moses was being set aside by Christ. But that their zeal was hateful to God and “not according to knowledge,” as the divine Paul writes, the Prophet would easily show when he says, “These things are not from the Lord Almighty.” Therefore they perished in fire and lost heart, consumed by war and wasted by famine. For such things befell the people of the Jews, who had committed outrage against the Son and, as I said, had killed the prophets before him.
“For the whole earth has been filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord, as abundant water covers the seas.”

Holy Scripture is often indifferent to tenses and presents future events as though already completed. We shall find this happening here too: where it should have said “will be filled,” it says “has been filled.” So when the divine wrath has been hurled upon Babylon and everything in it has been brought about through Cyrus and those with him, and the city once so formidable and unbreakable, which always roused its harsh cruelty against others, now appears pitiable and powerless, utterly desolate and under the feet of its enemies, then, yes then, the whole world under heaven will understand how great and how vast the glory of God is, and will be filled with the knowledge of it. For the empire of the Chaldeans held sway and was thus conspicuous, terrible and invincible, because God was patient and allowed it even to conquer Judea and to uproot countless cities. But when he decided to bring upon it the evils it deserved, it was shaken, it fell, and it was given over to desolation. The prophet Jeremiah says something similar about it: “How has the hammer of the whole earth been broken and shattered! How has Babylon become a ruin among the nations! They will set upon you, and you will be taken, Babylon, and you will not know it; you were found and seized, because you opposed the Lord. The Lord has opened his treasury and brought out the weapons of his wrath, for the Lord God has work to do in the land of the Chaldeans, because her times have come.”

It should be noted that after the sack of Jerusalem Christ passed over to the nations, and the whole world under heaven came to know the glory of God the Father, that is, Christ himself, flooding the earth like a torrent. For Christ turned toward them like a river, he who long ago said through the voice of the prophet, “Behold, I turn toward them like a river of peace, and like a torrent flooding the glory of the nations.” For when Israel once made the calf in the wilderness and thereby offended God, he promised the manifestation of the Savior and the abundance of the grace that comes through him, saying, “But as I live, and as my name lives, the glory of the Lord shall fill the whole earth.” For all things are full of Christ, who is the glory of the Father. That is why he also said, “I have glorified you on the earth; I have finished the work you gave me to do.”
“O he who gives his neighbour a muddy overthrow to drink and makes him drunk, so that he may look upon their caves! Drink your fill of dishonour instead of glory.”

Again he exclaims “O” over the unholy outrages of Nebuchadnezzar, foretelling what he will suffer and signifying by this that the blow will be full. He seems to call “muddy overthrow” undiluted grief or torment, which he, as it were, gave his captives to drink, making them appear little different from those overcome by wine and drunkenness. And what follows from this? As though opening a cave, he made each person's mind plain to everyone else. For, as I said, by inflicting bitter torments on the more distinguished of his captives, or perhaps even on kings themselves, he made them lament and, as if under unbearable compulsion, lay bare the faint-heartedness or cowardice that had sometimes lain hidden. And he was so harsh and hard-hearted that, when he ought to have grieved and pitied them, he gloated over their wailing and made it a boast of his own empire. This, I think, is what it means to give one's neighbour a muddy overthrow to drink so that he may look upon their [?], that is, the things hidden and secretly present in some people. Since, then, he gave free rein to his rage and, with all mercy cast aside, plunged small and great, illustrious and obscure alike into incurable calamities, the Lord of all therefore says, “Drink your fill of dishonour instead of glory”; that is, you were indeed famous, renowned and conspicuous to people everywhere, and most notorious for your cruelty; but now you will be dishonoured, and you will endure a punishment equal to the height of your renown.

If one wished, one might also say that this is true of the unholy Pharisees. For they gave their neighbour a muddy overthrow to drink; and this, we say, is their teaching, the commandments of men, and in addition their madness against Christ and the charges of their unbridled tongues. For he was calling people to life, but they slid into such madness as to say to his hearers, “He has a demon and is mad; why do you listen to him?” They did this so that, shaking off the word of salvation that illuminates the mind, people might look upon their caves, that is, upon their dark, lightless and dead teachings. Therefore they have drunk their fill of dishonour, though they were once illustrious and had attained no small glory. For they led flocks, and were priests and judges.

Such a saying would also fit the inventors of unholy doctrines, who truly give their neighbour a foul overturning to drink, pouring the poison of deceit into the souls of simpler people, so that they may look upon their caves. For their mind is dark, full of deceit, truly crammed with diabolical mist, and differs in nothing, I think, from caves, which are full of dead bodies and of every stench and uncleanness.

To explain what has been said more precisely, I think we should also mention this. The Hebrews say (and again the account comes from tradition) that after Nebuchadnezzar had ravaged Judea and all the other lands, and had carried off the leaders of the nations to his own country, he held drinking parties from time to time. Then he would bring in the captives, make them thoroughly drunk with elaborate drinks, and have them dance; and as they reeled and fell and were stripped, sometimes even exposing the hidden parts of the body, he would smile and make the spectacle his amusement and an occasion for good cheer. They say that these things are aptly called "caves", and the explanation is somewhat plausible. For the other translators have rendered "nakedness" in place of "caves", so that the saying runs like this: "Woe to him who gives his neighbour a foul overturning to drink and makes him drunk, so that he may look upon their nakedness."
And you, heart, be shaken and quake! The cup of the Lord's right hand has come around to you, and dishonour has gathered upon your glory.
For the impiety done to Lebanon will cover you, and the misery of wild beasts will terrify you, because of human blood and the impieties of the land and of the city and of all who dwell in it.

Somehow there is always present in the souls of the arrogant, and seen to be terribly ingrained in them, a very great insensibility of mind, and besides this the belief that they will hold their share of prosperity unshaken; they shake off, as it were, quite generally, any expectation at all that affairs will ever take a turn for the worse. Such is what is said through the voice of David, as if spoken by those living in comfort and luxury: "But I said in my prosperity, I shall never be moved." Since, then, the Babylonian's insensibility came from very great arrogance, the prophet all but rebukes him now as unyielding, saying, And you, heart, be shaken; that is, do not think you are set firm in unshakable prosperity. Admit at last thoughts of what brings grief, become aware of what is going to happen, and yield to experience, even though before it you did not deign, so to speak, to grasp even in bare thought that you too would one day be in gloomy circumstances, and that your heart would fall into things apt to cause no small distress. What, then, is it that shakes it and drives it into grief? The cup of the Lord's right hand has come around to you, and dishonour has gathered upon your glory. For as you yourself gave your neighbour a foul overturning to drink, in the same way, having drunk what divine wrath will bring upon you, you will be loathsome, dishonoured by all, pitiable and cast off, and utterly fallen from that former glory. By saying that the cup is of the Lord's right hand, the blessed prophet persuades us, as it were, to understand that it could not possibly go undrunk when God himself presents it. For he had by all means to endure what came from wrath: "For if he shuts a man in, who will open?" as it is written; and as the prophet says, "His uplifted hand, who will turn it back?" Why these things will happen, he makes clear when he says, For the impiety done to Lebanon will cover you, and the misery of wild beasts will terrify you. Now Lebanon is a mountain of Phoenicia, one of the most conspicuous, well wooded and fragrant, since it bears frankincense. Holy Scripture sometimes compares Jerusalem to it, because it is adorned with many holy heads, raised on high, minding the things in heaven, and steeped in the beauty of piety. Blessed David also recalls these, speaking thus to God: "The cedars of Lebanon which you planted; there the sparrows will make their nests." For each of the saints, as I said just now, is lifted on high like a cedar, because he refuses to mind what is cast down, that is, the things on earth; and he becomes a kind of shelter for others, receiving like sparrows those who wish to be taught under him. Therefore, since the Chaldean sacked Jerusalem, and acted impiously and offended God by burning the divine temple together with the city, and was found to have outraged even the holy things themselves, for this reason he says that the impiety done to Lebanon, the impiety committed against it, will cover him. By Lebanon, as I said, he means either Judea or Jerusalem; but one might perhaps think it is the temple itself, which had great fragrance and was crowned with the heads of the priests as with cedars. In what way the impiety committed against Lebanon was to cover him, he showed by adding, For the misery of wild beasts will terrify you. Here again he seems to call wild beasts the Persians and Medes armed alongside Cyrus, as being very savage and whetted to cruelty. And that God does not punish without cause, but brings penalties matching whatever someone has done, he taught by adding, Because of human blood and the impieties of the city and of all who dwell in it.

Each of the Pharisees, too, who became the inventors and contrivers of the madness against Christ, will hear: And you, heart, be shaken and quake. For the cup of the Lord's right hand has come around upon them [?], and dishonour has gathered upon their glory. They have drained the wrath that befell them as a cup of destruction, and have become dishonoured and as far as can be from all glory. For they too acted impiously against Lebanon. By Lebanon you will understand the Church, the truly fragrant one, the conspicuous mountain, best known to people everywhere. They persecuted the Church after the Saviour's cross. Therefore they were terrified as if by wild beasts, by those who ravaged them; and having become guilty of much blood, that of the holy prophets, they added to it also the blood of those who believed in our Lord Jesus Christ, whose firstfruits was blessed Stephen, shown to be the first offering, as it were the firstfruits, of the holy martyrs.
What does a carved image profit, that they carved it? He fashioned it as a molten image, a false appearance, because the one who fashioned it has trusted in his own handiwork, to make dumb idols.

The arrangement of the passage, then, is as follows: "For what does the carved image profit," it says, "that they carved it? And what does the one who fashioned it gain from his handiwork, that he has trusted in it?" But what, again, is the prophet's purpose? We shall explain as best we can. When Cyrus and the Medes had invaded the land of the Babylonians and war had been declared on every side, the magi, doing what was customary for them, called on their falsely named gods to help the endangered city, and offered sacrifices and libations to senseless things, placing their whole hope of being saved in them. But those things were nonsense and trickery, deceit and empty counsel, and nothing else; for the city was taken and sacked, though it had never imagined it would suffer this. So the God of all laughs to scorn the reasoning of those who had gone astray, and their hope in lifeless things. For what does the carved image profit, he says, since it is nothing other than a false appearance with nothing true in it? For how, or on what grounds, could divine power at all be believed to belong to things molded by human hands? It is futile, then, to trust in them, and the thing is truly laughable to those who have a sound mind and an alert understanding. Someone, however, thinks to unfold the sense of the passage in another way as well. Having taken the cities and laid waste, so to speak, all the lands, the Babylonian veered without restraint toward haughtiness and unbridled conduct; he was sick at last with arrogance, and the wretch, placing God's glory on his own head, had a golden image made, just as the divine prophet Daniel has written. Then he commanded tribes and tongues to worship it, and for those who would not do so the penalty was death. What profit, then, came of this? Tell me, he says. For he who thought himself even a god has now finally reached the limit of every evil and has fallen into calamities beyond words.

Woe to him who says to the wood, "Sober up, wake up!" and to the stone, "Be lifted up!" And it is an illusion; it is a plating of gold and silver, and there is no breath at all in it. But the Lord is in his holy temple; let all the earth revere him and stand in awe before him.

Again, as I said just now, the sense of the passage follows on. He rightly calls wretched those who have gone astray, who have abandoned the one God, who is God by nature and in truth, and have run off the road of reverence toward him, and rush to destruction, crying out to wood, "Sober up, wake up," and saying most foolishly to stone, "Be lifted up." For it is the custom of those who have gone astray, if some fear terrifies them, to kindle altars, open sanctuaries, and cry out to lifeless idols, "Have mercy, save us! Be lifted up, you too, O stone, and defend as a god those who revere your power and have chosen to worship you." Woe, then, rightly to such people, because, devoted to things made of gold and silver, things that have no breath, they utter words that would surely be better addressed to God, who dwells in heaven and has the city above as his own temple. For he is holy and dwells among the holy, and abides with those who revere him.

So the prophet adds something useful and necessary for us: Let all the earth revere him and stand in awe before him. For those who are truly of sound mind must worship the one God, who is God by nature and in truth. To him every wise person will offer reverence, to him he will bring his supplications, from him he will seek salvation, and him he will confess as Creator, Lord of all, Saviour and Redeemer, all-powerful, all-pure, who transforms the natures of things into whatever he chooses at the proper times, and who directs this whole universe by his own nod.
VOLUME TWO.
The Prayer of the Prophet Habakkuk, with a Song.

Having brought the oracle concerning Babylon to a very fitting close, and having foretold most fully that those who ravaged the holy city and carried Israel off captive would pay a bitter penalty, the prophet moves on, with good occasion, to the mystery of Christ. From the redemption that took place for a single nation, and only in part, he carries the discourse over to the redemption that is for all and most universal, by which the remnant of Israel has been saved, and the whole earth has been saved no less. For Cyrus son of Cambyses released Israel from captivity when he brought down the arrogant and God-hated kingdom—I mean, of course, that of the Chaldeans. But what was done was an image and outline of what has been accomplished through Christ. He found all humanity taken captive, as it were, and toiling under the tyrant's hand—for Satan had in a sense reigned over us through sin—and he set us free from bonds and toil, and releasing us from that strange slavery itself, he brought us back, as it were, to the holy city, the heavenly Jerusalem. For we have become, as it is written, "fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God," and from now on we have enrolled heaven as our homeland. So the prophet, astounded at the power of the mystery, and marveling beyond measure at the ineffable and God-befitting plan of the Only-begotten's coming in the flesh, offers his prayer in the form of a song, surely in keeping with that saying spoken through David: "My tongue will meditate on your righteousness, on your praise all the day long."
Lord, I have heard the report of you and was afraid; Lord, I have considered your works and was amazed.

This saying might be understood, if one should so choose, as addressed to the God and Father of all, as the one who reveals the Son and makes plain the report about him through the Spirit; or it might fittingly be taken as addressed to the incarnate Word himself. If someone should say it was addressed to the Father, we shall understand something like this: "O Master of all," he says, "I am astounded at the revelation given, that is, the report about your Offspring; for the accounts are awe-inspiring and beyond words, and the manner of the dispensation is beyond every mind. And if I direct the keen eye of my heart to look upon the power of your works, the result will be amazement and nothing else." But if the saying looks to the Son, we shall approach it no less in some such way as this: "O Lord and Ruler of all, even though you became flesh, when I received the report about you, that is, the message and revelation, I fell into fear. And I am struck with awe, and quite rightly, at the surpassing greatness of the matter. For I learn that, though you exist in the form of the one who begot you and in equality with him in every respect whatsoever, you will lower yourself into a voluntary self-emptying, and will become a man like us, born of a woman, and will endure the form of a slave, and will acknowledge your own Father as God together with us, and will become obedient 'to the point of death, even death on a cross.' So I have heard the report of you and was afraid; I have considered your works and was amazed. For you proclaimed the good news of sight to the blind, you preached release to captives, you healed the brokenhearted, you turned back what had strayed, you bound up what was broken, you became light to those in darkness, the door and the way to life and sanctification; you became peace, joining together through faith into one people those of the circumcision and those of the Gentiles; you became 'a cornerstone, chosen and precious'; you won the world for God the Father; you freed from sins those who had been taken captive through weakness; you rescued them from the devil's hand; what was a slave was made glorious by the grace of adoption; man, born of earth, has become a citizen of heaven. And besides these things, this too, I think, is worth hearing: you, who give life to all, endured with us the death of the flesh. Yet you became 'the firstborn from the dead' and 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' the first offering of humanity brought back to incorruption. For you came back to life as God, having trampled the harsh and grim beast, that is, death, and you undid the power of that ancient curse. In you and through you there has ceased what was spoken against us: 'You are earth, and to earth you shall return.'"
In the midst of two living creatures you will be known.

This has been interpreted by some in various ways. One said that the Spirit and the Son are called the two living creatures, in the midst of whom God the Father is known. To understand it so is, I think, ignorant and very foolish. For who would dare to say that Life—that is, the Son or the Holy Spirit—is a living creature? Life is rather that which gives life, while a living creature is that which partakes of life from another. It is absurd in another way, too, to think of the Father as being in the middle between the two, since he is named first in the order of the confession of the holy and consubstantial Trinity. And of course we do not say that, because he is placed before the Son and the Spirit in naming, he existed before them—that is nonsense and falsehood. Rather, we hold and believe that he has the Word who came forth from him as co-eternal with him, and that he was what he is not without his own Spirit; as soon as the Father is conceived of as God, there comes along with it immediately the existence of the one by reason of whom he is Father, and of his divine and holy Spirit as well. Since he is, as it were, a kind of source of his own Offspring, he is fittingly named first. How, then, he could be in the middle between the Son and the Spirit, I cannot conceive. But perhaps they will say, plausibly enough, that "the midst" should be understood as a place. But this too is absurd, for the divine is not in a place, since it is neither a quantity nor a body.

Others again have said that the two living creatures are the New and the Old Testament, in the midst of which Christ is known. In such speculations let each go whatever way he likes; but we, having once applied the passage to the person of Christ, will give an exposition of its meaning drawn from the law. Our Lord Jesus Christ, then, became a mercy seat through faith; for this is how the divine Paul too saw fit to think and speak. For through him we have been freed from every charge, and we have the Father gracious and approachable. The wise John will bear witness, saying: "Little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the whole world." Since the things sketched out long ago in riddles were types of what would come to be in truth, come, let us say something to show that the mercy seat made in the holy tabernacle at the Father's command points to the Son. The God of all commanded that an ark be made, and a lampstand, and also a table in the holy tabernacle; then in addition a mercy seat of gold and purple and fine twisted linen and spun scarlet; and this, raised on four pillars, hung over the holy ark. Then two cherubim made of gold stood around the mercy seat on the right and on the left, with their faces turned toward it. This thing was, again, a riddle of the mystery of Christ. For the Word became flesh, though he is God and Lord of all, as having come forth by nature from God the Father. But even though he became flesh, and was set forth by the Father as a mercy seat, he did not cast off what he was, that is, being God; even so he remains in God-befitting authority and glory, and again the powers above stand around him, carrying out the services assigned to them. That is why the cherubim stand around the mercy seat and look toward it continually. For it is the way of the powers above, being holy and all-pure, ever to contemplate the things of God, to look to him, and to be turned continually toward what pleases him and is dear to him. "You will be known, then, O Master," he says, "for who you will be when you have become like us; for that you are a mercy seat you will clearly be known, as from the pattern in the holy tabernacle. For you stand in the midst of two living creatures, that is, the cherubim, and your name is Mercy Seat." And the saying is true; for as Christ himself says: "The Father did not send the Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him." When the years draw near, you will be recognized; when the time is present, you will be shown forth. The law foretold the mystery of Christ in oracles; indeed, the choir of the holy prophets also proclaimed it beforehand. And those who initiate us into the mysteries, usefully comparing what happened and was accomplished at the time of his coming with what was written of him long ago, establish us in various ways more firmly in faith in him; and we shall find that they themselves very often confirmed their own understanding from this source. Such is what is said through the evangelists. For our Lord Jesus Christ drove out of the temple those selling sheep and oxen, and overturned the tables of the money-changers; "and making a whip of cords he drove them all out, saying, Do not make my Father's house a house of trade." And what followed? "His disciples remembered," it says, "that it was written, Zeal for your house will consume me." And when Joseph once supposed that the virgin betrothed to him had been defiled, and wished to dismiss her secretly, "an angel of the Lord appeared," it says, "in a dream, saying, Joseph son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary your wife; for what is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins." Then the evangelist brought in a sacred oracle for full assurance; for he spoke again thus: "All this took place to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet, saying, Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel." And we shall find Emmanuel himself strengthening faith in himself from what had been promised beforehand through the prophets, and asking to be recognized through the very facts, so that those who compared the outcome of events with what had been foretold should have no doubt at all that he himself was the one proclaimed beforehand through the law and the prophets. For some of John's disciples came to him, eager to learn, and said: "John the Baptist has sent us to you, saying, Are you the one who is to come, or should we look for another?" And he, although he could have said, "I am, and no other," persuades them to go back to the ancient prophecy, saying: "Go and report to John what you hear and see: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor have good news preached to them; and blessed is anyone who takes no offense at me." It is certain, then, that, as the prophet says, "when the years draw near you will be recognized," and that Christ was shown forth at the times appointed long ago, according to the will and counsel of God the Father. For in the last times of the age he appeared to us, and was recognized and confessed, just as Nathanael, indeed, cried out before the others, saying: "Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel." He was recognized, then, when the years drew near, that is, at the time of the dispensation in the flesh. And he was recognized by the saints, and by now by the whole world under heaven. For we have come to know the one in the midst of two living creatures, prefigured as a mercy seat in the riddles of the law, that is, Christ.
When my soul is troubled, in wrath you will remember mercy.

Human nature offended the Creator through the transgression in Adam, who held the commandment given him of very little account. Therefore we were troubled and perished, wretched as we were, falling under a curse and a penalty, and we were held fast by death, since God had been provoked to anger. For our forefather Adam, as the root of the race, heard: "You are earth, and to earth you shall return." Yet the Creator did not disregard us forever, but had mercy on us, as God. For even if "death prevailed and swallowed us up," in the prophet's words, yet "God has again taken away every tear from every face; he has taken away the reproach of the people from all the earth." For in Christ the power of death has been abolished, since sin, for which we were reproached, has been done away with. "For the Lord remembered us and had mercy on us," as the divine David sings. For he brought us back to incorruption and life, though we had been troubled, as I said just now, by the divine wrath, so that we suffered the failing of the spirit, that is, the laying aside and loss of the soul; for that is how death works in us. That we were condemned to death for offending God, and saved again by receiving mercy, the blessed David will confirm, saying to the Creator of all: "When you turn away your face they will be troubled, and they will return to their dust. You will send forth your Spirit and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth." For having suffered that turning away because of the transgression in Adam, we returned to the dust from which we were made. But since, in Christ and through Christ, we have again been enriched with the divine Spirit, becoming partakers of his nature, according to the Scriptures, we have been restored to what we were in the beginning, made new, and saved. For it is true, as the divine Paul himself wrote to us, that everything "in Christ is a new creation; the old has passed away; behold, all things have become new." So we were troubled from the beginning, enduring what came from the divine wrath. But since Christ was recognized when the years drew near, and shown forth at the times appointed long ago, God then remembered mercy. For we have been justified not "by works of the law," according to the Scriptures, nor even "by works of righteousness that we have done, but according to his great mercy."
God will come from Teman, and the Holy One from Mount Paran, shaded and thickly wooded.

The meaning of these words admits of a twofold interpretation, and we shall say what can be said about them. Teman is interpreted as "south"; and the wilderness of Paran lies very far to the south, where Mount Horeb is also said to be, the place where Moses presented the Israelites to God as he laid down the laws that define what they must do. So, applying one sense to the passage, we say this: God, he says, will come from Teman, from Mount Paran, that is, Horeb; that is to say, the one who long ago in the wilderness appeared to the fathers on Mount Horeb in the form of fire, the very one who long ago spoke the law, will come and will be seen in the flesh as one of us, in the role of prophet and mediator, just like the divine Moses, to whom God said: "I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers, and I will put my words in his mouth, and he will speak to them everything that I command him." But if someone wishes to approach the text in another way, it may also be taken thus. Teman, as I said, was what they called the southernmost wilderness. Now they say that Bethlehem, where Christ was born, lies in the most southerly parts of Judea; for somewhere it is addressed through the voice of a prophet: "And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrathah, are least among the thousands of Judah; from you shall come forth for me a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel." So God will come from Teman, that is, from Bethlehem in the south. For the one who is God by nature and in truth, the Only-begotten Word of the Father, having become like us, was born of a woman in Bethlehem. And since it is the custom of divine Scripture sometimes to liken the synagogue of the Jews to the more conspicuous among mountains, because it is seen to be thickly covered, as it were, with very many highly renowned men, so here too it compares it to Mount Paran, saying that he will come from a mountain shaded and thickly wooded. He calls the mountain shaded and thickly wooded because of the fathers from whom Christ's genealogy is traced. One can clearly hear the blessed Luke carrying the reckoning of the genealogy back from Joseph to Adam, and Matthew in turn bringing it down in order from David and Abraham, as I said, to Joseph. The synagogue, then, is a mountain thickly wooded and shaded, having produced over time many from whom Christ sprang. For how can anyone doubt that he is from the Jews? He was born of the blood of Abraham and David—according to the flesh, I mean—and he himself says somewhere about himself: "For salvation is from the Jews."
His excellence covered the heavens, and the earth is full of his praise.

For the Only-begotten Word of God became a mercy seat through faith for those on earth when he appeared like us and in the form of a slave, that is, as a man. For this reason he seemed in some way to be inferior even to the holy angels and to fall short of their glory; but he was again supreme, as God. The most wise Paul will confirm this, saying: "But we see Jesus, who for a little while was made lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death." For since he became "obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross," therefore, as the same apostle wrote again, "God highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father." So then the prophet [?] says, "His excellence covered the heavens, and the earth is full of his praise." For those who dwell in the holy city and live in the dwellings above "are all ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation"; but he is seated on the thrones of the Godhead. To none of them has God the Father said, "You are my Son"; but him he acknowledges as Son and names Beloved, and has him seated beside him, hymned and worshiped together with him. For the divine Paul again said of him: "And again, when he brings the firstborn into the world, he says, Let all God's angels worship him." So even though he became a mercy seat, having come down into humanity for us and on our behalf, he is no less God, and above all creation, visible, I mean, and invisible. For thus his excellence covers the heavens, and the earth too will be full of his praise. This the holy seraphim themselves clearly cried aloud as they stand around his divine throne and with their acclamations give him full honor as Lord of hosts and God of all; for they declare that heaven and earth are full of his glory. But if anyone wishes to say that Christ's excellence is so great and surpassing as to cover the very heavens, if it were conceived of as a measurable magnitude, that will be a plausible interpretation. For the blessed David too said somewhere: "Lord, your mercy is in heaven, and your truth reaches to the clouds," signifying the loftiness of his goodness and the surpassing greatness of his truth as if by bodily and spatial quantity.
And his brightness will be like light.

That the mercy seat through faith, that is, Christ, would come to give light to those in darkness may be made clear also through the voice of the holy prophets. For one said: "Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, and the rest who inhabit the coast, Galilee of the Gentiles: the people who sat in darkness have seen a great light." And another: "Shine, shine, Jerusalem, for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you." And God the Father himself bore witness, saying thus: "For Zion's sake I will not keep silent, and for Jerusalem's sake I will not rest, until my righteousness goes forth like light, and my salvation burns like a torch." For Christ is righteousness and salvation, "who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption," according to the Scriptures. So Christ was shown forth to us like a torch to those walking in darkness, freeing us through the teaching of the gospel from that ancient mist which the enemy of all cast over our minds, so that he would not let us behold the one who is God by nature and in truth, nor look upon the path of godliness and life. The brightness, then, that Christ showed us will be like light—that is, not dim or feeble, as was, of course, that given through Moses (for the law is in riddles and shadows), but like light that is pure and unmixed with mist, penetrating mind and heart, flashing its spiritual radiance upon us and making the ray of genuine knowledge dwell within us.
Horns are in his hands.

In the divinely inspired Scriptures the horn is always taken to mean either kingship and power, or arrogance. The blessed David teaches this, saying: "I said to the lawless, Do not act lawlessly, and to the sinners, Do not lift up your horn; do not lift up your horn on high, and do not speak injustice against God." For some, "uttering arrogant words of vanity," as it is written, speak injustice against God, falsifying the correctness of the doctrines about him, or insulting him in some other way.

But the horn signifies power when it is said of God the Father, who revealed the Son to us: "He has raised up a horn of salvation for us," and again, "His horn shall be exalted in glory." And everything accomplished so wondrously in the power of Christ is indeed glorious. So the Only-begotten came in a form like ours, and insofar as he came into flesh and humanity, he bore the appearance of our weakness. Yet as God he held all the horns in his hands, that is, the kingdoms, over the whole power of the opposing forces. When we say "in his hands," we mean "in his authority." Indeed, we have been taught to say to God in our prayers, "My lots are in your hands." Every diabolical power has been made subject to Christ, and so have the horns, that is, the tyrannies of the unclean spirits over cities and countries, for they had divided the whole earth among themselves. Who could doubt this? Some of them he drove out of people with authority, while others came to him "and begged him not to order them to depart into the abyss." That is what is written by the holy evangelists. And we shall see without any effort that he also drove away from his tyranny over us the very overseer of the unclean spirits, that is, Satan, since Christ himself says, "Now is the judgment of this world; now the ruler of this world will be cast out. And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself." So even though he became man, he still holds in his hands, that is, in his authority, the tyrannies or kingdoms, or rather powers, of the opposing forces. But someone may prefer to take it more simply: Christ has horns in his hands, that is, a strength that cannot be fought or overcome, which easily gores whichever enemies it chooses and readily ravages them, leaping on them irresistibly like a young bull. Such a reader too will understand it rightly.
And he established a mighty love of his strength.

Christ came to accomplish two things. The first was to destroy the adversaries, who had led astray the whole world under heaven. They had robbed God the Creator by stealing the glory that befits him alone and fastening it on their own heads. The second was to save those who had been deceived and who had suffered a rapacity that was truly hard to escape. He taught that the adversaries' power is gone and utterly destroyed by saying, "horns in his hands," meaning horns that overthrow their dominions and, as it were, gore their arrogance to pieces. And he goes on to show that he would save us by saying, "He established a mighty love of his strength." For we have been saved "not by works of righteousness that we ourselves have done," and not by boasting in the law, since the law made no one perfect. We have been saved by the gentleness of God the Father, who made the Son's love for us mighty, that is, strong and great. "For God the Father so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life." So we have been saved by the love of God the Father, and also by the love of the Son himself, who endured death for us. He came to life again, it is true, but he abolished the dominion of corruption and took our sin away from us. That is why he said, "No one has greater love than this, to lay down one's life for one's friends." Truly mighty, then, is the love of the strength of God the Father, through which we have been rescued from death and sin and the rapacity of the devil.
The word will go before his face.

He says that the announcement of him will walk ahead of him, the report about him will fly on ahead, and there will be much talk about him. No sooner was Christ born of the holy Virgin than the Magi came straight from the East. By God's providence, the star that appeared so wondrously in the sky all but announced his birth to them. And when, as time went on, he began to perform signs and become a worker of wonders, then "his fame went out," as the evangelist says, "into all Syria." In fact he became famous throughout the whole world under heaven. For who has not known the glory of Christ? What nation or country has remained without hearing of the power within him, or without experiencing it? As he himself said, the gospel has been preached to all the nations, and like the sun, the splendor of his deeds has traveled around the whole earth.
And his feet will go out into the plains.

It is as if he were saying: Nothing is uphill or impossible for him. In every matter he will walk as if on a bare, smooth road. Open plains can be crossed and are easy to travel, while ground that rises into hills is difficult, and horses cannot be driven over it. So everything is easy for Christ. Whatever road he wishes to travel, by which I mean the road of each of his deeds, is entirely free of every difficulty. For what would he not accomplish, and with no toil at all, since he is God by nature and the Lord of hosts? So the prophet uses a comparison with people travelling over plains to make clear the spiritual sense of these events. But someone may wish to understand the plains as the humble in heart, who are also called "a desirable land" and "God's field," since they receive the seed from above and from heaven and bear fruit, some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty. Such a reader too will understand it rightly. For the Son goes out as if to cultivate plains like these, just as he himself says in the form of a parable: "The sower went out to sow his seed." David too sings somewhere, "And your plains shall be filled with richness," and he added, "and the valleys shall abound in grain." And he let us know that the valleys too are to be understood spiritually by adding at once, "They will shout, yes, they will sing hymns." Senseless valleys do not sing hymns or cry aloud; spiritual ones do. And on these the divine word from above would settle like dew.
He stood, and the earth was shaken.

In the inspired Scripture, "he stood" can very often be understood of something that has been brought to completion. Someone might say, for example, "this matter stood," or "the account of it stood," meaning that it was settled and done. So too Zipporah, after she had circumcised Moses' child with a sharp stone, said to the destroying angel, "The blood of my child's circumcision has stood." She did not mean that the blood had stopped flowing, but that the work of circumcision had been done and what was required had been accomplished. For whoever is circumcised with the spiritual stone turns death away. That stone is the Spirit of Christ. In the same way Joshua, who succeeded Moses and led the sons of Israel across the Jordan, ordered them to be circumcised with knives of stone, fulfilling the type of circumcision in the Spirit. For just as Christ is called a rock, so his Spirit is called a sharp stone, or a knife of stone. So "stood" also often signifies that something has been fulfilled.

Christ, then, stood. That is, everything concerning him came to completion, and he was seen by those on earth. And the earth was shaken. By "earth" he means the inhabitants of the earth, who were indeed shaken. Come, let us say as best we can how this happened. There were people who once had minds, as it were, unshakably set on doing evil: they were settled in ungodliness, fixed in love of the flesh, and firmly planted in error. These have been shaken and moved, and have been brought over to the knowledge of God and the longing for virtue. In the same way those of Israel's blood have been moved away from worship according to the law by accepting faith in him. They have passed over to choosing to live according to the gospel and to order their lives by the Savior's laws. It becomes clear that being shaken sometimes means a change from one thing to another when blessed David sings and says, "You who are seated on the cherubim, let the earth be shaken." We surely do not claim that he is asking for the earth to be shaken, I mean the earth that lies beneath human feet and is perceived by the senses. Rather, he was seeking for it to change from worse to better.

That is one sense of the passage, but it also admits another, along these lines. "He stood," it says, "and the earth was shaken." The earth underwent two things: it both stood and was shaken. We must make clear what the explanation of each might be. It stood, then. For it was like someone drunk, easily swayed toward any absurdity whatever and, as it were, carried about by every wind; but now it has a firm and settled stance, because Christ has established it. This surely accords with what was said through the voice of Isaiah to the synagogue of the Jews: "Stand up, O Zion." And it was also shaken, as I said before, when it departed from its ancient deception and valued changing toward whatever pleases God. It is truly a paradox that the earth should both stand and be shaken at one and the same time. For it is Christ who makes it settled in every good work and persuades it to practice being shaken from worse to better.
He looked, and nations melted; the mountains were shattered by force.

God's looking on someone sometimes means a regard full of gentleness and love, but at other times a regard full of anger and threat. So he says, "On whom shall I look, if not on the meek and quiet, who trembles at my words?" And the inspired David pleads somewhere in these words: "Look upon me and have mercy on me." But through the voice of Ezekiel he said of someone, "I will set my face against that man, and I will make him a desert and a ruin, and I will cut him off from the midst of my people, and you shall know that I am the Lord." These were the words of one threatening wrath and destruction and the punishment that befits those who provoke him. As soon, then, as Christ looked, that is, turned his eye in anger on certain ones, they at once melted like wax, and the mountains were shattered by force as if fire were burning them up. By "nations" and "mountains" he means the unclean spirits, and those among them who are lofty and exalted and stand above the rest like mountains. But their eminence lies entirely in wickedness, and their superiority in arrogance, or perhaps also in strength, in proportion to the savagery within them. For the demons are arrogant: they even set themselves against God and are eager to fasten on themselves the glory that befits him. But they were shattered by force. For they are crushed by the power of Christ, have come to nothing, and have been placed under the feet of believers. Elsewhere too Satan is called a mountain, when God spoke to him through the prophet's voice, as if addressing Nebuchadnezzar: "Behold, I am against you, O corrupted mountain, which corrupts the whole earth."
The everlasting hills melted.

After alluding in riddles to the wicked and opposing powers, which work against the glory of Christ and turn those on earth toward sin, he had to bring in the leaders of the synagogue of the Jews as well. He calls them hills because they seem to be raised up high and to stand above everyone else, by virtue of their rank in the priestly service and the honor that comes from it. He calls them everlasting because of the perpetuity of their office. For the service of God never ends, since he is glorified at every season and in every age. Even if the force of the worship in shadows and types has ceased, the essence of that service has passed over into something better. For the leaders of the holy churches serve God no less, and offer him the bloodless sacrifice. So the hills are everlasting because the service is perpetual and unceasing. Yet they were shattered along with the spiritual mountains and melted along with the nations. For they set their minds on what pleases the demons and carried out the devil's will, handing over the Author of life to the cross and treating him outrageously in many ways. Therefore they justly suffered the same punishment as the demons. They have been brought down and have fallen, as the prophet says: "The house of Israel has fallen; there is no one to raise it up."
I saw his everlasting ways in place of toils.

The sacred writings sometimes call the divine commandments ways, roads and paths. So it is in what was said through the voice of Jeremiah: "Stand on the roads and ask for the everlasting paths of the Lord, and see which is the good way, and walk in it, and you will find purification for your souls." And also through the voice of blessed David: "I ran the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart." So the hills melted, he says. That is, those among the Jews who had obtained the glory of leadership and had taken on the boasts of the priestly service under the law. For the ways, that is, the commandments of Emmanuel, which clearly means the decrees of the gospel, and the teaching that is incomparably better and clearer than the ancient oracles, they "saw in place of toils." That is, they considered it burdensome and full of sweat. Yet Christ, the Savior of us all, plainly says, "Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is kind and my burden is light." Some also made his ways hard to bear in another way, though through them one could pass easily into eternal life. Our Lord Jesus Christ made clear what the power of the mystical blessing is when he said, "Truly, truly I say to you, unless you [?] of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you." But those who heard such holy words spoke foolishly, saying, "This saying is hard; who can listen to it? How can this man give us his flesh to eat?" And the evangelist bore witness, saying, "After this many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him." Then Christ also asked the disciples themselves whether they too would choose to leave him, saying, "Do you also wish to go away?" But Peter answered, crying out, "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life." They did not see his ways as toils; on the contrary, his word was truly sweet to them and worth hearing. He says that the ways are everlasting. For the saving proclamation of the gospel will never cease. Rather, it will extend throughout the present age and stand for all time. The older commandment of the law, by contrast, has grown old and was not faultless, as the most wise Paul says, and for this reason the second was brought in, which is said to have been enacted "on better promises." And indeed the inspired David cried out beforehand in the Spirit, saying to our Lord Jesus Christ, "Your righteousness is an everlasting righteousness, and your law is truth." For, as I said, the things in shadows have not remained. The types have come to an end, but the things of Christ stand firm and remain unshaken for all time.

The dwellings of the Ethiopians will be terrified, and the tents of the land of Midian. The better stories are always somehow worth hearing, and their message never grows tiresome, even if one tells them again in the same words. He has already described how the opposing powers were brought down into helplessness, and has shown them melting like the nations and indeed being crushed like mountains. Now he compares them again to the foreign peoples who made war on the land of the Jews. These were the Ethiopians to the east and south, who live along the Indian sea, and the Midianites too, who inhabited the neighboring desert. So those who fight against the holy city will be terrified, he says. By the holy city we are to understand the spiritual Zion, which is the Church of Christ. The saints inhabit it, the chosen race, as Israel did of old in type, since the name Israel is interpreted as "a mind that sees God." And Nathanael was admired as "truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit." So the Ethiopians and Midianites, who always wanted to harm the chosen race, that is, Israel, are an image and type, and in them we shall recognize the hordes of demons that oppose the saints. One might also say that idolaters are called Ethiopians in another sense, since their life is carnal, earthly and spent in impurity. Such people are Ethiopians because they do not have the divine light in their minds; they are all but black in heart and darkened in understanding. To them the dragon is said to have been given as food. For David sings somewhere, saying to the God of all, "You crushed the head of the dragon; you gave him as food to the peoples, the Ethiopians." Just as we have made the life-giving Word of God our spiritual and holy food, so too those who love sin and have not known the God who is God by nature all but feed on Satan: they have him in their minds, and think and speak as he does. The Midianites, again, would be, as I said, [?] striking, not pouring out his wrath on waters, not dividing the waves of the sea, not bringing destruction on human beings, but instead killing the murderous dragon himself. He destroyed the sin that was invented by him and came about through him, abolished the dreadful dominion of death, and called everyone to the knowledge of God through the holy apostles. They ran about the whole world under heaven, carrying the name of Christ everywhere, and were admired, and very justly. "O Master," he says, "the deeds that you yourself have performed are well worth hearing, and what you in turn have accomplished far surpasses what was done through Moses. You will not bring your wrath on rivers, and you will not rush against the sea. How could the wonder of your divine authority shine forth in those things? Instead you will mount your horses, and your riding is salvation." And who would the horses be? The blessed disciples, the apostles and evangelists. They were wholly yoked to his divine will, gentle and obedient to the rein, and ready for anything whatever that pleased him, with Christ as their rider and charioteer. One of them is blessed Paul, of whom Christ himself says, "This man is a chosen vessel to me, to carry my name before the nations." And the horses are very swift, travelling around the whole world under heaven. So too "the chariot of God is said to be ten thousandfold, with thousands of those who flourish." For very many, in their own times and after the apostles, have become leaders of peoples. They have bowed the neck of their minds to the Savior's yoke, carried his glory everywhere, rightly handled the word of truth, and made the whole earth ring, as it were, with hoofbeats. And the riding of the horses is salvation. For they did not run in vain, but in order to save cities and countries and nations alike, while Christ overthrew the dominions of the demons. The demons had divided, so to speak, the whole earth among themselves and subjected its inhabitants to their own will. Since the ancient dominions of the demons were about to collapse, he rightly says, "You will surely bend your bow against the scepters." For he will make his attack, as I said just now, not against rivers or seas; rather, he will overturn the scepters of the demons.
The land of rivers will be torn apart; the peoples will see you and be in anguish; scattering the waters of his course.

He again recalls the Savior's achievements. To the other nations against which the bow is bent, or rather will be bent, he says the land of the rivers will also be added. Perhaps he is hinting at the land of the Babylonians, since at that time Mesopotamia, the land between the rivers, was subject to it. So here again visible enemies serve as an image, and through it is signified the multitude of spiritual and invisible enemies against whom the saints wrestle. For the word of the prophets is always somehow hidden. So by the part, Mesopotamia, the land of the Babylonians is signified, and through it, in a riddle, the herd of demons.

Or perhaps the prophetic word is telling us something else as well. For it seems to call Judea "the land of rivers," because a great many prophets arose in it, who watered the nation like rivers and flooded it, as it were, with divine streams. It is about them, I think, that blessed David also says somewhere, "They shall clap their hands together." And indeed God says through Isaiah, "The beasts of the field will bless me, sirens and daughters of ostriches, because I have given water in the wilderness, rivers in a waterless land, to give drink to my race, [?] my people whom I acquired [?] my excellences." Our Lord Jesus Christ has perhaps been named a torrent of delight, and truly is one, and indeed a river too; for he said somewhere about himself through the voice of the saints, "Behold, I turn toward them like a river of peace, and like a torrent flooding the glory of the nations." It has also been said by the voice of David, "The rushing streams of the river [?] the city of God." Nothing prevents the saints themselves from also being called rivers, by their likeness to him, since they have been conformed to him spiritually. For just as he himself is the true light, and yet said to the holy apostles, "You are the light of the world," so too, being himself a river and indeed living water, he grants the saints also the dignity of the same titles. So the land of the spiritual rivers, that is, Judea, refused to drink the living water and did not receive the word of the holy prophets, nor indeed the word given through Moses. For if they had believed Moses, they would have believed Christ, since Moses wrote about him. This land, then, will be split open, that is, it will thirst; for thirsty ground cracks.

So the Prophet marvels, and says, as if with deep feeling: The land that once had many rivers and the most abundant supply of divine gifts will be thirsty and unwatered. But since, he says, O Master, the peoples have seen you appearing spiritually (that is, those from the gentiles who have understood the mystery concerning you), they at once conceived the good in birth pangs and have become fruitful. It would suit them also to say, "Because of the fear of you, Lord, we conceived in the womb, and travailed, and gave birth; we have brought forth the spirit of your salvation upon the earth." For those who have enrolled Emmanuel as their Savior and Redeemer are in labor with the fear of God; every conception of their mind will be a fruit of virtue, and their striving will end in a spirit of salvation. Therefore the peoples will see you and travail, drinking deep of your stream and filled to drunkenness with the streams of the gospel. For they came eagerly to the one who said, "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink." For you were so bountiful and good as to scatter waters even along your journeys, that is, the life-giving word of the gospel teaching. As Matthew says, "Jesus went about all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, and proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every [?] and every sickness among the people." This, I think, is "scattering the waters of his journeys." And that the word of divinely inspired teaching is everywhere called water in the holy Scriptures, how could anyone doubt?
The deep uttered its voice, the height of its display. The sun was lifted up, and the moon stood in its order for light.

He calls the peoples who travailed and have now become fruitful "the deep," showing that they are many and beyond number; for such is the deep. By this same name the multitude of the holy angels has also been called, through the voice of Ezekiel.
