Indeed God said somewhere, as though speaking of the ruler of Tyre but concerning Satan, "When I sent him down to Hades, the deep mourned over him." For when he who was above all and pre-eminent in glory had been brought down and had fallen, he who had even been set among the Cherubim, according to the words of that same prophet, it is not at all unlikely that the spiritual deep, that is, the hosts of the spirits above, grieved deeply, and all but turned gloomy over one who had suffered this and had offended the God of all. So, he says, the deep (that is, the measureless and incomprehensible multitude of those who have believed), and indeed also the height of its display (that is, again, everything in it that is splendid and exalted and adorned with the displays of this world, or empty glories), uttered its voice. For Christ is glorified by every nation of men, and one may see small and great doing this eagerly, the illustrious and the obscure, those more conspicuous than others and those who excel, whether perhaps in renown or in wealth and splendor of life. These things he very rightly called displays, or "the height of display"; for they are nothing to them but appearance, since "All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is like the flower of grass." That the deep uttered its voice, and that small and great honor our Lord Jesus Christ with praises, blessed David will also make clear when he says, "Praise the Lord from the earth, you dragons and all deeps." And having added to these mountains and hills, fruit-bearing trees and all cedars, wild beasts and cattle, creeping things and winged birds, he goes on again, "Rulers and all judges of the earth, young men and maidens, old men with the younger, let them praise the name of the Lord." And our Isaiah also said somewhere about him, "Kings shall see him and shall fear; rulers also, and they shall bow down to him."

He gives, as it were, the reason why the deep, and indeed the height of its display, uttered its voice, adding at once, "The sun was lifted up, and the moon stood in its order for light." Just as we have understood the deep not in its sensible meaning (that would be far too crude) but rather spiritually and intellectually, so now too we will not fix the eye of the mind on the elements, I mean the sun and the moon; rather, passing from them by likeness to higher things, we shall discern the force of the meanings. We say, then, that the sun is the luminous and radiant initiation into the oracles of the gospel, and the moon, in turn, the lesser and dimmer light of the law, which shone, as in night and darkness, in the time before the Advent. For the time in which Christ shone forth is called day: he is the sun of righteousness, the spiritual morning star, rising in the hearts of those who have believed. And indeed the divine David says, "This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it." Now the visible sun, while it is still low and scarcely rising above the earth, holds its light not yet broad and bright but drawn in, as it were, upon itself; yet when it leaps up on high, it sends forth its rays most brilliantly upon all things everywhere. So too the teaching given through Christ, that is, the gospel teaching, was confined at the beginning and unknown to many; but rising, all but like the sun, and climbing little by little to its height, and sending out everywhere the radiance of the knowledge of God, it astonishes the deep, that is, the whole human race. Therefore the deep also uttered its voice: for, as I said, it glorifies Emmanuel, names him God, and confesses him Lord and Redeemer of all.

So the sun was lifted up, and no less the moon too, that is, the law, stood in its order for light. For the teaching given through Moses comes after the gospel teaching, and this is its order, because it is shadow and type. But since Christ is the fulfillment of the law and the prophets, the law also shone forth. For comparing the outcome with what had been foretold through it long ago, we have now come to marvel at the light of the law itself as well, which in many ways elegantly prefigured for us the mystery of Christ. So it stood for light. And Christ himself blesses those who have joined in themselves the teaching of the law together with that of the gospel. For he spoke thus: "Therefore I tell you, every scribe" (that is, one who knows the law) "who has been made a disciple in the kingdom of [?] is like a rich man who brings out of his treasure things new and old."

We shall also accept another meaning for this passage, one that is not [?], as it seems to me, but rather comes close to what is likely. For we say, and quite rightly, that the sun is Emmanuel; for he is so named, and truly is. And by the moon we must take to be meant, by likeness to that element, the Church of God, which shines on those in darkness and gleams, as it were, in the night. So when the sun was lifted up, as the Prophet says (for Christ went up onto the precious cross for us), then the Church from the gentiles also shone forth and stood in its order for light; that is, like a full moon, keeping the order of its own cycle, it became a light to those in darkness, just as I said a moment ago. That it was when Christ was lifted up and endured the cross for the life of all that the Church came into being, he himself will again teach: "Truly, truly, I tell you, unless the grain of wheat falls and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit." And again, "And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself." So the lifting up of the sun signifies either the passion on the cross or the ascent into heaven; for we say that he was lifted up in this sense too.
Your darts shall go forth to the gleam of the lightning of your weapons.

By "darts" he here means the holy apostles and evangelists, who went through all the earth and were sent forth as if from a bow, or from a mighty hand. Of them blessed David also said somewhere, "Like arrows in the hand of a mighty man, so are the sons of those who were shaken off." For the nation of the Jews was shaken off and cast out because of its drunken outrage against Christ, who was calling them to life; but their sons, who were of the blood of Israel, the chosen disciples, became darts and arrows, speeding as if from a most valiant hand and easily piercing through everything they strike, to the death. Such darts are sent, as it were, from the hand of Christ; they lodge in the entrails of [?] and slay the dragon. And indeed blessed David sings somewhere, saying to our Lord Jesus Christ, "Your arrows are sharpened, O mighty one; peoples will fall beneath you; they are in the heart of the king's enemies." So by such darts the hosts of demons are consumed, and they bring destruction on the enemies; but for those who have recognized his appearing and honored it through faith, they serve another purpose. For they leave them wounded with love, like the bride in the Song of Songs who says, "For I am wounded with love."

In another way too they are found to be the gleam of the lightning of his weapons. His weapons may be understood as those which blessed Paul commands us also to fit ourselves with, saying, "Put on the whole armor of God." This is the breastplate of righteousness, the helmet of salvation, the shield of faith, having one's feet shod with the readiness of the gospel of peace, and the sword of the Spirit. Such, then, are the weapons of Christ: not ones that clothe him, but rather ones given by him to the worthy. And the weapons are bright and, as it were, full of lightning, for virtue is most radiant. So the darts will be for the gleam of the lightning of your weapons. For they themselves will bring to light that the weapons flash like lightning, by teaching those who did not know. To lovers of sin, virtue seems something without beauty and not yet bright; but to those who know her, she is nothing less than lightning, and she makes a man bright and shining and well known to all everywhere. So the divine disciples, having first possessed the lightning of your weapons, will also become its gleam for others. For just as those skilled in the practice of medicine, when they free from their affliction people who have fallen into diseases of the eyes and shrink from the light of the sun's rays, then persuade them to bear the light falling on them, and might quite fittingly be considered to have become a kind of light for them; so too the divine disciples, by admiring and praising the virtues, which are ranked as the weapons of Christ, are found to be for others something like the lightning that is in them, that is, their brilliance.
In threat you will diminish the land, and in wrath you will bring down nations.

By these words the Prophet indicates to us, in a veiled way, the ravaging of the land of the Jews and the destruction of the peoples living in it. For since they would not accept faith in Christ, but rose up against him and killed the Author of life, for this reason they have been given over to desolation. Isaiah foretold this to them, saying, "Woe to the lawless one! Evil will befall him according to his works."
You went forth for the salvation of your people, to save your anointed ones; you cast death upon the heads of the lawless; you raised bonds up to the neck, to the end.

Again he sets out for us, as it were, the whole economy of the incarnation of the Only-begotten. For he saved those who have been justified through faith, anointed with the Holy Spirit, and shown to be partakers of his divine nature; but he allowed those who chose to disobey to waste away in their sins. To them he said plainly, "Truly, truly, I tell you, unless you believe that I am he, you will die in your sins." So, he says, you went forth like one advancing against the troops of the enemy and armed according to the law of war. And the aim of your going forth was to save your anointed ones (clearly those anointed with the Holy Spirit, about whom he gave command long ago through the prophets, saying, "Do not touch my anointed ones, and do my prophets no harm"), but to prepare death for the lawless, which they themselves would be found to have poured out upon their own heads by refusing the faith that justifies. Therefore they are bound with unbreakable bonds and tied fast with the cords of their own offenses; and not partially, but as it were through the whole body, right up to the neck.

If the bonds should be said to be Christ's, let no one be troubled. For things that befall people by God's permission are always, in a way, said to be his doing, as in the saying, "There is no evil in a city that the Lord has not done." For he does not himself cause the [?], but rather often permits it to befall cities that sin. But if the bonds spoken of here should perhaps be understood as belonging to those who are praised, we say this again: death has been cast upon the heads of the lawless, but the God of all, as it were, binds to himself with bonds of love those who come to him, who are justified by faith and sanctified in the Spirit. This is surely in keeping with what was said by the voice of the prophet concerning those of the blood of Israel: "And I bound the feet of Ephraim; I took him up on my [?] them with the bonds of my love." And the bond up to the neck is to be understood here as the docility of those who have bowed the neck of their mind to him and have taken upon themselves the truly kind yoke of our Savior.

You cut off the heads of the mighty in ecstasy; they will be shaken in it. The word "ecstasy" is understood in various ways in divinely inspired Scripture. Sometimes it signifies astonishment, as when it is said, perhaps concerning the sins of those of Israel, "Heaven stood aghast at this," and again, "Astonishment and horrors have come about on the earth." At other times it signifies the departure from an earthly mind into a divine and spiritual state of character and life. Indeed the divine Paul writes to some and says, "For if we are beside ourselves, it is for God; if we are of sound mind, it is for you." And just as we say that the turning from what is more shameful to what is better is an ecstasy beloved by God, so too we maintain that the change from what is useful to what is more shameful is an ecstasy that is base and discredited.

So he says that you cut off the heads of the mighty, who had fallen into this kind of ecstasy. He means the heads of the leaders of Israel, surely the scribes and Pharisees and those who served as priests under the law. For they truly departed from right thinking and good sense and from love toward God, not accepting the Son, but rather killing him, even though they knew and said, "This is the heir." What the manner of this cutting off is to be understood as, the divine David will fittingly make clear, saying to God, the Savior of all, "Divide them in their life." For Israel was the "portion" of God and "the measured lot of his inheritance." But since they committed outrage against the Son in their unholiness, the beloved became an outcast and was divided off; he slipped away from the hope of those who have believed, disinherited and cast aside, put out of his presence, in second place, behind the gentiles, who say of themselves, "We are blessed by the Lord who made heaven and earth," and "God is the Lord, and he has shone upon us." So Israel was cut off, and having fallen from the blessing, became no longer God's portion, but rather a portion of the devil, utterly dishonored and profane. Then concerning the ecstasy he says that "they will be shaken in it," that is, they will fall. For what is quaking and tottering is close to falling. And the prophet also laments over them as utterly ruined in many ways, saying, "The house of Israel has fallen; there is none to raise it up."
They will open their bridles, like a poor man eating in secret.

The difficulty of both the construction and the wording of this passage is very great; but we will speak as best we can, distinguishing the force of the meanings with great care. Having described the state into which the heads of the mighty must surely come (that is, those appointed to lead the synagogue of the Jews), he passes at once to the holy apostles, who at first stood in great fear of their persecutors. For they were scourged in councils and ordered to speak to no one in the name of Christ; and gathering secretly they made supplication to God, saying, "For [?] there were gathered together in this city against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the gentiles and the peoples of Israel. And now, Lord, [?] their threats" (clearly those of the [?]), "and grant to your servants to speak your [?] with all boldness." So those who were all but held tight by fear as by a bridle and forced to keep silent, who were scourged and afflicted, who spoke to a few secretly and with difficulty, and were like a poor man eating, will open their bridles. It is as if he said: they will surely be set free into the boldness that is dearest and most fitting to them. For they will take no thought at all of the synagogue of the Jews; but, spurning the threats and all but bursting the bridle thrown over them, like proud and high-spirited horses, they will from then on neigh aloud with no one to check them, and fill the whole world under heaven with their voice. The divine Isaiah also says something of this kind to those who perform the sacred service of the gospel proclamation: "Upon a high mountain [?], you who bring good news to Zion; lift up your voice with strength, you who bring good news to Jerusalem; lift it up, do not [?]: Behold our God! Behold, the Lord comes with strength, and his arm with dominion." So, he says, those who were formerly like a poor man eating in secret, that is, who had no boldness, who were fed secretly and with difficulty on the faith of those who believed, will open their bridles for joy, in the manner already described. And that the faith of those being saved is a kind of food both for God and for the saints, Christ himself confirms when he says about the conversion of the Samaritans, "I have food to eat that you do not know about." And again, "My food is to do the will of him who sent me, and to accomplish his work."
And you mounted your horses into the sea, troubling many waters.

Again the passage has kept to the same figure of speech. For having spoken of bridles, he called the holy Apostles horses, on whom Christ himself rides, having settled, as it were, in their mind and heart. He is trying to teach that they would lead to faith not only those from Israel but also the vast and measureless multitude of the other nations. For he likens the world to the sea, as is sung in the Psalms: "This is the sea, great and wide; there are creeping things beyond number." And by many waters he means the herds of the nations throughout the whole earth; and by horses, as I said, the holy Apostles, who, traveling through all the world under heaven, troubled to good purpose the idolaters, who were all but snoring and lying at ease in their error. For they alarmed them, summoning them to fear as people who would go to punishment and suffer the penalty of fire unless they chose to repent and acknowledge the one who is God by nature and in truth. Indeed the divine Paul, speaking to the Athenians, and having called them more [?] than all others, alarmed them not a little when he added this: "So God, having overlooked the times of ignorance, now commands all people everywhere to repent, because he has set a day on which he will judge the [?] world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed, having [?] assurance to all by raising him from the dead." So the troubled water is the multitude throughout the world. It is sometimes likened to waters, and quite fittingly, since human life resembles the sea: great is the turmoil of affairs in it, and the surging and motion up and down and in every direction. And the troubled water is "many" in comparison with Israel; for they were one nation, while these are beyond all number.

I kept watch, and my heart was terrified at the sound of the prayer of my lips; trembling entered into my bones, and my frame was shaken beneath me. I will rest in the day of my affliction, so that I may go up to the people of my sojourning.

The holy prophets were in the habit of calling it a "watch" or a "hearing" when they turned the attention of heart and mind inward, as the Holy Spirit sounded within them the knowledge of things to come. So the same Habakkuk says, "I will stand at my watch, and climb up on a rock, and look out to see what he will say in me, and what I shall answer when I am reproved." Another prophet says, "I heard a report from the Lord, and he sent out a message to the nations." David says the same: "I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me." The Prophet hints at something of this kind here too with "I kept watch, and my heart was terrified." I paid close attention, he says, to the force of what was said, and then I was terribly frightened at the sound of the prayer of my lips. He was making his supplication to God in song, and his prophecy took the form of a melody. But his aim and his mind were not on the rhythm of what he was singing. Instead he was bitterly grieved and badly afraid, because the Spirit was making plain to him what would happen to Israel in the last times. In all likelihood, what disturbed him most and filled him with dread was perhaps this one thing: that he might be caught among these evils and see his people crushed. He might see death cast upon the heads of the lawless, and those heads split open in amazement and shaken by it, in the sense already explained. Then he learned that the vision was for appointed times and that what had been foretold was put off far into the future. As if he were finally recovering from utter despondency, he says, "I will rest in my day, so that I may go up to the people of my sojourning." I will not be caught up in such evils, he says, and I will not be found in this life when the time comes in which these evils will certainly befall Israel. I will go from here and depart to the people who were sojourners in this life, as I am myself. All the saints are sojourners and strangers in this world. That is why they say, "Here we have no lasting city, but we seek the city that is to come." And David sings to the God of all, "Spare me, for I am a sojourner on the earth and a stranger, as my fathers were." The aim of the saints is therefore admirable. They can hardly bear even to look on the things by which God is provoked, and they have trained themselves to think departure from this world sweeter than life itself if we do not uphold what serves the glory of God. Indeed the inspired Paul said that to depart and be with Christ is better. That is true for those who have reached such a frame of mind that they count life in the body as a sojourning.

For the fig tree will not bear fruit, and there will be no produce on the vines. The olive will fail in its work, and the fields [?] no food. The sheep have failed for lack of food, and there are no [?] oxen at the mangers, from their healing.

It is as though someone had asked him why he thought it so important to depart this life, or rather to go up to the people of his sojourning. In reply he describes, in very obscure terms, how the Synagogue of the Jews will be done away with, and he almost seems to lament the barrenness that will come upon it. He signifies it to us in many ways. He says it will be a fig tree that yields no fruit at all. The Savior himself called it this when he said in a parable, "A man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard." Since it was barren, he said that it must [?] so that it would not use up the soil. He also cursed the fig tree outside Jerusalem. Not finding [?] on it, he said, "May no fruit ever come from you again."

He also likens it to a vine with no clusters on it. For again, as the prophet Isaiah says, "The vineyard of the Lord of hosts [?] the man of Judah, beloved [?]." But "he fenced it, put a hedge around it, built a tower in it, and dug a winepress, and he waited for it to produce grapes, [?] thorns." That is why, David says, "a boar from the forest ravaged it, and a solitary wild beast fed on it." He pulled down "its hedge, and all who pass along the road have plucked its fruit."

The olive also failed in its work. Again, this means the Synagogue of the Jews. The prophet Jeremiah refers to it in the same way when he says, "A beautiful olive tree, well shaded in appearance: so the Lord called your name. At the sound of its circumcision a fire was kindled on it; great is the affliction upon you; its branches [?]; and the Lord of hosts who planted you has pronounced evil against you." As the Prophet says, its work failed: though they were trained for Christ by the law and the prophets, they did not accept the faith. For this reason it was cut down, and its branches fell. In their place the branches from the wild olive were grafted in, that is, those from the nations, and they "have come to share in the root and the richness" of the cultivated olive.

Then he says that the fields will produce no food. Here again, I think, he likens Israel to ruined crops, from which the farmer could not gather even enough to eat. That would be clear proof of the most extreme barrenness. They would suffer a famine of divine teaching and fall into the worst of all evils. He made this clear by adding that the sheep have failed for lack of food, that is, because they have none, and that the oxen do not low at the manger. This signifies that the sacred and chosen class among them has failed completely, namely the tribe of Levi. Like oxen, the Levites threshed the spiritual threshing floor. They stripped the word given through the all-wise Moses of its coverings of obscurity and set it before the others like grain to be understood, as a kind of spiritual food. They themselves were at the mangers, feeding on the people's offerings: tithes, firstfruits and thank offerings. So the sheep have failed for lack of food, and the oxen, that is, the leaders and teachers of the people, are no longer at the mangers. That is why the inspired Paul applies "You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain" to teachers, clearly interpreting for us what is in the law. He also says that the oxen have failed from their healing. The saying is obscure, but again I think it means this. They foolishly rejected healing from Christ, even though he strengthens the weak and justifies the ungodly. For this reason they have failed, that is, they have grown utterly weak and come to nothing. It is a dreadful thing, then, to offend God, and it leads to the most extreme barrenness. We too will lack spiritual food, and from then on we will be in a state worse than any evil.
But I will exult in the Lord; I will rejoice in God my Savior. The Lord God is my strength, and he will set my feet firm to the end. He sets me on the heights, so that I may conquer by his song.

Here, then, either the Prophet himself is plainly brought in speaking these words, or one might say that they are the words of those justified by faith. These make Christ their delight and rejoice in him. They record that he is the one who supplies the strength within them, and they say that in him they can do all things. So indeed the inspired Paul says, "I can do all things in Christ who strengthens me." And the blessed David sings somewhere, "For you are the boast of their strength." They also expect to be richly endowed by him, and by him alone, with steadfastness in godliness. That is surely all that "He will set my feet firm to the end" means. Indeed the Hebrew version has "safety" in place of "the end." And what else could feet set in safety indicate to us but, as I said, steadfastness in godliness, unshaken virtue, and a firm footing in faith and in love for Christ? The life of those justified in Christ is not lowly or groveling on the ground. It [?] every earthly and fleshly thing and has its dwelling on high. He shows this by saying, "He sets me on the heights." The glories of the gospel way of life are truly lofty in the sight of God.
We will prevail over those who oppose us and prove stronger than our enemies as we glorify him. He persuades us of this when he says, "so that I may conquer by his song."
By Cyril
BY THE ARCHBISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA
AN EXPOSITION IN THE FORM OF A COMMENTARY
ON THE PROPHET ZEPHANIAH.
BOOK ONE.
The word of the Lord which came to Zephaniah son of Cushi, son of Gedaliah, son of Amariah, son of Hezekiah, in the days of Josiah son of Amon, king of Judah.

The blessed Zephaniah prophesies in Jerusalem. He was not of obscure descent according to the flesh, nor was he one of those whose habit it was to speak falsely and to fabricate divine oracles for their hearers. Of these the inspired Ezekiel said, "Woe to those who prophesy from their own heart and see nothing at all," and indeed the God of all himself said through the voice of Jeremiah, "I did not send the prophets, yet they ran; I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied." No, he was a true prophet, conveying the words from the mouth of the Lord, filled with the Holy Spirit, and pouring forth good things as from the good spring of his heart. For the tongue of the saints does not know how to speak falsely.

The aim of the prophecy is to rebuke the two tribes that were in Jerusalem, Judah, I mean, and Benjamin. For they are charged with having acted impiously, with having wickedly inclined toward the deceptions of idols, and with rushing readily toward anything whatever that is displeasing to God. The time of the reign in which he spoke these things to the offenders has also usefully been added, so that by looking into the state of affairs at that time we may then understand why the divine wrath was stirred against them, and how greatly.

Well then (for I shall relate in turn what will benefit my readers), in his time Hezekiah reigned in Jerusalem, a man as devoted to God as any, a lover of piety, a champion of justice, an enemy of deceit, who cut away the harms of idolatry; for the sacred scripture clearly bears him witness in these things. While he held the royal office in Jerusalem, Sennacherib, the tyrant of the Assyrians, came up, took Samaria, and deported Israel, that is, the ten tribes, to the mountains of the Persians and Medes. And though he also burned a great many cities of the kingdom of Judah, he did not take Jerusalem, because God shielded it. But since the account of this history is plain, we must pass over it.

Then, when Hezekiah died, Manasseh, his son, succeeded to the kingdom. He was so impious that he left no form of wickedness unpractised. It is written of him thus in the Fourth Book of Kingdoms: "And he did what was evil in the eyes of the Lord, according to the abominations of the nations whom the Lord had driven out before the sons of Israel. And he turned back and rebuilt the high places which Hezekiah his father [had torn down], and set up an altar to Baal, and made groves, as Ahab king of Israel had done, and worshipped all the host of heaven and served them. And he built an altar in the house of the Lord, of which he had said, 'In Jerusalem I will put my name.' And he built an altar to all the host of heaven in the two courts of the house of the Lord. And he made his sons pass through fire, and practised divination and augury, and appointed mediums, and multiplied wizards, so as to do evil in the eyes of the Lord and provoke him to anger. And he set the carved image of the grove in the house of which [the Lord] had said to David and to Solomon his son, 'In this house and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, I will put my name there forever.'" Since Manasseh did these unholy things, the God of all was indignant, and quite rightly, and clearly threatened to bring the effects of his wrath upon Jerusalem before long. For again it is written thus: "And the Lord spoke by the hand of his servants the prophets, saying: Because Manasseh king of Judah has done these abominations, evils beyond all that the Amorite did before him, and has made Judah also sin with their idols, [?] thus says the Lord God of Israel: Behold, I am bringing evils upon Jerusalem and Judah, so that both ears of everyone who hears of them shall ring. And I will stretch over Jerusalem the measuring line of Samaria and the plummet of the house of Ahab, and I will wipe Jerusalem clean as an alabaster jar is wiped, wiped and turned upside down before them. And I will thrust away the remnant of my inheritance, and give them into the hands of their enemies, and they shall become plunder and spoil to all their enemies, because they have done evil in my eyes." These things, as I said, God threatened to bring before long upon those who lived in Jerusalem.

When Manasseh had passed away, his son Amon reigned. He fell in no way short of his father in the unholiness of his ways, but rivalled his impieties so closely that he perhaps even surpassed them. When he too died, Josiah reigned. He was Amon's son, but he emulated Hezekiah's love of God and was an excellent follower of his ways. For he pulled down altars and sacred precincts, cleansed the divine temple of the abominations of Manasseh, and commanded the lawful priests to perform the customary rites to the glory of God. Besides this he burned the chariot of the sun and drove out of Jerusalem the false diviners, augurs, tellers of portents, and wizards as well; he slaughtered a great multitude of the temple attendants and burned them on the altars of the idols; and he overturned the altar of the heifers at Bethel, which Jeroboam had made. Since he was so devoted to God and so good, God deferred his wrath and brought none of the things foretold. When Josiah too died, Jehoahaz reigned, whom Pharaoh Necho seized and took prisoner, crowning with the honour of kingship Jeconiah, another son of Josiah. In his reign Nebuchadnezzar marched against Judea; he ravaged the whole country, took Jerusalem, burned the divine temple, and carried Judah and Benjamin off as captives to his own land, together with the sacred vessels. It must also be known that the savagery of the Babylonian crushed and grievously maltreated the cities of the foreigners that lie by the sea, Gaza, I mean, and Ashkelon and others with them, as well as the Idumeans and the Ammonites. For the word of the prophecy mentions this too.

Let everything utterly fail from the face of the earth, says the Lord; let man and beasts fail, let the birds of the sky and the fish of the sea fail; and the ungodly shall grow weak, and I will cut off the lawless from the face of the earth, says the Lord.

Since their land was to be utterly desolate and was very soon to perish together with all who dwelt in it, he frames his prediction here in terms of hyperbole. For surely, if we are of sound mind, we do not say that the God of all lets loose his wrath on irrational animals, on swimming creatures and birds. Rather he persuades his hearers to understand that there will be no sparing of anything at all. Just as when a ship sinks together with its sailors no remnant is left, so, he says, when Judea is taken nothing will be saved: not man, not beast, not bird, not fish. But since it was very likely that there were some in it who lived lawfully and had practised a noble and admirable way of life, he does not want to seem to hurl his wrath at everyone simply and indiscriminately, destroying the righteous with the unrighteous and ruining the pious together with the profane and ungodly. For this reason he makes plain against whom the effects of his wrath would go. For he said, "And the ungodly shall grow weak, and I will cut off the lawless from the face of the earth." They will grow weak as they fall under the enemy's hand, and they are cut off either by dying and becoming the work of the sword, or by being carried off as captives to serve their conquerors.

But if someone should choose to transfer man and beasts and the rest elegantly to moral character and conduct, he will understand by "men" those who live according to the flesh, who have an earthly mind and are absorbed in temporal things, to whom the divine word said, "I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High; but you die like men." For the life of the saints is no longer human, but rather more divine and spiritual, if indeed it is true that they walk in the flesh but do not live according to the flesh, as it is written, but rather have their citizenship in heaven. By "beasts," again, he means those accustomed to live in great ignorance and sluggish of mind, of whom he says through the voice of David, "Man, being in honour, did not understand; he was compared to the senseless beasts and became like them"; and he further commands, saying, "Do not be like horse and mule, which have no understanding." [Birds] we shall take to be those who have an exalted and, as it were, soaring mind, whose intellect has practised being borne aloft and refuses to be led along with the lowly. Such, in a way, is the boaster, wholly caught in the charges of God-hated arrogance. By "fish" you will understand the most irrational multitude, for the kinds of fish are the most voiceless. Such are the many, who are surrounded by the turmoil of life as by a sea, feed on the salty and bitter pleasure of its affairs, and are kept for the nets of death, having destruction as the end of their life. These, then, will fail, as God sends punishment upon them and resolves at last to chastise them for leading a licentious and unrestrained life and not shrinking from provoking him.

And I will stretch out my hand against Judah and against all who dwell in Jerusalem, and I will cut off from this place the names of the Baals and the names of the priests together with the priests, and those who worship the host of heaven on the housetops, and those who swear by their king, and those who turn aside from the Lord, and those who do not seek the Lord, and those who do not [hold fast to] the Lord.

He now makes clear what was said obscurely, and declares plainly that the effects of wrath will befall the tribe of Judah and Jerusalem. For he says that he will stretch out his hand against it, as though seizing and striking it and subjecting the people to those who were expected very soon and who were going to ravage them and carry them away from their native land, caught in the nooses of slavery. He lays bare their offences, saying that the names of Baal will be removed from their midst and that those of the priests will vanish with them. By this he indicates that the multitude of objects of worship among them was great and the forms of their error varied. And by saying that the names of their idols, and indeed of the priests, would be cut off, he aptly hinted that they would be consumed by war and that the peoples of the Jews would be reduced to such a scarcity of men that there would perhaps be no one left to name Baal, that is, able to attend at the precincts of the idols. He says "names" in place of memories, that is, reputations. For so the most wise Solomon interprets it, saying, "A good name is more to be chosen than great riches." Together with the priests and the names of the Baals, he says, those who worship on the housetops will be destroyed; these, again, would be those accustomed to worship the moon and the Bear and the rest of the host of heaven. "I will cut off," he says, likewise "those who swear by their king and those who turn aside from the Lord." For it was the custom of some of those in error to swear by heaven and give free rein to their tongue on it, and with great ostentation to cry out, as it were, "By the king and lord Sun!" Those who chose to do this necessarily also fell savagely away from the love of God, even though the law had clearly declared, "You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve, and by his name you shall swear." And indeed the prophet once bore witness to those of Israel that they kept the commandment given through Moses, and said to God, seeking to turn his wrath away from them, "'The Lord lives,' they say." Those who do not seek the Lord, and take no care to hold fast to him, may reasonably be understood as those who live a wicked and shameful life and have prized a way of life outside the law. For the God of all is sought by us not in a place, but, I think, in deed: through true knowledge that is beyond reproach, through faith and gentleness, and through zeal and eagerness for anything whatever that is holily admired and pleasing to him.

It must be known that these things were also carried out by the very king who reigned in Jerusalem, Josiah, I mean, in whose time the word of the prophecy came. For he too pulled down altars and precincts and handmade idols, and slaughtered the priests, the false diviners and the augurs. But the prophet seems not to be describing present events at all, or speaking about things already done, but rather foretelling that these things will happen in due time. And they were indeed accomplished through Nebuchadnezzar, not because he acted for the glory of God (how could he, or on what grounds, when he even burned the divine temple?), but rather because he destroyed and burned those who worshipped the idols together with the idols themselves.
Be reverent before the face of the Lord God, for the day of the Lord is near, for the Lord has prepared his sacrifice; he has sanctified those he has called.

He usefully weaves exhortation into his threats, and having terrified them with fears, he urges them on toward what is better. He commands them to stand in awe of the God of all (for this, I think, is what "be reverent" means), to hasten to straighten the paths of their life, and to turn without delay to what is dear and pleasing to him. He says they must be seen to be such "before the face of the Lord," in keeping with what was said through the voice of Isaiah: "Wash yourselves, become clean; remove the evils from your souls before my eyes; cease from your evils." For surely it is not the same thing to remove wickedness from human eyes and to remove it before the face of God; the difference between the two is very great. For sometimes a wicked man, whose ways are not good, slips into a semblance of piety and wraps himself in the name of goodness, though in truth he is not so. Indeed Christ says, "Beware of those who come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly are ravenous." Such a man is reverent in the eyes of men, but certainly not in the sight of God. But the man who is truly free of malice before the face of God does not merely put on an outward show of goodness and the appearance of being good; he has rather an undefiled heart, and is indeed seen to be such. For Solomon says somewhere, "For the ways of a man are before the eyes of God, and he watches over all his paths." He calls the time of the capture "the day of the Lord," and says that it is near, so as not to let the more careless suppose and think among themselves that the fulfilment of what was foretold would be long postponed, and that they would escape suffering by reaching the end of their own lives first. For it was the custom of the Jews, when the gloomiest things were foretold, to think and say such things. Indeed God said to the blessed prophet Ezekiel, "Son of man, behold, the house of Israel, the provoking house, keep saying, 'The vision which this man sees is for many days hence, and he prophesies for distant times.' Therefore say to them, Thus says Adonai the Lord: None of my words which I speak shall be delayed any longer; for I will speak a word and do it, says Adonai the Lord." This, I think, is what he is saying now too, affirming that the day of the Lord has drawn near, that his sacrifice has been prepared and those he has called have been sanctified. By "sacrifice" he means the slaughter of the ungodly which will be carried out according to his will; and by "those he has called" he means the Chaldeans, whom he says have been sanctified, not as having become holy, but rather as having been appointed and called by God to burn Judea and, with all mercy set aside, to destroy those in it. The sacred scripture says something of the same kind elsewhere. For the Persians and Medes and those who fought alongside Cyrus had been called against Nineveh, and the God of all said of them, "They are sanctified, and I lead them; giants are coming to fulfil my wrath, rejoicing and insolent alike." So in these passages sanctification would signify neither the putting away of wickedness nor participation in the Holy Spirit, but rather that certain people have been predetermined and assigned to accomplish some such deed.

And it shall be on the day of the Lord's sacrifice that I will take vengeance on the rulers and on the house of the king and on all who are clothed in foreign garments; and I will take vengeance on all openly at the gateways on that day, those who [fill] the house of the Lord their God with ungodliness and deceit.

There are three things through which cities and countries prosper: the kingship, the ranks of authorities under it, and the renowned priesthood. If these are in good order, each as befits it, the affairs beneath them will also go well and the subjects are kept safe. But if they choose to honour the crooked path and rush along it, everything at once goes to ruin and all but reels drunkenly toward destruction. For just as, when pain arises in the head of the body, the other limbs must share its feeling and its sickness, so too, when those who lead have turned to wickedness and are sick with a leaning toward the worse, those yoked beneath them must somehow be ruined along with them. For subjects tend to follow, and be carried along by, the opinions of those who have come to rule. On the day, then, he says, of the sacrifice that pleases God, that is, at the time when the slaughter of those who have committed the most dreadful offences takes place, the effects of wrath will march first upon those who are distinguished above the rest in glory and stand foremost. These are the house of the king; next to it, those set in glory and prominence; and third along with them, the order of those who minister the divine rites, who are more honoured with God than the rest, for they too are rulers and leaders of peoples by virtue of the rank of the priesthood. He sharply blames them as clothed in foreign garments, that is, as having sunk so far into irreligion and contempt for what had been decreed long ago through Moses that they did not even keep the very dress of the priesthood when the occasion called them to perform the sacred rites.

Just as the sons of Aaron were consumed by fire, the charge and indictment against them being that they had placed foreign fire on the altar, so too, I think, those of whom the passage speaks are called to account, because, careless of the decorum proper to them, they did not robe themselves in priestly fashion as the lawgiver had ordained, but dared to perform the sacred rites dressed in foreign garments. This too is proof of the utmost contempt, and of the law's being held of no account among them. How then could one suppose that keeping the law was of any concern to the rest, if the leaders had no regard for it? He says, "I will take vengeance openly at the gateways," and what he means is this. When Israel frequently sinned and would not yield to the words spoken through the prophets, he called them to repentance, correcting them like a father with outward afflictions, and sometimes even touching their bodies. For example, he struck the crops in the field with blight, or sometimes sent down the locust and the grasshopper, or heaped up the caterpillar or what is called mildew; and he also afflicted them "with [?] and with mildew," as the prophet says. In bringing these things at various times, he struck them, as it were, covertly. "But now," he says, "I will take vengeance openly at the gateways"; that is, I will not bring the effects of my wrath covertly. It will not be locust and mildew that come against you, nor bodily sickness, but the enemy's sword, gleaming bare, threatening destruction to those who have been impious toward me, and savagely slaughtering, at the very gateways of the temple, those who fill the house of their God with ungodliness and deceit. What, then, is the ungodliness? And what is the [deceit]? Another prophet will make it clear to us, saying about Jerusalem, "Her leaders judged for bribes and her prophets divined for silver"; and indeed the wise Isaiah addresses her somewhere and says, "Your rulers are disobedient, companions of thieves, loving bribes, chasing after rewards; they do not judge for orphans, and they pay no heed to the widow's cause."

Those who minister at the divine altars must therefore take heed, lest they somehow fall under such indictments. For the men of old received the robe befitting the sacred rites as a type. But since the time of worship in spirit has come, let the bright garment and, as it were, the priestly robe of each of those called to ministry be this: a right and blameless faith, a life according to the Gospel, a dignified and thoroughly lawful conduct, an upright character not overcome by shameful gain, a concern that looks toward virtue and counts what pleases God worthy of all regard.
And it shall be on that day, says the Lord, that there will be a sound of crying from the gate of those who stab, and wailing from the second, and great destruction from the hills.

He clearly describes the calamities of the war, and shows people as it were falling, perishing and lamenting over themselves. He does this so that, overwhelmed by the sheer size of the evils to come, they might choose to change course and hurry to do what is better and more fitting, and so in the end escape the wrath. For the Creator is good, and does not desire "the death of the one who dies so much as that he should turn from his evil way and live," in the words of the prophet Ezekiel. At that time, then, he says, from one gate there will be a terrible and grim outcry: the gate of those who pierce through, that is, of those who slaughter whoever falls into their hands. For when enemies break into a city that is being taken, they always raise some dreadful war-cry. In this way they first break the spirit of those inside with fear, and they spur one another headlong to cruelty. And from the second gate, he says, there will be wailing and tears, as the captured crowd against one another and each hurries to leap out of the city as from a sinking ship. He says there will also be a great crushing from the hills. Perhaps he calls the so-called upper city in Jerusalem, that is, Zion, "hills," or perhaps he means something else. For when war sweeps over a land, the inhabitants always flee to the mountain peaks, thinking that the rough terrain will hinder the enemy and check the charge of those pursuing them. Indeed, our Lord Jesus Christ once said to the crowds of the Jews, "When you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then let those in Judea flee to the mountains."

So when God strikes, and demands punishment for their sins from those who have chosen to despise him, nothing will help the sufferers. No city with the finest towers will help them, nor unshakable circuits of walls, nor lofty mountains and savage rocks, nor trackless wild country. Repentance alone saves. It wins over the Judge, lulls his anger, and readily calls the Creator, who is good by nature, back to the gentleness that befits him. It is better, of course, to refuse with all one's strength to offend him at all. But human nature always leans toward what is bad, and "we all stumble in many ways," since we lack complete steadfastness in virtue. So let us at least strive to correct our own minds by running back to what is better, and by repentance call the Master of all to gentleness, since he is kind by nature, as I said just now.
Lament, you who inhabit the city that has been cut down, for all the people have become like Canaan; all who were exalted by silver have been utterly destroyed.

By these words he signifies that the iron of the Babylonians will spare none, but will utterly destroy everyone throughout all Judea. He has commanded those left in Jerusalem, who managed to escape, to lament for Judea as destroyed, and for the city famed among them, now cut down. This is because all the people in it vied with the ways of the Canaanites and chose to imitate their practices. In this way they made themselves equal to them in everything, so that perhaps they even surpassed them and left them behind. But the Canaanites were foreigners, hated by God, wicked and idolaters, and among the most notorious of all peoples for every kind of outrage. Indeed, in the sacred writings someone is reproached and hears, "Offspring of Canaan, and not of Judah." He further explains that their wealth is useless to them and a rotten prop, for he declares that those exalted by silver will perish. These are the people accustomed to think highly of themselves because of wealth and money, and to raise a haughty brow for that very reason. They were overcome by shameful gain and gaped after it, and so, as he himself says, "they filled the house of their God with ungodliness and deceit." For this reason wealth is justly exposed as powerless and useless, unable to save anyone. "A good name, then, is to be chosen rather than great riches," as it is written; "for treasures will not profit the lawless, but righteousness will deliver from death," and "Truly a small portion with the fear of God is better than great produce with injustice."

And it shall be on that day: I will search Jerusalem with a lamp, and I will take vengeance on the men who are contemptuous of their observances, who say in their hearts, "The Lord will not do good, nor will he do harm."

The enemies were going to rage unrestrained against the captured, and God attributes everything they would do to his own person. He does not mean that he himself is the doer of such monstrous things, but rather that he lets the effects of wrath come justly upon the ungodly. For what Solomon said in a riddle in Proverbs is true: "Not unjustly are nets spread for birds; for those who share in bloodshed store up evils for themselves." They could have gone as far as possible from punishment and penalty by choosing virtue instead of wickedness. Instead they sharpen the wrath against themselves, and anyone who knows how to judge rightly would convict them of casting their own souls into a destruction of their own seeking. Jerusalem, then, is searched with a lamp. For the Jews suffered something of this kind at the hands of the Romans, when Jerusalem was captured by Vespasian and Titus. The historian who lamented the sufferings of the Jews as if with countless mouths relates what happened. After the slaughter in battle and the countless multitude who perished throughout the city, the Romans searched with lamps for those who had leapt down into the caves and underground passages, brought them into the light, and slaughtered them cruelly and savagely. He says that he will take vengeance on them for being contemptuous of their observances. By "observances" he means either the laws laid down for each thing that had to be done, which they impiously transgressed, counting the keeping of them as nothing; or else he means specifically the customs of the priests. For the law required a great deal of careful observance concerning their vestments, their priestly garb, and indeed the sacrifices. They did not bring the victims to the altar in only one way, and anyone who consults the writings of Moses could learn the differences in these matters. But they had no regard for the observances, because they had sunk so far into nonsense and frigid notions that they perhaps even thought, and dared to say, that the God of all takes no account of any of us. They held that he has so neglected earthly affairs that he neither praises the good and grants them rewards worthy of their goodness, nor is roused against sinners and inflicts on them punishments to match their unholy deeds. This, I think, is the meaning of "The Lord will not do good, nor will he do harm." What they were bandying about, then, is a denial of providence and nothing else. The doctrine is so shameful and detestable that it did not please even the wise men of the Greeks. They called the man who introduced it godless; this was Epicurus, one of those famed among them for wisdom. One may therefore say that "the ways of a man are before the eyes of God, and he watches all his paths." He counts those who practice virtue worthy of rewards, but he utterly loathes the wicked, and renders to each according to his work, as it is written. We must therefore run along straight paths and take the road that pleases God, the Master of all. If we live lawfully in this way and practice the life that is truly best, we shall have the Master of all gracious and kindly toward us. We shall not let him grow bitter against us, so long as we renounce what is evil and hurry to correct by repentance the faults of sleep and sloth.
And their strength shall become plunder, and their houses a desolation; and they will build houses and will not [?dwell] in them, and they will plant vineyards and will not drink their wine.

Perhaps now too it will be timely for us to say, "Treasures will not profit the lawless." For wealth is always a runaway and has no stability. Rather, it reels as if drunk, leans toward desertion, and has rotten feet. And to want to think highly of oneself because of it is utterly foolish. It will not rescue in the least those who are under divine wrath, nor would it free anyone from the charges against them when God decrees punishment and brings upon offenders the penalty they deserve. What, then, is wealth? It serves only the flesh. It is the servant of unholy and loathsome pleasure, the father of boastfulness, the root and source of conceit. It procures a share in petty, fleeting glories that slip away from their owners like shadows. For it is true that "All flesh is like grass, and all the glory of man like the flower of grass." He teaches that zeal for wealth is entirely useless to the ungodly when he says that their strength will become plunder for the Chaldeans. For there are, indeed there are, people of whom one might very fittingly say what is sung in the Psalms: "Behold the man who did not make God his helper, but trusted in the abundance of his wealth and grew strong in his vanity." And if they have had houses lavishly adorned, these would not be theirs, for they will be burned. And if besides they have tended vines, they will not drink the wine. How could they? They will be led off as captives, leaving their homes behind, stripped of everything that can bring gladness. God made this clear through the voice of Jeremiah, speaking to one of those who had reigned in Samaria: "You have built yourself a well-proportioned house, airy upper rooms set off with windows, panelled with cedar and painted with vermilion. Will you reign because you were provoked in Ahab your father? They will not eat and will not drink. It would have been better for you to do judgment and good righteousness."

We must therefore desire nothing earthly. We must cast as far from us as possible all delight in temporal things and the pursuit of wealth, which flees and in the time of wrath can do its owners no good. Instead we must make our boast the life in Christ and the glories of an exceptional way of life, and consider nothing better than closeness to God. We must cry out and say, "Lord God of hosts, blessed is the man who hopes in you," and also, "Better is one day in your courts than thousands. I have chosen to be cast aside in the house of my God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners."

For the great day of the Lord is near, near and very swift; the sound of the day of the Lord is bitter and harsh; it has been appointed [?]. That day is a day of wrath, a day of affliction and distress, a day of untimely death and desolation, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and mist, a day of trumpet and outcry against the fortified cities and against the lofty corners.

Again he cuts off the hope of those who might sometimes suppose that the prophecies would be put off for a long time. For he declares that the punishment is, as it were, at the door, and that the calamity of war is running close on their heels. He calls the time when these things will happen the day of the Lord. He also called it swift, since it will come without delay and will be seen before long. He says that its voice is harsh and very mighty, hinting, I think, at the war-cry of the enemies. He calls it a day of wrath and affliction, of desolation and untimely death, of darkness and gloom. For which of these things will not befall those who have reached such a pitch of wretchedness that they find themselves amid the very terrors of death and lie in the depths of misery? When enemies have seized a city, what will not befall the captured? What outrage, however monstrous, is left undone? Are not boys destroyed before they reach manhood, and young girls flung down dead, like plants torn up before their season? Does not despondency, like a night and a darkness, blacken the hearts of the captured, so that they are at a loss for counsel and plans? It all but shrouds each one's mind in mist and clouds, and does not even let them perceive where they are. How then can any of this be in doubt? He adds that the day of the Lord will be a day of trumpet and outcry against the fortified cities and against the lofty corners. By this he shows that the enemy's assault will be unbearable both for populous cities trained in warfare and for others girded with circuits of walls. By "fortified" he means, as I said, cities that are well manned and have a great number of fighting men; and by "lofty corners" he means walled cities. For in the circuit of a wall the corners always rise up and stand as towers, higher than the rest. "It is a fearful thing, then, to fall into the hands of the living God," as it is written. No one at all will stand against him, for he is the Lord of hosts.

And I will afflict the people, and they will walk like the blind, because they have sinned against the Lord; and I will pour out their blood like dust, and their flesh like dung. And their silver and their gold will not be able to deliver them on the day of the Lord's wrath, for by the fire of his jealousy the whole earth will be consumed, because he will bring a full end, and haste, upon all who dwell on the earth.

The sense of the passage is very clear, and would need no explanation, I think. Nevertheless we will speak of it briefly. He threatens them with things beyond every evil, including darkness of mind. And he immediately explains the cause, adding, "because they have sinned against the Lord." It is as if he said: They have behaved outrageously toward their brothers, and they have also recklessly committed impiety against the Master of all himself, and would be convicted of rising up against the divine glory. For it is utterly harsh and unholy to rob the divine glory of its own honors and all but drive it from the thrones of deity, and to set up in its place, as it were, the creation and the forms of irrational beasts. Some offered their worship to heifers; others to some Astarte and Baal-Peor; others to the moon and stars. Therefore he threatens to bring upon them the calamities of war, "a full end and haste." The "full end" would signify the complete destruction of the land of the Jews; the "haste," that what was foretold would happen quickly and without delay. In the sacred writings the word "haste" also often denotes the onset of tumult. It is a very terrible thing, then, to sin against one's brothers. But if anyone's offenses go so far in wickedness that they grieve the ineffable nature itself, nothing will avert the effects of wrath.

It is settled, then, that the God-hated heretics deserve to be lamented. They sharpen their tongue against the Son of God, saying that he is created, and indeed that he holds a lesser rank than the Father. They too, as it were, fashion an idol to suit their own fancy, and command that it be worshiped. For suppose the Son has altogether fallen short of being God by nature and is a created being, and yet he is worshiped both by us and by the holy angels. How then are we not plainly serving the creation, just like the children of the Greeks, who out of folly and vanity of thought fashion an idol in the likeness of the sun or of some other created thing?

Gather together and be bound together, O undisciplined nation, before you become like a flower that passes away in a day, before the wrath of the Lord comes upon you, before the day of the Lord's anger comes upon you.

Having shown very clearly the savagery of the war and the magnitude of the coming calamity, he again turns his discourse, at the right moment, to the need to call them to repentance. Now he could easily persuade them, since they would naturally be afraid. For when the mind has sometimes grown hard and leaned far toward what is more shameful and utterly loathsome, we do not easily accept even the choice to repent; but fear often drives us to it even against our will. He therefore calls them back into close fellowship with himself. We say that they departed and became estranged when they served idols and gave their minds over to their own passions. In the same way, we shall understand them as turning back, as it were, and laying hold again of fellowship with God, when they choose to worship him alone and to follow his decrees. He calls the race of Israel an "undisciplined nation" because it dishonored even the ancient commandment and impiously thrust away the law, which acted as their tutor and could lead them to every kind of goodness. And he threatens again that unless they are bound together to him, in the ways we have just described, they will be no different from the flowers of the fields, which are frail and quick to wither, and will certainly fall under the effects of wrath.

So then, "while we have time, let us do good to all." While the Master, forbearing as God, still gives us room, let us repent and offer supplications. Let us cry out in tears, "Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorance." Let us bind ourselves to him through holiness and sobriety. For in this way we shall be sheltered on the day of wrath, and wash away the stain of our failings before the day of the Lord's anger comes upon us. For he will come, he will surely come in due time from heaven as Judge, and he will render to each according to his work.
Seek the Lord, all you humble of the earth; do judgment and seek righteousness, seek gentleness, and give answer with them, so that you may be sheltered on the day of the Lord's wrath.

He clearly shows how they might be bound to him, loathsome and undisciplined nation though they are. He commands them to seek the Lord, to do judgment and righteousness, and to give answer with them. We seek God, then, by choosing to thirst to do what pleases him, putting away all sloth. We shall do judgment by fulfilling his divine law and achieving virtue without the least hesitation. And in turn we shall gain the glory of righteousness, splendidly crowned with the honors of good deeds, as we travel the glorious and truly blameless road of piety toward God and love toward our brothers. For "love is the fulfilment of the law," as it is written. And to what I have said I think we must add "to give answer with them," that is, to speak to others as well and to admonish our brothers. In this way and no other shall we be complete in virtue. So too our Lord Jesus Christ said that whoever is most approved in deed and in word will be called great in the kingdom of heaven. But he said that whoever makes it his practice to teach and is content with that, without bringing himself also to do what he thinks good and commands others to achieve, will be called least. And somewhere he also pronounces woe on the teachers of the Jews, saying, "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, for you bind heavy burdens, hard to bear, and lay them on people; but you yourselves," he says, "do not touch them even with the tip of your finger." The proof of the most perfect godliness, then, is both to achieve virtue oneself and to teach others the things by which they too may become illustrious.

And the disciple of Christ makes it plain that the labor spent on this is not unrewarded, when he says, "[?] whoever turns a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins." But if anyone thinks that "give answer with them" indicates that we ought to make them the subject of our meditation, let him understand it this way too. For the law of Moses also commanded concerning the oracles of God, "And you shall speak of them when you sit down and when you walk in the marketplace, when you lie down and when you rise up." And David too sings, "And I will meditate on your statutes continually."
For Gaza will be plundered, and Ashkelon will become a desolation, and Ashdod will be cast out at noon, and Ekron will be uprooted.

Here again the word makes a provision: it plainly foretells what was to happen in due time, for the encouragement and comfort of the people of Israel. What this is I will explain. When Jerusalem had been sacked and all Judea taken by Nebuchadnezzar, the foreign cities round about gloated over the sufferers and laughed at the ruined. They even sacrificed to their own gods, as though they had destroyed a race hated by everyone. They dared to say that events themselves had proved it useless for the Jews to trust in God, and they supposed that the hand of the Babylonians had turned out stronger than the help from above and had got the better of it. And if any of the people of Judea left his home and fled his native land in time of war, coming to the neighbouring peoples in the hope of being saved, he found himself in worse straits, having fallen among people crueller than the Babylonians, the very people who ought to have pitied him. So the wretches treated the glory of God with arrogance; they met those who had fared miserably with hardness and without relenting, refusing to share their grief, or rather savagely loading the captives with their own malice besides. What then? Afterwards the people of Israel returned from captivity in due time, Cyrus having at last released them. Once in Jerusalem they rebuilt the walls of the city and raised up the divine temple itself, and now they had some hope at last of prospering, with God as their shield. But when the people of Gaza and Ascalon, and of Azotus too, and those of the place called Ekron, the Moabites, the Idumeans and the Ammonites, and some other nations besides, learned that things were going this way, they were consumed by the flame of envy and wanted to stop them fencing the city with a wall. So they gathered together and marched against those who had been called back from captivity. The battle was joined in the valley of Jehoshaphat, and they fell and were slain, for God strengthened Israel. And Israel took the cities of the nations by force so thoroughly that they reduced them to utter desolation and turned them into folds for flocks. This is the history the prophet recalls here, and it contains a promise, first of the return from captivity, and then of the glory to come and of victory over all. For he says that Gaza will be plundered, that Ascalon will go to destruction, and that Azotus will be cast out at noon. “At noon” means openly and not in the manner of brigands, but plainly and by the law of war. And Ekron, he says, will be uprooted. He frames the threat very aptly to show the meaning of the name, for Ekron means “uprooting.” He says that she will suffer exactly this, as though she carried in her very name the sign of the disaster that was to fall on her.
Woe to you who inhabit the coastland of the sea, sojourners [of the Cretans?]! The word of the Lord is against you, Canaan, land of the foreigners.

Having threatened sufficiently, and foretold what was soon to happen to the inhabitants of Palestine, I mean the people of Gaza and Ascalon, together with those of Azotus and Ekron, he weaves the same discourse against the cities of Phoenicia as well, and above all against those lying by the sea. That is why he says: Woe to you who inhabit the coastland of the sea. But since many of the cities of Palestine also lie by the sea, he sets apart, as it were, the cities he means, and here calls them sojourners of the Cretans, so that we may understand from this the inhabitants of Phoenicia, whom he names sojourners of the Cretans, as I said, for the following reason. The Cretans and the Libyans are separated from each other by the sea that lies between them, but only by a very short distance. For, as the common report goes, when the wind blows, the scent of Cretan herbs sometimes passes across and kills the beasts in Libya, I mean the reptiles and the various kinds of venomous creatures. So the Libyans and the Cretans were reckoned as one nation. From there they sent out a colony at some time and settled and built the cities of Phoenicia, just as the Cappadocians at some time did the cities of Palestine. Indeed God said somewhere through the voice of Amos: “Are you not like sons of the Ethiopians to me, sons of Israel? says the Lord. Did I not bring Israel up out of the land of Egypt, and the foreigners out of Cappadocia, and the Syrians out of the pit?” He calls the Palestinians foreigners, and the Phoenicians Syrians, and he declares that he brought these up out of the pit, calling Libya the pit, I think, because the country is perhaps hollow and low-lying. For the sea beside it spreads out into gulfs, the dry land all but retreating backwards, and the sea running deep into the most southerly regions. It should be noted that in place of “out of the pit” the other translators put “Cyrene,” so that the Phoenicians are shown more clearly to be colonists of the Libyans, for Cyrene is the most famous city of Libya.

So, he says, the word of the Lord is against you, you sojourners of the Cretans, that is, Libyans. By “sojourners” he means colonists and emigrants. And he also calls them Canaan, for all who inhabited the cities of Phoenicia were Canaanites, even if they had originally been colonists of the Cretans. It should be noted, again, that in place of “sojourners of the Cretans” the other translators have rendered: “The word of the Lord is against you, a nation destroyed.” But since it was necessary to follow once more the text of the Seventy, we have brought forward the facts of history, which tradition hands down to us and which the word of the prophet has also sealed as true.
And I will destroy you from your dwelling, and Crete shall be a pasture for flocks and a fold for sheep.

See, once more he addresses them as settlers from elsewhere and speaks to them as emigrants, and so bears witness to the truth of the history. For he says he will destroy them from their dwelling, that is, from the land in which they had settled and to which they had migrated. And he says their cities will come to such desolation that they become a pasture and a fold for flocks. Once again he calls Phoenicia “Crete,” or rather the people in Phoenicia, as being from Crete, the neighbour and borderer of the Libyans. In ancient times they were one, and the races were mingled with each other in blood, customs and laws.

And the coastland of the sea shall belong to the remnant of the house of Judah; on it they shall pasture. In the houses of Ascalon they shall lodge at evening, from before the face of the sons of Judah, because the Lord their God has visited them and turned back their captivity.

I have already said that all the nations, burning with envy, gathered together and marched against Jerusalem after the time of the captivity, and that when battle was joined in the valley of Jehoshaphat, those who were wickedly plotting against the redeemed were defeated and fell. So the people of Israel, having prevailed, grazed their flocks on the fields of the foreigners as on empty land, and used the deserted cities of the Philistines, that is, of the Palestinians, as folds, because everyone in them had been utterly destroyed. So, he says, the coastland of the sea, that is, the cities of the Palestinians by the sea, once so populous, so formidable and hard to overcome, shall be a pasture for flocks for the remnant of the house of Judah. For those who had been saved from captivity and had barely survived were the very ones who prevailed, and they will also lodge at evening in the houses of Ascalon. For towards evening shepherds shut their herds of cattle into the folds. What then is this great power? Or how will this come about, which is beyond all belief and reckoning? Because, he says, the Lord their God has visited them and turned back their captivity. It is as if he said: He has ceased from his anger against them, he has forgiven them their offences, and he takes up arms on the side of Israel as he did long ago, and grants them victory over their opponents, and that without toil.

So whenever God turns away from us because we sin, we shall lie under the feet of our enemies, and there is no one to save or defend us. But if he looks upon us again as people who long for virtue and want to live according to his law, we shall be stronger than any war, and shall very easily triumph over those who oppose us. And he himself will give us assurance, saying of every righteous person: “Because he has hoped in me, I will deliver him; I will shelter him, because he has known my name. He will cry to me and I will hear him; I am with him in affliction; I will rescue him and glorify him. I will fill him with length of days and show him my salvation.”

I have heard the taunts of Moab and the blows of the sons of Ammon, with which they taunted my people and boasted against my borders. Therefore, as I live, says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, Moab shall be like Sodom, and the sons of Ammon like Gomorrah, and Damascus abandoned like a heap on a threshing floor and wiped out for ever; and the remnant of my people shall plunder them, and the remnant of my nation shall inherit them.

When Jerusalem had been sacked and the people of Israel had fared miserably, the neighbouring nations, as I said, mocked them, and supposed that the capture of Judea was the work of their own falsely so-called gods, as though the hand that always helped them from above, plainly the hand of God the ruler of all, had been completely overthrown and had perhaps come to nothing. It is not unlikely that some should reach this degree of folly, since they were in error, had worshipped wood and stones, and did not know the one who is God by nature and in truth. So he says: I have heard the taunts of the Moabites and the blows of the sons of Ammon. For in my view the one who strikes sufferers with taunts, opening wide an unbridled mouth against them and spewing out words that would naturally embitter anyone to despondency and grief, differs in no way from the one who beats them, say, with a stick or a stone, and makes the assault of their misfortune heavier. And since they were convicted of speaking without restraint against the divine and ineffable glory itself, for this reason, he says, they will go to destruction, enduring the punishment of the Sodomites. Their own disasters will perhaps make the sufferings of Gomorrah look small, and only late and with difficulty, through what has happened to them, will they come to know the power of the one who punishes. As for Damascus, the metropolis of the Phoenicians, splendid and famous, where the royal palace was, it will be a heap of straw without an ear of grain, of no account, whose end is burning, or rather scattering. For the gusts of the winds scatter heaps of chaff in every direction, and in the same way the forces of the conquerors scatter in every direction the inhabitants of captured cities, falling on them like the most violent winds. And that these evils would in due time be accomplished not by anyone else but by the very people who had suffered and been taunted, he indicates when he says: The remnant of my people shall plunder them, and the remnant of my nation shall inherit them. For by “remnant of the nation,” as I said before, he means those saved from captivity, who prevailed over the nations, took the cities of the foreigners, and reduced them to utter desolation.

So whenever the God of all, in his providence, trains the Church by exercise, either bringing afflictions on it or permitting persecutions to happen, when its enemies attack it, whether pagans perhaps or unholy heretics, let no one laugh at it, but rather let them wait for the end of the whole contest. For those who sometimes laugh loudly and all but taunt Christ for not defending his own, or, as they suppose, for being too weak to do so, will suffer the fate of the Sodomites and become food for fire; and besides this, they will find that those whom they thought defeated have prevailed.

This shall be theirs in return for their insolence, because they taunted and boasted against the Lord Almighty. The Lord will be made manifest against them, and he will utterly destroy all the gods of the nations of the earth.

This, he says, is their portion and this their lot.
