For the wretches behaved outrageously against the ineffable glory itself, speaking without restraint and uttering blasphemous words, and all but rose up against the one who is beyond all things, showing a terrible and unbridled insolence in doing so. And since they ascribed the glory of being able to do all things to their own gods, the Lord will be made manifest against them, that is, he will show them his own power by destroying all their gods. For their sacred precincts were razed and fell by the hand of Israel, and their handmade idols became the work of fire everywhere and in every nation that was conquered. Where then is the power of the gods? Or how could they save others, when they cannot even defend themselves? Or rather, what at all is deaf and senseless matter? “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands”; and, if it is not offensive to say it, or rather it shall be said: “What is the carved image, that they carved it? They fashioned it as a molten image, a false phantom,” in the words of the prophet. And as the inspired David says: “May all who make them become like them, and all who trust in them.”
And they shall worship him, each from his own place, all the islands of the nations.

We say that the Lord was made manifest against them in destroying all their gods. Long ago this was done through the people of Israel, who along with the cities of the foreigners vigorously burned the images in the precincts and the altars in them. But one may see this happen more truly at the time of the incarnation of the Only-begotten, when the Word, being God, became like us and was made manifest. Indeed, the inspired disciples said that the one who was from the beginning, whom they had heard, [?] they had touched with their hands and seen with their eyes. For he who as God is beyond being seen was made manifest; and David too sings somewhere: “God will come manifestly, our God, and will not keep silent.” And when he was made manifest “and was seen on earth,” as it is written, “and lived among human beings,” then the loathsome and profane herds of idols perished, and the power of the devil was entirely destroyed. And now each of those who through faith in Christ have been brought to the knowledge of the truth offers worship to God the Father through him and with him from his own place. God is no longer known in Judea alone; rather the lands and cities of the nations too, even if they are cut off from Judea by the sea that lies between, come no less to Christ, offer their prayers, raise their doxologies, and honour him with unceasing praises. For long ago “his name was great in Israel,” but now it has become well known to people everywhere, and land and sea are full of his glory. And this, then, was the meaning of: “As I live, says the Lord, surely all the earth shall be filled with the glory of the Lord.” So he says: Each shall worship from his own place. For the law, prefiguring the beauty of the Church, set up for the people of Israel that ancient tabernacle, after whose pattern that famous temple was also built in Jerusalem. And the inspired Moses, or rather God through him, commanded the people of old that those who wished to worship should go up to Jerusalem from the whole land of the Jews and there sacrifice and worship God; and death was the penalty for those who sacrificed outside the temple. But since the time of the shadow has passed and the things in types have ceased, we now know that the divine is not confined to a place, nor does “the Most High dwell in temples made with hands,” but rather fills heaven and earth and what lies beneath. Therefore, believing that he is everywhere and in all things, each person offers worship wherever he happens to be, since he has near him the God who says: “I am a God who draws near, says the Lord, and not a God far off.”

It should be noted that holy Scripture sometimes calls the churches islands, as lying in a sea in this world, surrounded by the bitter waters of its troubles, and all but battered by the most violent waves of persecution, yet firmly grounded without falling, standing high, and not submerged by afflictions. For through Christ the churches are unshakeable, “and the gates of Hades shall not prevail against them.” So if anyone wishes to understand the islands of the nations as the churches from among the nations, he will not stray from the proper aim, since they are washed round by the surges of temptations, yet have their firmness in Christ, to whom be glory and power for ever and ever. Amen.
By the same author: on the same prophet, second volume.
You too, Ethiopians, are the wounded of my [?] sword.

He remembers every race, that is, every nation, that has made war on Israel and babbled against the divine glory. So he passes from the Idumaeans and Ammonites to the Ethiopians. These are either the peoples who lie to the east and south and inhabit the country bordering on the land of the Persians, or the Egyptians, who are neighbours bordering on the people of Israel. For the land of the Egyptians is also a part of Ethiopia, and indeed the sacred writings regularly call the rivers of Egypt rivers of Ethiopia. They too drink of the Gihon, about which Scripture says, “This is the one that encircles the whole land of Ethiopia.” So you too, Ethiopians, will be the wounded of my sword. He calls the sword of the Jews his own, because he himself brings it on those who have acted impiously against his glory, as I said, and also against Israel.

But the divinely inspired Scripture also knows of Ethiopians in a spiritual sense, so let us say something about them as well, without straying from the sense of the passage. The blessed David said somewhere in the Psalms, as if speaking to our Lord Jesus Christ, “You crushed the heads of the dragons upon the water. You shattered the head of the dragon; you gave him as food to the peoples, the Ethiopians.” And elsewhere: “Before him the Ethiopians shall fall down, and his enemies shall lick the dust.” The bride portrayed in the Song of Songs also confesses that she is both black and beautiful. So by Ethiopians we should understand those whose minds are, as it were, dark and without light, who have not yet been illumined and do not have the divine light. Those who fall down before Christ, as the bride does, are made radiant by him, for they have cried out in prayer, “Let the brightness of the Lord our God be upon us.” But those whose impurity is hard to wash away, and who have remained in their blackness, will feast on the heads of the dragon, for the apostate dragon is their food, and they will be subject to the sword. I think, however, that the force of the saying fits the unclean spirits best. Christ has wounded them, casting them out of their tyranny over us, and along with them he has destroyed the father of darkness, the inventor of all sin, who darkens “the minds of the unbelievers, so that the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ may not shine on them.” And this, I think, is what the wise Isaiah himself told us: “And it shall be in that day that God will bring his holy sword, great and strong, upon the dragon, the crooked serpent, upon the dragon, the fleeing serpent, and he will slay the dragon.”

And I will stretch out my hand against the north and destroy the Assyrian, and I will make Nineveh a waterless desolation, like a wilderness. Flocks will graze in her midst, and all the beasts of the earth; chameleons and hedgehogs will make their beds in her panelled ceilings; wild beasts will cry out in her breaches, and ravens in her gateways.

I will lay hold, he says, also of the lands and cities to the east and north. Along with the others I will destroy the Assyrians, and to the cities laid waste I will add the famous Nineveh itself, the capital of the Chaldeans. It will be waterless, on a par with untrodden and uninhabited lands. But here again the text very likely compares the multitude of the inhabitants to waters, for this is customary in the sacred writings. Indeed another of the holy prophets, announcing in advance the attack that the Assyrians made on Jerusalem, said, “Behold, waters are coming from the north, and they will become an overflowing torrent.” So when he says that Nineveh will be waterless, I would say he means that it will be empty of inhabitants. He insists, though, that flocks will graze in her midst, and I think he gives this as a sign of complete desolation, showing that no one lives there. For what grows in the fields does not grow in a town, and if grass should spring up even in a city, that is a plain admission, as it were, that it is entirely empty of people. He adds no small number of other signs too. He says that all the beasts of the earth will lodge in her, and that chameleons and hedgehogs will make their beds in the panelled ceilings. Moreover, in the breaches, that is, in pits or caves, the wild beasts will cry out, and ravens will roost in her gateways. No sensible person doubts that hedgehogs would not lodge in houses, nor wild beasts make their lairs in the middle of a city, nor night-ravens haunt the gateways, unless there were the deepest quiet, which is very pleasing to creatures of that nature. For wild beasts, and the other creatures he speaks of, do not like to live alongside people. How could they? They prefer places where there is great desolation and life is entirely undisturbed, where the very breadth of the wilderness all but guarantees their safety and removes them from all fear.

If something needful must be added to this, let us guard our own hearts and refuse with all our strength to offend God in any way at all, so that we do not become a dwelling place for evil and savage beasts, I mean the unclean spirits, once all virtue has been taken from us. And this, I think, is what was very well and wisely said to Jerusalem through the voice of Jeremiah: “With pain and the whip you will be disciplined, Jerusalem, lest my soul depart from you, lest I make you an untrodden land that will not be inhabited.” For when God removes virtue from us, foul and unholy passions will certainly invade our mind and heart and live there like wild beasts, and the savage horde of unclean spirits will break in along with them.

For her height is a cedar. This is the scornful city that dwells in confidence, that says in her heart, “I am, and there will be no other after me.” How she has become a desolation, a pasture for beasts! Everyone who passes through her will hiss and shake his hands.

Nineveh, which always chose to think great things of itself, is accused of being haughty and boastful. And this was really so. She raised her eyebrow as high as it would go against every nation and every kingdom, and held the strength of others in utterly small account. The prophet Habakkuk also bore witness to this, saying of the king of Assyria, “He will make sport of kings, and tyrants are his playthings, and he will mock every stronghold.” So the prophet again makes plain that the capital of the Chaldeans was exceedingly haughty, lifted high, and had risen to great unbridledness, comparing her to the height of a cedar and calling her scornful. You can learn that this is said rightly and accurately from the words of the Rabshakeh. When he came into Judea and then addressed those on the wall, he babbled against the supreme Glory. For he said, “Thus says the king: Do not let Hezekiah deceive you with words, which will not be able to deliver you, and do not let Hezekiah tell you that God will deliver you.” And a little later: “Have the gods of the nations each delivered their own land from the hand of the king of Assyria?” This, then, is the scornful city, which thinks highly of itself and says, “I am, and there is no other after me.” Since she likes to treat such shameful and accursed arrogance as a splendid ground for boasting, she will sink to such wretchedness that one must say of her, “How you have become a desolation, a pasture for beasts!” The “how” is not that of someone asking and wishing to find out, but rather of someone marvelling at a change beyond all expectation. For great and unexpected calamities are not without wonder; they tend to astonish those who see them or hear of them. So everyone will hiss over her and shake his hands, striking them together, I suppose, and clapping in amazement, and letting out from his mouth the rather inarticulate sound of hissing. With these words he paints for us very well, as it were, the person struck dumb by unexpected disasters.

“God, then, opposes the proud.” And I say that the precept is wise and worth taking to heart: “Do not exalt yourself, lest you fall,” and again, “Whoever makes his own house high seeks destruction.” Buildings that rise to a great height and beyond due measure are somehow more prone to shake, and are under serious suspicion of collapsing on themselves. In the same way a human soul, puffed up into arrogance by the vanity of its thoughts, is unsound, easily overturned and quick to fall. And if this is done against God, then there is nothing at all to hold it up.
O the renowned and redeemed city, the dove!

He passes at once to the remembrance of the city of the Jews, I mean Jerusalem. Because the Assyrians captured her, they have paid the penalty. The other nations too have been punished for mocking the glory of God. But he grieves, as it were, over Jerusalem for suffering what she never expected, and he blames no one else for her irremediable calamity, saying instead that she brought it on herself. So he laments and says, “O the renowned and redeemed city, the dove!”

Why, he says, have you become utterly dishonoured, pitiable and captive? You were so brilliant and conspicuous. You prevailed over every nation and defeated your opponents without effort, always harsh and hard to face for those who wished to march out against you and were armed according to the rules of war. You were redeemed from servitude in Egypt by many signs and wonders, and freed your neck from intolerable greed. For your sake rivers were turned into blood, and hail and darkness ravaged the land of the Egyptians; for you even the sea took up arms and drowned the pursuers; and countless other things worth hearing were done besides. O the city, the dove, that is, the most beautiful! For the divinely inspired Scripture always takes this bird as a figure of beauty. Indeed the bridegroom wished to honour the bride portrayed in the Song with the name of dove, saying, “Arise, come, my companion, my beautiful one, my dove.” Jerusalem was exceedingly beautiful because she was made radiant by the divine law, was seen to be distinguished by the glories of the priesthood, practised righteousness, worshipped the one who is God by nature and performed her services to him. This beauty is spiritual. But you could also understand Jerusalem to be called a dove in another way. It is always the habit of this bird, even if someone carries it very far from its beloved nest and then gives it the chance to fly, to return home again and come back to its own place. We will find that this happened in the case of Jerusalem too. She had piety from her forefathers, yet she went down into Egypt, and there, departing as it were from her ancestral worship, she worshipped idols. But she was called through Moses, and in a way flew away from the error in Egypt, hurrying back to God. But what, he says, was the reason that she was captured at all, and that she who had been redeemed came under the power of others again?
She did not listen to the voice.

She heard God saying on Mount Sinai, “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one Lord. You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor a likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or on the earth below, or in the waters under the earth.” But she ignored what had been proclaimed and foolishly slid into the error of many gods. So she did not listen to the voice, meaning either the voice that came to her on Mount Sinai, or else we may take “voice” to mean admonition.
She did not accept discipline.

She treated with contempt the law that served as her tutor and was leading her to righteousness, and turned to “teachings, the commandments of men.” Following her own opinions, she left the straight path and remained ignorant, with no share in the divine teaching.
She did not trust in the Lord.

When war was pressing hard, the struggle was upon her and dangers hung over her, she ought to have been eager to imitate the piety of her forefathers and to trust only in the God who saves. Instead, as it is written, “she called on Egypt, and they went to the Assyrians,” and she hired Syrians, or Arabs, all but dishonouring the divine power.

And she did not draw near to her God. We draw near to God through all goodness, choosing to accomplish what pleases him. We also draw near in another way, by believing that he alone is by nature and truly God, King and Creator of all, and by accepting no other at all besides him.
Her rulers within her are like roaring lions.

He lists the charges and sets out the reasons why he was rightly moved and inclined to anger, so that he might be seen to be justly punishing those who had acted impiously and had sunk so far into wickedness that the situation had become unbearable even to God himself. Her rulers, then, he says, were like lions. And what do lions do? When hunger sharpens them and drives them to look for food, they range vigorously over mountains and glens, roaring terribly and harshly. If they catch sight of anything fit to eat, they roar at it like thunder and terrify it so much that it seems frozen stiff and, as if bound in [?], waits for the one who will feast on it. Some of the leaders in Israel did the same. They threatened to inflict the death that the law prescribes for transgressors, sometimes even on people who had done nothing wrong, unless they chose to do what pleased and suited them; and those who gave way brought charges against others, or else surrendered their own possessions to the judges themselves [?]. He records such evils of theirs through another prophet as well, namely Micah, saying, “They were devising troubles and working evil on their beds, and at daybreak they carried them out, because they had not lifted up their hands to God. They coveted fields and plundered orphans, they oppressed households, and they plundered a man and his house, a man and his inheritance.”

The inventors of heresies too roar, as it were, at those who have chosen to live in simple faith. Opening their God-hated mouths, they all but devour those who know nothing, making them more ignorant still. They instil cold and twisted notions into them, spin their fables, and persuade them to think whatever seems right to the heretics themselves, so that those caught in their snares seem perhaps to have died outright and to differ little from senseless stones. To such people one might quite rightly cry out, “Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.” But, as the blessed David says, “God will break their teeth in their mouths; the Lord has shattered the jaw-teeth of the lions.”
Her judges are like the wolves of Arabia; they left nothing until morning.

They say that the wolves of Arabia surpass every other beast in savagery, are exceedingly given to an insatiable appetite for food, and are so swift that they easily outrun any pursuer. Through another prophet too he said of the horses from Babylon that they are “swifter than the wolves of Arabia.” So here he takes the greed of wolves as a figure of the judges. With full mouths and insatiable teeth, as it were, they devour those who come before them for judgement, demanding a great deal, even more than people can afford, for perverting justice, so that what the divine law approves is impiously twisted into whatever pleases certain others. It would have been better for them to consider what the author of Proverbs says: “The ways of one who takes gifts in his bosom do not prosper.” And, as it is written, “Gifts blind the eyes of the wise and corrupt righteous words.” What profit is there at all from bribery? What good will shameful petty gain do those who love it? Or rather, what harm will it not do them? For the blessed Paul speaks the truth when he says, “Those who want to be rich fall into temptation and a snare and many foolish and harmful desires, which plunge people into ruin and destruction.” So “a good name is to be chosen rather than great riches,” and the saying is truly very wise and accurate.
Her prophets are men who bear the Spirit, despisers.

The word “her” is well used here of the prophets, since they were not God’s prophets. As it is written, they spoke rashly “from their own heart and not from the mouth of the Lord.” The text speaks ironically when it calls them bearers of the Spirit. It does not mean that they truly shared in the Holy Spirit, but that they dared to fabricate prophecy and did not hesitate to say that they were filled with the Holy Spirit. So, he says, wanting to be both prophets and bearers of the Spirit, and wrapping that august name around their own heads, they became such despisers that they did not even know what decency is. They also brought ruin on others, to whom they spoke things out of their own heart, and the wretches did this for small and very cheap bits of gain, as the prophet Ezekiel says, “for a handful of barley and a piece of bread.” They slid into such madness that they called their own plans the counsels of the ineffable Glory, and insisted that words bubbling up from their own minds were divine words. Indeed he said of them through the voice of Jeremiah, “I did not send the prophets, yet they ran; I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied.” And when the prophet himself cried out plainly, saying, “O Lord, Master, you who are, behold, their prophets prophesy and say, ‘You shall not see the sword, and there will be no famine among you, for I will give truth and peace on the land and in this place,’” the God of all all but cried back, saying, “The prophets prophesy lies in my name. I did not send them, I did not command them, and I did not speak to them. They prophesy to you false visions and divinations and auguries and the choices of their own heart. If they are prophets, and if the word of the Lord is in them, let them come and meet me. What has chaff to do with wheat? So are my words, says the Lord. Are not my words like a burning fire, says the Lord, and like an axe splitting rock?” For the word that comes from God reaches into the depths of the mind and all but breaks open the hearts of those who hear it, while the word that comes from human will is cold and feeble, as was the word of the impious false prophets.
Her priests profane the holy things and act impiously against the law.

Not even the chosen race itself, that is, the tribe of Levi, has been found free of blame. He says that they too profane the holy things and act impiously against the law. For it is written, “The lips of the priest shall guard judgement, and they shall seek the law from his mouth.” But, as the Master of all says somewhere else, “The priests did not say, ‘Where is the Lord?’” Not wishing to make him known to those who do not know him, and not being eager to lead the peoples in their charge to what pleases God: this, I think, is what acting impiously against the law means. Nor do the charges against them stop there, for he says that they also profane the holy things. The law given through Moses pays very close attention to sacrifices and offerings, to when each must be performed and in what way. The priests, it seems, did offer the sacrifices, but carelessly and negligently. They did not see fit to observe either the proper times or the prescribed forms; perhaps they were not even purified, nor dressed in their vestments as priests should be, nor performing the sacred rites in good order. Instead they dishonoured that most venerable and admirable service as if it were something worthless.

So the ministers of the Church must take care not to profane the holy things. There is not just one way of profaning them; the ways are varied and many. They must be pure in both soul and body, shaking off every kind of foul pleasure, and must rather be adorned with zeal for good works, remembering the inspired Paul when he says, “Walk by the Spirit, and you will not carry out the desire of the flesh.”
But the Lord within her is righteous, and he will not do wrong. Morning by morning he will give his judgement, and he will not let injustice prevail.

The just is somehow always at odds with the unjust, and the pure could never walk the same road as the profane. "For what fellowship could light have with darkness?" Such things are at war with one another, and anyone can see how far they stand from any friendship between them. Since, then, God who rules all things loves righteousness and knows no injustice, how could the utterly wicked crimes of the Jews go on prevailing forever, that is, be carried through to the end without ever being checked? It seems a kind of injustice not to subject the guilty to punishment, and not to exact a penalty from someone who has chosen to live licentiously and impiously, who cares nothing for the laws and is so bent on wrongdoing that he counts the better course as nothing, and makes a splendid boast of things that ought to make him blush. Since, then, the Lord is righteous in her midst and will not do injustice (for he would not put up with those who are used to doing wrong), morning by morning he will execute his judgment. That is, he will do it at dawn, openly, as in broad daylight from now on. He will no longer hold back the effects of his wrath but will bring them out into the open, make them plain, and set before people's eyes, as it were, what he had announced beforehand. For he will not let injustice run on to victory. "To victory" means "to complete conquest," that is, "altogether." For once the ungodly have been punished, the practice of injustice will certainly come to an end too, since it no longer has anyone to carry it out.

Those who are truly sound of mind, then, must keep in view that the Master loves justice and will not put up with those who sin without restraint. If someone turns to repentance and sheds tears over his own sins, he will find the Lord most gentle, will obtain pardon, and will escape the snares and the punishment he deserved. But if someone is unyielding, with a mind hard to bring round to choosing what is more fitting, he will settle into his own failings, or rather will perish in them in the end, and will provoke the Master to act, because he does not bear with sinners forever.

I have dragged down the arrogant in destruction; their corners have vanished. I will lay waste their roads, so that no one passes along them at all. Their cities have failed, because there is no one left and no one dwelling there.

For since, as I said, the priests were profaning the holy things and some were acting impiously even toward the law itself, "the Lord is righteous in her midst; morning by morning he will execute his judgment." And what is this judgment? He shook down the arrogant in destruction, that is, he handed the boastful and insolent over to ruin. For are they not boastful, who are accustomed to fight against God, and who set up their own will against the decrees given through Moses as if leading out an opposing army? They cared very little for the divine laws, but veered off into utter unruliness, saying to the Lord, "Depart from me; I do not wish to know your ways." And how could anyone doubt that it is the one who is poor in spirit and humble of heart, as it is written, the bright [?], docile one, wholly intent on obedience, whom God counts worthy of his watchful care? Indeed the God of all said through one of the holy prophets, "And on whom shall I look, but on the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?" So the haughty race was dragged down to ruin, and their corners vanished too. By "corners" here I think he means the walls and the fortifications of the cities. For the corners are always high, with towers that stand out very clearly. So it is perhaps as if he were saying, "Their cities will be left without walls." In addition to this he also threatened to lay waste its roads, clearly the roads of Israel, so that no one passes along them at all. I think he means to suggest something like this. The law given through Moses commanded that whenever the Feast of Tabernacles was held at its appointed times, people should go up to Jerusalem from the whole land of the Jews and carry out the prescribed rites there. So when the cities had been shaken down and their inhabitants had perished, then we say the roads were laid waste too, since no one any longer traveled along them or hurried along them, as in former days, to keep the feast appointed for them. For the ranks of the Jews fell into such misery that there was no one left to keep the feast, and those who had barely been saved and had survived the war could not enjoy festivities. Indeed the prophet Jeremiah made this a part of his lamentations, saying, "The roads of Zion mourn, because there are none coming to the feast." And that this explanation is correct, the passage itself will make clear to us again, for it immediately adds: Their cities have failed, because there is no one left and no one dwelling there.

"It is a fearful thing, then, to fall into the hands of the living God." For when we provoke him by choosing to sin, and that without restraint, then indeed, and quite justly, we are caught, as it were, in the charge of arrogance and dragged down to destruction. We shall be stripped of the protection that comes from above, we shall find our heart within us easy to capture, like an unwalled city, and on top of this we shall not find the ways of righteousness. But whoever has chosen to follow the Master's will, and offers him the pliant neck of his soul, will easily turn away from such evils. I said: Only fear me and receive instruction, and you shall not be destroyed from before her eyes, all the things I have avenged upon her.

He tries to teach that, once again, they would be caught bringing the effects of wrath down on their own heads. For he had admonished them, commanding again and again that they must live in the fear of God and that they ought to receive instruction, clearly the instruction given through the law and the prophets. This, and nothing else, was the way to shake off the wrath and ward off what befell them. But since Israel was unyielding, hard and intractable, it fell away from instruction, that is, it ceased to be wise, and was destroyed as it were from before the eyes, although it ought [?] always to have dwelt on good teachings and been ready for whatever was needed of the things pleasing to God. For in this way, he says, it would have been possible to avoid all the things I avenged upon her.

So when we banish the fear of God from our minds, when we refuse instruction and think being wise worth very little, then we shall surely suffer what befits those who are accustomed to scorn; then God will also take vengeance and demand an account of our impiety. It is necessary, then, to remember the one who says, "The fear of the Lord makes life," and, "The fear of the Lord is glory and boasting." It is also "pure," that is, purifying, "enduring forever and ever," in the words of the psalmist.

Get ready, rise early: all their gleanings have been ruined. Since you did not accept, he says, the instruction that came from me, but thrust away and hated a life of fear and gentleness, get yourself ready for departure and for suffering now what you could have escaped if you had loved virtue and been wise. He commanded them to rise early to show that the time of calamity was at the doors, as if it would come tomorrow and would surely be there as dawn began. This was to cut off any hope of postponement and not to let them imagine that there would be some respite and delay, that a long time would pass in between, perhaps passing the effects of wrath on to their descendants. So, as in a matter that cannot be avoided, prepare yourself in advance and rise early for departure. For you will go off captive to your enemies, and leaving behind the land that bore you, you will be a pitiable figure among foreigners. Then the God of all says to the prophet, almost grieving over the captives: all their gleanings have been ruined. What this too is meant to show, we shall explain as best we can. The tyrants of the Babylonians sacked Samaria and other cities of Judea as well, first Pul, then after him Shalmaneser, and third Sennacherib. Like men who had harvested a vineyard, they went back to their own land, leaving Israel with only the scantiest remnants, as if they had left them nothing but the gleanings. By gleanings we mean the small clusters with only a few grapes, which are covered by the leaves and very often escape the eye of the harvester. Another of the holy prophets says something similar: "Woe is me, my soul! For I have become like one gathering straw at harvest, and like a gleaning at the vintage, when there is no cluster to eat the first-ripe fruit." So those kings did the harvesting, and after them came Nebuchadnezzar, who ruined even the gleanings, and having stripped the small remnant of Israel, went back home and continued to boast. Indeed the prophet Jeremiah lamented the capture of Jerusalem, saying of those who had laid it waste, "Let all their wickedness come before your face, and glean them as they have gleaned me"; and again, "See, Lord, and look upon whom you have gleaned in this way. Shall women eat the fruit of their womb? The cook has made a gleaning."

So when we provoke God, we shall be deprived of all help and stripped of his mercy and handed over to our enemies, and no remnant of virtue or goodness will be left in us. Satan will strip away every good thing in us and gather up the gleanings, as it were, perhaps even the very desires in the mind that carry it toward choosing to practice virtue.

Therefore wait for me, says the Lord, for the day of my rising up as a testimony. For since they had disregarded the divine commandments and had been handed over to their enemies, falling into the hand of the one who destroyed even the gleanings, he now commands them to wait and endure their hardship, bearing their slavery bravely, until he rises up to help them. That help he had all but solemnly testified to through the holy prophets and had clearly foretold would come in due time. So by the day of rising up as a testimony he means the time of help, which he had testified beforehand would surely come.

Such, then, is the historical sense. But we say that the contemplation of this passage reaches beyond it to declare the mystery of Christ, and is meant to point to the time of redemption, the universal and all-embracing redemption, that is, the one through Christ. For long ago, when the seventy years were completed, the God of all rose up to help those who had suffered those things; but in the last times of the age the Only-begotten became man, not only to rescue Israel, but to lead all the nations out of slavery to the devil, make them free, and release them from corruption, filth and sin, and above all from worshiping the creature rather than the Creator. And since he became man, "he endured the cross, despising the shame," so that by his own blood he might win for God the Father both those still living and those whom "death had already swallowed up," as it is written. "For to this end Christ died and lived again, that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living." Fittingly, then, it was said to those of old: Therefore wait for me, says the Lord, for the day of my rising up as a testimony. And the resurrection of Christ is a kind of testimony that death has been abolished. With him we too have been raised, justified through faith, and escaping along with death the mother of death, which is sin.
For my judgment is for the gatherings of nations, to receive kings, to pour out on them all the wrath of my anger; for in the fire of my jealousy all the earth shall be consumed.

He threatens the nations of the Chaldeans with devastation: the devastation brought about by Cyrus and by all who were his allies and invaded with him, overrunning the cities of the Babylonians and making a most terrifying assault on everyone. My judgment, then, he says, will be for gatherings of nations, so as to receive kings, clearly the ones already named, and through them to punish gatherings of nations as well, far inferior to them in might and strength, and subjected to every kind of cruelty; for I will pour out on them, he says, all the wrath of my anger. And it is indeed true that God does not punish great and outrageous sins with moderate stirrings of anger, but always brings penalties fully equal to the sins in which someone is caught. That the affairs of the Chaldeans were about to be all but burned up, he made clear by saying, For in the fire of my jealousy all the earth shall be consumed. What this jealousy is, and over what, the prophet Zechariah will make clear when he says: "Thus says the Lord Almighty: I have been jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion with great jealousy, and I am very angry with the nations that joined in the attack, because I was only a little angry, but they joined in to make things worse."

This is how we shall present the passage in its historical sense. But it may be understood in another way too, if the contemplation is carried over to the mystery of Christ. For he said in the words already read: Therefore wait for me, says the Lord, for the day of my rising up as a testimony; for my judgment is for the gatherings of nations, to receive kings, to pour out on them all the wrath of my anger. For Christ came back to life after despoiling Hades, since it was not possible, as it is written, for him who is Life by nature to be held by death. And he no longer left those who accepted faith in him in the devil's hands. Rather, he passes a holy judgment, worthy of God, on the gatherings of nations, that is, the herds of demons, and on those very ones who once held power and reigned over those who had gone astray. He receives them, as it were, and shuts them up, and casts them down into the deepest pit, that is, into Hades, pouring out all his wrath on them and all but burning them with fire by his ineffable and divine power, moved by great jealousy. For he himself was only a little angry, because of the transgression in Adam; "but they joined in to make things worse," turning the whole world under heaven away from God at once and choking the minds of those under their power with the rites of sin. So the Word of God was jealous for the spiritual Zion, that is, the Church. For he rescued her and "presented her to himself," as blessed Paul writes, "without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but rather holy and blameless."

For then I will change the tongue for the peoples for its generation, so that all may call upon the name of the Lord and serve him under one yoke. From the ends of the rivers of Ethiopia they will bring me sacrifices.

He is saying that once the land of the Babylonians has been sacked and the arrogant have been dragged down in destruction, the nations will recognize the power of God that shook them. Those who once laughed at Israel as it fell and perished will see it going home in splendor and returning again to the holy city, and will see those who once sacked it utterly destroyed. Then they will change their tongue and from then on take up the praises of God, though in the past they shook their heads, thinking and saying that Judea had been captured because the tyrant of the Babylonians had perhaps overpowered the one who helped them, that is, God. So when they see things turned completely around, then they will turn their tongues, according to their generations, that is, by tribes and races, to giving glory to God. They would also choose, I think, to serve under one yoke and to offer sacrifices, even if they lived far off in distant lands and inhabited the regions of the Ethiopians. Let this much be said for now about the letter. But we say that the word reaches beyond, to the time of the Lord's coming, and gives a clear sign in the changing of tongues. For it is written in the Acts of the holy apostles that in the days of holy Pentecost they were all gathered together, "and behold, there came from heaven a sound like the rush of a violent wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting; and behold, divided tongues as of fire appeared to them and rested on each one of them, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance." It is at that time, he says, that I will change the tongue for the peoples. For all of them heard the apostles speaking "in their own language," "Parthians and Medes and Elamites" and the rest of the nations. But notice the precision here. He said he would change the tongue for its generation, that is, so that it remained in those who had once spoken this way until the end of their life, or generation. For the sign extended only to those on whom, the sacred text said, the tongues rested. That is why he says, I will change the tongue for its generation, for the thing no longer happened to those who came after them. For what reason, let the wise Paul teach us. He said: "Tongues, then, are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers. For it is written: By people of other tongues and by the lips of others I will speak to this people, and even then they will not believe." In what way, then, changing the tongue for its generation was of benefit, he himself makes plain to us again when he says: so that all may call upon the name of the Lord and serve him under one yoke. From the ends of the rivers of Ethiopia they will bring me sacrifices. For when people saw the apostles speaking in other tongues, they were greatly amazed at the wonder and believed in Christ, and countless numbers of the people of that time called upon the name of him who is God by nature and in truth. They bowed their necks to the decrees of the Gospel; they became servants of Christ. And they offer sacrifices from the ends of the rivers of Ethiopia. The Ethiopian race stretches from east to west, and they drink from the Gihon, "for it is the one that encircles the whole land of Ethiopia." And so the word of the prophecy comes to its fulfillment in truth. For the Gospel has not only been preached in the land of the Romans; it also goes round among the barbarian nations. Indeed, there are churches everywhere, shepherds and teachers, guides and mystagogues, and divine altars, and the Lamb is spiritually sacrificed by holy priests even among the Indians and the Ethiopians. And this, then, was what was clearly said through another prophet: "For I am a great king, says the Lord, and my name has been glorified among the nations, and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure sacrifice."

On that day you shall not be put to shame for any of the practices by which you acted impiously against me; for then I will take away from you the disdainful acts of your insolence, and you shall no longer boast on my holy mountain.

Once again the God of all addresses two persons at the same time. One must, I think, bring a discerning mind to these words, for that is how we shall find their contemplation free of confusion. To the people of Israel he promises amnesty for their sins and forgiveness of their past failings, assuring them that they would no longer be put to shame for their practices and for the impious acts they once committed against God. But he threatens, as it were, the Babylonian, saying that he would no longer think highly of himself for having ravaged the holy city dedicated to God, that is, Zion, which he also calls a mountain. For after the return, I mean the return from captivity, Jerusalem remained unsacked and from then on never again experienced the inhumanity of the Babylonians.

No one would doubt that at the time of the Lord's coming amnesty and forgiveness were given to all who believed. For we have been justified "not by works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his great mercy." We have also been set free from shame, for the one who honors faith said to us somewhere, "Do not fear because you were put to shame, nor be confounded because you were reproached." For he brought us back to confidence, he who for our sake was among the dead and on our behalf went up to heaven into the Father's sight. For Christ went up as a forerunner for us, "now to appear in the presence of God." So he took away the charges against everyone, and freed those who believed from their failings, from shame and from disgrace. And to Satan, who once tyrannized over us, he also said: For I will take away from you the disdainful acts of your insolence, and you shall no longer boast on my holy mountain. For he will no longer look down on those on earth as people sorely afflicted with weakness, nor will he abuse those who have been sanctified, easily shaking them into doing whatever he pleases. For the old things have passed away, and the nature of things has passed into newness, since Christ has refashioned them to this end. He has made the weak very strong, strengthened toward godliness what was easily captured by sin, and made firm what had been shaken. So the disdainful acts of insolence, the devil's insolence, that is, have been taken away, and he would no longer think highly of himself against the holy mountain, that is, the spiritual Zion, "which is the church of the living God." For it has been founded on the rock, "and the gates of Hades shall not prevail against it." The prophet Isaiah too called the Church a mountain, saying: "In the last days the mountain of the Lord shall be manifest, and the house of God on the tops of the mountains, and it shall be raised above the hills, and all the nations shall come to it; and many nations shall go and say, Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will declare his way to us, and we will walk in it."

"And I will leave in you a meek and humble people, and the remnant of Israel shall fear the name of the Lord. They shall do no wrong and speak no vain words, and no deceitful tongue shall be found in their mouth."

Again he speaks to Zion, that is, to the holy city, I mean Jerusalem, and promises that the meekest and humble people will be left in it. The synagogue of the Jews behaved outrageously against Christ, the Saviour of all, and was shown to be the slayer of the Lord, and it is paying the penalty for this. Yet it has not perished entirely: the remnant has been kept and those who are left have been saved, for no small number of them have believed. These were the meek, who did not turn savage as bulls in rage against Christ, as did those who at that time brought him to Pilate, shouting him down and saying, "Away with him, away with him, crucify him!" and adding to this, "If you let this man go, you are not Caesar's friend." What could be harsher than such men, or more savage in their fury? They even poured that righteous blood out upon their own heads, saying without a care, "His blood be on us and on our children." So the meek people is the one that had no share in their savagery. It is also humble, in that it has been subjected to Christ, has bowed the neck of its mind under his yoke, and has obeyed him very gladly and out of love when he says, "Come to me, all you who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls." In this, too, they are conformed to Christ, who became poor for our sake and all but set aside his godlike glory and the preeminence that is his by nature, so that, for the sake of the divine plan, he might take on the measure of a servant. Those who are trained by his laws, then, are modest of mind as he is. These shall also fear the name of the Lord, for they have become lovers of God in the highest degree, and above all the rest the inspired disciples, who have even been made the light of the world. Those who love God and are good, he says, will renounce injustice and idle talk, for they will not speak vain words, and also a tongue that is not truthful, for that is what the deceitful tongue is. This is a spiritual adornment, like a crown made splendid by the glories of the virtues. For where there is meekness and humility, and also a longing for righteousness, and a tongue that has unlearned idle talk, one that is far from erring in speech but rather upright and a worker of truth, there surely virtue has shone forth bright and most perfect. Such virtue is fitting for those who are in Christ, since the beauty of godliness is not seen in the law, but rather shines forth in the power of the gospel's teaching.
"For they shall graze and lie down, and there shall be no one to make them afraid."

In former times the scribes and Pharisees shepherded the flocks of the Jews feebly. They had been appointed by the law to lead the people, because they were honoured with the prerogatives of the priesthood. So shepherds they were, but hirelings all the same, and, as men set over flocks that were not their own, they saw the wolf coming and abandoned the sheep, as the Saviour said. That they would be convicted of having utterly neglected the rational flocks and given them up to wild beasts, or rather of having become wolves themselves, one can easily see from what was said through the voice of the prophets. One of them said, as if in the person of God, "Woe to the shepherds who scatter and destroy the sheep of their pasture!" Another, again: "Thus says the Lord, the Lord: O shepherds of Israel, do shepherds feed themselves? Is it not the sheep that shepherds feed? See, you eat the milk and clothe yourselves with the wool and slaughter the fat ones, but my sheep you do not feed. The weak you have not strengthened, the broken you have not bound up, the straying you have not brought back, the lost you have not sought, and the strong you have worn down with toil. And my sheep were scattered because there were no shepherds, and they became food for all the beasts of the field and the birds of the sky." And somewhere he says to the shepherds themselves, "Shepherd the sheep destined for slaughter, which their owners slaughtered and felt no remorse; and those who sold them said, 'Blessed be the Lord, for we have become rich.'"

So the shepherds were destroying the flocks of rational sheep; they had no need of wild beasts, or rather they themselves imitated the ways of wild beasts. But when at last Christ shone forth, the good shepherd who laid down his life for the sheep, we were pastured in gardens and shepherded among lilies, as it is written, and we lay down in folds; for we have made our dwelling in churches and holy temples. No one frightens us away or snatches us; no wolf springs upon us, no lion tramples us, no thief breaks in; no one comes against us any longer "to steal and kill and destroy." Rather, we live on in safety and security and in the sharing of every good thing, having as our overseer the Saviour of all, I mean Christ. God the Father made this plain to us through the voice of Ezekiel, saying, "Thus says the Lord: I will save my sheep, and I will judge between ram and ram, and I will raise up over them one shepherd, my servant David, and he shall be their shepherd."

"Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; proclaim it, daughter of Jerusalem; be glad and delight with all your heart, daughter of Jerusalem. The Lord has taken away your iniquities; he has redeemed you from the hand of your enemy. The Lord will reign in your midst; you shall see evil no more."

As far as the historical sense is concerned, he clearly promises them peace after the return from Babylon, when God, forgiving them their old offences, promises to be with them and to defend them. But as far as the inner meaning is concerned, he has commanded her, as was fitting, to rejoice greatly, to be exceedingly glad, and indeed to delight with all her heart [?], since her offences have been taken away, through Christ, of course. For the spiritual and holy Zion, that is, the Church, or the holy multitude of believers, has been justified in Christ and in him alone, and we have been saved through him and by him, escaping the harm done by our invisible enemies, and having in our midst the King and God of all, who appeared in a form like ours, that is, the Word from God the Father. Through him we no longer see evil; that is, we have been freed from everything that has power to harm. For he is the shield of favour, the peace, the wall, the giver of incorruption, the president of the games who awards the crowns, who wards off the war of the spiritual Assyrians and lightens the plots of the demons; who grants us "to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy," through whom we have trodden upon the asp and the basilisk and trample the lion and the dragon; through whom we have come to good hopes of incorruption and life, of adoption and glory; through whom we shall see evil no more.

"At that time the Lord will say to Jerusalem: Take heart, Zion; do not let your hands grow slack. The Lord your God is in you; the Mighty One will save you. He will bring gladness upon you and will renew you in his love, and he will rejoice over you with delight as on a feast day. And I will gather your broken ones."

The proclamation that we must take heart is plain, and the one who made the promise does not lie. We have heard this from Christ himself, as though he were renewing the ancient oracle, or rather setting before our eyes what had been foretold. For he said, "In the world you will have tribulation; but take heart, I have overcome the world." When he came to be "in the midst" of us, then our hands were no longer slack, our knees no longer feeble; rather, we turned to works and labours aimed at good deeds, whose "fruit," it has been said and truly is, "is glorious." Then too we took heart, because Christ who is in us, being all-powerful as God, delivers and saves those who believe in him. For he has made his dwelling in our hearts through the Spirit, and has brought upon us this gladness, spiritual, that is, and worth gaining. What else could sharing in the Holy Spirit be but delight and joy and every kind of gladness? So when he brought upon us the gladness that comes through the Spirit, then he also renewed us in his love, that is, at the time of his coming in the flesh, when, dying "one for all," he said truly, "Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends." And when he had laid down his life and gone among the dead for our sake, being life by nature, he came to life again, reshaping human nature into newness of life and reforging it into what it was at the beginning.

"For if anyone is in Christ," it says, "he is a new creation." For God the Father was pleased to "sum up all things" in him, as it is written; and what is summed up is in a way taken up again and, as it were, brought back to what it was at the beginning. When he had renewed us, then Christ also rejoiced over us, as with delight and as on a feast day. How could the Divine not exult in our state, when we have been freed from sin, have risen above death and corruption, and share in the Spirit and in sanctification? Then too he gathered the broken ones. As the wise Paul writes, "Christ came into the world to save sinners"; and he himself says somewhere, "I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." So Christ gathered those whom Satan had crushed through sin and left crippled, not knowing how to walk upright or to go along the paths of righteousness. But though Satan crushed them, Christ bound them up. He healed those who were sick, and "he himself takes away our infirmities," as it is written.
"Woe! Who has taken up a reproach against her?"

We who have chosen to think rightly will firmly maintain that the Saviour's cross, raised up for the life and incorruption of the world, is the boast of the Church. The most wise Paul himself confesses it, writing thus: "But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world." Yet he also said that the cross has become "a stumbling block to Jews and folly to the Gentiles." For the wretches laugh loudly, being wholly ignorant of the power of the mystery. But they will not escape justice. How could they? Nor will they have the last laugh against Christ, that is, against the churches; rather, in due time they will be fuel for a savage fire, the work of a long and unquenchable flame. For some among the Greeks reached such a pitch of madness and perversity of mind that they sharpened an insolent tongue against the divine message of the gospel and left their invective written in books, so that not only do their sins go before them to judgment, but they also follow them even after death, since they have left their sin behind them as if it were a living thing. So he pronounces woe, and with very good reason, on those who have taken up reproach against the holy Church; for them the word "Woe" is entirely fitting.

"Behold, I am at work in you for your sake at that time, says the Lord, and I will save her who was oppressed and receive her who was thrust away, and I will make them a boast and renowned in all the earth. And they shall be put to shame at that time, when I do well by you, and at the time when I receive you."

Again the discourse has turned to Zion, and it promises the wonders accomplished through Christ for the flocks from the Gentiles and for rejected Israel. For he says, "In you, for your sake, I will act." Since some were carried away by greed into drunkenness, while others failed to recognize God who became man for the salvation of all, the Creator of all lavishes his mercy on both, and for our sake he has worked wonders among us. She who was oppressed has been saved, that is, the multitude of those who had gone astray, once afflicted and brought to such misery by Satan who crushed them that they lost all their vital sap; for a mind gone astray is dead. And she who was thrust away will also be received, namely [?] the synagogue of the Jews. It behaved outrageously against Christ, and for this reason it was justly sent away, fell from its hope, and was cut off from intimacy with Christ. Yet mercy has been shown to it as well, for in the last times of the age it will be called to repentance and to the cleansing that comes through faith. So they will be a boast and renowned, and as far as possible from shame. And who are these but surely the two peoples, no longer divided, as they once were, holding views that could not be reconciled and split in their opinions about God, but firmly bound together by the unity of the Spirit in one soul and one faith? For it is written, "Now the multitude of those who believed were of one heart and soul." And Christ created "the two peoples into one new man, making peace, and reconciling both in one Spirit," as it is written. When they become enviable, then, he says, their enemies will surely be put to shame, astounded at the greatness of the glory given them, the unshakeable firmness of their prosperity, and the steadfastness of their hope. One may see from the facts themselves that the promise is already true. For the Church of Christ has been glorified and, filled with splendid glories, is admired by all. But he also specifies the time when these things will happen, for he says, "at the time when I receive you." What comes after faith would not reasonably be understood as coming before faith, but rather after it. We were called, then, in the time of the Only-begotten's dispensation in the flesh, for it was then, precisely then, that the promise reached its true fulfilment. "For I will make you renowned and a boast among all the peoples of the earth, when I turn back your captivity before your eyes, says the Lord."

In a way he sums up the purpose of God's generosity, and through these words he shows us clearly in what state believers will surely be. He says they will be famous, set amid splendid glories and in better standing than every nation. He adds again the time at which these things will happen, everywhere keeping in mind the Only-begotten's dispensation in the flesh, when, as I said just now, every good was revealed and every wonder came to pass for us. For it was then, precisely then, that he wondrously rescued those who were under the devil's hand and yoked to the passions of the flesh; then he freed them from the error of many gods and brought them over to the truth; then he rescued them from the bonds of death, giving himself as a ransom for us and winning the whole world under heaven for God the Father. For we have been called through him, and through him we have been enriched with access in the Spirit and intimacy with God; I mean through Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
A COMMENTARY ON THE PROPHET HAGGAI BY THE SAME AUTHOR.

We can see that the purpose of Haggai's prophecy arose from other circumstances, and not from those one might suppose gave rise to the words of the other prophets. The inspired Hosea, and those after him down to Zephaniah, foretold what would happen to the Jews in their own times. As though the time of captivity were about to arrive at any moment, they tried to frighten Israel, naming the enemy armies over and over, and usefully announcing in advance, to those who had chosen to scorn God, the overthrow of cities, the burnings, the plundering, and the devastation of the whole land. For they thought that even if the people would not choose to do what pleases God out of a good disposition, and to hold to efforts for the better, they would at least do so out of dread at the scale of the disaster. Haggai, however, speaks when the time of captivity has already ended and Israel has been brought back to the holy city from the land of the Persians and Medes, and he does so for the following reasons. Cyrus released them from captivity and ordered them to go home together with the sacred vessels, to rebuild the divine temple in Jerusalem, and in addition to wall the city itself if they wished. When this had happened and the temple was at the stage of its first foundations, certain people in Samaria, Belemus and those with him, grew envious and wrote accusations against the Israelites. Pretending goodwill toward the rulers of the Babylonians, they said that Jerusalem had been warlike and hard to deal with, and intolerable even to the kings of the Persians. Then they persuaded the king to order the Jews to keep quiet, and neither to raise the temple any further nor to continue their work on the city. After a short time Darius succeeded to the kingdom, and it was the second year of his reign. Since some of the Jews in Babylon came to him and earnestly begged that they might at last be allowed to raise the divine temple, Darius gave the order. He wrote to those who held office throughout Phoenicia not to hinder the Jews if they chose to restore the temple, but even to supply them generously with funds, and to let them carry down the cedars of Lebanon without hindrance, so that, lacking nothing they needed, they might at last easily complete what served the honor and glory of the God who rules over all. Since this history is related in detail and clearly in the first book of Ezra, I think it superfluous to go through it minutely here. So then, although the Israelites were now free to labor, to build the divine temple, to offer sacrifices and prayers, and to live by the customs of the law, they neglected it. Each of them set his own affairs in good order, turned wholly toward what was pleasant and dear to himself, and made very little account of what served the glory of God. So they were afflicted again, God striking them, not with war this time, but rather with famines, failed harvests, and the destruction of their livestock. For he wanted to make them better, not by subjecting them to punishments equal to their sins, but at once pitying them as people who had suffered, and correcting them as out of love. This, in brief, is the occasion of Haggai's prophecy. The discourse is mixed, however: beneath the historical deeds and words lies buried a mystical and most inward contemplation, fitting for those who are spiritual.
In the second year of Darius the king, in the sixth month, on the first day of the month, the word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai the prophet, saying:

I said earlier that the Israelites had a plausible excuse for their sloth over the temple, since their freedom to act had been taken from them, and the people of Samaria had been envious about it and had made a great many accusations against Jerusalem before those who governed the Persian empire. But once Darius was already in the second year of his reign, and had granted them unhindered and free license for the work, ordering them to do as they saw fit and to pursue holy undertakings, and had in addition assigned them funds, their sloth no longer had any plausible excuse; it now appeared utterly unreasonable, and their pretext entirely unconvincing. So the word comes by the hand of Haggai. You will understand "by the hand" to mean "while he handled," that is, while he ministered the words from God and carried out the service of prophecy. And he usefully notes the very time at which Darius issued these orders, cutting off in advance, as I said, the senseless excuses by which the Israelites might again choose to remain slothful.

Speak now to Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, of the tribe of Judah, and to Joshua the son of Jozadak, the great priest, saying: Thus says the Lord Almighty: This people says, "The time has [not] come to build the house of the Lord."

Shealtiel was the son of Jeconiah, who was of the tribe and blood of David. While Jeconiah held royal power over Judah in Jerusalem, the city was sacked and all Israel went away captive, Nebuchadnezzar at that time burning even the divine temple; Jeconiah himself was taken and was a captive along with the rest. Shealtiel's son was Zerubbabel. So when Israel returned to Jerusalem, Zerubbabel, being of the blood of the tribe to which kingship belonged, reigned over Judah. Joshua, being of the tribe and blood of Levi and of the root of Aaron, held the honor that is set apart and chosen above all others: he was the great priest. For so the law named the one whose lot it was to lead the sacred orders, when it said that those in the cities of refuge must not be released from their exile, but must remain wherever each of them was "until the great priest dies," that is, the high priest. The word came to both of them, I mean to the king and to the head of the sacred orders, since it was fitting that they should announce the oracle to all the rest. The God of all commanded them to report the people's excuses, of which, I think, they were not unaware; and it was as if he smiled at people who were falling back into sloth at the wrong time, and who were greatly neglecting the very things they ought to have cared for most earnestly. It would have been better for them to consider that, if they had held the things of God in higher regard, they would surely have been kept in prosperity by his care and grace, and would have lived in good fortune and wealth, with the necessities of life in abundance. So through the prophet's voice he in effect testifies that Israel had impiously neglected the things most useful to it and directed toward the glory of God. For, cloaking their faults, as they suppose among themselves, with plausible excuses, they say that the time has not yet come to build the temple of the Lord. But the time for willing to act rightly is always present, and the good and reasonable are always free to accomplish what serves the glory of God. And if whatever seemed to hinder and oppose them has somehow gone out of the way, then delay is truly most grievous, and whatever might be said about it would amount to charges of sluggishness and of extreme unwillingness to work. And this, I think, is what is said through the voice of David: "Do not incline my heart to words of wickedness, to make excuses for sins."
And the word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai the prophet: Is it a time for you to dwell in your houses with carved doorposts, while this house lies desolate?

This is a second oracle from God to Haggai, condemning Israel with a clear rebuke and showing that they valued their own ease and luxury more than the glory of God. "Has the time," he says, "not yet arrived when the God of all must be honored by the raising of the temple, while your affairs have reached such a degree of comfort and splendor that you live in luxury in richly furnished homes and pride yourselves on halls with carved doorposts? Then does it not seem burdensome and unbearable to you to see the temple so shamefully outraged, overturned, most unsightly to look at, and all but crying out against the impiety of the Babylonians and those burnings of old? Yet how much better would it be to see it in good repair and in its former appearance! For then you could also sacrifice to God and offer prayers for whatever you choose." By houses with carved doorposts he means, I think, those whose jambs, that is, the posts of the doors, have been hollowed out with iron, craftsmen chiseling them around and engraving on them ornaments of their own skill. Such a thing is a sign of people already living in luxury and priding themselves on wealth. For such extravagance in the building of houses, beyond what is needed, would be a very clear proof of an abundance of money.
It is truly dreadful, then, and a sin without excuse, if we put the things of God second and rank them below human concerns.

And now thus says the Lord Almighty: Set your hearts on your ways. You have sown much and brought in little; you have eaten, and not to the full; you have drunk, and not to drunkenness; you have clothed yourselves, and were not warmed by your clothes; and he who gathers wages has gathered them into a bag full of holes.

The Israelites, as I said, neglected what was more important and disregarded what served the glory of God, and turned instead to their own concerns, putting up lavishly furnished houses, and then foolishly saying, "The time has not come to build the house of the Lord." Since they had to contribute toward the construction of the divine temple and were unwilling to do so, they pleaded lack of money, claiming that they must first gather wealth and, as it were, rub off their poverty beforehand, meanwhile farming, or trading, or building up herds of livestock, or pursuing some other such occupation. But it would have been better to trust in God, who finds ways even where there are none, who is able to make people rich and to bless those who till the soil, and who opens up the paths of holy gain. But since they had no share in pious thoughts, they also fell from the favor from above and succeeded at nothing. That is why he necessarily says: Set your hearts on your ways. It is as if he said, "Consider carefully what paths of life you have walked, or which of your pursuits of gain has turned out as you wished." You have sown much and brought in little. But it would have been better, with God's blessing, to sow little and to gather much. Since what was necessary was absent, however, the labors were many and the fruits very few. You have eaten, and not to the full. This is dreadful, and shows the utmost want and misery: much was sown, but the fruits were so few that those who labored were hung up, as it were, to suffer famine, and their food fell short of satisfying them. You have drunk, and not to drunkenness. For the vineyard did not bear good clusters; even the trees with the richest branches sickened along with the cornfields. You have clothed yourselves, and were not warmed by your clothes, perhaps because a plague had also struck the flocks of sheep, so that even those who owned much came to lack clothing. And he who gathers wages has gathered them into a bag full of holes. By this he means those engaged in trade, who in a way collect the wages of commerce, always adding a markup to everything they have bought and fattening their purses by raising the prices. But not even these, he says, had any profit from their love of gain. For falling perhaps into losses and unexpected shipwrecks, they seemed no different from people dropping silver into a bag full of holes. It is better, then, and wise, to seek to be blessed by God, who supplies us with everything. And this would easily come to those who have chosen what is his and have honored what serves his glory above their own affairs. So the Savior himself has told us: "Do not worry about your life, what you will eat, or about your body, what you will wear. But seek rather the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you."

Since the narrative of the history, I think, is complete in itself, come, let us turn our minds to spiritual contemplation and observe that what happened to the Jews would be a type, and a very clear one, of the universal and most general dispensation accomplished through Christ. They were in Babylon, weighed down by the yoke of an unwanted slavery and paying the penalty for their sins; for that reason they had been placed and were living under the hands of enemies. But in due time they were redeemed, God taking pity on them, and they were brought home again and settled in the holy land, with Zerubbabel and Joshua leading and presiding over them. And Darius, although still devoted to the worship of idols, is seen to have ordered that the divine temple be rebuilt, supplying timber from Lebanon and funds besides; yet they were still sluggish and slow to do what pleases God. They were caught setting up excuses, saying: The time has not come to build the house of the Lord. In the same way the whole earth lay subject to Satan, who had led it astray and ruled it as a tyrant; it was captive, caught in his net through sin and through not knowing him who by nature and in truth is God and the Creator of all. But God rescued it in Christ, breaking the bonds of slavery. For through him we have been led on our way: we have left our sojourn among enemies, abandoned the error of many gods as if it were a land of foreigners, and hurried up to Zion, the spiritual Zion, that is, the Church.

See how Christ is portrayed for us in Joshua and in Zerubbabel. Zerubbabel, as I said, was of the tribe of Judah, and from that tribe our Lord Jesus Christ also arose. Therefore he also reigned over Israel. For thus he says through the voice of David: "But I have been set up as king by him on Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming the decree of the Lord." Joshua, moreover, was of the tribe and blood of Levi, and was great priest; and Christ too has become our high priest, offering himself as a sacrifice for us, as an unblemished victim, presenting himself as a true lamb for a fragrant aroma to God the Father. For those who choose to examine this point closely, even the explanation, that is, the interpretation, of the names will somehow confirm the argument. Zerubbabel means "a flowing transferred," and Shealtiel "God's turning aside." And Christ also said somewhere: "Behold, I turn toward them like a river of peace, and like a torrent flooding over with the glory of the nations." For he himself is admittedly the torrent of delight and, as it were, the flowing of peace. But he has turned aside toward us and has all but been transferred, having left Israel behind. He has gone over, as I said, to those called from the nations, giving them in rich abundance the outpouring of heavenly and spiritual goods. Joshua, again, signifies "salvation of Iao," and Jozadak "righteousness of Iao"; and Iao is the God of all. Christ has become for us salvation and righteousness from God the Father. For in him we have been saved, escaping the net of death, and we have been justified through faith, shaking off the sin that tyrannized over us. So then (for I will bring the discussion back to where it began), we shall see him as king in Zerubbabel and as high priest in Joshua. But let the lover of learning again observe how the Jews fell back into sloth when it came to choosing to labor at building up the divine temple, the Church of Christ. And let him also observe, besides this, the eagerness of the nations and how greatly they were roused to diligent work. For Darius, as I said, ordered that the temple be raised and that what served the glory of the God who rules over all be carried out; but they were sluggish and most unwilling to work, putting their own affairs before what pleases God, and having inclined very much toward more earthly things. For they were building, he says, houses with carved doorposts. That is why the inspired David says about the nations: "You have heard the desire of the poor, O Lord; your ear has attended to the readiness of their heart." For those from the nations were more ready to believe, while those from Israel were very sluggish. You can see what I mean in the Gospel writings too, that is, in the parables. Those sent to call the guests to the banquet ran about gathering people to the wedding, but they would not come and invented excuses for their sins. One said, "I have bought a field"; another, "I have married a wife"; and others went off to their business. So those found in the roads and by the hedges were called and ran into the wedding, and truly the first became last and the last first. So too Christ said through the voice of David, concerning those of Israel's blood and the nations: "A people I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me. Foreign sons lied to me; foreign sons grew old and limped away from their paths."

Thus says the Lord Almighty: Set your hearts on your ways. Go up to the mountain, cut wood, and build the house, and I will take pleasure in it and be glorified, said the Lord. You looked for much, and it came to little; and it was brought into the house, and I blew it away.

He reminds them repeatedly, knowing that this is useful to his hearers. So too the inspired Paul writes to some: "To write the same things to you is no trouble to me, and for you it is safe." "Consider, then," he says, "the ways you have now taken." And what these are he makes clear at once: You looked for much, and it came to little; and it was brought into the house, and I blew it away. For they were disappointed in their hope, I mean the hope they had in choosing to farm. Having spent long labor and sweat, they barely gathered a little. Yet they were deprived even of this, for it was blown away, that is, it came to belong to others: it was used up not by them at all, but rather by those accustomed to take more than their share. Their effort and toil were therefore in vain, because they did not choose instead to accomplish what seemed good to the Master, and gave greater importance to concern for baser and more earthly things than to diligence in better things. Did he then leave Israel unadmonished, and not show those who had gone astray the way of correction? On the contrary, we shall see this done immediately.
