For he said: Go up to the mountain, cut wood, and build the house, and I will again be glorified in it, and I will take pleasure, that is, I will accept and praise the zeal and eagerness of those who have labored for it.

It is good, then, and pleasing to God, to hasten to accomplish whatever appears useful and necessary for establishing the Church and building it up. And we shall do this very wisely if we gather, as most useful material, the spiritual insights in the divinely inspired Scripture, cutting them like timber from a forest. Through them one can make one's belief, that is, one's understanding, about God secure and firmly grounded, and will show the manner of the dispensation in the flesh to be sound and excellently wrought; and in addition one will attain an accurate knowledge of spiritual skill and of the goodness understood in character and conduct. It is through these things, we say, that the house of God is built and the Church is established.

I will add to this that each of us also may be understood as a temple and house of God. For Christ has dwelt in us through the Spirit, and we are temples of the living God, according to the Scriptures. So let each of us build up his own heart through right faith, and let him have as its foundation Christ himself, the Savior of all, who is truly precious. And let him bring other material in addition to these: I mean obedience and docility in everything whatever, courage, endurance, self-control. For being fitted together in this way "through every joint of supply," "we shall grow up into a holy temple and into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit." But those who are slow to believe, or who have believed but are still somehow sluggish about departing from passions, sin, and worldly love of pleasure, for that very reason all but cry out, "The time has not come to build the house of the Lord." That is why they fall into want of heavenly goods and into spiritual barrenness, their mind wasting away like a piece of land, so that they have neither grain, that is, strength, nor wine, which is a symbol of gladness. For it is written: "Bread strengthens the heart of man, and wine gladdens the heart of man."

Therefore thus says the Lord Almighty: Because my house is desolate, while each of you runs to his own house, therefore the heaven will withhold its dew, and the earth will hold back its produce from you. And I will bring a sword upon the land, and upon the mountains, and upon the grain, and upon the wine, and upon the oil, and upon all that the earth brings forth, and upon people, and upon livestock, and upon all the labors of their hands.

He does not allow those who neglect divine things to set their own affairs, absurdly, among the better things, or to rank what is more earthly ahead of what serves his glory. Rather, he urges them to consider that if the things which stand incomparably higher are not in good order, then good order would never attend the lesser things either, not even the very things they have set their hearts on. That is why he says, Because my house is desolate, while you run each to his own house, therefore this and that will happen, things by which the crops in the fields would at once waste away: the sky no longer letting fall its dew, the earth holding back its own strength, and moreover the sword, that is, wrath, being brought upon them, the olive withering together with the cornfields and the vines, and besides this, the sword devouring both people and cattle.

So for those who shrink from accomplishing what serves the glory of God, and the things by which his house, that is, the Church, would be seen to stand firm, there would be no spiritual dew, that is, the consolation from heaven that enriches souls and hearts; nor the fruitfulness of the earth, that is, the good deeds done through the body; no grain, no wine, no use of oil. For they will be wholly and utterly without strength, and far from gladness; they would never be anointed with the spiritual oil of rejoicing, and, in short, they will remain without taste or share of the blessing that comes through Christ. And on top of this they will fall under the sword, and will endure toil wholly without reward, even if they practise some form of upright conduct. For no one is crowned “unless he competes according to the rules,” as it is written. Zeal for the better things, then, and for what is most venerable of all, is to be pursued with all eagerness; let our own affairs be ranked as of lesser account and follow behind what serves the glory of God. And not only homes and money and things that make for empty glory, but kin as well, and brothers, and fathers. For so Christ too says somewhere: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me; and whoever does not take up his cross and follow after me is not worthy of me.”

And Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, of the tribe of Judah, and Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and all the remnant of the people listened to the voice of the Lord their God and to the words of Haggai the prophet, as the Lord their God had sent him to them; and the people were afraid before the Lord.

That he does not make his threats in vain, and that fear is no unprofitable thing for those accustomed to negligence, one can easily see from this as well. For look: as soon as they heard the divine words, they turned at once to diligent work, and now they yield to those whose lot it was to lead them, I mean Zerubbabel and Joshua; they treat the prophet's words with the greatest reverence and stand in awe of his mission, although long before they had thought the matter worth very little regard. So the truth of this is seen in the events themselves: “Whom the Lord loves he disciplines, and he scourges every son whom he receives.” For at times the dread of punishment moves the mind over to better things, and the onset of grim events steers us across into the fear of God. And true is the saying in the book of Proverbs, “He who fears the Lord, this one [?],” and again, “The fear of the Lord is life for a man.” And likewise the Wisdom says, “The fear of the Lord is glory and [?],” and “The fear of the Lord will delight the heart, and will give besides gladness and joy and length of days.” But see how gently, and as befits him, God strikes us. For he does not at once bring the effects of his wrath upon human bodies; rather, he alarms them with small fears from outside, and through the loss of their food he changes them for the better, so that they choose at last to do his work.
And Haggai, the angel, that is, messenger, of the Lord, said to the people: I am with you, says the Lord.

See how loving-kindness at once accompanies a change for the better. For the God of all, as it were, changes along with those who have chosen to repent, and promises to be with them. What could equal that? For when God is with us, every harm will depart out of our way, good things will surely come pouring in, the paths of prosperity will at once appear firm, and every one of the sweetest things will come to pass. But if the sacred text calls Haggai an angel of the Lord, let no one suppose that he was an angel by nature and yet was born a human being of a woman, as we are; to think so is utterly senseless. Rather, if we are of sound mind and have an understanding that looks to the truth, we shall suppose that he is said and named an “angel,” that is, a messenger, from his bringing a message. Otherwise nothing prevents us from slipping into another absurdity as well, and confessing that those who reported to Job what had happened in the fields and at the hands of the horsemen, and moreover that his children had died when the house collapsed, were angels by nature. The Word of God, too, is called “Angel of great counsel,” for he brought us the message of the will of God the Father. So he is called an angel from his bringing a message, and certainly not, if the title happens to be applied to human beings, from their being by nature something other than we are.

And the Lord stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, of the tribe of Judah, and the spirit of Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and the spirit of the remnant of all the people; and they came in and did the work in the house of the Lord Almighty, their God, on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month.

The people of Israel were afraid before the Lord. But observe again, I ask you, that they did not go on to choose to do what pleases God until he was with them and stirred up their spirit. From this, then, we shall learn that even if someone chooses to work willingly at what is good, and even if he happens to be full of such eagerness, he will still accomplish nothing at all unless God is with him, rousing him to courage, sharpening him for endurance, and cutting away the sloth that weighs on diligent work. So the divine Paul too, speaking of those entrusted with the divine preaching, says, “I labored more abundantly than all of them”; and he added, most wisely, “yet not I, but the grace of God that is with me.” And indeed the Savior himself says to the holy apostles, “Without me you can do nothing.” For he is our desire and our eagerness for every good thing; he is our strength. When he is with us we shall win approval, building ourselves up “into a holy temple, into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit”; but when he departs and withdraws, how could anyone doubt that we shall accomplish nothing, overcome by sloth and cowardice, and shaking off the toil as profitless?

But see how those who had formerly fallen under wrath through their great disobedience now run into the house of the Lord and work, with Zerubbabel and Joshua the priest [?] with them. The matter, again, would be a type of the calling of Israel that will take place in the last times of the age. They indeed disobeyed at the beginning, and for that reason remained fruitless, without dew and grain and wine and oil; they also fell under the sword. But when at last they fear before the Lord and revere the words of the holy prophets, they will have the God of all with them, and their spirit will be stirred up, and they too will work at what concerns the temple of the Lord, that is, the Church. And these things too are in Christ, for he is portrayed, as it were, in Zerubbabel and Joshua: he is at once king as God, and high priest, in turn, as man, and mediator between God and men; for it is the priest who mediates.

The words on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month have necessarily been added as well, and they show very clearly how quickly the mind of the Israelites turned. For the word came to them by the hand of Haggai in the second year of King Darius, in the sixth month, on the first day of the month, and they hurried to the labors on the temple on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month; so the days in between, the days of delay or deliberation, number twenty-three.

In the second year of King Darius, in the seventh month, on the twenty-first day of the month, the Lord spoke by the hand of Haggai the prophet, saying: Speak now to Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, of the tribe of Judah, and to Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and to all the remnant of the people, saying: Who among you saw this house in its former glory? And how do you see it now, as though it were not there before you?

They went into the house of God and took up the work on the twenty-fourth of the sixth month; then, straight after, on the twenty-first of the following, seventh, month, the word of God came to the blessed prophet Haggai. What, then, are we to reckon about this, and what was the reason for it? It must be explained. Having begun to endure hardship and having taken in hand the cares of the divine temple, and having continued at this for twenty-seven days, they were found losing heart, perhaps whispering, either to themselves or to one another, that they were laboring in vain, and that even if they did manage to rebuild the temple, it would in no way resemble the first. For that one was exceedingly splendid, built by a lavish hand and beautiful with offerings of gold and silver; this one would be without beauty, lacking all adornment, and deprived of the lavishness that wealth provides. That first temple the kings who reigned in Jerusalem from time to time, while still abounding in wealth, had richly adorned, and Solomon before all the others. But this one they were ordered to build when they had scarcely recovered, still dripping with the sweat of captivity and having nothing at all at home. Tossed about and distraught by reasonings of this kind, they did work, but they were found once again to have become unwilling and sluggish. For this reason God strengthens them in their weakness and puts to them a most useful question: whether there is anyone among them who had seen the former temple in its first glory. There were very few, and they were old. For the temple had been sacked by Nebuchadnezzar, and Israel had been taken captive, and was released only when seventy years had been completed. Hard to find, then, and very old indeed would be anyone who had lived before the sacking, had lived through the captivity, and had returned again to Jerusalem. That is why he says, Who is there among you who saw this house in its former glory, and will then see the one that is to be, the new one, as nothing at all? There is reproach in the question, since they did not consider that, even if they themselves were in great straits and short of money, God would not be found lacking in strength, but would himself suffice, I mean, for what was needed to make his own temple glorious and renowned.

And now be strong, Zerubbabel, says the Lord; and be strong, Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest; and let all the people of the land be strong, says the Lord; and do the work, for I am with you, says the Lord Almighty, and so is my word which I covenanted with you when you came out of the land of Egypt, and my Spirit stands in your midst. Take courage.

He does not let them be shaken into despondency, nor be overcome by fears that lead to sloth; rather, he opens their hearts to diligent work and makes their eagerness vigorous. At the same time he trains them in faith and makes them firmly grounded, telling them they must take courage; and, what goes beyond all this and is truly most to be prayed for, he promises to be with them. And he went on to say in what way, saying: My Spirit stands in your midst. Take courage.

No one of sound mind and steady understanding would doubt that to all who labor at building the divine temple, that is, the Church, he grants strength and gives courage, since he will be with them through the Holy Spirit and will bring to completion for them everything by which they could make their own life splendid and approved. So too our Lord Jesus Christ, speaking to the holy apostles, who were about to build the Church and gather the believers into a holy temple, necessarily said, “Behold, I am with you all the days, even to the end of the age.” And that he would again be with them through the Spirit he himself will make clear once more, at one time saying, “I will not leave you orphans; I am coming to you,” and at another making plain the manner of his coming, by saying again, “It is to your advantage that I go away. For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you.” So he is with those who build his house, but he departs and turns wholly away from those who try to shake it down. These, again, would be those who say by Beelzebul, “Jesus is accursed,” who pervert everything that is right and pour the poison of destruction into the souls of the simpler sort.

For thus says the Lord Almighty: Yet once more I will shake the heaven and the earth and the sea and the dry land, and I will shake all the nations together, and the choice treasures of all the nations will come, and I will fill this house with glory, says the Lord Almighty. Mine is the silver and mine is the gold, says the Lord Almighty.

He carries the prophecy over to the Church drawn from the nations, and to the time of our Savior's coming among us. At that time, he promises, he will shake violently heaven itself and the earth and the sea as well, and all the nations besides. For he said, Yet once more I will shake. This seems to me to suggest a meaning of the following kind, at least as it seems right to me. When he resolved to set free Israel, who had worshiped idols and been brought up in the customs and laws of the Egyptians, and wished to bring them over to the knowledge of the truth, he is seen to have all but shaken everything: the waters were changed into blood, heaven sent down hail, the sea was cut in two and its waves stood frozen like walls, heaven rained down manna. And the psalmist suggests something of this kind when he says, “O God, when you went forth before your people, when you passed through the wilderness, the earth shook, and the heavens dripped.” We say that the earth was shaken at that time, not because it underwent an ordinary quake, but because the exodus of the children of Israel became famous and escaped the notice of no one on earth. He says there will again be a shaking of this kind at the time of our Savior's coming, since no one would remain ignorant of the great deeds accomplished through it. For heaven came to know the mystery, and Paul is witness to this when he says, “so that the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known through the Church to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places, according to the eternal purpose which he accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord.” Likewise the whole earth came to know it, and the sea too, that is, the islands. For who is seen to have no share at all in the knowledge of this? What sea, what nation, what region under heaven? “The gospel has been preached to all the nations,” as the Savior said. Therefore, he says, Yet once more I will shake the heaven and the earth, and then the choice treasures of all the nations will come, and I will fill this house with glory. For a great many from every nation, both illustrious and choice, have become believers; they have been gathered into the house of God like splendid offerings, and through this they bring glory to it, making it renowned and celebrated, while they themselves are glorified by Christ. For they have learned to pray and [?]: “And let the splendor of the Lord our God be upon [?],” and again, “Blessed are we by the Lord, who made heaven and earth.” That God needs no lifeless matter, but spiritual adornment, he indicates by saying, Mine is the silver and mine is the gold, says the Lord Almighty. It is as if he were saying: Do not think the temple without glory because it may perhaps have no share of gold and silver and the splendor that wealth brings. I have no need of such things. How could I? For all the silver is mine and the gold is mine, says the Lord Almighty. Rather, I seek genuine worshipers; with the splendor of such as these I will gild my temple. For just as, when he was weaning Israel away from the sacrifices of the law, he necessarily said, “I will not accept calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks; for all the beasts of the [?] are mine, cattle on the mountains, and oxen,” so here too, declining adornment from [?] and seeking rather the spiritual kind, he says, Mine is the silver and mine is the gold; that is: I have enough, I am full, and I need none of these things. Rather, let him come who has right faith, who is distinguished by the glories of virtue, who is adorned with love for me, the pure in heart, the poor in spirit, the compassionate and good. For when they are gathered in this way into my temple, that is, the Church, they will make it renowned and conspicuous.

For great will be the glory of this house, the latter greater than the former, says the Lord Almighty; and in this place I will give peace, says the Lord Almighty, and peace of soul as a possession to everyone who builds, to raise up this temple.

For at the time of our Savior's coming the divine temple was shown to be incomparably more glorious, better than the old one and surpassing it by as much as one would judge the worship in Christ and in the gospel to differ from the worship under the law, and the truth from the shadows. Besides this, and I think it useful to mention it too, the old temple was one, and in Jerusalem alone, and one nation, Israel, performed the sacrifices in it. But since the Only-begotten, being God, became as we are, and, being “the Lord, has appeared to us,” according to the Scriptures, the whole earth under heaven has now been filled with holy houses and with countless worshipers, who honor the God of all with spiritual sacrifices and spiritual fragrances. And this, I think, is what was foretold through the voice of the prophet Malachi, as spoken in the person of God: “For I am a great king, says the Lord, and my name is glorified among the nations, and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure sacrifice.” True, then, is the word that the glory of the last temple, that is, the Church, will be greater.

That to those who have taken care to build it Christ, the peace of all, will be given as a kind of guest-gift from the Father and a present from heaven, he through whom “we have access in one Spirit to the Father,” he makes clear by saying, I will give peace in this place, and peace of soul as a possession to everyone who builds, to raise up this temple. For Christ himself also said somewhere, “My peace I give to you, my peace I leave with you.” And how it benefits those who have loved him Paul will teach us in turn, when he writes, “The peace of Christ, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your bodies.” And the wise Isaiah also entreated somewhere, saying, “O Lord our God, give us peace, for you have given us all things.” So those who have been counted worthy to receive the peace of Christ can readily save their own souls and direct their minds toward the achievement of virtue. He says, then, that peace will be given to everyone who builds. For whether someone builds the Church and has been appointed as one who initiates others into the mysteries over the house of God, or whether he benefits his own soul, presenting himself as a living and spiritual stone “into a holy temple, into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit,” such a person will in every way and without fail have the power to save his own soul with ease.

On the twenty-[?] day of the ninth month, in the second year of Darius, the word of the Lord came to Haggai the prophet, saying: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Ask the priests for a ruling of the law, saying: If a man carries holy meat in the fold of his garment, and the fold of his garment touches bread or stew or wine or oil or any food, will it be made holy? And the priests answered and said, No. And Haggai said: If someone who is defiled by a dead body touches any of these, will it be defiled? And the priests answered and said, It will be defiled. And Haggai answered and said: So is this people, and so is this nation before me, says the Lord, and so are all the works of their hands; and whoever comes near there will be defiled.

This is another oracle given through the prophet to Israel, and we say it came about for the following reason. In the second year of the reign of Darius, in the seventh month, God reproached those who had been redeemed from captivity and charged them with sloth, I mean with regard to their duty to work on the temple. They barely set about it, and from then on took their share in the sweat of hard work. When they had done this, God praised them, promised to be with them and to bless them, and told them to take courage, since the Spirit stood in their midst. But they were no less sluggish and reluctant workers than before. Barely two months or so had passed when they fell back into slackness and were caught again, badly distracted. They had turned to the business of trade with dreadful and extravagant eagerness, and had no restraint in their love of gain. So they gave way to listlessness, as though otherwise they could not attend at full leisure to their trading concerns. Then they offered sacrifices and said that this would suffice for their sanctification, even if the divine temple perhaps were not yet built. The prophet is therefore commanded to wound them with apt reproofs and to teach them this: even if they chose to fulfil vows and offer sacrifices, as long as they were found slack about their duty to complete the house of God, it would bring them no benefit. Rather, their wish to sacrifice oxen out of season and approach the divine altar would bring them wrath and judgment. Besides this he makes it plain that, for the sake of the trade in front of them, they were mixing with wicked and foreign men, and no doubt with idolaters too, and so were utterly defiled. The question is very much a matter of the law, and it is hard to interpret. Nevertheless I will explain it as far as possible, setting out what is meant in such words as I can.

So the prophet asks the priests about the law, for it is written: "The lips of the priest shall guard judgment, and they shall seek the law from his mouth." And what is the question? "If a man takes holy meat in the fold of his garment, and the fold of his garment touches bread or stew or wine or oil or any food, will it be sanctified?" And the priests answered and said, "No." By holy meat he means meat taken from an animal offered to God in sacrifice. But this is what he wants to teach them. When the priests performed the sacrifices prescribed by the law, they sometimes touched the meat that was to be burned, even with their garments. So, he says, if a sacred garment that has perhaps been sanctified by holy meat touches something else that has not been offered to God, will that also be holy? The priests answered no, in accordance with the law. Let us then go from the example to the truer meaning. If the one who offers a sacrifice provokes God in other ways, will he be sanctified by it? By no means. Rather, he is condemned, because he offered sacrifice before he had cleansed himself. To see that this account is true, hear what the lawgiver says in Leviticus: "Any meat that touches anything unclean shall not be eaten; it shall be burned in fire. Everyone who is clean shall eat meat. But the person who eats of the meat of the sacrifice of peace offering, which belongs to the Lord, while his uncleanness is upon him, that person shall be cut off from his people. And the person who touches any unclean thing, whether human uncleanness or unclean four-footed beasts or any unclean abomination, and then eats of the meat of the sacrifice of peace offering, which belongs to the Lord, that person shall be cut off from his people." You see that offering sacrifices with unwashed hands is useless, and worse, that it brings wrath and death. The priests' garments, though sanctified by the meat of the sacrifice, could not sanctify anything that touched them. In the same way, he says, sacrificing to God will not make holy those who have chosen to grieve him in other ways and are content to do nothing about what pleases God.

As I said, because of their trading and the gains it brought, they were mixing with profane men, and so they would certainly share in those men's foulness as well. He makes this clear through the second question, for he said again: "If one who is defiled by a corpse touches any of these, will it be defiled?" And the priests answered and said, "It will be defiled." The law given through Moses commanded those who were consecrated not to touch a dead body, nor to go near people who had died. Indeed it said that the ministering priests must not defile themselves except for father, mother and brothers alone, and that the one who presides over the sacred orders and stands first among them must not do so even for these. But the command was a riddle, for the law is a shadow. The corpse, in turn, would be a type of dead works and worldly uncleanness. I think those who have practised a holy and wholly pure life must keep themselves from dead works and make a habit of standing aloof from worldly rottenness. Now if it happened that someone who had been near a corpse then touched something else, perhaps a person or some food, by the law this was certainly defiled. So the prophet asks whether, when someone has touched a dead body and then, still unwashed, touches something else, he wholly and entirely defiles it. When they said, "He will defile it," God then adds: "So is this people, and so is this nation before me, says the Lord, and so are all the works of their hands, says the Lord; and whoever comes near there will be defiled." For since he touches dead works, he says, not only is he himself defiled, but he has sunk to such a pitch of wickedness that he is fully able to defile others, and thoroughly.

We must therefore take care to do good works. Let us be eager to fulfil whatever is truly dearest to God, and so let us offer sacrifice spiritually. For then he will accept it, and our prayer will bring us not condemnation but benefit and blessing. Let us also shake off dead desires, those soulless pleasures, as it were, and worldly uncleanness. For God will be with those who have been cleansed and sanctified in this way.
"Because of their early-morning gains they will be pained on account of their wickedness, and you hated those who reproved you in the gates."

They say that neither the Hebrew text nor the other translators contain these words or know of them. Even so, they clearly carry a meaning consistent with what came before. As I said, they had become greatly excited about the love of gain and getting more. This had shown itself to be the pretext for their slackness, even though they had been commanded to build the divine temple. So he necessarily accuses them on these grounds. He speaks of early-morning gains because their going out at dawn and their efforts in the morning were for nothing else than this alone, I mean the desire for gain. And he says they will be pained over these gains, because the object of their longing does not reach its goal [?]. For when God does not direct us and smooth the path of what we must do, any human effort about anything at all is surely vain and useless. For it is written: "Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have labored in vain." So they preferred their gains, made as it were at dawn and first light, to raising the divine temple, and put the baser things ahead of the better. In this they were found sick with another dreadful thing besides, for they hated those who reproved them in the gates. You should take "in the gates" to mean "openly." And why did they hate them? To those who have once been mastered by wicked pleasures and have slipped, unbridled, into choosing to do what is not lawful, people able to correct them are not pleasant. They find them burdensome and loathsome. And indeed, what would such people not be counted as?

It is therefore a dreadful sickness of the mind to lean toward what is base, to loathe those who know how to help, and to be quite content with the disease that has befallen one, even when it is seen to be something utterly outrageous. It is better and wiser, as a general rule, to fend off the harms that pour into the soul and mind. But if one does happen to suffer something, one should seek the physicians as quickly as possible, love those who reprove, and fall down before God, saying as it were, "Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved; for you are my boast."

"And now set it in your hearts from this day and beyond. Before stone was laid upon stone in the temple of the Lord, what were you? When you put twenty sata of barley into a bin, there came to be ten sata of barley; and when you went into the wine vat to draw out fifty measures, there came to be twenty. I struck you with barrenness and wind-blight and hail in all the works of your hands, and you did not turn to me, says the Lord."

He uses compelling arguments to persuade them that they acted rightly in choosing to build the divine temple, and that they are better off than before, now that they have taken up this work. Consider, he says, and remember what you were, that is, how and in what state you were, before stone was laid upon stone in the temple of the Lord. Back then, he says, you would gather twenty sata of barley from the fields and the threshing floor, barely, with long sweat. (The saton, I think, is a measure.) You would store it in a bin, which should also be understood as a kind of storehouse for produce, and there came to be ten sata of barley. Evidently a moth was devouring the crops, perhaps, and grinding them to dust by divine wrath. And if someone came to the winepress to draw out and decant fifty measures, he found the measure unexpectedly diminished and was left dumbfounded. You were struck, he says, with other plagues too, barrenness, wind-blight and hail, and still you were hard. "For you did not turn to me," he says.

What, then, shall we learn from this? Clearly some are unwilling to build the house of the Lord, that is, the Church, or are outrageously reluctant to make their own souls into a temple of God. For them even the good things they have already gained will come to nothing. On top of this they will certainly suffer harm from the unclean spirits, barrenness and hail, that is, unbearable onslaughts of temptations that drive them toward every kind of evil, and the effects of divine wrath will befall them.

"Set your hearts from this day and beyond, from the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, and from the day on which the temple of the Lord was founded. Set it in your hearts whether it will be known on the threshing floor, and in the vine and the fig tree and the pomegranate and the olive trees that bear no fruit. From this day I will bless."

By what we have just discussed he first persuaded them thoroughly that, because they had chosen to be idle about the divine temple, a great onslaught of troubles had come upon them. Now he says that they will be fully assured, by experience that brings gladness, of two things. As the fruit of their zeal for what pleases him they will have prosperity, and as the reward of their devotion to his house they will be enlarged in every good thing. He promises to supply them with such abundant crops from the fields that the thing will be almost past belief, and the heaps on the threshing floor will appear far beyond hope. Among the trees that grow in gardens, the vine will be seen heavy with clusters, and so too the fig and the pomegranate. In short, the produce of the seasons will flourish richly for them, and the olive too will yield its fruit for them in unexpected abundance, because they are blessed by God.

Some choose to shrink from building the Church, that is, from presenting themselves to Christ as a holy temple. For them everything slides toward the worse, and indeed they are seen to be constantly in temptations and in spiritual barrenness. The reverse is just as true. To those who are willing to build and have valued the sweat of virtue, God will grant that they be seen in every good thing and be enriched with fruitfulness of mind. Their innermost self will be like a garden blooming with the various glories of the virtues, all but laden with ripe fruit, so that they can then cry out boldly the words of the Song of Songs: "Let my beloved come down into his garden and eat the fruit of his trees." For the shoots of the virtues and the grace of spiritual fruitfulness are like food to God.

"And the word of the Lord came a second time to Haggai the prophet on the twenty-fourth day of the month, saying: Say to Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, of the tribe of Judah: Once more I shake heaven and earth, the sea and the dry land. I will overturn the thrones of kings and destroy the power of the kings of the nations. I will overturn chariots and riders, and horses and their riders will go up, each with the sword against his brother."

The prophetic word somehow always sets out from particulars and from the matters at hand, and ranges out toward universal and most general things. If it mentions the redemption of certain people, it often passes on to the redemption that comes through Christ. The prophetic word gives us a hint of something like this here. These words too are necessarily added to what has already been said, and they subtly introduce the proclamation of the mystery of Christ, still as if in riddles and shadows. The prophet is sent to Zerubbabel of the tribe of Judah to tell him that heaven and earth will be shaken, and the sea and dry land as well, and that the thrones of kings will be brought down. The most wise Paul, turning to the contemplation of these words, says that "will be shaken" signifies that the things that are shaken will be removed, "so that the things that are not shaken may remain." But this had to be accomplished through Christ, for in him all things are new and "the old things have passed away," the things that reel and are shaken. What comes through him has become new, namely the things that stand firm, are established and endure. See, then, how the word is arranged. He promised them an admirable abundance of crops and said he would richly provide everything for their good cheer and delight. Then he immediately introduced the time of true fruitfulness, that is, clearly, the abundant supply of spiritual blessing from above. I shook the world under heaven, he says, when I brought Israel out of the land of Egypt. But I will shake it yet again, that is, I will once more do something notable and renowned among people throughout the whole earth, all but shaking everything.

I will bring down the thrones of kings, he says, and wipe out all their power. There are some who, like horsemen, have overrun the whole world under heaven, and I will throw them out of their domination over all. But I will raise up other horsemen, that is, warriors, who draw the sword against their kin and brothers. Through these words he seems to hint to us of the wicked and hostile powers that have been brought down by the might of our Saviour. These are the principalities and authorities over which he triumphed by his own cross. He threw them out of their domination over all and came to the defence of the wronged, that is, of us. Indeed, the holy and spotless Virgin, while she was still carrying Christ in her womb, cried out such things beforehand, since her mind was filled with the Holy Spirit. She said: "My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Saviour." And after some other words she said again: "And holy is his name, and his mercy is from generation to generation for those who fear him. He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts. He has brought down rulers from their thrones and lifted up the lowly. He has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty. He has helped his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy, as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his offspring for ever."

So the rulers have been brought down and have fallen from their thrones. But the achievements of our Saviour's coming do not stop there. A swarm of horsemen has been raised up, fighting men who are experienced in war and skilled in command, and who march out in general against the wiles of the devil. These, in turn, would be the inspired disciples. In a spiritual sense they drew the sword of the Spirit, that is, the word of the sacred teaching, which is living, active and sharpest of all. They went out against every person, against kin and against brothers. They did not strike them dead. Rather, they slew the ignorance in them, put them to death, as it were, to the world, and prepared them to die to their sins, so that they might live to God, having come to love the glorious and blameless life, that is, clearly, the life of the gospel. And how can anyone doubt that, for the love of Christ, sons would be set against fathers, daughters against mothers, and brothers against brothers? The Saviour says plainly: "Do not think that I came to bring peace on earth. I did not come to bring peace, but a sword. For I came to set a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man's enemies will be those of his own household." They are enemies, then, insofar as they think differently. But they will be friends before long, being of one mind in faith and united in the Spirit and in love in Christ.
"On that day, says the Lord Almighty, I will take you [?], Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, my servant, says the Lord, and I will make you like a seal, because I have chosen you, says the Lord Almighty."

In truth this word is not addressed to Zerubbabel. Rather, it is addressed to our Lord Jesus Christ, who is very well portrayed in Zerubbabel. For Zerubbabel was of the tribe of Judah, he was also a king, and he was the leader of those redeemed from captivity and, as it were, the overseer of those who were building the house of the Lord. So, he says, I will take you, my servant. That is, he means the one who appeared in the form of a servant but is free by nature. At the time when I choose to bring down rulers from their thrones and throw out the principalities, he says, I will make you like a seal. For the Son is the seal of God the Father. He bears the Father's likeness whole and pure, and in his own beauty he makes the nature of the one who begot him shine forth. And in him God seals us too into his own likeness, since by being formed into Christ we gain the image of God. The Son, then, is the exact impress of God the Father, and the Father chose him, that is, made him chosen and elect. Indeed, at the waters of the Jordan he acknowledged him, saying: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him." For God the Father was pleased to refashion all things and restore them to what they were in the beginning, and, as the inspired Paul writes, "to sum up all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth." Through him and with him be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
OF THE HOLY
Cyril
On the Prophet Zechariah
Volume One
Chapter 1. In the eighth month of the second year under Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo the prophet, saying:

The blessed Zechariah prophesies in Jerusalem, at the same time, I think, as Zephaniah. After the return from the captivity, Israel no longer lived divided, part in Judea and part in Samaria. They had all been gathered into one city, namely Jerusalem, and throughout the whole of Judea. Zerubbabel of the tribe of Judah reigned over them, and Joshua son of Jozadak, the high priest, presided over the priesthood. Zechariah weaves the discourse of his prophecy with great skill. Most of those who had been carried off into captivity from Judea or Samaria returned here knowing everything the Babylonians had dared to do against Jerusalem over the years, and they were also aware of the things that had grieved God. But those born in the land of the Persians and Medes did not know who or what Jerusalem was. They did not know Judea, nor what divine wrath had brought on their fathers, nor even why they had paid such harsh penalties, except perhaps from half-forgotten stories. So the God of all necessarily appoints the blessed Zechariah as a kind of tutor and governor for these redeemed people who were still so young. Zechariah was of priestly blood, that is, of the tribe of Levi. According to the flesh he was born of his father Berechiah, but according to the spirit he was also called the son of Iddo the prophet. He had been brought up, as is likely, in Iddo's ways, and became an imitator of his noble deeds.

What, then, is the substance of his prophecy, and through what accounts does it proceed? Surely it is right to say something more about this. He confronts the redeemed with the punishment they are under, since they had neglected the divine commandment in no small way and were in the habit of disregarding what had been decreed through the all-wise Moses. He frightens them greatly and urges them to change course and choose instead to win God's approval by ready obedience and submission in everything. He adds that unless they are good and tractable and yield to the divine laws, they too will suffer things heavier than what befell their fathers. Broadening, as it were, the scope of his instruction, he tries to teach them what their fathers' practices were long ago, and for what reasons the divine anger fell on them drop by drop, and in what way they perished. He also teaches how they were redeemed, threw off the yoke of captivity, and were brought back to Judea. To this he adds that, as I have just said, they will suffer worse things if they are eager to follow in the footsteps of their fathers' lack of love for God. Throughout, he also keeps in mind the redemption through Christ that would come in due time, and he describes to us the mystery concerning him in many ways.

Those who wish to examine each part of the prophecy closely must not, then, regard its contents as repetition and a superfluous retelling of events already past. They should rather remember that for those who had come back from the captivity to Judea, the account of what had already happened was most necessary. By calling these things to mind, he corrected those who knew what they had already suffered. For the very young, who did not know the past, he secured their safety in advance, so that they might not fall into the same evils by loving a profane and utterly lawless life.
The Lord was angry with your fathers with great anger.

Do you see how he alarms them with these accounts? By setting before the very young what befell those who came before them, and explaining it, he frightens them toward what is better. It is as if he were threatening that they will lament bitterly, subjected to the same or even more grievous evils, unless they wisely choose to turn away from their fathers' ways and count what pleases God worthy of all care and attention. He says that God, who holds sway over all, was angry with great anger. He does not leave the truth of the statement unproven, but from what they have already experienced and suffered he shows that he is not speaking falsely. It would be no sign of ordinary indignation to allow the Babylonians to ravage all Judea, and Samaria with it, to burn the sanctuary itself, and to raze Jerusalem. It would be no ordinary indignation to make chosen Israel an exile, serving pitiably and wretchedly in a foreign land and enduring unbearable hardship. Israel no longer touched sacrifices, no longer entered the sacred court, no longer offered thanksgivings, tithes or firstfruits as the law required. Through compulsion and fear it was even barred from celebrating its customary and most beloved festivals. Therefore, the Lord was angry with their fathers with great anger.

One might also proclaim such things to the Jewish people, if one chose to initiate them into the mystery of Christ. Because they killed the prophets and crucified "the Lord of glory" himself, they were captured and plundered. Even the famous temple itself was torn down, and what was spoken through Hosea has now been fulfilled in them: "For the children of Israel shall remain many days without king or ruler, without sacrifice or altar, without priesthood or manifestations." They are captives, for now under the devil's hand, since they have offended God. They have been cast off and are outside all mercy from above. Who could doubt it? But if in due time they should be redeemed, accepting the faith and acknowledging Christ as God and King and Lord, then indeed, and very fittingly, one might wisely exhort them and say these words at the right moment: The Lord was angry with your fathers with great anger.

And you shall say to them, "Thus says the Lord Almighty: Return to me, and I will return to you," says the Lord Almighty. "Do not be like your fathers. The former prophets rebuked them, saying, 'Thus says the Lord: Turn back from your evil ways and from your evil practices.' But they did not pay attention to hear me," says the Lord.

As I said, they had been called back from the captivity and had hurried back to Judea, but they became careless about what pleases God. For the time being they were not devoted to idols, nor did they take up the old error again, but they were found provoking him in other ways. As it is written in Ezra, they married foreign women. They brought wives from the neighboring nations into their homes and became fathers of foreign children, although the law forbade the practice as outrageous. They also neglected to celebrate the feasts and to offer the sacrifices, and they were found unwilling to rebuild the divine temple. For this reason, as it is written in Haggai, he struck them with barrenness and blight, and with hail in all the works of their hands. They put twenty measures of barley into the bin, and it came to ten. They went again to draw fifty measures, and it came to twenty. He therefore promises them that if they choose to change for the better and return to him by choosing to do what seems good and pleasing to him, then he too will return to them. That is, he will hold back his anger against them, turn back to mercy, and once again count them worthy of forbearance and compassion. But he declares that choosing to imitate those who came before them would bring destruction. Through the holy prophets he had given those earlier people a great deal of exhortation and comfort, calling them to turn from their shameful practices. But it all proved quite useless, since they had inclined toward disobedience.

Those who follow their fathers' ignorance are therefore ridiculous. They always put forward ancestral custom as an unanswerable defense, even when they are blamed for the worst evils. This is especially the habit of idol worshippers. When they are called to the knowledge of the truth, they keep recalling their fathers' delusion. They embrace their fathers' ignorance as a kind of family inheritance and remain blind. And I think that even if someone advised those of the circumcision to unlearn what is shameful and choose to honor what is profitable, they too would take refuge in the custom of their fathers. It is useful, then, to proclaim to those who are in error: Return to me, and I will return to you, says the Lord Almighty. And further: Do not be like your fathers. He means, of course, those who went astray and remained in ignorance to the very end.

"Your fathers, where are they? And the prophets, will they live forever? But receive my words and my statutes, all that I command by my Spirit to my servants the prophets, which overtook your fathers." And they answered and said, "Just as the Lord Almighty determined to deal with us according to our ways and according to our practices, so he has done to us."

Before Judea and Jerusalem itself were captured, some people put on the name of prophecy like a mask. They spoke to the people of that earlier time things "from their own heart," as it is written, "and not from the mouth of the Lord." These men lied. They said that the holy city would never be taken by enemies, and that Israel would never be easy prey for those who wished to ravage it. Instead, they said, it would enjoy firmly established prosperity and lie secure in unshaken comfort, with God as its shield, since he always honors and loves the chosen race. As I have just said, these wretches spoke such things falsely. Israel was already careless, and they lulled it further into complacency. Yet they ought to have persuaded the people to appease God, to throw as far away as possible the things that grieved him, and to choose to turn to what pleases him. But they cared little for the truth. Overcome by small and utterly paltry gains, they led Israel astray. The prophet Jeremiah accused them severely, saying, "O Lord, who are, behold, their prophets prophesy and say, 'You shall not see the sword, and there shall be no famine among you, for I will give truth and peace on the land and in this place.'" And God replied to this: "The prophets prophesy lies in my name. I did not send them, and I did not command them, and I did not speak to them. They prophesy to you false visions and divinations and omens and the inclinations of their own heart." Elsewhere again he says, "I did not send the prophets, yet they ran. I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied." So, as I said, Israel was led astray, foolishly carried away by the deceits of the false seers. It would never have been taken by enemies, nor have experienced such bitter and crushing servitude, had it paid attention to the prophets sent by God. They foretold to the people that such things would happen, and declared plainly that they would surely experience disaster if they did not choose to do what pleases God. For this reason he calls to mind both the unholy false prophets and those they deceived, and says: Your fathers, where are they? And the prophets, will they live forever? It is as if he said: "Your fathers have perished, and pitiably, in captivity. With them perished the liars and deceivers who peddled the name and business of prophecy. If your fathers were still alive, perhaps they would have made you better men by constantly lamenting what befell them and loudly denouncing the false prophets of their own day. But they received the wages of their laxity and disobedience: to perish together with those who had deceived them. As for you, accept the words of the holy prophets and set great value on the oracles given through them." For these prophets also spoke to those before you, saying that the Lord had determined to act. Clearly this means the captivity and the miseries that would come with it. They also convicted them, saying openly that he has done to you according to your ways and your practices. The God of all does not punish without cause. Nor does the divine judgment, which is unerring and supremely just, pass sentence on anything without examination. Only after it has been patient beyond measure does it finally weigh out to sinners exactly what is most fitting for them.

So docility is wise, and following the divine laws will rid us of every evil. So will honoring the predictions of the saints and believing the words of the Spirit. Knowing that what has been foretold will come to pass in every way and without fail, we should be reshaped for the better and turn to repentance. In this way we shall shake off the effects of wrath and find the Master gentle. For he justifies the ungodly, and he releases from punishment those who have fallen into sin through ignorance or weakness.

On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month (this is the month of Shebat), in the second year under Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo the prophet, saying: I saw in the night, and behold, a man mounted on a red horse. He was standing between the two shaded mountains, and behind him were horses, red, grey, dappled and white. And I said, "What are these, my lord?" And the angel who was speaking in me said to me, "I will show you what these are." And the man who was standing between the mountains answered and said to me, "These are the ones whom the Lord has sent out to go about the earth." And they answered the angel of the Lord who stood between the mountains and said, "We have gone about the whole earth, and behold, the whole earth is inhabited and at rest."

God revealed visions to the holy prophets in part and at particular times. We do not say that the grace of seeing God and the revelation of things to come was granted to them always, continually, and without any break at all. It came rather at times suited to each matter, and as it seemed good to the one who reveals hidden things. They were taught sometimes this, sometimes that, in many different ways. Sometimes they received simple knowledge, with the Holy Spirit sounding within them. At other times they were also placed within the very visions of what they saw, as God shaped things for them in one way or another and revealed mysteries in riddles. The blessed Isaiah says that he saw "the Lord of hosts sitting on a throne, high and lifted up," with the Seraphim standing around him and praising him in turn. The inspired Ezekiel says that he saw a throne upon a firmament, with the Seraphim beneath it. He said that the one seated on the throne appeared twofold to him: from the loins downward he was plainly seen in the form of fire, and above in the appearance of amber. A deep and long discussion could be devoted to each of these, if one chose to inquire into the reasons why God gave the prophets visions of so many forms.

In the same way the blessed Zechariah, after clearly specifying the time, the day and the month, says that he saw the Lord in a form like ours. Behold, he says, a man mounted on a red horse. By this he hints at someone who is, so to speak, experienced in war and skilled in tactics. To sit on a horse, and a red one at that, with a color like blood, signifies something of this kind, I think. For the God of all fights against those who oppose him. Like an enemy, he takes up arms against those who raise against him the disobedient and arrogant neck of their minds. This is what the people of Israel's blood did, and very brazenly: both those who lived in Judea and Jerusalem itself, and those who held the land of the Samaritans, that is, the ten tribes. They turned to the worship of many gods, devoting their reverence to handmade objects. They cried out to the golden heifers, "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt." Besides this, they utterly disregarded the decrees of the law and turned heedlessly to whatever each of them liked. For this reason, then, the God of all comes upon them in a riddle, on horseback as it were, in a form like ours.

He stands between the two shaded mountains. By shaded mountains I think he means the mountain of Judea, that is, Zion, and the mountain of Samaria. God said of them somewhere, "Woe to those who despise Zion and to those who trust in the mountain of Samaria." Both are shaded, perhaps because they were crowded with a countless multitude of inhabitants and so resembled a thick, dense forest. Behind the rider of the red horse came other horses, which did not all look alike. They were red, grey, dappled and white. These too signify kings, or warlike and most belligerent nations. They were not content to hold only the land that bore them, but spread as it were over the whole earth and strove to bring everything under heaven under their power. Such were the kings of the Babylonians. First was Pul, who took the tribes beyond the Jordan. Then after him came Shalmaneser, who sacked Samaria. Third was Sennacherib, who savagely ravaged what remained of Samaria and also burned many cities of Judea. Fourth was Nebuchadnezzar, who took Jerusalem itself and carried Israel off into captivity. The fact that the horses appear in different kinds perhaps signifies the difference in each king's disposition, and one might quite reasonably take their different colors as a riddle for the mind of each. The prophet, then, was perplexed and asks for a revelation. He learns that these are the ones whom the Lord sent out to go about the whole earth. Those who were sent say this themselves, affirming that they have gone about the whole earth. They also say that it is at rest, since it cannot resist their greed, and that it endures their yoke, which is unwelcome but unavoidable.
And the angel of the Lord answered and [?]: "Lord, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judea, which you have disregarded? This is now the seventieth year."

The horses that had been sent out, that is, the nations and kings, went about the whole earth and then stated plainly that it was inhabited and at rest and was enduring the yoke laid on it by force. At once the blessed angel turns to supplications on behalf of Jerusalem and Judea. Perhaps God had appointed him to guide the nation of the Jews. We shall find that when they fled out of the land of the Egyptians, the mad Pharaoh terrified them with dreadful threats, armed for war, and then tried to pursue them. Then, Scripture says, the angel of the Lord stood between them, "and they did not come near one another all night." Moreover, Paul, learned in the law, said that the law itself was spoken through angels. The meaning of the Gospel parable also hints at something of this kind. Speaking of the synagogue of the Jews, Christ said somewhere, foretelling in a riddle what would happen to it: "A man had a fig tree planted in his field." Since it was fruitless, he wanted to cut it down, and he ordered this to be done, saying to the vinedresser, "Cut it down. Why should it even use up the ground?" The vinedresser replied, "Lord, leave it this year too, until I dig around it and put on manure. If it bears fruit in the future, [well and good]; but if not, you will cut it down." [?] What else does the figure of the vinedresser hint at here, except the angel set over the synagogue and commanded, as I said, to guide it? God had fixed the end of the captivity at the seventieth year. While that time had not yet run its course, the angel had to keep silent, so as not to appear to oppose the Master's will. But once the time had been completed, he makes his supplications. The suspicion of offending had, as it were, been removed. Knowing that the Master does not lie, he asks to learn whether the effects of wrath against the sinners had come to an end in the seventieth year, as had long ago been decided. Or would there be yet another postponement because more sins had been added, so that their hardship would stretch on still longer? Therefore he says: How long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and her cities, which have now been disregarded for seventy years?

Those who worship God, then, have a good and [?] sure hope. If they should happen to offend through weakness, they still have people who plead for them before God. These are not only human beings but the holy angels themselves. By their own purity they calm his anger, make God gentle and kindly, and, as it were, win over the displeased Judge by their entreaties. Back then an angel made supplications for the synagogue of the Jews. But we who have believed and have now been sanctified in the Spirit "have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. He is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not for ours only, but for the whole world." And as the inspired Paul writes, "God set him forth as an atoning sacrifice through faith," freeing from their sins those who come to him.

And the Lord Almighty answered the angel who spoke in me with good words and words of comfort. And the angel who spoke in me said to me, "Cry out, saying: Thus says the Lord Almighty: I have been jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion with a great jealousy, and with great anger I am angry with the nations that joined in the attack, because while I was angry only a little, they joined in the attack to do harm."

It is true to say, in the words of the psalmist, that "the Lord is compassionate and merciful," and the very experience of events would proclaim that it is so and not otherwise. Observe how he at once accepts the supplications made on behalf of those who had fared so wretchedly, who had been crushed in a foreign land and had borne the yoke of captivity. He all but anticipates the request of the one interceding, and immediately answers with good words and words of comfort. By "words of comfort" he means words able to restore and console those who had suffered. For through the whole time of their captivity he had perhaps not spoken a single kind word, nor granted them any of the other things that usually bring consolation; now he begins to speak kindly, and lays the foundation of his gentleness toward them. So out of exceeding joy the divine angel commands the prophet to cry aloud at last and to deliver to everyone the message from God. He says he has been jealous for Jerusalem with jealousy, not directing that jealousy against her, as before, when she had been led astray into strange forms of worship, but on her behalf against those who had sacked her. He says he is angry with them too, not, it may be, with a simple and measured emotion, but with an unmixed and unrestrained wrath. "For I," he says, "was disciplining my own, and wanted them to suffer nothing beyond measure; but they turned the savagery of their own disposition upon them, terribly and without restraint, leaving out nothing that makes for cruelty and inhumanity."

This, I think, is what is meant by "I was angry only a little, but they joined in the attack to do harm." For the God of all disciplines out of love those who have sinned, and by bringing upon us measured afflictions or hardships he drives us on toward what is better. But those who have been taken up for this purpose sometimes leap upon the ones being disciplined like wild beasts. Yet God is angry with them with great anger. For he, like a father, wished to correct through the afflictions; but they, as if under full sail and straining every rope, rushed upon the sufferers with unrestrained violence.

When the Church suffers this, the persecutors fail to recognize that they will have to give account for their savagery toward her, and that bitter penalties will be exacted from them by the God who watches over her.
Therefore thus says the Lord: I will return to Jerusalem in compassion, and my house will be rebuilt in it, says the Lord Almighty, and a measuring line will once more be stretched out over [?].

He has shown that she slid into this wretchedness and misery because she suffered the turning away of the one who has power to save; but that she will again, without effort and with great ease, be as she was of old, once the one she had provoked, plainly the all-powerful God, has been turned to gentleness, and all but comes back to her by once more counting her worthy of mercy and love, and, bearing no grudge, letting her charges drop. For he promises both to raise up the house and to make Jerusalem very long. The temple had been burned, and the very walls of the city had been torn down, so that it looked altogether small and shrunken and had few inhabitants. But, as I said just now, he promises to restore it to its original state, and this was in fact accomplished: Cyrus released them from captivity, and Darius ordered the temple itself to be rebuilt and permitted the city to be fortified with walls.

We see that God at times, in order to exercise the faith of the saints and the love of those devoted to him, allows the Church to be persecuted from time to time. But when she has suffered a little, he at once raises her up, rebuilds her walls with his help, and crowns his own house with grace from above. And each of those who have chosen to live piously is also a city and a house of God. Such a person is often tested, when fleshly pleasure and worldly care provoke him toward wickedness, so that the soul of the one who suffers this seems to have been burned and left bare of walls, that is, of security. But when God has compassion and is moved to gentleness by the prayers of the saints, it is built up again "into a holy temple, into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit"; and once all impurity has been driven out, it is walled again by God and becomes the city of the great King, that is, of Christ.

And the angel who spoke in me said to me, "Cry out, saying: Thus says the Lord Almighty: They will yet overflow with good things, and the Lord will yet have mercy on Zion and will yet choose Jerusalem."

As the time of the captivity dragged on, the cities of Judea, and no less those of the Samaritans, had been made utterly desolate. Houses had been burned and all but cried out against the cruelty of the Babylonians, and the very shape of the cities had been obliterated and completely overturned. Since the inhabitants were very few, one could not see any man of distinction or of any other note, nor anyone living in comfort; all were downcast, weighed down by famine and poverty. He promises that there will be an end to all this. For he says that the cities will overflow with good things, that is, they will enjoy their former prosperity, and with good things set before them in abundance they will change their appearance and return once more to the condition they had prayed for. For the Lord will yet have mercy on Zion and will yet choose Jerusalem.

Observe how skilfully the word of the prophecy proceeds for us. He does not promise to have mercy on her forever, nor to choose her for all time; rather he says "yet," as though promising a limited time of gentleness. For after this she was going to be caught in still worse evils, condemned for her outrages against Christ. So the word "yet" all but measures out the time of gentleness, and carries a veiled threat of what would befall her at the time of our Savior's coming.

And I lifted up my eyes and looked, and behold, four horns. And I said to the angel who spoke in me, "What are these, lord?" And he said to me, "These are the horns that scattered Judah and Israel." And the Lord showed me four craftsmen. And I said, "What are these coming to do?" And he said to me, "These horns that scattered Judah and Israel, they shattered them, and none of them lifted up his head; and these have come in to sharpen them in their hands: the four horns, the nations that lift up a horn against the land [?] to scatter it."

The prophet comes to another vision, and not long afterward, so that he might be taught the future not by word alone, but, having beheld in visions the very things that were to happen, might know precisely and in detail what was being signified. What, then, the meaning of the vision is, I shall try to explain as best I can. In the divinely inspired Scripture the horn is always taken partly as an image and figure of strength, that is, of kingship; but very often it also signifies arrogance, as when blessed David says to some, "I said to the lawless, 'Do not act lawlessly,' and to the sinners, 'Do not lift up the horn; do not lift your horn on high, nor speak injustice against God.'" And somewhere he sings also of Christ, "His horn will be exalted in glory," that is, his kingdom, and his strength and authority to rule over all things.

So the prophet sees four horns, that is, four nations, harsh and exceedingly mighty, able easily to gore cities and countries alike. Some say that these are the kingdom of the Assyrians, then besides that the kingdom of the Babylonians, and third that of the Macedonians, since Antiochus, surnamed Epiphanes, who was from Macedonia, ravaged Judea. To these they add the kingdom of the Romans, which after the Savior's cross took Jerusalem by force. But since the divine angel, interpreting the vision to the prophet, said of the horns, "These horns that scattered [?] and Israel, they shattered them," I think it necessary now to set those views aside and turn rather to the nations that crushed Israel. There were, then, four powers through which we shall find that Judea suffered this. First Pul, as I said, took the tribes beyond the streams of the Jordan; after him came Shalmaneser, third Sennacherib, and last after them Nebuchadnezzar. So it would be more fitting to understand of these that they are the four horns that scattered Judah and Israel. Then, as God showed the prophet more and widened the vision, four craftsmen are seen. He asked again where and for what purpose they were going; and the angel who spoke in him says that they had come in to sharpen the four horns that crushed and scattered Judah and Israel.

What, then, shall we say is signified by this in turn? Were those who had already ravaged Israel being sharpened against Israel, and was God making those whom he had brought upon them in anger even fiercer? Yet he plainly cries out and says, "I have been jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion with a great jealousy, and with great wrath I am angry with the nations that joined in the attack, because I was angry only a little, but they joined in the attack to do harm." How then could he who was angry only a little and in due measure, and who turned his jealousy upon the ravagers because their outrages against the captives went beyond all reason, command the horns to be sharpened against them? They are sharpened, then, but not against Israel; rather against one another. For they rose up against each other, and the Persians and Medes made war on the Assyrians and Babylonians when Cyrus became king, as has already been said.

So if the horns had not been sharpened and the land of the Babylonians had not been ravaged, Israel would not have been freed from slavery, nor released from its bonds and its unbearable misery. The four craftsmen, then, who whet the horns in their hands, that is, in the hands of those who hold them, the rulers (so that we understand those who reigned over the Persians), might be understood as angels, appointed to carry out admirably what God had decided. And this was the capture of Babylon and its falling under the power of the Persians and Medes, of whom the God and Lord of all says somewhere else, "They are consecrated, and I lead them; giants are coming to fulfill my wrath, rejoicing and insolent alike."

And I lifted up my eyes and looked, and behold, a man, and in his hand a measuring line. And I said to him, "Where are you going?" And he said to me, "To measure Jerusalem, to see how great its breadth is and how great its length." And behold, the angel who spoke in me was standing there, and another angel was going out to meet him, and he said, "Run and speak to that young man, saying: Jerusalem will be inhabited, abounding in fruit, because of the multitude of people and livestock in her midst; and I will be for her, says the Lord, a wall of fire all around, and for glory in her midst."

That the horns were sharpened not against Israel but rather against those who had captured and ravaged Jerusalem, and Judea as well, the vision that follows would show, and very easily. For the prophet again lifts up his eyes, not at all those of the body, since such visions are beyond the sight of the eyes of flesh, but rather the inner, spiritual eyes, clearly those of the heart and mind. Then he says that he saw someone in the form of a man holding a measuring line, and he asked again for what purpose he was going and what his aim was. When he said, "To measure Jerusalem, to see how great its breadth is and how great its length," one angel told another to go and announce to him that Jerusalem would be inhabited, abounding in fruit, because of the multitude of people and livestock that were in her midst. For since Jerusalem had been made desolate, the divine temple itself had been burned as well, and the houses and cities throughout all Judea had been overturned, the hope that she might ever recover had in a way been destroyed. But God shows that when the horns, that is, the nations or kingdoms, had been sharpened and had joined battle with one another, Israel would be set free and would again inhabit Jerusalem, enlarged, divinely fortified, and girded as with an invincible flame by the favor from above. So the angel runs to measure Jerusalem, and, as it were, to mark her out as broad and very long.

So much for the historical sense. But I would say that the vision may also fittingly be understood of the Church of Christ itself. For Satan had tyrannized over everyone on earth, and we had become captives, brought under his yokes. But the Savior's grace ground down his horn and shattered his arrogance. For he triumphed over the principalities and authorities of the world-ruler and over the opposing powers. He rescued us and freed us from his bonds; he raised up for us the Church, the truly holy and renowned city, broad and very long, which we inhabit abounding in fruit, people and livestock alike, that is, those who have already come to maturity of reason and those who have not yet reached that measure but are on the way to it and are being instructed in the mysteries: a city which Christ himself walls, consuming those who oppose it with powers beyond words, filling it with his own glory, and standing, as it were, in the midst of those who dwell in it. For he promised, saying, "Behold, I am with you all the days, even to the end of the age." [?] of this city, saying, "Your eyes will see Jerusalem, a rich city, tents that will not be shaken, nor will the pegs of her tent be moved, nor will her cords be torn apart"; and to her he says, "Enlarge the place of your tent and of your curtains; fix them firmly, do not hold back; spread out still further to the right and to the left." For the Church of Christ is widened and stretched out to an immense measure, ever receiving countless people who worship him.
Ho, ho! Flee from the land of the north, says the Lord, for I will gather you from the four winds of heaven, says the Lord. Escape to Zion, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon.

He is, as it were, saddened for those who suffered captivity, since they had endured a misery hard to bear; and now he bids them leave the land of the Chaldeans, since they are now able to do so with no one hindering them, and he himself is gathering from every place those who had been scattered by the onslaught of war. He calls the land of the Chaldeans the daughter of Babylon and the land of the north; for metropolises are ranked as mothers of the other cities that are subject to them. And the land of the Chaldeans lies somewhat toward the north and the east.

Let this be said once more as regards the historical sense. But the discourse now passes over to spiritual contemplation, and the person of the Savior is in some way introduced, grieving in a manner and all but weeping over those on earth, because all had fallen into the worship of Satan the tyrant and endured a slavery so harsh that they were seen to be weighed down by his will. So he urges them to flee as from the land of the north, that is, as from the country of [?], so that by this we may indirectly understand a worldly disposition and condition of character. Whoever has it and is seen to dwell in it would not be fervent in spirit, nor would he have the fiery word of God dwelling in him. For blessed David sings somewhere to God, "Your word is exceedingly refined by fire, and your servant has loved it." And he himself said somewhere to the blessed prophet Jeremiah, "Are not my words like a burning fire, says the Lord, and like an axe that splits rock?" So whoever does not have the fervent and fiery word of God would be chilled and dead. For the love of many will grow cold because lawlessness has multiplied; and blessed Paul also said [?]. Sin will be called the daughter of Babylon, and very fittingly, if it is true that Babylon means "confusion"; for sinning is the work not of a settled and firmly grounded mind, but rather of one that is confused and, as it were, drunk with its inclinations toward wickedness.
