We must therefore depart from such things, and, as from a foreign land, from the chilled and dead disposition of the mind, move over to Zion, that is, to the truth, so that we understand the Church of Christ. Once we are in her we shall discern what pleases God, we shall contemplate the doctrines concerning the holy and consubstantial Trinity, and we shall find Christ himself gathering us together from every quarter and binding us spiritually into one mind and soul. For he said somewhere concerning us, "And I have other sheep, which are not of this fold; those too I must bring, and they will become one flock, one shepherd."
For thus says the Lord Almighty: Behind glory he has sent me against the nations that plundered you, for whoever touches you is like one who touches the pupil of his own eye.

That Christ defended and redeemed the peoples of old as well, no one would doubt, if he had a mind that loves accuracy. For if he was the rock that gave drink to thirsty Israel in the desert, and if he is the one through whom all things come from God the Father, how can anyone doubt that through him also every redemption in its season and every kind of help was accomplished? But in this passage we say that he is addressing those who have been justified by faith and sanctified in the Spirit, and is pointing to the manner of the incarnation. For he says that he was sent "behind glory." And he would by no means speak falsely. For if God the Word, who is from God the Father and in him, being in the form of God the Father, "did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped," as it is written, but came down even into the form of a servant and humbled himself, becoming as we are, how did he not come to be behind the dignity that most befits him?

What, then, is the reason why he had to undergo this temporary loss of glory? He came to plunder those who had ravaged the people of the earth and brought them under their own yokes, that is, us, whom the wicked and opposing powers were carrying off as spoil without restraint. And they are now being plundered, as Christ the Savior of us all gathers us to himself through faith, makes those who had been burdened by their greed his own worshipers, and extends to us such security that whoever wishes to harm us all but touches the pupil of his own eye; for the outcome of events is always somehow turned to the very opposite. Of each of those who persecute the Church the words of the Psalms might be said: "He dug a pit and hollowed it out, and he will fall into the hole he has made; his mischief will return upon his own head, and his injustice will come down upon his own crown." He will touch himself, then, he says, who plots against the souls of those who have believed in me. This is what he says also through the voice of the psalmist: "Do not touch my anointed ones, and do my prophets no harm." For if we are "the body of Christ and individually members," how would he abandon his own body to those who love sin? Or how could anyone be permitted to fill the members of Christ with evil? Rather, how would those who wickedly plot against those who have come under him not pay the ultimate penalty?
For behold, I am bringing my hand upon them, and they will be plunder for those who served them, and you will know that the Lord Almighty has sent me.

For Christ laid his hand on the world-rulers of this age, and with an irresistible hand crushed the heads of the murderous dragon, and gave us power "to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy." And those who were once terrible and exceedingly harsh, whose onslaught was hard to withstand, have become plunder for those who were his slaves. For we who were once tyrannized by sins have been justified in Christ, and have now come to such spiritual strength that we can excel in every virtue and achieve the life that is in Christ and according to the Gospel, and then be filled with the gifts that come from him, and receive authority over unclean spirits and rebuke unholy demons, as Christ lays low and crushes under the feet of the saints Satan himself and the evil powers under him.

In another way too one might plunder those who once held sway. For when we overcome our own passions and count it of the utmost importance to master worldly and fleshly pleasures and every unnatural and foul desire, then we have conquered those who once held sway over us. And if we see ourselves in this state, then indeed we shall know by experience itself that the Word, being God, was sent with flesh into this world by God the Father, and came to be behind glory for no other reason than to bind up what was broken, to give strength to what was weak, to raise up what was cast down, to make the feeble strong, to heal what was sick, and to save what was lost.

Delight and rejoice, daughter of Zion, for behold, I am coming, and I will dwell in your midst, says the Lord. And many nations will flee for refuge to the Lord on that day, and they will become his people, and they will dwell in your midst, and you will know that the Lord Almighty has sent me to you. And the Lord will take Judah as his inheritance, his portion in the holy land, and will yet choose Jerusalem.

From this you may learn that the Savior's coming will be an occasion of the highest joy for those on earth. For he has bidden the spiritual Zion, as was fitting, to delight and rejoice. That Zion is "the church of the living God," that is, the most holy multitude of those saved through faith. And he promised that he would come and would surely be in her midst. For the divine John tells us, "He was in the world." Being God, the Word was not estranged from his own creatures. He himself was the one who gives life to all that share in life and holds all things together so that they may exist and live well. Yet "the world did not know him," for it worshiped the creation in his place. But he came to be with us when he took on our likeness and was born of the holy Virgin. Then too "he was seen on earth and lived among men," and the divine David will bear witness, saying, "God will come manifestly, our God, and will not keep silent." Then he also became a refuge for the nations. No longer was it only the race of Israel that was instructed, through that ancient commandment. Instead the whole world under heaven was gilded with the proclamation of the gospel, and among every nation and in every land "his name became great." For he was "the expectation of the nations," in the prophet's words, and to him "every knee shall bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father." For those from the ends of the earth have taken refuge [?] in him through faith and have come to dwell with him in the holy and spiritual Zion. They have clearly come to know that "God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life." For the Father sent us the Son from heaven as Savior and Redeemer. He did so that we might believe in him and marvel at the Father in him, and that, seeing the one who is from the Father by nature as an exact image of the one who begot him, we might contemplate the archetype. Then indeed Judah became Christ's portion, that is, everyone who confesses and glorifies him, for "Judah" is interpreted as "confession." As Paul says, "A Jew is not one outwardly, nor is circumcision something outward in the flesh. He is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter; his praise is not from men but from God." So all of us who have [?] the circumcision in the spirit through Christ have become his portion upon the holy land. By that land we are to understand the city above, the spiritual Jerusalem, "whose architect and builder is God," who makes her dear to himself and chosen. For he says, "He will yet choose Jerusalem." Then again, if one preferred, it would not be implausible to suppose that here too the church is called Jerusalem. The divine David also calls her the city of God, saying, "As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God."
Let all flesh be in awe before the Lord, for he has roused himself from his holy clouds.

This is a fine and profitable exclamation and a good summons to those who wish to win approval, whether Christ himself spoke it or it is spoken in the person of the prophet. But one thing must be noted. He commanded them to be in awe because those who do not believe in him will perish utterly and completely. Christ himself declared this to those of Israel who would not accept faith in him: "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you believe that I am he, you will die in your sins." And again: "Whoever believes in the Son is not judged, but whoever does not believe is judged already, because he has not believed in the name of the Son of God." For this reason Christ has also been named "a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense." Crowning him with faith is good and saving. In the same way, it brings destruction not to revere the one who came to share our condition for our sake. He came for no other reason than to save what was lost, turn back what was straying, and give life to what had been corrupted. He came to enlighten what was in darkness, to cleanse from its offenses what was liable for sins, and to make healthy and strong what had grown weak.

Again, we will take the words "he has roused himself from his holy clouds" to mean that he has passed from his former stillness and silence into active care for us. He was born of the seed of the holy Abraham, Jesse and David, and of those reckoned with them in the genealogy. These he calls clouds because the minds of the saints are borne aloft. They renounce earthly things and a groveling mind and seek instead the things above and in the heavens. Like clouds, they also water others with spiritual rains. Here I take the rising to mean that the ineffable nature was moved to care for us, and the Savior himself will again assure us that this reading is not implausible. He says through the psalmist's voice: "Because of the misery of the poor and the groaning of the needy, now I will arise, says the Lord." So he has been roused, that is, he has at last been moved to help those on earth who had fared so miserably. He is the deliverance of all, the end of the ancient curse, the beginning of every good, and the giver of hope for the age to come.

And the Lord showed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the Lord, and the devil was standing at his right hand to oppose him. And he said to the devil, "May the Lord rebuke you, devil; may the Lord who chose Jerusalem rebuke you! Is not this like a brand plucked from the fire?"

The account is a vision, yet it carries a historical meaning. That meaning enters in the form of a riddle and is once again sketched in advance, as in an image, in the person of Joshua. It must be understood that the prophet speaks about things in the visions that came to fulfillment. He does not speak idly at all. Nor does he come after the events and heap upon us a crowd of superfluous narratives. Rather, as I said at the beginning, he takes great care to announce what he saw before the events took place. In this way he makes Israel wise and secure, so that it may not fall into the same offenses and be caught a second time. Israel would know that it had been saved only with toil, and that its redemption and the grace shown to it had been almost a concern even to the angels in heaven. He says, then, that he saw the angel standing, and before him Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest. The angel stood as an image and type of Christ, while the priest may be understood as standing for the whole people, for that is how the divine Scriptures take him. Thus God said somewhere to Moses, "And I, behold, I have taken the Levites in place of all the sons of Israel; they are given to me as a gift." So our interpretation does not miss the proper mark when it takes the priest in place of the whole people. Israel had fallen from the presence of God by worshiping idols and dishonoring the very law given through Moses. Then, when the just wrath against it had run its course, God took pity on it and called it back into his sight. This, I think, is the riddling sense of the priest standing before the angel of the Lord. For in anger God turns away and withdraws his eyes from those who habitually despise him, but when he has pity he looks upon them and visits them. Thus the divine psalmist prayed, "Do not turn your face from me, and do not turn away in anger from your servant." And again: "Look upon me and have mercy on me." God, who is by nature good and compassionate, was freeing Israel from sin. But Satan, who had cast it into that sin, stood there again, opposing and contending against it and still accusing it. As far as it lay in him to say what he pleased, he would not allow it to be pitied, since it was in offenses, guilty of the charges of impiety, and had nothing right about it. For the prophet says that he stood at its right hand, as though to paralyze what is right. He wars not against what is left-handed and wrong in us, but against what is right and praiseworthy. The blessed David prayed that this would befall one of those who had acted impiously against Christ, saying, "And let the devil stand at his right hand." So Satan stood in opposition, but he was rebuked by the voice of the angel. He heard the angel say, "May the Lord rebuke you, devil; may the Lord who chose Jerusalem rebuke you."

Observe how the angel at once showed him to be a fighter against God, wickedly setting himself against the decrees from above. God was already pitying Israel and releasing it from its offense, receiving it and in a way already making Jerusalem his chosen one. Yet Satan does not stop accusing, and he dares to condemn those who have found mercy. So the angel exposes him as insatiable in his wrath, saying, "Is not this like a brand plucked from the fire?" It is as if he were saying: "Israel has admittedly sinned, and it is plainly caught in your fault-finding. But it has paid no small penalty and endured its calamities, and it was plucked out only with difficulty, like a half-burned torch from the fire. It has not yet shaken off the damage of the captivity. Only just, and barely, has it escaped the flame of incurable misery. So stop accusing those who have found mercy. 'It is God who justifies; who is to condemn?'"

And Joshua was clothed in filthy garments and stood before the angel. And he answered and said to those standing before him, "Take the filthy garments off him." And he said to him, "Behold, I have taken away your iniquities. And clothe him in a full-length robe, and put a clean turban on his head." And they clothed him in garments and put a clean turban on his head.

Once we have accepted that the one whose lot was to serve as priest represents the whole people, it is enough, I think, to say only this: the filthy garments are a quite clear symbol of the people's impurity. Clothed, as it were, in their own sins, and bearing the stain of impiety that was hard to wash off, they remained in captivity. There they were subjected to punishments and paid the penalty for their unholy offenses. But when God took pity on them, he commanded that they be released from sin, freed from the filthy clothing, and in a way clothed instead with justifying grace. He grants them an end to their toil and release from what had befallen them. For where sin is forgiven, release from what was brought on because of it must surely follow. So the blessed angel, acting in the role of God, commanded those who stood by and served him to remove the soiled garment, and he says, "Behold, I have taken away your iniquities." Then he said that a full-length robe should be given to him and a clean turban for his head. From this let us understand that the glory of the priesthood always somehow goes along with the condition of the people. The purity of those under their care is the boast of the priests. Their priesthood is renowned and splendidly glorious when the people are approved: when they go blamelessly toward what pleases God, gently submit the neck of their mind to his decrees, and for this reason see God gracious and friendly toward them. But the negligence of those under the yoke, and their heedless rush into wrongdoing, are a reproach and a blemish. When the people were in their sins, the priest's vestments were somehow filthy too. In the same way, if the people are again seen to be approved, the form of the priesthood will be clean and radiant and will have great boldness before God. Thus the divine Paul had served the gospel of Christ as a priest to the Gentiles. When he saw them approved through their progress toward the better and holding a firm faith in Christ, he wrote, "I swear by my boast in you, brothers, which I have in Christ Jesus," and again, "my joy and crown."

And the angel of the Lord stood, and the angel of the Lord solemnly charged Joshua, saying, "Thus says the Lord Almighty: If you walk in my ways and keep my ordinances, then you shall judge my house; and if you also guard my court, I will give you people who walk among these who stand here."

We have taken Joshua the high priest as a figure of Christ, the Savior of us all, for he was set down for this purpose at the beginning as well [?]. In the passage before us, however, we say that the following words were addressed to the son of Jehozadak himself: "Thus says the Lord Almighty: If you walk in my ways and keep my ordinances, then you shall judge my house," and what follows. Such things would not have been said to Christ. He himself is the way, he himself is the ordinances of God the Father, and he himself has judged his own house, holding authority over it as Son.

For the divine "Moses was faithful as a servant in all God's house, but Christ as a Son over his house, and we are his house." So let such words be taken as said to the son of Jehozadak, and not to Christ. God promised that the priesthood according to the law would still prevail even after the time of the captivity, so that the priests would govern Israel and administer the holy tabernacle. When the captivity had come, the holy places had been burned and sacrifice was no longer offered. So some thought that the institutions of Moses had gone to utter ruin and that the law would no longer be in force, even though the time had not yet come when the Only-begotten was to be revealed as made man. For this reason God wanted to persuade them that Israel would again be subject to its ancient customs and would be under the hand of the priests, as before the captivity. So he had to say that if Joshua proved to be a true guardian of the law, he would again judge his house and be established in his former glory, with holy angels also ministering alongside him. We would not claim, I suppose, that the ancient law was bereft of rational powers. Even if the things in the law were types and shadows, they were nevertheless performed for the glory of God. This, I think, is what the words "I will give you people who walk among these who stand here" signify: angels who, so to speak, serve as priests and ministers alongside him. Notice how the sacred text everywhere says that the holy angels stand. By the word "standing" it shows that they do not sink down into negligence. Their minds are always upright, as it were, and will not allow themselves to weaken, but stand with God. So too we shall find it written in Ezekiel of the cherubim that "their legs were straight." The human mind bends, and very easily, and readily falls sick with negligence. But the holy multitude of the spirits above stands firm. For this reason God said to Zion, "Stand up, O Zion." And the blessed David somewhere offered songs of thanksgiving, saying, "He set my feet upon a rock." In these passages the Spirit-bearer used the word "standing" to signify a mind that does not swerve and is firmly fixed.

Hear now, Joshua the high priest, you and your companions who sit before you, for they are men who watch for portents. For behold, I am bringing my servant the Dayspring. For the stone that I have set before Joshua: on the one stone are seven eyes.

The words we have just discussed contained a promise to Joshua, or, more truly, to the priesthood according to the law. It would judge its house, still rule the people, and carry out the types of the worship prescribed by the law. But observe, please, the divine plan, and the great skill of God's purposes. Soon, and not long after, the things of the law were to be changed into true worship, and the unloveliness of the types was to be reshaped into a lovely and spiritual way of life. The tenants who killed the Lord were to be driven out of the vineyard, and the estate was to be let out to others. These others were clearly the holy apostles and evangelists, who would make it fruitful and flourishing, thinking it worthy of the utmost care. In the prophet's words, "A king was to reign in righteousness, and rulers to rule with justice." Another high priest was to arise, not after the order of Aaron but after the order of Melchizedek: "a minister of the holy places and of the true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched, not man." For our Lord Jesus Christ entered the holy of holies "not through the blood of goats and calves, but through his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption," and "by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified." God had always and continually promised the priesthood according to the law that it would oversee and judge his house. So, lest he appear false and idle in his speech, he had to foretell the mystery of Christ. He foretold that the things of the law would come to an end, and that he himself would judge his own house through his own offspring, that is, the Son. For this reason he solemnly charges, as it were, Joshua himself, his companions, and those sitting before him. By these we are to understand Levites and priests. The Levitical order stood beside the high priest when he officiated, while the elders and priests, being superior to the Levites and still holier according to the law, were also honored with a seat in council. He calls them men who watch for portents, that is, men who are always seeking to see signs and are eager for wonders. For the Jewish nation is somehow always like this by nature. Thus, when Christ "made a kind of whip out of cords and drove them all out of the temple, saying, 'Take these things away from here; do not make my Father's house a house of trade,'" they came up and said, "What sign do you show us for doing these things?" and "Who gave you this authority?" We shall also find others coming to him and saying, "Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you." So, he says, since they are men who watch for portents, let them learn along with you what is to come. Let them learn of the all-powerful worker of the signs they are forever asking for. And who is he? "Behold, I am bringing my servant the Dayspring." The Only-begotten appeared as God by nature and from God the Father, and as such he is free. Yet he emptied himself, according to the Scriptures, descending into what he was not. He was called a servant on account of his humanity, although as God he is Lord of all. But even so he was the Dayspring, that is, the Sun of Righteousness. We were living as if in darkness, all but stupefied by worldly pleasures as if by night and sleep, with the eye of our mind darkened. He rose and shone upon us, roused us to sobriety, and made us radiant by his own grace. Accordingly the wise Paul writes to us, pointing to this very thing: "The night is far gone, the day is at hand. Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light; let us walk decently, as in the day." And again: "Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you." So the prophet proclaims in advance the splendid achievements of our Savior's coming. He calls him a servant because he came down in the form of a servant. He calls him the Dayspring because he is the true light, radiance and day, and the bright morning star that rises in the mind and makes hearts shine. He also calls him a stone and says that it has been set before Joshua, and he firmly insists that it has seven eyes. The priesthood according to the law, which we have taken Joshua to represent, most of all needed to keep the stone always before its face and eyes, as it were. This is the chosen stone, the cornerstone, the precious stone laid in the foundations of Zion, the very precious pearl, that is, Christ, who watches over all things with many [?] eyes. For the number seven always somehow signifies what is complete. Thus the barren woman is said to have borne seven. No one would doubt that the divine and ineffable nature of the Son looks upon all things with countless eyes and watches over our affairs. As it is written: "For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart. No creature is hidden from his sight, but all things are naked and laid bare to his eyes."
Behold, I am digging a pit, says the Lord Almighty, and I will search out all the iniquity of that land in a single day.

He has shown that our Lord Jesus Christ is both light and the Dawn, and that he will shine out like daybreak on those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death, that is, on those who have gone astray. But it was also necessary to announce in advance the end of the divine plan, that is, the death he willingly endured for all of us when he handed his own body over to the cross. The Jewish nation stumbled at this and was cast out of its kinship with him. Because the wretches did not understand the mystery of his plan in the flesh, they became murderers of the Lord. For that very reason, and quite rightly, they slipped away from their hope, and the wicked perished wickedly, caught in terrible and inescapable disasters. So he likens the Saviour's cross to a pit. Those who shed the Master's blood and dared to hand the Author of life over to the cross have fallen as if into a pit. And if the Father himself is said to have dug the pit, let no one be scandalized. Let him consider instead that the saying is in some way full of the divine plan. It is like what Christ said wisely and accurately: "For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind." Surely it is true to say that he did not come for this reason, so that some might become blind. Rather, the depravity of those who did not understand all but distorted the character of that excellent plan. They did not want to see, although they had the opportunity to share in the divine light. You should understand this passage in the same way. The Father sent the Son "so that the world might be saved through him". But because of the folly of those who did not understand, the one who was sent became a pit and a snare for those who crucified him, and so perhaps the one who sent him has been thought to have dug the pit. "I will dig the pit," then, he says, "and I will search out all the iniquity of that land in one day." By "I will search out" he means "I will seek out and examine closely." They killed the holy prophets and leapt like wild beasts on the servants sent to them from time to time. Some they insulted, some they stoned, some they killed. But God was still patient, because those who suffered were servants and fellow slaves of those who killed them. But they rushed into this with unbridled impulses and looked far into impiety. They behaved with outrageous violence toward the Son himself and slid down into the pit of the cross. So he no longer left their sin unsearched. He sought it out and made the impious pay the penalty. He decreed the destruction of the whole land of the Jews in one day, the day on which they brought him to Pilate and said, "His blood be on us and on our children." The effects of divine wrath may not have followed immediately, and they may not have paid the penalty without delay. Even so, God's just sentence was passed on them, pouring destruction, as I said, on the land of the Jews. Indeed, as the Saviour was being led away to the cross, women followed him, lamenting and weeping. And what did he say to them when he turned around? "Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children." They have been handed over to destruction and slaughter, and what was spoken through Isaiah has come upon them: "Your land is desolate, your cities are burned with fire; strangers devour your country before your eyes, and it lies waste, overthrown by foreign peoples."
"On that day," says the Lord Almighty, "each of you will invite your neighbor under the vine and under the fig tree."

He has clearly foretold that every kind of evil will come on those who were brought down as if into a pit by crucifying Christ, when their sin is searched out. Now he usefully predicts that for those who believe in him and love him, this will not be without gain. Rather, it will bring them gladness and holy delights. The righteous Simeon will bear witness to this. When he saw the divine infant and took him in his arms, he prophesied, saying, "See, this child is set for the fall and the rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that will be opposed." Those who poured the righteous blood on their own heads have fallen. They lie as if thrown to the ground, under the feet of the devil. But those from the Gentiles have been raised up. And Christ himself foretold to his holy disciples his suffering on the cross. When he saw that they had become downcast, he comforted them, saying, "A woman has pain when she is giving birth, because her hour has come; but when she has given birth to the child, she rejoices with joy, because a human being has been born into the world. So you have pain now, but later you will see me and your heart will rejoice." In the same way, when he had risen from the dead, he greeted the women who were weeping at the [?] with "Rejoice!" It would also be fitting for each of those who love him to say, in view of the cross and the resurrection, "You have turned my mourning into joy for me; you have torn off my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness." Once Christ has risen and destroyed the power of death, mourning is surely gone from our path, and "every tear has been taken away from every face," in the prophet's words. For he was life by nature, as God, even though he appeared in the flesh. So "on that day," he says, that is, at the time when he comes back to life from the dead after those who crucified him have been cast into the pit, "each of you will invite your neighbor under the vine and under the fig tree." If someone wishes to take the meaning in a simple and obvious way, he will insist that the things named are symbols of spiritual delights. But I say it is not implausible to add that he seems to call the Church a fig tree and a vine. The inspired psalmist also mentions her, speaking in a riddle to the Bridegroom who is from above and from heaven, that is, Christ: "Your wife will be like a flourishing vine on the sides of your house." And the Bridegroom himself says somewhere, "The vines are in blossom, they have given off their fragrance; the fig tree has put forth its early figs." The churches had already begun to give off a sweet fragrance in the world through faith in him. That is why he said that the vines were in blossom and that the early figs were appearing. These figs could be understood as the multitude of new believers, not yet ripe and sweet, but soon to become so as they advance toward what is better. Once we have grown to full size and "attained to the mature man, to the fullness of Christ," we will be like sweet fruit for God, attached to the Church as to a mother. So if the churches are understood by the fig tree and the vine, we will be under them and will lodge in them, eagerly saying to one another those prophetic words: "Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will show us his way, and we will walk in it." And if we succeed in this, we will count those who called us to it worthy of every praise, saying again, "I was glad when they said to me, 'Let us go to the house of the Lord.'" The fruit of this would rightly be understood as the highest delight for us. So we will say again with the holy psalmist, "One thing I have asked of the Lord, and this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to behold the delight of the Lord and to visit his holy temple." BOOK 1.
ON THE PROPHET ZECHARIAH. SECOND VOLUME.

And the angel who spoke in me returned and roused me, as a man is roused from his sleep, and said to me, “What do you see?” And I said, “I have looked, and behold, a lampstand all of gold, with the torch on top of it, and seven lamps on it, and seven oil-funnels for its lamps, and two olive trees above it, one on the right of its torch and one on the left.”

We will not take “returned” here to mean returning from a place, for that would be quite simple-minded. Rather, we will take it as a passing from the vision at hand straight on to another one next to it, and clearly a spiritual passing. There was need of an undiluted sobriety, one beyond the human mind, and especially in these matters. So God instilled a fine wakefulness in the prophet through the mediation of the angel who spoke in him, so that he seemed to have been roused from sleep. For the condition of our understanding is somehow of this kind, and much inferior to that of the holy angels, so that one might say that theirs is wakefulness, while ours is like being asleep. The divine angel saw that the prophet had been brought to this state of disposition and mind, so that he was well able to grasp the vision with precision. So he questioned him, asking what he thought the things shown to him were. The prophet in turn gave a most accurate account of the vision. He said he had seen a lampstand, golden through and through, with the torch on top of it, and seven lamps as well, with the same number of oil-funnels, and two olive trees, one on the right of the torch and the other placed on the left. The more obvious explanation of what was shown would be no other than this. But I say that those who direct their minds to the innermost meanings must examine what is signified with special care and make every effort to view it from all sides, and must link these things too, with some skill, to what has already been said.

The God of all said that he would dig a pit and search out all the iniquity of that land in a single day, and he urged others to call to one another beneath the vine and beneath the fig tree. We made the aim of the prophecy clear and said that a pit, as it were, has been dug for those who chose to disobey and ignorantly dishonor the salvation that comes through Christ, and it carries them down to destruction. That pit is their drunken outrage at the cross and the charges of bloodguilt against Christ. For the wretches perished, having impiously killed the Lord. But those who loved his appearing had delight and luxury, and indeed what good thing did they not have? For in the churches they came to be as if under fig tree and vine. But see, the prophet beholds the power of the mystery in another way as well. We say that the golden lampstand is again the Church: it is honored in the world, it shines most brightly in virtues, and it is raised very high by the doctrines of the true knowledge of God. On it is the torch, that is, Christ, of whom God the Father says, “For Zion's sake I will not keep silent, and for Jerusalem's sake I will not rest, until my righteousness goes forth as light, and my salvation burns like a torch.” God the Father has set this torch, which enlightens the whole world under heaven, on the lampstand, so that “all who come in may see the light” and it “may shine on all who are in the house.” The seven lamps have no light of their own; their light is brought in from outside and fed by supplies of oil. They too signify the holy apostles, as well as the evangelists and the teachers of the churches in every age. Like lamps, these receive into mind and heart the illumination that comes from Christ and have it fed by the supplies of the Spirit. They give the light out to those in the house and, together with the torch, shine upon those who have believed.

Notice that the seven lamps had oil-funnels through which the oil was poured into them, but the torch has no funnel. For what reason? Because the Son is the true light. He did not obtain the ability to give light from outside, nor was it brought in or given by another. He himself is the light by nature, and it is in the saints by participation and from him. The wise John will assure us of this when he says, “From his fullness we have all received.” Since the Son is the true light, he called those who had come to share in his brightness the light of the world, for he said to the holy apostles, “You are the light of the world.” The two olive trees, placed one on the right and one on the left of the torch, signify the two peoples, who stand almost in a circle around Christ. They are honored with such a position because they have received mercy. The one people came from the cultivated olive, that is, from the synagogue of the Jews. The other sprang from the wild olive, that is, from the multitude of the gentiles, but they were grafted into the cultivated olive and became sharers in the richness of its root, as blessed Paul says. Observe how the lamps and the two olive trees are on the lampstand together with the torch. For Christ is with us in the Church, and the multitude of believers who have received mercy is shone upon by his light. It is also enlightened through lamps, which have their light by participation and from him.

It should be known that in the construction of the holy tabernacle, a golden lampstand with seven lamps was placed in the holy of holies. God commanded Aaron, saying, “The seven lamps shall give light in front of the lampstand, on one side.” For the illumination through the lamps is not given to those behind it, but to those who have been brought by faith, as it were, before the face of Christ. Indeed the Jews, placed as it were behind him and at his back, have their minds darkened. But those of the gentiles who believed have the lamps before their faces, for the illumination through the saints has come to them freely and [?] completely. One lamp also burned in the first tabernacle. This signifies to us that the teaching of the law comes behind the instruction of the gospel. For see how, for those in the first tabernacle, only a single lamp burned, while for those who had come into the holy of holies the seven lamps and the torch gave out, as it were, a most abundant radiance. And I asked and said to the angel who spoke in me, “What are these, lord?” And the angel who spoke in me answered and said to me, “Do you not know what these are?” And I said, “No, lord.” And the angel answered and said to me, “This is the word of the Lord to Zerubbabel, saying: Not by great power, nor by strength, but by my Spirit, says the Lord Almighty.” The mind of the spiritual powers is better and holier than our understanding and surpasses ours beyond all comparison, and you can learn this from here as well. For “the angel returned,” as the prophet says, “and roused him, as a man is roused from his sleep.” Suppose someone chose to compare the measure of human understanding with the mind of the powers above. He will find it falling short by as much as the feeble images of our dreams would be thought to fall short of the understanding of people who are awake. So the prophet was roused to wakefulness. Yet even in that state, and greatly sharpened, he is no less slow when it comes to being able to understand what is shown. For this reason, and quite fittingly, he inquires and asks to learn from the wise angel. The angel, almost astonished that he had not understood, asks whether he really does not know. The prophet openly confesses his ignorance and is not ashamed of his slowness to learn. The angel then makes the riddle of the vision plain and, as if from a clear and visible image, interprets the purpose hidden within it. For he says, “This is the word of the Lord to Zerubbabel, saying: Not by great power, nor by strength, but by my Spirit, says the Lord Almighty.” It is as if he were saying: The meaning of the vision and the purpose of what was shown all but cry aloud God's words to Zerubbabel. They declare that all these things that are seen will come to completion in their own time. They will be accomplished not by human power, nor by the strength of the flesh, but by the power of the Holy Spirit and by divine assent. For the Only-begotten became a man like us, yet he did not wage war in the flesh in order to set up the Church for the world like a lampstand. He did not set visible weapons and phalanxes of warriors in motion to present the two peoples to himself or to set the spiritual lamps on the lampstand. Rather, in the strength of his own Spirit he appointed in the churches “first apostles, second prophets and evangelists,” and all the rest of the assembly of the saints. He filled them with divine gifts and richly enriched them with the outpouring of his favor. So Christ's work was not done by great power, nor by the strength of the flesh. It was by the power of the Spirit that Satan was despoiled and the hosts of the opposing powers fell with him. And so both those from Israel and those who had formerly worshiped the creation instead of the Creator were called through faith to the knowledge of God.

In the churches, too, the lamps were displayed, that is, the saints, shining together with the torch, I mean Christ. For, as the most wise Paul writes, they became “lights in the world, holding fast the word of life.” Emmanuel saved the world under heaven not by human hand but by his own powers as God, and he bore witness to this through the voice of Hosea as well. The passage runs thus: “But I will have mercy on the sons of Judah, and I will save them by the Lord their God, and I will not save them by bow, nor by sword, nor by war, nor by chariots, nor by horses, nor by horsemen.” The word was very fittingly addressed to Zerubbabel, who was of the tribe of Judah and at that time held the throne of the kingdom in Jerusalem. Such splendid and admirable achievements had been foretold to him, and God did not want him to suppose that wars and battles would be waged in their time. So God of necessity removed him from such feeble human notions and commanded him rather to be convinced that the working of Christ, who brings such things to completion, befits God, and that his power is not human. We remember that we said Zerubbabel himself, being of the tribe of Judah and a king, points in his own person to Christ, with Joshua son of Jehozadak joined to him. In this way Emmanuel may be understood as king and high priest at once in the same person.
Who are you, O great mountain, before Zerubbabel, to accomplish the work? And I will bring out the stone of the inheritance; equality of grace is its grace.

The passage before us is very hard to grasp, but we will say what seems best and right. The word seems almost to rebuke the great mountain, that is, Satan. He rose up against Christ and set the power of his own perversity against him, which was also written for us in riddles above. For the prophet said he had seen “Joshua the great priest standing before the angel of the Lord, and the devil standing at his right hand to oppose him.” As far as he could and as far as it lay in his power, the devil made war and rose up fiercely against the Savior's saving plan as he called the world under heaven to salvation. No one would doubt this who considers the following. First, the devil approached him as he fasted in the desert. Seeing him saving the world under heaven, the devil wanted to make him his own worshiper, showing him “all the kingdoms of the world” and saying that all would be his if he would fall down and worship him. Then, in addition to this, he snatched the betrayer disciple from the very company of the holy apostles and persuaded him to become the instrument of the Jews' perversity. So the word rebukes him and says, “Who are you, O great mountain, before Zerubbabel, to accomplish the work?” The words “Who are you?” must be understood not as coming from someone who wants to learn who he is and where he comes from, for being God he would not be ignorant of this. Rather, they come from one who belittles him and counts him as worth nothing, even if the mountain is great and hard to face. It lies in the way of Christ, who wished to accomplish such things, and of whom Zerubbabel is a type, as we have already said. For although the apostate dragon has a perversity beyond compare, Christ trampled him without toil or sweat. For he was God by nature, the one who conquers all things.

We may approach these words in some such way as this, or otherwise, if one prefers. We said that the things that lead to life will be accomplished for the world not by human power. The lampstand will stand, holding the torch, that is, Christ. The lamps will shine out, and on the right and on the left of the torch the two olive trees will surely stand, signifying the two peoples. Then it is as if someone were asking, “Who then are you, who promise to accomplish such great things without any war and without toil?” And God the Father answers, saying, “I am the great mountain before Zerubbabel, to accomplish the work.” That is: I am the nature that surpasses all things, that soars with heights befitting God into the glory beyond all things, and that in due time will be sufficient to accomplish what was promised, even before Zerubbabel. For Christ did not ignore his own Father but made him a kind of co-worker in his own achievements, saying, “I do nothing of myself, but the Father who sent me, abiding in me, does the works himself.” For the Father worked through the Son as through his own power, and through him he also brought all things into being in the beginning, for which he is rightly admired. We remember that in the most wise Daniel, too, God the Father is again called a mountain, from which “a stone was cut without hands, and it crushed the gold, the silver, the bronze, the iron,” and this too was a type of Christ. For the Son, begotten from God the Father ineffably and beyond understanding, crushed all the kingdoms, so that from then on dominion might belong to him. “For every knee shall bow to him, and every tongue shall confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” So the Son, cut out from the mountain, God the Father, as a chosen cornerstone, has become our inheritance. For we have been called to adoption by him and have become heirs of the living God, gaining equality of grace in return for grace. And what does this mean?

Grace was given to Israel, that ancient and celebrated grace. They were redeemed from Egypt in the flesh and shook off the slavery imposed on them out of greed. They were brought through the midst of the sea, they ate the manna in the wilderness, and they crossed rivers on foot, for that is how they crossed the Jordan. They were brought into the land of promise. This, then, is the first grace. But in equality and likeness to that ancient grace, another grace has been given to us by Christ. He has become for us a stone, as a foundation, or rather a cornerstone, and also an inheritance, for through him we have become heirs of God. How, then, is the second grace equal to the first? What was done for them in the flesh, that is, in perceptible ways, Christ has accomplished for us spiritually and in ways perceived by the mind. He rescued us from slavery to the devil, as if from clay and brickmaking. He set us free from the passions of the world and the impurities of the flesh. He brought us across as through a sea, for we have passed through the surge of this present life and the bitterness of its cares. We have eaten the bread from heaven; the saying is a mystical one. We have been brought across the Jordan, we have received circumcision in the Spirit, and we have inherited the city above, the truly holy land. Christ himself spoke of it when he said, “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the land.” I think the most wise evangelist John wants to show this very thing when he says of Christ, “From his fullness we have all received, grace in return for grace. For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.” Moses became the minister and mediator of that ancient grace, but Christ is the giver of the second. The second grace bears a likeness to the first, for those things were types pointing to the truth, as it were in labor with the beauty of the truth. Yet it is better and higher, as much as the things perceived by the mind would rightly surpass the things perceived by the senses. Paul will bear witness to this when he writes, “Jesus has become the guarantee of a better covenant.”

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house, and his hands will complete it, and you shall know that the Lord Almighty has sent me to you. See, once more he describes for us spiritual realities in terms of perceptible events. As a type of what was wonderfully accomplished through Christ, he sets before us what was brought to completion in its own time by the hand of Zerubbabel. Babylon had been taken by the Persians and Cyrus, and the people of Israel had been released from the bonds of slavery and had gone back to Jerusalem. Then, while Darius was governing the dominion, or rather the kingdom, of the Chaldeans, God urged those who had returned to rebuild the divine temple at once. Zerubbabel was reigning as king, and Joshua son of Jehozadak, the great priest, was serving as priest. They set their hands to the work, and the work was at the first laying of the foundations. The walls had been raised high by then. But in the meantime some people hindered them, and the envy of the surrounding nations got in the way. So there was a halt and a postponement of their zeal for the work.

When God once more granted them the ability to succeed, the temple was finished, though with difficulty, while Joshua served as priest and Zerubbabel presided as king. With this the historical account comes to an end. But we have taken Zerubbabel of the tribe of Judah as a type of Christ. So come, let me say how and in what way Christ himself began to build the house of the Lord and then completed it in a spiritual way perceived by the mind. In the beginning he established the synagogue of the Jews as a house, a kind of dwelling fit for God, for himself and for the Father. For that is what he called it when he said through the all-wise Moses, “If there is a prophet of the Lord among you, I will make myself known to him in a vision and speak to him in sleep. Not so with my servant Moses: he is faithful in all my house. Mouth to mouth I will speak to him, in visible form and not through riddles.” So the house was founded, as it were, through Christ, but in the meantime it was torn down. Indeed the prophet Jeremiah lamented it as fallen and shaken, saying, “The house of Israel has fallen; there is no one to raise it up.” Because they behaved outrageously toward Christ, it fell, and from then on there was no one left to raise it up. Yet it has been raised up through Christ and remade for the better. The gentiles have been brought into it, and the Church has been displayed in the world, “which is the house of God,” and the Lord and God of all has come to love its beauty. The temple raised in the last times, that is, the Church, is better than the first beyond all comparison. He gave assurance of this when he said through the voice of the prophet Haggai, “Who is there among you who saw this house in its former glory? And how do you see it now, as though it were not there before you?” And after some other things: “For the latter glory of this house shall be great, beyond the former, says the Lord Almighty.” No one would doubt that it is senseless to understand such things historically, if he considers the following. How could the glory of the divine temple in the last times be thought superior to the first? Nebuchadnezzar the Babylonian burned and plundered the first temple. The one raised after it, after the time of the captivity, was burned no less by the Romans, and with it Jerusalem itself and the whole land of the Jews. So the historical explanation is not sufficient to reach the truth. The latter glory is better and superior to the first because the Church has been taken up “into a holy temple, into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit.” For we are built up “upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets,” “joined and fitted together by every ligament of supply, according to the working of each member.” In a way we fit together with one another, as by unity of faith and love through the Spirit, into a holy temple, for we are living stones. Indeed the divine Paul called the multitude of believers sometimes “God's field” and at other times God's building. And “as a wise master builder” he laid a foundation, and this is Jesus Christ. On him we all rest, and through him we stand and are called temples, since we have him dwelling and lodging in mind and heart through the Spirit.
For who has despised the small days? And they will rejoice and see the stone of tin in the hand of Zerubbabel. These seven are the eyes of the Lord that look out over all the earth.

The vision does not concern things that would happen at once. It concerns things that would be brought to fulfilment at the end, at the time of the coming of Christ, the Saviour of us all. That coming did take place in the last times of the present age, though not, I think, very many years after the prophecy before us, that is, after the building of the temple raised up by the hand of Zerubbabel. So, he says, if anyone should make little of the few, easily counted days in between, and reckon the delay short without growing weary over it, he will in every way be filled with all gladness. For he will rejoice and see the tin stone in the hand of Zerubbabel. Now he has called Christ the tin stone. If anyone wishes to learn why, I will at once give the explanation that some hold and that we ourselves also take to be correct. Some say that tin is a blend of bronze and lead. For this reason it is neither wholly free of hardness nor does it refuse to be soft. In somewhat the same way we too hold that Emmanuel is composed of the unbreakable Godhead and a humanity that is, so to speak, capable of suffering. One should also know that the adamant stone is said to be easily shattered by lead, although it cannot be made to suffer this by any other material. We say, then, that although Christ is exceedingly kind and all-powerful and has nothing harsh in him, being God, he shatters Satan like a piece of adamant. Of Satan it is written: "His heart is set like stone, and stands like an anvil that cannot be beaten." Others again think that tin, or simply lead, is necessarily used to purify other material by fire, and that it is especially useful and necessary to those who are accustomed to work in silver. And indeed God said somewhere through the voice of Jeremiah, showing this very thing in a riddle: "The bellows has failed from the fire, the lead has failed; in vain the silversmith works the silver; their wickedness has not been melted away."

So he likens Christ to tin, or lead, because he melts away filth, removes what is superfluous, and purifies spiritually. If anyone, then, he says, should rise above the intervening times and count the few days in between as nothing, he will rejoice and see the tin stone in the hand of Zerubbabel. And what does "in the hand of Zerubbabel" mean? The divinely inspired Scripture takes the hand to mean both power and authority. So it is in the power and authority of Zerubbabel, that is, of Christ, that he will see the tin stone. For Zerubbabel, as I said, was of the tribe of Judah and reigned over Israel. In the same way our Lord Jesus Christ sprang according to the flesh from the blood and tribe of Judah, and he too reigned over Israel. He did not reign in the manner proper to us, with a kingdom that can be measured and is limited in time, but as truly God, with a kingdom extending to endless ages. The blessed Gabriel will bear witness to this when he says to the holy Virgin about him that she will bear a son and call his name Jesus, and adds: "And the Lord God will give him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Israel forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end." In the hand of Zerubbabel, then, that is, in the power and authority of Zerubbabel, the tin stone will be seen in due time. The word of the prophecy immediately adds: "These seven are the eyes of the Lord that look upon all the earth." And who might these be? One possibility is that he has called the seven lamps, which he saw with the lampstand, the eyes of the Lord, so that we should understand the saints, through whom the whole earth is enlightened and shown to have been counted worthy of God's oversight. Alternatively, we will say that it signifies, I think, that the God and Father of all would not neglect his own creatures. Rather, surveying all things as if with many sleepless eyes, he will graciously grant to the earth the tin stone, that is, Christ, through whom the gift of visitation, or of watchful care, has come to us. For "the dawn from on high has visited us," as it is written. And if we are "the body of Christ and individually members," I think it is not at all unreasonable to say that the holy teachers of the mysteries have been placed in the rank of eyes, since they stand out above the rest and are set over them. For this reason, I believe, they are also called overseers. Through them our Lord Jesus Christ watches over those who believe in him. The tin stone might also be understood as our Lord Jesus Christ in another way. Tin joins divided things into a union, since it is adhesive by nature. Christ has done something like this for us as well, if it is true that he "creates the two peoples into one new man, making peace and reconciling both in one body" into the union that comes through the Spirit. Hence he is also called the cornerstone, binding the two peoples into a union, as I said. He also joined those on earth to the angels, and, more than that, joined us through himself to God the Father, pulling down the sin that lay between us and had long walled us off.

And I answered and said to him: What are these two olive trees, on the right of the lampstand and on the left? And I asked a second time and said to him: What are the two branches of the olive trees that are in the hands of the two golden nozzles, which pour into and draw up the golden oil vessels? And he said to me: Do you not know what these are? And I said: No, lord. And he said: These are the two sons of fatness who stand beside the Lord of all the earth.

The mind of the saints is exceedingly eager to learn. So the Prophet passes over nothing shown in the vision. He is very inquisitive and asks carefully about each thing, wanting to know what it means. Since he was of this disposition, it had to be made plain through the voice of the Prophet [?] what the placing of the olive trees on the right and the left of the lampstand might symbolize. This is why he takes pains to learn. Notice how he adds a second question and even recasts the form of his question to make it more exact. At first he named two olive trees. But as he turned the eye of his mind more closely on what he saw, he no longer called them olive trees but rather branches of olive trees. To this skilful question the blessed angel at last replies and says: "These are the two sons of fatness who stand beside the Lord of all the earth." By sons of fatness he surely means the two peoples, Israel and the people from the Gentiles, as having been brought into spiritual fatness. This is why he says they were placed at the nozzles of the lamps. They rejoice and luxuriate in the oil that comes from Christ and are richly fattened by the grace of the Spirit. For we have received mercy, "being justified freely through faith," and have been made "partakers of his divine nature" by sharing in the Holy Spirit. So the two peoples are set and stand among oil and lamps. For our calling is in light, and, as it were, in the oil that comes from God. It is indeed accurate to say that we have received mercy, having been freed from death and sin and having released our necks from the old slavery. We have also been enlightened, since we acknowledge the one God who is God by nature and have come out of the darkness of the error of many gods.

But what might be the reason for this careful observation? What persuaded the blessed Prophet that he should no longer call them olive trees, but rather branches of olive trees? Come, let us look into it. The synagogue of the Jews has been called a cultivated olive, while the multitude of the Gentiles is a wild olive. This is how the blessed Paul also speaks of them when he says to the Gentiles who believed: "For if you were cut from what is by nature a wild olive and grafted, contrary to nature, into a cultivated olive, how much more will these, the natural branches, be grafted into their own olive tree." So the synagogue is the cultivated olive, as I just said, and the herd of the Gentiles is the wild olive. The one had the instruction of the law and did not remain fruitless. The others were dwellings of wild wasps, their minds full of demons, and they were wholly fruitless. Yet neither did the whole synagogue of the Jews accept faith in Christ, nor did the whole multitude of the Gentiles. But many, plucked as it were from each, have received mercy and been called through faith to the enlightenment that comes through the Spirit. Those who were broken off may therefore fittingly be understood as branches of olive trees. They have received mercy through grace and have come to be, as it were, in the light of the lampstand, that is, Christ, and of the seven lamps that shine together with it, that is, the multitude of the saints. Notice how the divine angel takes the lampstand as an image and figure of Emmanuel. The branches are set on its right and left, and he called them the two sons of fatness. He says that they stand beside the Lord of all the earth. Here the "standing beside" signifies very well their spiritual closeness and their readiness of mind to be subject to him and serve him. In this sense Christ might be understood as having presented to himself the Church gathered from the two peoples. In this way too, I think, the divine Moses was honoured with the term "standing beside," since God said to him: "But you, stand here with me." For instruction through the law is not rejected by God, who knows all things. Why? Because it leads us like a tutor to Christ, and in types and shadows, as it were, it is in labour with the truth itself for us. The Son himself will assure us of this when he says to the disobedient Jews: "If you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote about me."

And I turned and lifted up my eyes and looked, and behold, a flying sickle. And he said to me: What do you see? And I said: I see a flying sickle, twenty cubits long and ten cubits wide. And he said to me: This is the curse that goes out over the face of all the earth. For every thief will be punished by it to the point of death, and every perjurer will be punished by it to the point of death. And I will bring it out, says the Lord Almighty, and it will enter the house of the thief and the house of the one who swears falsely by my name. It will lodge in the midst of his house and destroy it, both its timbers and its stones.

Here again, I think, no one would take the words "I turned" to mean a change of place. They mean rather a change to another vision. The first vision was cut off, as it were, and his sight passed over to another contemplation, so he indicates what happened with the word "turning." He lifts the eyes of his mind on high, and then sees a sickle raised aloft like a bird and darting, as it were, over all the earth. It was very broad and long: twenty cubits in length and half that in breadth. When he asked again what it might be and said that he did not know, the angel said: "This is the curse that goes out over the face of all the earth." It inflicts on the perjurer, and with him on the thief, the penalties that fit them. As far as the plainer meaning of what was shown is concerned, there is no difficulty. A divine curse will in every way consume thieves and, besides them, those who are in the habit of swearing falsely. All but mowing the insolent down with a sickle, it makes them grass on the housetops and gives them as food to the fire. It will drive into the house of such a man, destroy it, and shake it down completely.

But I think we must eagerly inquire into the reasons why the present vision, which is now before us, has necessarily been brought in along with the others. A fair-minded person might ask: there are very many offences in life, and the people of Israel at that time stood under various charges, so why does he say that the punishment of the sickle hangs over thieves and perjurers alone? Why does the curse go out against them only, mowing down those it catches and destroying them completely? To this we reply that God spoke through the holy prophets whatever was useful for each time, and in this way always helped the present circumstances. So it was especially necessary that this vision be made clear to the people of that time. We will set out the reasons and show that it was most timely. The people of Israel had with difficulty left the land of the Chaldeans, thrown off the yoke of slavery, returned to Judea, and were living in Jerusalem. They should have kept away from those old offences. By turning back to better ways they should have set right what had gone before and gladdened their Redeemer by choosing to do what pleased him. Yet they were no different from what they had been before, and carelessly set aside what the law required. Moses had forbidden them to mingle with foreign women. But they cared little for what had been commanded. They became entangled with the daughters of the neighbouring nations, fathered foreign children, and once again filled the holy city with unholy seed. Even some of the more prominent among them were caught in such faults. When this happened, Ezra lamented, went to the divine house, and made supplication for those who had sinned. What happened next we shall learn from what he himself wrote. It reads as follows: "And while Ezra was praying and making confession, weeping and lying on the ground before the temple, a very great crowd gathered to him from Jerusalem, men and women and youths, for there was great weeping among the multitude. And Jechoniah son of Jeelus, of the sons of Israel, called out and said: Ezra, we have sinned against the Lord God, and we have married foreign women from the peoples of the land; and now all Israel is lifted up. In this matter let us take an oath to the Lord to put away all our wives of foreign race together with their children, as has been decided by you and by all who obey the law of the Lord. Arise and carry it out, for the matter is in your hands, and we are with you to act with strength. And Ezra arose and made the leaders of the priests and Levites of all Israel swear to do these things, and they swore." Since they had sworn to do what the law required, it was in some way necessary to make ready the curse that falls harshly on those who are in the habit of swearing falsely, so that they might keep what they had sworn.

Moreover, while the divine temple was being built, a great deal of money was collected, partly granted by Darius and partly brought in by the people. It was likely, then, that some of those appointed to manage such things would embezzle part of what had been brought for the glory of God. That is why he says, very aptly, that the curse also goes out against thieves. In this way they too would rise above shameful gain and would not lay hands on the sacred funds and spend them on their own needs. This, then, is the occasion of the vision. But I say that those who are in the habit of stealing or swearing falsely must fear the curse and the cutting of the sickle. They should bear in mind that God will in every way bring what he has decreed to fulfilment and will spare neither thieves nor the others. For he always holds in abhorrence those who despise his divine glory and those who with insatiable minds covet what in no way belongs to them.

And the angel who spoke in me went out and said to me: Lift up your eyes and see this thing that is going out. And I said: What is it? And he said: This is the measure that is going out. And he said: This is their iniquity in all the earth. And behold, a talent of lead was being lifted up; and behold, a woman was sitting in the midst of the measure. And he said: This is lawlessness. And he threw her into the midst of the measure, and threw the stone of lead into her mouth.

I said earlier, when I began explaining the Prophet, that after the return from Babylon he usefully relates to those who had been redeemed the things he had seen during the time of the captivity. He saw that they too were very negligent about doing what had been prescribed. They were turning aside without restraint to whatever was pleasant and dear to themselves, while caring very little for the laws given through Moses. They were entangled with foreign women, and some had already gone altogether beyond what was fitting and been initiated into the worship of idols, and besides this were doing things that should not even be spoken of. So the Prophet gives the necessary account of the visions. He wanted those who had barely been redeemed to know how many prayers of men and of holy angels it had taken to win them this boon, and that by becoming caught again in the grip of their old offences they were once more provoking the God of all against themselves.

He said, then, that the angel who spoke in me went out. But went out where? Where had he been at all? The going out, then, was from the showing of the sickle to the present vision, I mean the one about the measure. The Prophet raises his eyes on high, and it is fitting that eyes trained to soar on high should be able to behold divine mysteries. So he asked what it was that was being shown. And the angel said to him: "This is the measure that goes out. This is their iniquity in all the earth." We must consider what the measure is. We say that the Master of all is by nature kind and loving toward humanity. He bears patiently with those who offend and puts up with transgressors, waiting for each one to repent. But if someone goes on offending for a long time and finally reaches the end of the forbearance allotted to him, then at last he will be subject to punishment. He will have no excuse for such long negligence, and no one could rescue him from receiving penalties equal in measure to what he is shown to have done. Indeed Christ said somewhere to the crowds of the Jews, who were rushing in unbridled folly into every kind of outrage: "Fill up, then, the measure of your fathers." So what he saw was a measure, showing in itself that the people's offence had been filled up. A woman was seated in the measure, representing the figure of lawlessness. She filled its capacity by herself, as it were, and was perhaps even overflowing and peeping out over the top. "But behold," he says, "a talent of lead lifted up, and he threw it into her mouth." The vision fittingly depicts lawlessness for us in the form of a woman. For woman is a figure of pleasure and also of weakness. All lawlessness is committed in no other way than through some pleasure that lures us toward evil, with weakness of mind coming in as well. If the mind stood firm in itself and was manly, it would not choose to give way to the pull toward evil. But if it is softened and bewitched by pleasure, it will suffer what brings grief. So the woman is quite rightly depicted as lawlessness. The talent of lead that is lifted up and that stops her mouth could be understood, I think, as nothing other than our Lord Jesus Christ. He was lifted up on the precious cross, "bore our sins in his body on the tree," and triumphed over the bond that stood against us, so that, as the divine psalmist says, "all lawlessness shall stop its mouth." He too is likened to lead. As I said, lead is used by those accustomed to cast silver to purify what is being smelted. Such too is the power of Christ in us: if it enters the mind and heart, it melts away every impurity entirely. Some think that the lead was thrown into the mouth of lawlessness to show God stopping it up and no longer allowing it to cry out beyond measure against those who have sinned. This, they think, is why it is also enclosed in a measure: God, who has compassion on all, measures out, I think, the penalty for each case in proportion to the charges brought for the offences.

And I lifted up my eyes and looked, and behold, two women coming out, and there was wind in their wings, and they had wings like the wings of a hoopoe. And they lifted up the measure between the earth and the sky. And I said to the angel who spoke in me: Where are they taking the measure? And he said to me: To build a house for it in the land of Babylon and to prepare it; and they will set it there on its prepared place.

Before anything else, I think it necessary to say what the pair of women is meant to signify, or what they might be a figure of. The God of all said to the prophet Ezekiel: "Son of man, there were two women, daughters of one mother, and they played the harlot in Egypt. In their youth they played the harlot; there their breasts fell." He added to this, making his meaning clear: "And their names were Samaria, Oholah, and Jerusalem, Oholibah." At the beginning the synagogue of the Jews was one. But in the time of Rehoboam's reign, the ten tribes broke away from the rest and settled in Samaria. There they played the harlot with the golden heifers that Jeroboam son of Nebat had made. Yet the other, that is, Jerusalem, was not free of blame, for she too [?] in many ways. On the one hand, some worshipped idols and sacrificed to Baal, to Astarte, on the hills, and to the sun and moon and the other stars. On the other hand, they readily went into every kind of impurity and counted as nothing what had been commanded through the all-wise Moses.

So the vision again likens the two congregations of Israel to two women, and it says that they had wings like a hoopoe's. This shows very clearly the impure disposition within them and their readiness for every kind of outrage. The hoopoe is a well-known bird, but it loves filth and eats dung, it attacks swarms of worms in a frenzy, and its habit is always to take its pleasure in the worst uncleanness. Something like this is the mind of idolaters too. It does not go straight toward what is fitting. It strays outside what is reasonable, it does not know the divine law, it is full of every uncleanness, and it counts every kind of wickedness as pleasure. That is why the account of the vision said that the women had been fitted with hoopoe's wings: it teaches that they had the same disposition as that bird. And they take up the measure that is filled with lawlessness.

For each soul must be loaded with its own burden, the burden of sin, I mean. The charges against both were equal and of the same kind, against Samaria, I mean, and against Jerusalem. So both were weighed down in the same way by the measure and by the lawlessness. With wind falling on their wings, they are carried swiftly and without hindrance to the land of the foreigners, which is clearly the land of the Babylonians. The unclean spirit drove them on together into wrongdoing and loaded them with lawlessness, and so they were carried off into captivity and fell beneath the feet of their enemies. The blessed angel says that they are carrying the measure away to build a house for it in the land of Babylon. From this we must understand that Israel would spend a long time among its enemies. The sign of this is that a house is built for lawlessness, so that it gains, as it were, a settled seat and a fixed place among the enemies. And this did in fact come to pass, for they were released from the bonds of captivity only when the seventieth year had been completed.

And I turned and lifted up my eyes and looked, and behold, four chariots were coming out from between two mountains, and the mountains were mountains of bronze. In the first chariot were red horses, in the second chariot black horses, in the third chariot white horses, and in the fourth chariot dappled grey horses. And I answered and said to the angel who spoke in me, “What are these, Lord?” And the angel who spoke in me answered and said, “These are the four winds of heaven. They are going out to stand before the Lord of all the earth.” The chariot with the black horses went out toward the land of the north, and the white went out after them, and the dappled went out toward the land of the south. And the grey went out and were eager to go and travel throughout all the earth. And he said, “Go and travel throughout all the earth,” and they traveled throughout all the earth. And he cried out and spoke to me, saying, “Behold, those who go out toward the land of the north have set my wrath at rest in the land of the north.”

He showed beforehand that, caught in their own snares and bound tight by the cords of their own sins, as it is written, they went away to a foreign land and lived among enemies, enduring the unaccustomed yoke of slavery. But it was also necessary to mention the times of their redemption, and so he makes these known, with other matters woven in. For the Prophet was being taught, all at once, everything that would happen to the nation over the course of time. We say, then, that the four chariots between the bronze mountains are again the most famous of the kingdoms, those that arose at different times in the four regions, or winds, under heaven. By the bronze mountains I think he means the two divisions of the inhabited world, since some divide the whole earth into Europe and Asia. Its parts are bronze because they are always firmly set and unshaken and suffer no harm. For the divine David too sings somewhere to the Creator of all, “You established the earth, and it endures.” These kingdoms, then, which come as it were from the four winds, were mightier than the others, as we said, and won great renown, and they went out to stand before the Lord of all the earth. Their standing before him points to their servitude, for they were servants of his will. If they became strong and famous, they gained this too through him. And if they accomplished anything and conquered lands or cities, it was again by his consent that they rose to such strength.
