For if the prophet is telling the truth when he says, “There shall be no evil in a city which the Lord has not done,” and here we take “evil” to mean affliction, how could those kingdoms have prevailed over nations or lands unless he, again, in his providence granted them to prevail?

It is now time to say which kingdoms these are. In the first chariot, he says, were red horses. They represent in themselves the cruelty of the Chaldean kingdom. Redness would naturally suggest to us the shedding of blood, and the Babylonians were extremely bloodthirsty: they took Judea and the cities of Samaria and cast aside all mercy. In the second chariot were black horses. This seems to point to the kingdom of the Persians and Medes, the one under Cyrus, I mean. He has given these too a black color, because, I think, they hurled a vast and immeasurable death on the Chaldean nations and brought their whole land into mourning. And darkness would be a symbol of mourning and of death. He says that the horses in the third chariot were white, perhaps pointing to the dominion of the Greeks and Macedonians, that is, the kingdom of Alexander. They are white because the Greek nations live in luxury and for the most part wear white robes, and because they are clear in speech and lack the obscurity, so to speak, of barbarian tongues. In the fourth chariot, he says, were horses that were dappled and grey.

It should be noted that both the Hebrew text and certain other translators have put “strong” instead of “grey.” Even so, we say that this is the kingdom of the Romans. Those who have reigned over it from time to time have always had a varied gift for quick learning and a certain depth of mind. For those who have wielded the power of the Roman empire have been, and still are, extremely intelligent and, besides, extremely brave. And in order of time they are placed last, after the first ones.

Let us look also at the going out of each chariot, that is, of each kingdom: where it turned and against whom it goes. This will make the explanation of the meaning clearest for us. The Prophet says that there are four, but he mentions three, and he says nothing of the first one's going out. As I said, I will remind you briefly. He says that the horses in the first chariot were red. But he begins from the second and says, “The chariot with the black horses went out toward the land of the north, and the white went out after them, and the dappled went out toward the land of the south.” And even if we count the grey, he will not have mentioned four chariots, for we have granted that these are the same as the dappled, since he says, “In the fourth chariot were dappled grey horses.” So he does not mention four, having passed over the first in silence. What, then, is the reason for this whole arrangement? Come, let us explain it as best we can for the more teachable. We affirmed that the red horses are the bloodthirsty dominion of the Chaldeans. It swept away all Judea, burned its cities, and carried Israel off into captivity. We took the black to be the kingdom of the Persians and of Cyrus. And the kingdom of Alexander and the Macedonians was depicted in the white. Both of these made war on the land of the Chaldeans and took it by force: first Cyrus, then after him Alexander, who also defeated Darius himself near the place called Issus, a city of the Cilicians, and killed countless tens of thousands of Persians. They say, at any rate, that a great heap of the bones of those who fell there has been piled up, and that an inscription has been carved there with this meaning:

It was likely that Israel would be grieved not a little to hear about the kingdom of the Chaldeans, by which it had been laid waste. So the Prophet usefully passes over the account of them, so as not to seem to cause grief, and that at the wrong time. But what would most gladden them he sets out brilliantly: I mean what concerns the kingdom of Cyrus, and that of Alexander as well. These were all but sent to call the arrogance of the Chaldeans to account for its cruelty toward Israel. That is why he added, as if in the person of God, “Behold, those who go out toward the land of the north have set my wrath at rest in the land of the north.” For the land of the Chaldeans lies somewhat to the north, and the God of all was angry with the Babylonians. This too would become clear again when he says plainly, “I have been jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion with great jealousy, and I am very angry with the nations that join in the attack, because I was only a little angry, but they joined in to do harm.” Since the land of the Chaldeans paid the penalty, ravaged first by Cyrus together with the Persians and Medes, and after him by Alexander, he therefore says that “those who go out toward the land of the north have set my wrath at rest in the land of the north.” But although the prophet, by design, kept silent about the Chaldean invasion, for he passed over the red horses, as I said, he did not stay silent about the affairs of the Roman dominion. For the dappled, he says, went out toward the land of the south.

Notice how skilfully, and as if in passing, he gives the explanation of the passage. After the Savior's cross, Vespasian and his son Titus overran the land of the Jews. They stripped it completely bare and burned the holy city itself. And the Prophet aptly says, “They went out toward the land of the south,” for the land of the Jews lies very far to the south. These same dappled and grey horses were ordered to travel throughout the earth, and they did so, for they have ruled all that is under heaven and become lords of all the earth. God consented to this and kindled a brilliant glory in it for those who wield the power of the Romans, for, being God, he knew beforehand how great their piety would be.

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying, “Take the things from the captivity, from its rulers and from its useful men and from those who have come to know it. On that day you shall go into the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah, who has come from Babylon. You shall take silver and gold and make crowns, and you shall place them on the head of Jesus son of Jozadak, the high priest. And you shall say to him, ‘Thus says the Lord Almighty: Behold, a man whose name is Rising, and he shall rise up from beneath him, and he shall build the house of the Lord. He shall receive excellence, and he shall sit and rule upon his throne, and the priest shall be at his right hand, and there shall be a counsel of peace between them both. And the crown shall be for those who endure, and for its useful men, and for those who have come to know it, and for the favor of the son of Zephaniah, and for a psalm in the house of the Lord. And those far from them shall come and build in the house of the Lord, and you shall know that the Lord Almighty has sent me to you. And this shall be, if you truly listen to the voice of the Lord your God.’”

God's word was addressed to the blessed Prophet Zechariah, or rather through him to everyone, and it concerned Zerubbabel. He was of the tribe of Judah, and he led the people of Israel, since the royal tribe called him to this. We must first recall what God said about him. He said, then, “The hands of Zerubbabel laid the foundation of this house, and his hands shall complete it.” But with him, as he laid the foundation of the house and as he completed it, was Jesus son of Jozadak, the high priest. That is why the God of all commanded the divine Prophet to take the things from the captivity, from its rulers and from its useful men and from those who had come to know it. Who these people might be, and what the things from the captivity are, I will explain, since it is useful.

The people of Israel were brought back from the land of the Babylonians not in a disorderly crowd but in good order and arrangement. They came by clans and by tribes, with leaders set over them, as is written in Ezra. When they finally arrived in Jerusalem, since God was urging them to raise up the temple, they set up a treasury. There money could be collected to build the works, to provide the priests' vestments, and to pay for the sacrifices appointed for them by the law. Josiah son of Zephaniah was appointed treasurer of the money. So the God of all commands the Prophet to take gold and silver from what the rulers of the captivity had brought, which was stored with Josiah. Then he is to make crowns and place them on the head of Jesus son of Jozadak, the high priest, and say to him about Zerubbabel, “Behold, a man whose name is Rising.” For “rising” the Hebrew text has the word “shoot.” “And he shall rise up from beneath him”: that is, many shall spring up from his root. “He shall also receive excellence”: that is, comeliness, or glory, for the other translators have rendered it that way. To this he added that both of them, Jesus and Zerubbabel, would sit on the same throne. So the kingship would be shared by the one who holds the priestly service in his hands, and the priesthood would also belong to the one who reigns. And the two of them would have one counsel, a counsel of peace, so that they would never be seen to disagree in anything at all. Then he commanded that the crowns be brought into God's house as a splendid offering to him. In this way they would become a favor, or a source of pride, for those who had brought them: Josiah, I mean, and the useful men of the captivity and its rulers. And they were to be dedicated not in vain, but so as to give the singers and sacred psalmists of the temple a reason for song. For then, he says, those far from them also, that is, those from the other nations, will come and worship the Lord. These things will happen, he says, if they choose to adorn themselves with the beauty of obedience and to listen to the voice of the Lord God. And then, when what was foretold has finally been fulfilled, they will know clearly that the Prophet was sent to make God's will clear. He did not, like some who are in the habit of lying, speak things out of his own heart. Rather, he is truthful and no false messenger.

This, then, is the most ready and obvious explanation of the historical events. But if the matter is examined closely, no one could doubt that it reveals the mystery of Christ. We affirmed at the beginning that Christ is foreshadowed in Zerubbabel and also in Jesus: partly in each of them, and in both together, as one. For he is at once both king of Israel and great high priest, “holy, innocent, undefiled.” Those of the tribe of Judah occupied the thrones of the kingdom, while those of Levi were appointed to the priesthood, and it was not possible to see kingship and priesthood in one man. So Christ is wisely portrayed as one through the two. Therefore, when God says of Zerubbabel, “The hands of Zerubbabel laid the foundation of this house, and his hands shall complete it,” you will understand this historically of him, but you will refer the force of the mystery spiritually to Christ. For he has become our foundation, and on him we are all built up spiritually into a holy temple. He is our beginning and our end. For he presents us sanctified in the Spirit as a splendid and holy dwelling for himself and for the Father, with sin wholly taken away and corruption abolished. He is Jesus, as I said, the high priest. And the name Jesus is interpreted as “Salvation of the people.” This is how the divine Gabriel spoke to the holy Virgin: “And behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.” Jozadak is understood as “Righteousness of God,” for we have been justified in him through faith and have washed away the filth of our old offences. When we were captives, he rescued us and delivered us from spiritual slavery. He brought us back, as if from a foreign country and a land of strangers, out of the deception of demons into the knowledge of God, and into the beautiful city of the saints, the truly holy Jerusalem, which is the Church. That is why we crown him with right and blameless faith, with the glories of virtue, and with hymns of thanksgiving. The crowns of that time were of gold and silver and were made from perishable material. But the crowns that we weave and fasten on him have nothing earthly about them. They are made instead of the glory that befits God. For we offer him, as gold, the unerring contemplation of the doctrines concerning him, and, as silver, the spiritual brightness that comes from good works. In another sense, too, the salvation of those he has saved is Christ's crown and glory. And it is not one nation that has been saved, as Israel was long ago through Moses, but now the whole world under heaven, for this too was fitting for Christ. Notice also how the materials for making the crowns are brought from the rulers of the captivity, from its useful men, and from those who had come to know it. There are those who lead the peoples and have been appointed by God to such offices. There are those who know the manner of our former captivity and are useful to the redeemed, as guides and teachers who are able to admonish them and lead them well toward a life fully in keeping with the law. These are the ones who bring gifts on behalf of all, making up by their own efforts for the weaknesses of those who are unable.

When the crowns have been placed on the head of Jesus, these words are spoken to him about Zerubbabel: “Behold, a man whose name is Rising, and he shall rise up from beneath him.” You have seen Jesus crowned as priest. Now see him again pre-eminent, as in Zerubbabel, in royal glory as well. And understand that he is the Rising, that is, the Shoot, of whom the divine Isaiah says, “And a rod shall come up from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall come up from the root.” And we have blossomed from beneath him. For Christ has become the second root of humanity, that is, of those called through faith. He is not like the first root, by which I mean Adam, but incomparably better. For we no longer blossom toward corruption and death because of the curse, but toward life and incorruption, since our root is life itself, that is, Christ. He is “the vine, and we are the branches,” joined to him by spiritual communion. In the same way he is the rod and the shoot, that is, the new growth and the rising, while we have sprouted under him, grown up and blossomed into incorruption, as I said, and life. He built the house of the Lord. And he is full of all excellence, that is, of the glory most fitting for God. “His excellence covered the heavens, and the earth was full of his praise,” says the prophet Habakkuk. The wise John also wrote somewhere, “And we have seen his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.” He has sat upon a throne, for he reigns as God, shares the throne of his own Father, and rules all things together with him. He showed that Zerubbabel and Jesus, brought together as if into a unity, very clearly signify Christ when he added, concerning Zerubbabel, “And the priest shall be at his right hand,” that is, in honor and glory, “and there shall be a counsel of peace between them both.” For, as I have already said, the same one is at once king and high priest, so that he is portrayed through two as the one Emmanuel. Yet the labor of those who crown Christ is not without reward. Their fruitfulness will pass into an everlasting memory. He confirms that this word is true by adding, “And the crown shall be for those who endure, and for its useful men, and for those who have come to know it, and for the favor of Zephaniah, and for a psalm in the house of the Lord.” For the things brought will be a favor to those who dedicated them, and they will also become a reason for giving glory. For the piety of leaders becomes for others a road to love for God. And when Christ is crowned by us, then the flock of the nations too will run to know him. Those who were far off because of their error will be called through faith, and they will build in the house of God. What will they build? Themselves, clearly, as they are fitted together with the saints and joined in faith into unity with those of Israel. Christ is the cornerstone, and through himself he binds into one mind what was formerly divided. For he created “the two into one new man, making peace, and reconciling all things in his body to the [?]” [?] Since these things have been fulfilled, we bear witness that the holy prophets spoke the truth, and we know clearly that it was God in them who spoke and revealed to us beforehand the mystery of Christ.
On the Prophet Zechariah. Book Three.

And it came to pass in the fourth year of King Darius that the word of the Lord came to Zechariah on the fourth day of the ninth month, which is Chislev. And Sarasar and Arbeseer the king and his men sent to Bethel to propitiate the Lord, speaking to the priests who were in the house of the Lord Almighty and to the prophets, and saying: “Has the consecration come in here in the fifth month, as they have already done for a good many years?”

After the visions had been shown, further words came from God, once a short interval of time had passed. Before the visions it is written: “On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, which is the month Shebat, in the second year of Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo, the prophet, saying.” But in the passage now before us, another time, later than that one, is fixed: in the fourth year, on the fourth day of the ninth month, which is Chislev (in the language of the Hebrews, that is), the manner of divine revelation to the Prophet changed. What the occasion was, an account of the history will make very clear. Indeed, the sense of the passage cannot be grasped in any other way. Who, after all, were Sarasar and Arbeseer the king and the men with him? Surely we must learn this before anything else. And what is the “consecration” in the fifth month? Then there is the form of the question itself: what does it have in view, and what could the purpose of those asking it be?

Now, when Hoshea son of Elah was reigning over the ten tribes in Samaria and had turned far toward apostasy (for he worshiped idols), God was provoked against Israel. Then Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, marched against the land, took Samaria and carried Israel into exile, and arranged for some people from the land of the Chaldeans to settle the country, so that it might become Persian, since from then on it would have its inhabitants from there. You have the story in 2 Kings, where it is written: “In the twelfth year of Ahaz king of Judah, Hoshea son of Elah began to reign in Samaria over Israel for nine years. And he did what was evil in the sight of the Lord, yet not like the kings of Israel who were before him. Shalmaneser king of the Assyrians came up against him, and he became his servant.” And again, after other things: “And Israel was carried away from its own land to the Assyrians, to this day. And the king of the Assyrians brought people from Babylon, from Cuthah, from Avva, from Hamath and Sepharvaim, and they were settled in the cities of Samaria in place of the sons of Israel; and they inherited Samaria and dwelt in its cities.” These, then, who received the land of the Samaritans as their lot, settled the country, presumably had children, and inclined toward the customs of the Jews, terrified by the attacks of the lions. From them came Sarasar and Arbeseer. Arbeseer is also called king, because at that time he led those who had been resettled in Samaria from the land of the Persians.

So much for the men. Now, about the consecration, come, let us again say what is reasonable. Before Judea was taken by Nebuchadnezzar, the blessed prophet Joel had proclaimed in advance what was going to happen. He urged the priests to mourn, and the peoples under their charge as well, since Jerusalem was all but about to be trampled under the feet of enemies and the divine temple itself burned. He spoke thus: “Gird yourselves and lament, you priests; wail, you who minister at the altar; come, lie all night in sackcloth, you who minister to God, for sacrifice and drink offering are withheld from the house of our God. Sanctify a fast, proclaim a service, gather the elders, all who dwell in the land, into the house of our God, and cry out earnestly to the Lord: Alas, alas, for [?]” So the prophet. How what had been foretold was brought to pass I will again make clear by setting out the sacred text itself. It is written thus in 2 Kings: “In the fifth month, on the seventh day of the month (this was the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon), Nebuzaradan the chief cook, who stood before the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem and burned the house of the Lord and the house of the king and all the houses of Jerusalem; every house the cook burned.” Then he appointed Gedaliah over the people of Israel who were left; and in the seventh month Ishmael son of Nethaniah, son of Elishama, of the royal line, came upon him, overpowered him and killed him. For so it is written. Since, then, it happened that Jerusalem was taken and the temple burned in the fifth month, on the seventh day, and that Gedaliah also died in the seventh month, the remnant of the Jews, perhaps moved to remember the prophet’s words, made it a rule that everyone from the whole surrounding region should go up to Jerusalem in the fifth month, on the seventh of the month, to sanctify a fast and make lamentation as over a corpse, to bewail the temple lying, as it were, dead, and to pour out over the burned city the tears of belated regret. They thought they had very wisely found a form of worship pleasing to God. This was practiced while Israel still lay under the yoke of captivity and the divine temple had received no care at all.

But when they had come back, leaving the land of the Persians and Medes, and had settled in the holy city and then rebuilt the divine temple, it somehow seemed to them that the custom was no longer being kept at the proper time or fittingly. For in view of what had happened they ought rather to have turned to gladness, to keep festivals and send up songs of thanksgiving to the one who had called them to freedom. Being in doubt, then, the men we are speaking of, Sarasar and Arbeseer, send some people to ask the priests and the prophets: “Has the consecration come in here in the fifth month, as they have already done for a good many years?” That is: have those who are accustomed to mourn in Jerusalem come together, and will they themselves still accept the custom, which had arisen as a kind of consecration, even though the divine temple had been raised up and the captivity brought to an end? For, as I said, they sanctified a fast, as they had done for many years. While Israel was in captivity, they too had kept on observing the season of mourning and sanctifying the fast, as I said before. So the question is that of people in doubt: must the consecration and the mourning still be observed even after the rebuilding of the temple, or should they now refrain from it, since the cause of the mourning had been removed?

And the word of the Lord of hosts came to me, saying: Say to all the people of the land and to the priests: If you fasted or lamented in the fifth months or in the seventh, and look, for seventy years, was it for me that you fasted the fast? And if you eat or drink, is it not you who eat and you who drink? Are these not the words which he spoke by the hand of the former prophets, when Jerusalem was inhabited and prosperous, with her cities round about her, and the hill country and the lowland were inhabited?

Some people, as I said already, asked the priests and the prophets about the so-called consecration. Then God answers, presumably because the priests and prophets had offered up prayers and earnestly sought a wise answer for those who had chosen to inquire into such matters. What, then, is the word from God? It is brief and yet long, with nothing intricate about it, but, so to speak, plain and readily giving knowledge of what is profitable. “What does it matter,” he says, “even if perhaps you have fasted in the fifth and the seventh months? Or what achievement of virtue is it at all to wail ignorantly over burned stones and timbers? How could God take pleasure in what you do, when you have done nothing of what is needed for your good, and yet suppose that you are achieving the best of all things? If I had need of such a fast, and womanish wailing deserved praise, why,” he says, “have you passed this seventieth year without fasting?” For while they were still living among the Babylonians they did not keep a public fast, nor would they be found to have been eager to carry out any of the other customary observances, those, that is, according to the law of Moses. “How then,” he says, “did I have mercy on you and rescue you from the hand of your rulers? So I have no need of such a fast. In the same way, if you choose to eat and drink,” he says, “you are gratifying yourselves rather than me.” So when someone fasts at random and for no useful purpose, the tears are profitless and the sweat goes unrewarded. Are these not the words of the former prophets, when Jerusalem was inhabited and prosperous, abounding in good things and still boasting of her own cities unharmed, both in the hill country and in the lowland? For the prophet Joel said that the priests and the peoples ought to lament and, besides this, to sanctify a fast. And the aim of that exhortation was to call them to repentance. He did not want you to wait until you experienced what happened, so as to lament the temple once it was burned, but rather, as I said, before the experience, to appease God with wailing and lamentation and so escape the evils. Are these not, then, the words of the former prophets? You have not understood them, and so you bewail in vain and drip tears of ignorance on fallen stones, when you ought to correct the path of your own way of life and walk the glorious and blameless road, firmly resolved to carry out what the law approves.

And the word of the Lord came to Zechariah, saying: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Judge righteous judgment, and show mercy and compassion each to his brother; and do not oppress [?] the orphan, the stranger and the poor; and let none of you bear malice in your hearts against his brother.

Having discredited the mourning as useless and unprofitable, and ridiculed their pointless sweat, he now leads them to what contributes most of all to their good. He makes the path of the way of life that pleases him clear and evident, and, as it were, brings to light the meaning both of the law itself and of the prophetic preaching. For the lawgiver delights in right and blameless judgment. He holds mercy and mutual love in the highest and most earnest esteem; he deems worthy of praise love toward orphans and kindness toward women weighed down by widowhood; but he shakes off greed as profane, along with any crushing of the weaker, and he wants those who have chosen to share his mind to be kind and free of malice. Christ himself said somewhere: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven.” And indeed he taught those who pray to say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors; and lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.” For the compassionate God remits the offenses of those who remit others’, but “the ways of those who bear grudges lead to death,” as is written in the book of Proverbs. And that love contains the fulfillment of the whole law, how could anyone doubt, since the inspired Paul wrote just that? The things mentioned above are the fruits of love, and whoever practices them is an exact keeper of the law.

But they refused to pay heed, and turned a senseless back, and made their ears heavy so as not to hear, and set their heart in disobedience so as not to hear my law and the words which the Lord Almighty sent by his Spirit through the hands of the former prophets. And great wrath came from the Lord Almighty. And it shall be that, just as he spoke and they did not listen to him, so they will cry out and I will not listen to them, says the Lord Almighty; and I will cast them out among all the nations whom they have not known, and the land shall be made desolate behind them, with no one passing through or returning; and they made a choice land a desolation.

By these words he has made it fully certain that it was they themselves who never stopped provoking the Judge of all against themselves. They could have been persuaded by the words of the holy prophets, cast as far from themselves as possible their stubborn resistance to the will of the lawgiver, chosen instead a glorious and fully lawful life, and walked the blameless path. Instead they became hard, held their instructor of no account, and kept their heart unbending and unyielding. They never stopped outrageously insulting the divine words and fiercely and impiously rebuking those who conveyed them, the ones who exercised the office of prophecy, even though they spoke in the Holy Spirit. They sank to such savagery and incorrigible folly that they would not choose to repent until what had been foretold came to pass for them, and they fell under what divine wrath brought upon them. And when God says here, “I will cast them out among all the nations, and the land shall be made desolate, with no one passing through or returning,” let us understand that these things too are spoken in the manner of prophetic prediction. For they had been cast out to the Persians and Medes and had already experienced captivity; the land had been laid waste, and the best of all countries had been made, as the text says, a desolation, with no one passing through or returning. Some had been consumed by war, while others, weighed down by the yoke of slavery, had been driven into captivity. So let us understand these words too as joined with the rest in the manner of prediction. That disobeying the divine words is harmful, or rather brings ruin, anyone could see from what befell the people of old. Nor would long arguments be needed to prove it: the matter is clear to everyone, at least to anyone who has once known the good things that come from obedience.

And the word of the Lord Almighty came to me, saying: Thus says the Lord Almighty: I have been jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion with great jealousy, and with great wrath I have been jealous for her.

Having sufficiently condemned the disobedience and unruliness of the earlier generations, on the evidence of what happened to them, and having shown that it was the cause of all their evils, he moves the discourse on to the blessings that come from his gentleness. He now undertakes to promise them times of prosperity and to enrich them abundantly with all the good things they could wish for, since they had already paid the penalty for their impious outrages and had, as it were, washed away the charges of their former wickedness by being punished among their enemies and enduring the yoke of slavery. He cries out, as it were, against the cruelty of the Babylonians, who went beyond all bounds of audacity and did to them what not even the divine wrath itself had wanted. For he said plainly: “I was angry a little, but they joined in to do evil.” “I have been jealous for Jerusalem,” that is, I have taken up zeal on her behalf, “and with great wrath I have been jealous for her.” It is as if he said: It will befall the Babylonians in their turn to suffer harsher things than they did, and I will bring the effects of my wrath upon those who ravaged her so.

Christ fulfilled this. Grieved over us who were wretchedly perishing, and, as it were, jealous for the Church, which was foreknown to him but not yet revealed in the world, he crushed the hosts of demons, cast the overseer of their madness out of his tyranny over us, and, subjecting him to the stirrings of his wrath, made the assembly of those who worship him free from that one’s perversity from then on.
Thus says the Lord: I will return to Zion and dwell in the midst of Jerusalem, and Jerusalem shall be called a true city, and the mountain of the Lord Almighty a holy mountain.

God fills all things, and all things are full of his ineffable nature. Yet he is sometimes said to depart from those who have sinned, not by being divided by distances of place (it would be utterly foolish to think that), but by no longer being willing to stay close to them and grant them his kindness and love. This, we say, is also what his wrath is like. Israel turned to false worship, and Jerusalem played the harlot. And the God of all, as it were, departed and handed them over to the evils that come from his turning away. But since he now has pity on them, he says, “I return,” that is: I will cease from my wrath, I will show her to be worthy of my care, and I will make her my house again. And just as, when he had turned away, the holy mountain, that is, the temple in Jerusalem, no longer seemed in any way venerable to those who saw it burned, so again, when God chooses to dwell in it and it has been raised up, the reverence paid to it will rise again and be renewed. And Jerusalem will be true again, no longer offering worship, as in the past, to hand-carved gods and falsely named idols, but serving the one God, who is true by nature, with uprightness, since she will from then on choose to live according to the law and to be obedient in everything.

You might fittingly apply such words to the Word, who for our sake became like us. Being in the form of the one who begot him and equal to him in every respect, “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,” and became man, and “became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might become rich.” So he who of old had justly turned away, because of the transgression in Adam and because “the mind of man is bent on evil from his youth,” returned to us out of his innate gentleness, came to dwell in the Church, and made those who have been sanctified his city and his holy abode. For he said somewhere about her, clearly meaning the Church: “Here I will dwell, for I have chosen her.” And the blessed David sings: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, O city of God.” The prophet Isaiah also pointed her out to us, saying: “In the last days the mountain of the Lord shall be manifest, and the house of God on the tops of the mountains, and it shall be exalted above the hills, and all the nations shall come to it.” For the Church of Christ is visible from all around, and, as though set on a mountain, she is known to people everywhere. She is also called true, because she does not worship in types and shadows at all, but has instead received the truth, which is Christ, and offers worship in spirit and truth.

Thus says the Lord Almighty: Old men and old women shall again sit in the streets of Jerusalem, each with his staff in his hand because of the great number of his days; and the streets of the city shall be filled with boys and girls playing in its streets.

When war had consumed the Jewish nation, their cities inevitably became empty of inhabitants, and their houses, along with the beauty of their buildings, were to be seen thrown down. But see, he promises to grant them a long and much longed-for peace, which the children of the Greeks quite rightly call the “nurse of the young.” For peace brings those who are born to maturity, and for those already young it, as it were, smooths the road to old age, with no one ravaging, no war crushing, no battle consuming. We must suppose, then, and quite rightly, that in peace cities, however broad and long they may be, turn out to be cramped and are outmatched by the number of their inhabitants. Such is the meaning that the passage once again brings forth for us. For he said that old men and old women will sit in the streets of Jerusalem, barely relieving a little the weakness of age with a staff, and holding a stick to guide their old age. The thing is a commendation of times free of war and of deep peace, which, as I said, brings infants to maturity and sends to old age those who are already grown men and have run through the whole span of their lives without battle. And if lads are to dance in the city and little girls to dance in the middle of the streets, this too would be clear proof that no bitter care hung over them. For they would not have put up with anyone playing if it were a time of gloom.

Christ, too, has become peace for us. He has crushed every war and made the Church full of saints. In her there are those gray-haired in mind, countless and outstanding, to whom the wise John writes, saying: “I have written to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning.” And the more childlike multitude of those newly come to faith are like boys not yet grown and little girls; with their spiritual leaping they all but adorn the truly holy city, that is, the Church. To them it would be fitting to say: “Come, let us rejoice in the Lord, let us shout aloud to God our Savior.” And if the old men are said to lean on a staff, you will perceive that Christ supports both small and great: he is the rod from Jesse, and the one called the rod of power, which God the Father [?] for us out of the Zion above, so that we rejoice in it and say: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me.”
Thus says the Lord Almighty: If it seems impossible in the sight of the remnant of this people in those days, will it also be impossible in my sight? says the Lord Almighty.

Things that are great and beyond nature tend somehow to meet with disbelief, and the way they come to fulfilment is a marvel. Sarah, for example, laughed in disbelief at the promise of Isaac, because she looked at her old age and set the impossibility of it against the laws of human nature. Yet she gave birth beyond hope, because God made the thing possible for her. It was therefore quite natural that those who had been redeemed from captivity should be shaken by doubts, and should not feel very confident that their affairs would come to such prosperity that Jerusalem would be filled with old people, that choirs of boys and dancing girls would be seen in it, and that they would enjoy the blessings of deep peace. For they saw the walls thrown down and the houses burned, and all the cities round about had become the lairs of wild beasts, because they had been completely emptied of their inhabitants. The fields, once so fertile and full of flowers, were full of thorns and bore no harvest, and the whole race of country people had perished entirely. So, as I said, it was natural for them to doubt that what had been promised would ever be fulfilled for them. That is why God does not let them waver. He bids them take courage and confirms his word, saying: If it is impossible in the sight of the remnant of this people in those days, will it also be impossible in my sight? says the Lord Almighty. What is impossible for us is very easily accomplished by God, who is able to do all things. For he is the Lord of hosts, who by his mere will fulfils even what is utterly beyond nature and brings his purpose to completion without delay.

Somewhere too God the Father spoke to the Jews, proclaiming in advance the achievements that would come from the coming of our Saviour: "Look, you despisers, and see, and perish, for I am working a work in your days, a work that you will not believe if anyone tells it to you." As far as our human reasoning goes, the very mystery of the Incarnation is beyond wonder and beyond words, and no less so the achievements that have resulted from it for us. For is it not close to unbelievable that the Word begotten of God should be united to flesh, take the form of a slave, endure the cross, and bear insults and abuse and the injuries inflicted by the folly of the Jews? Or how could anyone not marvel at the outcome of the dispensation, in which sin has been destroyed, death abolished, corruption driven away, and man, once a runaway, is now seen made glorious by the grace of adoption? So let Christ say about these very things: If it is impossible in the sight of the remnant of this people in those days, will it also be impossible in my sight? For to him everything is smooth and open road, and when he wishes to accomplish anything needful, nothing, I think, could ever stand in his way.

Thus says the Lord Almighty: Behold, I will save my people from the land of the east and from the land of the west, and I will bring them in, and I will dwell in the midst of Jerusalem; and they shall be my people, and I will be their God, in truth and in righteousness.

In the past God did save those of the blood of Israel who had been scattered by war, gathering them together to Jerusalem and dwelling among them, in that he had them raise up the divine temple and allowed them once more to appease him with the sacrifices of the law, to fulfil their vows and to keep their feasts. But to say that he saves his own people from east and west would rightly befit Emmanuel, who called the whole world under heaven, drawing in by faith, as in a net, those from the ends of the earth, and gathering every flock of the nations into the truly holy and renowned city, "which is the church of the living God," the heavenly Jerusalem. And how could it be anything but true to say that he dwelt in its midst? For he became like us and "lived among men" in the flesh. God foretold this to us through another prophet, saying: "Take courage, Zion, let your hands not grow slack; the Lord your God is in you; the Mighty One will save you; he will bring gladness upon you and [?] you in his love." And he is with us still now. For he has not left us orphans; he has sent us the Paraclete in his place, and through him he is present with those who love him. He gives us full assurance, saying: "Behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age." So we have become his people, we who once were not a people, we who once served stones. Loathing that ancient and profane error, we have enrolled ourselves under him as our God, and that in truth and righteousness. For we do not cling to types and shadows, as the lovers of the letter do. Rather, we have received into mind and heart the splendour of the gospel preaching, and so we offer the true worship; and holding fast to the righteousness that pleases him, we offer worship in spirit. For "God is spirit," as the Son himself says, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.

Thus says the Lord Almighty: Let your hands be strong, you who in these days hear these words from the mouth of the prophets, from the day when the house of the Lord Almighty was founded and from when the temple was built.

The God of all often promises those who love him things beyond hope, but he never speaks falsely. By his own power and by certain ineffable workings he accomplishes in due season whatever he wills, and with no effort at all. It befits us, then, who are not weak in faith, to bear witness to him in every way and at every point that he can easily accomplish all things; and to act manfully in the works by which we shall become illustrious and win the glorious crown of goodness; and to obey his words, and to be eager to take as our guides those who in each age are the most unerring bearers of the divine oracles to us. Our Lord Jesus Christ also promised through the holy prophets the blessings of the Incarnation, and as far as human thought goes, his words, in describing the greatness of these gifts, came, as I said, not far from seeming incredible. But by faith we have accepted what is beyond nature; and turning our minds to these supernatural works, we have in a way offered the neck of our understanding to the teachers of godliness, pliant and easy to guide. And the time fitting for this bestowal of good things, and for our own submission, is the manifestation of the Church. For see how the God of all commanded those before us too to be strong and to carry out their works and to obey the words of the prophets, from the day when the house of the Lord Almighty was founded and from when the temple was built.

For before those days the wages of men will not be for profit, and the wages of beasts there are none; and for the one who goes out and the one who comes in there will be no peace from affliction; and I will send out all people, each against his neighbour.

The Hebrew text does not put these words in the future tense but uses the past. For before those days, it says, the wages of men were not for profit, and the wages of beasts there were none; and again, For the one who went out and the one who came in there was no peace; and instead of saying, And I will send out all people, they have put, I sent out all people. This reading is very plausible, and the sense of the passages will show what is accurate here. For it means something like this. Those of Israel had come from Babylon to the holy city. But they had no place for a sanctuary, since the former temple had been demolished; there was no sacrifice and no libation, since no altar was standing. Then the God of all urged them to make what was so necessary for them their foremost concern: to build the temple and to set up again the divine altar in it, so that they might properly perform what the law prescribed and appease the God of all. But they made all kinds of excuses, sometimes pretending a shortage of money, sometimes pleading the obstruction of those who were hindering the building. Then, because they offended God in this, they were struck by frequent and repeated blows, I mean crop failures, blights caused by wind, and the attacks and raids of the neighbouring nations. The God of all reproached them for their idleness, speaking thus through the voice of the prophet Haggai: "This people says, The time has not come to build the house of the Lord. Is it time for you to live in panelled houses, while the house of the Lord has not been built?" Since, as I said, they had grown slack from idleness, they were often struck by lack of necessities and by wars with their neighbours. But once they had raised up the temple, the effects of wrath ceased, they had plenty of everything, and great prosperity lay before them. That is why he says that before those days, that is, before the temple was raised, the wages of men were not for profit, and the wages of beasts there were none. For the farmers went without wages; gathering nothing at all, they left the fields along with their exhausted oxen. Nor was there peace for those going out or coming in. By those coming in and going out he means those who travel from city to city, sometimes because they have a trade to pursue, or else for other reasons. Even for them there was no peace, since, as I said, the neighbouring nations had grown frenzied against Israel, and each man looked on his blood relative, or even his brother or his neighbour, as one of his worst enemies.

It should be understood that before the Only-begotten became man and the Church was manifested, there were no wages for man, nor indeed for beasts. For those in this life who were more rational and had a reputation for understanding, who might indeed be counted as men, had a zeal for learning that was unprofitable and useless: they neither wrote anything needful, nor were they able to understand it or speak it to others. Likewise those who led a herd-like and bestial life remained without wages, for it was not possible to do anything praised by God. Nor was there any peace at all on earth, since the horde of demons was throwing everything into confusion and filling the earth with turmoil, so that everyone's affairs, and indeed their minds, were as if shaken and tossed about, with nothing stable.

And now I will not deal with the remnant of this people as in the former days, says the Lord Almighty; but I will show peace: the vine will give its fruit, and the earth will give its produce, and the heaven its dew; and I will give all these things as an inheritance to the remnant of my people.

Together with his anger he also removes what follows from it, and he says that the punishments will pass away together with the times of transgression. For now that sin has ceased, or rather now that Israel has already paid the penalty for it, he says that their misfortunes will come to an end, and very reasonably, and that the onslaught of distress will no longer prevail. For his purposes for them are not like the former ones, but all tend toward gentleness. This was the bestowal of peace and an abundant supply of the most delightful things, so that the vine would be seen rich in clusters, and the ploughland, thick with crops, would repay the farmers' sweat, with heaven, of course, almost working along with it and enriching the fields and all that is in them with dew. For heaven and earth, and in a word all creation, will certainly follow the Master's nod. These things are Israel's portion, as God widens their prosperity and frees them from everything that naturally causes grief.

The passage at this point would also fit Christ, the Saviour of us all. For before the time of his coming each of us walked according to what seemed good to himself, living a bestial and utterly irrational life, yoked to the deceptions of the demons. But when the Father took pity on us, who had all but been sold, thrown to the ground, and trodden under the feet of enemies, he no longer dealt with us as in the former days. For he no longer allowed us to be exploited and to live under a cruel tyrant who carried us off into every kind of the most shameful deeds. Rather, he gave us the peace from heaven, that is, Christ, who has also granted us an abundant supply of every spiritual fruitfulness. For we have been filled with grain and wine, and the true vine, that is, Christ, has given us its own fruit, which gladdens the heart of man, as it is written. He himself, being both the grain of wheat and the holy sheaf, has been shown to be for us the bread of life. And he has made us flourish abundantly, enriching us with dew from heaven, clearly the spiritual dew given through the Spirit, which the divine David also mentions, saying: "Like the dew of Hermon that comes down on the mountains of Zion." These things are given us by God as our allotted portion and our good share, since we have become Israel, that is, a mind that sees God; for we have beheld the Father in the Son.
And it shall be that, just as you were a curse among the nations, O house of Judah and house of Israel, so I will save you, and you shall be a blessing. Take courage, and let your hands be strong.

When those of Israel became captives and fell prey to the greed of their conquerors, they were even called accursed, since some people, naturally enough, would say, "May I never become like Israel." But when the compassionate God saved them and they returned to their former blessings, they cast off, together with their misfortunes, the reputation of being accursed. For they were blessed, and became no less enviable than in former times, as God gladdened them with blessings from above and granted them a share in every joy.

This same thing may be seen to hold true of us as well. For we were accursed, yoked under the hordes of demons and dragged down to every kind of wickedness by their perversity. But when we came to know God, the Creator of all, and were known by Christ, then indeed we were taught to sing of ourselves: "Blessed are we by the Lord, who made heaven and earth." And since we have been called to such honour and glory, we must be diligent, master our passions, hate sin, and shine in keeping the laws of the gospel, so as to be eager to accomplish what pleases Christ. For we have heard him call out to us, Take courage, and let your hands be strong; and we have received from Christ the reason why we ought to take courage. For he has conquered the world on our behalf, trampled our enemies, shown his own temple to be stronger than death, and stopped the mouth of lawlessness, so that we too, through him, might share in these victories. For, as I said, he conquered not for himself so much as for us, the weak, securing for us the blessings of his victory.

For thus says the Lord Almighty: Just as I purposed to do you harm when your fathers provoked me to anger, says the Lord Almighty, and I did not relent, so I have set myself in array and purposed in these days to do good to Jerusalem and to the house of Judah. Take courage. Here again he lets us understand that nothing can withstand the divine purposes or counsels. For whatever God plans and chooses to carry out will certainly come to pass and reach the end he intends. So he says somewhere also through the voice of Isaiah, showing the almighty power of his nature: "And I said, My every counsel shall stand, and all that I have planned I will do." So from what they suffered when divine wrath was brought upon them, from those very things it is possible to understand, and very clearly, that the path of joy too is being widened for them, since he wills and permits them to prosper, or rather, in his love for mankind, holds out to them the prospect of enjoying every good thing. For, he says, just as nothing held me back when I wished to harm you because of your many sins, so too, now that I am planning good things and wish to have pity on you who have suffered enough, nothing will stand in the way. For I have set myself in array to do good to Jerusalem and to the house of Judah. The wording is very expressive. For he did not say only, I have planned and perhaps purposed, but that I have come to such a resolve and such gentleness toward you that I have even set myself in array. This is a clear indication of an intense resolve. And he seals the promise as true by adding, Take courage.

In the same way Christ gives assurance to us too, who have been called through faith to the knowledge of the truth. For just as, before our calling, when we had slid into every kind of wickedness, he handed us over to a debased mind and afflicted us because of our impurity, so too in these days he has purposed and, as he himself says, set himself in array to do good to the Church and to the house of Judah, that is, to us who confess him and honour him with praises as Master, Saviour and Redeemer; for Judah is interpreted as "praise." The house of Judah could also be understood as the Church in another way. For it has been called the house of Christ, who "arose from Judah," and he is called so in the divinely inspired Scripture as well. The patriarch Jacob, for instance, mentions him in this way, saying: "Judah, may your brothers praise you," and again: "From a shoot you have come up, my son Judah." For Christ sprang up from the root of Jesse, and from the holy Virgin as from a shoot, "a glorious staff and the rod of majesty," in the words of the prophet. So the words Take courage will also be spoken to us, and very fittingly. For the Father has crowned us "with the shield of his good pleasure" through the salvation and grace that come through Christ.

These are the words that you shall do: speak the truth, each to his neighbour; render peaceable judgment in your gates; let none of you devise evil against his neighbour in your hearts; and do not love a false oath. For all these things I hate, says the Lord Almighty.

It is not to those who choose to disobey and are in the habit of falling away into a corrupt way of life that God promises to bestow the blessings that come from his gentleness, and to set himself in array to do them good from now on. It is rather to those who love to walk the way pleasing to him and have chosen to live in holiness. For he has commanded that they should by no means be found speaking falsely, but should rather speak with truthfulness; that they should love uprightness in [?], and in every matter deliver a verdict that is straight and blameless in every way, not overcome by shameful gains or looking to dishonest profit and corrupting the grace of justice for the sake of money, but looking only to what pleases God; that they should forgive their brothers if ever they stumble in deed or word; and in addition that they should firmly reject false swearing. For he declares emphatically that he hates such evils. Notice how he commands nothing to be done of what belongs to shadows or types. He does not command the sacrifice of oxen or honour with incense; rather, he wants us to practise a life that is, so to speak, spare and finely wrought, all but evangelical. For since no small part of the discourse here has concerned the coming of our Saviour, it is natural that a commandment should be introduced along with it, voicing the precepts given through him. For if we must follow the divine words and speak the truth, we shall certainly speak of the things of Christ; for Christ is the truth. That is why the most wise Peter also commanded us to be fully ready "to make a defence to anyone who asks us for an account of the hope that is in us." And those who are accustomed to speak of the things of Christ, who always have him on their tongue and have made him the study of mind and heart, would surely be righteous and distinguished by uprightness in every respect, peaceable and gentle and, besides this, patient under wrong, not knowing how to swear falsely, or rather not swearing at all. For they remember him saying: "Let your word be yes, yes, and no, no; anything more than this comes from the evil one."

And the word of the Lord Almighty came to me, saying: Thus says the Lord Almighty: The fast of the fourth month, and the fast of the fifth, and the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth shall become for the house of Judah joy and gladness and good feasts; and you shall rejoice, and you shall love truth and peace.

I think it is necessary for the studious first to explain the reasons for the fasts mentioned here: which the fourth is, and which the fifth, and the seventh and tenth that follow them. In this way we shall bring out, at the proper point and in good order, the force of what is commanded. After the holy city had been captured and the temple burned, and Israel carried off captive together with the sacred vessels, those who had been saved and left behind in Judaea regarded the days on which these things had happened as ill-omened and hateful; and gathering in crowds, they beat their breasts and lamented, going without food as on fasts. So what were these events, and what happened on each of the days we have just named? Come, let us tell it from the sacred writings.

Blessed Jeremiah says: "And it came to pass in the ninth year of his reign" (clearly meaning Zedekiah's) "in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came against Jerusalem with all his army. They put up a palisade around it and built around it with squared stones on every side, and the city was under siege until the eleventh year of King Zedekiah, in the fourth month, on the ninth day of the month. The famine grew severe in the city, and there was no bread for the people of the land. Then the city was breached, and all the men of war went out by night by way of the gate between the wall and the outer wall, which was by the king's garden." Then, after recording in between the slaughter of Zedekiah's sons and his own blinding, he says again: "In the fifth month, on the tenth day of the month, Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, who stood before the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem. He burned the house of the Lord and the house of the king and all the houses of the city, and every great house he burned with fire; and the army of the Chaldeans that was with the captain of the guard tore down every wall around Jerusalem." You hear how Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem in the tenth year. He then says that the city was breached in the fourth month of the eleventh year, and he affirms that in the fifth month the temple itself and the whole city were burned by the captain of the guard. So they made the fourth, the fifth and the tenth into days of ill omen, carrying the names of the months over to the days. We must also explain what the seventh was. When the captain of the guard had taken Jerusalem, he appointed Gedaliah as governor over the Jews who were left in Jerusalem, and having done this he departed for Babylon. When the Jews who had survived learned that this had been done, they gathered in Jerusalem, hoping to go on living in the land. But in the seventh month, as it is written, Ishmael killed Gedaliah. Then all the people were scattered and fled to Egypt, and there they perished. So for this reason they made the seventh day hateful too, and that whole month as well. This, then, was the reason for the fasts. But once the effects of wrath had ceased, and Israel had been brought back to Jerusalem, and the days of gloom had passed, it was fitting that they should no longer fast and lament. So he commands them to turn their mourning into gladness and to rejoice instead in what they had received from God; or rather, to keep in memory the things for which they had been punished at various times, when they sinned without restraint and slid shamelessly into every kind of outrage.

Christ has done this for us too. "For he turned our mourning into joy; he tore off our sackcloth and girded us with gladness," in the words of the psalmist. We do not dwell at all on accusing ourselves because once, not knowing God and worshiping the creature instead of the Creator, we fell under the feet of our enemies and into a debased mind. Rather, we give thanks that we have received mercy and been saved, that we have been redeemed from the hand of our enemies, that we dwell in the holy city, that is, the Church, and that we have been counted worthy from now on to honor him with prayers and spiritual sacrifices. And we love, as it were, peace and truth, and we have been taught by the divinely inspired Scripture to count this a cause of the highest gladness. "For he is our peace"; he, as I said, is the truth; and through him we live in good hopes and ought to rejoice, now that all dejection has been taken away.

Thus says the Lord Almighty: Many peoples will yet come, and the inhabitants of many cities, and the inhabitants of five cities will gather into one city, saying, "Let us go to entreat the face of the Lord and to seek the face of the Lord Almighty; I too will go." And many peoples and many nations will come to seek the face of the Lord Almighty in Jerusalem and to propitiate the face of the Lord.

When Christ transforms our mourning into joy, into a feast and into good gladness, and turns our lamentations into delight, those called to salvation will no longer, he says, approach one by one in faith and draw near to God through sanctification. Instead, cities will urge one another on to this, and all the nations will come in multitudes, those who come second always calling out to those who arrived first, "I too will go." For it is written, "Iron sharpens iron, and a man sharpens the face of another." The eagerness of some is always found to be a spur to others to accomplish what is good. And what is the aim of these cities, or nations? To propitiate and to seek the face of the Lord, that is, Christ, who is the exact image of God the Father and, as it is written, "the imprint of his being and the radiance of his glory." Of him the inspired David also says, "Make your face shine upon your servant." For the image and, as I said, the face of God the Father has shone upon us. With him gracious and merciful toward us, we shall also ward off the harm that comes from sin, being justified through faith, "not by works of righteousness that we have done, but according to his great mercy." For he is compassionate and good, and forgives the offenses of those who come to him. If we seek him eagerly, and by fulfilling what is required, we shall certainly find him in every way, and through him we are joined to God the Father; for he is our peace, according to the Scriptures.

Thus says the Lord Almighty: In [those days] ten men from all the languages of the nations will take hold, they will take hold of the hem of a Jew's garment, saying, "We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you."

He makes plain once more how those who seek the face of the Lord will come, city by city and nation by nation. This will happen, he says, in those days, that is, at the time when ten men take hold of one Jew, saying, "We will go with you." By the ten you will understand the complete number of those who come, for the number ten is in some way a symbol of completeness. That those of the Gentiles who cleaved to the holy apostles set out to walk the same road as they did, being justified through faith in Christ, he makes clear by the very figure he uses, which is very well drawn from an image taken from our own life. When little children choose to follow their fathers, they grasp the hem of their garment and, steadying themselves by touch and hanging on to their clothes, they walk without straying and without danger. In the same way, I think, those who once worshiped the creation instead of the Maker of all claim as their true fathers the teachers of the gospel doctrines and are united with them in one soul. They follow them while still infants in understanding and set out on the same path, showing themselves in every way zealous imitators of their way of life, and by constant progress toward what is better they grow up "to mature manhood, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ." And why do they follow? Because they are fully convinced that God is with them, that is, Emmanuel, which is interpreted "God with us." That the call at that time would belong not only to those of Israel's blood, but rather to all the nations throughout the whole world, he has shown by saying that those who take hold of the hem will come from all languages. And when were the nations called to the knowledge of the truth, when did they wish to seek the face of the Lord and to propitiate it, and to travel, as it were, the same road as the holy apostles, if not when the Only-begotten became one of us? He is the expectation of the nations; to him the inspired David also sings, "All the nations you have made will come and worship before you, O Lord." For through him the multitude of the nations too has been saved.
The burden of the word of the Lord in the land of Hadrach, and Damascus is his resting place, for the Lord looks upon men and upon all the tribes of Israel; and Hamath within its borders.

The passage before us is not without difficulty, and the very arrangement of the words is quite hard to grasp. Still, we shall explain it as best we can. It is necessary, however, to state first the events to which we take these words to refer, for only in this way, and even so with difficulty, can the meaning of the prophecy be understood. When Israel was in time loosed and set free from the bonds of captivity, and came at last into Judea and set about rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem, then the surrounding nations, both those who lived in Samaria and those who occupied the cities of Palestine and Phoenicia, were consumed with envy. At the same time they were afraid that, if Israel's fortunes returned to what they had been at the beginning and the nation grew to a countless multitude, they would then have a city so hard to capture and so strongly fortified with towers that they would march against them again and, as in the old days, raise against them a hand no one could withstand. For this reason they wanted to prevent them from building the walls, devising bitter schemes and even launching raids against them like bandits. They went so far in malice and envy that they wrote to the king of the Persians at that time the letter recorded in Ezra. It reads as follows: "To King Artaxerxes, our lord, from your servants Rathumus the recorder and Samellius the scribe, and the rest of their council, and the judges in Coele-Syria and Phoenicia. Now let it be known to our lord the king that the Jews who came up from you to us have come to Jerusalem, that rebellious and wicked city, and are building it, repairing its marketplaces and walls, and laying the foundations of a temple. Now if this city is built and the walls are finished, they will refuse to pay tribute and will even resist kings. And since the work on the temple is under way, we think it right not to overlook such a matter." So, since they had mocked Israel without restraint when it was captured and suffered captivity, and when it had barely been saved and loosed from its bonds they attacked it again no less, subjecting it to countless hardships, plotting against it in many ways, and allowing it neither to raise up the divine temple nor to build the walls of the holy city, God was necessarily provoked against them and delivered them into the hands of Israel. For once the work was finished and the temple raised, the Israelites laid waste all their cities, brought their inhabitants under their power, and became masters of countless riches.

"The burden," then, he says, "of the word of the Lord in the land of Hadrach and Damascus." That is, the word from God that we have in our hands will come against the land of Hadrach and against Damascus, and also against Hamath, which lies within its borders, clearly meaning those of Damascus. The land of Hadrach is certainly some region lying to the east, whose neighbors are Hamath (which is now Epiphania, a little beyond the city of Antioch) and Damascus, which is the metropolis of the Phoenicians and the Palestinians. Naturally, the cities under these metropolises will be subject to the same fate. Why, then, is the burden directed against them? Because in them too he found his rest, that is, the rest of the God who rules over all. And he rested because he saw them punished. For he who oversees all things would not have kept silent, since he counts the chosen race, that is, Israel, worthy of sparing and of his care. The God of all looks upon men and observes each one's path; on those who do wrong he brings the effects of his wrath, but he rescues those who are wronged.

We must remember that earlier too, after he had given the account of the four chariots and the appearances of the horses, he went on to add, "Behold, those going out to the land of the north have given rest to my wrath in the land of the north." The Master's wrath, which hates evil, comes to rest, as it were, when those who have offended him by such great and unbridled sin have paid the penalty. Tyre and Sidon, because they thought themselves very wise; and Tyre built strongholds for herself, and heaped up silver like dust, and gathered gold like the mud of the streets. Therefore [the Lord will take possession of] her [?], and will strike her power into the sea, and she will be consumed with fire.

The text runs through what happened to the cities against which he declared that the "burden of the Lord" had come. He begins with Tyre and Sidon, which were held in honor far above the others, excelling in strength and wealth and in the fine manhood of their inhabitants, keeping the other cities, as it were, under their hand and standing out above their neighbors. Since, then, he says, Sidon and Tyre raise their brows high and think themselves formidable and unbreakable, and trust in their strongholds, that is, in the circuit of their walls, or in other things by which a city may prosper and be kept safe, and also pride themselves greatly on their wealth, they will learn by experience itself that the Lord will take possession of her. For when those from Israel [?], or perhaps Vespasian and Titus, had sacked her, he says that she would be taken as an inheritance by God. For it was he who handed her over and put her under the power of those who captured her. The Romans, as they brought the whole earth under their scepter, were gentle and kind to those who yielded without a fight, but against those who chose to resist they too fell upon them fiercely and warlike. So he says she will be burned, her strongholds hurled down into the sea and her wealth plundered, even though her gold was like dust and her silver like the mud of the streets. For the inhabitants of Tyre had become clever merchants and exceedingly greedy for gain, and a long and full discourse on this subject is found in the writings of the prophet Ezekiel. Nothing, then, will ever profit those who offend God, who mock the saints if they happen to suffer anything and laugh loudly when God tests the faith of his own. All their strongholds will fail, that is, every wall and every means of safety; their wealth will be nothing at all, but will rather become food for war and an added lure to the eagerness of those accustomed to plunder.

One can see even now the children of the Greeks priding themselves greatly on worldly wisdom and, as if in strongholds, on the deceptions of their intricate syllogisms, all but fortifying their own error with the power of eloquence, and greatly enriched with brilliance of diction, like silver, and with the value of their thoughts, like gold. Yet even so Christ has taken them as his inheritance. He has torn down their strongholds, that is, the inventions of deceit have fallen, and their gold and silver have been plundered. For those who have presided over the churches in their time, learned and wise men, seized for themselves the power of their eloquence and made it a sacred offering to God, contending for the doctrines of the faith and delivering a most thorough and true refutation of the deception found among the Greeks. The Israelites did something similar. They borrowed vessels of gold and silver from the Egyptians and despoiled those who had wronged them, and then brought these to the all-holy God in the wilderness when the holy tabernacle and the sacred vessels within it were being made.

So those who govern the Church with worldly wisdom and brilliance of speech plunder the children of the Greeks and, having in their great fairness enriched themselves, as it were, with their gold and silver, make it God's portion, speaking to others the things that serve his glory, overthrowing the strongholds of the Greeks and building up spiritually the holy city, that is, the Church. Ashkelon will see and be afraid, and Gaza, and will be in great anguish, and Ekron, because she has been put to shame in her hope; and the king will perish from Gaza, and Ashkelon will not be inhabited. And aliens will dwell in Ashdod, and I will bring down the arrogance of the foreigners.

When the invasion of war and battle overruns a country, the cities in it are somewhat bolder and sometimes even in good hopes, for they think they will overcome their enemies either through the number of their inhabitants, or through the strength of their walls and the skill of their tacticians. But if one of their cities should be taken, one that might be called the most powerful, then every city sinks down in fear, shakes off its hope (I mean the hope of being able to escape), and mourns as though it had already fallen. So when the city of Tyre is taken, so splendid, so valiant and so rich in wealth, Ashkelon, he says, will be afraid, and Gaza and Ekron too will be in anguish. These are cities of the Palestinians. She will be in anguish because she has been put to shame in her hope. For they thought that the strength of Tyre would be enough to help them; but since they have seen her laid low, they have accordingly fallen away from their hope. And the ruler of Gaza will be gone, he says, clearly because he has perished, and aliens will dwell in Ashdod, since the native inhabitants, naturally, will have been consumed by the war. To this he adds, "I will bring down the arrogance of the foreigners." By "foreigners" he customarily means the Philistines, that is, the Palestinians. But the word might also, if anyone thinks so, apply to the other nations that had wronged Israel, which bordered on Judea and were its neighbors. This, then, is what we have to say as regards the literal sense.

We must recognize that when, as I said, the Church is at times persecuted by its enemies, those enemies join in the assault fiercely and sneer at it, perhaps saying, "Aha, aha!" as it is written. But Christ comes to its defense. He will shatter all their power, raising up his own temple and bringing upon those who plot against it the effects of his undiluted wrath, shaking down, like so many cities, the assemblies of the heretics, and besides these the unholy hordes of the idolaters.

And I will take away their blood from their mouth, and their abominations from between their teeth; and these too will be left for our God, and they will be like a commander of a thousand in Judah, and Ekron like the Jebusite.

These too devoured Israel, and like wild beasts their mouths were all but stained with blood. And since they were idolaters devoted to the worship of vain things, they always had the names of their own abominations on their tongues, or rather between their teeth, calling handmade things gods up and down, and saying to lifeless stones, in the words of the prophet, "You are my god, and you gave birth to me." They have paid the fitting and sufficient penalty for their savage wrongs against Israel. Yet they have not perished entirely, for God foresees their conversion in Christ that would come in due time. "I will take away," then, he says, "their blood from their mouth." That is, even if they all but swallowed Israel down like wild beasts, a time will come when they will be pure and freed from guilt for these things; for they too will be justified by faith and will wash away the defilement of their former wickedness. "And I will take away the names of their abominations from between their teeth." For they will no longer remember the falsely named gods, nor name them; but they too will be left for our God, just as Israel itself was, for its remnant too has been saved, even though it acted impiously against Emmanuel himself. And since the multitude of the nations, once called, has been joined spiritually to those of Israel's blood who believed, Christ binding them together into unity ("For he is our peace, who has made both one and has broken down the dividing wall, creating the two peoples into one new man, so making peace, and reconciling both in one Spirit to the Father"), he therefore says that they will be like a commander of a thousand in Judah. That is, they will advance so far in genuineness, I mean in faith and goodness, that leaders of Judah will come even from among them. And Ekron, that is, the foreigner from the land of the Philistines, will be like the Jebusite, that is, like the very people who live in Jerusalem. For Jerusalem was originally called Jebus, so here the Jebusite is understood to mean the inhabitant of Jerusalem. And many commanders of thousands, that is, leaders and those set over peoples, have come from the Gentiles too, and are found now throughout the whole world. By "in Judah" you will understand those who are accustomed to give praise, that is, us who have been called in faith, who are accustomed to crown Christ, who called us, with unceasing doxologies.
And I will set up a bulwark for my house, so that none may pass through or return, and no oppressor will ever again come upon them, for now I have seen with my eyes.

See, he plainly calls Christ a rampart and a wall, through whom and in whom we have been fortified as with towers, by the good pleasure, of course, and the will of God the Father.
