For we who have believed are surely the spiritual house and God's building, in Paul's words, if it is true that he dwells in our hearts through the Spirit and makes his home in those who love him. For he himself said through the prophet's voice: “I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.” Christ, then, is the rampart raised up for the Church by the Father's counsel, so that no longer, as in the past, may certain ones pass through us and turn back again, going up and down, trampling us like a road through waste ground, and filling our hearts with every kind of harm.

For somewhere he said concerning those of Israel, who was of old the vineyard belonging to the beloved: “I will take away its hedge, and it shall be for plunder; and I will pull down its wall, and it shall be for trampling.” But for us who have come to know his appearing, Emmanuel himself has been raised up as a wall and a hedge. He surrounds us with ineffable power, drives the unclean demons away from our minds, and does not let us be laid down beneath their feet. That is why the prophet also says to him: “And you shall be called a builder of hedges, and you shall put an end to the paths in between.” For just as those who fence in vineyards that have gone to waste put a stop to the paths running through the middle, no longer letting them be trodden by the feet of those going up and down, so also our Lord Jesus Christ has placed himself around us like an unbreakable wall and, fencing us about with angelic powers, has made us safe from being trampled. And he said besides that no longer shall the one who drives out come upon them. For in the past we were easily captured and very easily led astray, readily going off after anything at all that was out of place, while Satan led us and carried us off and all but drove us from one thing to another. But Christ has put a stop to this too. The plunderer will not come against us; he will not cast us out, as before, wherever he pleases. For we have been planted firmly in Christ, and we have a heart that is secure and settled, no longer shaken toward what is unfitting, not going off into polytheism, not driven out into wandering, but standing firm, as it were, in faith and in love toward God, so that we rejoice at this and say: “And he set my feet upon a rock.” And by saying “For now I have seen with my eyes,” he clearly showed that the time of the Saviour's coming was a time of visitation. “For the dayspring from on high has visited us,” and, as David says, “The Lord looked down from heaven upon the earth.” Yet in the past, because of the sin in us, he did not count us worthy of his oversight, nor of his sparing or his love, nor of anything else of that kind at all, but had, as it were, turned away. That is why we were also troubled. And blessed David will bear witness, saying: “When you turn away your face, they will be troubled, and they will return to their dust.” But since now, that is, at the time of his coming, he has seen with his eyes, we have been saved and have received mercy. Indeed, which of the things that are beyond words and truly admirable have we not gained?
VOLUME III.
On the Prophet Zechariah.
BOOK FOUR
Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; proclaim it, daughter of Jerusalem! See, your king comes to you, righteous and saving; he is meek, and mounted on a beast of burden and a young colt.

Here, then, he openly proclaims the manifestation of our Saviour, so that nothing at all difficult is to be seen in it. He has good reason to command the spiritual Zion to rejoice, since all our dejection has been removed. For where is there any dejection now, and what could we possibly have to lament, when sin has been driven away, death has been trampled down, and human nature has been called to the dignity of freedom, crowned with the grace of adoption as sons, and made splendid with gifts from above, from heaven?

Notice that, in speaking of our Saviour's coming, he at once calls Zion "daughter." He does well, then, to command that she must rejoice greatly. He also urges Jerusalem to announce that her king will soon be present and will be revealed in the flesh, righteous and saving. For Christ has justified us by faith, and he widens the path of salvation for those who come to him. Besides this, he is meek. He does not bring the severity of the law, or punish those who break the commandment with death. Rather, he saves out of gentleness and raises up those who have slipped. And if anyone sins, he himself becomes an advocate with God the Father.

We have read that "the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life." The letter is the law that punishes, the shadow and the type; but the life-giving Spirit is Christ, for through the teaching of the gospel we have been taught to worship in spirit and in truth. As for his mounting a young colt and entering Jerusalem in this way, no long argument will be needed to establish it. The inspired evangelist who wrote these things is enough for our faith. Christ sat on the colt, while its mother followed, and what was done was a sign to us of something of the greatest importance. For Christ came to rest upon the new people, that is, the people called to the knowledge of the truth who had once worshipped idols. It was like a colt not yet broken in, and it did not know how to walk properly, since it had never been trained by the divine law. But he who leads all to spiritual skill first set the colt under himself. By the she-ass that followed, he gave us to understand that in due time the synagogue of the Jews will also follow. Yet the synagogue had seniority in time with respect to the calling, for it had been called beforehand through Moses and the prophets. But since it stumbled against the saving King and did not accept the faith, it rightly comes behind the colt, barely keeping up. It has become the tail, that is, something trailing along behind those from the Gentiles, and the first has become last. Observe how he who knows hearts and minds showed that human nature had been carried off into the utmost irrationality. Both the synagogue of the Jews and the multitude of the Gentiles are likened to the ass, a most irrational animal. The Gentiles worshipped the creation rather than God the Creator, and the Jews dishonoured the law that was their tutor. So both have abandoned good sense and sound understanding and turned aside to every kind of wickedness, and "they have been compared to the senseless beasts and have become like them," as the Psalmist says. The ass is also a symbol of impurity in another way. The animal is unclean and lies under the ban of the law (Exod 13:13). Such are all who wander astray and love sin.

And he will utterly destroy chariots from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem, and the bow of war will be utterly destroyed, and there will be abundance and peace from the nations; and he will rule over the waters from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the ends of the earth.

Here the prophetic word hints to us in a riddle that the Only-begotten, once he became man, would put principalities and powers and the world-rulers of this darkness under the feet of those who love him. These are the loathsome hordes of demons. He would make every enemy, visible and invisible, subject to them, crush every war, and gladden them with the blessings of peace. At various times the Babylonians, and also certain other neighbouring nations, came against Jerusalem riding horses and chariots "and shooting with bows," as it is written. In this way they overpowered the city and inflicted bitter sufferings on it. Starting from what usually happened, then, the prophet shows the splendour of what Christ achieved. The saving king, he says, righteous and most meek, will come, and before long. Yet he will not come escorted by a great crowd of shield-bearers, or with countless men skilled in the arts of war. He will have so trained himself in modesty of character that he will barely sit on a bare colt. Yet he will be so great in virtue, and will so benefit those who trust in him, that he will take away chariots from Ephraim, remove the horse from Jerusalem, destroy the bow of war, and spread abroad a deep peace that comes from all the nations. By Ephraim he means the ten tribes in Samaria, and by Jerusalem those who lived in it, namely Judah and Benjamin. So the prophetic word brings us a promise of security and peace. For the holy city, he says, will not be easily overrun by those who wish to harm it. This is the spiritual Zion, or Jerusalem, "which is the Church of the living God." And he who saves it will so widen his kingdom that he will rule over the whole of Judea, from the sea to the rivers. For these are the outlets of the land, that is, its limits. The inspired David also sings somewhere, speaking of the synagogue of the Jews as a vine: "It stretched out its branches to the sea, and its shoots to the rivers." For the land of the Jews is bounded by the southern sea, the Indian Sea, and by the region called Mesopotamia, "between the rivers." But the kingdom of Christ does not stay within these bounds, far from it. Rather, the passage moves from a particular example to what is universal and most general. For he has reigned not over Judea alone, but over the whole earth under heaven, and his authority extends from one end of the earth to the other.

And you, by the blood of the covenant, have sent forth your prisoners from a pit that has no water. You shall sit in a stronghold, you prisoners of the synagogue, and for one day of your sojourning I will repay you double.

The passage now turns to the righteous and saving king himself, who is also meek, that is, Christ, and it makes vivid the splendid and admirable achievements of his coming. For the only-begotten Word of God willingly emptied himself and became man. He endured the cross as well, despising the shame. He laid down his own life as the price for the life of all, and won the whole earth under heaven for God the Father by the blood of an eternal covenant. The type of this covenant was the blood sprinkled on the people of old through the all-wise Moses. For Moses, it says, took the blood "and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying, 'This is the blood of the covenant that God has made with you.'" But those things were types and a sketch of the truth, whereas the truth itself is Christ, who bought us all by the blood of the covenant. For, as his disciple says, we have been redeemed "not with perishable things, silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot." You, then, he says, O most righteous and most meek king, by the blood of the covenant have sent forth those who became your prisoners. These are the people you have bound tightly with bonds of love, and have clearly persuaded to bow the neck of their mind under your yokes and be fastened to them. "Sent forth" means brought out, led out, or brought up, from a pit that has no water. By this, we say, he means either Hades, which has no life, since we take water as a figure of life because it is life-giving; or else, and quite rightly, we will take the pit to be the deception about the falsely named gods. For that thing truly is a pit, and anyone who slips into it at all will have no share in life in the age to come. That Christ emptied Hades by his death and opened the gates below to the spirits in prison is surely clear to everyone. The God of all also spoke through the voice of Jeremiah about those of Israel who had forsaken him and foolishly turned to the madness of idolatry: "Heaven was astonished at this and shuddered exceedingly, says the Lord; for my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water." For just as right and unerring knowledge of God is life-giving and a fountain of life, so the playthings of idolatry and error about God may be understood as waterless, like broken cisterns. Then he speaks to the prisoners themselves and spurs them on to good hopes, saying: You shall sit in a stronghold, you prisoners of the synagogue. By "stronghold" he means, I think, the Church, since it is walled about in Christ and cannot be shaken. By "sitting" he means being firmly established in faith. For it is written of God, "For you sit enthroned for ever," that is, you have a nature that is established and unshaken. So you will be in safety, he says, standing firm in faith, O prisoners of my synagogue. These would be the holy multitude of those justified in Christ. He shows that their endurance in every excellent thing, and their steadfast love for God, will not go unrewarded, when he says: And for one day of your sojourning I will repay you double.

What he means is something like this. All the saints are sojourners and strangers on the earth, and every person's life in the body is very short. If anyone measures it against the age to come, he will see that it is altogether small, so small that it might perhaps be compared to a single day. So he says, "for one day of your sojourning." That is, in return for the short and cramped time of life in the body, I will repay rewards double and in abundance. Christ too said somewhere, "Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, they will pour into your lap." For we do not expect rewards that merely equal what we may have done, but rewards with a great increase, since the giver is rich in gifts.
For I have bent you, Judah, as a bow for myself; I have filled Ephraim.

Here again he makes clear how the flock from the nations will be called and will enter through faith, and how he who once lived in luxury, that is, Satan, will be made wretched, driven away from the worshippers he had gained by greed. He addresses his words, however, to the holy apostles, that is, the teachers from Israel. These went all around the lands of the Gentiles, calling the people there to the knowledge of the truth and gathering them in like a net. "O Judah," then, he says, "I have bent you as a bow for myself," that is, through you I will shoot down the adversaries; "and you, O Ephraim, I have filled." And I will explain again what this means. When skilled archers draw the string back to the breast and bring the iron head of the arrow close to the bow, they are said to "fill" the bow. Then they shoot the arrow, or shaft, as something terrible and inescapable, leaping off with unchecked force and flying straight through. So the same thing is expressed in two ways: "I have made you a bow," he says, "O Judah," and "I have filled you, O Ephraim." Judah and Ephraim together are the whole race of Israel. So he has made a kind of bow out of those Jews who believed before the others. They advanced so far in understanding that they could instruct nations, drive the herds of demons away from those who had gone astray, and strike down Satan and, in short, all who oppose the divine doctrines and fight against the sacred teaching conveyed through those doctrines. So too the inspired David says to God, the Saviour of all: "Your arrows are sharpened, O mighty one; peoples will fall beneath you, in the heart of the king's enemies." For "the arrows of the mighty one," that is, of Christ, strike the enemies of God the Father deep within, in heart and mind. And his arrows, again, are the teachers of the mysteries. They strike those who have gone astray and do not know him who is God by nature and in truth. Yet they strike them not to death, but carry them away into love in Christ, so that they may fall beneath him. Such is the bride described in the Song of Songs, who says plainly: "For I am wounded with love." The most wise psalmist, speaking in the Spirit, will confirm that the inspired disciples became most valiant and strong, when he says of them: "Like arrows in the hand of a mighty one, so are the sons of those who have been shaken off." He calls those of Israel "shaken off" because they fell away from divine grace through their drunken outrage against Christ. But their sons became arrows, as if shot from the hand of the mighty one. Habakkuk also said somewhere, again addressing Emmanuel himself and speaking about the holy apostles: "For your darts will go forth into the brightness of the lightning of your weapons."
And I will rouse your children, Zion, against the children of the Greeks, and I will wield you like a warrior's sword.

See, he plainly calls the teachers of the mysteries who came from the Jews his own bow. For who are the children of Zion who rise up against the children of the Greeks, if not the inspired disciples and those who in each age lead the churches and rightly handle the word of truth? For how could the spiritual Zion be understood as anything other than the Church? They defeat the children of the Greeks and make war on those who have gone astray, because God has made them like a warrior's sword. In the same way the inspired Paul is seen equipping the soldier who is understood to be in Christ. He puts on him the breastplate of righteousness in Christ, and also the helmet of salvation. Then he gives him the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. Using this sword against the children of the Greeks, they cut away the deception growing in them. They bring to bear on them the word of God, which is sharper than any blade, living and active, and with it they cut out the wicked and unclean spirit. In this way the Greeks may then receive the word of the true knowledge of God with a mind that is pure and free, released from the greed of the demons.
And the Lord will be over them, and a dart will go forth like lightning.

By these words he indicates that the Lord God will also be with them. He will fight beside them like a shield-bearer and help them lay waste those who oppose them. For "the Lord will be over them," he says, meaning clearly those who have made it their business to rise up against the men who serve his gospel as priests. Each dart is a teacher of the mysteries or an apostle, for again he likens them to an arrow or dart sent by God. Each, he says, will run like lightning, meaning that it falls effortlessly on everyone's eyes. For the inspired disciples, the heralds of the Saviour's gospel, and those after them who led the peoples and presided over the churches, became so brilliant that no one failed to see the radiance of the virtue in them. The Saviour himself said this: "No one who lights a lamp covers it with a vessel or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a lampstand, so that those who come in may see the light." And again elsewhere: "In the same way, let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven" (Matt 5:16).

And the Lord Almighty will blow the trumpet, and will go forth in the storm of his threat. The Lord Almighty will shield them; and they will consume them and bury them under sling-stones, and they will drink their blood like wine and fill the altar like bowls. And the Lord will save them on that day, his people, like sheep.

As I said, the passage clearly presents the God who rules over all as their shield-bearer and comrade in arms. He is drawn up for battle and has chosen to fight beside them, so that he already seems armed for war. Like someone about to march against enemies, he will use all his power and the strength that is in him. The prophet is quite right to say that he makes war, not on those who are caught in the net through faith and brought to justification, but on those who wickedly opposed the divine message. Paul also pointed to these when he said, "For a great and effective door has opened to me, and there are many adversaries." The Lord, then, he says, will blow the trumpet. For Christ has spoken the message of the gospel, which flashes through the whole earth under heaven, and the mystery of Christ is heard by people everywhere. Moses was weak of voice and slow of tongue, so he was barely heard, and in Judea alone. But the word that comes from Christ is not like that at all. It has rung out like a long and most resonant trumpet, sending a piercing sound into the ears of all. And he will march as in the storm of his threat. He will so shield his own bodyguards that their opponents are consumed as if by fire, and they all but bury them with slings as they strike them down valiantly. "They will drink their blood" means that, like wild beasts leaping on them, they will easily overcome them and leave them dead. And they will bring bowls filled with the blood of the fallen to the altar, as a kind of libation. For the death of those who do not allow the lost to be saved is a fragrant offering to God and an acceptable sacrifice. If those who murder bodies do not deserve pity, but should rather be brought to justice and suffer what they inflicted, what can one say of those who have become the destroyers and corrupters of souls?

These, again, would be the elite among the Greeks, who have grasped at the glory of worldly wisdom. They name gods and goddesses above and below, persuade people to worship the creation rather than the Maker, and assign to each of the elements the glory that belongs to God. These men have led the whole earth under heaven astray, and not only during the time of their life in the body, but in the ages that followed as well. Countless people in every age have perished, overcome by their lying words and paying attention to frigid old wives' tales. Such men, then, have now been done away with. The profanity of their writings is gone, the myths are powerless, and their blood has, so to speak, been drunk up. Struck by the doctrines of the truth as if by stones from a sling, they are buried. And, as I said, the destruction of their unbridled talk has become a fragrant offering to God. And the Lord has saved his people like sheep. Since he himself is the Maker of all, even those who once went astray might reasonably be called his people. But Christ saved them like a flock driven off by robbers. He cast out the false shepherds and placed the human race under his own hand. For he is the good shepherd, who laid down his life for the sheep.
For holy stones roll upon his land. For if there is anything good that is his, and anything fair that comes from him, it is grain for young men and fragrant wine for virgins.

By the holy stones rolling in the land of God, we say, are meant those who in each age are holy in the churches, who become teachers of the mysteries and instructors. For they have been conformed to the chosen, precious cornerstone that God the Father laid in the foundations of Zion. If the foundation is a stone, then those who are fitted and joined together and built up into a holy temple for God may fittingly be called stones like him. He does well to say that they roll. By this, I think, he means that the saints are, so to speak, nimble and quick to turn to anything at all. For round, that is, spherical, stones somehow overcome inertia and are readier to move than others, if one chooses to move them. Likewise the mind of the saints is very easily led to whatever pleases God. Since this is what the stones mean for us, it would befit us to be firmly disposed in the same way. "For if there is anything good that is his, and anything fair that comes from him" refers, clearly, to God, who gives us everything that pertains to godliness and life. And what are these gifts? Grain for young men and fragrant wine for virgins. To those who have turned with youthful spirit to what pleases him, and have chosen to do what is good, he will give still greater strength, which is meant by the grain. For bread strengthens the human heart. But to those already thoroughly purified, whose minds are undefiled, and who may fittingly be likened to holy and chaste virgins, he will give wine. This is clear and unadulterated knowledge of God, which gladdens the human heart. So the young men and the virgins, in the sense we have just explained, will rightly be called to a broad and abundant share in the blessings from above. And they will hear God saying, "Eat and drink, and be drunk, you who are near." For such people are near to God, not in any spatial sense, since it is nonsense to think or say that. They are near through a most valiant readiness of mind, a longing for everything excellent, and love for him. For just as wickedness removes us and carries us far away, so virtue brings us close to God. It causes the thing that separates us and stands between us, I mean sin, to be taken out of the way.
Ask the Lord for rain in its season, the early rain and the late.

Grain does not grow in the fields without toil, nor does a vineyard yield good clusters and good wine. In the same way there can be no spiritual fruitfulness in us unless God sends down, like rain upon mind and heart, the revelation of his oracles, and as it were lets fall on us drop by drop the knowledge of both the old and the new letter, that is, of the law and of the gospel. These would be the early and the late rains. The knowledge and spiritual contemplation of the law does contribute to our benefit; rather, it acts as our tutor, leading us through type and shadow to the mystery of Christ. The Savior himself will confirm this when he says to the crowds of the Jews: “Do not think that I will accuse you before the Father; the one who accuses you is Moses, on whom you have set your hope. For if you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote about me.” And somewhere he also spoke about the scribes and Pharisees as being called from the instruction of the law to something better, namely the instruction of the gospel: “Therefore every scribe who has been trained for the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings out of his treasure what is new and what is old.” So if we ask God for knowledge of both the law and the gospel, and show ourselves worthy to receive it, we shall certainly receive it. We shall fill the treasuries within the mind, gathering together the old and the new, and filling the mind with the richest spiritual fruitfulness.

The Lord has made flashes of light, and he will give them winter rain, grass in the field for each one. For those who utter oracles have spoken troubles, and the diviners have told false visions and false dreams; they gave empty comfort. Therefore they withered as though they had no rain, and they were afflicted like sheep, because there was no healing.

This passage is pregnant with a hidden meaning, and I think it necessary to make it clear first, for in this way lovers of learning will grasp the aim of the prophet's words. He had been speaking about the saints, whom he also called holy stones. He said that grain especially befits them, since they act manfully, as young men do, and also fragrant wine, since they are virgins, that is, pure and undefiled. “For those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires,” as the inspired Paul says. He also commanded them to ask for the early and the late rain. Then, after a mention of those who have been led astray breaks in, he gives in these words, as it were, the reason why these people have neither grain nor wine, and are not watered by the spiritual rains either, so that consequently they have no grass in the field. The words are framed as if they were about things of the senses, but the contemplation they contain is very subtle and very pure. For he says that although God makes flashes of light, that is, lightning, and pours the winter rain upon the earth, which is useful, and gives grass to each one (namely to the beasts in the fields), those who utter oracles have led them astray. These are the false speakers and liars who tell divinations out of their own heart. They have spoken troubles, that is, not what brings rest to those who believe them, but things that were bound to bring them toil, since they would offend God and be overlooked by him. The diviners too gave comfort with false dreams. Evidently they sounded in their ears what they wanted to hear and fattened them on fine hopes, yet said nothing true. Instead they carried them off into deceit and error. They did not in the least point out to them the giver and supplier of spiritual things, but rather persuaded them to ask for prosperity from the falsely named gods. That is why he says: They withered as though they had no rain, and were afflicted like sheep. For there was no grass, there was no healing. There was no one among them to bind up what was broken, to raise up what was shattered, to restore what had been afflicted.

We must therefore pay heed, not to those who utter vain things, to false speakers, buffoons and dreamers, but rather to God. He flashes into our mind the light of the true knowledge of God and pours down spiritual rains, by which I mean the consolations that come through the Holy Spirit. He makes grass spring up for those in the field; that is, again, he pastures us as it were on the most flowery grass, the blameless knowledge of the divinely inspired Scripture. “For man, though he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to the senseless beasts and became like them.” But if he should somehow take into his mind the knowledge of the divine oracles and share in spiritual food, then indeed he will throw off his sluggishness and be in honor again. He will be governed by sober reason, having recovered the mind that befits a human being.
My anger has been provoked against the shepherds, and I will visit the lambs.

Here, as I think, he calls the false prophets and false diviners shepherds, along with the leaders of deceit. They became destruction and a snare to some who missed the true glory of God, gave the honor and worship that befit him to creation instead, “and worshiped the works of their own hands,” as it is written.

It is not unreasonable to join the elite of the Greeks to the false diviners as well. They were exceedingly wise in their own conceit and used their eloquence to lead astray those devoted to them. Like bad shepherds, they grazed them among thorns and brought them into the great worthlessness of rotten notions. For what is there among them that helps toward the knowledge of the truth? The effects of divine wrath would also fall on these, and very justly, for they destroyed not only their own souls but those of others besides. As I said, they led people astray by the pomp of their diction, all but gilding falsehood and spending the use of speech on deceptions. But he visits the lambs, evidently out of pity. He moves them from deceit to the knowledge of the truth and drives them out of their wandering onto a straight road. It was fitting to hang over those who had wronged them the punishment [?] that their wrongs deserved. In the same way, the merciful judgment on those who had suffered would in no way lack godlike gentleness and a just verdict. For it was necessary, truly necessary, that those who had been wronged be saved. God bears no grudge, and he frees from punishment those who were carried off by the greed of the others, perhaps even against their will.

And the Lord God Almighty will visit his flock, the house of Judah, and will set them as his comely horse in battle. From him he looked out, and from him he arrayed, and from him comes the bow in wrath, and from him will come forth everyone who drives out in the same. And they will be like warriors treading mud in the streets in battle, and they will draw up in array, because the Lord is with them.

He makes clear how he will bring the effects of his wrath on the shepherds while visiting and saving the lambs. He raised up from among the Jews those who would initiate the world into the mysteries, the holy apostles and evangelists. Through them he overcame the wise men of the Greeks, rescued the lambs from their unbridled talk, freed them from the nooses of deceit, and brought them over to the true and blameless knowledge of God. So, he says, he will visit his flock, the house of Judah. And he will make it like a comely and most warlike horse. Mounted on it, as it were, in a spiritual sense, he will campaign, as I said, against the tongue of the Greeks, and condemn the ugliness and uselessness of the wisdom found among them. Who could doubt that among the Greeks to whom they were dispersed the inspired disciples became like horses, all but neighing down their unbridled talk and their God-hated deceit? Christ said to Ananias concerning blessed Paul: “Go, for this man is a chosen vessel of mine, to carry my name before the gentiles and kings and the sons of Israel.” And Habakkuk too said somewhere, addressing our Lord Jesus Christ himself: “You will mount your horses, and your riding is salvation.” So he says: him as a comely horse in battle, and from him he looked out. It is as if he were saying: As God he surveyed those who were fit for the ministry of the gospel preaching, but he chose those from Judah. And from him he arrayed: for he chose them to become the servants and ministers of his own will, and as it were the mediators and stewards of his grace. And from him too, he says (clearly from Judah), comes the bow drawn in wrath against the adversaries. And from him again will come forth the one who drives out in the same. By one who drives out he means, I think, one who plunders and takes captives.

This is what the inspired disciples did. They seized people from among the Greeks and brought them to the great King, I mean Christ, so that they might be under him and choose to think as he does, having at long last and with difficulty shaken off the yoke of the devil's greed. The inspired disciples so overpowered the wise men of the Greeks that they seemed to be trampling scattered mud. For the Lord was with them, he who does “great and unsearchable things, glorious and marvelous things without number.” And somewhere Christ said to those who believed in him: “Behold, I have given you power to tread on snakes and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy.”

It should be understood that we say such things as we weave a spiritual interpretation. The Jews, however, do not see the matter this way. They take it rather historically. They say that after the time of the captivity Antiochus, surnamed Epiphanes, made war on them. He had gathered a vast host of fighters from the land of the Greeks and was proud of the reinforcements they provided. But, as they say, Israel conquered and won a better name than his perversity did. For it was then that those of the Maccabees who bore witness bound on the crown of approval. As proof of their view they cite both the words we have just discussed and those a little further on, which run as follows: “For I have bent you, Judah, as a bow for myself; I have filled Ephraim; and I will rouse your children, O Zion, against the children of the Greeks, and I will wield you like a warrior's sword. The Lord will be over them, and his dart will go forth like lightning. The Lord Almighty will sound the trumpet and will go forth in the storm of his threat. The Lord Almighty will shield them.”
And the riders of horses will be put to shame, and I will strengthen the house of Judah and save the house of Joseph, and I will settle them, because I have loved them.

Again, those who champion the Jewish accounts say that when battle was joined against the Greeks, the Greek cavalry was destroyed, but those of the blood of Israel prevailed. So they lived in the land (clearly Judea) free of all fear, and no one at all was deported, that is, taken captive. But we are anxious to make our interpretation consistent with and akin to what came before. We say that the riders of horses who were put to shame are none other than the leaders of the Greek doctrines, who were accustomed to fight in defense of God-hated deceit. When they were dashed to the ground, Judah prevailed, and the house of Joseph too was saved. These names signify the blood and race of Israel, that is, the multitude of those justified in Christ. They carry the Jew about in their mind and heart, they have received the circumcision that is in the spirit, and they have a mind that sees God, for that is what Israel means. And since they have been loved by God, they have for that reason been settled, that is, they have gained a firmly grounded permanence in every excellent thing. For it is written, “The Lord settles the solitary in a house.” And somewhere the inspired Isaiah said about one who practices the exceptional life: “He who walks in righteousness, speaks of a straight way, hates lawlessness and injustice, keeps his hands from bribes, stops his ears so as not to hear of bloodshed, and shuts his eyes so as not to see injustice, he will dwell in a lofty cave of a strong rock.” It is not unreasonable to say that the house God has given to the saints is the Church, or the dwelling places above. Indeed blessed David considers this a thing worthy of all wonder, when he says to the Savior and God of all: “Blessed are all who dwell in your house; they will praise you forever and ever.” And again: “For one day in your courts is better than thousands. I have chosen to be cast aside in the house of my God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners.”
And they will be as they were when I had not rejected them, for I am the Lord their God, and I will hear them, and they will be like the warriors of Ephraim.

Now that the wise men of the Greeks, who were also called horsemen, have been put to shame, he promises to strengthen and settle those who have received mercy, adding, “Because I have loved them.” And he goes on to explain what they will gain from being loved by God. For he says: As I did not reject them. For I did not disregard them altogether, but visited them when they were in danger, because I am the Lord their God. For he is not “the God of the Jews only, but of the gentiles also,” since he is the Creator and Lord of all. That is why he also says, and I will hear them, that is, I will accept their prayers. And they will be like the warriors of Ephraim. Again it is as if he were saying: Those who were once as it were paralyzed and prostrate through weakness of mind and understanding will now be brought to such spiritual strength that they seem to rank equally with those of Ephraim who won renown, that is, with the apostles and evangelists from among the Jews. For such men have become spiritual warriors. They overpower enemies and strike down adversaries; they conquer principalities, powers and dominions and the spiritual forces of wickedness, and they prevail without a fight over those who resist the divine preaching. From the multitude of the gentiles as well, called through faith to the knowledge of Christ, there have arisen holy and Spirit-bearing men who are like the warriors of Ephraim. For they have imitated the apostles' way of life as far as possible, and following in the track of their virtue they too have fought manfully against the enemies of the truth, against the passions, and against sin.
And their heart will rejoice as with wine, and their children will see it and be glad, and their heart will rejoice in the Lord.

The mind of those who have drunk wine is always carefree in a way, and disdainful of worry. It does not admit what usually causes grief, but is relaxed and rises above every care. So, he says, if they become like the warriors of Ephraim, then indeed they will receive gladness in themselves. As illustrious and highly approved men they will rejoice in the hope of the good things to come, and they will have as imitators of their exceptional way of life the sons born of them, spiritual sons, of course. The inspired Paul was such a man, when he wrote to those called through him: “Even if you have ten thousand guardians in Christ, you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel.” So the children who will be born of them will see and be glad. For they will have come to the contemplation of Christ, learned the power of the mystery, and been enlightened by the gifts of the Spirit. They will act rightly, will find their gladness in Christ the Savior himself, and will make him the joy, delight and exultation of their soul and heart. This too would be clear proof that they have chosen to live in a way that pleases God. For those who turn the inclination of their mind to the things of the world and lean toward what is more shameful rejoice in these things and make them their gladness. They delight in the pleasures of the flesh, and being accustomed to wallow in the other luxuries of the present life, they think the things of God worth very little. But those who seek him with their whole heart, who are enriched by the contemplation of him and who widen the eye of their understanding, will welcome gladness in him and in him alone.

I will signal to them and receive them, because I will redeem them, and they will become as many as they once were. I will sow them among the peoples, and those far off will remember me, and they will rear their children and will return.

Again he calls to mind the flock of the Jews. He promises to gather them though they are scattered, and to assemble them from all the earth into Judea, so that not a single one is left apart. And again he indicates how the gathering will take place. They say that beekeepers make certain signals, whistling or doing other things they customarily do, and in this way gather the swarms of bees that have left the hives. Something like this was said through the voice of Isaiah: “For in that day,” he says, “the Lord will whistle for the flies that rule over part of the river of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of the Assyrians.” Others say that in times of war too, if the fighters happen to be scattered, whether in pursuit or in flight, the generals raise some signal on high, and the soldiers look to it, gather together and rush back to the same place. Something of this sort is suggested also by what we find in the prophet Isaiah: “And it will be like a mast on a mountain, and like a standard raised on a hill.” So he draws the comparison from what commonly happens. For he says: I will signal to them and receive them. A great and conspicuous sign has been raised among us, the Savior's cross. Through it we have become acceptable to God the Father, we have been redeemed, and we who believe have spread out into a countless multitude. He added: and I will sow them among the peoples, and those far from them will come and remember me. Here again we say this, and not beside the mark, for the interpretation is very probable. The inspired disciples and heralds of the divine gospels were sown, as it were, among many nations and in every land and city. Those who had moved very far from God because of the sin and error that came between them, they caused to remember him and to take into their mind the Savior and Creator of all, although they had long given their reverence to creation and had therefore abandoned their closeness to God. Indeed the inspired Paul addressed those called through him to the knowledge of Christ, saying: “But now you who once were far off have been brought near.” They will come, then, remembering God. And the blessed prophet Jeremiah hints at something like this when he says to Israel: “You who are far away, remember the Lord, and let Jerusalem come into your heart.” And if they once remember the one who is God by nature, then indeed they will advance to such spiritual vigor that they become fathers of children, rear their own children in the words of godliness, and take pride in this very thing. The inspired Paul writes somewhere to those he had reared, who had grown up to mature manhood and reached the measure of the stature that is in Christ, at one time “My joy and crown,” and at another, “By the pride in you, brothers, which I have in Christ Jesus.” For “children's children are the crown of the aged,” as it is written, “and the glory of children is their fathers.”
And I will bring them back from the land of Egypt and receive them from among the Assyrians, and I will bring them into Gilead and into Lebanon, and not one of them will be left behind.

When Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Judea by force and the divine temple was burned, and Jerusalem itself, all Israel suffered misery. Some were taken captive and carried off to the Assyrians and Medes. Others escaped the cruelty of these enemies and managed to flee, but fearing to be caught in the same fate and trying to avoid it, they went over to the Egyptians as deserters. There they bowed beneath the yoke of servitude under them, a yoke they had not wanted but that necessity had forced on them. So, since he promised to gather them from everywhere, he also names the places to which they had been carried off: some, as I said, as captives, others driven by unbearable terrors into what they did not want.

But since those who most love contemplation and are spiritual ought to pursue the spiritual interpretation, we say that he promises to drag them out of the country, or rather the hand, of the invisible enemies and to free them from every fear. They are captives and, as it were, lie subject to others, but he all but refashions them into freedom.

Or else, in another sense, he says that they will be set free from darkness and confusion. For "Egypt" is interpreted as "Darkness", and "Babylon" as "Confusion". Scripture often makes no distinction here and counts the Assyrians and Babylonians as one nation, because they lay under one sceptre and a single kingdom was set over them. So he promises that, once they have been redeemed from the hand of their oppressors, he will bring them into the land of Gilead, which is the most productive and fruitful part of the land of the Jews, and also into Lebanon, which is a great mountain covered with fine timber, lying on the border between the land of the Jews and that of the Phoenicians. I think both of these signify the following. Our Lord Jesus Christ freed us as if from Egypt and the Assyrians, that is, from the greed of those who had taken us captive, who are the wicked and unclean demons. He then brought us into the Church as into a land rich in timber and exceedingly fertile. In it the fruit of those who are well approved is very plentiful, and the heads of the saints cannot easily be counted. Their virtue has raised them on high, and they have flourished like cedars. One might very fittingly say of them the words addressed by David to the God of the universe: "The cedars of Lebanon, which you planted." The inspired Paul, too, plainly calls those who have been justified in faith "God's field".

And they shall pass through a narrow sea, and they shall strike the waves in the sea, and all the depths of the river shall be dried up. All the arrogance of the Assyrians shall be taken away, and the sceptre of Egypt shall be removed. And I will strengthen them in the Lord their God, and they shall boast in his name, says the Lord.

The promise of help is given to those who believe in Christ by analogy with what was granted to the people of old. Israel was brought across the Red Sea and prevailed over its waves, "for the waters were made firm like a wall", since God accomplished the deed in a wondrous way. Israel also crossed the Jordan on foot. In the same way, he says, those who have been called through Moses to the knowledge of Christ, and saved by the sacred teachings of the holy apostles, will cross the surge of this present life as though it were a sea raging with savage waves. Once they are clear of the world's turmoil, they will be free to serve the One who is God by nature. They will also pass through temptations as though through flooding rivers, so that they rejoice greatly over this very thing and say: "If the Lord had not been among us—let Israel now say—if the Lord had not been among us when men rose up against us, then they would have swallowed us alive. When their anger was kindled against us, then the water would have drowned us. Our soul passed through a torrent; our soul then passed through the overwhelming water." Israel, he says, was taken captive and carried off to the Assyrians and Medes, and yet escaped their outrages and greed, for it was brought back again to Judea. It also shook off the greed of the Egyptians, who were always pressing upon them and were in the habit of making war on them. In the same way, he says, those redeemed through Christ will be stronger than their enemies, both visible and invisible. Those enemies all but forced them into slavery against their will, and held them like captives in bonds forged by their own perversity. But the redeemed will prove stronger than these as well, and will escape their outrages and greed, because God gives them strength, and in this they will boast. For we take great pride in Christ. We have made him our strength, we have taken courage in him, and we have placed in him every hope of our life. "For not an envoy, not an angel, but the Lord himself saved us." And as the blessed psalmist says: "Our God is our refuge and strength, a helper in the afflictions that have come upon us greatly."

Open your doors, O Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars. Let the pine wail, because the cedar has fallen, because the mighty have suffered great misery. Wail, you oaks of Bashan, because the close-grown forest has been torn down.

He now turns the meaning of his words onto another path of thought. He has given a quite sufficient account of the calling of the nations in Christ through faith. Now he clearly foretells the disobedience toward Christ that would come from those of Israel at the time of the incarnation. He also foretells that for this reason the temple itself, and Jerusalem too, must be burned, and that the very cities of Israel must be captured and perish together with those who lived in them. These things were carried out by the hand of the Romans, under the command of Vespasian and Titus at the time. It seems superfluous to relate in detail everything that befell the cities and people of the Jews because of their drunken outrage against Christ. Those who wish can read the writings of Josephus and learn clearly, in as much detail as they like, whatever they choose.

So he turns his discourse to those who are of the blood of Israel. He likens Judea to Lebanon. For what reason? Lebanon is a mountain rich in timber, thickly covered with spreading forests. The land of the Jews, too, was very populous, with a multitude of inhabitants beyond counting. Like very tall cedars or pines, it had men more prominent than the rest. I mean the priests, and those of the tribe of Judah who reigned at various times. These towered above the others in the glories of their rule. They were known to people throughout the whole land, and their glory was raised on high. But they acted impiously toward Christ. For they "took away the key of knowledge, and neither entered themselves nor allowed those who were entering" to enter, and in the end they crucified him, even though they recognized that he was the heir. For this reason they justly perished utterly, together with their homes, their cities and those dearest to them. So, as I said, he speaks figuratively when he calls Judea Lebanon, and he likens its inhabitants to very tall trees, since they were raised above the rest and far surpassed them. The land was going to be captured easily, and like a city without gates it would receive the Roman army pouring in and be consumed, like a forest when flame is set to it. He indicates this when he says: "Open your doors, O Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars; let the pine wail, because the cedar has fallen."

The language here is metaphorical. Having named Lebanon, that is, having likened the land of the Jews to a mountain, he must also liken those who live in it to pines and oaks. It is easy to see that the discourse is about men, for he immediately said that "they suffered great misery". He showed what kind of misery should be understood when he said, "Let the pine wail, because the cedar has fallen." As the hand of the Romans ravaged the cities of Judea, the illustrious men in them were being captured every day. Those who had not yet suffered this mourned for the captured, and took up the lament for themselves as well. They were despondent and terrified, since they expected to suffer the same fate very soon. This, I think, is what "Let the pine wail, because the cedar has fallen" means. By "the oaks of Bashan", on the other hand, he perhaps means specifically those in Jerusalem. For Bashan is a district in Judea with good soil, extremely fertile, which nourishes very tall trees. Since those in Jerusalem were superior to the rest (I mean the priests and the leaders of the people), he called them the oaks of Bashan. These oaks fittingly lamented, because the close-grown forest was torn down. For they learned that the multitude throughout the whole land had been consumed like a forest, cut down as if with axes by the savage assaults of the enemy. But by the close-grown forest which he says was torn down, you may equally understand the multitude in Jerusalem itself. They perished by famine and war, while the oaks of Bashan, that is, the leaders, wailed over them.
A sound of shepherds lamenting, because their greatness has come to misery; a sound of lions roaring, because the pride of the Jordan has come to misery.

Here, as I said just now, he makes his meaning clearer. He no longer speaks of pine or oak, but openly indicates the leaders of the Jewish orders. He says that they lament and raise their voices, as it were, wailing because their greatness has come to misery. For they became pitiable and cast down, wretched and utterly dishonoured, though once they had enjoyed a most conspicuous glory. Since the shepherds sent through Christ had now been appointed, that is, the inspired disciples, the greatness of the false shepherds fittingly came to misery. The Master of the flock had accused them through the holy prophets, saying: "Woe to the shepherds who scatter and destroy the sheep of their pasture." And again: "For the shepherds have acted foolishly and have not sought the Lord; therefore the whole flock did not understand, and they were scattered." But he promised those who believe in him that he would appoint genuine shepherds, saying again: "And I will bring you into Zion, and I will give you shepherds after my own heart, and they will shepherd you with knowledge." And who, again, are these? They are the inspired disciples and those who at various times lead the churches, "rightly handling the word of truth". They know how to lead the flocks in their care toward everything that brings spiritual benefit.

So the false shepherds lamented, because their greatness had come to misery. He indicates this in another way too, adding at once: "A sound of lions roaring, because the pride of the Jordan has come to misery." Strictly speaking, "howling" is the cry of wolves, which they make when they cry out from hunger and want of food. But divine Scripture applies the word to lions as well. So those who presided over the Jewish orders were exposed as lions roaring, that is, hungry and crying out, because they no longer received the offerings of the people: tithes, firstfruits and thank-offerings. Since they had lost the flock, they no longer enjoyed the fruits it produced.

Someone might think that the scribes and Pharisees roared against Christ like lions. For they [?] against him and let loose cries of envy, malice and unmixed madness. They called him a Samaritan, a drunkard, one born of fornication, and they cried, "Away, away, crucify him!" Anyone who thinks this will also be thinking reasonably. Yet although they roared against him, they came to no small misery, and the pride of the Jordan was brought to nothing. What this means I will explain in turn. The Jordan flows past Jericho, and a great many lions live around it. They roar fearsomely and strike unbearable terror into the inhabitants. The scribes and Pharisees were like this in their ways. They roared at the flock and terrified the weaker with the fears their authority inspired. But the dread of the lions came to misery, and this, he says, is the pride of the Jordan. The word for "pride" properly means the snorting of horses and mules, the sound sent out through the nostrils and bursting forth with a wild blast of breath. But it is also used of arrogance. The inspired David, for instance, said of those who acted outrageously against Christ: "Why did the nations snort with insolence, and the peoples devise vain things?" So when he speaks of "the pride of the Jordan", you should understand arrogance, and not that of the river at all, but that of the lions around it. For sometimes the things in a place are signified by the place itself.

Thus says the Lord Almighty: Shepherd the sheep for slaughter. Their owners slaughtered them and did not repent, and those who sold them said, "Blessed be the Lord, for we have become rich", and their shepherds felt no grief for them.

The word is addressed to the very shepherds who lament and who roar like lions. He still allows them to pasture the sheep for slaughter, although they had been utterly neglectful and had felt not the slightest grief, so to speak, when the sheep were sold and slaughtered. Some shepherds are less scrupulous than others. They look only to their own pleasure and care very little for the master of the flock. Some of the sheep they slaughter without fear, as though imitating the attacks of wild beasts. Others they sell, feeling, as I said, no grief at all, but delighting in the most outrageous gains and giving in to so shameful a love of profit. In the same way, I think, the leaders of the Jewish people would be found to have had no pity on the flocks under them. They fattened their own wealth and widened their purses, as it were, with an insatiable hand. And indeed the Saviour, rebuking such men, said: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faith." They were such hair-splitters that they would rebuke those who did not bring the tithes required by the law even for the cheapest things. Yet they took no account whatever of the weightier commandments, that is, the more necessary and most profitable ones. He also makes clear through the voice of Ezekiel that they were not good shepherds, but rather looked only to profit, when he says: "O shepherds of Israel, do shepherds feed themselves? Do not the shepherds feed the sheep? See, you eat the milk, you clothe yourselves with the wool, you slaughter the fat, and you feed yourselves on my sheep." So, he says, pasture the sheep for slaughter. These are either the sheep that will very soon die by the hand of the Romans, or else those whom you yourselves slaughter, although you hold the rank of shepherds. For the time when they will go to the slaughter has not yet come. It was after the Saviour's coming that the multitude of the Jews was consumed by the Roman sword, even though God had borne with them very patiently. He showed that the peoples under their hand had become the shepherds' own possession when he said: "Their owners slaughtered them and did not repent." The spiritual vineyard belonged to the Master. I mean Israel, or the man of Judah, the new planting, the beloved. Yet they made it their own possession. In the same way they all but took the flocks as their own property. They harvested the fruits the flocks produced, always somehow drawing an abundant profit from them, while abandoning them as plunder to anyone who wished. So the owners slaughtered them, and those who sold them said, "Blessed be the Lord, for we have become rich." These sellers might also be understood as the judges. They made a trade of right judgment and all but said farewell to the law given through Moses, although it says clearly: "You shall not show partiality in judgment, for the judgment is God's." They found it sweet and pleasant to sell the verdict in every case to whoever wished to buy it. This too will be made plain to us, once again, through the voice of the saints. One of the holy prophets said of Jerusalem: "Her leaders judged for bribes." And the inspired Habakkuk all but cries out against God, saying: "How long, O Lord, shall I cry out, and you will not hear? Shall I shout to you when I am wronged, and you will not save? Why have you made me look upon toil and trouble, misery and ungodliness? Judgment has come before me, and the judge takes bribes. Therefore the law is scattered, and judgment is never carried through to the end, because the ungodly man overpowers the righteous. For this reason judgment will go forth perverted." So those who gather wealth from unjust gains, who pervert justice and, as it were, sell the verdict in every case, would be the judges, as I said just now. They are also the ones who say, "Blessed be the Lord, for we have become rich." In saying this they would rightly be convicted of the utmost folly and absurdity. They pretend to bless God, as though God allowed them to amass wealth through injustice and grow rich from bloodshed. It would have been better for them to hold right judgment in high honour and to say: "Blessed be the Lord, for we have shown ourselves illustrious and genuine guardians of the divine commandments, giving a right verdict in every case." Fair words, then, are a deception and a disgrace, unless we do the things in which God takes pleasure.

Therefore I will no longer spare those who live in the land, says the Lord. See, I am handing these people over, each into the hands of his neighbour and into the hands of his king. They will cut the land to pieces, and I will not rescue them from their hand. And I will shepherd the sheep for slaughter into the land of Canaan.

He threatens the flocks with destruction, with exile and with the calamities of war. It had been open to them to come under the hand of the chief shepherd of all, I mean Christ, and to live under him. Instead they foolishly attached themselves to those who slaughtered and sold them. For the only-begotten Word of God became man, and he spoke plainly, showing both their perversity and the true nature of his saving plan for us: "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. But the hired hand, who is not a shepherd and does not own the sheep, sees the wolf coming and abandons the sheep and runs away, and the wolf snatches them and scatters them. He runs away because he is a hired hand and does not care about the sheep. I am the good shepherd." The wretched Jews ought to have cried out against the hired shepherds, but they did not do so. Instead they grieved the good shepherd in countless ways, the one who laid down his own life as a ransom for the life of all. They tried to stone him, they reviled him, and in the end they opened an unguarded mouth against him. For they joined their own leaders in crying out to Pilate, "Away, away, crucify him!", and they poured the righteous blood itself on their own heads. Again, they said, "His blood be on us and on our children!" "Therefore," he says, "I will no longer spare those who live in the land." They are no longer judged worthy of God's mercy. Instead, each has been handed over into the hands of his neighbour and into the hands of his king, that is, his ruler. For they crucified Emmanuel and became murderers of the Lord, filled with every kind of unholiness. Yet God called them to repentance and did not at once inflict the consequences of his wrath. But when the thirtieth year after the Saviour's cross had already passed, peace departed from the land of the Jews. There were wars everywhere, city marching against city, and the people in each city split into factions and fought one another, so that the evils they inflicted on themselves seemed as great as the calamities of the war. For the bravest of the Roman generals conquered the land of the Jews. They burned its cities together with their inhabitants and placed the land under the yoke of slavery. Those who managed to escape settled in the lands of the gentiles, as can be seen even to this day.

This, I think, is what he means when he says, "I will shepherd the sheep for slaughter into the land of Canaan", that is, into the country and land of the Canaanites. The Canaanites are the gentiles. Among them the sheep for slaughter are still, in some way, shepherded by God up to the present day, or rather they seem to be shepherded. For they observe some of the things in the law, and one would not find that they have entirely abandoned their ancient customs. Indeed they circumcise the flesh, keep the Sabbath, and consider certain other things besides to be worthy of attention and account. This, then, was what God said through the voice of the prophet: "And I will be a little sanctuary to them in the countries to which they go." As for the civil wars throughout all Judea, and in Jerusalem too, and what happened in each city, these were clearly recorded by the man who wrote the tragic history of the Jews' calamities. This was Josephus, a learned and wise man.
And I will take for myself two staffs. One I called Beauty, and the other I called Line, and I will shepherd the sheep.

In the divinely inspired Scriptures we understand the staff, or rod, in many ways. Sometimes it signifies kingship, as when it is said to Christ: "A rod of uprightness [?] is the rod of your kingdom." Sometimes it signifies strength, as in the saying: "The Lord will send forth a rod of power out of Zion, and you shall rule in the midst of your enemies." Sometimes it is also taken to mean discipline and the shepherd's skill. Indeed, it was said again through the voice of a prophet to the Son: "Shepherd your people with the rod of your tribe, the sheep of your inheritance." But in the present passage the staffs signify ways of practising the shepherd's skill, a twofold form of instruction, in a manner that appears blameless. The staffs are received by the chief shepherd of all, "who laid down his life for the sheep", that is, Christ, so that he may shepherd his own sheep with them.

For of old, that is, even before the time of the incarnation, the Word who is from God the Father, being God and lawgiver, pastured Israel as though using a single staff: the training given by the law. Somewhere he said to Israel through the voice of a prophet, “I shepherded you in the wilderness.” But when he became a human being like us, he took two staffs. For he pastures, as it were, his own worshippers, those plainly who have been justified through faith and sanctified in the Spirit, with the ordinances of both the law and the gospel. He does not persuade them to sacrifice oxen, nor does he teach them to devote themselves to the offerings prescribed by the law; rather, he has commanded them to make the power of worship in the Spirit their manner of bloodless sacrifice. For the shadow has been changed into truth, and what was in types has been re-minted into the excellence of the way of life in Christ and in the gospel. As for the names of the staffs, the one is Beauty, which is the new covenant, beautiful and worthy of wonder, which the Son himself has spoken, he who is “fair in beauty beyond the sons of men.” The other is Allotment, that is, a portion, so that we understand it as the law, which was accustomed to train the allotment set apart for God. For it is written, “When the Most High divided the nations, when he scattered the sons of Adam, he set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God, and his people Jacob became the Lord’s portion, Israel the allotment of his inheritance.” With these two staffs, then, the great chief shepherd promises to pasture his own sheep, and the word is true. For he gathered into one fold both those from Israel and those from the nations, setting before them the training of both the law and the gospel for their delight, supplying it for them to share like a kind of spiritual pasture, and richly fattening the souls of the saints.

And I will remove the three shepherds in one month, and my soul will be weighed down against them, for their souls also howled against me. And I said, “I will not shepherd you. What is dying, let it die, and what is failing, let it fail, and let the rest devour, each one, the flesh of his neighbor.”

Once the true and good shepherd had appeared, it was surely quite fitting, or rather by then even necessary, that the hirelings and false shepherds should at last be taken out of the way, that is, the Jews’ teachers under the law. Some of these “slaughtered the sheep and felt no remorse,” while others, “selling them, said, ‘Blessed be the Lord, and we have grown rich.’” Then someone might ask why he calls them three shepherds, and in what way they are removed, as he says, in one month. Come, let us speak, setting out evidence from the sacred writings to make it credible. I think, then, that he calls three shepherds those who served as priests under the law, those appointed as judges of the people, and in addition to these the scribes, or the lawyers. For it was these who, so to speak, pastured Israel. Those who held the dignity of the priesthood were from the tribe of Levi alone, and concerning them Moses said, “The lips of a priest will guard judgment, and they will seek the law from his mouth.” Those who received the authority to judge were likewise chosen men, but they were appointed from every tribe. And in the same way, I think, were the scribes, or, as I just said, the lawyers, who always sat beside those appointed to judge and brought forward the writings of the law as proof in each case. Now that those who performed the sacred rites at the divine altars were, as I said, from the tribe of Levi alone would need no argument to prove it. But that the judges were also chosen from every tribe, being taken as men learned in the law, the blessed Moses will make plain when he says to the sons of Israel in Deuteronomy, “You shall appoint for yourself judges and scribes in all your cities which the Lord your God gives you, according to your tribes, and they shall judge the people with righteous judgment. They shall not pervert judgment, they shall not show partiality, nor shall they take gifts; for gifts blind the eyes of the wise and pervert the words of the righteous.” Moses came to say such things, and indeed to command that they be carried out, admittedly following divine and secret promptings, but also not disregarding the counsel of Jethro, who was his father-in-law. For it is written, “And it came to pass on the next day that Moses sat to judge the people, and all the people stood beside Moses from morning until evening. And when Jethro saw all that he was doing for the people, he said, ‘What is this that you are doing for the people? Why do you sit alone, while all the people stand beside you from morning until evening?’” Then, when Moses said that for the sake of judging justly and according to the law he chose to take on the labor involved, Jethro said again, “Now therefore listen to me, and I will advise you, and God will be with you. Be for the people in matters before God, and you shall bring their words to God, and you shall solemnly declare to them the ordinances of God and his law, and you shall show them the ways in which they are to walk and the works they are to do. And you yourself look out from all the people capable men, God-fearing, righteous men who hate arrogance, and you shall set them over them.” Then what does the sacred text say? “And Moses listened to his father-in-law and did all that he told him. And Moses chose capable men from all Israel and made them rulers over them, commanders of thousands and of hundreds and of fifties and of tens. And they judged the people at all times; every weighty matter they brought to Moses, but every light matter they judged themselves.” So, then, there are three shepherds: priests, judges, and those learned in the writings of the law, that is, the lawyers.

We will also find our Lord Jesus Christ himself pronouncing woe separately on the Pharisees, the scribes, and the lawyers. For he said, “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees.” As he was saying this, one of the lawyers answered him, saying, “Teacher, in saying these things you insult us too.” And he said, it says, “Woe to you lawyers also, for you load people with burdens hard to bear, and you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers.” Now I know that the kings from the tribe of Judah who reigned in Jerusalem at various times also filled the role of shepherds for the peoples under their hand. But since, when Christ was born, the line of the kings had come to an end, or rather had been ejected from rule (for at that time Judea was ruled by Herod the Ascalonite, son of Antipater, and by Pontius Pilate), we have of necessity passed over in silence those from the tribe of Judah. That they had come to an end when Christ was born, what is written will make plain: “A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until the things laid up for him come, and he shall be the expectation of the nations.” Since, then, the expectation of the nations, that is, Christ, had at last arrived and been born, a ruler from Judah and a leader from his thighs necessarily failed.

There are, then, as I said, three shepherds: priests, judges, and teachers of the law, who also remained in their own offices, that is, in their ranks and positions, right up to the time of the advent. These are removed, and quite justly, in one month. For since they killed the author of life, for this very reason they are cut off, and in the month of new things, as it were, in which Emmanuel endured slaughter on our behalf. For they did remain, still governing Israel even after the Savior’s cross, while God who rules over all still bore with them and pitied them and called them to repentance. But we say that they were removed, as far as the sentence God passed on this matter is concerned, at that very time when, as I said, they handed over to the cross the Savior and Redeemer of all. Accordingly, they were removed in one month.

So much for the shepherds. But the judgment on the flock itself is “I will not shepherd you,” and that they may, if they choose, devour and bite one another, and crush and consume one another without any mercy. For since they have been cast out of the divine fold and were not counted worthy of the mercy of the chief shepherd of all, they have both devoured one another and been given as the readiest prey to those who wish to plunder them. And concerning the three shepherds who were removed in one month he said, quite fittingly, “My soul will be weighed down against them,” that is, “I will bring a heavy punishment upon them,” “for their souls also howled against me.” For, differing in no way from wild beasts, they repeatedly sprang upon Christ, and in the end they brought him to Pilate, saying, “Away with him, away with him, crucify him!” He also recalls this through the voice of Jeremiah, saying, “I have forsaken my house, I have abandoned my inheritance, I have given my beloved soul into the hands of her enemies. My inheritance has become to me like a lion in the forest; she has raised her voice against me; therefore I have hated her.”

And I will take my beautiful staff and cast it away, to break my covenant which I made with all the peoples. And it will be broken on that day, and the Canaanites, the sheep that are guarded, will know that it is the word of the Lord.

He calls the beautiful staff the training given through the mystical teaching of the gospel, which is exceptional in its beauty, plainly its spiritual beauty. As for saying that he casts it away and breaks it, this would presumably suggest, not that he will send it off and scatter it, annulling it or doing away with it as useless (far from it), but rather, I would say, we ought to understand the following. Those who are accustomed to tend flocks, if they see some of the sheep that have bolted from the herd and gone as far as possible from the rest, then without fail they throw the staff at them and immediately scare them back, so that they choose to herd together with the others. The word of the prophecy, then, has kept to the customary practice of the shepherd’s craft. For it says that the beautiful staff will be cast away, that is, sent even to those farthest off, plainly to the nations; for they were the ones who were far away, but they have come near through faith. And it says that the staff will be cast away in such a way that it is scattered over the whole earth, that is, distributed, so that the word about Christ, or the preaching of the gospel, seems as it were to have been scattered everywhere. For it says it will be scattered on that day, that is, at that time when Christ, having trampled the power of death, would come back to life and say to the holy apostles, “Go and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” For then the word of our Savior traveled through the whole world under heaven, and it is true to say of the holy apostles, “Their voice has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.” That it was not without benefit to the nations that the beautiful staff was cast away and scattered over the earth, that is, distributed even in their own lands (the staff being the covenant which he made no longer with Israel alone but rather with all the nations), we can see with very little effort once we understand the word of the prophecy. For it says, “The Canaanites, the sheep that are guarded, will know that it is the word of the Lord.” By the Canaanites it means the nations. These might be understood as the sheep that are guarded. For they have been kept for Christ, since he is the expectation of the nations. And since the covenant made with all was scattered even in their own lands, they have believed that it is the word of the Lord. For we who have been called from the nations through faith maintain that the only-begotten Word of God, being God and begotten of God by nature and existing from him, has himself addressed to us in his own person the divine laws of the gospel. For this reason we have worshipped him and we serve him, having abandoned that ancient and inglorious deception and having been brought over from belief in many gods. And this, then, was what was sung to him through the voice of David: “All the nations that you have made will come and worship before you, O Lord.” “For at the name of Jesus Christ every knee will bend, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.”

And I will say to them, “If it is good in your sight, fix my wages and give them, or refuse.” And they fixed my wages at thirty pieces of silver. And the Lord said to me, “Put them into the furnace, and see whether it is genuine, in the way I was tested for them.” And I took the thirty pieces of silver and threw them into the house of the Lord, into the furnace.

Through the ordinances of the gospel, that is, through the beautiful staff, the exceptional training, we have been taught the mystery of the Only-begotten’s dispensation in the flesh.
