For we have heard and believed that the Word who is from God the Father, being God, as I said, “became flesh and dwelt among us,” and that he came down even into the form of a slave, and though he existed in the form of the one who begot him and in equality with him, he became “obedient to death, even death on a cross,” and “though he was rich, he became poor for our sake, so that we by his poverty might become rich.” For he rescued us from the bonds of death, set us free from sin, and made us sons of God; and indeed, what good thing has he not given us? We have learned besides that we were bought at a price, “not with perishable things, silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot,” and so from then on we owe him our very life. For if “one died for all, then all died” in him, and we ought to live no longer for ourselves, by any fitting and right reckoning, but rather “for him who died and was raised for us.” And for this reason he says, “If it is good in your sight”; that is, plainly, the mystery of the dispensation in the flesh. If you have been saved through it and fared well, and have come to know me as Savior and Redeemer, the one who endured death for the life of all, “fix,” that is, set, “my wages and give them, or refuse.” But those from the nations are grateful. For they fixed the wages, by no means equal to, but in some way resembling, what we have received from him. For just as he died for us, so we too have laid down our lives for the sake of our sincere devotion and love toward him; and it would be fitting for the holy martyrs to say, “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Shall affliction, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?” For nothing has overcome the courage of the saints. So the likeness to what Christ has done for us is in some way suggested by saying that thirty pieces of silver were given to him as wages. For Judas, the traitor, truly most loathsome and hateful to God, took thirty denarii and betrayed Christ to those thirsting for his blood, and sold the author of our salvation to the wicked. But thirty pieces of silver were brought by the nations as wages for him, and at God’s command these are thrown into the furnace, being thoroughly tested, just as Christ himself was tested for us. For our faith will not go unexamined before God, who knows all things, nor will our life go untested; rather, as the blessed Paul says, “the fire itself will test what sort of work each one has done.” And it is also written of Christ, “Suddenly the Lord whom you seek will come to his temple, and the messenger of the covenant whom you desire. Behold, he is coming, says the Lord Almighty. And who will endure the day of his coming? Or who will stand when he appears? For he comes in like a refiner’s fire and like the fullers’ herb, and he will sit refining and purifying as silver and as gold.” And somewhere the divinely inspired David also sings, as though in the person of everyone who has believed in Christ and wishes to live according to the gospel, “Test me, O Lord, and try me; refine my kidneys and my heart.” But the prophet says that the furnace is in the house of the Lord. For the Church of Christ tests each person’s character and the sincerity of his love for Christ, and, “having the discernment of spirits,” it knows precisely who speaks in the Holy Spirit when calling Jesus Lord, and who speaks by Beelzebul when he calls him accursed; and who are “the true worshippers,” and who, on the other hand, are the “wolves” who come to us “in sheep’s clothing.”
And I cast away my second staff, the Allotment, to break the covenant between Judah and Israel.

He said that Christ would take two staffs and so pasture with them his own sheep, plainly the holy multitude of those called through faith. And we said that the beautiful staff is the training, that is, the preaching of the gospel, while the other, that is, the Allotment, is the commandment given through Moses, given as a help to the allotment set apart for God, that is, to Israel, in accordance with the voice of the prophet: “For he has given the law as a help,” he says. Now, that the multitude of the nations was to be trained not only by these teachings, but also by the very commandments given of old through Moses, plainly with the shadow in the law being refashioned into truth, the present passage makes clear to us as well. For just as he said that the beautiful staff would be cast away and scattered (for the training of the gospel was spread abroad, as it were, in the lands of the Canaanites, carried about, of course, by the holy apostles), so too the other staff, or training, that is, the Allotment, namely the law, which God had established as a covenant between Judah and Israel, that is, among the whole race descended from Israel. (By Judah he means the two tribes in Jerusalem, I mean Judah itself and Benjamin, and by Israel the other ten, which settled in Samaria together with Jeroboam.) So the law too has been given to those from Canaan; for we are instructed in the mysteries, as I said, by the ordinances of both the law and the gospel. That is why Christ said, “Do not think that I came to abolish the law or the prophets. I did not come to abolish but to fulfill. For I tell you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke will pass from the law until all is accomplished.” For he fulfills the law by teaching what is beyond the law, without putting the one he trains outside the law, as for example when he says, “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not murder,’ and whoever murders will be liable to judgment. But I tell you that everyone who is angry with his brother without cause will be liable to judgment.” And again, “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I tell you that everyone who looks at a woman with desire has already committed adultery with her in his heart.” For “You shall not murder” is brought to completion by renouncing anger as well, which is the root and origin of murder; and by not admitting desires at all, that is, by restraining pleasures, the very possibility of adultery is surely done away with at the same time, just as we say that when roots are damaged the shoots that spring from them wither along with them, or rather would not spring up at all.
BOOK 4
ON THE PROPHET ZECHARIAH. BOOK FIVE.

And the Lord said to me: “Take for yourself once more the gear of a shepherd, an unskilled shepherd. For behold, I am raising up a shepherd over the land. He will not look after what is failing, he will not seek what is scattered, he will not heal what is broken, and he will not guide what is whole. He will devour the flesh of the choice ones and wrench their ankles out of joint.”

The good shepherd, wise and skilled, that is, Christ, cast away the two staffs and scattered them in the lands of the Canaanites, in the ways already explained. Some then recognized that this is the word of the Lord. As I said, they have believed that the Word, who is from God the Father and in him, was begotten of him in a way beyond telling. Yet because he became like us and was proclaimed chief shepherd of all, he set before them both the teaching and illumination of the gospel and also that of the law. These were meant to initiate them into the mystery concerning himself and to give them exact knowledge of it. We said that these are the two staffs by which Christ shepherds us “in good pasture and in a rich place,” as it is written. But the Jews did not understand the mystery. They did not recognize the staff called Beauty, that is, the preaching of the gospel. Besides this, they dishonored the other staff, whose name is Cord, that is, the law given through Moses. So they did not accept the faith, and they failed to recognize the one foretold through the law and the prophets. The Savior himself told them this plainly: “Do not think that I will accuse you before the Father. The one who accuses you is Moses, on whom you have set your hope. For if you believed Moses, you would believe me, since he wrote about me. But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?” So it is beyond all dispute that they believed neither the writings of Moses nor the words of the Savior.

Since they did not receive the knowledge of the truth, “God will send them,” as the most wise Paul says, “a working of error, so that they believe the lie.” He says that this working of error is the Antichrist, and the Jews will be condemned because they attach themselves to him. The Savior confirms this when he says to them, after they had chosen to disobey: “I have come in my Father's name, and you do not receive me. If another comes in his own name, him you will receive.” The Jews, then, were going to receive without delay the son of lawlessness when he appears in his time, the one “who opposes and exalts himself above every so-called god or object of worship, so that he takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God.” For this reason God commands the prophet to act out beforehand a figure of the one who does not know how to shepherd rightly and skillfully. He says: Take for yourself once more the gear of an unskilled shepherd. The kindest shepherds, who are skilled in the work at hand, carry slender staffs, so that if the time comes to strike, the animal struck is not crushed. But a man who does not understand the business, and stands as far as possible from the shepherd's skill, crushes them with the heaviest clubs. These, I think, are the gear of the unskilled shepherd. In due time the son of lawlessness, clothed with royal honor, would appear to those on earth to hold the rank of a shepherd. Yet he would think the peoples under his hand, and those outside it too, worthy of no mercy. Therefore he says: Behold, I am raising up a shepherd over the land; he will not look after what is failing. It is as if he said: what has slipped into little faith he will not strengthen with sacred instruction. He will not seek what is scattered: what has strayed, he says, from the straight way and is used to bolting from the flock he will not seek. That is, he will not bring it back to what is better and right. He will not heal what is broken. A person is broken when he is overcome by wicked pleasure and, as it were, cannot bear the weight of his love of the flesh. Or he is broken when the deceits of the unholy heretics have carried him off, so that his mind is not sound in the matter of right belief. The good shepherd heals this too, but the unskilled one no longer does. He will not guide what is whole; instead he will even devour the flesh of the choice ones and wrench their ankles. For the son of lawlessness will make war on the saints. He will let loose his unbridled anger on them and all but carve them up and devour them like a wild beast. He will also wrench their ankles, so that no one is able to walk upright. He will force them to worship him, overwhelming them with wonders. For his “coming is according to the working of Satan,” and by Beelzebul he will perform “wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect.” As the Savior says, “no flesh would have been saved,” since his greed rages against all, “but for the sake of the elect those days will be cut short.” “For the Lord will slay him with the breath, and destroy him by the manifestation of his coming.”
O you who shepherd vain things and have abandoned the sheep! A sword upon his arm and upon his right eye! His arm will wither away completely, and his right eye will be utterly blinded.

Having spoken once of the unskilled shepherd, he now all but scowls at the shepherds who are not good. He speaks in a very general way, announcing beforehand what will happen to those who think as they do. Notice how he describes them as already paying the penalty for their negligence. Perhaps he even grieves with them out of his natural gentleness. He accuses them of having become shepherds of vain things, that is, caretakers of what is temporary. They are so negligent that they rejoice over sheep that perish miserably. Some sold them and said, “Blessed be the Lord, and we have become rich.” Others slaughtered them and felt nothing for them, for among them there was no thought at all of the duty to shepherd rightly. These were the teachers of the Jews. As Christ says, they shut the kingdom of heaven, neither entering themselves nor letting others enter. They travel around “sea and land to make one proselyte, and if that happens, they make him twice as much a son of Gehenna as themselves.”

What, then, will happen to such wicked shepherds? A sword, he says, upon his arm and upon his right eye. The arm is taken to mean power, and as a figure of spiritual activity. Indeed, when animals were slaughtered in the holy tabernacle, the arm was the part set apart for the divine altar as a holy offering to God. I think the law was hinting by this riddle that one must dedicate one's own strength, both bodily and spiritual, to God. That the arm signifies power is confirmed by one of the saints, who cried out to the God of all: “By the greatness of your arm let them be turned to stone.” The eye is taken as a figure of the mind. So the one who does not shepherd rightly will suffer the maiming of arm and eye. That is, he will be stripped of spiritual strength, for he will not be able to accomplish anything good without God giving him strength. He will also be darkened in mind, since he has no share in the divine light and is seen to have none. He will not be able to say with confidence, “For you will light my lamp, O Lord; my God, you will lighten my darkness.” It is the right arm that is cut by the sword, and the right eye that is blinded. For among the Jewish people there is nothing on the right hand: no good deed, no strength in such things, none of what comes from divine light into mind and heart. As Paul says, “To this day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart.” And somewhere David sings of them, “Let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see.” So everything among them is on the left hand, sinister and perverse, whether you mean their way of life, their thinking, or anything else believed to belong to them. To have the things on the left taken away would, I know, benefit those who undergo it, for casting off perversity would free them from every charge and blame. But to lose the things on the right would do no small harm, since it leads straight into what is more shameful and utterly abominable. It is fitting, and quite reasonable, for the Jews to be deprived of the things on the right. But for us who are in Christ it is fitting to cast off what is perverse and to take pride in the things on the right.
The burden of the word of the Lord concerning Israel, says the Lord, who stretches out the heaven, lays the foundation of the earth, and forms the spirit of man within him.

The prophet has now given a full account of the good shepherd, that is, Christ. He has also described the unskilled and utterly cruel shepherd who carves up the sheep, whom we say is the Antichrist. Next he usefully mentions the persecutions that would come in their time against Israel. He does not mean Israel according to the flesh at all, but rather the spiritual Israel, and the truly holy Jerusalem, “which is the church of the living God.” We say that the spiritual Jew is the one who has circumcision of the heart, by the Spirit, and not the circumcision in the flesh by the letter. In the same way, one could say that Israel should be understood not as Israel by blood, but rather as the one whose mind sees God. Such, above all, are all those who have been called to holiness through faith in Christ, and who have come to know God the Father through him and in him. For this is the one true and exceptional way of seeing God.

The word, then, is to be understood as concerning the Israel we have just described. The prophet shows that the Creator of all, who foretells these things to us, is all-powerful, when he says: who stretches out the heaven, and lays the foundation of the earth, and forms the spirit of man within him. He means that God, who has power over all things, takes up the burden of the word concerning Israel. In the psalmist's words, he is the one “stretching out the heaven like a skin.” He made the earth so firmly established that it stands always and forever unshaken, though it is founded upon the seas, for so the inspired Scripture said. He it is who forms the spirit of man within him. How could the maker and craftsman of such great things fail to accomplish whatever he wills, without sweat and with perfect ease? God forms the spirit of man within him. He does not call it into the beginning of its being, even though it did come into being through him. Rather he transforms it, as it were, from weakness to power and from cowardice to endurance. In short, he spiritually remakes it from worse to better. The divine David too sings somewhere: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.” No one with any sense would say that he wanted to receive a heart or a spirit as if he had none to begin with. One would suppose instead that he was asking for a clean heart and a right spirit to be created within him. This is the re-forming. It is the custom of the holy prophets, when they are about to foretell matters of real weight, first to try to show the God of all as all-powerful and supremely mighty. In this way their word has firm grounds for belief on every side, even if they say something beyond hope, something that to our way of thinking seems beyond reason and incredible. Behold, I am making Jerusalem like shaken doorways to all the peoples round about, and in Judea there will be a siege against Jerusalem. And on that day I will make Jerusalem a stone trampled by all the nations. Everyone who tramples it will mock it to the full, and all the nations of the earth will be gathered against it.

The earlier prophecies clearly spoke of the war that the Roman army would wage against Judea. Indeed he said, “A voice of shepherds lamenting, because their greatness has been brought to misery.” And after other things he said again, “Therefore I will no longer spare those who inhabit the land, says the Lord. Behold, I am handing over the people, each into the hands of his neighbor and into the hands of his king. They will cut the land to pieces, and I will not rescue it from their hand.” In the present passage, however, he clearly foretells the persecutions that came upon the Church. For they made war on those who believed in Christ. First of all came the leaders of the Jewish synagogue. They ordered the holy apostles not to speak in the name of Christ, had them scourged in their councils, and arranged for them to be stoned. What utterly unholy thing did they not do and say? Then the word about Christ went out into the lands of the nations as well, and the people there heard the preaching of the gospel. So other persecutions arose in turn, carried out by those who ruled at various times and in various lands. These men were eager to hold on to profane and abominable idolatry and had become servants of diabolical impiety. They killed the saints, summoning them to the contests of martyrdom. The Church seemed somehow to suffer easily, with no one coming to her aid. She seemed like shaken and falling doorways, or a trampled stone. The Savior of all could easily have lulled every war to sleep, or rather removed it entirely from those who worship him. He could have made them stronger than every trial and than the hand of their enemies, who were exalting themselves over them. Yet in his saving plan he allowed them to be made glorious through sufferings, so that, conformed to him, they might be glorified and reign with him. As it is written, if we suffer with him, “we shall also reign with” him; and if we are “partakers of the sufferings,” we shall also share in the glory. So he says: Behold, I am making Jerusalem like shaken doorways. Suppose this happens, and the siege is set around her, that is, she is besieged by everyone. When she seems to be like a trampled stone, then every mocker will mock. As I said just now, this was done in the persecutions that came from time to time. They fastened on the saints and tormented them in many ways, and perhaps even smiled at them as they died, the wretches. No doubt they did not know the glory that comes from suffering, or that the toil would surely lead the saints to everlasting gladness. Notice how he says that the trampling of the Church is not the work of the strength of the nations. It comes from his own will, which, as I said, allows his own worshipers to be perfected through sufferings. For behold, he says, I am making Jerusalem like shaken doorways to all the peoples round about. I think this is similar to what the Savior said very clearly to Pilate: “You would have no authority over me unless it had been given you from above.” The spiritual Jerusalem, that is, the Church, might in her turn rightly say to the world that persecutes her: You would have no authority over me unless it had been given you from above.

On that day, says the Lord Almighty, I will strike every horse with bewilderment and its rider with madness. But upon the house of Judah I will open my eyes, and I will strike all the horses of the peoples with blindness.

He says that he will strike horse and rider with bewilderment, madness, and blindness. By this he gives us to understand that he will lull every war to sleep and make the attacks of the persecutors come to nothing. Suffering bewilderment is, I think, the same as undergoing madness, for to be out of one's mind may quite reasonably be understood as bewilderment. When this has happened and has come upon the murderers, the saints will surely be able to say of those who fought against them, “Our enemies are senseless,” and also, “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will be magnified in the name of the Lord our God. They were hobbled and fell, but we have risen and stand upright.” There is another way, too, in which the one who wickedly assails the patient endurance of the saints is driven mad. He will undergo an unexpected bewilderment, that is, amazement, when he sees that they conquer in their calamities and are crowned when they fall. Though they seem to be defeated, it is then above all that they prevail all the more. For it is true that they are seen to be glorious above all in their suffering, and that grace from above accompanies the greatness of their toils. How then could the blessed martyrs fail to astound those who fought against them? They conquer even Satan himself and rebuke wicked and unclean spirits. Sometimes they even fill their very killers with great amazement at the glory that is in them. So he promises to strike rider and horse together. By these I understand the battle lines of the enemy, drawn up against the gentleness of the saints.

He said that upon the house of Judah he would open his eyes. Here he gives the name Judah to Christ, who came forth from the root of Jesse and from the tribe of Judah. His house is the Church, that is, the holy multitude of those who have been justified by faith. The opening of the eyes signifies, I think, that he will watch over them very generously, as it were with his whole gaze. This would be a clear sign of his kindness toward them, and also of his tender care and love, for it is written, “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous.” He would surely make those he looks upon thrice blessed, if it may truly be said that he punishes the insolent and the wicked by turning away from them, but gladdens the pious and virtuous by visiting them. The divine David makes plain both the loss that comes from his turning away and the gain that comes from his visiting. At one time he said, “Do not turn your face away from me, and do not turn aside in anger from your servant.” At another he said, “Look upon me and have mercy on me.” For anger and all that comes from it will surely follow when he turns away, but receiving mercy follows when he looks upon us.
And all the captains of thousands of Judah will say in their hearts: We shall find for ourselves those who dwell in Jerusalem in the Lord Almighty, their God.

We say that the holy apostles have been named captains of thousands of Judah. Christ appointed them as if to the rank of generals, and their lot was to lead Judah, that is, those called to confession and praise, for the name Judah means “praise.” These would be all those from the nations. The divine psalmist also commands them to glorify Emmanuel, saying in the Spirit, “Bless our God, you nations, and make the voice of his praise heard.” Here, then, Judah means those called through faith to praise and confession. The captains of thousands set over them, its commanders and leaders, are the divine disciples. Indeed, one can see them shouting to the worshipers of the Savior as if to soldiers: “Stand, therefore, having girded your loins with truth, having put on the breastplate of righteousness, and having shod your feet with the readiness of the gospel of peace. In all things take up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to quench all the flaming darts of the evil one. And receive the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.” The divine Paul also said that we must be seen to be shining and living a life worthy of approval: “with the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left.” Besides this, he all but pointed out the enemy's battle lines when he said, “Finally, be strong in Christ and in the might of his strength. For our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against the principalities, against the authorities, against the world rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.” So the divine disciples are quite rightly the captains of thousands. They, he says, will say in their hearts: We shall find for ourselves those who dwell in Jerusalem in the Lord Almighty, their God. The divine disciples longed to see the truly holy Jerusalem, that is, the Church, filled with worshipers. They longed to see her, like some famous and celebrated city, greatly adorned with a large multitude of inhabitants. So they proclaimed the faith and preached the good news of Jesus, sealing their words with signs and wonders. But they did not persuade Israel. Israel remained hard and unbending, like an unbridled horse. For this reason they then sought for themselves people who would dwell in the holy city in the Lord Almighty their God, that is, in Christ. And so they turned to the nations, crying out to the Jewish people: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first. But since you thrust it away and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the nations, for so God has commanded us.” From there they sought the citizens of the Church, the city that the divine David also mentions when he says, “Glorious things have been spoken of you, O city of God.” By seeking they grew rich and gathered a multitude beyond number. They say to the holy city: “Enlarge the place of your tent and of your curtains. Fix them firmly, do not hold back. Lengthen your cords and strengthen your stakes. Spread out further still, to the right and to the left.” She rejoices in the multitude of her inhabitants. All but marveling at the gathering of her own children, she says: “But I was childless and a widow. Who has borne me these? And where were these?”

In that day I will make the commanders of thousands of Judah like a firebrand among wood and like a torch of fire in stubble, and they shall devour all the peoples round about, on the right and on the left.

As I said before, he calls the holy apostles the commanders of thousands of Judah, or indeed simply all who lead the holy churches. He said that the word they preached, that is, their initiation into the mysteries, would so prevail over the hearts of the Gentiles that it would seem like a firebrand fallen among wood, or a torch dropped into stubble that easily catches fire. For they shall devour, he says, all the peoples round about, on the right and on the left. That is, wherever they wish to go, they will be able to go, everywhere and in every way, calling people to awareness and warming those who had grown cold, as it were with the divine and spiritual fire. The God of all said something like this to the blessed prophet Jeremiah too: "Behold, I have made my words in your mouth fire, and this people wood, and it shall devour them." This means that it will call them to [?], and will make those who had grown cold in sin fervent again in the spirit. For the heart of those who have gone astray has grown cold, and their mind is dead, since they worship "the creation rather than the Creator," God, and offer their reverence to wood and stones.

But when they receive the divine word they become, as I said, fervent in spirit and warm toward righteousness. For we have been baptized, as the inspired John says, "with the Holy Spirit and with fire": a spiritual fire, which consumes like rubbish the sin that has settled in our souls and melts away the filth of love for the flesh. Indeed, it was said to someone through the voice of Isaiah: "Because you have coals of fire, sit upon them; they will be a help to you." And Isaiah himself says of himself: "And one of the seraphim was sent to me, and in his hand he had a coal of fire, which he had taken with the tongs from the altar. He touched my mouth and said, Behold, this has touched your lips, and it will take away your iniquities and cleanse you of your sins." By the coal he means, in all likelihood, Christ, who is divine and most holy and melts away sins. So the inspired disciples became like a firebrand among wood and like torches of fire in stubble, and they devoured the nations round about. Yet they did not consume them to destruction. Rather, they burned up the foul and profane doctrines of the knowledge falsely so called that was among them, and melted away the filth of the ancient deception. Nor did they any longer allow the minds of those who had once believed to grow cold and turn to useless follies, so that the believers leap for joy at their own state and say to Christ, the Savior of all: "Your word is exceedingly refined by fire, and your servant has loved it." That the word of God is hot and very sharp would become clear when he says to Jeremiah: "Are not my words like a blazing fire, says the Lord, and like an axe that splits rock?" For the all-powerful Word of God is admirably suited to rekindle a mind grown cold in sin, and easily to open it up when it has, so to speak, dried out, hardened and been packed down. For it is "living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart." And it was said somewhere through the voice of the prophets to the harsh and unyielding Jew: "Be circumcised to our God, and take away your hardness of heart, men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem." And: "Rend your hearts and not your garments."

And Jerusalem shall dwell again by herself, and the Lord will save the tents of Judah as at the beginning, so that the boast of the house of David and the exaltation of the inhabitants of Jerusalem may not be magnified over Judah.

He says that the Church will not always be in turmoil, nor will she endure unending persecutions. At times she will be at rest and will dwell by herself, that is, alone, with no one troubling her, no one bringing affliction on her, no one instilling fear, and no one heaping on her the despondency that comes from trials. For the Lord will save the tents of Judah as at the beginning. The Lord of all, plainly Christ, will shield his own churches, that is, his own tents, and will give them care equal to that which was once granted to the Israelites redeemed from Egypt. For the God of all brought Israel out of the house of bondage and "out of the iron furnace," as it is written, and out of unbearable oppression, "with a mighty hand and an uplifted arm," when he also "drowned" their pursuers "in the Red Sea; the deep covered them, they sank like lead in the mighty waters." The redeemed were brought across. A pillar of fire led them by night and showed them the way, and a cloud hung over them by day. Then they ate bread from heaven, escaped the bites of the serpents in the desert, proved stronger than their enemies, were brought across the Jordan, were circumcised with knives of stone, and entered the land of promise.

These things Christ will grant to those who seek his tents, that is, the Church. In the same way he will save them too. He frees them from bondage, I mean bondage under the devil, and rescues them from the oppression of the demons. He brings them across the distractions and senseless turmoil of this world as through a sea. He sets himself up for them as a pillar and a bright foundation, enlightening those in darkness, and like a cloud he waters them with spiritual dew. He becomes for them the bread of life too, and renders the bites of the spiritual serpents ineffective and powerless. He brings them across the Jordan, makes them clean by the circumcision that comes through the Spirit, and brings them into the kingdom of heaven. These things he will grant to his own worshipers, and he will save them in such ways, so that the boast of the house of David, that is, the leaders of the Jews, may not be magnified; nor may there be exaltation, that is, occasions for exaltation, for the inhabitants of the visible and earthly Jerusalem over Judah. For they thought highly of themselves and looked down with great disdain on those who believed in Christ, and even on Emmanuel himself, constantly holding up the gifts given through Moses to the ancients and pointing to the favor shown to their fathers. So at one time they said: "What sign do you do, then, that we may see it and believe you? What work do you perform? Our fathers ate the manna in the desert, as it is written, He gave them bread from heaven to eat." And at another time: "We know that God has spoken to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he comes from." So the God of all will work wonders for us too, if not visibly, as he did then, yet spiritually. In this way he will save us who are in his own tents, so that the Jews, that is, their leaders, may not be arrogant toward us. For this, I think, is what "the boast of the house of David" signifies.

And it shall be in that day that the Lord will shield the inhabitants of Jerusalem; and the one who is weak among them in that day shall be like the house of David, and the house of David like the house of God, like an angel of the Lord before them.

God the Father has crowned us "as with a shield of favor." For he has given us his own Son as our defender and champion, through whom we have been saved. Through him we easily slip free of every temptation and regularly prevail over war from our enemies and the perversity of our persecutors. Something of this kind is shown in the present passage too, though one would find the saying shrouded in much obscurity. For the God of all said that he would shield those who dwell in Jerusalem, and not rather those who merely sojourn by it. Here Jerusalem is admittedly understood as the Church of Christ. The one who sojourns by it is someone who is not very secure but is, as it were, shaken and very easily led toward what is not right, or else is careless about learning. The one who dwells in it, on the other hand, stands firm, is grounded in love for Christ, and devotes himself constantly to the benefits of the divine teachings, so that he can say what was spoken through the voice of David: "How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth." He will shield those who dwell there, then, he says, and the one who is weak among them in that day shall be like the house of David. By the house of David here we say that the most honored among the Jews are meant. For kings from the tribe of Judah, to which Jesse and David belonged, reigned at various times in Jerusalem. By the one who is weak among those who dwell in the holy city, the spiritual Jerusalem, which is the Church, he perhaps means someone who is still a catechumen. Such a person has not yet been baptized but is still sick, as it were, weighed down by the burden of sin and not yet freed from his old ailments, that is, his passions. Yet even so, because he has believed, has departed from the shadow of the law, and has wholly inclined toward choosing to live out the life of the Spirit and the glories of life in Christ, he shall be, he says, like the house of David. That is, he will be in no way inferior in understanding to those who are wise and most honored among the Jews. The most wise Paul hints at something of this kind when he addresses the Jewish people. For he says: "When Gentiles, who do not have the law, by nature do what the law requires, they are a law to themselves, even though they do not have the law. They show that the work of the law is written on their hearts." And again: "Circumcision is indeed of value if you keep the law; but if you break the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision. So if an uncircumcised man keeps the precepts of the law, will not his uncircumcision be counted as circumcision? And the one who is physically uncircumcised but fulfills the law will judge you, who have the written code and circumcision but break the law. For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is circumcision something outward in the flesh. He is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the Spirit, not the letter. His praise is not from men but from God." So the one who has rejected circumcision in the flesh as stale, has come to love rather the circumcision in the Spirit, and bears within himself the Jew who is one inwardly, "whose praise is not from men but from God": how would he not be better than those learned in the law and most honored among the Jews, and in no way inferior to them, even if he perhaps still has some remnant of weakness because he is not yet baptized? For by the healthy part of his heart, that is, by his faith, he will surely surpass the one who does not accept the faith. But if any of the house of David, that is, of those who are illustrious and most honored among them, should accept the faith, understand the mystery of Christ well and become his worshiper, he will be like the house of God and like an angel of the Lord before them. The Savior himself is found saying something of this kind, for he said: "Therefore every scribe who has been trained for the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings out of his treasure what is new and what is old." For the one who already has the knowledge of the law stored up within him, if he adds to it the knowledge of the gospel, will be rich in understanding, and will set new and old insights before those eager to learn, as if from storehouses. Such a one was the inspired Paul. At times he sought to confirm the message about Christ with proofs from the law; at other times, by the mysteries that go beyond the law, he in a way drove his hearers to choose to glory in faith in Christ. At one point he said: "Tell me, you who want to be under the law, do you not hear the law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman. But the son of the slave woman was born according to the flesh, and the son of the free woman through the promise. These things are an allegory: the women are two covenants. One is from Mount Sinai, bearing children for slavery; she is Hagar. For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia; she corresponds to the present Jerusalem, for she is in slavery with her children. But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother." And at another point he said of the Son: "He is the radiance of his glory and the exact imprint of his being, and he upholds all things by the word of his power. When he had made purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high." Do you see, then, how he benefits the souls of those being initiated with teachings both old and new? The house of David, then, he says, will be like the house of God, like an angel of the Lord before them.

And it shall be in that day that I will seek to destroy all the nations that come against Jerusalem, and I will pour out on the house of David and on the inhabitants of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and compassion, and they shall look upon me.

"It will be my purpose," he says, "to destroy all the nations that have fought against the holy city," that is, the Church, "and to surround with grace and compassion the house of Judah and those who dwell in Jerusalem." These are the citizens of the Church, those counted among the ones who ought to give praise. They would again be those who worship Christ, have chosen to follow the commands of the gospel, and lead a glorious and blameless life. That the enemies of the truth were going to be utterly and completely powerless, the Savior himself makes clear when he says: "You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it." By the gates of Hades he means those who wish to persecute the Church. They are, as it were, destruction and corruption, and they habitually drag down to the pit of Hades those who attach themselves to them. So those who have made war on her will grow weak, or rather will be destroyed, and will go off to perdition. "Many indeed are the afflictions of the righteous, but the Lord will deliver them out of them all." And it is true that "all who desire to live a godly life in Christ will be persecuted." Yet Christ makes the schemes, and even the attempts, of those who plot against us useless and ineffective. He has given us power "to tread on serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy," and he encourages us, saying: "In the world you will have tribulation; but take courage, I have overcome the world." So those who rise up against the Church from time to time are destroyed, while on those within her, that is, the believers, a spirit of grace and compassion is richly poured out. For God the Father crowns us with good things from above and fills us with spiritual gifts, so that, lifting the eye of the mind to him, we may place all our hope in him. This, I think, is the meaning of "they shall look upon me." In this state we rejoice at our lot, and then we say in praise of God: "Bless the Lord, O my soul, who is gracious toward all your iniquities, who heals all your diseases, who redeems your life from corruption, who crowns you with mercy and compassion, who satisfies your desire with good things."
Because they mocked, they shall also mourn for him with a lamentation as for a beloved one, and they shall grieve with grief as for a firstborn.

The Hebrew version begins the present section with "And they shall look upon me," but in this it does not agree with the tradition and translation of the Seventy. For the Hebrews say "They shall see" instead of "They shall look upon," and "him whom they pierced" instead of "they mocked." Yet we say that neither the Hebrew nor the Seventy has missed what is fitting. For the Jews mocked Christ, and besides this they also pierced him, since Pilate's soldiers pierced his side, as it is written. So we will rightly apply the saying here to the person of Christ. We say it means this: They shall see him whom they pierced, or whom they mocked, and they shall mourn for him with a lamentation as for a beloved one, and grieve with grief as for a firstborn. For after they had nailed the divine temple to the wood, those who crucified him stood around him, mocking him impiously. Some said: "You who destroy the temple and build it in three days, save yourself!" Others in turn said: "He saved others; he cannot save himself." But when he had laid down his own life for us, had preached to the spirits in Hades and had come back to life, and an earthquake had taken place, those keeping watch at the tomb marveled and said, "Truly this was the Son of God"; and many were filled with remorse. Later the Roman war fell upon them: their country was ravaged, their cities burned, their houses left deserted, Jerusalem itself was besieged, and famine wasted them from within. Then some were at last, with difficulty, brought to recognize their outrages against Christ. At last they knew the causes of their sufferings, and that their impious acts against him had brought these sufferings upon them. So because they mocked, they shall mourn for him with a lamentation as for a beloved one, and grieve with grief as for a firstborn. For when a beloved firstborn son lies dead, his parents shed uncontrollable tears; their beating of breasts and dirges cannot bear to come to an end, and their grief is long and, as it were, unceasing, wasting the soul with sharp and unbearable assaults. Christ foretold that the Jews were going to experience such evils when he rebuked the women who were weeping over him, saying: "Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children."

In that day the mourning in Jerusalem shall be as great as the mourning for a pomegranate grove cut down in the plain, and the land [will mourn?] tribe by tribe: each tribe by itself, and their women by themselves; the tribe of the house of David by itself, and their women by themselves; the tribe of the house of Nathan by itself, and their women by themselves; the tribe of the house of Levi by itself, and their women by themselves; the tribe of Simeon by itself, and their women by themselves. All the tribes that remain, each tribe by itself, and their women by themselves.

While all Judea was being ravaged at various times by the Roman army, and Jerusalem itself was under siege, he says that the mourning of those within it will be like the mourning a farmer would make when a pomegranate tree is cut down. For it is a plant that flowers beautifully, and from its root it sends up many shoots, straight and very tall. And if it is also adorned with its fruit, then above all it is held in great admiration. For the pomegranate is a lovely thing, distinguished by its natural beauty as it hangs from the branches, its rind tinged with the same red as the seeds within. But it is a terrible and grievous thing, as I said, for the plant to be cut down together with its fruit. Yet one could see something of this kind happening to the Jews. For as far as the honours given by the law were concerned, the leading men among them might fittingly be compared to fruitful pomegranates: those from the tribe of Judah, who occupied the thrones of the kingdom, had attained a glorious lot among them, while those from the tribe of Levi, richly crowned with the distinctions of the priesthood, were illustrious and renowned. And why should I mention the judges and the lawyers and those adorned with other honours? But since they behaved outrageously toward Christ, they were handed over to their enemies: Vespasian and Titus ravaged their country, Jerusalem was besieged, and everyone in it wasted away with famine, and everything was filled with lamentation and mourning. Josephus too will bear witness, for in composing his books on the Capture he says somewhere about Jerusalem, in these very words: "There was wailing everywhere throughout the city, piercing cries, and lament as if at a word of command." And just as he called it Lebanon and a forest, saying, "Open your doors, O Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars. Let the pine wail, for the cedar has fallen, because the mighty have been grievously afflicted; wail, you oaks of Bashan, for the dense forest has been torn down," so too he calls it a pomegranate tree being cut down. The inspired John will also confirm the statement, when he cried out to the crowds of the Jews: "Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees; every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire," "and burned." So the mourning in it, he says, will be as great as the mourning over a pomegranate tree would be, when its fruit has come into full bloom and it is unexpectedly cut down. And the land will mourn tribe by tribe, and their wives by themselves. Now we do not suppose that the blessed prophet means that in each tribe the males would stand on one side and the females on the other, and so make their mourning; that, it seems, would be a superfluous and pointless thing. Rather, he teaches that each tribe, together with the women in it, will have its own particular reason for lament. That is why he says, the tribe of the house of David by itself, and their wives by themselves. So come, let us describe, as far as we can, the grief of each. Those from the tribe of David, that is, of Judah, falling from the kingship, will wail uncontrollably, as people deprived of so conspicuous a glory; those from the tribe of Levi, thrust out of the privileges of the priesthood, will make their lament together with their wives. Those from the tribe of Nathan—he was a prophet, and not altogether a truthful one—will mourn in their turn. For they would no longer be able to prophesy unjust things and speak what came from their own hearts, to sell their own words to the foolish as though they came from God, and to collect the shameful gains that came from it. Tradition holds that the Jews took the judges appointed from time to time from the tribe of Simeon, since it had men of great understanding, learned in the law, and far superior to the others in choosing to live lawfully. That is why he says that the tribe of Simeon will mourn by itself. These too have a lament of their own. For they did not judge rightly, nor did they yield to the divine laws and strive to accomplish what pleases God; rather they were greedy for gain and very easily bought, and, as the prophet says, "Her judges are like wolves of Arabia." And the other tribes were bound, in a way, to join these in lamenting, since they were being driven out from the customs and places dearest to them, or rather because death itself hung over their heads, with famine itself, as it were, outstripping even the enemy's sword.
Chapter 13. On that day every place will be opened in the house of David and for those who live in Jerusalem, both for change and for sprinkling.

The text runs on to what will again happen after this to "those who have loved the appearing" of Christ. Those who have behaved insolently through their disobedience will be under siege, he says, and will wail over their own evils. But in the spiritual and truly holy Jerusalem, and in the house of David, that is, in the Church of Christ, who appeared from the seed of David according to the flesh, every place will be opened; that is, there will be great spaciousness and, as it were, a relaxed way of life, much longed for and wholly free of toil.

It should be known that the Hebrews have again rendered the passage differently. Instead of "every place will be opened," they said that every spring will gush forth. And it is very likely that the aim of the translation of the Seventy also tends toward this very thing, even if the manner of expression differs, so that the meaning is something like this. The disobedient and unbridled Jerusalem, the wicked and apostate one, "who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her," will pay penalties proportionate to her own outrages; for she will be cut down like a pomegranate tree. But for those who dwell in the spiritual Jerusalem, that is, in the house of Judah, which is to say of Christ, every place will be opened; that is, in every place there will be a spring gushing forth the water of cleansing—clearly that of holy baptism—so that it is of use to believers both for change and for sprinkling. And what is the change? For Jews it is from the discipline of the law to the way of life in Christ, from shadow to truth, from type and letter to spiritual worship. For Greeks the change is a passage from unbelief to faith in Christ, from their former ignorance to pure knowledge of the God who truly is, from darkness to illumination. And there is a common change, fitting for everyone who has been called through faith, Jew and Greek alike: from minding the things of the flesh to choosing to live holily and purely and to walk in the Spirit, as blessed Paul says; from honouring the things in the world to loving the things above the world. And who could doubt that when we receive divine and sacred baptism we are sprinkled with the blood of Christ for cleansing from sin? So the way to change and to sprinkling for those in the house of Judah is saving baptism, that is, every place opened, namely every spring that is widened and gushes forth the water of cleansing.

And it shall be on that day, says the Lord, that I will utterly destroy the names of the idols from the land, and there will no longer be any memory of them; and I will remove the false prophets and the unclean spirit from the land.

All things have changed for the better in Christ, and what is in him is a new creation, having cast off the blemish of the old decay. Anyone who wished could see from the facts themselves that this statement is accurate. Before the time of his coming, when the Only-begotten had not yet become one of us, nor yet flashed his divine light around all things, there was still mist and darkness in the hearts of the nations. For they served idols, and had slid into such folly as to offer their reverence to wood and stones, and to pay to unclean demons the honours fitting for God. Such were the charges against the stupidity of those who had gone astray. But in Israel, which was chosen and was "the Lord's portion," as it is written, "the allotted measure of his inheritance," there was such a decay of morals and manners that the law was held in little account, though it had been given to help them and was by no means incapable of training them to live rightly; instead they leaned toward being heedlessly carried away along with the errors of the nations and slipping into the superstitions of their neighbours. For they were devoted, quite outrageously, to the oracles of the false prophets. Some of these, servants of idols who sat in profane precincts, were oracle-mongers and speakers of lies; others had "Thus says the Lord" on their tongues and pretended to be pious, cloaking the wolf, as it were, in a sheep's skin. The wretches took the name of prophecy for themselves and impiously snatched the glory that goes with it, belching out whatever they pleased, and claiming that the reasonings of their own hearts were the counsel of God. Concerning those accustomed to such audacity the prophet Jeremiah also said to God, who holds sway over all things: "O Lord, you who are, see, their prophets prophesy and say, You shall not see the sword, and there shall be no famine among you, for I will give truth and peace on the land and in this place." And to this God says: "The prophets prophesy lies in my name. I did not send them, I did not command them, and I did not speak to them; for they prophesy to you false visions and divinations and auguries and the inclinations of their own hearts." And again: "I did not send the prophets, yet they ran; I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied." For they were liars, as I said, and, overcome by shameful petty gains, they spoke to their hearers things "from their own hearts," as it is written, "and not from the mouth of the Lord." Then, when the Jews ought to have been indignant at this, they did the opposite: they held these men in reverence and were eager to crown them with the highest honours. But now that the Only-begotten Word of God has appeared to us, the cold and childish toys of idolatry are utterly gone and wholly destroyed, and along with idolatry has been removed the outlandish and impious practice of the false prophets, who were full of an evil and unclean spirit and could quite rightly be found to suffer from an error akin and next door to that of the idol-worshippers. For both had one and the same master of their impiety, namely Satan. So, he says, I will remove the names of the idols from the land, and there will be no memory of them on that day, that is, at that time when the divine and heavenly light shines, and the spiritual morning star rises in the hearts of those who had gone astray, as it is written, and the day dawns, the former night and the deeds done in it having been driven away; so that, with the ancient uncleanness removed, the true and holy worshippers may henceforth appear, having taken up the glories of a pure way of life and honouring the life that is in Christ.

And it shall be that if a man still prophesies, his father and his mother who bore him will say to him, You shall not live, for you have spoken lies in the name of the Lord; and his father and his mother who bore him will bind his feet when he prophesies.

So great, he says, will be the reverence for the divine among the people of that time, and so much will they care for the utmost decency and an admirable life, that even parents will be provoked against their own children if they choose to imitate the liars, pretending to prophesy, and utter something from their own hearts as though God had spoken. For they will bind his feet, he says, that is, they will tie him up as one senseless and mad, and without delay they will even decree death for him, if he persists stubbornly and shamelessly in this sickness. For it is enough for them, to decree every penalty for their child, that he has spoken lies in the name of the Lord.

See how true the word is, and how firm a claim to belief the prediction has. For who among us at the present time would put up with someone prophesying? How would he not at once regard such a person as out of his mind, and how would he not consider someone so minded detestable? What father will leave his child unrebuked if he is caught in such dreadful offences? This, then, I think, would be a very clear proof that we must hold firmly that the nature of our affairs has changed much for the better compared with before, as God refashions it according to his own will and toward what is good. Indeed, the things that were once honoured and admired by many are now detestable and accursed, intolerable to decent people, and not exempt from deserving punishment.

And it shall be on that day that the prophets will be put to shame, each by his vision when he prophesies; and they will put on a garment of hair because they lied. And he will say, I am not a prophet, for a man begot me from my youth. And I will say to him, What are these wounds between your hands? And he will say, Those with which I was struck in the house of my beloved.

That the things once admired are regarded among us as deserving penalty and punishment can be seen without difficulty from the sense of the passage before us. For, as I said, liars and cheats used to prophesy in Israel, people in the habit of leading others astray "for a handful of barley and a crust of bread," as it is written. Yet when they dared such things, no one rebuked them or was willing to restrain them as people who had chosen impiety; rather, the wretched people thought fit to crown them with praises and the highest honours. That is why these men went from bad to worse, the disease being fed in them, as it were, by the frivolity of those who admired them. But at the present time, he says, they will be put to shame—false prophecy being clearly not accepted but rather rebuked, and the penalties for their madness being demanded of those accustomed to such audacity—so that, once convicted, they at once abstain from the evil and put on a garment of hair because they lied. That is, they mourn over the evil and lament their offence, repenting that they slid into such ignorance of mind as to speak lies against God, and without blushing at all they confess their sin and ask for pardon, saying plainly, I am not a prophet, for a man begot me from my youth, that is, I am a human being's child. And human nature is very weak and quite easily led into what is not right, and somehow readier for sin. Such would be the words of those who repent. And if I should wish to ask him, he says, "What is the meaning of these wounds or blows that can be seen on your hands?" he will answer in turn, Those with which I was struck in the house of my beloved—his father and mother, clearly, having bound him and exacted the penalty for his rashness. For to each of us the beloved house is the house of our parents.

See, then, how great the difference is between the affairs of former times and those of now. The false prophets among them were admired, enjoyed glory and good repute, and, doing these things, did not even repent. But at the present time, if any should choose to follow their madness, they are rebuked, put to shame, and punished by the verdicts of their parents; they repent as having sinned, they mourn and weep, they ask for pardon, confessing the weakness of human nature and how easily it slips into sin. For "the unclean spirit" has been removed "from the land" by the power and authority of our Saviour Jesus Christ.

Awake, O sword, against my shepherd and against the man who is his fellow citizen, says the Lord Almighty. I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered; and I will bring my hand upon the shepherds.

God the Father gave his own Son for us, permitting him in the plan of salvation—though he is God and was ineffably begotten from him by nature—to descend into the form of a servant, to become a man like us, and to endure the cross, so that he might save the world and put an end to Satan's greedy grasp over all, and also overthrow profane idolatry and abolish divinations, false prophecies and the deceptions that come from the heart, and remove "the unclean spirit from the land"; and in addition to these things, so that he might win over the whole world under heaven, bringing those who had gone astray to the knowledge of God and persuading them to choose a pious and seemly way of life and to be seen honouring every form of virtue. For this reason, then, he willingly endured death on the tree, though it carried very great disgrace, "despising the shame," since this was the good pleasure of God the Father himself. And the Son himself suggests something of this kind to us when he says: "For I have come down from heaven not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me. And this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day." For, as the inspired Paul writes, "For this reason Christ died and lived again, that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living." So he willingly laid down his life for us, with God the Father all but handing him over, as man, by his own decree, and permitting him, as I said, to purchase the life of all with his precious blood. Indeed, when Pilate thought he had authority over him, the Saviour countered him, saying, "You would have no authority over me at all, unless it had been given you from above."

Through the voice of the Prophet he has already foretold that, once he has suffered death in the flesh, human affairs will change greatly for the better. Now he all but hurries on the arrival of the time when these things will happen, and he orders the mystery of the passion to be set in motion. He gives his charge to the sword itself, saying: Awake against my shepherd and against the man who is his fellow citizen, says the Lord Almighty. By “sword” here, we say, is meant the trial, pictured as a blade, or else the passion itself, which the madness of the Jews brought upon Emmanuel. This seems to be how the righteous Simeon understood it, and indeed spoke of it, when the holy Virgin brought Jesus at eight days old: “And a sword will pierce your own soul too.” For she was all but slain by a sword when she saw the one born of her (according to the flesh, I mean) being crucified. “O sword,” then, he says, “awake against my shepherd”; that is, let the saving passion now be set in motion, and let the time come when good things are revealed. Christ has been set over us as chief shepherd, and all of us who have believed are under him, yet not outside the hand of God the Father. For the Father rules over us in the Son; through him and in him we have been saved, and through him we have gained access. Indeed the Savior said: “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand. My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one can snatch them out of the Father's hand. I and the Father are one.” The Son, then, is God the Father's own shepherd. He does not tend someone else's flocks; he tends his own, which are also the Father's. The hired shepherds are not counted as his own. They slaughtered the sheep without any mercy, “and as they sold them they said, ‘Blessed be the Lord, we have become rich.’” The good shepherd's fellow citizens, that is, his kin and acquaintances, are those placed under him, and first of all the divine disciples, who were scattered and fled when the shepherd was struck. For when the servants of the Jews came to seize Jesus, and with them the betrayer together with the cohort, “all left him and fled”; so the Gospel text tells us. God the Father gave his own Son over to death for us, and he is said in some sense to strike him because he allowed him to suffer at all. The Son himself will confirm this. Through the voice of the psalmist he speaks about those who did unholy things against him, clearly meaning the Jews: “For they persecuted the one whom you struck, and they added to the pain of my wounds. Add iniquity to their iniquity.” So, as I said, he undertook the passion willingly, so that what his suffering achieved might be plainly seen. But the deed will bring destruction on those who crucified him, and those who led such a plot and its undertakings will fall into the evils that come from divine wrath. These were the leaders of the peoples. He makes this plain when he says: And I will bring my hand upon the shepherds. For they destroyed “his vineyard,” as the prophet says; “they made his desirable portion a trackless wilderness; it was made a desolation of destruction.” So God brings his hand upon the shepherds, as though it were the sword striking them down and exacting the penalty for their impiety. He does this not only because they themselves acted outrageously against Christ, but also because they became for others the beginning and the path of unrestrained madness. As the blessed evangelist Matthew says, when Pilate set Christ and Barabbas before the Jews and called out to them, “Which of the two do you want me to release to you?”, “the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowds to ask for Barabbas and to destroy Jesus.” They also persuaded them to shout, “Crucify him, crucify him!” So what was said through the voice of the prophet is true: “For the shepherds acted foolishly and did not seek the Lord; therefore the whole pasture did not understand, and they were scattered.” The watchfulness of good shepherds benefits the flock, and in the same way their slackness destroys it, since those under their hand always follow in the shepherds' footsteps.

And on that day, says the Lord, two parts will be utterly destroyed and will perish, but the third will be left in it. And I will bring the third through fire, and I will refine them as silver is refined, and I will test them as gold is tested. He will call on my name, and I will hear him, and I will say, “This is my people,” and he will say, “The Lord is my God.”

God's hand has been brought upon the unholy false shepherds who destroyed the Master's vineyard. Now he says that those who very foolishly went along with their unholy schemes will not escape penalty and punishment either. He clearly means the populace of the Jews, the common crowd under the shepherds' hand. For they were consumed by war. Cities perished together with their inhabitants, and villages with their men, burned to the ground in utter destruction. A remnant was barely saved, about a third of the whole multitude, so to speak, for Israel was not wholly destroyed, since God took pity on them for the sake of their fathers. The blessed Isaiah himself says this: “And if the Lord of hosts had not left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah.” But the third part, meaning the remnant, that is, those of Israel's blood who believed, he says he will bring through fire and refine like silver and gold. For the life of the saints is not without hardship. It is true that “all who want to live a godly life in Christ will be persecuted.” The divine disciples proved to be the most thoroughly tested, and so were all who became their fellow workers at that time and labored with them, serving the gospel of Christ as priests among the nations. They were called to endure many afflictions and persecutions. They were all but refined in fire, tested by trials, so that they could say boldly: “For you have tested us, O God; you have refined us as silver is refined.” What benefit, then, comes from this? What reward will there be for those who have labored and been tested in this way? They have become God's own, his acquaintances and beloved. For they were counted as “a holy nation, a royal priesthood, and a people for his own possession, so that they might proclaim the excellencies of him who called them out of darkness into his marvelous light.” Once they were not a people, but now they have become a people. Once they heard: “When you stretch out your hands to me, I will turn my eyes away from you; and even if you multiply your prayers, I will not listen to you.” But now he says: He will call on my name, and I will hear him, and I will say, “This is my people.” So they have become the portion of God the Father, and they have been given to the Son, for the Son rules over all things together with the one who begot him. They have the Creator and Master of all as gracious and merciful to them.
VOLUME FIVE
BOOK SIX.

Behold, days of the Lord are coming, and your spoils will be divided in your midst; and I will gather all the nations to Jerusalem for war, and the city will be taken, and the houses plundered, and the women defiled, and half of the city will go out into captivity.

Pointing to the venerable and saving passion on the cross, he said a little earlier: “O sword, awake against my shepherd and against the man who is his fellow citizen, says the Lord Almighty; strike the shepherd, and let the sheep be scattered.” And that the multitude of the Jews would be subjected to the utmost penalties — and quite rightly, for that all-daring people had killed the Lord — he taught by adding: “And I will bring my hand upon the shepherds, and it shall be in that day, says the Lord, that two parts shall be utterly destroyed and shall fail, but the third I will bring through fire, and I will refine them as silver is refined, and I will test them as gold is tested.” How such things are to be understood we have already explained, as far as we could, and not beyond what is reasonable. Now the aim of the present passage has turned toward Jerusalem, which committed impiety without restraint, and it indicates to us the manner of its capture. For behold, he says, days of the Lord will come, that is, days which he himself brings on by a just verdict and a holy judgment. For what he says through another prophet as well is true: “Shall there be evil in a city which the Lord has not done?” For nothing capable of harming a whole city could happen which we do not say is done with his permission, when he wishes to exact the penalty for their offenses from those who rush toward wickedness with unbridled impulses. So he says that the days are his, because they are brought on in accordance with his wrath. For their drunken outrage was no longer bearable: they had killed the prophets, and on top of them the Son as well.

What will happen in those days he makes clear, saying: And your spoils will be divided in your midst — evidently by all the nations gathered together, plundering the houses and dragging off women together with their infants. For then, he says, half of the city will go out into captivity. For they say that the Romans, having taken the city and lost all patience with the shamelessness of those fighting against them, burned both the temple itself and the houses of the town. But they spared those inhabitants of the upper city and of the temple who threw themselves at their feet. Observe how he says the victors will reach such a pitch of insolence that, having plundered the houses, they will not at once go off with the booty and make the division at leisure once they have reached their own tents, but will do it in the captured city itself — which would not have happened if there had been anyone at all to help those in their wretched plight and to fight against the ravagers. And he says that the women will be defiled, dragged off against their will by others and stripped of the customs of modesty, often in the very sight of their lawful husbands. Such are the sufferings of war, and such the misfortunes that befall those who have once been captured and are wholly without help.
But the remnant of my people shall not be utterly destroyed from the city.

This, I think, is nothing other than what I said just now: that some mercy was shown to those who lived in the upper city, and part of Jerusalem was saved. For the Roman generals checked the fury of their fighting men whenever they saw people weeping, falling at their feet, and running to them without resistance. So either he calls those in the part of the city that was saved the remnant of his people, or perhaps those who believed in Christ the Savior of all, about whom he also says that they would not be utterly destroyed from the city. For they will always be citizens of the Church; even if they are cast out of the earthly and destroyed Jerusalem, they nonetheless have the city above, about which the inspired Paul also writes: “But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother.” The blessed David too seems to hint at something of this kind when he says somewhere: “He who dwells in Jerusalem shall never be shaken.” For if the Church is unshakable, “and the gates of Hades shall not prevail against it,” according to the Savior's word — for it has him as its foundation — it is entirely necessary that those who dwell in it should henceforth be seen to be stronger than destruction, reckoned as God's people and ranked among his true-born children.

And the Lord will go forth and will do battle against those nations, as on the day of his battle, on a day of war. And his feet will stand on that day upon the Mount of Olives, which faces Jerusalem on the east; and the Mount of Olives will be split, half of it toward the east and half of it toward the sea, a very great chasm; and half of the mountain will lean toward the north, and half of it toward the south. And the valley of my mountains will be blocked up, and the valley of the mountains will be joined as far as Asael, just as it was blocked up in the days of the earthquake, in the days of Uzziah king of Judah.

The language is framed as if of one of the noblest generals, spurring on his comrades in arms to battle and rousing their fighting spirit against the enemy's ranks; yet it is to be understood of God, as all but present with and fighting alongside the nations who ravaged Judea and sacked Jerusalem itself.

We recall that in the gospel parables too he says something of this kind. The king who was holding the wedding feast for his son sent his servants to gather those who had been invited. But they wickedly insulted and killed those who were calling them to the festival, and finally, on top of them, they slew the son. Then what does the parable say? “But the king was angry, and sending his armies he destroyed those murderers and burned their city.” He will therefore be, he says, like those who rise up nobly against the foe on a day of battle and consume their enemies. This is a demonstration of wrath come to its limit and of the most extreme measures, as he brings a penalty equal to the offense upon those who outraged him. For they killed, as I said, the Author of life. But since things beyond reason and wonder could fittingly be accomplished only by the nature that is sovereign over all, for this reason he says that his feet — evidently Christ's — will stand on that day upon the Mount of Olives, and that the mountain will undergo four rents: two toward the east and the west, that is, toward the sea (for it is the custom of the inspired Scripture to call the region of the west by that name), and the other two inclining, one toward the north and Boreas, the other toward the southern region. He said that the peaks themselves would also be broken down, so as to fill the ravines between them, which were unexpectedly shaken, as far as Asael; this is a village lying, as the story goes, at the far edge of the mountain.

He compares this so severe earthquake to the one that occurred once in the time of Uzziah, who was also called Azariah. For while he occupied the royal throne in Jerusalem, being as he was of the tribe of Judah, he dared unlawfully to take hold of the ministries of the priesthood, and was at once struck with leprosy; and as God then displayed his wrath at these things, the land of the Jews and Jerusalem itself were terribly shaken. Indeed they say that Mount Zion underwent such a shock that it was rent into two parts and dropped its peaks into the adjacent ravines.

By these words the Prophet seems to be hinting to us at the earthquake which the ministers of the gospel proclamation say took place at the precious cross. The Prophet recalls the event at greater length here, but our most wise Matthew, abridging the narrative, says: “And Jesus cried out again with a loud voice and gave up his spirit. And behold, the curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom, and the earth shook, and the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised.” But since we must fit a plausible explanation to what happened, the splitting of the rocks and the blocking up of the ravines seem to hint at the hardening of the Jews and at the turning to better things of those who had served idols. For those who worshiped the creation rather than the Creator had, as it were, a heart of stone, hard and unyielding, like rocks that bear no fruit. But what did God say about them through the voice of Ezekiel? “And I will tear out their heart of stone from their flesh, and I will give them a heart of flesh, so that they may know me, that I am the Lord.” So the hearts of those who were in error were split, as God opened them, so that they might receive the word of the saving proclamation.
