And he hints at something of this kind through the voice of Jeremiah, saying: “Are not my words like a burning fire, says the Lord, and like an axe splitting rock?” For the word of God is “living and active and sharper than any sword, piercing to the division of soul and spirit.” So, as I said, the splitting of the rocks would be a sign, and a very clear one, of the turning to better things of those who had gone astray. The blocking up of the ravines, on the other hand, hints, as I said, at the hardening of the Jews. For the inspired Isaiah also said something of this kind: “And it shall be in that day that the Lord will block up from the channel of the river as far as Rhinocorura” — that is, the mind of those throughout all Judea will be blocked up, “so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not hear, nor understand.” “For a veil lies upon their heart,” as it is written, “at the reading of the old covenant.” The shaking of the earth, I suppose, would indicate a change from one state of things to another. Indeed the inspired David cried aloud, saying: “You who sit upon the cherubim, let the earth be shaken.” We certainly do not say that he is asking for the earth under heaven to be shaken bodily and perceptibly — that would be a silly thing, and would bring us no benefit at all. Rather, the Spirit-bearer was asking that the earth be changed from worshiping idols to knowing at last the One who is God by nature and in truth, from minding the things of the flesh to wishing to live spiritually, and, in a word, from earthly things to heavenly. And if he also says that the very tombs of those who had fallen asleep were opened, we say that death itself had to be seen to be conquered, when Christ died in the flesh for our sake according to the divine plan, “so that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living.”
And the Lord my God will come, and all the saints with him.
On that day there will be no light, and there will be cold and frost for one day; and that day is known to the Lord, and it will be neither day nor night, and toward evening there will be light.

Having run quickly through the wicked deeds of the Jews against Christ the Savior of us all, and the capture of Judea and of Jerusalem itself, he now comes to the very end of the present age, and to our profit describes the descent of Emmanuel from heaven. For he will come down with the holy angels in the glory of God the Father, to “judge the world in righteousness.” For as the inspired Paul writes: “We must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or bad.” He will come, then, he will come, he says, and all the saints with him — that is, the most pure multitude of his own angels, escorting him as his guard, no doubt, and standing by in attendance. For Emmanuel is Lord of all, and is glorified by all as God and as co-ruler with the one who begot him. But if anyone should say that the saints themselves will also stand beside him, caught up “in the clouds to meet him in the air” after the resurrection from the dead, as the most wise Paul also holds, he would by no means miss what is fitting. For the inspired Isaiah too said something of this kind about them: “There the deer met and saw one another's faces; they passed by in number, and not one of them perished; one did not look for the other, for the Lord commanded them and his Spirit gathered them.” And the inspired David too sings to us somewhere, foretelling the descent from heaven of Christ the Savior of us all: “For the Lord will not reject his people, and he will not forsake his inheritance, until righteousness returns to judgment, and all the upright in heart hold fast to it.” For he calls Christ righteousness, and says that he will return for judgment. He was taken up after trampling down death, and ascended to his Father and God in heaven; but in due time he will return for judgment, and with him all the upright in heart, that is, the saints, as I said just now.

That at the time of the consummation the condition of the visible creation will be different, and that it too will pass over to something better, renewed through Christ, the Prophet will confirm when he says: On that day there will be no light, and there will be cold and frost for one day, and that day is known to the Lord. For now day and night are kept distinct and have divided the times between them by the Maker's commands: the light of day rises, and then night follows. But when the Judge arrives, who refashions all things as he sees fit, the creation, as I said, will receive a different ordering. For there will no longer be light and cold and frost for one day. By light he signifies the day, and by frost and cold the night; for night and day together are reckoned as one day.

It is as if he were saying: At that time when he has come from heaven and remolds all things and refashions them for the better, as Creator, there will be no light nor night for one day. The blessed prophet Isaiah also says something of this kind: “And the sun will no longer be your light by day, nor will the rising of the moon light up the night for you; but the Lord will be your everlasting light, and God your glory.” That the use of the elements themselves will in due time cease, Christ himself will confirm, saying: “Immediately after the tribulation of those days the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light.” For Christ will suffice as everlasting light for us, and he himself will be a long and unending day. And he says that that day is known to the Lord. For God the Father alone knows the day of the consummation. The Son himself also assures us of this, saying: “But concerning that day or hour no one knows, not the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but the Father alone.” For insofar as he is understood to be a man like us, he would not know what is in the Father; but insofar as he is God by nature and has come forth from him, he surely knows the last day too, even if he says he does not know it because of his humanity. The Prophet, interpreting for us and making clearer what he had said, adds to this: And it will be neither day nor night, but toward evening there will be light; that is, at the time of night there will again be light — the light that comes through Christ — and it will flash over all that is under heaven, darkness having been wholly abolished and no longer lying over the eyes of the saints. And it is reasonable to think that creation itself will be remade for the better. A worthy witness to this is the Savior's disciple, who says that the day of the Lord will come like a thief, on which the heavens will pass away with a roar, the elements will be burned and dissolved, the earth and all the works in it will be burned up, and we look for new heavens and a new earth and his promises. Besides, we shall arrive at this by necessary reasoning. For if our existence is certainly to be in newness of life, we needed a new creation as well. For as the inspired Paul writes: “The creation itself too will in due time be set free from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.” On that day living water will go out from Jerusalem, half of it to the first sea and half of it to the last sea, and so it will be in summer and in spring. And the Lord will be king over all the earth.

Again he explains to us in a riddle that a very great and abundant outpouring of the Holy Spirit will be bestowed on the saints, especially at that time when they are brought back to a holy and unending life — I mean the life in the age to come. For now, through faith in Christ, we have been enriched with the firstfruits of the Holy Spirit by way of a pledge; but after the resurrection from the dead, when sin has been entirely abolished, the divine Spirit will no longer be in us by way of pledge and in measure, but richly and abundantly, as I said, and we shall then delight perfectly in the gifts that come through Christ. So he calls the Spirit living water, which he also says will go out from the Jerusalem above. For since the inspired Scripture said that the God of all dwells in heaven — even though he is everywhere and fills all things — for this reason he says that the life-giving Spirit will go out from heaven.

That it is the custom of the holy writings to compare the divine Spirit to waters, its Giver himself, that is, the Son, will confirm, saying: “Whoever believes in me, as the scripture has said, out of his belly will flow rivers of living water.” And the inspired evangelist, interpreting this and making it plain, says: “Now this he said about the Spirit, which those who believed in him were to receive.” For since the Spirit is life-giving, it is for this reason compared to water, which gives life to bodies — and quite rightly.

That those who are deemed worthy of the holy life will have richly at hand a share in the bounty of the Holy Spirit, and will be filled as it were with life-giving waters, he indicates by saying that of the water expected in due time to go out from Jerusalem, half will go to the first sea and half to the last sea. And what does this mean? The divine Scripture often likens the many nations of humanity and a multitude beyond number to seas and waters. Thus it says somewhere through one of the holy prophets: “For the whole earth was filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as abundant water covers the seas.” And the inspired Daniel too, foreseeing what would befall those throughout the whole world in the last times, said: “I, Daniel, was watching, and behold, the four winds of heaven were striking upon the great sea, and four great beasts were coming up out of the sea, different from one another.” Making this very point clearer, the blessed David sings out: “This is the sea, great and wide; there are creeping things without number, small creatures with great; there ships pass through; this is the dragon which you formed to make sport of.” For what dragon do we say there is in the visible sea, formed to be made sport of by God who rules over all? It is therefore the custom of the holy writings to liken to seas both the whole world and sometimes a great multitude of people.

That the grace of the Spirit will be distributed by God without measure both to those from Israel who believed and to those from the nations, he indicates by saying of the life-giving water that half of it will go to the first sea and the other half to the last sea. By the first sea he means Israel, and by the last the multitude of those who believed after them, that is, the nations. And we certainly do not say that the Holy Spirit has been divided, and that because of the word “half” he will be incomplete in each of them — far from it. Rather, we shall consider that the Prophet means to indicate that the distribution of grace will be allotted equally to the one and to the other. For half and half will signify an evenly balanced generosity and equality. And that the grace is perpetual, and the participation in it is at every time, is easy to see from his saying again that so it will be in summer and in spring.

It should be noted that instead of “in spring” the Hebrew edition says “in winter.” So, he says, the outpouring of the spiritual waters will be the same and alike in winter and in summer, that is, at every time. But there is no harm in saying “spring” instead of “winter,” according to the text of the Seventy; for spring lies, as it were, in between and shares in both winter and summer, so that even if someone assigns it to the season of winter, he will not do violence to what is reasonable, or indeed correct.

Someone may wish to understand in another way what is said about the spiritual water: that half of it will go out into the first sea and half of it into the last sea, and that it will be so in summer and in spring. Such a reader will arrive at an interpretation of the passage something like this. By the first sea he probably means the one that lies toward the dawn, that is, the sea beyond the limits of the whole earth. By the last sea he means the one at the far edges of the west. He treats the east as the face, so to speak, and the beginning of the inhabited world. By summer, I think, he means the hot and southern parts of the world, and by spring the northern and cold parts. The divine David spoke in the same way when he wished to point to the four regions under heaven. He cried out to God, "Summer and spring, you made them," and again, "The north and the sea, you created them." So the living water, he says, will go out in equal measure and with grace equally shared, both into the first sea and into the last, that is, to east and west. It will go out in summer and in spring, which again means to south and north. For the whole world under heaven will be filled with the gifts that come through Christ, and the gift will remain for good with those who have received it. Then, at that very time, "the Lord will be king over all the earth." We shall be subject to him alone, and he will rule over all. The world-rulers of this age will have been completely abolished and every evil principality led away in triumph. Satan himself and the evil powers with him will have been driven out of their greedy tyranny over us.

On that day the Lord will be one and his name one, encircling all the earth and the desert from Gabel to Remmon, south of Jerusalem. Ramah will remain in its place, from the Gate of Benjamin to the first gate, and to the Gate of the Corners, and to the Tower of Hananel, to the king's winepresses. They will dwell in it, and there will be no more curse, and Jerusalem will dwell in safety.

The words of the holy prophets are always somewhat obscure. This, I think, is God's wise arrangement, so that holy things may not be set before dogs, and the truly precious pearl may not be carelessly thrown at the feet of swine and trampled with contempt. But in the Spirit Christ reveals this knowledge to those who are worthy, and he makes the powers of the age to come plain to them. As a rule, hidden and spiritual things are sketched out in things that can be perceived by the senses, and what is visible becomes a kind of body for what is less visible. So he said that on that day, that is, at that time, the Lord will be one and his name one, encircling all the earth. This will be when our condition has been changed into newness of life and creation itself has been remade into something better than before. Of course there always was, is, and will be one Lord, who is by nature and in truth the God of all and who brought into being things that once did not exist. But the inventor of sin, that is, Satan, led the world under heaven astray, and we wretched people were drawn off into false and profane worship. We went on living in the world blind and foolish. We called those who had deceived us lords, and in our ignorance we gave the name of deity to unclean demons. Through Christ we have been called to the knowledge of the truth even in this world. Yet when the present age has passed away and reached its end, all madness will have been taken from us and the enemies placed beneath Christ's feet. Then at last there will be one Lord over all the earth, and no one will snatch from him the glory of lordship. Christ will also be the one Lord in another sense, when every earthly kingdom has ceased to act and the world under heaven assigns power over all to him alone. The most wise Daniel said something of this kind. In explaining what the visions meant, he says: "Just as you saw that a stone was cut from a mountain without hands, and it crushed the earthenware, the iron, the bronze, the silver, and the gold, so the great God has made known to the king what must happen after these things. The dream is true, and its interpretation is trustworthy."

So he will be one and alone, and he will fill the holy city with his own glory, that is, the spiritual Jerusalem. Here again he shows its breadth and length through the earthly Jerusalem, as in a type, saying that it will be broadened from Gabel to Remmon. Gabel, or Gabe, is a village belonging to the allotment of the tribe of Benjamin, and it is said to lie in the parts north of Jerusalem. Remmon is a rock in the southern desert. So the breadth of Jerusalem runs from Gabel to Remmon. He also marks out its length, saying: From the Gate of Benjamin to the first gate, to the Gate of the Corners, and to the Tower of Hananel, to the king's winepresses. The first gate and the Gate of the Corners were names of certain gates in Jerusalem. Between them was a tower called Hananel, and immediately after it came the king's winepresses. These places mark out the length of Jerusalem, as in a type. The God of all commanded the blessed prophet Ezekiel to measure the house with a reed, passing this way and that, to show that there are many dwelling places with the Father and that the abodes of the saints are countless. In the same way, it seems to me, he describes for us here, through visible places, the breadth and length of the spiritual Jerusalem, that is, the Church of Christ. The divine Isaiah also cried out to her: "Enlarge the place of your tent and of your curtains; set them up, do not hold back; lengthen your cords and strengthen your stakes; spread out further to the right and to the left." So the saints will dwell in the holy city, which has been broadened and stretched to the length fitting for it. And there will no longer be a curse, he says. This means that it will in no way be estranged from God, for he will grant it a love that does not fail. They will no longer fall into offending God, since, as I said, sin will have been completely abolished, and Satan the tempter along with it. "For no lion will be there, nor will any of the evil beasts go up onto it, nor will any be found there." Therefore they will dwell in safety. Between these statements stands "Ramah will remain in its place," and here again we shall explain the sense of the passage as far as we can. Ramah is a small town or village belonging to the allotment of the tribe of Asher, and besides it there is another Ramah belonging to the tribe of Naphtali. A holy prophet also mentions either one of these or yet another Ramah. He said: "A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation and weeping and wailing: Rachel weeping for her children, and she would not be comforted, because they are no more." We say that this took place at Bethlehem, when Herod ordered the infants there to be slaughtered. So he calls Jerusalem Ramah because there was great lamentation in it when it was captured. Indeed, the prophet Jeremiah portrays it as all but shedding tears and wailing over its own lost children. He said: "She wept bitterly in the night, and her tears are on her cheeks." And what is her lament? "My virgins and my young men have gone into captivity. You have killed with sword and famine; in the day of your wrath you have slaughtered, you have not spared."

Someone may wish to apply the name to the spiritual Jerusalem, that is, the Church, and take it that the Church is now called Ramah. We say that this reading is also quite correct. For many people weep in the churches and have "godly grief, which produces a repentance that leads to salvation and brings no regret." Christ himself welcomes such people, saying, "Blessed are those who mourn now, for they will be comforted," and again, "Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh." So even if the prophet's words call the Church Ramah, this interpretation will also be convincing. But it will remain in its place, he says, that is, it will not be shaken. For, as I said, the Church of Christ is firmly founded and cannot be moved.

And this will be the fall with which the Lord will strike all the peoples who have made war against Jerusalem: their flesh will melt away while they are standing on their feet, their eyes will flow out of their sockets, and their tongue will melt away in their mouth.

"You will have tribulation in the world," Christ said to those who had believed in him. But he made them braver by adding something helpful: "But take courage; I have overcome the world." And: "I have given you power to tread on serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy." Who, then, are the scorpions, and who are the serpents? Clearly they are the foul and bloodthirsty ranks of the accursed demons, and those who persecute the saints. These persecutors have become servants of the unrestrained madness of the spirits in the world. Those spirits roam this whole universe and plot against the saints in many ways, even though Christ has triumphed over them. He nailed the bond that stood against us to his own cross so that he might free us from their greedy tyranny.

He had said that Jerusalem, which is the Church of the living God, would dwell in safety. It was quite right to expect this to come about only when the enemies had been destroyed and those who usually persecute it had been overthrown. So he must also give us an account of these things. This, he says, will be the fall with which the Lord will strike all the peoples who have made war against Jerusalem: their flesh will melt away, and their eyes will flow out, while their tongue also wastes away. This common death that comes to all by nature does melt everyone's flesh, empty their eyes, and rot their tongues. But it would surely be utterly dreadful, a calamity at its very extreme, for the flesh of people still alive and standing to melt, for their eyes to flow out, and for their tongues to be punished. He says, and very fittingly, that such things will happen to those who have lived a God-hated and accursed life. They will pay the penalty not only for the wrongs they committed against the saints, but also for the love of the flesh they had in this world. It was this that caused them neither to accept the faith nor to choose a godly life, nor to love the glory of the way of life in Christ. As I said, they gave themselves over without restraint to outrageous pleasures. They had unrestrained eyes that all but gulped down, open-mouthed, their desire for each thing they saw. They also sharpened their tongue against Christ and made unholy attacks on the sacred doctrines of the Church. So it is fitting that their punishment fell on their flesh, their eyes, and their tongues. The woman who drank the water of testing after swearing falsely was punished in the thigh, the part where the charges of fornication arise: "For her thigh," it says, "will swell and fall away." In the same way, I think, the punishment of those who persecute the holy city falls on their flesh, eyes, and tongues. The charges against them are love of the flesh and self-indulgence, the sins committed through the eyes, and the words of an undisciplined tongue.

And on that day there will be a great panic from the Lord upon them, and each will seize his neighbor's hand, and his hand will be clasped with his neighbor's hand. And Judah will draw up for battle in Jerusalem, and will gather the strength of all the peoples round about: gold and silver and clothing in very great abundance. Here again by "panic" he means fear, that is, terror. He is saying that the enemies of the Church will see one another falling under such dreadful punishments, and at that time they will be struck with terror. Then they will give up daring to persecute the holy city any longer and will run off as fugitives. They will all but clasp hands as they seek help from one another in vain, and they will be pitiful, cast down beneath the feet of the saints. But Judah, he says, will draw up for battle in Jerusalem. Judah means those who have been justified through faith in Christ, who carry within them the spiritual Jew and are rich in the circumcision that is in the Holy Spirit. They will march against the enemies and act boldly against their opponents. They will trample them like scorpions and tread on the asp and the basilisk, and they will show no mercy at all to the lion and the dragon. They will be radiant and admirable, gathering the wealth won by such achievements, as gold and silver and clothing. Who could doubt that the meaning of the prophecy does not lie in things perceived by the senses? For the wealth of the saints is not perishable and earthly, but spiritual, heavenly, and everlasting. Those who teach, and those who distinguish themselves in other ways in the churches, gather this wealth for their own souls. They plunder, as it were, the strength of all the peoples by bringing the choicest of the nations to Christ through faith. Christ himself spoke in this way when he said that he had plundered the goods of the strong man.

Someone might say that Judah gathers the strength of all the peoples round about, gold and silver and clothing, so that we may understand that they also collect the wisdom of the world and are made brilliant by it as they fight for the doctrines of godliness. That interpretation would also be reasonable. For the wise women of Israel once despoiled the Egyptians by borrowing "from their neighbor and from the woman who lodged with them vessels of gold and silver, and clothing." So the splendor of spiritual goods is signified through things perceived by the senses and through visible materials. And the wealth of teachers is above all their disciples. Indeed, the divine Paul cried out to those who had been saved and had believed through him: "By the pride I take in you, brothers, which I have in Christ Jesus." Elsewhere he called them his own "crown and joy."
And this will be the fall of the horses and the mules and the camels and the donkeys and all the beasts that are in those camps, like this fall.

He has already set out the kinds of punishment that will surely come, in due time, upon those who made war against the holy city. They became persecutors and insolent men, loathsome and quick to bring accusations. They spoke unrighteousness against God and lifted up their horn on high, in the words of the Psalmist. He now adds, to good purpose: This will be the fall of the horses and the mules and the camels and the donkeys and all the beasts. By the beasts of burden he means those who ride on them. For the nations, both distant and neighboring, attacked the Jews and Jerusalem itself. Some were mounted on horses: the Babylonians and Syrians, and also the peoples of Egypt. Others harnessed camels, donkeys, and mules, such as the Moabites and the nomads of the desert. The prophet Isaiah mentions these, saying: "In affliction and distress, the lion and the lion's whelp, and from there also asps and the offspring of flying asps, who carried their wealth on donkeys and camels." Elsewhere he says that he saw "a rider on a donkey and a rider on a camel." So, as in a type, he portrays the enemies of the truth through the nations that were always at war with the earthly Jerusalem. From them we are to understand the enemies, visible and invisible, that we must fight against. Someone may also wish to apply the traits of these animals to the characters of the Church's enemies. There is no harm in saying and thinking this. Some of them are impetuous and bold, perhaps like horses, and one might very reasonably also ascribe to them love of pleasure and a lustful craving for women. Others are wild and harsh, like mules; indeed, the Greek poets are in the habit of calling mules "the wilder ones." Others resemble camels in their nature: they are lopsided and boastful, and their minds are lifted high by folly. Still others are no different from donkeys and suffer from the worst stupidity of all, for the donkey is sluggish and slow to perceive, and is an image of utter stupidity. It should be noted that he compares those who have made war on the Church to none of the tame and clean animals, such as the sheep and the ox. He likens them instead to the loathsome and untamed animals, which the words of the law also condemned as profane and unclean.

And it will be that all who are left of all the nations that came against Jerusalem will go up year by year to worship the King, the Lord God Almighty, and to keep the feast of Tabernacles. And it will be that any of all the tribes of the earth who do not go up to Jerusalem to worship the King, the Lord God Almighty, will be added to those others.

Some made war against the churches and raised a proud and arrogant brow against holy Jerusalem. He has said that they will fall into the punishments they deserve. Now he foretells the worship offered by those who are left after them, which is clearly worship in Christ through faith. For Christ is the expectation of the nations, as the patriarch said. And he has been appointed "as a light for the nations and a covenant for the race, to open the eyes of the blind, to bring those who are bound out of their bonds, and to bring out of the prison house those who sit in darkness." Those from the nations will leave the gloom of idolatry and break the bonds of the devil's perversity. Then they will come to the light of the truth and submit to the Savior's yoke. He makes this clear by saying that those left of the ones who were punished, that is, of those who fought against the churches, will go up year by year to worship the Lord God Almighty and to keep the feast of Tabernacles. And these are too many to count. The law given through Moses commanded that the feast of Tabernacles be celebrated on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, once the harvest of the fields had been gathered into storehouses. For this reason it calls the feast the closing festival, since the work in the fields had already come to an end. It commanded them to take "fronds of palm trees, the fruit of a beautiful tree, leafy branches, willows, and branches of the chaste tree," to drink water from a brook, and to rejoice in it. The law gave as the reason for the feast that Israel had lived in tents after it was rescued from the oppression of the Egyptians.

But in fact this was a type of the mystery of Christ. For we too have been rescued from the devil's oppression and, as I said, have been called to freedom through Christ. We have come under him, the King and God of all, and have turned our backs on the perversity of those who once ruled over us. And we celebrate the true feast of Tabernacles, that is, the day of Christ's resurrection. On that day the bodies of all were, as it were, set up again in him like tents, even though they had been taken down by corruption and held captive by death. For he is the resurrection, he is the life, the firstborn, as it were, from the dead and "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep." He fills us with a spiritual harvest and makes us ready to store up, as it were, the fruit of our labors in the fields in the storehouses above. He will give back to us the life and delight of paradise, clearly a spiritual one, once we have overcome sin. We are spiritually fragrant, we bear the beautiful and lovely fruit of the gospel way of life, and we have lived in purity and holiness. Another sign of this would be the fronds of palm and the fruit of a beautiful tree that are held bound together with the other branches. He is the torrent of delight from which God the Father has given us to drink. He is the fountain of life and the river of peace that has turned toward us who were called from the nations. We have spoken briefly about these things elsewhere. So those who go up to worship the Lord Almighty and to keep the feast of Tabernacles are those who have been justified in Christ through faith. But to those who do not go up he threatens destruction, and the same punishments that the persecutors and the insolent would suffer. For those who have not chosen to love will share the same lot as the enemies. And this, I think, is what Christ himself said: "Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters."

And if the tribe of Egypt does not go up or come there, then the fall will come upon them too, the fall with which the Lord will strike all the nations that do not go up to keep the feast of Tabernacles. This will be the sin of Egypt and the sin of all the nations that do not go up to keep the feast of Tabernacles.

Using one nation, the Egyptians, as an example, he points to those who have gone to the extreme of error and have chosen to practise idolatry in the most outrageous way. For them it will be a terrible and inescapable penalty, and the cause of their destruction, that they did not choose to honour the grace of salvation through Christ, a grace so worth taking hold of. They would be found to be little short of murderers of their own souls. It was open to them to lay hold of eternal life and of the gentleness from above that is set before all who wish to take a share in it, and also to unload their sin. Yet they have died in their own errors. They have kept the stain of their error and the pollution of their offence unwashed, and they have stayed in error to the end, even though the divine light shines all around and calls to recover their sight those who sit in mist and darkness. Of each such person I would say, "Better off than he is the [stillborn child], for it came in vanity and goes into darkness, and its name will be covered in darkness." For "it would be good for them if they had not been born," in the Savior's words. The statement is not directed against the Egyptians alone. It will also come upon all the nations, which will be punished in every way and without fail because they disregarded the salvation that comes through Christ and did not honour the festival held in him. The prophet confirms this when he says: "This will be the sin of Egypt and the sin of all the nations that do not go up to celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles." Before the Savior came, the nations perhaps still had some partial ground for excuse, since they said that no one had called them; after all, no one had preached to them. So the Savior, showing this very point in his gospel parables, said that the workers called at about the eleventh hour answered, "No one hired us." But now Christ has shone forth. He has bound the strong man, rescued from his perversity those who lay under his power, justified by faith those who come to him, and laid down his own life for the life of all. Those who have not accepted so holy a grace will no longer find any adequate excuse. So Christ would be speaking the truth about these nations too if he said, "If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin."
On that day what is on the horse's bridle will be holy to the Lord Almighty.

He speaks as though all war had already been laid to rest, battle abolished, the enemies routed, and an unbreakable peace at last crowned the holy city, that is, the Church. So he says that the gear of war, both the horse's trappings and its bridles, will now lie idle. What use would a horseman have for such things, however skilled he is at winning glory in battle, if there is no one at all to take the field against him? So, he says, the things that are useful to warriors will become sacred vessels and offerings to God. Since God is the one who awards peace, the gear of war, now superfluous and idle, will rightly be dedicated to him. The blessed prophet Isaiah said of certain people that "they will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into sickles, and nation will not lift up sword against nation, and they will no longer learn war." The times of peace all but persuade them to hand over their weapons to the needs of farming and to turn, as it were, to other pursuits, giving up the study of tactics. In the same way the inspired Zechariah, seeing that God has at last granted an unbreakable peace, says that the gear useful to fighting men will be refashioned into an offering to God. For the warlike spirit will certainly fall idle. It will care nothing for horse, bridles or trappings, and will turn instead to the conviction that one must excel in the pursuit of virtue and godliness.

Some think that the meaning of the prophecy was also fulfilled in another way. They say that in due time the wood of the cross was found, with the nails still fixed in it. The pious Constantine took one of these and had it made into a bridle for his own horse, believing that through this too he would be blessed by God. If the story is true, one might say it is not implausible. It could reasonably be understood, and would not go beyond what is fitting, that the most pious emperor should be remembered before God and honoured in a prophetic prediction. For at various times the word of the holy prophets mentioned and foretold a great many people, Josiah, for instance, and some others. Sometimes, too, the gentleness and piety of an age is signified through those who rule in it. So it is not at all unlikely that the prophet Zechariah here also records a most noteworthy event: an act truly dear to God, a pious reign, and times devoted to the love of Christ. When a nail taken from the precious cross adorns even the horses of emperors, what else could this show us but the very great and truly admirable piety of those who rule?
And the cauldrons in the house of the Lord will be like bowls before the altar.

There were cauldrons in the holy tabernacle and in the temple built after it. The meat of the sacrifices was boiled in them, and the priests ate it in a holy place. The law commanded that this be done so that what had been sanctified would not be carried anywhere outside the sacred precincts. But those ancient customs have now ceased, and for us the mysteries have passed over into another mode of worship. Through faith we have been taught to honour the God of all no longer with the slaughter of sheep and with incense, but rather with bloodless sacrifices, and in the churches we spiritually offer Christ himself, the Savior of all. So in place of the cauldrons we use other sacred vessels, which the prophet here calls bowls. These vessels are of the greatest use to those who drink. The wise hearer will surely grasp the meaning of what is signified, even if our account has been somewhat more obscure than it should be, because hidden things must be explained with reserve. So then there were cauldrons, but now there are bowls before the altar.
And every cauldron in Jerusalem and in Judah will be holy to the Lord Almighty; and all who sacrifice will come and take from them and boil for themselves.

Still using the old names, he calls the mystical vessels "cauldrons." They are holy, venerable and precious both to those in Jerusalem, that is, the Church, by which he clearly means the divine ministers, and in Judah itself, that is, again, to those who have received circumcision in the spirit. These, once more, would be the believers. For no one at all takes the vessels of the holy altar for common use. As I said, they are holy and set apart for the glory of God, and they serve only the needs of the holy table. Through them and in them the sacrifices of those who make offerings are performed. Each person does not bring his own vessel; all use only the sacred ones. For "every cauldron," he says, "will be holy to the Lord." So the prophet speaks as though he were still dealing with the sacrifices of the law, and he mentions cauldrons, boiling and those who sacrifice. We, however, shall understand it in a way that fits the times of Christ and the worship we perform in the Spirit. We say that it was by divine design that the word of the holy prophets became obscure and was not simply laid open to all. This was so that they would not throw holy things to the dogs, and so that the word that befits only the saints would not be uncovered to the profane and the utterly abominable.
And there will no longer be a Canaanite in the house of the Lord Almighty on that day.

One could see with no effort at all that the mind of the people of old was unsound and easily broken. The Israelites were redeemed from Egypt through Moses and shook off the yoke of an unbearable slavery. After a great many admirable signs had been performed for them, they barely got away. They were brought across through the sea itself, they ate the bread from heaven, and in the desert they drank water that came out of a rock against all expectation. What did the wretches do then? While Moses was away they made a calf, and, as the prophet says, they took up "the tent of Moloch and the star of their god Rephan, the images that they made to worship." But those people perished, for their corpses fell in the desert, as it is written. Their descendants were brought across the Jordan under Joshua's command. But again, as time went on and they came under the judges, they served idols. Even in the times of the holy prophets they sacrificed to the golden heifers that the accursed Jeroboam had made for them. Besides these, they set up sacred precincts and altars, and they worshipped Baal, Chemosh, Astarte and Baal-Peor no less. And something worse than all these evils: we do not say that only the common rabble took part in these things, for we shall find that many even of the priests themselves had turned aside. This is why God said through the prophet: "The priests did not say, 'Where is the Lord?' Those who handle my law did not know me, the shepherds acted impiously against me, the prophets prophesied by Baal and went after what does not profit." The prophet Ezekiel also saw "about twenty-five men of the elders of Israel with only their backs toward the temple of the Lord and their faces turned the other way, worshipping the sun toward the east." It would be no trouble to pile up a great many other examples, but I think these will be enough to expose their unwillingness to learn. So the mind of the people of old was unsteady and very easily led astray. This is why God said of them, "They loved to move their feet and did not hold back, and God took no pleasure in them." They were easily carried off into outlandish idolatries, and though they were of the blood of Israel, they were eager to imitate the foreign Canaanites.

But the only-begotten Word of God became as we are. He justified by faith those who come to his grace and sealed them with the Holy Spirit, and so our mind has become firm, secure and unshakable, fixed in godliness. No one will persuade those who have been sanctified to acknowledge any god besides the one who is God by nature and in truth, whom we have come to know as God in Christ. For he showed us the Father in himself when he said, "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father." So "on that day," he says, that is, at that time, "there will not be a Canaanite," that is, a foreigner and idolater, "in the house of the Lord Almighty." For, as I said, we have been established in faith, and through Christ we have been crowned with that in which we can securely boast. Through him and with him be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, forever. Amen.
By the Same Author
COMMENTARY
ON THE PROPHET MALACHI
VOLUME ONE
Here too, with the prophecy of Malachi, a few words of introduction are needed, so that readers may follow easily and understand each thing he says.

When the time of the captivity had come to an end, Israel was brought back from Babylon to Judea and came again to the holy city, having thrown off the yoke of slavery. The divine temple had also been rebuilt, with Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, of the tribe of Judah, and Joshua son of Jozadak, the high priest, overseeing the work. At that time Haggai and Zechariah were prophesying to those who had been redeemed from the captivity, and Ezra and Nehemiah were with them among those who served the sacred rites. The inspired Malachi lived at the same time as these holy prophets, or a little after them. He is also called Angel, for that is what the name Malachi means.

We should not accept what some people say about him. They have spun idle tales, supposing and claiming that he was an angel by nature who took on a body by God's will and served the Israelites as a prophet. He is called angel, as I said, chiefly because his name carries that meaning. Then too, since he announced to the Israelites the words that came from above and from God, he could quite reasonably be called an angel, that is, a messenger. Indeed the prophet Malachi himself says further on about every priest: "For the lips of a priest will guard knowledge, and they will seek the law from his mouth, because he is a messenger of the Lord Almighty." And about Emmanuel the prophet Isaiah says: "And they will wish they had been burned with fire, for a child has been born, a son has also been given to us, and his name is called Angel of Great Counsel." Do you see that announcing the will of the supreme nature to others has caused some to be called angels, even though they are not angels by nature? For the priests who interpret the divine law to us are human beings, while the Son is God, and from God by nature.

The prophet Malachi, then, was a man like us. The whole aim of his prophecy comes down, as it were, to two things. Once the divine temple had been rebuilt, the time had come that called the leaders of the people, that is, those of the blood of Levi, to perform the sacred rites, and it also allowed the Israelites themselves to fulfil their vows under the law if they wished. They did keep the commandments given through Moses, but not blamelessly or properly. The people brought the usual offerings for sacrifice, but without much care. They did so sluggishly and carelessly, bringing to the altar the poorest of their flocks, the sick and the worthless. And the priests accepted them without inspecting them for blemishes as the law required, to see whether what was brought was lame, or had its ears cut off or its nose or tail docked, or had mange or ringworm, or had one testicle. The law had made such animals unacceptable, and the whole business was nothing but an insult. The priests were negligent in another way too toward the people under their charge. They did not teach them rightly what is in the law or guide them well toward what pleases God, but let them turn aside into strange [?] ways and stray from the straight path. This is one kind of rebuke. There is a second, addressed to the Israelites for reasons like these. Some of them said farewell to their love for their wives and threw a certificate of divorce at them, sometimes though they had been convicted of no wrongdoing, and then joined themselves to other women. They thought that they did not grieve God in any way, even if they chose to do this. Others again were mad with desire for the daughters of foreigners, although the law clearly cries out: "You shall not give your daughter to his son, and you shall not take his daughter for your son; for she will turn your son away from me, and he will go and serve other gods." There is also a long account of this in the books of Ezra, which is why some suppose that Ezra is Malachi; but that is not the truth. So much for the rebukes. At the end of the prophecy he speaks of the revealing of our Savior, since at that time a pure and bloodless sacrifice was to be offered to God, and the charges against all were to come to an end, sin being destroyed and those on earth being reshaped into newness of life. For, as it is written, what is in Christ is a new creation, and the old things have passed away.
The oracle of the word of the Lord upon Israel, by the hand of his angel.

By "oracle" (lēmma) of the word of prophecy from God he means, as it were, its "receiving" (lēpsis). For the blessed prophets received through the Holy Spirit the knowledge of things to come, and they gave counsel and also rebuked people, not drawing from their own hearts whatever words they happened to choose, or speaking falsely against anyone, but interpreting what came from God and conveying the words from above to others purely and blamelessly. So he says that the receiving of the prophecy came from the Lord. By these words he also hints that this prophecy does not foretell some grievous and painful event about to befall the Israelites, nor does it praise them for having lived rightly; it is rather a rebuke of priests and people. You should understand "by the hand of his angel" as follows: the oracle came upon Israel while the one called Angel handled, that is, carried out, the ministry of prophecy. Malachi is called angel for the reasons I have already given.
Lay it to your hearts: I have loved you, says the Lord.

He commands them not to listen to what is about to be said as a side matter, but earnestly, with the greatest attention and understanding. This is the right disposition for those who are about to hear divine words, whose benefit will be immense and abundant once they are poured into the mind itself. For the inspired David sings somewhere: "I have hidden your sayings in my heart, so that I may not sin against you." It is possible for someone who hears to seem not to have heard at all, if the words do not touch the mind but fly off, as it were, from the speaker's tongue, strike only the bodily hearing, and are then counted as so much idle noise [?]. Such were those of whom one of the holy prophets said: "Look, a foolish and senseless people; they have eyes and do not see, they have ears and do not hear." So the prophet necessarily urges them, saying, "Lay it to your hearts." That is: store the divine words deep within your mind and heart, grasp the force of the oracles from above, and agree fully that "I have loved you, says the Lord," and counted you worthy of every gentleness and mercy, and of the generosity that befits those who are loved. In saying this he reproaches them sharply for repaying him evil for good, when, having been deemed worthy of love, they ought to have delighted him in return with their goodness and with zeal and eagerness for everything that pleases him. For if it is wrong to refuse to repay those of our own kind, what could be said of someone who will not repay God for his gifts, God who richly bestows on us all that makes for gladness? Those who are truly right-minded should above all say: "What shall we give back to the Lord for all that he has given us?"

And you said, "In what have you loved us?" Was not Esau Jacob's brother, says the Lord? Yet I loved Jacob, but Esau I hated, and I made his borders a desolation and his inheritance dwellings of the desert.

From time to time the Jews were struck by what comes from God's wrath, since they had been impious in many ways. They went off into captivity; their land was ravaged, their houses laid waste, and Jerusalem burned together with the divine temple. The reason they suffered such things was that they chose to abandon their true devotion to God and thought reverence for the law worth almost nothing. So when God says that he loved them, and loved them greatly, they would probably remember the evils of the captivity and might well say, "In what have you loved us?" The God of all, with great wisdom, passes over what happened in between and runs past any account of it, and instead carries the proof of his love back to the beginning of the race, I mean Jacob. He declares that he loved Jacob but made Esau hated, even though by the laws of nature Esau was bound in brotherhood to the one who was honored. For as the inspired Paul writes, "Before they were born or had done anything good or bad," God chose Jacob, from whom the race of the Jews sprang, and rejected Esau. And we certainly do not say that this was out of partiality. God is not unjust, nor does he carry out an unequal or one-sided judgment on anyone on earth. Rather, since as God he foreknew what each of the two would do and the character of each, he deemed the better and holier one worthy of his love. In the same way he says that he knew the blessed Jeremiah before he formed him in the womb, and sanctified him before he came out of the womb. For he knew, he truly knew, that Jeremiah would be a prophet, fit for the mission ahead of him, which was to foretell what was to come. So too the inspired Paul says that we ourselves, who have been justified by faith, have been sanctified: "For those whom God the Father foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son," and these, it is said, he called and sanctified. So it was according to foreknowledge that Jacob was deemed worthy of love and Esau was justly hated.

"O Israel," he says, "I have loved you. I would by no means be telling a lie if I said this to you. Rather, you will know that the word is right and true if you trace the manner of my love back to the beginning of your race. Both were sons of Isaac, but Jacob was good in character and loved God, while the other was harsh, hard to deal with, and ready for profanity. That is why I favored Jacob. I wiped out the lot assigned to Esau and gave it over to desolation, but I upheld by my mercy the lot of Jacob, that is, you, or the land you have settled." We should know that Esau means "Oak." Esau was hard and unbending, hardly yielding anything to oak timber. And since he sold his birthright for a single meal, he was also named Edom, which means "earthy." That is why sacred scripture says that the land of Esau's descendants was called Idumea, the land which the Jews at various times conquered and made completely impassable and uninhabited. What, then, does the sense of the prophecy mean to show the Israelites? This, I think. He says that he loved Jacob for no other reason than that he was "a plain man, dwelling in a house," and that he hated Esau because he became earthy and "profane," in the words of the blessed Paul. So the Jews needed to know that they would not have suffered desolation and been carried off from their native land to foreigners if they had imitated Jacob. But since they became zealous imitators of Esau, like him in character, and were caught following in the footsteps of his perversity, in the end they were handed over to their enemies.

If anyone wishes to apply a spiritual interpretation to these words as well, let him understand clearly that Jacob means "Supplanter," and so he would be a type of everyone who supplants sin. Esau, as I said, means "Oak," and Edom means "Earthy," and so he too would be a type of everyone who sets his mind only on things on earth. God, then, loves Jacob the supplanter, but he has hated Esau the unbending and hard, that is, Edom, the one who inclines toward earthly things and foolishly prefers what is temporary and perishing to spiritual goods. Our God, who loves virtue, will wipe out the lot of those who are used to living this way. For the things on earth are not secure, nor do they stand unshaken. That they will certainly fall is shown, as in a type, by the lot of the Idumeans, which was utterly laid waste. But the one who clings to God will have a sure and firmly grounded hope, and will cry out to God, the giver of good things: "My lots are in your hands."

Because if Idumea should say, "It has been overthrown, but let us return and rebuild the desolate places," thus says the Lord Almighty: They will build, and I will tear down; and they will be called borders of lawlessness, and a people against whom the Lord has set himself in battle forever.

The construction of the wording is very difficult, but the sense of the passage is not hard to see. "I," he says, "have given Esau's inheritance over to destruction and desolation, since you, the descendants of Jacob, laid it waste. The Idumean will perhaps say, 'Even if the land we have lived in has been utterly overthrown and has come to the utmost of evils, still we who survive will return, raise up the ruined cities and villages, and live in them.'" What does he say to this? "Thus says the Lord: They will build, and I will tear down." Idumea will certainly be called "borders of lawlessness," since it was overthrown because of its very great sin, "and a people against whom the Lord has set himself in battle forever."

I think the literal sense is nothing other than this. But I would add that the lot of those who have a fleshly and earthly mind (for Idumean, as I said, means "earthy") will fall utterly and completely, since God will overthrow it. The affairs of this world have no stability, nor can we share in them forever. Desire for temporary things slips away from those who have it and passes like a shadow, either when someone is cut off by death or when some unexpected misfortune strikes. If any of these spiritual Idumeans chooses to build up his own lot, whether by heaping up wealth gained through injustice, or by reveling in empty little honors, or by wanting to pride himself on worldly power, he will find the God of all practically standing against him and fighting him. For as the inspired disciple wrote, "Whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God." He will not cease, as I said, to oppose those who have chosen to set their minds on earthly things, nor will he end his war against them. For he always hates the wicked and casts away the one who loves sin.
And your eyes will see, and you will say, "The Lord has been magnified beyond the borders of Israel."

"When you observe the nature of events," he says, "and see clearly, with the eyes of your mind open, what I have just said, then you will certainly agree and say that the Lord has been glorified and magnified within the borders of Israel." Those descended from Jacob, that is, the Jews, gave offense, as I said, through very great impiety, and became exiles, captives, and prey to their enemies. But when God took pity on them, since they had fared miserably and had been sufficiently punished, they were brought back to their former state, and their affairs turned for the better. The land prospered; they settled the cities, rebuilt the temple, walled Jerusalem again, and once more found themselves in a condition beyond their hopes and as they had prayed. But the land of the Idumeans has been laid waste and has remained in misery, without recovering to a better state. So God has been glorified within the borders of Israel.

We should know that in the innermost sense too, even if some of those who know God fall into offense, and even if they are disciplined for their sin, they still do not perish completely. God has pity on them once he has disciplined them enough and brings them back to gladness. But against those who love an earthly mind and look only to the things of the flesh he fights continually, and he will prolong the time of his wrath against them. For he says, "They will be called borders of the lawless, and a people against whom the Lord has set himself in battle forever."
A son glorifies his father, and a servant will fear his master. If, then, I am a father, where is my glory? And if I am a lord, where is the one who fears me? says the Lord Almighty.

He shows that they have gone beyond what is fitting in every way and have chosen to neglect what they should least have neglected. It would be fitting, and very reasonable, for good sons to care greatly about their father's glory, so that they may be called children of a most renowned father. And if someone is a faithful servant, he will surely pray that his own master may become famous and celebrated, not obscure and trampled underfoot. For in this way he himself will share in that good fortune, will make it his boast, and will count it a cause of the highest joy. "But you," he says, "who ought to glorify me as a father and fear me as a master, will be found to have fallen far short of what is fitting on both counts, giving me neither glory as a father nor fear as a master. Where is my glory? Where is the fear of me, if you will do nothing that looks to my glory, and do not yield to your master's laws out of fear of punishment?" He said something like this through the mouth of Isaiah as well: "Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken: I have begotten sons and raised them up, but they have rejected me."

We must therefore seek what makes for God's glory and press on to accomplish it, knowing what is written: "As I live, says the Lord, those who glorify me I will glorify, and the one who despises me will be despised." We will glorify the God of all as Father not by striving to do what is pleasant and agreeable to ourselves, but rather by devoting our minds to him and following his will in everything. And we will fear him as Lord by checking our tendency toward wickedness out of reverence, so as not to offend him, and by keeping in mind the examination before the divine judgment seat. "For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or bad."

You priests who despise my name, and you said, "How have we despised your name?" By offering polluted bread on my altar. And you said, "How have we polluted it?" By your saying, "The table of the Lord is contemptible, and the food placed on it is contemptible."

He sharply blames the indifference of the Jewish priests, to whom the law also proclaims, "Make the children of Israel reverent." For the multitude under their charge will generally follow the good example of its leaders, and it is badly wronged when it sees them neglecting reverence toward God. It immediately falls in with them, grows slack along with them in piety, and is molded by its teachers' negligence. That this is true the God of all will confirm, saying: "Because the shepherds have acted foolishly and have not sought the Lord, therefore the whole flock did not understand and was scattered." So, as a rule, the ministers of the divine mysteries prove to be the cause for others of an honorable life, if they choose to live rightly and to show reverence to God in the fitting way, but of shameful and abominable practices if they are found to be sick with such evils before anyone else. That is why the inspired Paul wisely told those who hold the office of teaching that they ought to be examples to their flocks. "You, then," he says, "who are distinguished by the glories of the priesthood, are the ones who despise my name. And if you want to learn how you despise it, you will hear him cry out: by offering polluted bread on my altar. And if you ask again, 'How have we polluted it?' I will tell you: you perhaps think, or rather you proclaim by your very deeds, that 'the table of the Lord is contemptible, and the food placed on it is contemptible.'"

Since each of these sayings must be unfolded and clearly explained, let us say what the polluted bread is meant to signify. By "polluted" he means defiled and unclean. We need to know that, according to the lawgiver's ordinance, loaves were also brought with the sacrifices that were offered, but they were unleavened and pure. He commanded that only the sacrifice of praise be offered with leavened loaves. What the mystical meaning of these things would be, we have explained sufficiently elsewhere. Still, I will go over it briefly now, so that I may not seem lazy about matters so very profitable. Unleavened bread, then, would be a sign of an unleavened and pure life. So the inspired Paul writes to those justified by faith: "Therefore let us celebrate the feast, not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth." And again: "Clean out the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump, as you really are unleavened." And Christ warns the holy apostles, saying, "Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees." So bread is a sign of a pure, sanctified, and unleavened life. Those who brought offerings, then, still living in types and shadows, presented unleavened loaves in place of themselves and received unleavened ones in accordance with the law.

When we glorify God, we do not send out of the churches those who are still catechumens and have not yet had their sin washed away through holy baptism. Instead we make them our partners in offering the sacrifice of praise. This is why the law says that it must be performed with leavened bread. By "leavened bread" it means, in a figure, a person who has not yet been cleansed through holy baptism, as I said, and who still carries in himself the remnants of the old wickedness, like a kind of leaven.

"You, then," he says, "are the priests who despise my name by offering defiled bread on my altar." So those who hold the divine priesthood must take great care that nothing of this kind is done in the churches. They must also know that careful watchfulness will gladden God, while choosing to be careless and to neglect such holy things will grieve him deeply. The negligent cannot escape the penalty for this, and that is plain to see when they hear, "You priests who despise my name." The priests' carelessness is a kind of contempt toward God himself, and the offense reaches up to the glory that befits him and is owed to him.

For if you bring a blind animal for sacrifice, is it not evil? And if you bring a lame or sick one, is it not evil? Offer it, then, to your governor. Will he accept you? Will he show you favor? says the Lord Almighty.

The law commanded that sacrificial victims be inspected for blemishes, that maimed animals be rejected, and that only unblemished ones be consecrated. Yet at that time they brought them to the altar in a heap, without telling one from another. They had almost no concern at all for the glory due to God. What they cared about most was gathering as many victims as possible and having plenty of meat at home, and perhaps even in the holy tabernacle itself. So then, you guardians of the law, if someone brings a blind animal for sacrifice, is the victim not evil? And if it is lame or sick, will it escape the charge of being maimed? Will you not count such animals as bad and unfit for sacrifice? But if you think privately that this is not so, let someone carry them as a present, by way of a gift, to one of your rulers. "He would not accept it," he says. Nor would he put up with such a thing out of respect for the person who brought it. He would be very angry, as one who had been insulted.

It is utterly outrageous to dare to offer God what not one of you would choose to accept. Yet this offense is common among us too. When we are about to bring something to God, we wretched people look for the shabbier and second-rate things we have. We do not consider that God did not accept Cain's sacrifice because, though he offered rightly, he did not divide rightly. He kept the first and choicest portions for himself and thought he could honor God with the second-rate. And the God of all did not regard his sacrifices, for he will not count the carelessness of those who offer as honor.

The law made blind animals unacceptable for sacrifice, and also lame and sick ones. In a figure, the blind animal signifies those who do not have the divine eye in their heart. The lame signifies those who do not know how to walk uprightly in good works. The sick signifies those who carry out their service to God without vigor, slackly and as if they did not care. Somewhere he also said through the voice of a prophet, "Cursed are those who do the work of the Lord negligently." We must therefore have a mind that is enlightened, that walks uprightly, and that is strong. Then we shall be acceptable to the Lord and holy before God, who loves humankind.
And now entreat the face of your God, says the Lord Almighty, and make your petition to him. These things have come about by your hands. Shall I show favor to any of you? says the Lord Almighty.

He calls the ungodly to repentance. He says that they very much ought to turn to better ways, and so shake off in advance the wrath their outrages deserve. For he is good: he raises up those who have been thrown down, heals what is broken, and turns back what has gone astray. By saying, "Entreat the face of our God," he hints, quite fittingly, that God turns away from those who will not stop offending him. He withdraws his eyes, as it were, from those who do not seek his glory, and does not count them worthy of his mercy, his love, or his watchful care. For as it is written, "The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous." And he said to some of the wicked through the voice of Isaiah: "When you stretch out your hands to me, I will turn my eyes away from you; and even if you multiply your prayers, I will not listen to you, for your hands are full of blood."

So those who have sinned must seek to appease God, in the hope that they might turn his face back toward themselves and ward off the harm that his turning away would bring. He pins down the priests' offense and rules out any denial. He is not speaking falsely when he says, "These things have come about by your hands." It is as if he were saying: "It is not that others sinned while you kept silent. You yourselves have done these impieties against me with your own hands, as it were, and you are their cause. The charges for them belong to your carelessness, with no one else in between. Perhaps some people are afraid to reprove you for these things. Still, I myself will not be like one of you, and I will not show favor to the ungodly." Something similar was said through the voice of David: "You thought, in your lawlessness, that I would be like you. I will rebuke you, and set your sins before your face." For the judge knows no partiality. Since he is God, he is upright and cannot be bribed.
For among you too the doors will be shut, and you will not kindle my altar for nothing.

Very aptly, and for now by way of prophecy, he gives a glimpse in advance of the beauty of the way of life in Christ. The shadow of the law was about to come to an end, and so was that ancient priesthood. In due time the ministers of the truth were to be revealed. They would be ministers of worship in the Spirit and would seek the glory of God very eagerly. So he says that the doors will be shut on them, and that there will be no sweet savor for those who serve as priests according to the law. As it says elsewhere, "If he shuts a man in, who will open?" In other words, once the truer tabernacle, which is the Church, has been revealed, those who still keep the priesthood of the law will not enter it. Shut out, as it were, by their unbelief, they will stay outside and will not touch the holy things. That they have fallen from the priestly ministry is clear from what God says through the voice of Hosea: "For the sons of Israel will remain many days without a king, without a ruler, without sacrifice, without an altar, without a priesthood, without manifestations." So, as it seems to me, the saying that the doors must be shut on them signifies the abandonment, so to speak, of the worship of the law, and the closing down of the priesthood that belongs to it, since the Church does not admit them. For it is no longer the time for slaughtering sheep. The God of all is now honored with unbloody sacrifices.

He adds to this, "You will not kindle my altar for nothing," and we say that this was spoken with feeling. He wants to show that they were called to the priestly ministry, and to set fire on the altar, not to undo the glory of the one who called them. They were called to honor him in fitting ways and to enjoy the privileges of the priesthood. But those who give no thought to such sacred duties, and who out of reverence for the ministry do not refrain from offending God, would rightly be punished now. It is no small charge, and with good reason, to treat a share in God's gifts as worthless and to throw away the honors that come from God so thoughtlessly. Indeed Esau was called earthly and profane because "for a single meal he gave away his birthright." So when he says, "You will not kindle my altar for nothing," he means that the priesthood is not without its reward. But neither is it beyond punishment, if one does not approach it in the manner and for the reason that befit it.

It should be known that the Hebrew version renders the sense differently, and even the arrangement of the wording itself. It says: "For you, the Levites, and also the priests, and those who hold the lowest rank in the temple and have been appointed by you to shut the doors, will not kindle my altar for nothing." That is, you do not perform the service, meaning the priesthood, without pay, since the people bring you tithes, firstfruits, and thank-offerings.
Since, then, the things of God have been neglected, and what matters most has not been cared for,—

I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord Almighty, and I will not accept a sacrifice from your hands. For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name has been glorified among the nations, and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure sacrifice; for my name is great among the nations, says the Lord Almighty.

He now plainly rejects the offering of sacrifices under the law. He all but withdraws his love for the Jews. He makes the priesthood unwanted and the shadow unacceptable, by which I mean the sacrifices of oxen and the smoke, because this was not his purpose even at the beginning. He made this plain to us through other prophets as well. Through the voice of Isaiah he said: "I am full of whole burnt offerings of rams; I do not want the fat of lambs or the blood of bulls and goats, not even if you come to appear before me. Who required these things from your hands? You shall no longer trample my courts. If you bring fine flour, it is futile; incense is an abomination to me." Through the voice of Jeremiah he said: "Add your whole burnt offerings to your sacrifices and eat the meat. For I did not speak to your fathers about whole burnt offerings and sacrifices on the day I brought them up out of the land of Egypt." The law was a kind of outline and advance announcement of worship in spirit and truth. As the divine Paul writes, it was "regulations for the flesh, imposed until the time of reformation." And the time of reformation, I think, is nothing other than the coming of our Savior. The first covenant was not faultless, and so it is said to have been done away with, for it had grown old. But a place was sought for the new and second covenant, which is beyond all fault and blame. For it was spoken through the Son himself, who has been named the Angel of Great Counsel. That is why he said, "I do not speak on my own; the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment about what to say and what to speak."

So he plainly told those who serve as priests according to the law that he does not want them. Or rather, he has no pleasure in them while they perform their sacrifices in shadows and types, and he would not accept what they offer. He also foretells that his name will be great and renowned among people throughout the whole world under heaven. In every place and among every nation, pure and unbloody sacrifices will be brought to his name. The priests will no longer belittle him, or offer him their spiritual worship carelessly. With zeal, reverence, and holiness they will strive to send up the fragrance of spiritual incense: faith, hope, love, and the glories that come from good [?]. And set before all these, of course, is Christ's heavenly and life-giving sacrifice. Through it death has been abolished, and this corruptible, earthly flesh is clothed with incorruption.
But you profane it when you say, "The table of the Lord is defiled, and the food set on it is despised."

Through these words, too, he makes it plain to us that those called from the nations will be better and more reverent than those from Israel. Among the nations the sacrifices are pure, the incense is fragrant, and his name is great from the rising of the sun to its setting. "But among you," he says, "the altar is not held in great glory, the glory that befits God. For you profane it when you say, 'The table of the Lord is defiled, and what is on it is despised.'" Probably the priests did not use these actual words. They proclaimed this by their deeds, just as "The fool says in his heart, 'There is no God.'" In the things that show his contempt, he may not say it aloud, yet by his very deeds and the perversity of his life he all but shouts, "There is no God." People who are used to living as though God were not watching, who do everything without care and commit monstrous impieties, deny God by their very deeds and actions. In the same way, those who have made no effort to keep for the holy altar the reverence that most befits it and is owed to it are saying by what they do, "The table of the Lord is defiled."

So carelessness in these matters must be shunned. Let no one choose to act this way, or he will surely hear God saying, "I have no pleasure in you, and I will not accept a sacrifice from your hands." And how could anyone in his right mind doubt that offending God is a most terrible thing?

And you said, "These come from hardship," and I blew them away, says the Lord Almighty. And you brought in what had been snatched by beasts, and the lame and the ailing, and you offered them as a sacrifice. Shall I accept them from your hands? says the Lord Almighty.

He sharply accused the priests. They did not choose to inspect the victims brought to them for blemishes at all. Instead they carelessly and without examination accepted animals that were lame, blind, and sick, even though the law clearly commanded that maimed victims be rejected. And if some priest held to the law and drove away a person bringing something useless for sacrifice, the people bringing them persisted. They brought up the captivity over and over, and insisted quite brashly that the animals were not bad, but had suffered hardship on the road as they came back from Babylon to Judea. So they brought what had been snatched, and the lame and the ailing. Wild beasts sometimes attack and ravage the flocks. If they happen to snatch an animal, the shepherd may run up and pull it from their teeth, scaring them off with barking dogs or by throwing his crook. That, I think, is what is meant by the "snatched" animal. They brought these along with animals crippled in the feet that could no longer graze with the rest. They also brought the "ailing," that is, animals already dying. In this way they insulted the God of all rather than honoring him. "But I blew them away," says the Lord Almighty. He means: "Since you have chosen to sacrifice in an unholy way, I will not accept anything from you at all, and I will not count such lawless and unclean offerings as a fragrant aroma."

We must therefore sacrifice very reverently and with great care. We must not offer God whatever comes to hand, things thrown aside, utterly worthless, and of no account. We must offer what is excellent and choice. And someone may offer himself to God as a sacrifice, for we remember that the blessed Paul wrote: "Present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship." Let such a person examine his own condition closely and become, as it were, a careful inspector of the blemishes in his own soul. Let him see whether he is blind, that is, without the light of truth in his mind. Let him see whether he limps, unable to walk uprightly toward any good thing at all. Let him see whether there is anything in him that has been snatched or is sick. For we must not be forever asleep, "because our adversary the devil prowls around like a lion, looking for someone to devour." When we are found sleepless and watchful, the beast runs past us. But if he sees us drowsy and negligent, he makes us his prey and leaves us sick, that is, dead, and wholly powerless to achieve virtue. Let him also be far from being "ailing," that is, troubled.
