Let him rise above faint-heartedness and excel in endurance. For just as endurance leads to life, so faint-heartedness leads to death. We call it a weakness of the mind and a paralysis of the heart. That is why the blessed prophet Isaiah advises us to be rid of such passions, saying: "Be strong, you slack hands and paralyzed knees. Take courage, you who are faint-hearted; be strong, do not fear. Behold our God! Behold, the Lord comes with strength, and his arm with dominion."

And cursed is the one who was able, who had a male in his flock and was bound by his vow, yet sacrifices what is blemished to the Lord. For I am a great king, says the Lord Almighty, and my name is renowned among the nations.

He now pronounces the curse on anyone who sacrifices in an unholy way, and quite rightly. If someone makes a vow, he says, and has in his own flocks a male without blemish, why does he not bring that to God, and instead collect animals that are worth nothing at all? Such a thing is an insult and nothing else. We are not like some who sit in darkness, in errors and profane idolatries, serving stones and wood. We serve God Almighty, the Creator of all things, before whom the heavens tremble, and the earth and everything in it shudders. And again he bears witness to the great reverence of those from the nations, saying that the name of the Godhead is renowned among them, revered and admired. For that is exactly how we will be disposed toward it.

Our Lord Jesus Christ, too, welcomed the centurion, though he was an idolater, and said, "Truly I tell you, I have not found such faith in anyone in Israel." Cursed, then, is the one who sacrifices to God what is blemished, when he could honor him with something better because, as I just said, he has an unblemished male in his flocks. Note that he asks for a male for the sacrifice, although the law also commanded that females be sacrificed to God. Our answer is this. Sacrifices made under a vow, that is, freewill offerings, required an unblemished male victim, and this was a type pointing to the one who offered it. It was as if the law were all but urging etc. that those who wish to rise up to God as a sweet savor must be manly, superior to the passions, and as far as possible from every blemish. Sacrifices offered for sins, however, always required a female from the lambs or the kids. This too was a figure, of the weakness of those who offered them. For the female is weak and second to the male in strength. And every sin is committed when the mind has grown weak and no longer keeps its spiritual vigor.

And now this commandment is for you, O priests. If you do not listen, and if you do not take it to heart to give glory to my name, says the Lord Almighty, I will send the curse upon you, and I will curse your blessing, yes, I will curse it. I will scatter your blessing, and it will not be among you, because you do not take it to heart.

Out of his goodness he lets go of the charges for what has already happened and extends mercy, setting the sinners back, as it were, at the starting point of reverence. I think this is what he means when he says kindly, "And now this commandment is for you, O priests." Then he threatens them. They must choose to do what they ought to be seen doing, and take the meaning of the divine oracles into their mind and heart. They must become better than they were before and seek the glory of God. They must no longer belittle the altar as they used to [?], or perform the prescribed rites carelessly and without examination. If they do not, he will show them to be utterly accursed and under divine wrath. For my part, I think "I will curse your blessing and scatter it" probably means this. When God grants prosperity to people, their fields will bear well and be fruitful and abundant. Their flocks will multiply beyond counting, and they themselves will be spared bodily decay. But when he takes his blessing away, everything turns to the very opposite. Prosperity vanishes completely, and what prevails instead are the things a person would rightly grieve over.

This is what the passage says with regard to sensible and temporal things. But it is necessary to understand this: if anyone does not choose to keep the divine commandments in mind, his spiritual goods will vanish into nothing. He will have no fruit from a God-loving life. He will be deprived of the blessing that comes from above, from God, and will fall under the curses and the punishments that follow from them. We must therefore seek God's gift [?]. The Savior himself taught us how we can achieve this when he said: "Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven." Then we shall receive the blessing and a gladness that cannot be shaken. We shall delight in spiritual fruitfulness, and, filled with every good thing, we shall live a life that is truly worthy and praiseworthy.

Behold, I [?] the shoulder for you, and I will scatter dung on your faces, the [?] of your feasts, and I will take you away together. And you will know that I, the Lord, have sent this commandment to you, so that my covenant may be with the Levites, says the Lord Almighty.

Again, something lies hidden in the passage before us, and I think I must make it plain to those who love to listen, for then they will understand the meaning very well. The law given through Moses crowned the one who stands at the divine altars and performs the sacred rites with the highest honours, and placed him, as it were, in the rank of God. For it said, "The offering of the Lord is his portion." And the inspired Paul also says somewhere, "Consider Israel according to the flesh: are not those who [?] at the altar partners in the altar?" For it was the custom to dedicate to God, from each sacrifice, the breast and the arm, the lobe of the liver, the two kidneys and also the maw, that is, the stomach. In this way the letter of the law hinted in a riddle that all the inner parts of us who offer ourselves to God as a fragrant aroma ought to be holy and sanctified. The entrails are brought forward only after they have been cleansed of the impurity in them. The arm, moreover, may be understood as a sign of strength. And I say that we must be strong and act manfully for every good work, and wisely sing out what was sung on the psalmist's lyre: "Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name."

We have already written a very detailed discussion of the entrails and of the sacrifices offered under the law in other works (cf. On Adoration). So we will leave that subject aside for now and do our best to explain the passage before us. The law had commanded that the victims be inspected for blemishes, that no victim be brought to the altar without being examined, and that portions of the victims be set apart for those appointed to the sacred service. The priests neglected the duty of inspecting for blemishes, but they kept the commandment about what are called the "portions taken off." They did not put what pleases God ahead of their own wishes. Instead they enforced and worked to secure what they thought profited them, gathering up the meat from the sacrifices. He brings this forward as a reproach and says, "Behold, I set apart for you the shoulder." Here he has put "I set apart" in place of "I have already set it apart, and I want the custom kept from now on." And it is as if he said, "I have flung, or I fling, the maw too into your faces." For since they dishonour the altar, God says "I will scatter," as if insulting them in return. For he says, "Whoever despises me shall be despised." "I will take you to the same," that is, "In this very matter I will get the better of you and convict you of impiety. You have kept the law about your portions and will not tolerate any neglect of the share given to you, yet you think it pointless to inspect for blemishes. So when the doors are shut against you, that is, when you are shut out and expelled from the sacred service, you will know that I have given this commandment," that is, the covenant that he made with the Levites. What, then, follows from this? Those who minister to the divine mysteries ought to know that they must do what pleases God, and must put everything that otherwise seems to profit them behind the Master's commands. In this way they will be holy ministers, and not lovers of temporal things and slaves to shameful gain.
My covenant was with him, a covenant of life and of peace.

He turns the discussion back to the holy men who served as priests with distinction. He shows that the priesthood is a truly admirable thing, at least as far as the law is concerned, and that the divine oracles bring benefit and security. For as the most wise Paul writes, "The law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good." So when he seems to be speaking about Levi, we must not refer the force of these ideas entirely to the Levi who sprang from Jacob and was counted among the twelve sons, for that Levi never served as priest at all. Rather, we will understand the institution of the priesthood, sacred ministry itself, as all but given shape in the person of Levi. "My covenant," then, he says, "was with him, a covenant of life and of peace." For the written law was spoken to the most holy Moses, delivered through angels, and laid down through Moses as mediator for those of Israel's blood. It held out a promise of life and peace to those who were willing to live rightly and to make what pleases the lawgiver the rule of their own lives.

But here the passage also seems to hint at something more essential for us to contemplate. The law was given to the people of old, that is, to those of Israel's blood, to serve as a tutor leading to Christ, and as a kind of image and clear outline of truer things. The truth is Christ, who is life and peace, and the shadows given through Moses portray him to us. That is why, speaking to the Jews, he said, "If you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote about me." He was signified by the lamb slaughtered in the first month on the fourteenth day, by whose blood God meant to save those willing to smear the doorposts of their houses. He was signified by the red, unblemished heifer, whose ashes mixed with water sanctified the defiled "for the purification of the flesh," as it is written. He was signified by the unleavened bread, the turtledoves and the young pigeons. In short, the law was full of the contemplation of Christ. It is fitting, then, that it is called a covenant of life and peace. For we have been made alive in him, and through him in turn we have gained access to the God and Father, and we are at peace with him through obedience and faith.
And I gave him the fear of me, that he should fear me with fear and stand in awe before the face of my name.

He usefully lists the splendid glories of the priesthood, which were raised high by the instruction of the law. For the law especially instilled the fear of God in the priests. It persuaded them to stand in awe before the face of his name, that is, it trained them to revere and shrink before the Master's name, and it persuaded them that they must show that name reverence, not casually but in earnest. What could be more precious than this? For it is written, "Whoever fears the Lord is sound." And again, "The fear of the Lord is glory and a boast." So he has borne witness that those who served as priests in holiness and truth stood firm and secure. For he does not say simply that they feared, but that they feared with fear, that is, that they received the fear of God with their whole soul and heart. The emphasis in these words and the doubling of the terms show the hearers how firmly the men being praised were grounded in virtue.
The law of truth was in his mouth, and no injustice was found on his lips.

For the law commanded them to keep away from falsehood, to speak what is right and just, and to love making true and undistorted judgments in every matter. Yet here again he seems to give the name "truth" to our Lord Jesus Christ, and he says that those who lived as befits priests carried Christ's law on their lips. For even if the law, as I said, was in shadows, the form of the truth was still in it, and the outline, written in letters, of the decrees of the gospel. In the types we will find the power of worship in spirit. The Saviour himself will convince us that the law given long ago through Moses to the people of old was also Christ's law, when he says, "Do not think that I came to abolish the law or the prophets. I did not come to abolish but to fulfil. For truly I tell you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota, not one stroke, will pass from the law until all things have taken place."
He walked with me in peace, keeping a straight course, and he turned many away from injustice.

What else could being at peace with God mean, both for ourselves and for others who are skilled in the divine oracles, than choosing to think and do what he wills, never offending him in any way, but rather striving to achieve a glorious way of life, an admirable life wholly in keeping with the law? This is how the divine Paul has addressed us: "Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, let us have peace with God." For in this way we know and honour the one who is Master by nature and in truth. But when we attach our reverence to the creation, and profane and filthy sin overpowers our thoughts, we have set ourselves against the Master and, as it were, risen up to fight against him, stiffening our necks and still practising disobedience and unruliness. The Saviour's disciple will confirm this when he says, "Do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God? Whoever wants to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God." But once we have turned to the God of all through faith and sin has been taken away, nothing stands between us, and no one could bar us from intimacy with him. Rather, we cleave to him, as it were, in all gentleness. We will walk along the straight road and travel the truly good path, guiding both ourselves and others onto it.

It would be especially fitting for holy priests to be engaged in these things, so that it could quite rightly be said of them, "He walked with me in peace, keeping a straight course, and he turned many away from injustice." For those under authority tend somehow to follow in the tracks of their leaders' virtues. Leaders who go by the straight road save many. They readily persuade them to abandon a licentious and accursed life and the ways of injustice, and to choose and love instead what is better and admirable, which must win praise from God and from people.
For the lips of a priest will guard knowledge, and they will seek the law from his mouth, because he is an angel of the Lord Almighty.

He makes clear how the priest turned many away from injustice and walked with God, keeping a straight course in peace. He says that the priest carried on his lips, that is, on his tongue, the knowledge of everything necessary for life. He became "an instructor of the foolish and a teacher of infants," and for those wishing to learn what the law requires he was a true and wholly reliable interpreter. He did not twist the sense of the divine oracles in some other direction, nor did he teach "as doctrines the commandments of men." Instead, like an angel of God, he made perfectly clear to the peoples in his care what the oracles sometimes express obscurely. For he does not announce his own will, nor does he pour out words of his own devising; rather, he serves the Master's decrees. And I would say that what is said in the book of Proverbs also holds true for such men: "A desirable treasure will rest on the mouth of the wise, but foolish men will swallow it up." It is to the credit of those who announce anything from God that they add nothing to what they announce and do not dare take anything away. The unholy bands of the Pharisees thought very little of this, and in their ignorance they slid into such nonsense that they taught "as doctrines the commandments of men" and nullified the divine commandments for the sake of their tradition. These were the charges Christ brought against them. So the law about the divine oracles is firm: nothing may be added to them, and nothing may be taken away from them. The lips of the priests, then, will guard the knowledge of the law and proclaim it without adding anything. This is also why the priest is called an angel of the Lord Almighty, though he is a man by nature: he clearly announces what pleases God, and the law governs every movement of his tongue.
But you have turned aside from the way, you have made many weak in the law, and you have corrupted the covenant of Levi, says the Lord Almighty.

In a way, he sets the charges against the negligent beside the virtues of the distinguished, and exposes what is base by comparing it with what is better. For just as light shines in darkness and "power is made perfect in weakness," so the beauty of virtue shows itself more plainly [?] when some baseness or sin lies beside it. Some men, then, lived as befits priests, keeping themselves and others on a straight course in peace. They were with God and turned many away from injustice, for they carried knowledge on their lips and became precise interpreters of the divine words. But those who came after them, to whom this word is addressed, have turned aside from the way. They slipped away from what was fitting and did great wrong both to themselves and to others. And they made many weak in the law, that is, they left them weak and utterly feeble when it came to choosing to live by the law. For if those in charge stray beyond what is fitting, how could those under them not wander off with them entirely? How could those of lower station, who fall short in understanding, not slide down along with their superiors? A law-abiding and holy priest will make the peoples in his care imitators of his own good deeds, and the opposite is also true. If the priests themselves have corrupted the covenant of Levi, how could those they instructed be expected to regard the law as venerable?
And I have made you despised and cast off among all the nations, because you did not keep my ways but showed partiality in the law.

He goes back to the sins of their fathers and also reminds them of the old charges. Since they had not been steadfast in keeping the law, he says that for this reason they were handed over to those who carried them off into captivity, pitiable, cast down and deprived of all mercy. For what grief did they not suffer? What misfortunes did the wretches not share in? "But if you want to learn the causes of the wrath that came upon you," he says, "you will hear him say: Because you did not keep my ways but showed partiality in the law." This, I think, is what it means to corrupt the covenant of Levi: refusing to keep to the way of life set out in the law, and passing the most outrageous judgments in every case, although God says plainly, "You shall not show partiality in judgment; you shall judge the small and the great alike." And with the very words in which he says that this is why they were handed over to their enemies and became outcasts, he skilfully issues a threat. If they do not choose to live rightly, he himself will not hold back from punishing them; those who outrage the law will meet the penalty that is fitting and most appropriate for people accustomed to doing such things.

Did not one God create you? Is there not one father of you all? Why has each of you forsaken his brother, so as to profane the covenant of your fathers? Judah has been forsaken, and an abomination has been committed in Israel and in Jerusalem.

At the beginning of our treatise on this Prophet, we said that after the return from Babylon and from the land of the Assyrians, the people of Israel paid little heed to the commandment of the law and began joining themselves to foreign women. The practice grew so degenerate that even those who served as priests were carried along with the rest. They treated the wives already living with them, who were of Israel's blood, as utterly worthless and sent them away from their homes, and brought in foreign women instead: Ammonites, Moabites and Idumeans. This brought great profanation on Israel. For those women did not give up their ancestral customs. They still worshipped idols and bowed down to the host of heaven, and it was all but inevitable that the men who had unlawfully married women so corrupted in mind would be defiled along with them and offend God. A great deal is said on this subject in the books of Ezra. So the God of all accuses them of dishonouring the women of Israel's blood, that is, of Judah, and of attaching themselves in an unholy way to the daughters of foreigners, even though the law forbade such unions. But somehow they made light of these sacred things. Either they were swept away into licentious pleasures by the women's charms, or perhaps they wanted to gain the upper hand through friendship with the foreigners, so that those peoples would not make war on them, since they were now acquaintances and related by marriage. But this was nothing other than outraging God through little faith, as though he were unable to rescue them from those peoples' hands or to make them stronger than the greed of foreigners. So the affair grieved God in every way.

That is why, seeing them disregard even their natural affection, he says, "Did not one God create you? Is there not one father of you all? Why has each of you forsaken his brother?" For there is one Creator of all, and all belong to one Master, who wants what he has made to be bound together in unity and concord by the laws of love. If there were two gods and lords, or even more, it would be no surprise if their creatures were forced to go along with the wills of their makers and readily accepted strife with one another, as those in power saw fit. But since there is one God, who is through all and in all and over all, what excuse could there be for dissension? And since, besides this, all the Jews have one father according to the flesh, the inspired Abraham, what could persuade them to take on the disease of hating one another? Is it not only right to give love to those close in blood as a kind of debt? And is it not close to madness to rave after the daughters of foreigners while dishonouring the women at home and of their own race, "so as to profane the covenant of your fathers"? For their fathers kept what the divine laws prescribed about foreign women. They heard: "You shall not give your daughter to his son, and you shall not take his daughter for your son, for she will turn your son away from me, and he will go and serve other gods." But these men counted the oracle as nothing. They trampled on the law and, as far as it lay with them, made the covenant powerless and profane, grieving the Best of beings by their transgressions of the laws. And as though astonished at what was done, and seeing the women of Judah's blood overwhelmed by the most unjust hatred, he goes on to say, "Judah has been forsaken, and among those who dwell in Jerusalem." "What a strange thing!" he says. "Not to the Assyrians, not to the Medes, not to the Persians, not to the Elamites, not to the enemies next door, but to Israel itself and to those who dwell in Jerusalem, Judah has become loathsome and hated"—that is, the race of Judah and the wretched crowd of kindred wives.

It should be noted that by "Israel" he means the ten tribes who lived in Samaria before the time of the captivity, whom Shalmaneser was the first to deport to the Assyrians and Medes. By those who dwell in Jerusalem he means the people whom Nebuchadnezzar captured in the last captivity, when he burned Jerusalem and the divine temple itself, and whom he carried off to Babylon. So he accuses them, or rather raises no small outcry against them, because they put away the wives from Judah and unlawfully took in women from foreign peoples, even though, as I said before, these women clung tightly to their ancestral customs and still wallowed in the mire of idolatry.

We too must be on our guard, we who have been justified in Christ and, through faith in him, have been granted a share in the Holy Spirit. We must not mingle with people who are perverse in mind, profane in heart and lacking right faith. For these are foreigners, of barbarous speech, "speaking perverse things," and anyone who mingles with them will be wholly and utterly defiled. For it is written, "Whoever touches pitch will be defiled." Since we can bear spiritual fruit in the Church of Christ, what reason could there be for wanting to join ourselves in any way to other assemblies, to share in profane synagogues, and to stir up the God of all against ourselves?

For Judah has profaned the holy things of the Lord, which he loved, and has gone after foreign gods. The Lord will destroy the man who does these things, until he is brought low and cut off from the tents of Jacob and from those who offer sacrifice to the Lord Almighty.

He says that Judah has been hated, not by any of the foreigners, but by Judah itself, which profaned the law by being inclined to love foreign women, choosing to imitate their ways, loving apostasy from God and devoting itself to the worship of idols. For, as I said, some were carried away to this by following the women unlawfully joined to them and doing everything in their power to satisfy their wishes. In just the same way, at Shittim, those who had been redeemed from Egypt joined themselves to the women of the Midianites, or rather of the Moabites. Little by little they slid into such folly and unholy thinking that they were even initiated into the rites of Baal of Peor, and for this reason the wretches perished. So the God of all curses the man who does these things, the unholy lover of such outrageous practices. If he is counted among the people, the curse holds "until he is destroyed from the tents of Jacob," that is, until he perishes completely and loses even the memory of having existed. But if he is one of those appointed to the sacred service, it holds "until he is brought low from among those who offer sacrifice to the Lord Almighty," that is, until he perishes and is struck from the priestly rolls. For, as I said, some of the priests also slid along with the others into the people's offences and were overcome by foreign women, having completely disregarded the divine oracles.

So if anyone who provokes God, and tries to set the pleasures of the world against his decrees, is accursed, let us turn away the curse. Let us take no account of those pleasures, and hasten instead to make our souls shine with the glories of obedience. In this way the curse will lose its force, and the Lord of all will enrich us with the good things of his own gentleness.

“And these things which I hated you did: you covered the altar of the Lord with tears, and with weeping and groaning from your toils. Is it still fitting for me to look upon a sacrifice, or to accept anything acceptable from your hands?”

Under the law there were a great many kinds of sacrifice. Some were offered as a freewill vow, others were thank offerings, and still others were for sin. Tithes and firstfruits, and the tax of the double drachma, were brought to the priests by command of the law. So when they brought their freewill offerings to God as sacrifices, they presented, as I said, the lame and the blind and things seized as plunder in the captivity. They were forever talking of their misfortunes, harping up and down on the devastation and on the poverty it had brought upon them, even though, after the return from Babylon, God who is mighty in all things was gladdening them with incomparable gentleness and lavishly giving them things in which they might well take no small delight. So they brought their offerings downcast and in tears, all but wailing over the victims, and saying to the priests, “These come from toil,” that is, they were not obtained without effort but scraped together with difficulty, by sweat and labor. Then he says: How is it still fitting for me to look upon the sacrifice, or how could I still accept what comes from an ungracious disposition? For one ought to sacrifice cheerfully, keeping festival and rejoicing. And this, I think, is what was rightly said through the voice of Paul to those who were gathering the contributions for the ministry: “Not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.”

So if we sacrifice cheerfully, God will look upon it, accept it and approve it, and having accepted it he will honor and bless us. But I think it is also necessary, for our benefit, to apply another interpretation to the passage before us. The God of all declared accursed, and very justly, the one who profaned the covenant of the fathers by marrying foreign women, after driving out the women of his own race, who had often been condemned for no reason at all. Besides this, he was accusing some of the priests of showing partiality in the law, and so he said: “The Lord will utterly destroy the man who does these things, until he is brought low from the tents of Jacob and from among those who bring a sacrifice to the Lord Almighty.” Then he immediately added: “You covered the altar of the Lord with tears, and with weeping and groaning from your toils.” “You covered” must be understood to mean: you caused the divine altar to be filled with lamentation and wailing. For the women who had been driven out without reason, and those who had suffered outrageously unjust judgment at your hands, you priests, stand around the altar, bewailing the injustice done to them and weeping uncontrollably over the troubles brought upon them. Then he says: How is it fitting for me to look upon a sacrifice, or to accept anything acceptable from your hands? For just as what is written in the book of Proverbs is true, “Vows paid from a harlot’s hire are not pure,” so a priest could not be reckoned pure and blameless if, having all but bidden farewell to the divine decrees and trampled on the proper ordinance of the priestly service, he offered the sacrifice as though he had in no way given offense. It is a fearful thing, then, to perform sacred service to God with unwashed hands, so to speak. For my part I say that one must be cleansed with all one’s strength, as far as possible, before laying hold of so venerable a ministry. Such a person is found free of all blame and of the stirrings of wrath.

“And you said, ‘For what reason?’ Because the Lord bore witness between you and the wife of your youth, whom you abandoned; and she was your partner and the wife of your covenant. And he did not make her otherwise, and she is a remnant of his spirit. And you said, ‘What else does God seek but offspring?’”

Since God was frequently finding fault with such conduct, urging them to love the women of their own race, to keep away from foreign women, and to shun marriages that the divine law itself had forbidden, they said in their folly, “What else does God seek but offspring?” It was said, they argue, through the commandment of Moses, “There shall be no one childless or barren among the children of Israel.” And somewhere the God of all also said to Abraham, “I will surely multiply your offspring, like the stars of heaven in number.” So the divine purpose, they say, looks to multitude and the begetting of children, so that the grace promised to Abraham concerning his offspring may be brought to its proper fulfillment. Whether we accomplish this through foreign women or through women of our own race makes no difference to God, for the promise is carried through to its fulfillment either way. “Tell me, then,” he says, “why the Lord bore witness between you and the wife of your youth, whom you abandoned.” But if you choose to ask, “For what reason did he bear witness and command that the wife who shares one’s home must not be sent away?”, I too will answer this: Consider that she is your partner and the wife of your covenant, that is, one flesh with you and joined to you in lawful marriage, and God did not create her otherwise. And she is also, I think, a remnant of his spirit, as if to say: a husband is somehow blended, in body and in soul, with the woman lawfully joined to him. Just as they have become one body, so in a certain way they are also one soul, since love binds them together and the divine law gathers them into oneness of soul. So he calls the wife a remnant of the husband’s spirit, as it were a part of his own soul, because of their union, I mean the union in that oneness of soul which comes through love. Do not, then, go beyond what is fitting and accuse God, as though he were perhaps unjust in rebuking those who send away from their home the wife of their youth, the partner of their covenant and of their spirit, who has been united to them in the flesh. For my part I think that the most wise Paul was moved by this passage when he wrote to those who had believed in Christ, “Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be released.” And somewhere the Savior himself also said, “Whoever divorces his wife, except on the ground of sexual immorality, makes her commit adultery; and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.” And when the Sadducees, fond of disputing, asked why “Moses commanded to give a certificate of divorce” and be rid of a wife, he said again, “Because of your hardness of heart Moses commanded it; but from the beginning it was not so. For he who formed them made them male and female. So what God has joined together, let no one separate.” “And take heed in your spirit, and do not abandon the wife of your youth. But if you hate her and send her away, says the Lord Almighty, the God of Israel, ungodliness will cover your thoughts, says the Lord. And take heed in your spirit, and do not abandon the covenant.”

Since the law declared clearly and openly that those who wished might hand their wives a certificate of divorce and be rid of the woman who shared their home without incurring blame, what was said through the Prophet’s voice seemed in some way to contradict what had been decreed long ago, since he brings to judgment, and charges with the crime of lawlessness, the man who dares to put away his wife and cut himself off from her. So with great prudence, by these words, he neither declares the ancient commandment void nor allows anyone to make it a pretext for unholy undertakings. It is as if he said: The law permitted the certificate to be given, but that does not mean you are free of guilt when you give it in order to attach yourselves to foreign women. Even if it is permitted to leave a wife, and to do so by legal decree, take heed in your spirit not to abandon the wife of your youth. This is the better course, even if the law permitted divorce to those who wanted it. “But if you hate her and send her away, says the Lord, the God of Israel”: that is, if, to make the dismissal plausible and well grounded, you write in the certificate, “I have come to hate her, and I will send her away,” and then ungodliness covers your thoughts, that is, if an ungodly and profane pleasure should [?] cover your thoughts, and hatred is only an idle pretext, while in fact you are found to be overcome by the beauty of others and wanting to attach yourself to foreign women, then take heed, do not abandon her, or you will be accursed altogether and without fail. For I said, “The Lord will utterly destroy the man who does these things, until he is brought low from the tents of Jacob and from among those who bring a sacrifice to the Lord Almighty.” So much for the plain and obvious sense. But those who have been called through faith to sanctification must also be on their guard, lest they somehow be carried off into profane heresies, as though to women hateful to God and foreign. For the pure and blameless instruction of the Church’s teachers is enough for them to bear spiritual fruit, and it all but makes them fathers of noble children, as they beget spiritually, from a good heart, the glories of love for God, to whom be glory and might forever and ever. Amen.
BY THE SAME AUTHOR, ON THE SAME PROPHET. SECOND VOLUME.

You who provoke God with your words; and you said, “In what have we provoked him?” In your saying, “Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and he himself has taken pleasure in them; and where is the God of justice?”

It has already been said that the God of all was angered against those of the blood of Levi, not in one way only but in many. Rebuking the negligence of the priests, he said, “And you brought in what was stolen, and the lame, and the sickly,” and to this he added, “and you showed partiality in the law.” For they gave honour where it was not due, and out of an ill-timed deference made much of some of those who came to them, while they wickedly condemned the weaker, and helped some to get the better of others. They did not judge justly, according to the law, but delivered a slanted [?] and unequal verdict; or perhaps they even seized inheritances that in no way belonged to them. They delighted in bribes, abused the honours of the priesthood, and lorded it over those placed under them. Some of those who had endured these injustices, seeing them lead a life so disgraceful and so utterly lawless, were all but dumbfounded. For no rebuke came upon them from God, nor the things that sometimes befall the habitually contemptuous as a result of his wrath; instead they lived in comfort and luxury. Vexed at this, and no longer able, it seems, to keep in mind the incomparable gentleness of God, they all but cried out in their faintheartedness, saying, “Everyone who does evil is good in his sight, and he himself has taken pleasure in them”; that is, perhaps the worker of wicked deeds is actually good in the eyes of God, and he delights in those who have chosen to live so shamefully. “For if this is not true,” they say, “where is the God of justice? The ruler of justice ought, surely he ought, not to have put up so long with priests who are grasping and who defile the altar, men utterly bent on doing what is unjust, unholy and outside the law.” Such, then, are the charges that sprang from their faintheartedness. But it should be understood that, according to the sense of the passage, those who use such ignorant words provoke God. For they have all but resolved to rebuke God for his forbearance, though he waits, and most kindly, for the return of those who have gone astray and for the turning to better things of those who have slipped into sin. Indeed the divine Paul rebuked those who still hesitated and shrank back from repentance, saying, “Or do you despise the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God’s kindness leads you to repentance? But by your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God.” So those who are overcome by such feeble faintheartedness and let loose an unbridled tongue against God certainly give offence in every way; yet those who gave them occasion for this weakness would also be guilty of wrongdoing.

It is necessary, therefore, that the chosen ministers in the Church, that is, those called to the priesthood, should live holy lives and walk uprightly. For in this way they will be a pattern of good order and of every virtue to the peoples under them, who will in turn glorify the God of all when they behold the splendid and exceptional beauty of the priests’ way of life. And this, I think, is what was rightly said by the Saviour: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” For just as the people are scandalized when the priests choose to live outrageously, so they will gain the greatest and most abundant benefit if they see them fulfilling what is good and choosing to live as is pleasing to God.

Behold, I send out my angel, and he will survey the way before my face; and suddenly the Lord whom you seek will come to his temple, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire. Since they were saying, “Where is the God of justice?”, the word of the prophecy before us very fittingly passes over to the mystery of Christ. For Emmanuel has become for us, from God the Father, “righteousness and sanctification and redemption,” and the cleansing of all filth, the putting away of sins, the casting off of shameful things, the way to what is better and more fitting, and a kind of door and path leading to eternal life. Through him every restoration has come about, the overthrow of greed and the discovery of righteousness; and indeed, which of the marvellous things have we not been enriched with through him? “Behold,” then, he says, “I will send my angel, and he will survey the way before my face.” By these words he seems to foretell the ministry of the holy Baptist. For Christ himself said somewhere, “This is he of whom it is written, ‘Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’” In the same way the divine Isaiah also pointed him out to us, saying, “A voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, make straight the paths of our God.” When this has happened, he says, and the one appointed to announce these things has gone a little ahead, “Suddenly the Lord whom you seek will come to his temple, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire.” The blessed John also affirms it, saying to those who came to the baptism of repentance, “I baptize you with water, but after me comes a man the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to stoop down and untie. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire.” You see, then, how Christ came immediately after his forerunner, all but on his heels, making himself manifest to those throughout all Judea and appearing, as it were, suddenly and unexpectedly. We say, however, that the divine Baptist was called an angel not on account of his nature, for he was born of a woman and was a human being like us, but because he was entrusted with the ministry of proclaiming and announcing these things to us. The name, then, comes from his function and does not signify the essence of an angel.

He says that he will come to his temple either because the Word became flesh and dwelt, as in a temple, in the all-pure body taken from the holy Virgin, that is, in a complete human being, consisting, I mean, of soul and body, to which he is believed to have been united directly and in accordance with the economy of salvation; or else he simply calls “temple” the city that was, as it were, holy and dedicated to him, clearly Jerusalem, or, as in a type pointing to it, the Church. He proclaimed his own coming by working wonders of many kinds, “preaching the gospel of the kingdom and healing every disease and every sickness among the people,” as it is written. So, he says, the Lord will come whom you seek, you who say in your faintheartedness, “Where is the God of justice?” And he will come teaching what is above the law and beyond the shadow and the types. For he will be the angel of the covenant that was announced long ago by the voice of God the Father. For he said somewhere to Moses, the revealer of sacred things, “I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers, and I will put my words in his mouth, and he will speak to them everything that I command him.” That Christ was the angel of a new covenant the blessed Isaiah also makes clear, saying concerning him, “For they shall repay every garment gathered by deceit and every cloak gained by exchange, and they will wish they had been burned with fire. For a child has been born to us, a son also has been given to us, whose rule is upon his shoulder, and his name is called Angel of Great Counsel,” clearly that of God the Father. That is why he also said, “I do not speak on my own, but the Father who sent me has himself given me a command about what to say and what to speak.” For the Saviour’s word was not human; rather, it came to us from God the Father through his Son by nature. For he is the Word of the one who begot him, and he will confirm this, saying through the voice of David, “My heart has poured forth a good word.”
Behold, he comes, says the Lord Almighty; and who will endure the day of his coming in? Or who will stand at his appearing?

Like this, and very similar to it, is what was said through the voice of Isaiah: “Be strong, you slack hands and paralysed knees; take comfort, you who are fainthearted in mind; be strong, do not fear. Behold, the Lord comes with strength, and his arm with dominion.” For by showing him as about to be present, or rather as already present, he declares plainly that the time of his sojourn in this world will not be long postponed. And that the power of the economy will not be easily despised by anyone, nor would it be bearable to the disobedient, he teaches when he says, “And who will endure the day of his coming in? Or who will stand at his appearing?” By “coming in” he means the entry of the Only-begotten into this world with flesh, and by “appearing” his manifestation, so to speak. For although by nature he is invisible as God, he became visible by taking on our likeness. The psalmist too had plainly cried this out beforehand in the Spirit, saying, “God will come visibly, our God, and he will not keep silent.” For “the Word became flesh,” as the divine John says, “and dwelt among us,” and he came in the form of a servant. And to “those who have loved his appearing” he was by no means burdensome; rather, he was gentle and meek, and the giver of eternal life. God the Father too said of him somewhere, “Behold, my servant will understand, my beloved, in whom I am well pleased. He will not quarrel or cry out, nor will his voice be heard outside. A bruised reed he will not break, and a smouldering wick he will not quench, but he will bring forth judgment in truth.” Those, however, who dishonoured the salvation that comes through him and would not accept the cleansing that comes through faith suffered the most shameful of all evils; for the wretches perished utterly. That is why he said to the crowds of the Jews, “Truly I tell you, unless you believe that I am he, you will die in your sins.” And John also said somewhere, “Whoever believes in him is not judged; but whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he has not believed in the name of the Son of God.” The Baptist too declared to those of Israel, “Already the axe is laid at the root of the trees; every tree, therefore, that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.” So for the disobedient the time of his coming in and of his appearing proved unbearable and hardly to be endured. For they were convicted of destroying their own souls and of being about to die in their own sins, because they did not choose to think rightly or to receive into mind and heart the cleansing that comes through faith. “Who, then,” he says, “will endure the day of his coming in? Or who will stand at his appearing?” That is, who will be so formidable and so harsh as to stand firm and remain unbroken at the time and on the day of his entry into the world, clearly his entry with flesh, through which he became tangible, that is, visible? For such a one will be punished in every way, and will pay a bitter penalty for his folly.

For he enters like the fire of a smelting furnace and like the soap of launderers; and he will sit smelting and purifying as silver and as gold, and he will purify the sons of Levi and pour them out like gold and silver.

Here the language is framed by analogy with things familiar to us, but to the more discerning it would convey the disclosure of an ineffable mystery. Those skilled in such things assay silver and gold by melting away with fire everything in them that is counterfeit and unsightly. But the divine and heavenly fire, that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit, through which we are made alive in the spirit, when it enters mind and heart, Christ sending it in, then indeed scours away all the filth of sin and consumes the defilement of our former transgressions. It renders those who possess it thus purified and thoroughly proven, and all but reforges them spiritually into newness of life, and makes them henceforth bright and sanctified vessels, prepared for honour and useful for the great house, that is, the Church. This divine and spiritual fire the divine John signified when he said, “I baptize you with water, but after me comes a man the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to stoop down and untie; he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire.” And we remember Christ himself saying, “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and how I wish it were already kindled!” Since, then, those of the blood of Israel complained in no small measure about the impurity, that is, the injustice, of the Levites, or rather on their account kept provoking the God of all, uttering blasphemies and daring to say, “Everyone who does evil is good in his sight, and he himself has taken pleasure in them; and where is the God of justice?”, he usefully foretells that in due time Christ will shine forth, who takes away all our sin, makes his own priests all-pure, and tests them like gold or silver in the fire, that is, renders them proven and resplendent.

For such, generally speaking, are the ministers of the Church, to whom it would be very fitting to say the words spoken through David: “For you have tested us, O God; you have refined us as silver is refined.” For the sons of Aaron wore the vestment prescribed by the law; but for those chosen in Christ and appointed to the priestly ministry, Christ himself will be a splendid garment, befitting priests and holy. That is why God the Father, through the lyre of the psalmist, said concerning the Church from the Gentiles, “I will clothe her priests with salvation, and her holy ones will rejoice with exultation.” For Christ himself, the salvation, is the admirable garment of his own priests, or rather of all who have believed: “For as many of you,” he says, “as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.”
And they will be offering sacrifices to the Lord in righteousness; and the sacrifice of Judah and Jerusalem will please the Lord, as in the days of the age and as in the former years.

They will be dedicated to God, he says; for this, I think, is the meaning of “They will be offering to the Lord.” And we will be dedicated to God when we no longer live for ourselves but devote ourselves wholly to love for him, and choose with all our strength to accomplish what is pleasing to his divine will. The divine Paul said something like this concerning Christ, the Saviour of us all: “For one died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and was raised for them.” And depicting for us, as it were, the beauty of his own way of life, and making plain the power of the mystery of Christ, he said again, “I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.” So, he says, they will be offering to the Lord, that is, they will be devoted to his will alone, not “setting their minds on earthly things,” not loving the defilements of injustice, not choosing to prize gain at the expense of others, but rather offering sacrifices of righteousness. And it seems to me that Paul spoke very wisely: “For when the priesthood is changed, there is necessarily a change of the law as well.” For we who have been called in Christ to the priestly ministry approach no longer with blood and smoke, nor do we bring lambs or kids to God; rather, in the churches we perform the holy and spiritual sacrifice understood in Christ, setting him forth for sanctification and also for participation in eternal life. And like some choice incense we offer the fragrance of good works, and sacrificing righteousness to him, we are confident that we will be accepted. For it is written, “Honour the Lord from your righteous labours, and give him the firstfruits of your fruits of righteousness.” For the God of all is pleased, I think, with no other sacrifices than these.

He has said, then, concerning those called in Christ to the priestly ministry, that they will be better than the former ones, not slaughtering sheep as they did, nor profaning the altar by offering polluted bread, but bringing to God righteousness in place of incense, and the spiritual fragrance of the gospel way of life. And they will perform a worship so acceptable that it will in no way fall short of the sacrifices befitting the days of the age, that is, the life of the holy spirits in heaven, who pass continual and long days, that is, ages; and it will also be equal to the former years, that is, to the worship of the saints who lived in former times. For among the more ancient it was through obedience that good repute was won. Thus Abraham offered his son to God, “and it was reckoned to him as righteousness, and he was called the friend of God.” Thus Noah too “built the ark for the salvation of his household,” as it is written. So, he says, the sacrifice of Judah will please, that is, of the people that bears the circumcision of the heart and spirit, and of Jerusalem, clearly the spiritual Jerusalem, that is, the Church; just as did the sacrifice of those who possess the days of the age, and that of the saints who lived in former times, who became well pleasing through obedience and faith. These the divine Paul lists in the Epistle to the Hebrews, saying that many were justified by faith.

And I will draw near to you in judgment, and I will be a swift witness against the sorceresses and against the adulteresses and against those who swear falsely by my name, and against those who withhold the wages of the hired worker, and those who oppress the widow, and those who beat orphans with their fists, and those who pervert the judgment of the stranger, and those who do not fear me, says the Lord Almighty.

Here too our text proceeds in keeping with the matter at hand. For those of Israel, in their ignorance, said, “Everyone who does evil is good in his sight, and he himself has taken pleasure in them; and where is the God of justice?” What gave rise to such dreadful loose talk has already been stated, but it will be stated again. Since some of the priests, and indeed of the others who were more prominent and distinguished by the highest honours, recklessly gave themselves to every kind of perversity and wicked enterprise, and God seemed to bear with them beyond measure, for he is good, kind, gentle and loving toward humankind, for this reason some belched out words born of unmixed faintheartedness. But he has clearly indicated that in due time there will be a change for the better in those appointed to the priestly ministry, as Christ refashions them into newness of life and transforms them into good order and a glorious way of life and conduct. And that he would not then accept those who practise wickedness, nor deem them worthy of praise or consideration, but would rather judge them and exact a penalty for their outrageous lives, he makes plain when he says, “And I will draw near to you in judgment,” that is, I will come forward as judge, “and I will be a swift witness,” clearly of my own accord and summoned by no one. For I will pass sentence on the wicked. And I will bring judgment upon them, not with someone else uncovering what is in them, but knowing, as God, what is unseen and hidden, and bearing witness against each of the sinners through his own conscience. The divine Paul too said somewhere that in due time all those throughout the whole earth will stand before the judge, “their thoughts accusing or else excusing one another, on the day when God will judge the secrets of people, according to my gospel, through Jesus Christ.”

Notice how he says that those who have committed both hidden and open offences will be brought to judgment. First he names sorceresses and adulteresses, and then those who swear falsely. These things are hidden and done in secret; for who would ever practise sorcery openly? Or how would an adulteress choose to be seen by anyone? And those who choose to perjure themselves, I think, are eager to escape notice. The blessed David will expose such people as lacking understanding, saying, “Understand, you senseless among the people; and you fools, when will you be wise? He who planted the ear, does he not hear? Or he who formed the eye, does he not perceive?” For nothing at all is hidden from God; he alone knows both the hidden and the open evils. Those, then, are the things done in secret and as in darkness; but to them he adds the open ones as well: withholding the wages of the hired worker, I mean, and the greed and oppression that some practise against the weaker, namely widows and orphans. To these he adds those who pervert right judgments and those who do not fear him. These would be the ones who grieve God in some other way besides those we have just mentioned. “I will be,” then, he says, “a judge and a swift witness, of my own accord, against sorceresses and adulteresses, and against those who practise the other evils.” It is likely that such things were being dared by some at that time, and that because of them the many were railing against God.

We must therefore reject evil with all our strength, run eagerly toward better things, and hurry to carry out whatever will make a person full of all praise and goodness. In this way he will have no share in what divine wrath will bring on those who make a habit of sinning, but will have a place among the honours and glory that God grants to those who love him.
For I am the Lord your God, and I have not changed; and you, sons of Jacob, have not kept away from the sins of your fathers. You turned aside from my statutes and did not keep them.

Again he draws them away from unholy thoughts, and from unholy words as well. Some suppose that the God of all has turned from willing what is good to its opposite, or that he no longer loves righteousness but welcomes the lovers of wickedness. How is this not ignorant, or rather entirely jarring and unholy, and full of the most extreme impiety? So when you see them summoned to judgment, he says, the sorceresses among you, that is, the enchantresses (these are surely whispering, scurrilous women), and those who practise the other evils, then, he says, you will learn from the facts themselves that I am the Lord your God, who was good and a lover of virtue long ago and is so now. For I know no turning or alteration. I am always and unchangeably what I am. But you, he says, though you are descended from Jacob, a man who loved God, a good man who always hated unruliness and served God, have not become imitators of his ways. You have imitated instead the disobedience and stubbornness of your own fathers. For this very reason they went away as captives, leaving the land that bore them, and became slaves to the enemies who had conquered them. You too turned aside from my statutes and did not keep them. So God is always unchanging, fixed, as it were, in goodness and unshakable in righteousness. They, on the other hand, have all but kept their own unchangeableness in wickedness, and have become the most faithful imitators of their fathers' unholiness.

Christ too is found saying something of this kind. He rightly pronounces woe on that workshop of ignorant scribes and Pharisees, speaking as follows: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you build the tombs of the prophets and adorn the monuments of the righteous, and you say, 'If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have taken part with them in the blood of the prophets.' So you testify against yourselves that you are sons of those who murdered the prophets. Fill up, then, the measure of your fathers." It is necessary, then, if we are truly sound of mind and in our settled senses, to imitate as far as possible the most approved of our fathers and to shake off any imitation of those who were not good. If someone does not choose to do this, but simply and without examination follows those who came before him in time, he will be just like the children of the Greeks. If anyone blames them because they have abandoned the knowledge of the truth, forsaken the God who is God by nature, and worship stones, they forever plead the custom of their own fathers.

Return to me, and I will return to you, says the Lord Almighty. And you said, "In what shall we return?" Will a man cheat God? For you are cheating me. And you said, "In what have we cheated you?" In that the tithes and firstfruits are still with you. You keep your eyes fixed on them, and you are cheating me. The year has been completed, and you have brought all the produce into the storehouses, and in his house will be its plundering.

Having thoroughly turned them away from their railing against him, and having shamed them as far as possible with fitting defences of himself, he calls the sinners to repentance, saying that he will very gladly grant them his accustomed gentleness again. For just as he brings fitting punishments on those who choose to live outrageously, so he truly rejoices over those who turn back, as it were, and give up sinning any further, and everywhere he cuts away despair as the agent of destruction. From this we can see what a dreadful disease is brought into life by those who debase the grace of repentance and ignorantly give themselves the name of 'the pure'. Yet would it not be better to realize that to think oneself pure, and to insist on saying so, brings on them the charge of the worst impurity? For it is written, "State your sins first, so that you may be justified"; and somewhere the divine David sings to us, "For I know my iniquity, and my sin is ever before me." "For no one is clean from filth," as it is written. So those who are sick with such weakness need the good things that come from repentance, and the gentleness from above that thoroughly washes the defiled and justifies the ungodly. He therefore calls sinners to repentance out of gentleness. And when they in turn ask and wish to learn what their offence was, he says, Will a man cheat God? For you are cheating me. To 'cheat' means to snatch something away or to deceive, and to suppose one can escape notice while lying, perhaps, or even while doing something utterly outrageous. Esau, for instance, bore a grudge against Jacob, and explaining his reason for wanting to kill him he said, "For he has cheated me now a second time: he took my birthright, and now he has taken my blessing." Will a man, then, he says, get the better of God, that is, outwit the one who knows all things? Why then do you cheat me?

I think that, for an exact explanation of the ideas before us, I should now also say a few things that are written in the books of Ezra. When those from Israel left the land of the Babylonians and returned to Judaea, they settled in Jerusalem. The divine temple was raised up, and the orders of priests were now in good order, the singers, the sacred psalmists, and those in charge of the gates. Then what happened after this? The redeemed grew careless about holding fast to the divine ordinances. They did not keep the law, and they counted the transgression of the divine commandment as nothing. Reluctantly and grudgingly they brought for sacrifice the blind, the stolen, the lame, and the sick. Then, after reaping the grain and the other crops in the fields in season, gathering the grapes from the vines, and pressing the fruit of the olive, they did not bring tithes and the firstfruits required by the law, so that the orders of priests, having enough to live on, might devote themselves without distraction to the worship of God and persevere in the ministries appointed for them by the law. Since nothing was brought, the ministers of the divine altars were scattered, and the temple was thus left deserted, with no sacrifice being offered and nothing else being done that serves the glory of God. So from then on everything in the fields was ruined, and they were oppressed by famine. They sank into such need and helplessness that they were even willing to sell their own children to those who had food, until Ezra, brought to an awareness of the divine wrath, laid a charge about these matters on the leaders of Israel. And so, with difficulty, they brought tithes and firstfruits, and the ministers at last hurried back and took their places, performing the customary rites in the temple. Why then, he says, are you cheating me? The year has been completed, the crops have been gathered in, and the tithes and the firstfruits required by the law are still with you.

And in his house, he says, will be its plundering. It is as though he were saying: You have gathered the crops from the fields into your houses, and perhaps you think they are being kept safe for you and are very well stored; but they will vanish in those very houses, and the matter will be no different from plunder. For you will be oppressed by famine, he says, even though you have gathered what you found by the sweat of your brow and with great effort. From this we too shall learn how great a fault it is not to bring God our thank-offerings, and not to return due thanks to his glory for what he graciously gives. If we do this, he will bless us in every way and by all means, and will lavish good things on us abundantly. But if we draw back our hand and keep what has been given for our own pleasures alone, he will not give readily; rather, he will scatter even what was gathered with such difficulty. For we must be generous and ready to share, and must set out the gifts of God for others to partake of.

Return, then, in this, says the Lord Almighty: see if I will not open for you the floodgates of heaven and pour out my blessing on you until you have enough. And I will set apart food for you, and I will not destroy the fruit of your land, and your vine in the field shall not fail, says the Lord Almighty. And all the nations will call you blessed, for you will be a desirable land, says the Lord Almighty.

Again he releases them from the charges and frees them from all blame, and he promises kindly, holding no grudge, to grant them what they pray for and to delight them with generosity beyond words. He wants them to learn by experience and from the facts themselves that bearing fruit will certainly be to their benefit. If they choose to do this, he promises to send down an abundant supply of rain and to bestow his blessing lavishly, so that they will have plenty of food, and in short a sufficient share of the good things of the earth. For he says, I will set apart food for you. You will understand 'I will set apart' as 'I will mark off', meaning that each of the things that grow from the earth has its own season in which it either springs up or ripens. He clearly promises that the fruit of the land will be safe from all harm, and that the vine in the fields will be laden with clusters and give the finest wine. When these things are fulfilled, he says, they will at last be blessed and will be called a kind of desirable land, that is, a land worth loving for its fruitfulness and fertility.

So if anyone has a heart of compassion, he will surely find God to be like this. He will store up treasure in heaven and will eat the fruit of his own labours, as it is written. He will not be like that harsh and utterly senseless rich man whose land, the Saviour says in the parables of the Gospel, produced plentifully. For he said, "What shall I do? I will pull down my barns and build bigger ones, and I will say to my soul, 'Soul, you have many good things laid up for many years; eat, drink, be merry.'" But as he was pondering such things in his folly, God said, "Fool, this very night your soul is demanded of you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?" So, as I said, the one who shares is full of blessing. Such a person will have spiritual rains watering his heart and greatly gladdening it, and he will yield the fruits of godliness at different times and in different ways, as if set apart, excelling now in love, now in kindness and mutual affection, now in courage and endurance. He will be like a fruitful and most fertile land, brilliant, renowned, and truly thrice-blessed. "A good name is more to be chosen than great riches," as it is written.

You have made your words heavy against me, says the Lord, and you said, "In what have we spoken against you?" You said, "It is futile to serve God. What did we gain by keeping his charges and by walking as suppliants before the Lord Almighty? And now we call strangers blessed; those who do lawless things are built up; they opposed God and were saved." These things those who fear the Lord spoke against him, each to his neighbour; and the Lord paid heed and heard.

When God wishes to set right some of those close to him who have slipped into sin, he brings their failings out into the open, convicts them plainly, and strikes them, as it were, with reproaches, so that, blushing at their own offences, they may choose to move over to what is better and more profitable, and so be saved by seeking his mercy. So he accuses those from Israel of yet another fault, and weaves a reproof that is, as it were, common to those who came after them too, knowing that this is beneficial and saving for all. For whatever happened to those before us as a type, "these things were written for our admonition," as the most wise Paul says. He accuses them, then, of unbridled speech and of choosing to grieve him with blasphemous words. For he says, You have made your words heavy against me. And what form did their slander take? You said, he says, "It is futile to serve God," and that there is no gain in wanting to keep his charges, that is, the ordinances given through the law. Besides this, you say, it is pointless even to entreat him, that is, to offer prayers for whatever you might wish.

The God of all is certainly truthful when he says these things and accuses those from Israel. But we must explain what occasion the babblers had for their sinful words. Countless nations grazed the earth, but out of them all God chose the one from Israel, and it has been called his portion, his allotted measure, and his inheritance. Having made it his own, he trained it by the law and helped it through the prophets. And what did foolish Israel do in return? It worshipped the host of heaven, served idols, and said to carved images, "You are our gods." The God of all, rightly indignant at such dreadful acts of impiety, chastened them in many ways, calling them to repentance by famines, blight, failures of crops, locust and caterpillar, mildew and grubs. For he did not yet want to strike them with a mighty hand, but rather to drive them on, as it were, with frights and still moderate stirrings to choose to do what was beneficial and to love the God who is God by nature and in truth. But since they paid no heed even to being struck in moderation, and ran off unbridled into every kind of impurity, he sent them into captivity and arranged for them to fall into the hands of the Babylonians. When they were called back again to Judaea through God's compassion, rebuilt the walls of the city, and raised up the temple, they turned once more to carelessness. They did not fulfil their vows, did not follow the ordinances of the law, and did not bring tithes or firstfruits. Instead, they came to sacrifice reluctantly and grudgingly, slaughtering the lame, the blind, and the sick. Since they behaved so outrageously, God chastened them no less with famine and barrenness. They ought, if they were good and understood what was to their advantage, to have appeased the grieved God of all by turning back to what was better; instead they raised a senseless outcry. For when they saw the neighbouring nations, which did not know God but rather worshipped carved images and were sick with the worst error, living in comfort and luxury, they said senselessly, "It is futile to serve God; and what did we gain by keeping his commands?" For we, they say, the keepers of the law, suffer barren seasons and blows, and we even went away as captives, though we were always falling down and making ourselves suppliants to the Lord Almighty; but those who do none of these things suffer no blow and no hardship. "So we call strangers blessed; those who do lawless things are built up; they opposed God and were saved." For those who are in error truly act against the glory of God in many ways, offering sacrifices to molten images, "saying to the wood, 'You are my god,' and to the stone, 'You gave birth to me.'" These things, he says, those who fear the Lord spoke against him. Again the charge is blasphemy, and a clear proof of the most extreme sickness. For these are the words of a diseased mind, and to say anything against God is the God-hated froth of a drunken intellect. He has assured us that he listens to such words not casually but attentively, when he says, And the Lord paid heed and heard. "For the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world, and that which holds all things together has knowledge of every voice." And if any word is spoken against his divine glory, it will be heavy and, as it were, unbearable, even to one who is accustomed to be very forbearing. That is why he said, You have made your words heavy against me.

So even if we are in hardships, while God is chastening us for our good, we must not lose heart too much, nor suppose that one who so loves virtue has withheld good things. Rather, we should search out the ways in which we have offended, and so appease him and ask for his mercy. And if some lovers of sin are living in worldly comfort and enjoying temporary pleasures, we should, as is fitting, ascribe the reasons for his forbearance toward them to his secret dispensations.

And he wrote a book of remembrance before him for those who fear the Lord and revere his name. And they shall be mine, says the Lord Almighty, on the day that I make, for a possession; and I will choose them as a man chooses his son who serves him.

When those from Israel mocked him and babbled unholy things against him, "he paid heed and heard." Then, although he ought to have inflicted fitting punishment on the sinners and called them to account for their unbridled words, he passes over this too, as God, holding no grudge. Instead he inscribes a book of remembrance for those who fear him, concerning whom, I think, David himself also said to the one who writes the book, "And in your book all shall be written."

We shall find our Lord Jesus Christ himself saying to the holy disciples, "Do not rejoice that the demons are subject to you; rejoice rather that your names have been written in heaven." And the inspired David very fittingly curses the Jewish people who killed Christ, saying, "Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and let them not be written with the righteous." So the book of remembrance is written for those who fear God. He says that they will be his own and most intimately known to him at the time of possession, when Christ sits on the throne of his glory, attended by angels, "and he will set the sheep on his right and the goats on his left, and will say to those on his right, 'Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.'" For then he will choose them, that is, make them his chosen ones, yielding nothing in affection to our human fathers, who rejoice over their own children, especially when they are wise and obedient and treat their parents with the greatest respect.
And you will turn and see the difference between the righteous and the unrighteous, and between the one who serves God and the one who does not serve him.

Then, then indeed, he says, you will stop such rotten idle talk and check your unrestrained and undisciplined tongue. You will no longer rail against God, the lover of virtue; but, having all but shaken off your drunkenness and turned back, as it were, from error, you will clearly see what the difference is, and how great it is, between the righteous and the lawless, between the one who serves God and the one who does not. For the lawless and unruly, who shake off the yoke of his service, will go away to destruction and endless punishment—"there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth," as it is written. But the good, who love God, understand the divine laws, and care for every virtue, being radiant and sanctified, will be crowned with the crown of incorruption. Having come into the dwelling places above, they will live together with the holy angels, and, shown to be sharers in the glory of Christ, they will delight in the good things of the age-long life, "which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have they entered into the heart of man," as it is written. Yet some of the saints, seeing the lovers of wickedness prospering in this life, have been troubled in their thoughts, though they were not unaware that such people will end their life in destruction. Blessed Jeremiah, for instance, says something like this: "You are righteous, O Lord, when I plead my case with you; yet I will speak of judgments with you. Why does the way of the ungodly prosper? Why do all who deal treacherously thrive? You planted them, and they took root; they had children and bore fruit. You are near to their mouth, but far from their hearts. And you, O Lord, know me; you have tested my heart before you." Then he says again, "Set them apart for the day of their slaughter. How long will the land mourn?" You see how he fell into perplexity of thought, yet he was not ignorant of the end of the ungodly. "For all flesh is grass, and all the glory of man like the flower of grass," as it is written.

For behold, a day is coming, burning like an oven, and it will burn them up; and all the foreigners and all who do lawless things will be stubble, and the coming day will set them ablaze, says the Lord Almighty, and there shall not be left of them root or branch.

It follows that we should understand the day of judgment to be in fire, "in which the heavens will pass away with a roar, and the elements will be dissolved with burning, and the earth and all the works in it will be burned up. But according to his promises we wait for new heavens and a new earth." So said one of the holy disciples. The day of the Lord, then, he says, will come like an oven and will burn up all the foreigners, and it will add to them those who do lawless things, for the same punishment will fall on both. Notice how very aptly he now mentions the foreigners. Since they had called them blessed, saying, "And now we call strangers blessed; those who do lawless things are built up; they opposed God and were saved," he therefore says that they will be burned up, as people who have waged war on the glory of God and have chosen to worship the creation rather than the Creator.

We shall also take "foreigners" in another sense, as a name for idolaters and for those who in some other way have become estranged from the holy and chosen race. I mean, for example, the heretics, of whom it might very fittingly be said: "They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have remained with us."
