These people have thrown away their divine nobility and cut themselves off from the holy and chosen race that has become God's own possession, through faith in Christ, that is. Such people, then, will be food for the all-devouring fire. And those who do lawless deeds will share the same lot before God, even if they happen to be counted among those who have believed and been chosen and who know the one who is God by nature and in truth. For this is not enough to wash away their sin, if it is indeed true that "faith without works is dead." Faith in Christ does justify, and it frees us from the stain of earlier failings. But if after this someone is found idle and slack and inclined toward the passions of the flesh and of the world, he has in a way killed the faith within himself. He has added nothing worthy of praise, and has instead run back to the old perversity of his life. Of such people the inspired disciple also says: "It would have been better for them never to have known the way of righteousness than, having known it, to turn back from the holy commandment handed down to them. What the true proverb says has happened to them: A dog returns to its own vomit, and a sow that has been washed goes back to wallowing in the mud." So those who do lawless deeds stand on the same footing as the foreigners. They too will be stubble, and they will be burned up just as stubble is when fire is brought to it. For the wheat is gathered into the barn, as the Saviour also says concerning the holy reapers, but the chaff is burned with unquenchable fire. *And neither root nor branch will be left to them.* That is, they will have no hope of springing up again to life. By life I mean the life that is truly to be desired, life in glory with God, understood as a life of holiness and blessedness. For when a root has not been cut out entirely, and a branch has not been torn up from the depths, some hope remains that it may spring up again. "For there is hope for a tree," as it is written; "if it is cut down, it will blossom again, and its shoot will not fail." But if it is dug up from below, from the root itself, as I said, and suffers a savage cutting of its growth, every hope that it might spring up to life again perishes with it entirely. So, drawing a comparison with plants, he says that all the hope of those who love sin has been taken away. Isaiah plainly declares this when he says: "Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be quenched, and they will be a spectacle to all flesh."

But for you who fear my name the sun of righteousness will rise, with healing in its wings; and you will go out and leap like calves set loose from their bonds. And you will trample the lawless, for they will be ashes under the soles of your feet on the day that I am making, says the Lord Almighty.

The only-begotten Word of God has shone forth. He appeared in this world after taking on our likeness, for "the Word became flesh," it says, "and dwelt among us." We were in mist and darkness, and he flashed his own radiance around us like a sun. Sending the bright ray of the true knowledge of God into the hearts of believers, he made them pure and wise and skilled in every good work. He showed us the Father in himself. Through his ineffable initiation into the mysteries he made us most expert and wise, and filled our minds with the knowledge of him. Yet even though we have been brought to this degree of brightness and have been enriched, as blessed Paul says, "in all speech and all knowledge and all wisdom," still "we see now in a mirror and in a riddle, and we know in part." But in due time the perfect will come, and then we shall have the fullest knowledge. Christ will shine on us again from heaven. He will do away with knowledge that is partial and in riddles, shine upon us as upon those who are fully perfect, fill our minds with a divine and ineffable light, and make them radiant with the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. For the inspired Paul said: "As for prophecies, they will be done away with; as for knowledge, it will cease." But we say that we shall not pass from knowing in part to knowing nothing at all. Far from it! Otherwise, how would the time of our future hope not be a loss to the souls of the saints? They would have to slip away even from what they already have. They would gain nothing better and lift their minds to nothing higher, but would instead throw away what they had already acquired, sometimes with no little hardship. Prophecies are done away with, and knowledge will cease, because a far higher knowledge is admitted into our souls. Suppose a single lamp is shining in a house and giving a modest light to those who see it, and someone brings in a torch. The light of the lamp must then all but cease to do its work, giving way to the vastness of the greater light. Likewise, when the sun lights up everything under heaven, the brightness of the stars is left somehow powerless. In the same way, when a brighter knowledge has been brought into us, the lesser will in some way be done away with. Christ also said somewhere to the holy apostles: "I have spoken these things to you in figures. The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures, but will tell you plainly about the Father."

So upon the saints, who have deeply feared the name of God and have devoted themselves to every virtue in this world, Christ will shine forth. Like a sun of righteousness he will send into them the rays of the most perfect knowledge, free them from every sickness of soul, and put their former affliction as far away as possible. This is the meaning of "healing in his wings." It is said as of an eagle and its young, surely in line with what the all-wise Moses said about God and those redeemed from Egypt: "As an eagle shelters its nest, spreading its wings, he received them." So there will also be healing in his wings, he says. For in this age the leapings of the flesh in us are somehow terrible. The flesh sharpens the mind toward monstrous pleasures, and the law of sin rages in our members, even if it is perhaps overcome by the virtue of the saints, with Christ coming to their aid. The mind also becomes drunk, as it were, when the passions test it in other ways: arrogance assails it, along with worldly ambition, anger, greed and the other evils. Since through Christ we have been enriched with the pledge of the Spirit, we have grown used to overcoming the passions, though not without sweat. But in the age to come we shall have the full radiance of the knowledge of God and be rich in the perfect gift of the Holy Spirit. We shall have stripped off corruption and the passions of the flesh, and we shall serve God completely. We shall not be divided toward sin or troubled by any of the old passions, but shall live a pure life, free from harm, ranked equally with the holy angels. For it is written of the saints that they will forget their affliction, and it will not rise into their heart. "And there will be everlasting joy upon their head," it says, "for upon their head will be praise and gladness, and exultation will overtake them; pain and sorrow and sighing have fled away." This is why the Prophet, or rather God, who works and gives these things, says: *And you will go out and leap like calves set loose from their bonds.* Suckling calves, when they are set loose from their bonds, frolic over the fields, bounding and lowing in the flowering grass. In the same way, in due time, the saints will be set loose, as it were, from the bonds of affliction and care, sweat and toil, that belong to this life. They will go out into the cheerfulness that befits the holy, trampling the lawless. These will no longer be fighting and resisting, but already fallen and defeated, lying as it were under their feet, because the war they waged has been entirely abolished. "For there will be no lion there, and none of the evil beasts will go up there," as it is written; "rather there will be a pure way, and it will be called a holy way." For at that time above all, the life of the saints will be free of war and released from every stain. *Behold, I am sending you Elijah the Tishbite before the great and glorious day of the Lord comes. He will turn the heart of the father back to the son, and the heart of a man to his neighbour, so that I do not come and strike the earth utterly.*

It is a proof of God's gentleness and forbearance that in due time Elijah the Tishbite will shine forth before us, announcing in advance to people throughout the whole world that the Judge is at last about to appear. For the Son will come down as Judge in the glory of God the Father, escorted by angels, and will sit "on the throne of his glory," judging the world in righteousness. He will certainly repay each person according to his deeds. Since we are caught up in very many sins, the inspired prophet usefully goes ahead of him to bring those on earth into one mind. In this way all may be brought into the unity that comes through faith, cease from their zeal for wickedness, and choose to do what is good, and so be saved when the Judge comes down. Blessed John the Baptist had already gone ahead "in the spirit and power of Elijah." But just as John proclaimed, "Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight," so the inspired Elijah will then proclaim that the Judge is near and is all but present, coming to judge the world in righteousness. Now, perhaps, some people are at odds, and father is divided against son and son against father. One has believed in Christ, while the other is numbered among the unbelievers. Others have broken away from love for one another and are separated by enmity, unending anger, and quarrels over all sorts of worldly affairs. But the prophet will restore them. He will gather into one faith those who were long divided and reconcile each person to his neighbour, *so that I do not come*, he says, *and strike the earth utterly*, that is, completely and entirely. So you see the gentleness of the Master of all. He persuades those on earth in advance and all but solemnly testifies to them through Elijah's voice that the Judge will come. Then those living on earth at that time may amend their lives by turning toward what is better. They will not meet a harsh Judge who sends them into the flame and the outer darkness, but will rather hear: "Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world."
Remember the law of my servant Moses, as I commanded it to him at Horeb for all Israel, ordinances and statutes.

Once again he urges those who will read the Prophet's words to understand that the preaching about Christ is nothing new or unusual. Nor was it foretold only by the words of Malachi. It was foretold from above and from the beginning, from the earliest times, so to speak, when Israel was called to the knowledge of God and God gave the oracles of the laws at Horeb through Moses. The God of all came down in the form of fire upon Mount Sinai. Smoke appeared, and flames darted on high and struck great dread into those who saw them. There was darkness and gloom and storm, and "the sound of the trumpet rang out loudly." Then, at that very moment, the sons of Israel were terrified, and they came to their mediator and guide, who was Moses, and said: "You speak to us, and do not let God speak to us, or we shall die." To this God said: "All that they have spoken is right. I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers, and I will put my words in his mouth, and he will speak to them everything that I command him." Do you see how Holy Scripture proclaimed Christ beforehand, from long ages past? Indeed, if someone is willing to examine closely the very shadows of the law, he will find Christ depicted there, together with the mystery concerning him. That is why he said to the Jews: "If you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote about me." For Christ is the fulfilment of the law and the prophets. Through him and with him be glory to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
